0.title: The Son of God on the Move: The Gospel According to Mark
0.overview:
Mark's gospel is the sound of boots on cobblestones. No genealogy, no annunciation, no infancy narrative — the very first sentence plants a flag and the rest of the book is a march: 'The beginning of the gospel of Jesus Christ, the Son of God.' Everything else is commentary on that title. Before a parable is told or a sermon delivered, demons have been cast out, fevers have broken, a leper has been made clean, and four fishermen have walked away from their nets to follow a man they have known for minutes. Mark writes at full sprint.

The tradition connecting this gospel to the apostle Peter is ancient and remarkably consistent. Papias, writing around 125 AD, records that Mark was Peter's 'interpreter' and wrote down accurately — though not in strict chronological order — what Peter preached about the Lord's words and deeds. Irenaeus, Clement of Alexandria, Origen, and Eusebius all confirm the connection. The internal evidence supports it: the gospel is saturated with the vivid, concrete, eyewitness detail of a man who was there — the green grass at the feeding (6:39), the look of anger on Jesus's face (3:5), the specific towns and houses and times of day. Peter's voice is everywhere. Mark's pen is the instrument by which that voice was preserved. The gospel was almost certainly written for a Roman audience — Mark explains Jewish customs (7:3–4), translates Aramaic phrases (3:17; 5:41; 7:34; 14:36; 15:22, 34), and sprinkles in Latin loanwords that would feel natural to Roman ears (centurion, legion, denarius, praetorium). Scholars place the composition in the late 50s to mid-60s AD, either during Peter's lifetime or in the immediate aftermath of his death.

Which Mark? The Gospel itself names no author, but the early church agreed that it was John Mark, whose mother’s house in Jerusalem was a meeting place for the first believers (Acts 12:12). He set out with Paul and Barnabas and turned back (Acts 13:13), was the cause of their parting (Acts 15:37–39), was later restored to Paul’s confidence, he is very useful to me for ministry (2 Tim 4:11), and was with Peter in Rome, who calls him Mark, my son (1 Pet 5:13). That is the man the tradition makes Peter’s interpreter.

Why is it so much shorter than Matthew and Luke, with no birth story? Mark gives mostly what Jesus did, and gives a large share of the book to his last week, rather than long blocks of teaching. He begins where the apostles’ preaching began, with John the Baptist and the public ministry (cf. Acts 10:37–38), and leaves the birth to Matthew and Luke. Shorter is not lesser; what Mark gives is the most vivid of the four.

The word that unlocks Mark is euthys — immediately, at once, straightway. It appears some forty-one times. This is not careless repetition; it is a theological statement about the nature of the kingdom. When the King arrives, things happen. The blind see, the lame walk, the demons flee — and they do not do so on a leisurely timetable. The gospel's organizing question is not 'Who teaches about God?' but 'Who has authority over everything?' — over disease, over death, over the demonic, over the sea, over sin, over the law, over the grave. The answer Mark gives is Jesus of Nazareth, the Son of God. The theological heart of the entire book is found in 10:45: 'The Son of Man came not to be served but to serve, and to give his life as a ransom for many.' Everything before that verse is the demonstration of who he is; everything after it is the unfolding of what that service costs. Mark is a passion narrative with a long introduction — and the introduction is glorious.

1.title: The Kingdom Breaks In
1.text: <sup>1</sup>The beginning of the gospel of Jesus Christ, the Son of God. <sup>2</sup>As it is written in Isaiah the prophet, “Behold, I send my messenger before your face, who will prepare your way, <sup>3</sup>the voice of one crying in the wilderness: Prepare the way of the Lord, make his paths straight”— <sup>4</sup>John appeared, baptizing in the wilderness and proclaiming a baptism of repentance for the forgiveness of sins. <sup>5</sup>And all the country of Judea and all Jerusalem were going out to him and were being baptized by him in the river Jordan, confessing their sins. <sup>6</sup>Now John was clothed with camel’s hair and wore a leather belt around his waist and ate locusts and wild honey. <sup>7</sup>And he preached, saying, “After me comes he who is mightier than I, the strap of whose sandals I am not worthy to stoop down and untie. <sup>8</sup>I have baptized you with water, but he will baptize you with the Holy Spirit.” <sup>9</sup>In those days Jesus came from Nazareth of Galilee and was baptized by John in the Jordan. <sup>10</sup>And when he came up out of the water, immediately he saw the heavens being torn open and the Spirit descending on him like a dove. <sup>11</sup>And a voice came from heaven, “You are my beloved Son; with you I am well pleased.” <sup>12</sup>The Spirit immediately drove him out into the wilderness. <sup>13</sup>And he was in the wilderness forty days, being tempted by Satan. And he was with the wild animals, and the angels were ministering to him. <sup>14</sup>Now after John was arrested, Jesus came into Galilee, proclaiming the gospel of God, <sup>15</sup>and saying, “The time is fulfilled, and the kingdom of God is at hand; repent and believe in the gospel.” <sup>16</sup>Passing alongside the Sea of Galilee, he saw Simon and Andrew the brother of Simon casting a net into the sea, for they were fishermen. <sup>17</sup>And Jesus said to them, “Follow me, and I will make you become fishers of men.” <sup>18</sup>And immediately they left their nets and followed him. <sup>19</sup>And going on a little farther, he saw James the son of Zebedee and John his brother, who were in their boat mending the nets. <sup>20</sup>And immediately he called them, and they left their father Zebedee in the boat with the hired servants and followed him. <sup>21</sup>And they went into Capernaum, and immediately on the Sabbath he entered the synagogue and was teaching. <sup>22</sup>And they were astonished at his teaching, for he taught them as one who had authority, and not as the scribes. <sup>23</sup>And immediately there was in their synagogue a man with an unclean spirit. And he cried out, <sup>24</sup>“What have you to do with us, Jesus of Nazareth? Have you come to destroy us? I know who you are—the Holy One of God.” <sup>25</sup>But Jesus rebuked him, saying, “Be silent, and come out of him!” <sup>26</sup>And the unclean spirit, convulsing him and crying out with a loud voice, came out of him. <sup>27</sup>And they were all amazed, so that they questioned among themselves, saying, “What is this? A new teaching with authority! He commands even the unclean spirits, and they obey him.” <sup>28</sup>And at once his fame spread everywhere throughout all the surrounding region of Galilee. <sup>29</sup>And immediately he left the synagogue and entered the house of Simon and Andrew, with James and John. <sup>30</sup>Now Simon’s mother-in-law lay ill with a fever, and immediately they told him about her. <sup>31</sup>And he came and took her by the hand and lifted her up, and the fever left her, and she began to serve them. <sup>32</sup>That evening at sundown they brought to him all who were sick or oppressed by demons. <sup>33</sup>And the whole city was gathered together at the door. <sup>34</sup>And he healed many who were sick with various diseases, and cast out many demons. And he would not permit the demons to speak, because they knew him. <sup>35</sup>And rising very early in the morning, while it was still dark, he departed and went out to a desolate place, and there he prayed. <sup>36</sup>And Simon and those who were with him searched for him, <sup>37</sup>and they found him and said to him, “Everyone is looking for you.” <sup>38</sup>And he said to them, “Let us go on to the next towns, that I may preach there also, for that is why I came out.” <sup>39</sup>And he went throughout all Galilee, preaching in their synagogues and casting out demons. <sup>40</sup>And a leper came to him, imploring him, and kneeling said to him, “If you will, you can make me clean.” <sup>41</sup>Moved with pity, he stretched out his hand and touched him and said to him, “I will; be clean.” <sup>42</sup>And immediately the leprosy left him, and he was made clean. <sup>43</sup>And Jesus sternly charged him and sent him away at once, <sup>44</sup>and said to him, “See that you say nothing to anyone, but go, show yourself to the priest and offer for your cleansing what Moses commanded, for a proof to them.” <sup>45</sup>But he went out and began to talk freely about it, and to spread the news, so that Jesus could no longer openly enter a town, but was out in desolate places, and people were coming to him from every quarter.
1.overview:
No other chapter in the New Testament moves at the pace of Mark 1. Forty-five verses carry us from the wilderness prophet to a leper made clean — and along the way we see a baptism attended by the Holy Spirit and the Father's voice, a forty-day confrontation with Satan, four fishermen leaving their boats in a single morning, a man delivered from an unclean spirit in a synagogue, a fever cured with a touch, an entire town gathered at a doorstep after dark, and a solitary prayer in the pre-dawn dark before another preaching circuit begins. The word 'immediately' appears nine times. Mark is not interested in biographical completeness; he is interested in demonstrating authority — who this man is and what he does when he arrives.

The chapter divides into four movements: the prologue (vv. 1–13) establishes the cosmic identity of Jesus before his public ministry begins; the kingdom announcement (vv. 14–20) gives the content of his message and shows what responding to it looks like; the day in Capernaum (vv. 21–34) demonstrates his authority over the demonic and the physical in the most public possible setting; and the morning prayer followed by the preaching circuit (vv. 35–45) reveals the inner life that powers the outward mission, and ends with a healing that Mark's Jewish readers would have found staggering. The King has come. Everything is about to change.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–13 — Prologue: The Son Announced, Baptized, and Tested
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Mark's opening thirteen verses constitute a compressed prologue that accomplishes everything a careful reader needs before the public ministry begins. Three things are established: who Jesus is, what voices announce him, and that he has already engaged and survived the primary enemy. The Son of God is identified before a single synagogue hears him speak. This matters enormously for how we read everything that follows — every healing, every confrontation, every silencing of a demon is performed by the one the Father called 'my beloved Son' at the Jordan.

The temptation account in Mark (vv. 12–13) is the most compressed of the Synoptic versions — no dialogue, no three-part structure, only the bare essentials: the Spirit drives Jesus out, Satan is present, wild animals are there, angels minister. Mark gives us not the content of the temptation but its texture: isolation, exposure, the presence of the adversary, the sustaining of heaven. The brevity is itself eloquent. Mark's Jesus does not need to explain his victory over Satan. The reader will see the evidence throughout the gospel as demons flee before him.
verseByVerse.theology:
The baptism of Jesus (vv. 9–11) is one of the most theologically dense moments in Scripture. The Trinity appears in undisguised form: the Son is baptized, the Spirit descends like a dove, and the Father speaks. The Father's words — 'You are my beloved Son; with you I am well pleased' — are a composite of Psalm 2:7 (the coronation Psalm of the Davidic king) and Isaiah 42:1 (the Servant of the Lord on whom God's Spirit rests). In a single sentence, Jesus is identified as both the Messianic King and the Suffering Servant. The two identities that the Old Testament held in tension are here placed on one person. The reader who knows their Hebrew Bible should feel the ground move.

Why was Jesus baptized with a baptism of repentance when he had no sin to repent of? The New Testament answer: he who knew no sin was being made sin for us (2 Cor. 5:21). His identification with sinful humanity at the Jordan is the beginning of the identification that will be completed on the cross. He goes into the water as the representative of those he came to save. He comes out of it as the Spirit-anointed King, confirmed by his Father, commissioned for the mission.
verseByVerse.examples: John in the wilderness wore camel's hair and ate locusts and wild honey — the clothing and diet of Elijah (2 Kgs. 1:8). The garment was a prophetic uniform, a visible claim. He stood in the desert rather than Jerusalem for the same reason the word of God in every revival comes from the margins rather than the religious centre: the establishment had calcified, and God's next move was being prepared outside it. Then: the religious capital full of priests and scribes who had been waiting for centuries and missed the moment. Now: the same danger faces any church or tradition that mistakes institutional health for spiritual vitality. The voice of preparation rarely comes from where we expect it.

verseByVerse.quote: The beginning of the gospel of Jesus Christ, the Son of God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Mark’s first sentence is a title for the whole book: this is the beginning of the good news about Jesus, who is the Messiah and the Son of God.

Meaning first. Mark 1 moves at a run. The prophets are fulfilled, John prepares the way, heaven is torn open over Jesus at his baptism, and the Spirit drives him into the wilderness to face Satan. Then Jesus announces that God’s kingdom has come near, calls four fishermen, silences a demon, heals a fevered woman and a whole town at the door, prays alone before dawn, and touches a leper. Mark’s first line names him: the Messiah and the Son of God. Every scene after it shows his authority over demons, disease and men’s lives, and shows him spending it to come near the unclean and take their place outside.

The setting. Mark is probably the earliest Gospel, written in the AD 50s or 60s. Early church writers from Papias (about AD 120) onwards say that John Mark wrote down the preaching of the apostle Peter, in Rome, for mostly Gentile Christians facing persecution under Nero. Mark was the cousin of Barnabas (Colossians 4:10); his mother’s house in Jerusalem was a meeting place of the church (Acts 12:12); and he travelled with Paul and later with Peter (1 Peter 5:13). His Gospel is short and vivid, uses immediately (euthys) over forty times, and gives half its length to Jesus’ last week: a passion story with a long introduction.

A title, not an introduction. Verse 1 is not a warm-up; it is a title. The beginning of the gospel of Jesus Christ, the Son of God, works the way In the beginning, God created works in Genesis 1:1: it announces what the whole document is about. Something new is starting, and it is as large as creation. It may also mean that the whole story of Jesus’ life is only the beginning of the gospel, which continues to run on through the church to the ends of the earth, and has reached you.

Of the gospel. Euangelion means good news, and in the first century it was not chiefly a religious word. It was political and military. When a battle was won, a herald ran back to the city with the gospel of victory. When an emperor was born or came to the throne, cities announced it as good news. An inscription from Priene in 9 BC calls the birthday of Caesar Augustus the beginning of the good news for the world. Mark’s first readers lived in Rome, under Caesar’s statues and Caesar’s coins, and Mark takes Caesar’s word and gives it to a crucified Galilean. The real good news is not about the emperor. In Isaiah the good news is that God reigns and comes himself to save his people (Isaiah 40:9; 52:7), and Mark is announcing that the decisive battle has been joined and won, and that the one who won it is Jesus of Nazareth.

Of Jesus Christ. Jesus means the LORD saves. Christ is the Greek for Messiah, the Anointed One, the King God promised to send. It is not a surname but a title, and to say it in Rome was to name a king other than Caesar.

The Son of God. The title that frames the whole Gospel. It stands here at the start; at the baptism the Father calls him his beloved Son (1:11); on the mountain of transfiguration he says it again (9:7); and at the cross, when the body hangs dead and there is nobody left to impress, a Roman centurion says it aloud: Truly this man was the Son of God (15:39). The demons know it too, and scream it (3:11; 5:7). The great question of this Gospel is who Jesus is, and Mark tells the reader the answer in the first sentence. The disciples will take eight chapters to see half of it.

Textual note. A few early manuscripts omit the Son of God, including the original hand of the great fourth-century Codex Sinaiticus. Most, including Codex Vaticanus and very early and diverse witnesses and translations, include it. The likeliest explanation is mechanical rather than theological. Ancient copies wrote the sacred names as abbreviations, two letters with a stroke above, and in this phrase four such contractions fall one after another, of Jesus Christ, Son of God, a row of nearly identical short forms. That is exactly where a copyist’s eye slips and a phrase drops out. Verdict: probably original; it fits the shape of the whole Gospel. And nothing depends on it. Strike it out and Mark is still about what verse 1 says, because he spends sixteen chapters proving it from every direction. The title does not rest on a disputed line in the first sentence. It rests on the book.

Who was Mark, and can his account be trusted if he was not one of the Twelve? Mark is the young man who left Paul and Barnabas halfway through their first journey (Acts 13:13), so badly that Paul refused to take him again (Acts 15:37–39). Years later Paul writes that Mark is very useful to him for ministry (2 Timothy 4:11). So the earliest Gospel was written by a man who had once failed and been restored, which is a gospel in itself. His account rests on Peter, an eyewitness from the first day at the lake to the empty tomb, and the ancient church received it on that basis. The vivid details only an eyewitness would keep, the cushion in the boat, the green grass, the hired servants, are Peter’s memory on Mark’s page.

In a sentence. Mark announces that his book is the good news of Jesus, the Messiah and the Son of God.

On a Tuesday. You will hear a great deal of news this week, most of it about who is winning and who is in charge. Notice how much of it you receive as though it were the news that decides your life. Then remember that the one announcement that does decide it has already been made, and it was not about Caesar. The news people around you need most is not the latest headline but the good news about Jesus. Think of one person who has never heard it told plainly, and ask God for an opening to tell them.

For worship. Before Mark tells a single story, he sets a crown on the head of Jesus. The world had heralds for its emperors, and they are dust; their gospels are inscriptions in museums. But the good news of this King has outlived every empire that tried to silence it, because it is not the news of a man who seized a throne but of the Son of God who came down from one. He is the Anointed King and the eternal Son, and the battle he went out to fight he has won. Every page that follows is the herald running in from the field.
verseByVerse.note: “Gospel” means good news. “Christ” is the Greek form of the Hebrew “Messiah” — the anointed one, the promised king. The ESV notes that some manuscripts omit “the Son of God.”

parallels.desc: John’s opening: the Word who was God

verseByVerse.quote: As it is written in Isaiah the prophet, "Behold, I send my messenger before your face, who will prepare your way, the voice of one crying in the wilderness: Prepare the way of the Lord, make his paths straight"—
verseByVerse.commentary:
Mark begins with Scripture. God had promised to send a messenger ahead of the Lord, a voice in the wilderness calling people to prepare the way. John the Baptist is that messenger.

As it is written in Isaiah the prophet. Mark combines three Old Testament texts: Exodus 23:20, where God sends an angel before Israel on the road; Malachi 3:1, behold, I send my messenger, and he will prepare the way before me; and Isaiah 40:3, a voice crying in the wilderness to prepare the way of the LORD. He names Isaiah, the most prominent prophet and the source of the main theme, as Jewish writers often did when they combined texts. The Jewish interpreters of the time read these passages together as one prophecy about the forerunner of the Lord, and Mark follows them. The claim is simple and enormous: the voice has cried, the way is being prepared, and the Lord himself is coming.

Behold, I send my messenger before your face, who will prepare your way. Look at what Malachi actually said, because a claim is buried here that is one of the largest in the New Testament. In Malachi, God is speaking about himself: the messenger goes ahead of the LORD, and the next line says that the Lord whom you seek will suddenly come to his temple. The one being prepared for is God. Here, in Mark, it becomes your way: the way of Jesus.

The voice of one crying in the wilderness. In Isaiah 40 this voice announces comfort to God’s people in exile: their warfare is ended, their iniquity is pardoned, and God himself is coming to lead them home through the desert in a new exodus. It is one of the tenderest chapters in the Old Testament. Comfort, comfort my people, says your God. Mark begins his Gospel inside that comfort.

Prepare the way of the Lord, make his paths straight. Before a king visited a province, roads were repaired and straightened, valleys filled and hills levelled. John prepares hearts by calling them to repent. And the word behind LORD in Isaiah, in small capitals in your Bible, is the divine name itself, the name given at the burning bush. Now watch what Mark does. He takes two passages about clearing a road for the arrival of God and applies them, without argument or apology, to the arrival of a Galilean carpenter. He is two sentences into his Gospel and he has already identified Jesus with the God of Israel, simply by choosing which verses to quote. It is the quietest enormous claim in Scripture.

The terms for everything that follows. When this man forgives sins in chapter 2, the scribes will ask who can forgive sins but God alone, and they will be asking the right question. When he tells the sea to be still in chapter 4, the disciples will ask who this is, that even the wind and the sea obey him, and they will be asking the right question too. Mark answered both in his second verse, before either was raised.

What it does not mean. Not that Mark made a mistake in naming only Isaiah. Combining texts under the name of the leading prophet was an accepted practice. Later scribes, puzzled, changed it to the prophets in some manuscripts; the original reads Isaiah.

Why does Mark start with old prophecies instead of with Jesus himself? Because the good news is not a new idea that turned up in the first century. It is the keeping of a promise. Mark wants his Gentile readers in Rome to know that Jesus is not a religious novelty but the arrival of the God whom Israel’s prophets had promised for centuries. It also tells you how to read your Old Testament: not as a different religion that the New Testament replaced, but as the road on which the Lord was always coming. When you read Isaiah or Malachi, you are reading about Jesus before he arrived.

In a sentence. As the prophets promised, God sent a messenger to prepare the way for the Lord himself, who has come in Jesus.

On a Tuesday. A road is prepared by taking out what is in the way: the hill of pride, the hollow of discouragement, the crooked place where you have learned to go round a sin instead of dealing with it. Ask what in your heart needs straightening out to make way for Christ, and name one thing. Repentance is how we prepare the way, and he does not wait for the road to be perfect before he walks it.

For worship. The God of the burning bush, whose name the prophets wrote in trembling, did not send a deputy. He came himself, by the road Isaiah promised, on the feet of a man from Nazareth. Every comfort spoken to the exiles was a promise he meant to keep in person. He is the Lord who comes, and he has come.
verseByVerse.note: Mark names Isaiah, the better-known prophet, though the first line comes from Malachi.

verseByVerse.quote: John appeared, baptizing in the wilderness and proclaiming a baptism of repentance for the forgiveness of sins. And all the country of Judea and all Jerusalem were going out to him and were being baptized by him in the river Jordan, confessing their sins.
verseByVerse.commentary:
John appeared in the wilderness, baptising and preaching a baptism of repentance for the forgiveness of sins. People from all Judea and Jerusalem went out to him, confessing their sins, and were baptised in the river Jordan.

John appeared, baptizing in the wilderness. After about four hundred years with no prophet in Israel, God was speaking again. Mark gives John no birth story; he simply stands up in the barren country near the Jordan, north of the Dead Sea. And the place is chosen. The wilderness is where Israel was born as a nation, where God met them, fed them and gave them the law, and where the prophets said the restoration would begin (Isaiah 40:3; Hosea 2:14). To go out there was to go back to the beginning, past the temple, the priesthood and the whole apparatus of religion in Jerusalem, and start again.

And proclaiming a baptism of repentance. Baptism means washing, immersion. Ritual washing was ordinary in Judaism, but it was something you did to yourself, repeatedly, for ceremonial uncleanness. Later Jewish sources also describe a washing for Gentiles converting to Judaism, a once-for-all washing that marked an outsider coming in, though how early it began is disputed. John gives the rite for outsiders to the descendants of Abraham, telling the covenant people that their ancestry will not carry them and that they must be washed like pagans to be ready for what is coming. Repentance (metanoia) means a change of mind and heart, turning from sin to God, and the baptism expressed it.

For the forgiveness of sins. Repentance leads to forgiveness. John’s baptism pointed to the forgiveness God would give through the one coming after him (v. 8). Paul says John told the people to believe in the one who was to come after him, that is, Jesus (Acts 19:4).

And all the country of Judea and all Jerusalem were going out to him. All is a natural exaggeration for very many, but the statement is meant to be taken seriously. The movement was huge. And it tells us the country knew something was wrong. People do not walk into a river and confess their sins in public because a preacher is eloquent. They do it because he has said out loud what they already suspected about themselves.

And were being baptized by him in the river Jordan, confessing their sins. The Jordan, where Israel had crossed into the promised land under Joshua (Joshua 3). John brings them back to the edge of the land, as if Israel had to cross in again. Confessing means openly admitting, naming one’s sins before God. The crowds at the Jordan were not the notorious; they were the ordinary religious population of a religious country, and what John got them to admit was that religion had not dealt with them. That is still the hardest admission a churchgoer ever makes, and there is no way to the rest of this book that goes round it.

The one who came down into the same river. John could wash bodies and name sins; he could not carry them away. The crowds went home from the Jordan confessed but not yet cleansed, and the forgiveness John preached still had to be paid for. Within a few verses the one who would pay it walks down into the same water, the only man in Israel with nothing to confess, and takes his place in the line. Israel had once crossed this river behind the ark, the waters held back before it, under a leader called Joshua (Joshua 3:15–17). Jesus bears that same name, the LORD saves, and he goes down into the Jordan ahead of his people to lead them into a rest Joshua never gave (Hebrews 4:8–10).

What it does not mean. Not that water baptism itself forgives sins. Forgiveness comes from God to those who repent and believe; baptism is the outward sign. No rite can take away sin by itself (Hebrews 10:4). Nor is John’s baptism the same as Christian baptism into the name of the Father, Son and Spirit (Matthew 28:19; Acts 19:1–5). It prepared the way for it.

How is John’s baptism different from Christian baptism, and what does that mean for me? John’s baptism looked forward to a Saviour who had not yet died and risen; Christian baptism looks back to one who has, and is into his name. What carries across is the order. People came to John repenting and confessing, and then were baptised. That is why this commentary holds to believer’s baptism, as the 1689 London Baptist Confession does: baptism is for those who personally repent and believe. Many faithful brothers and sisters baptise the infants of believers, and we honour them as fellow servants of the same Christ. If you have repented and trusted Christ and have never been baptised as a believer, speak to your church about it. It is the ordinary first step of obedience, not a reward for advanced Christians.

In a sentence. John called Israel to be baptised as a sign of turning back to God, and great crowds came, confessing their sins.

On a Tuesday. Is there a sin you need to name before God today, not sin in general but the particular thing? Confession is the doorway to forgiveness (1 John 1:9). And ask whether your religion has become the reason you never make that walk to the river. Being in church is not the same as being clean, and the Lord is kind to the person who stops pretending it is.

For worship. God did not leave his people to drift in their religion. He sent a prophet to the riverbank to tell them the truth about themselves, and every sin confessed in that water was a sin his Son had already resolved to carry. John’s washing could only point. The cleansing it pointed to was bought with blood, and the Lamb who bought it did not stand at a distance from the guilty, pronouncing on them. He came down among them, wet with the same river, so that the whole crowd of the confessing might be washed in a way no water reaches.
verseByVerse.note: The Jordan runs south from the Sea of Galilee to the Dead Sea. John’s baptism was a public washing that marked a turning from sin; confession came with it.

verseByVerse.quote: Now John was clothed with camel's hair and wore a leather belt around his waist and ate locusts and wild honey. And he preached, saying, "After me comes he who is mightier than I, the strap of whose sandals I am not worthy to stoop down and untie. I have baptized you with water, but he will baptize you with the Holy Spirit."
verseByVerse.commentary:
John dressed in camel’s hair with a leather belt, like the prophet Elijah, and lived on locusts and wild honey. He preached: one mightier than I is coming after me. I am not worthy to stoop down and untie his sandals. I have baptised you with water, but he will baptise you with the Holy Spirit.

Now John was clothed with camel’s hair and wore a leather belt around his waist. Mark’s first readers would have stopped dead at this, because it is not a note about desert practicality. It is a quotation. When King Ahaziah’s messengers described the prophet who had intercepted them, they said he wore a garment of hair with a belt of leather about his waist, and the king answered at once: It is Elijah the Tishbite (2 Kings 1:8). The clothing was as recognisable as a uniform. John is not dressed like a hermit; he is dressed like Elijah, deliberately, in public. Malachi had closed the Old Testament by promising that Elijah would come before the great and awesome day of the LORD (Malachi 4:5). Mark has just quoted Malachi. Now he shows you a man wearing the fulfilment of it. Jesus later confirms it: Elijah has come (9:11–13).

And ate locusts and wild honey. The food of the desert, permitted by the law (Leviticus 11:22). It is not penance. It is what the wilderness gives to a man who has walked out of the economy and taken nothing with him: a life stripped to what God supplies, lived outside the system he was sent to confront.

If John was Elijah, why did he deny it? When the priests asked him, Are you Elijah? he said, I am not (John 1:21). He was denying that he was Elijah returned in person, which is what they meant. He was not the old prophet come back from heaven. He was the one who came in the spirit and power of Elijah (Luke 1:17), fulfilling Malachi’s promise. Scripture knows nothing of reincarnation: it is appointed for man to die once, and after that comes judgment (Hebrews 9:27). John was a new man, born to Zechariah and Elizabeth, sent in Elijah’s role. The costume was telling the truth before John ever opened his mouth.

The strap of whose sandals I am not worthy to stoop down and untie. John points away from himself to the one coming after him; his whole ministry is to point to Jesus. Untying a master’s sandals was a slave’s task, so lowly that some rabbis said a disciple could do every service for his teacher except this one. John places himself below that. The greatest of the prophets (Matthew 11:11) sees himself as less than a slave before Jesus. This is what genuine preparation looks like: not building a movement around yourself, but pointing away from yourself so insistently that when the one you announce arrives, people recognise him.

The stronger one. Mightier is the comparative of the ordinary Greek word for strong (ischyros), and Jesus picks up that word himself when he is accused of casting out demons by Satan: no one can plunder a strong man’s house unless he first binds the strong man (3:27). Luke’s telling uses John’s exact word: one stronger than he attacks him and overcomes him (Luke 11:22). John is announcing the stronger one, who walks into the enemy’s house and takes back what was stolen. Within weeks of this sermon Jesus is facing that strong man in the wilderness, and soon demons are crying out in a synagogue at the sight of him. He is stronger than the strong man, and he came to empty his house.

I have baptized you with water, but he will baptize you with the Holy Spirit. John’s baptism was outward, with water. Jesus would do what only God can: pour out the Holy Spirit, as the prophets promised for the last days (Joel 2:28; Ezekiel 36:26–27). What John began in the physical element, Jesus completes with the divine Person. This happened at Pentecost (Acts 1:5; 2:33). To be baptised with the Spirit is to be brought into new life by the Spirit, cleansed and indwelt. Every believer receives this (1 Corinthians 12:13).

What it does not mean. Not that Spirit baptism is a second experience after conversion for some believers only, as some Pentecostal traditions teach. Paul says all believers were baptised in one Spirit into one body (1 Corinthians 12:13). Verdict: Spirit baptism happens at conversion; believers are then filled with the Spirit again and again (Ephesians 5:18).

How do I know I have the Spirit if I have never had a dramatic experience? By what he does, not by how it felt. The Spirit makes you call God Father with real trust (Romans 8:15–16). He makes Jesus precious to you and teaches you to confess him as Lord (1 Corinthians 12:3). He makes you hate the sin you once loved and fight it. He produces, slowly, love, joy, patience and kindness (Galatians 5:22–23). If you have turned from sin and are trusting Christ, you have the Spirit, whether or not you can name the day (Romans 8:9). Ask him to fill you afresh, and keep in step with him.

In a sentence. John, dressed like Elijah, pointed away from himself to the mightier one coming, who would baptise not with water but with the Holy Spirit.

On a Tuesday. Notice in your conversations this week how often the story drifts back to you: your opinion, your experience, your credit. Like John, point people away from yourself to Jesus. He is the one they need. And if you serve in any visible way, ask whether the people you serve are more impressed with you or with him. The only success John wanted was to be forgotten in the light of someone else.

For worship. The greatest man born of women knelt in spirit below the place of a slave, because he had seen who was coming. And the one he could not stoop to unshod came to pour out God himself into the hearts of fishermen, tax collectors and sinners. John gave water; Christ gives the Spirit of the living God. He is mightier than every prophet, and his might is spent in filling the empty.
verseByVerse.note: Untying a master’s sandals was a slave’s job.

parallels.desc: Elijah’s dress: hair and a leather belt

verseByVerse.quote: In those days Jesus came from Nazareth of Galilee and was baptized by John in the Jordan.
verseByVerse.commentary:
In those days Jesus came from Nazareth in Galilee and was baptised by John in the Jordan.

In those days Jesus came from Nazareth of Galilee. One sentence, and it is Mark’s entire account of the first thirty years of the Lord’s life. No genealogy, no annunciation, no manger, no shepherds, no flight to Egypt, no boy in the temple. Matthew and Luke give us those; Mark opens the door and Jesus is simply standing there, a grown man of about thirty (Luke 3:23) walking into a river. That is a deliberate decision, and it tells you what this Gospel is for. Mark is not writing a life. He is writing a case, and the case begins the moment the subject steps into public view.

From Nazareth of Galilee. Both words were a problem, and Mark’s readers knew it. Galilee was the northern province, agricultural, mixed, and looked down on by Jerusalem; a Galilean accent gave you away as a countryman, which is exactly how Peter would later be identified in a courtyard (14:70). And Nazareth was not even a notable town in Galilee: a village of a few hundred people, never mentioned in the Old Testament, in Josephus or in the Talmud. Nathanael’s reaction is the honest one: Can anything good come out of Nazareth? (John 1:46). The Messiah was to come from Bethlehem, of David’s line, and be revealed in Jerusalem. This man arrives on foot from a village nobody could place, at the wrong end of the country. The Lord whose way was prepared comes from nowhere important.

The walk itself. Nobody makes it by accident. From Nazareth to the Jordan crossings where John was baptising is something like sixty or seventy miles: three or four days on the road, alone, with the deliberate intention of joining a queue of people confessing their sins. He was not swept up in a revival meeting. He set out from home to be there.

And was baptized by John in the Jordan. A surprise. John’s baptism was for repentance and confession of sins, and Jesus had no sin to confess (2 Corinthians 5:21; Hebrews 4:15). Why was he baptised? Matthew records his answer: to fulfil all righteousness (Matthew 3:15). He identified himself with sinners, standing in the water with them, as he would later take their place on the cross (10:45). He obeyed every command of God on our behalf, so that his perfect obedience could be counted to people who have none. And his baptism marked the start of his public ministry, when he was anointed with the Spirit for his work. He steps into the sinners’ water at the beginning exactly as he will step onto the sinners’ cross at the end, and for the same reason: for our sake God made him to be sin who knew no sin. The identification that finishes at Golgotha starts here, waist-deep in the Jordan.

What it does not mean. Not that Jesus needed forgiveness. He came to the water as the sinless one standing with sinners, not as a sinner himself.

Why do the Gospels differ so much in what they include? Each writer selected from far more than he could record (John 21:25) and arranged it for his purpose and his readers. Matthew, writing for Jewish believers, opens with the genealogy from Abraham; Luke, the careful historian, gives the birth; John begins before creation. Mark, writing for persecuted believers in Rome who needed to know who Jesus is and what following him costs, goes straight to the action. The four do not compete. They are four witnesses to one Lord, and together they give a fuller portrait than any one could alone.

In a sentence. Jesus came from obscure Nazareth and was baptised by John, standing with sinners though he had no sin.

On a Tuesday. If you have ever thought that the important things happen elsewhere, among people with better names and better postcodes, notice where the Son of God grew up and which way he walked. And if you feel that your sin puts you at the back of the queue, remember who chose to stand in it. Jesus stood with sinners in the water, so that sinners could stand with him before God. He is not ashamed to stand with you.

For worship. He walked for days to stand in a line he did not belong in. The Holy One of God, who had nothing to confess, waded into the river where Israel’s sins were being named, and took his place among them without a word of protest. It was the first public act of his ministry, and it told the truth about all the rest: he came to be numbered with the transgressors, and he stayed numbered with them to the end, crucified between two robbers (Isaiah 53:12; Mark 15:27).
verseByVerse.note: Nazareth was a small village in the hill country of Galilee, never mentioned in the Old Testament.

parallels.desc: “Can anything good come out of Nazareth?”

verseByVerse.quote: And when he came up out of the water, immediately he saw the heavens being torn open and the Spirit descending on him like a dove. And a voice came from heaven, "You are my beloved Son; with you I am well pleased."
verseByVerse.commentary:
As Jesus came up out of the water, he saw the heavens being torn open and the Spirit coming down on him like a dove. A voice came from heaven: you are my beloved Son; with you I am well pleased.

And when he came up out of the water, immediately. Mark’s favourite word, euthys, here for the first time. It beats through this chapter like footsteps and gives his Gospel its urgency.

He saw the heavens being torn open. Torn open (schizomenous) is a strong, violent word. Matthew and Luke say the heavens were opened; Mark says they were ripped. Isaiah had prayed: Oh that you would rend the heavens and come down (Isaiah 64:1). Now God has done it. Mark uses the same word only once more: when the temple curtain is torn in two from top to bottom at Jesus’ death (15:38). At the start and the end of his ministry, the barrier between God and people is torn open, and the tearing at his baptism and the tearing at his death frame the whole Gospel. Heaven has been broken open. Something is getting through that was not getting through before.

And the Spirit descending on him like a dove. The Spirit anoints Jesus for his work as Messiah, as the prophets promised (Isaiah 11:2; 42:1; 61:1). The dove may recall the Spirit hovering over the waters at creation (Genesis 1:2), signalling a new creation, or the dove that came back to Noah with peace after the flood (Genesis 8:8–12).

You are my beloved Son; with you I am well pleased. The voice comes from heaven, and the Father speaks directly to Jesus. Matthew records the words as an announcement, this is my beloved Son; Mark gives them as the Father addressed them to the Son himself, an intimate word of identity spoken before the battle begins. And the words are not freshly composed. They are Scriptures laid across one man. You are my Son comes from Psalm 2:7, the coronation psalm, spoken over the Davidic king on the day he takes the throne. Beloved recalls Genesis 22:2, your son, your only son, whom you love, spoken of Isaac, who was to be offered on the mountain. With you I am well pleased echoes Isaiah 42:1, the first Servant Song, spoken over the Servant in whom God’s soul delights, who will not break a bruised reed, and who will bear the sin of many. Israel had held these figures apart for centuries. In a single sentence at the Jordan, the Father lays all of them on Jesus: the royal Son, the beloved Son who will be offered, and the Servant who will suffer.

Before he has done anything. Notice when the Father says it: before a single miracle, before one sermon, before the cross. The Father affirms before the Son serves. The Son knows who he is before the world tries to define him. And this becomes the pattern of the Christian life, because those who are in Christ are accepted in the Beloved (Ephesians 1:6): we serve from the security of the Father’s voice, not in search of it.

The Trinity. The Father speaks from the torn heaven, the Son stands in the water, the Spirit descends upon him: the three persons of the one God, revealed together, in the open, at the start.

What it does not mean. Not that Jesus became the Son of God at his baptism, as the early heresy called adoptionism taught. Mark’s first verse already calls him the Son of God. The baptism reveals and anoints who he already is.

Does God still speak from heaven like this? Not with new words to be added to Scripture. The voice at the Jordan was part of God’s once-for-all revelation of his Son, and it was written down so that we could hear it. God now speaks to us by his Son through the Scriptures, which are complete and sufficient (Hebrews 1:1–2; 2 Timothy 3:16–17). That is not a smaller gift. When you open your Bible to this verse, you are hearing the same Father say the same thing about the same Son, and, if you are in Christ, you are hearing how he regards you for his Son’s sake.

In a sentence. As Jesus came out of the water, heaven was torn open, the Spirit descended on him, and the Father declared him his beloved Son.

On a Tuesday. Most of us work for approval: from a boss, a parent, a congregation, ourselves. Notice this week where you are labouring to earn a verdict. If you are in Christ, the Father’s delight in his Son covers you too (Ephesians 1:6). You do not serve to become accepted; you serve because you are. Rest in that today, and let it take the fear out of your work.

For worship. Heaven was torn open, and what came through was not thunder but love. The eternal Father looked on his eternal Son, standing in the river with sinners, and said: my beloved, my delight. The Spirit rested on him. All three persons of the one God were glad together over the work about to begin. And the delight the Father has in his Son is not rationed out to us. In him it reaches the people he came to save, and it rests on them as it rested on him, undiminished.

parallels.desc: the servant in whom God delights

verseByVerse.note: “Torn open” (schizō) is the word Mark uses again when the temple curtain is torn at Jesus’ death (15:38).

verseByVerse.quote: The Spirit immediately drove him out into the wilderness. And he was in the wilderness forty days, being tempted by Satan. And he was with the wild animals, and the angels were ministering to him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Immediately the Spirit drove Jesus out into the wilderness. He was there forty days, tempted by Satan. He was with the wild animals, and the angels served him.

The Spirit immediately drove him out into the wilderness. Drove out (ekballei) is a strong word, the one Mark uses again and again for casting out demons. The same Spirit who descended at the baptism thrusts Jesus into the desert. The test was not an accident but God’s purpose. From the voice of the Father straight into the face of the enemy: that is the order. Matthew and Luke describe three temptations; Mark gives only the bare facts, and the brevity is its own statement.

And he was in the wilderness forty days. The number is never decorative in Scripture. Israel was forty years in the wilderness, tested and failed (Deuteronomy 8:2). Moses was forty days on the mountain (Exodus 34:28). Elijah walked forty days to Horeb in the strength of the food an angel gave him (1 Kings 19:8). Mark is putting Jesus where Israel was, and where the lawgiver and the great prophet were, and letting the reader draw the line. Jesus relives Israel’s story and succeeds where Israel failed.

Being tempted by Satan. Satan means adversary. He is a real, personal enemy who tempted the first Adam and succeeded (Genesis 3). Now he tempts the last Adam. And note what this settles, because it is a comfort people badly need and often miss: being tempted is not sinning. Jesus was tempted, genuinely, over forty days, by the enemy himself, and remained without sin. Hebrews makes the pastoral point: we do not have a high priest who is unable to sympathise with our weaknesses, but one who in every respect has been tempted as we are, yet without sin (Hebrews 4:15). So the arrival of a foul thought is not evidence that you are a fraud, only that you are being tempted, as the sinless Son of God was. What you do next is where the moral weight falls.

And he was with the wild animals. Only Mark mentions this. Readers divide over the meaning. Some hear menace: the danger and loneliness of the place, the beasts as part of the ordeal. Others hear Eden and Isaiah: the second Adam among the animals as the first Adam was before the fall, and the peaceable kingdom where the wolf shall dwell with the lamb (Isaiah 11:6–9). The text will not settle it, and it may hold both: a man in real danger, and a sign of the creation that is coming. In Jesus, the peace of Eden is returning. And Mark’s first readers in Rome, some of whom Nero had sewn into the skins of animals to be torn by dogs, as Tacitus records, would take comfort that Jesus too had been among wild beasts and was kept.

And the angels were ministering to him. Serving him, perhaps with food, as an angel fed the exhausted Elijah in the desert (1 Kings 19:5–8). God cared for his Son. Notice the shape of the sentence: Satan is there, the wild animals are there, the angels are there, and heaven is feeding him in the middle of it. That is a fair picture of the Christian life: real opposition, real exposure and real provision, all in the same wilderness at the same time.

Two men tested. Adam was tested in a garden, with every good thing to hand, full and safe and in company, and he fell. The Son of God was tested in a desert, hungry, alone, among the beasts, for forty days, with the adversary himself at his ear, and he did not. Where the first man surrendered paradise, the second man held the line in a wasteland. Everything that follows in this Gospel, every demon that flees, every disease that lifts, the tomb that empties, rests on the fact that the enemy came at him with everything and could not move him.

If the Spirit led Jesus into temptation, why do we pray, lead us not into temptation? Because God and Satan had different purposes in the same wilderness. Satan meant it as a trap; God meant it as a test, to prove his Son and to begin his victory. God himself tempts no one to sin (James 1:13), but he does lead his people through testing for their good (James 1:2–4). Jesus went in our place into the full strength of the enemy’s attack, so we pray humbly, as he taught us, not to be brought into it, and to be delivered from evil. And when testing comes, we are not alone in it. He has been there, and won, and God provides the way of escape (1 Corinthians 10:13).

In a sentence. The Spirit drove Jesus into the desert for forty days of testing by Satan, among wild animals, where angels served him.

On a Tuesday. Being tested is not a sign that God has abandoned you. Jesus was led into the wilderness by the Spirit straight after the Father had called him beloved, and God sent help. When the hard thing arrives this week, the temptation that will not leave or the season that feels like a desert, do not conclude that the voice of the Father was a mistake. Ask what the provision is in the same wilderness, because there will be some, and look for the angels.

For worship. He went from the Father’s voice straight into the enemy’s country, and he was not moved. For forty days the serpent who had ruined a garden worked on a hungry man in a wasteland and found nothing in him to take hold of. The beasts prowled near him and did not have him; the angels of God waited on him at the end of it. That is our Lord. He does not send his people into a wilderness he has not walked, and he walked out of this one the victor, with the first spoils of his war already in his hands.
verseByVerse.note: Matthew and Luke record the three temptations; Mark gives only the fact.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 14–20 — The Kingdom Announced and the First Disciples Called
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The transition from John to Jesus is marked by John's arrest. Mark notes it without elaboration — the forerunner's work is done, and the one he announced steps forward. The kingdom announcement of vv. 14–15 is the gospel compressed into four phrases: the time is fulfilled, the kingdom is at hand, repent, believe. This is not an offer to consider; it is the announcement of a reality that demands a response.

The calling of the first four disciples (vv. 16–20) is astonishing when read at face value. Jesus walks past a lake, says a sentence, and two sets of brothers leave their work, their equipment, their livelihoods, and their families to follow him. No extended conversation, no theological discussion, no discernment process. They came, he called, they went. Mark does not explain this — he presents it as the natural result of encountering a person with absolute authority.
verseByVerse.theology: 'The time is fulfilled, and the kingdom of God is at hand; repent and believe in the gospel' (v. 15) — this four-part announcement is the theological thesis of the entire gospel. 'The time is fulfilled': the appointed moment in God's redemptive calendar has arrived. History has been building to this. 'The kingdom of God is at hand': the sovereign rule of God is not merely near as a future hope — it is present in the person of the King. 'Repent': turn, change direction, reorient the whole self. 'Believe the gospel': stake everything on the good news that the King has come. The kingdom is not a programme or an idea; it is a Person, and you are either with him or not.
verseByVerse.examples: Simon, Andrew, James, and John left their nets and their father without, as far as Mark tells us, a moment's hesitation. Zebedee is left in the boat with the hired servants — not abandoned cruelly, but left because the new claim on his sons was greater than the old. The call of Jesus has always done this: it places a weight on the scales that makes everything else feel lighter by comparison. Then: fishermen who knew the lake and the nets and the dawn routines. Now: every person who has heard the call and left something — a career, a worldview, a former self — to follow the one who calls. The response always precedes the understanding.

verseByVerse.quote: Now after John was arrested, Jesus came into Galilee, proclaiming the gospel of God, and saying,
verseByVerse.commentary:
After John was arrested, Jesus came into Galilee proclaiming the gospel of God.

Now after John was arrested. Literally handed over. Herod Antipas imprisoned John for condemning his marriage to his brother’s wife (6:17–18). The arrest is noted in a subordinate clause; Mark will return to it in chapter 6 with devastating detail. The same word is later used of Jesus being handed over to death (9:31; 10:33; 15:1). The forerunner’s fate foreshadows the Messiah’s. Here it is a hinge: one era ends and another begins. The silence of the forerunner is the cue for the voice of the one he announced.

Jesus came into Galilee. The northern region around the Sea of Galilee, with a mixed population of Jews and Gentiles, looked down on by people in Judea. Not Jerusalem, not the temple, not the religious centre. The public ministry of the Son of God begins in the provinces, among the farms and fishing villages of the north, at a distance from the temple, the Sanhedrin and every institution with the authority to certify him. He will get to Jerusalem, and when he does, it will kill him. But the years of teaching and healing happen out where ordinary people live, and Mark never treats that as second best.

Proclaiming the gospel of God. Proclaiming means announcing as a herald. In verse 1 it was the gospel of Jesus Christ; now it is the gospel of God: the good news that comes from God and is about what God is doing. It is God’s own announcement, not a proposal Jesus puts forward for consideration. Good news in the ancient world was not advice about how to live; it was a herald’s report that something had happened, usually a battle won or a king enthroned. Nobody debates a herald. You either believe the report or you do not.

In a sentence. When John was arrested, Jesus began announcing God’s good news in Galilee.

On a Tuesday. The silencing of one messenger did not stop God’s word; opposition never stops the gospel. And if you have quietly concluded that the significant things happen elsewhere, in bigger churches, in cities, among people with platforms, remember that the most important preaching tour in the history of the world was conducted in a rural province by a man from a village nobody had heard of. The religious capital found out about it late and did not like it. Your small place is not outside his interest.

For worship. They silenced John, and God opened the mouth of his Son. The enemies of the word have never yet found a prison strong enough to hold it. The King chose to begin among fishermen and farmers, far from every throne, and from there his news has gone out into all the earth. He is the God who does his greatest things where the world is not looking.
verseByVerse.note: Galilee was the northern region of the land, around the lake. John was imprisoned by its ruler, Herod Antipas.

verseByVerse.quote: "The time is fulfilled, and the kingdom of God is at hand; repent and believe in the gospel."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus’ message: the time is fulfilled, and the kingdom of God is at hand; repent and believe in the gospel.

The time is fulfilled. Time (kairos) means the appointed time, the decisive moment, not the ticking of the clock. The long wait of the Old Testament is over. Everything God promised is now coming true. When the fullness of time had come, God sent forth his Son (Galatians 4:4).

And the kingdom of God is at hand. The kingdom of God is God’s reign: God acting as King to save his people and judge evil, as the prophets promised (Isaiah 52:7; Daniel 2:44; 7:13–14). It is not a place, nor merely a future heaven. At hand means it has come near, so near as to be within reach. It is not coming sometime soon; it is arriving in Jesus himself. His healings and exorcisms show it (3:23–27).

Is the kingdom present or still to come? Both. It is God’s saving rule arriving in the person of the King: where Jesus is, casting out demons and forgiving sins, the kingdom has come near. Yet it waits for its completion when he returns in glory (9:1; 13:26). It was not the political kingdom many expected, a free Israel under a Jewish king. It is God’s reign begun now in Christ and finished at his coming.

Repent. Turn around: a change of mind so thorough that it changes direction, away from sin and self-rule toward God. It is not an emotion, and it is not self-improvement. You can feel dreadful about your sin for years and never repent, because remorse looks at yourself while repentance turns to God. In practice it is concrete and unglamorous: naming the particular thing rather than sin in general, agreeing with God about it instead of managing the account downward, and turning, which usually means a decision this week that costs something. And it is not a gate you pass through once. Luther opened the Reformation by saying that the whole life of a believer is repentance, and he was right; you will be doing this on your last day.

And believe in the gospel. Trust the good news: rely on it, stake your life on it. It does not mean achieving a level of certainty. Its object is a report: the news that the King has come and has done what was needed. Believing that a chair will hold you and sitting down in it are two different things, and only one of them is faith. Repentance and faith are two sides of one turning: you stop trusting yourself and start trusting Christ. Repentance without faith is mere moral reformation; faith without repentance is intellectual assent. Only Mark records the words believe in the gospel: the response to the kingdom is not first to do better, but to trust the good news.

What it does not mean. Not that repentance and faith earn the kingdom. They receive it. Nor that the kingdom is only spiritual and future, or only political and present. It is God’s saving reign, already begun in Jesus and to be completed at his return.

How do I know whether I have really repented and believed? Look at direction rather than intensity. Repentance is measured by which way you are facing, not by how much you felt on the day. Ask: is Christ my hope, and am I fighting my sin rather than making peace with it? And if you find you cannot turn, ask for it. Scripture speaks of repentance as something God grants (Acts 11:18; 2 Timothy 2:25), which means the very thing commanded here can be requested from the one commanding it. That is why this is good news and not a hurdle. The King does not stand at a distance demanding that you climb; he has come near, and the command to turn is itself the outstretched hand.

Is the kingdom of God the same as the church? Not quite. The kingdom is God’s reign; the church is the people gathered under that reign, the community where it is confessed, preached and lived. The kingdom is wider: Christ already reigns over all things for his church (Ephesians 1:22), and one day his rule will fill a new heaven and a new earth. But the church is where the kingdom shows its face now, in forgiven sinners worshipping their King, so belonging to a local church is not optional for a citizen of the kingdom.

In a sentence. Jesus announced that the appointed time had come and God’s reign was arriving, and called everyone to turn to God and trust the good news.

On a Tuesday. Repent and believe is not only the first step of the Christian life but every step. Name one specific thing you need to turn from this week, not your sins in general, and one thing you need to trust God with instead of carrying it yourself. Then do the turning in a concrete act: the conversation, the deletion, the apology, the surrendered worry. Faith is sitting in the chair.

For worship. The waiting of centuries ended in a sentence. The King whom prophets and kings had longed to see came walking through Galilee and said that the hour had struck and his reign had begun. He did not set his kingdom on a mountain for rebels to climb; he carried it to them in his own person and held it out in two words, repent and believe. He is the appointed time. Every promise God ever made arrived on the road from Nazareth, and every one of them finds its yes in him.
verseByVerse.note: “The kingdom of God” means God’s reign, his rule as King. “At hand” means it has come near.

verseByVerse.quote: Passing alongside the Sea of Galilee, he saw Simon and Andrew the brother of Simon casting a net into the sea, for they were fishermen. And Jesus said to them, "Follow me, and I will make you become fishers of men." And immediately they left their nets and followed him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Walking by the Sea of Galilee, Jesus saw Simon and his brother Andrew casting a net, for they were fishermen. He said: follow me, and I will make you become fishers of men. Immediately they left their nets and followed him.

Passing alongside the Sea of Galilee. A freshwater lake about thirteen miles long and eight wide, full of fish, with fishing towns around its shore. Mark grounds the call in an ordinary working morning.

He saw Simon and Andrew the brother of Simon casting a net into the sea. Mark even adds for they were fishermen, as though writing for readers who had never seen it done. The net is the circular casting net, a mesh weighted round the rim, thrown by hand from the shallows so that it opens in the air and drops over the fish. It is close work, done wet, and it takes years to learn. This is not a hobby he is interrupting. It is a skill, an income and an identity. Simon, later called Peter, would become the leader of the apostles; Mark’s Gospel probably comes from his preaching, so this is Peter telling the story of the morning his life changed.

Had they met Jesus before? Yes. John’s Gospel records an earlier meeting: Andrew was a disciple of the Baptist, heard him point at Jesus and say, Behold, the Lamb of God, spent a day with him, and went to find his brother with the words, We have found the Messiah; and Jesus looked at Simon and renamed him (John 1:35–42). That happened at the Jordan, months before. By the time Jesus comes up the shoreline, these are not strangers. This does not damage Mark’s point; it puts a floor under it. Mark is compressing a history he assumes you know. What he records is not their conversion but their conscription: the men had believed already, and at the lake following became leaving. That is the harder step, and the one Mark wants you to see.

Follow me. Literally come behind me. Students usually chose their rabbi; Jesus chooses his disciples. He calls them not to a set of teachings but to himself. The authority of the one calling is the point: Jesus passes, sees, speaks, and they leave their nets at once: following Jesus costs something from the start. No backstory, no deliberation. Mark is not writing biography; he is writing testimony.

And I will make you become fishers of men. Men means people. They would gather people into God’s kingdom as they had gathered fish. And the image is chosen with a craftsman’s care. He does not tell them to abandon what they are; he tells them what they are for. Every instinct the lake taught them, patience, early starts, working all night for nothing, will be needed, aimed now at people. And I will make you become is a promise of process. Jesus is not recruiting people who are already prepared; he is calling people he will transform, and he takes responsibility for forming them. The disciples in Mark are often confused, fearful and faithless, and yet they are the ones he chose and the ones he is making. The calling comes before the competence.

What it does not mean. Not that every Christian must leave their job. These men were called to be apostles. But every disciple must put Jesus before everything, and every disciple is called to bring others to him.

I am not a preacher. What does fishing for people look like for me? Mostly it looks like ordinary faithfulness where you already are. Pray by name for a few people who do not know Christ. Be the kind of neighbour and colleague whose life raises questions, and answer them gently when they come (1 Peter 3:15). Invite people to your home and to church. Tell your own story of what Christ has done, simply. Fishermen work in teams, and so do Christians: you may never be the one who draws the net in, but the one who cast it, mended it or rowed the boat is part of the catch.

In a sentence. Jesus called Simon and Andrew to follow him and become fishers of people, and they left their nets at once.

On a Tuesday. What nets would be hardest for you to leave if Jesus asked: a career plan, a comfort, a reputation, a relationship? Hold them loosely. And look at the skills and habits you picked up in years you thought were unrelated to anything. Ask how they might be aimed at people. They are usually the equipment.

For worship. He walked along a beach and spoke two words, and four working men walked out of their lives into his. That is the voice that called the worlds into being, and it has not weakened. He chose them before they were ready and promised to make them what he needed, and he kept his word: the frightened fisherman of this shore became the rock who preached at Pentecost. He still calls people he intends to transform, and he still finishes what he starts.
verseByVerse.note: The Sea of Galilee is a freshwater lake about 13 miles long. A casting net was a round net thrown by hand into shallow water.

parallels.desc: Luke’s account of the call by the lake
Andrew and Simon first meet Jesus

verseByVerse.quote: And going on a little farther, he saw James the son of Zebedee and John his brother, who were in their boat mending the nets. And immediately he called them, and they left their father Zebedee in the boat with the hired servants and followed him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A little farther on, Jesus saw James and John, the sons of Zebedee, in their boat mending the nets. Immediately he called them, and they left their father Zebedee in the boat with the hired servants and followed him.

He saw James the son of Zebedee and John his brother, who were in their boat mending the nets. The second pair are called off a different job: not casting nets but mending them, which is the unglamorous half of fishing and the half that never ends. Nets tore every night, and a fisherman who did not mend was a fisherman who did not eat. James and John, with Peter, became Jesus’ inner circle (5:37; 9:2; 14:33). Jesus nicknamed them Sons of Thunder (3:17), and John became the disciple who wrote of love.

And immediately he called them, and they left their father Zebedee in the boat. No more of the call is recorded; it was enough. Only Mark mentions the hired servants, and the detail is worth having. Zebedee ran a business with employees; the family was reasonably well off. The brothers left a prosperous family firm, and their father in mid-work. Mark leaves Zebedee sitting in the boat and does not soften it. But the detail also quietly answers a charge sometimes brought against this scene: the family was not destitute, and the business would survive. This is a real cost and it is not a cruelty, and Mark expects the reader to hold both.

The Son who left his Father’s house. The call costs James and John a father in a boat, and the one calling them knows that cost from the other side. He had left far more than a family firm. The eternal Son came out from the Father into a world that did not receive him (John 1:11; 16:28), and before long his own family would come to take him home, convinced he was out of his mind (3:21). He never asks a disciple to leave anything he did not leave first, and more. And what he calls them into is a family of his own: whoever does the will of God, he says, is his brother and sister and mother (3:35).

What if following Jesus divides me from my family? Jesus warned it would sometimes happen (10:29–30; Matthew 10:34–37), and promised that no one who leaves home or family for his sake will lose out, in this age or the next. Following him first does not mean despising your family. Keep honouring your parents, keep loving them, keep serving them in practical ways; the hired servants show that these sons did not leave their father helpless. But when their wishes and Christ’s commands collide, Christ comes first. Do it gently, without self-righteousness, and keep praying. Many families who were hurt by a believer’s choice have later been won by the same believer’s patient love.

In a sentence. Jesus called James and John, and they left their father and the family fishing business to follow him.

On a Tuesday. Following Jesus may mean disappointing family expectations, or giving up the security of a path that was all mapped out. Honour your family, but follow him first. And be faithful in the mending: the unseen, repetitive work you do every day is not beneath his notice, and it is often from there that he calls.

For worship. He called them, nothing more, and it was enough to empty a boat. The Lord who is worth more than father and family firm is the one who gives back a hundredfold, brothers and sisters and homes beyond counting, and in the age to come eternal life. No one has ever left anything for him and found themselves the poorer.
verseByVerse.note: James and John left “hired servants” with their father, so Zebedee ran a working fishing business.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 21–45 — Authority in Capernaum and Beyond
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
What follows from verse 21 through verse 45 is a compressed day that functions as a demonstration of Jesus's authority across every domain. In the synagogue: authority over teaching and over the demonic. In the house: authority over disease. At the door after dark: authority over sickness and possession in numbers. Before dawn: the inner life of prayer that sustains the outer life of power. On the road: authority to cleanse the untouchable.

The crowd's reaction names exactly what Mark wants his readers to see: 'A new teaching — with authority! He commands even the unclean spirits, and they obey him.' The scribes taught by citing precedent. Jesus taught declaratively — from his own authority, as one who does not need to appeal to a tradition because he is the source of the tradition.
verseByVerse.theology: The exorcism in the synagogue (vv. 21–28) raises the question of the Messianic Secret — one of Mark's dominant themes. The unclean spirit identifies Jesus accurately: 'the Holy One of God.' Jesus silences him and casts him out. Why the silence? Several things converge: the testimony of a demon is unreliable as a vehicle of revelation even when technically accurate; Jesus's identity must be understood through the cross, not merely through power encounters; and a premature popular messianism would derail the mission. Throughout Mark, Jesus consistently refuses to let the wrong voices tell the right story.
verseByVerse.examples: The leper of vv. 40–45 approaches Jesus with the most honest prayer in the chapter: 'If you will, you can make me clean.' Not 'if you are able' — he has already seen enough to know the ability is there. The question is the willingness. Jesus's response answers the question permanently: 'I will; be clean.' The will of God toward the broken and the defiled is never in doubt when he reaches out and touches the untouchable. Then: a man excluded from community, from worship, from human touch — brought back by a hand that chose to land on his skin. Now: the same question echoes in every person who approaches God uncertain whether he actually wants them. He does. He reaches. He wills it.

verseByVerse.quote: And they went into Capernaum, and immediately on the Sabbath he entered the synagogue and was teaching. And they were astonished at his teaching, for he taught them as one who had authority, and not as the scribes.
verseByVerse.commentary:
They went into Capernaum, and on the Sabbath Jesus went into the synagogue and taught. The people were astonished at his teaching, because he taught them as one who had authority, not as the scribes.

And they went into Capernaum. A fishing town on the north-west shore of the lake, on the trade road, with a customs post and a garrison, which became the base of the Galilean ministry (2:1). Archaeologists have found remains of its synagogue and of a house venerated from early times as Peter’s.

And immediately on the Sabbath he entered the synagogue and was teaching. The synagogue was the local meeting place for prayer and for the reading and teaching of Scripture, the most public platform a town had: the whole community present, the leaders in their seats, the law being read. Visiting teachers could be invited to speak (Luke 4:16; Acts 13:15). And the first thing Jesus does in his new town is go to the service and teach.

For he taught them as one who had authority, and not as the scribes. They were astonished: struck, knocked out of their composure. The word for authority is exousia: the right to act, the entitlement that stands behind a command. And the comparison the crowd reaches for is not that Jesus was more interesting than the scribes, or a better speaker. It is about the basis on which he spoke. The scribes were experts in the law who taught by citation, tracing a ruling back through a chain of rabbis; their authority was always borrowed, and borrowing it correctly was the skill. Jesus quotes nobody. He teaches as a man reporting what is the case, I say to you, and the effect on a room trained to expect footnotes is the word Mark uses. They had come for an exposition of the tradition. They got the person the tradition was about, saying so, in the room. Mark does not record what he taught here; the focus is on who he is.

Should my pastor teach with authority like this? Only in a borrowed and lesser way, and that is right. Jesus’ authority was his own. A faithful preacher’s authority is exactly as great as his faithfulness to Scripture: when he says what the text says, he speaks with Christ’s authority, and you should receive it as God’s word (1 Thessalonians 2:13); when he goes beyond it, he speaks only as a man. So test what you hear by the Bible, as the Bereans did (Acts 17:11), and when it is true, do not treat it as one opinion among many. The scribes’ failure was not that they quoted others but that they never brought people face to face with God’s own voice.

In a sentence. In the Capernaum synagogue, Jesus amazed the people by teaching with his own authority, unlike the scribes.

On a Tuesday. When you read Jesus’ words this week, notice whether you are reading opinions to consider or the words of the one with all authority. Pick one thing he says plainly, about worry, money, forgiveness or anger, that you have been treating as advice, and treat it as a command from the one who has the right to give it.

For worship. He did not need to cite anyone, because there is no one above him to cite. Every true word the scribes ever handed down came from him first. When he speaks, the source of the law is speaking about the law, the Author is reading his own book aloud. Blessed are the people who have heard his voice, and who have it still, written, in their hands.
verseByVerse.note: Capernaum was a fishing town on the north-west shore of the lake, and became Jesus’ base in Galilee. Scribes were the trained teachers of the law of Moses.

parallels.desc: the same astonishment after the Sermon on the Mount

verseByVerse.quote: And immediately there was in their synagogue a man with an unclean spirit. And he cried out, "What have you to do with us, Jesus of Nazareth? Have you come to destroy us? I know who you are—the Holy One of God."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Immediately a man in the synagogue with an unclean spirit cried out: what have you to do with us, Jesus of Nazareth? Have you come to destroy us? I know who you are: the Holy One of God.

And immediately there was in their synagogue a man with an unclean spirit. An unclean spirit is a demon: a fallen angel, morally impure, which defiles and torments the person it controls. And notice where it happens. Not in a graveyard, not in a pagan temple, not among the tombs on the far shore where Mark will take us in chapter 5.
