In the synagogue, on the Sabbath, during the service. Whatever was in him had sat quietly through the readings and prayers, week after week, until the day Jesus of Nazareth walked in, and it could not stay quiet for one more sentence. The presence of Christ does not create the problem; it surfaces it. Things that have coexisted comfortably with religion for years become unbearable the moment he is actually in the room.

What have you to do with us, Jesus of Nazareth? A Hebrew idiom: what is there between us? Leave us alone. And us: the demon speaks for the whole kingdom of evil spirits.

Have you come to destroy us? It is not defiance but panic. The demons know that Jesus has come to defeat them; the Son of God appeared to destroy the works of the devil (1 John 3:8). It knows exactly who has walked in and exactly how the story ends.

I know who you are, the Holy One of God. The demon recognises what the people do not: Jesus is the Holy One, set apart by God, God’s own. There is terrible irony here. Demons in Mark repeatedly recognise Jesus before the people and even the disciples do (1:34; 3:11; 5:7). Knowing who Jesus is does not make them his followers; they believe and shudder (James 2:19). Some suggest that naming him was an attempt to gain power over him, as ancient magic believed that knowing a name gave control. If so, it failed in the next breath.

What is an unclean spirit, and does any of this happen now? This is the first exorcism in Mark and there will be many, so the question is best met here. Scripture treats demons as real personal beings, fallen and malevolent, not a first-century label for illness that we have since outgrown. And the Gospel writers themselves keep the categories apart. A few verses on, Mark says the people brought all who were sick or oppressed by demons, and that Jesus healed many who were sick and cast out many demons (vv. 32, 34): two groups, two verbs, listed side by side by a writer who plainly did not think they were the same thing. Luke, who was a doctor, keeps the same distinction. These men were not confusing epilepsy with the devil for want of a better word.

In a sentence. In the synagogue, a demon cried out that it knew Jesus to be the Holy One of God, come to destroy the powers of evil.

On a Tuesday. Knowing facts about Jesus is not enough; even demons know them, and know them accurately. Ask yourself whether your knowledge of him has become love and trust. And when the nearness of Christ in his word stirs something uncomfortable in you, do not run from the discomfort. It may be the first sign that something long hidden is being brought into the light to be dealt with.

For worship. Hell knew him the moment he walked in. The powers that had held a man for years and sat unmoved through every service in that building looked at the carpenter from Nazareth and cried out in terror, because they knew the Holy One of God. Our Lord is not a teacher whom evil can ignore. He is the one it fears, and the one who came to destroy its works.
verseByVerse.note: An “unclean spirit” is a demon. “The Holy One of God” is a title for the one set apart by God — the demon names who Jesus is.

verseByVerse.quote: But Jesus rebuked him, saying, "Be silent, and come out of him!" And the unclean spirit, convulsing him and crying out with a loud voice, came out of him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus rebuked it: be silent, and come out of him! The unclean spirit threw the man into convulsions, cried out with a loud voice and came out of him.

But Jesus rebuked him, saying, “Be silent”. Literally be muzzled. Jesus silences the demon. Why, when it was telling the truth? Because Jesus would not accept testimony from demons, and because he did not want his identity proclaimed before people understood that the Messiah must suffer (1:34; 3:12). This is part of what is called the messianic secret in Mark: he will not be proclaimed Messiah until the cross can define the word.

And come out of him! Five words in all, and it is over. Set that against how exorcism was done everywhere else in the ancient world. The technique involved naming a superior spirit, invoking a formula, sometimes using a ring or a root or a bowl of water; the practitioner’s power was borrowed, and the procedure could take a long time and might not work. There are surviving handbooks. Later in Acts we meet seven men attempting it by borrowing the name of a Jesus they did not know, and being beaten for their trouble (Acts 19:13–16). Jesus uses no name but his own authority, no formula, no ritual and no delay. He tells it to be quiet and to get out, and it is quiet and it gets out.

And the unclean spirit, convulsing him and crying out with a loud voice, came out of him. A final violent display, but it had to obey. Luke adds that it did the man no harm (Luke 4:35). This is not a contest between equal powers. Jesus does not wrestle, argue or perform; he speaks, and the thing goes.

What it does not mean. Not that every illness or mental disorder is demonic. The Gospels distinguish demon possession from disease (1:34). Nor should Christians try to cast out demons by formulas. Jesus’ authority is his own.

Two ditches. Does it still happen? Yes, and there are two ditches, both of which have hurt people. One is to deny the whole category, which is a modern reflex rather than a biblical conclusion; missionaries working where the occult is openly practised do not generally find it hard to believe. The other, and in our churches by far the more damaging, is to see a demon behind everything. Treating depression, epilepsy, trauma or a chemical illness as a spirit to be cast out has done real and lasting harm to people who needed a doctor and got an exorcism instead. Notice how little space this occupies in the New Testament letters. When the apostles write to churches about the Christian’s daily struggle, they speak overwhelmingly of sin, the flesh and the world, and the weapons they prescribe are ordinary and unspectacular: Scripture, prayer, truth, the armour of God, the company of the church (Ephesians 6:10–18). If you are unwell, see a doctor; that is not a failure of faith but an ordinary mercy God provides.

Can a Christian be possessed by a demon? No. You cannot be owned by what has already been beaten. He who is in you is greater than he who is in the world (1 John 4:4), and a person indwelt by the Spirit of God is not available for occupation: harassed sometimes, tempted certainly, but not possessed. You belong to Christ, bought with a price (1 Corinthians 6:19–20). So if you read a passage like this at night and feel afraid, resist the devil by the ordinary means and he will flee from you (James 4:7). And if you have dabbled in the occult in the past, renounce it plainly before God, get rid of anything connected with it (Acts 19:18–19), tell a pastor, and rest in Christ’s finished victory.

In a sentence. Jesus silenced the demon and commanded it out, and it left the man with a final convulsion.

On a Tuesday. No power of evil can resist Jesus’ word. Whatever has a grip on you, a habit, a fear, a darkness you cannot shake, it must obey him. Bring it to him by name in prayer, and tell one trusted believer about it. Shame keeps things in the dark; Christ’s word brings them out.

For worship. Five words from the Son of God, and the enemy fled screaming. All the massed power of hell, in a synagogue on a Sabbath morning, lasted one sentence against him. There was never going to be a struggle. This is the Lord Jesus Christ, and there is nothing in heaven or on earth or under the earth that can hold its ground in front of him a moment longer than he permits. He holds his people, and no one can snatch them from his hand.
verseByVerse.note: Jesus uses no ritual, no formula and no appeal to another power — a command alone.

verseByVerse.quote: And they were all amazed, so that they questioned among themselves, saying, "What is this? A new teaching with authority! He commands even the unclean spirits, and they obey him." And at once his fame spread everywhere throughout all the surrounding region of Galilee.
verseByVerse.commentary:
They were all amazed and asked each other: what is this? A new teaching with authority! He commands even the unclean spirits, and they obey him. And at once his fame spread everywhere throughout the region of Galilee.

What is this? A new teaching with authority! They were all amazed, first at his teaching and now at his power. Read the crowd’s sentence carefully, because they have got it exactly right and exactly incomplete. What is this? Not who is this. That question comes later in Mark, and it is the question the whole Gospel is driving at (4:41; 8:29). Here they ask what, as though it were a phenomenon rather than a person. New (kainē) means new in kind, fresh. And they connect the two things Mark has laid side by side, the astonishing teaching in verse 22 and the expulsion in verse 26. They are right to connect them. In this Gospel the word and the power are never two departments. What he says happens, whether he is saying it to a room or to a spirit.

He commands even the unclean spirits, and they obey him. The evidence that the kingdom of God has arrived: Satan’s power is being broken; the strong man is being bound (3:27). But notice what they call it. They have watched a man command a demonic power out of a neighbour with a sentence, and their category for it is a new teaching, a very good lesson. It is not wrong. It is nowhere near big enough.

And at once his fame spread everywhere. Mark’s immediately again. The news is out of the building before the Sabbath is over, and by the end of the verse it has the whole district. News travelled fast in the towns of Galilee. And that spreading fame is the thing Jesus will spend the rest of the chapter, and much of the Gospel, trying to manage: silencing demons, silencing the healed, withdrawing to desolate places. Not because the reports were false, but because a reputation built on power would fix in people’s minds a Messiah who was never going to be crucified. He is not building a following. He is going to a cross, and a crowd that wants a miracle worker will not follow him there.

Is it wrong to be amazed by Jesus without fully understanding him? No, it is often where faith begins. But amazement is a doorway, not a room to live in. These crowds were amazed and many of them later drifted away. The amazement that saves moves from what is this? to who is this? and then to you are the Christ, and finally to the trust that follows him even to the cross. If you are amazed by Jesus but not yet sure who he is, keep reading Mark. Its whole purpose is to take you from wonder to faith.

In a sentence. The people were amazed at Jesus’ authoritative teaching and his command over demons, and his fame spread throughout Galilee.

On a Tuesday. Amazement is a beginning, not an end. Let wonder at Jesus become trust in him. Ask whether your categories for him are big enough: whether you think of him as a very good teacher whose lessons you consult, or as the Lord whose word does what it says. Live this week as though his commands are as effective in your life as they were in that synagogue.

For worship. They called it a new teaching, and they did not know the half of it. It was the voice of the Creator in a village synagogue, the word that said let there be light now saying come out, and being obeyed. His teaching and his power are one, because he is one: the living Word of the living God. No category is big enough for him, and all our wonder only begins to tell the truth.

verseByVerse.quote: And immediately he left the synagogue and entered the house of Simon and Andrew, with James and John. Now Simon's mother-in-law lay ill with a fever, and immediately they told him about her. And he came and took her by the hand and lifted her up, and the fever left her, and she began to serve them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Leaving the synagogue, they went straight to the house of Simon and Andrew, with James and John. Simon’s mother-in-law lay ill with a fever, and they told Jesus about her at once. He came, took her by the hand and lifted her up; the fever left her, and she began to serve them.

And immediately he left the synagogue and entered the house of Simon and Andrew. From public ministry to a private home, from synagogue to kitchen. The kingdom has no restricted zones. Jesus’ power is for ordinary households, not only for public spectacles.

Now Simon’s mother-in-law lay ill with a fever. The verse drops a fact so quietly that most readers step over it. A man does not come by a mother-in-law any other way: Peter was married. And since the earliest witnesses tell us Mark wrote down Peter’s preaching, this cramped domestic scene, whose house it was, who was lying ill in it, the hand that lifted her, is very likely Peter describing his own front room. A fever in the ancient world could be dangerous; fevers killed.

Peter’s wife. It is not a private matter, because a great deal has been built on Peter. Rome names him the first pope and requires that those who stand in his succession be unmarried. Yet here is his wife’s mother in his house, and Paul, writing decades later, asks the Corinthians whether he does not have the right to take along a believing wife, as do the other apostles and the brothers of the Lord and Cephas (1 Corinthians 9:5). Cephas is Peter, still married and still travelling with her, years into the work. Let the point be made narrowly and fairly. This is no argument against celibacy freely chosen; Paul commended it warmly and lived it (1 Corinthians 7:7–8), and the Lord himself spoke of those who give up marriage for the sake of the kingdom (Matthew 19:12). But a rule that forbids marriage to the men who hold Peter’s office cannot appeal to Peter, who held it with a wife. Scripture expects that a pastor may well be the husband of one wife (1 Timothy 3:2).

And immediately they told him about her, and he came and took her by the hand and lifted her up. They brought her need to Jesus, which is the beginning of every answer to prayer. Then a personal touch: lifted her up is the word used for resurrection (16:6), a small picture of what Jesus came to do. And the fever left her, instantly and completely.

And she began to serve them. No time of recovery needed. The word (diēkonei) is the one used two paragraphs earlier of the angels ministering to Jesus in the wilderness (1:13), and the one Jesus will use of himself: the Son of Man came not to be served but to serve (10:45). Her response to healing was service, the mark of every disciple. She does not sit and contemplate her recovery; she moves toward others in love.

Is it demeaning that the healed woman goes straight to the kitchen? Not in Mark’s eyes. He uses for her work the same word he uses for angels serving the Son of God and for the Son of God giving his life. Serving a meal to Jesus and his friends puts her in very high company. Hospitality is honoured throughout Scripture (Romans 12:13; Hebrews 13:2), and many women served Jesus out of their means and were the faithful witnesses at the cross and the tomb (15:40–41). Every Christian, man or woman, is healed in order to serve, and no service done for Christ is small.

In a sentence. In Simon’s house, Jesus took his feverish mother-in-law by the hand and raised her up healed, and she served them.

On a Tuesday. Tell Jesus about the people you love who are suffering, simply and by name, as Peter’s household did. And when he helps you, serve: look for the person in your home or church whom you could serve today in some practical, unnoticed way.

For worship. The kingdom’s first stop after the synagogue was a sickroom off somebody’s kitchen. The first person served by the Son of God in a private house was an older woman with a fever, whom nobody outside that family would have named. He took her hand. She got up and made the meal. That is where this kingdom lands, and that is the kind of King he is: Lord of angels, and not too great to take a feverish woman by the hand.

parallels.desc: Peter was married, and his wife travelled with him

verseByVerse.quote: That evening at sundown they brought to him all who were sick or oppressed by demons. And the whole city was gathered together at the door. And he healed many who were sick with various diseases, and cast out many demons. And he would not permit the demons to speak, because they knew him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
That evening at sundown, people brought to Jesus all who were sick or oppressed by demons, and the whole town gathered at the door. He healed many who were sick with various diseases and cast out many demons. And he would not allow the demons to speak, because they knew him.

That evening at sundown. The Sabbath ended at sunset. Only then could people carry the sick without breaking the Sabbath rules about carrying burdens.

They brought to him all who were sick or oppressed by demons. News of the synagogue exorcism had spread. Mark distinguishes sickness and demonic oppression.

And the whole city was gathered together at the door. Peter, telling the story to Mark, could remember the crowd at his own front door. Word travels fast when the synagogue has just witnessed what happened.

And he healed many who were sick with various diseases, and cast out many demons. Many, not necessarily all: a Hebrew way of saying a great number. Matthew, describing the same evening, writes that he healed all who were sick (Matthew 8:16), and there is no contradiction: Mark is reporting the scale of an extraordinary night, not drawing a boundary round it. But the word is worth pausing on, because a chapter this full of healing raises a question in anyone who has prayed for healing and not received it.

And he would not permit the demons to speak, because they knew him. He would not have his identity announced by demons, nor have people take him for a mere wonder worker before they understood his cross.

Why does Jesus keep telling people to be quiet about him? This silencing runs right through Mark, and scholars call it the messianic secret. It is not that Jesus is hiding; the crowds see everything he does. He refuses to let the word Messiah be shouted before it can be rightly understood. In first-century Galilee that word meant a conquering king who would drive out Rome; a premature acclamation would light a political fire. Jesus will not be crowned before he is crucified. So he controls the timing, moving deliberately toward Jerusalem, so that when the title is finally confessed it will be defined by his death and not by the crowd’s dreams. With demons there is a further reason: praise from liars to the core is no honour to the Holy One. The secret is not concealment but protection: the right truth, at the right time, on the right lips.

Does he heal everybody, and if not, why not me? Say the honest thing first. What happened in Capernaum that night was not normal and was never claimed to be. Such miracles clustered around Jesus and then his apostles to authenticate the message while it was being given (Hebrews 2:3–4); we are nowhere promised that abundance now, and anyone who guarantees it is promising what Scripture does not. At the same time God has not retired. He remains entirely free to heal, and still does, and the church is told plainly to pray for the sick and expect him to act (James 5:14–15). So we ask, honestly and often, and we leave the outcome where it belongs.

The signpost is not the country. Then say the deeper thing, because it is where the comfort is. Every person healed in this chapter died later. Peter’s mother-in-law got up, made a meal, and in due course was buried. The leper of verse 40 walked away clean and did not walk away immortal. Not one of these healings was the destination; every one was a signpost, a piece of the new creation pushed early into the old, so that we would know what the King is going to do with the whole of it. What is guaranteed to the believer is not healing now but resurrection then, and a body that will never need healing again (1 Corinthians 15:42–44; Revelation 21:4). If you are not healed, it is not that your faith was too small or that he was unwilling. It is that the signpost is not the country, and you are still on the road to it.

In a sentence. When the Sabbath ended, the whole town brought its sick and possessed to Jesus, and he healed many and silenced the demons who knew him.

On a Tuesday. Jesus received everyone who came to his door. Bring your needs, and the needs of others, to him in prayer tonight: the sick friend, the troubled child, the neighbour in distress, by name. Ask boldly, and leave the answer with him. And if you are carrying an illness that has not lifted, tell him honestly how it feels, and fix your hope on the day when every signpost gives way to the country itself.

For worship. Picture the door of that little house at dusk, the whole town pressing round it, and one man moving among them, touching, speaking, healing, until the last of them went home. He never turned anyone away for being too much trouble. And every healing that night was a promise in miniature: one day he will stand at the door of the whole creation, and the sickness and the darkness will go out for ever, and death will be no more. The King has shown us what he means to do, and he will do it.
verseByVerse.note: The Sabbath ended at sundown. Only then could people carry the sick through the town without breaking the Sabbath rules.

verseByVerse.quote: And rising very early in the morning, while it was still dark, he departed and went out to a desolate place, and there he prayed. And Simon and those who were with him searched for him, and they found him and said to him, "Everyone is looking for you."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Very early in the morning, while it was still dark, Jesus got up and went out to a solitary place, and there he prayed. Simon and those with him searched for him, and when they found him they said: everyone is looking for you.

And rising very early in the morning, while it was still dark. After a long, exhausting evening, Jesus got up before dawn. This is perhaps the most important verse in the chapter for understanding what powered everything before it. The authority over demons, the healing touch, the astonishing teaching: all of it flows from this, a solitary communion with the Father in the dark.

He departed and went out to a desolate place, and there he prayed. Desolate place (erēmon) is the word for wilderness. Jesus withdrew from the crowds to be alone with his Father. Mark shows Jesus praying at three key moments, each at night: here, after feeding the five thousand (6:46), and in Gethsemane (14:32–39). Notice what the verse gives us: a time, a place and a priority. Very early, while it was still dark: before anyone could reach him. A desolate place: he went somewhere, deliberately, out of range. And before the day’s demands arrived rather than after they were satisfied. Those three are the anatomy of the thing.

Do I have to pray at five in the morning? No. This passage often leaves readers feeling condemned, so it is worth working out properly. Mark is recording what Jesus did, not legislating an hour. Scripture nowhere commands a time of day, and the Lord himself kept no fixed slot: he prayed through an entire night before choosing the Twelve (Luke 6:12) and went up the mountain to pray in the evening after feeding the crowd (6:46). What is constant is not the clock but the withdrawal. The hour mattered only because of what it protected. He was not being austere; he was getting somewhere he could not be reached. In a life with no margin in it, prayer is never found. It has to be taken.

What should I actually do when I get alone with God? Keep it simple and scriptural. Open the Bible and read a passage slowly, perhaps a chapter of a Gospel or a psalm, and ask what it shows you of God and of yourself. Then pray from it: praise him for what you have seen, confess what it exposed, thank him for his mercies, and bring your requests and other people’s by name. The Lord’s Prayer is a pattern for exactly this (Matthew 6:9–13). Ten honest minutes most days is better than an hour you never reach. If your mind wanders, bring it back without fuss. You are not performing; you are a child talking to your Father.

And Simon and those who were with him searched for him. Searched (katediōxen) means hunted him down, pursued him. They were eager to bring him back to the excited crowds.

And they found him and said to him, “Everyone is looking for you”. The disciples saw a great opportunity: popularity, crowds, success. They wanted Jesus to go back. In effect they tell him he is missing his moment.

In a sentence. Jesus rose before dawn to pray alone, and the disciples hunted him down to bring him back to the crowds.

On a Tuesday. When will you be alone with God today? Name the time and the place, and guard them, even when everyone is looking for you. If your day has no margin at all, ask what would have to go to make some. And if you have failed at this for years, do not start with guilt. Start tomorrow, small.

For worship. The eternal Son, who shared the Father’s glory before the world was, slipped out of a sleeping house in the dark to be with him. His communion with the Father was the very centre of his life, and it was never broken until the cross, when he cried out as one forsaken, so that we who never pray as we should might be brought near to God for ever. He prayed in the dark while his friends slept. He prays for us still, and his intercession never fails.

verseByVerse.quote: And he said to them, "Let us go on to the next towns, that I may preach there also, for that is why I came out." And he went throughout all Galilee, preaching in their synagogues and casting out demons.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus said to them: let us go on to the next towns, so that I may preach there also, for that is why I came out. And he went throughout all Galilee, preaching in their synagogues and casting out demons.

Let us go on to the next towns, that I may preach there also. And see what his hour of prayer in the dark had bought. A whole town wants him. It is a genuinely good thing being offered: more healing, more crowds, more obvious fruit. And he says no. He refuses to be held by popularity. Prayer had clarified his purpose. The crowds wanted miracles; Jesus’ priority was preaching. The towns of Galilee were many and close together.

For that is why I came out. Perhaps came out from Capernaum, or more deeply, came from the Father into the world (John 16:28). His mission was to proclaim the kingdom. He could say no to a good thing because he had already settled in the dark what the day was for. That is what the desolate place is for. If you do not decide before the demands arrive, the demands will decide, and you will spend your life on whatever shouts loudest, which is usually good, and usually not what you were sent to do.

And he went throughout all Galilee, preaching in their synagogues and casting out demons. Word and power together, inseparable. The word of the kingdom is not merely information; it is an event that changes the territory it enters.

What it does not mean. Not that Jesus did not care about the sick in Capernaum. But the healings served the message, not the other way round. Good things can distract from the main thing.

How do I know what my main calling is? Start with what is plain in Scripture for every Christian: to love God, to love your neighbour, to belong to and serve a church, to make Christ known. Then add what your place in life gives you: a spouse to love, children to raise, a job to do faithfully, parents to honour. Your gifts, the church’s wise counsel and the needs in front of you help to fill in the rest. Most people do not need a new calling so much as the courage to say no to good things that crowd out the ones already given.

In a sentence. Refusing to stay where he was popular, Jesus went on to preach throughout Galilee, because preaching was his purpose.

On a Tuesday. What has God called you to do first? Write it down. Then look at this week’s diary and ask where good opportunities are crowding out your main calling. Take the principle rather than the alarm clock: somewhere out of reach, before the noise, often enough to keep the question of what you are for from being answered by other people. And remember that when his friends woke he did not rebuke them for missing the prayer. He went out to preach, which is what they needed him to do. He has prayed for you far more faithfully than you have ever prayed for yourself.

For worship. Everyone was looking for him, and he went looking for everyone else. The Son of God would not be kept by the crowd that loved him, because he had come for the towns that had not yet heard. That is his heart: the next village, the far country, the lost sheep. He came out from the Father on purpose, and he did not turn aside from it until it was finished.

verseByVerse.quote: And a leper came to him, imploring him, and kneeling said to him, "If you will, you can make me clean." Moved with pity, he stretched out his hand and touched him and said to him, "I will; be clean." And immediately the leprosy left him, and he was made clean.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A man with leprosy came to Jesus, knelt and begged him: if you are willing, you can make me clean. Moved with pity, Jesus stretched out his hand, touched him and said: I am willing; be clean. Immediately the leprosy left him, and he was made clean.

And a leper came to him. Leprosy in the Bible covers a range of skin diseases (Leviticus 13–14). A leper was ritually unclean, had to live outside the town, wear torn clothes, cover his lip and call out Unclean, unclean! (Leviticus 13:45–46). Anyone who touched him became unclean. He was cut off from worship, from family and from all human touch. Curing leprosy was thought as hard as raising the dead (2 Kings 5:7). This man approaches Jesus, already breaking the law by coming near, and kneels.

Imploring him, and kneeling said to him, “If you will, you can make me clean”. He had no doubt about Jesus’ power, only about his willingness. Would Jesus want to help someone like him? His prayer is a small masterpiece of faith: he does not doubt the power; he leans his whole weight on it. He is uncertain only about the heart.

Moved with pity. Pity (splanchnistheis) is deep, gut-level compassion. But one ancient Greek manuscript and several early Latin translations read moved with anger (orgistheis). The two words look nothing alike in Greek, so a slip of the eye is unlikely; a scribe softening a startling anger to a gentle pity is the easier change to explain, which is why some scholars think the harder reading may be original. Verdict: the evidence is divided; pity is better supported, though anger may be the harder and therefore original reading. Either way, Jesus is moved deeply.

If Mark wrote anger, at what? Not at the man; Jesus touches him in the same breath. At the thing that has him: at the disfiguring, isolating cruelty of a disease that is sin’s shadow on the body, at the whole ruin the enemy has worked in God’s good world. It is the same holy indignation with which he would groan in spirit at the tomb of Lazarus (John 11:33, 38). Pity and anger are not rivals here. Love for the sufferer is fury at what is destroying him, and both bend the same hand toward the untouchable to make him clean.

He stretched out his hand and touched him. Astonishing. Jesus touched the untouchable. Perhaps no one had touched this man for years. He did not need to touch him; elsewhere he heals at a distance. The touch is deliberate solidarity. When Jesus touches a leper, the uncleanness does not pass to him; his cleanness passes to the leper. That is the direction grace always moves, and it is what he will do with the moral uncleanness of his people at the cross.

And said to him, “I will; be clean”. The direct answer to the man’s question: I am willing. Not I might, or under the right circumstances. I will. And immediately the leprosy left him, and he was not only healed but clean: restored to God’s people and to worship.

What it does not mean. Not that we should pray if you are willing about forgiveness. God has promised to forgive all who come to him (1 John 1:9). We may pray if you are willing about healing or circumstances, which he has not promised.

A guard on I will. It is a sentence that can be misheard. What Jesus settles here for all time is his willingness to receive and cleanse the person nobody else would touch, the one who wonders whether he is wanted. That question is closed. It is not a promise that every disease will be removed on request; Mark has just said he healed many at Simon’s door, not every illness on request; healing now is his free gift, resurrection is his promise. Keep the two apart and both stand. Whether he will heal your body today, you must ask him and leave with him. Whether he is willing to have you, unclean as you come, he has already stretched out his hand and answered.

What if what makes me feel unclean is something I did, not something that happened to me? Then this story is still for you, and even more so. The leper’s disease was a picture of sin: it spread, it defiled, it cut people off from God and from one another. The cleansing Jesus gives reaches the guilty conscience as well as the wounded body. The blood of Jesus cleanses us from all sin (1 John 1:7), including the thing you are most ashamed of. Come as the leper came, kneeling and honest. You do not need to clean yourself up first. That is exactly what he came to do.

In a sentence. A leper asked if Jesus was willing to cleanse him, and Jesus, moved with compassion, touched him and made him clean.

On a Tuesday. Is there something that makes you feel untouchable to God, a sin, a history, an addiction, a secret? Jesus is willing. Come to him today and say so in words. And ask who in your world is treated as untouchable: the lonely, the ill, the disgraced, the person everyone avoids. A hand on the shoulder, a meal, a visit may be the first human touch they have had in a long time.

For worship. He did not wait for the leper to make himself touchable. The hand through which all things were made reached across years of exile and rested on a ruined body, and the Holy One was not stained by it. That is the Lord Jesus. Every outcast who has ever knelt and wondered whether he is wanted has the same answer, spoken once on a Galilean road and sealed when those hands were nailed open on the cross: I will; be clean.
verseByVerse.note: “Leprosy” in the Bible covers a range of skin diseases. A leper had to live apart from others — so touching one was unheard of.

parallels.desc: the leper must live alone, crying “Unclean”

verseByVerse.quote: And Jesus sternly charged him and sent him away at once, and said to him, "See that you say nothing to anyone, but go, show yourself to the priest and offer for your cleansing what Moses commanded, for a proof to them." But he went out and began to talk freely about it, and to spread the news, so that Jesus could no longer openly enter a town, but was out in desolate places, and people were coming to him from every quarter.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus sternly warned him and sent him away at once: see that you say nothing to anyone, but go, show yourself to the priest and offer for your cleansing what Moses commanded, as a proof to them. But the man went out and began to talk about it freely and spread the news, so that Jesus could no longer openly enter a town, but stayed out in desolate places, and people came to him from everywhere.

And Jesus sternly charged him. The word behind sternly charged (embrimēsamenos) is a strong one, used of snorting with indignation, and it is the same verb John uses of Jesus at the grave of Lazarus. It is a startling word to use of a man being sent home healed. But if Mark wrote in verse 41, as some manuscripts read, that Jesus was moved with anger, then verse 43 is of a piece with it: two fierce words within three verses, in a scene that is otherwise pure tenderness. Whatever burned in him at the sight of that ruined body had not gone out by the time he sent the man away.

See that you say nothing to anyone. The same command comes again and again in Mark (1:34; 3:12; 5:43; 8:30). Jesus did not want to be known chiefly as a wonder worker, drawing crowds that would make his preaching impossible, as happened here (v. 45), or to stir up political hopes; the titles that would follow, Messiah and King, would be heard as a call to revolt. Who he is had to be defined by the cross before it was proclaimed.

But go, show yourself to the priest and offer for your cleansing what Moses commanded. The law required a priest to examine and declare a leper clean, with offerings of birds, lambs, flour and oil (Leviticus 14:1–32). Only then could he return to society and worship. Jesus respects the law and wants the man fully restored, not only in his skin but in his place among God’s people. What the man was told to do instead of talking was the proper public witness.

For a proof to them. A testimony to the priests that something extraordinary had happened, evidence they could not deny. Rabbis said cleansing a leper was as hard as raising the dead, and now a cleansed leper would be standing in front of them with his offering.

But he went out and began to talk freely about it, and to spread the news. He disobeyed, out of joy. It is entirely understandable. He had been untouchable, excluded from worship and from his own family, required by law to shout his own contamination at anyone who came near, and a man had put a hand on him and made him clean. Of course he talked. Anyone would. But disobedience, even happy disobedience, had consequences.

So that Jesus could no longer openly enter a town, but was out in desolate places. Look at what it cost, because Mark records the consequence in the same breath. The man who had been shut out of the towns is now free to walk into any of them; and the one who freed him has taken his place outside. Mark does not draw the moral, and it would be a shame to flatten it. But the exchange is unmistakable, and it is the shape of everything this Gospel is moving toward. Jesus took the leper’s place, a picture of what he would do at the cross, when he suffered outside the gate to sanctify the people through his own blood (Hebrews 13:12). The clean man goes in. The one who made him clean goes out. And even there people kept coming to him from every quarter; he could not be hidden.

So should I keep quiet about what Jesus has done for me? No. This command was for a particular moment, before the cross, when talk of a miracle worker would hinder his mission. After the resurrection the command is the opposite: go and tell (16:7; Matthew 28:19–20). Even in Mark, the healed man of Gerasa, in Gentile territory, is told to go home and tell how much the Lord has done for him (5:19). The lesson for us is not silence but obedience: to tell what he has done in the way and at the time he commands, which now means gladly, plainly and often.

In a sentence. Jesus told the cleansed leper to keep silent and go to the priest, but he spread the news, so that Jesus had to stay outside the towns.

On a Tuesday. Gratitude is good, but obedience is better. Ask how Jesus wants you to respond to what he has done for you, and do it his way rather than yours. Is there an instruction of his you have quietly replaced with something you thought would serve him better? Enthusiasm that ignores his word can still get in the way of his work.

For worship. The leper went home, and his Lord went out to the lonely places. It was a rehearsal in miniature of the great day when the Son of God would be led outside the city wall, bearing the uncleanness of his people, and cry out as one forsaken, so that the shut-out might be brought into the very presence of God. He took the outside place willingly, and he holds it open still as a door: from every nation and every kind of ruin they come to him, and not one is sent away unclean.
verseByVerse.note: The cleansing involved the priest’s inspection, two birds, and offerings on the eighth day.

1.theology:
Chapter 1 establishes the theological framework for everything that follows. Jesus is identified from three directions before his ministry begins: by the Father ('my beloved Son'), by Scripture ('as it is written'), and by his own announcement ('the kingdom of God is at hand'). The reader is positioned to understand all subsequent events in light of these identifications. When the demons recognize him, when the crowds are astonished, when the disciples follow without explanation — the reader knows why.

The Messianic Secret — Jesus silencing the demons and commanding the healed not to speak — is not evasion but strategy. The kind of Messiah the popular imagination expected was a military deliverer. Jesus is doing something far more radical, and a premature popular messianism based on power-encounters would derail the mission before it reached its necessary destination. The secret must be kept until the cross redefines what messianic identity means. Fittingly, the climactic declaration will be made by a Roman soldier standing at the foot of the cross (15:39).
1.examples: The disciples in this chapter are responsive but unformed. They leave their nets, they follow, they find Jesus praying and report the crowds waiting — but they have no framework yet for what they are following. This is where discipleship always begins: responding to a presence before you have the categories to explain it. The categories will come, often painfully, over the three years ahead.

keyVerse.quote: The time is fulfilled, and the kingdom of God is at hand; repent and believe in the gospel.

2.title: Who Has Authority to Forgive?
2.text: <sup>1</sup>And when he returned to Capernaum after some days, it was reported that he was at home. <sup>2</sup>And many were gathered together, so that there was no more room, not even at the door. And he was preaching the word to them. <sup>3</sup>And they came, bringing to him a paralytic carried by four men. <sup>4</sup>And when they could not get near him because of the crowd, they removed the roof above him, and when they had made an opening, they let down the bed on which the paralytic lay. <sup>5</sup>And when Jesus saw their faith, he said to the paralytic, “Son, your sins are forgiven.” <sup>6</sup>Now some of the scribes were sitting there, questioning in their hearts, <sup>7</sup>“Why does this man speak like that? He is blaspheming! Who can forgive sins but God alone?” <sup>8</sup>And immediately Jesus, perceiving in his spirit that they thus questioned within themselves, said to them, “Why do you question these things in your hearts? <sup>9</sup>Which is easier, to say to the paralytic, ‘Your sins are forgiven,’ or to say, ‘Rise, take up your bed and walk’? <sup>10</sup>But that you may know that the Son of Man has authority on earth to forgive sins”—he said to the paralytic— <sup>11</sup>“I say to you, rise, pick up your bed, and go home.” <sup>12</sup>And he rose and immediately picked up his bed and went out before them all, so that they were all amazed and glorified God, saying, “We never saw anything like this!” <sup>13</sup>He went out again beside the sea, and all the crowd was coming to him, and he was teaching them. <sup>14</sup>And as he passed by, he saw Levi the son of Alphaeus sitting at the tax booth, and he said to him, “Follow me.” And he rose and followed him. <sup>15</sup>And as he reclined at table in his house, many tax collectors and sinners were reclining with Jesus and his disciples, for there were many who followed him. <sup>16</sup>And the scribes of the Pharisees, when they saw that he was eating with sinners and tax collectors, said to his disciples, “Why does he eat with tax collectors and sinners?” <sup>17</sup>And when Jesus heard it, he said to them, “Those who are well have no need of a physician, but those who are sick. I came not to call the righteous, but sinners.” <sup>18</sup>Now John’s disciples and the Pharisees were fasting. And people came and said to him, “Why do John’s disciples and the disciples of the Pharisees fast, but your disciples do not fast?” <sup>19</sup>And Jesus said to them, “Can the wedding guests fast while the bridegroom is with them? As long as they have the bridegroom with them, they cannot fast. <sup>20</sup>The days will come when the bridegroom is taken away from them, and then they will fast in that day. <sup>21</sup>No one sews a piece of unshrunk cloth on an old garment. If he does, the patch tears away from it, the new from the old, and a worse tear is made. <sup>22</sup>And no one puts new wine into old wineskins. If he does, the wine will burst the skins—and the wine is destroyed, and so are the skins. But new wine is for fresh wineskins.” <sup>23</sup>One Sabbath he was going through the grainfields, and as they made their way, his disciples began to pluck heads of grain. <sup>24</sup>And the Pharisees were saying to him, “Look, why are they doing what is not lawful on the Sabbath?” <sup>25</sup>And he said to them, “Have you never read what David did, when he was in need and was hungry, he and those who were with him: <sup>26</sup>how he entered the house of God, in the time of Abiathar the high priest, and ate the bread of the Presence, which it is not lawful for any but the priests to eat, and also gave it to those who were with him?” <sup>27</sup>And he said to them, “The Sabbath was made for man, not man for the Sabbath. <sup>28</sup>So the Son of Man is lord even of the Sabbath.”
2.overview:
Chapter 2 is the first gathering storm. Four episodes — the paralytic, the call of Levi and the dinner with sinners, the question about fasting, and the grain plucked on the Sabbath — form a sustained controversy sequence in which the question of Jesus's authority escalates from Who can forgive sins? to Why does he eat with tax collectors and sinners? to Why do John's disciples and the disciples of the Pharisees fast, but your disciples do not fast? to Why are they doing what is not lawful on the Sabbath? Each is a deeper probe of who this man thinks he is and by what right he does what he does. Read straight on into 3:6, where the Pharisees go out and take counsel how to destroy him, and you can watch a decision being reached. The shadow of the cross falls across this Gospel from chapter 2 onward.

The key that unlocks the chapter is the sentence Jesus speaks over the paralytic: Son, your sins are forgiven. The scribes immediately and correctly identify it as a claim to a divine prerogative — Who can forgive sins but God alone? Their premise is right; their conclusion about him is wrong. He is not blaspheming. The miracle that follows is the public receipt for the invisible claim, offered in terms Jesus himself set in advance.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–12 — The Paralytic and the Authority to Forgive
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The room (vv. 1–2). Jesus comes back to Capernaum and the town finds out within hours. The house fills, the doorway fills, the street outside the doorway fills — and Mark ends the sentence not with healing but with preaching. Whatever the crowd came for, what it got was the word.

The roof (vv. 3–4). Four men carry a fifth through the streets, find the door impassable, climb the outside stair, and dig through a mud-and-branch roof over the head of the preacher. Mark does not tell us their names, their theology, or whose ceiling it was.

The sentence nobody expected (vv. 5–7). Jesus looks at a paralysed man and speaks about his sins. The scribes say nothing aloud and think something precise: only God forgives sins, therefore this is blasphemy. Their premise is right out of Isaiah. Their conclusion about the man in front of them is the error the whole Gospel exists to correct.

The proof (vv. 8–12). Jesus answers the unspoken thought, stakes an invisible claim on a visible test, and the man walks home carrying the bed that carried him.
verseByVerse.theology:
This is the first place in Mark where Jesus does something that belongs to God alone, and it is worth being clear about why the scribes reacted as they did. A priest could pronounce a man clean; a prophet could announce that God had forgiven; a rabbi could teach the way of repentance. Nobody in Israel forgave sins in the first person. When God says I, I am he who blots out your transgressions for my own sake (Isa. 43:25), the doubled pronoun is the whole point — pardon is his own act, not a delegated one.

So the scribes are not being obtuse. They have correctly identified that the man in the room has done something only the God of Israel does, and they draw the only conclusion their categories allow. Mark lets their logic stand unchallenged, because he intends the reader to run it to the end: if the premise is true and Jesus is not blaspheming, there is exactly one thing left that he can be.

Note also where the forgiveness happens. Not in the temple, ninety miles south, through a priest and a lamb. On earth (v. 10) — in a crowded fishing-village house, from the mouth of a carpenter, to a man who had not brought a sacrifice.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: four men digging through someone else's roof because the door was blocked by people who had come to hear Jesus. The obstacle was not his enemies; it was the crowd around him.

Now: the friend or parent who keeps carrying a name to God when the person attached to it will not come — who has been carrying it for years, and has watched the door stay shut. Mark records that Jesus saw their faith, and did not ask the man on the mat for a statement first.

There is a warning folded into the same scene. The people blocking the door were not opponents. They were admirers who had got there early and would not move. It is possible to be so close to Jesus, and so pleased to be close, that you become the reason somebody else cannot reach him. The four went over the top of that crowd, and the crowd got a shower of dried mud for its trouble.

verseByVerse.quote: And when he returned to Capernaum after some days, it was reported that he was at home. And many were gathered together, so that there was no more room, not even at the door. And he was preaching the word to them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When Jesus returned to Capernaum some days later, word spread that he was at home. So many people gathered that there was no room left, not even at the door, and he was preaching the word to them.

Meaning first. Mark 2 sets the authority of Jesus against the religious leaders. He forgives a paralysed man’s sins and proves it by making him walk, doing what only God can do. He calls Levi, a despised tax collector, and eats with sinners, because he came as a doctor for the sick. He says his disciples do not fast because the bridegroom is with them, a title that belongs to God, and that his new life cannot be patched onto old religion. And he defends his hungry disciples on the Sabbath and claims to be its Lord. In every scene the question is Mark’s first one, who is this, and the answer keeps coming back larger than anyone expected, and full of mercy.

The connection. Mark 2:1–3:6 is a series of five conflict stories in which Jesus is challenged by the religious leaders: over forgiving sins (2:1–12), eating with sinners (2:13–17), fasting (2:18–22), and the Sabbath (2:23–28; 3:1–6). Each reveals more of who Jesus is, and the opposition grows from silent questioning to open plotting, until the leaders agree to destroy him (3:6).

And when he returned to Capernaum after some days. After his preaching tour of Galilee (1:39). And Mark has just told us why there was a gap. At the end of chapter 1 the healed leper spread the news so widely that Jesus could no longer openly enter a town (1:45). He had been driven into the countryside by his own success. Coming back to Capernaum was a deliberate return, and the town found out in hours.

It was reported that he was at home. Probably Peter’s house (1:29). Capernaum was a fishing village of perhaps fifteen hundred people, with single-storey houses of black basalt round a courtyard, roofed with beams, branches and packed mud; a family room might be eighteen feet square. Archaeologists have dug up a house a few steps from the synagogue that Christians venerated as Peter’s within a couple of generations. That is probably the address Mark means when he writes, with no ceremony at all, that he was at home. The Son of God, in this Gospel, does not have a headquarters. He has a friend’s spare room.

And many were gathered together, so that there was no more room, not even at the door. The room, the doorway and the courtyard are packed, and people in the street crane at a window slot. This is why the four could not get near, and it is worth being honest about who was in the way. Not the authorities, not enemies. People who had come to hear Jesus, had arrived first, and were not moving.

And he was preaching the word to them. Mark saves this clause for last, and most readers skip it. The crowd has come because of a demon silenced, a fever broken, a leper touched, and what Jesus is doing when they arrive is talking. The word is the message of the kingdom (1:15), and the miracles were never the ministry; they were its credentials. But this preaching is like no other. The voice filling Peter’s front room is the voice that said let there be light, and within the hour it will forgive a man’s sins and stand him on his feet. When Jesus preaches, the word does what it says.

Is my faith fake if I first came to Jesus because I wanted help with a problem? No. Many came to him first for healing, and he received them. The four friends who brought a paralysed man to this very house came for legs, and he gave them more. What matters is where your coming leads. If you came for help and stayed for Christ himself, that is the ordinary story of countless believers. The danger is only in never moving past the problem: wanting Jesus as a means to something else rather than as the one worth having even if the problem stays.

In a sentence. Back in Capernaum, Jesus preached the word to a crowd so large that it filled the house and blocked the door.

On a Tuesday. Try the test the chapter is quietly running on the crowd. Suppose the healing you are waiting for never comes, and what remains is a Person who speaks and asks to be believed. Would you still have made the walk to the door? People crowd to Jesus for many reasons. Make sure you come to him for his word. And if you are a regular in the crowded room, notice whether anyone is being kept outside because those already inside are comfortable where they are.

For worship. The Lord of glory came back to a fishing village and sat in a borrowed room, and the first thing he gave the crowd was his word. He did not make himself scarce or charge for admission. He opened his mouth and taught them, as he still does wherever his word is preached. The house was too small for the people who came, and he was too great for the house, and yet he was content to be there, at home among his friends.
verseByVerse.note: “At home” probably means Peter’s house in Capernaum (1:29).

verseByVerse.quote: And they came, bringing to him a paralytic carried by four men. And when they could not get near him because of the crowd, they removed the roof above him, and when they had made an opening, they let down the bed on which the paralytic lay.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Four men came carrying a paralysed man on a mat. Unable to get near Jesus because of the crowd, they removed the roof above him, dug through it, and let down the mat on which the paralysed man lay.

And they came, bringing to him a paralytic carried by four men. Only Mark mentions that there were four, one at each corner of the mat. The man could not come on his own. The bed is not a bed frame but a poor man’s pallet, a mat you could roll and carry. His whole world was a piece of quilted matting and four friends. They are never named. They say nothing in the entire episode. They do not appear again in Scripture. When the crowd blocked the door, most people would have given up. Their whole recorded contribution to the kingdom of God is that they would not accept a blocked door.

They removed the roof above him, and when they had made an opening, they let down the bed on which the paralytic lay. Houses had flat roofs, reached by an outside staircase, because the roof was usable space: you dried figs on it and slept on it in summer. It was beams of rough timber, branches and reed matting, and a thick layer of mud and straw rolled flat on top. What they did next was not repairable in an afternoon. Mark’s words are blunt: literally they unroofed the roof, and dug it out. Mud, straw and matting came down in a shower on a packed room, and then a man on ropes. Luke, writing for readers who lived in Greek cities, translates the scene into tiles (Luke 5:19); Mark, closer to the ground, gives you the dirt. It was bold, inventive, costly and disruptive.

Whose roof? If this is Peter’s house, then a man who had just left his nets to follow Jesus watched his own ceiling come down into his own front room, and Peter, telling the story to Mark, would have remembered it. Mark records not one word of complaint from anybody. There was a man outside who needed to get in. The roof was only a roof.

The one beneath the hole. Nobody digs through a roof for a lecture. These four were not gambling on a teacher. They had seen the town crowd Simon’s door at sunset, and a leper walk back into Capernaum clean, and they were sure of two things: that this man could, and that this man would. Their whole wild effort is a confession of who Jesus is, faith that will not be stopped and love for a friend who cannot help himself. And it was not misplaced. There is one door in the world that is never finally blocked, because the one behind it has promised that whoever comes to him he will never cast out (John 6:37). Friends can carry a man to the edge. Only Christ can deal with what is lying on the mat.

What does carrying someone to Jesus look like today? Mostly ordinary things done stubbornly. Praying for someone by name, for years if necessary. Inviting them to church and offering to drive them there and sit with them. Reading a Gospel with them. Meeting a practical need so that a barrier comes down: the childcare, the lift, the meal. Bringing them into your home among other believers. Sometimes it means removing obstacles that Christians themselves have put up, like jargon, unfriendliness or a church that is hard for an outsider to enter. You cannot make anyone believe, but you can get them to the place where Jesus speaks.

In a sentence. When four men could not get their paralysed friend through the crowd, they dug through the roof and lowered him to Jesus.

On a Tuesday. Whom could you carry to Jesus: in prayer, by inviting them, by helping them past obstacles? Be one of the four. And ask what you would let be damaged to get one person in front of Christ: your dignity, your schedule, your carefully managed reputation as a reasonable person. Friends like these are usually one of three or four. Who would be the other three with you?

For worship. The Lord did not rebuke the hole in the roof. He looked up through the falling dust and saw faith, and he loved it. He had come down from a far greater height than any ceiling to reach people who could not reach him, and he is glad, still, to be interrupted by the desperate. The mat came down on four ropes. The mercy had come down from heaven long before, and it was waiting on the floor to meet him.
verseByVerse.note: Houses had flat roofs of beams covered with branches and packed clay, reached by an outside stair. An opening could be dug through and repaired.

verseByVerse.quote: And when Jesus saw their faith, he said to the paralytic, "Son, your sins are forgiven."
verseByVerse.commentary:
When Jesus saw their faith, he said to the paralysed man: son, your sins are forgiven.

And when Jesus saw their faith. Their faith was visible in their action. Faith in Scripture is not a private feeling; it climbs stairs and digs through roofs. And their faith: the four friends, and probably the man himself, though Mark tells us nothing of what he believed. What Jesus saw and honoured above all was the faith of the men on the roof.

Can my faith do for someone else what these four did for their friend? Yes and no, and both halves matter. Yes: your faith can carry a person to the place where Jesus is, and that is precisely what intercession does. You can bring them, again and again, under the preached word and into the company of his people, and refuse to accept that the case is closed. And no: the man did not stay a spectator of his own healing. He heard your sins are forgiven, and he rose and walked. No one was forgiven in his place, and no one repented for him. Each must finally meet Christ himself. So your part is the roof and the ropes; the rising is God’s to give and theirs to receive. Many a believer walking with Christ today was once only a name on somebody’s stubborn, seemingly unanswered prayer list. Do not stop digging.

He said to the paralytic, “Son, your sins are forgiven”. Unexpected. Everyone expected him to say, Get up and walk. Instead Jesus addresses the man’s deepest need. Son is literally child (teknon), a warm, domestic word, the word a father uses. The man has been lowered into a room full of strangers and religious professionals, filthy from the ceiling, at the centre of everyone’s attention, and the first word spoken to him is a family word. Before anything is said about his sins or his legs, he is told where he stands. And are forgiven is present tense: it is happening now, on Jesus’ word.

Why this, and not the legs? The legs are what everyone in the room is looking at. Jesus saw the ruined man, not only the ruined body, and went first to his greatest need. Paralysis would end at death; unforgiven sin would last for ever. A paralytic who walked home that afternoon and died unforgiven would still be lost; one forgiven and carried on that mat to the end of his life would be eternally safe. Jesus will heal the legs to prove that he has dealt with the soul, but he leaves nobody in doubt about which was the emergency. He begins where you would not have begun, with the thing you were not asking about, because he is treating you as a man and not as a case.

Sin and sickness. Was his paralysis caused by a particular sin? Not necessarily. Scripture is careful here. Sometimes suffering is tied to a specific sin: Jesus tells another healed man to sin no more, that nothing worse may happen to him (John 5:14). Very often it is not at all: of the man born blind Jesus says it was not that this man sinned, or his parents (John 9:1–3). But all sickness belongs to a world broken by sin. Jesus deals with the root first.

What it does not mean. Not that the friends’ faith saved the man apart from his own faith. But Jesus honoured the faith of those who brought him. Intercession matters.

How can I know that my sins are forgiven? In the same way this man did: by Jesus’ word. He did not feel forgiven first and then believe it; he was told, and the healing confirmed it. Your confirmation is greater than his legs, because you know the cross and the empty tomb. God promises that everyone who believes in Christ is forgiven and has peace with him (Acts 10:43; Romans 5:1), and that if we confess our sins he is faithful and just to forgive us (1 John 1:9). Feelings come and go. Rest your assurance on what he has said and on what Christ has done, not on how you feel this morning.

In a sentence. Seeing their faith, Jesus first met the man’s deepest need, telling him his sins were forgiven.

On a Tuesday. Your deepest need is not your circumstances, but forgiveness. Have you received it from Jesus? Write down the things you are most anxious about this week. Then ask how many of them would still matter in a hundred years, and set beside them the one thing that will. If you are forgiven, the worst problem you have is already solved.

For worship. The first word he spoke to a filthy, helpless man in front of the whole village was child. And the second was the word every human being most needs to hear and no human being can say on God’s behalf: your sins are forgiven. He said it on his own authority, because it was his to give, and he would pay for it himself. Blessed is the one whose transgression is forgiven, whose sin is covered, and blessed is the Saviour who says so and makes it true.
verseByVerse.note: “Son” is a warm address, like “my child.”

verseByVerse.quote: Now some of the scribes were sitting there, questioning in their hearts, "Why does this man speak like that? He is blaspheming! Who can forgive sins but God alone?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Some of the scribes sitting there questioned in their hearts: why does this man speak like that? He is blaspheming! Who can forgive sins but God alone?

Now some of the scribes were sitting there. Experts in the law, perhaps sent to investigate this new teacher. Seated, while others stood, which in that culture is the posture of the qualified man, the one who has come to assess rather than to listen.

Questioning in their hearts. Silently. Nobody has said a word. The whole exchange that follows begins as an argument that was never spoken aloud.

Why does this man speak like that? He is blaspheming! Blasphemy means speaking against God or claiming for oneself what belongs to God alone. It was punishable by death by stoning (Leviticus 24:16). Fix the word in your mind, because it is a death sentence, and it lands in chapter 2. When Mark reaches the night trial, the high priest tears his garments and says, You have heard his blasphemy, and they all condemn him as deserving death (14:63–64). The verdict that kills Jesus is reached, silently, in a crowded front room in Capernaum, twelve chapters before it is carried out. Everything in between is the trial.

Who can forgive sins but God alone? They were right. The scribes in this room are not fools and they are not straw men; they know their Bible. A person can forgive wrongs done to himself, but all sin is ultimately against God (Psalm 51:4), and only God can forgive it. I, I am he who blots out your transgressions for my own sake (Isaiah 43:25), and the doubled pronoun is the whole force of it. A priest could declare a leper clean and a prophet could announce God’s pardon, but none of them ever stood in front of a man and forgave him. Nor was this something anyone expected the Messiah to do. Israel hoped for a king who would reign and drive out the Romans; no known Jewish writing before Jesus has the Messiah forgiving sins in his own name. This is a category the hope did not contain.

No third option. Run the scribes’ logic honestly, because Mark wants you to. Their first premise is true: only God forgives sins. Their second premise is true: this man has just forgiven sins. Either Jesus is blaspheming, or he is God. There is no third option. What has never been available, whatever the century decides to say about him, is the comfortable middle position that he was a fine moral teacher who would be appalled at what his followers made of him. Fine moral teachers do not do this. The scribes’ theology was correct; their conclusion about Jesus was wrong.

Did Jesus ever actually claim to be God? Yes, and often in exactly this way: not by announcing a doctrine but by doing what only God does and accepting what only God receives. He forgives sins against others as if he were the one offended. He reads hearts (v. 8). He calls himself the bridegroom of God’s people (v. 19) and lord of the Sabbath God gave (v. 28). He stills storms with a word (4:39). Elsewhere he says that before Abraham was, I am (John 8:58), and accepts Thomas’s worship, my Lord and my God (John 20:28). His enemies understood the claim perfectly. That is why they called it blasphemy.

In a sentence. The scribes silently accused Jesus of blasphemy, rightly reasoning that only God can forgive sins.

On a Tuesday. The scribes were right about God and wrong about Jesus. They had the doctrine of divine pardon perfectly in place, and it was the very shelf on which they filed him as an enemy. It is entirely possible to hold every article of the faith correctly and be undone by the Person the articles are about. Before you enjoy their mistake too much, ask whether your settled convictions about how God works have room in them for God turning up and working. The scribes saw the issue clearly: only God forgives. Who do you say Jesus is?

For worship. Every sin we have committed was finally against God, and so only God could cancel it, and the cancelling has now been done face to face. The pardon Isaiah heard God speak, I, I am he, was spoken aloud in a fishing village by a man you could touch, with dirt from the roof still on the floor. The theologians in the room had every premise and missed the Person. We bow to him: the Son who forgives as only the offended God can, because he is that God, and every offence was against him.
verseByVerse.note: Blasphemy is speaking against God or claiming what belongs to him alone.

parallels.desc: the same charge at his trial

verseByVerse.quote: And immediately Jesus, perceiving in his spirit that they thus questioned within themselves, said to them, "Why do you question these things in your hearts? Which is easier, to say to the paralytic, 'Your sins are forgiven,' or to say, 'Rise, take up your bed and walk'?
verseByVerse.commentary:
Immediately Jesus, knowing in his spirit what they were thinking, said to them: why do you question these things in your hearts? Which is easier, to say to the paralysed man, your sins are forgiven, or to say, rise, take up your bed and walk?

And immediately Jesus, perceiving in his spirit that they thus questioned within themselves. Before Jesus answers the objection, he demonstrates something nobody in the room stops to comment on: he answers an objection that was never spoken. The scribes have not moved a muscle. He reads the silence. Only God knows the heart. Solomon, dedicating the temple, prayed to the God who alone can do that: you, you only, know the hearts of all the children of mankind (1 Kings 8:39). The heart is deceitful above all things, says Jeremiah, and who can understand it? And God answers: I the LORD search the heart (Jeremiah 17:9–10; 1 Samuel 16:7). So two divine prerogatives are exercised in ninety seconds, forgiving sin and reading the heart, and the men best equipped to notice are the ones being read.

Why do you question these things in your hearts? He brings their hidden thoughts into the open, not to shame them but to answer them.

Which is easier. A clever question, and not the trick it first appears. Easier to say: that is the exact wording, and it decides the whole argument. To say your sins are forgiven is the easy sentence, because nothing in the visible world changes when you say it. There is no test. A charlatan could say it in every village in Galilee for a decade and never be caught. To say rise and walk is the hard sentence, because it is checkable in about four seconds in front of a packed room, and if the man does not move you are finished. Every religious fraud in history has preferred claims that cannot be tested. But to actually do either requires the power of God.

The reverse of a fraud. So Jesus does the opposite of what a fraud does. He deliberately hangs the invisible claim on a visible, immediate, public test, and tells the room in advance that this is what he is doing. He is not hiding behind mystery. He is inviting verification. That instinct runs right through the faith. Paul does not tell the Corinthians to have an experience. He says that if Christ has not been raised, our preaching is in vain and your faith is in vain and you are still in your sins (1 Corinthians 15:14, 17), and he lists the surviving eyewitnesses and in effect invites the reader to go and ask them. Christianity has always staked itself on things that happened in public.

Is my faith only a feeling, then? It should not be. A fair question to put to yourself is what your faith actually rests on. If the honest answer is a mood or an experience that nothing could ever touch, it may be more fragile than you think. Christian faith rests on facts that are public and historical: a man who lived, died under Pontius Pilate, was buried and rose bodily on the third day, seen by many witnesses. Feelings are good gifts, but they are the weather; the facts are the ground. Read the Gospels as the testimony they claim to be, and let your trust stand on what God has done.

In a sentence. Jesus read the scribes’ thoughts and asked which is easier to say: your sins are forgiven, or get up and walk.

On a Tuesday. Jesus knows your thoughts, including the ones you would never say aloud in church. That is a warning against secret sin and a comfort in secret pain. Name one thought you have been nursing privately, a grudge, a doubt, a fear, and bring it to him in words, since he already knows it. There is relief in being known by the one who forgives.

For worship. Nothing is hidden from him. He looked into the silence of the scribes and read every thought, as he reads ours. And the one who knows the worst about us is the same one who says, your sins are forgiven. He does not need to be persuaded of our guilt; he has seen it all. He forgives with his eyes open, and that is why his forgiveness can be trusted.

verseByVerse.quote: But that you may know that the Son of Man has authority on earth to forgive sins"—he said to the paralytic— "I say to you, rise, pick up your bed, and go home."
verseByVerse.commentary:
But so that you may know that the Son of Man has authority on earth to forgive sins, he said to the paralysed man: I say to you, rise, pick up your bed and go home.

But that you may know. The visible healing will prove the invisible forgiveness. Read the sentence and notice that it breaks in half. Jesus is speaking to the scribes, and then mid-argument Mark inserts a stage direction: he said to the paralytic. The dashes in your Bible mark the swivel. The theological point is aimed at the professionals; the command is aimed at the man on the floor. Jesus never finishes the sentence to the scribes. The finish is the man standing up.

That the Son of Man has authority on earth to forgive sins. This is the first time in Mark that Jesus names himself, and it is his favourite name for himself all the way to the cross. In ordinary Aramaic the phrase could mean simply a human being, but Jesus is reaching for something enormous. It comes from Daniel 7, where the prophet watches thrones set in place and the Ancient of Days taking his seat, and then sees one like a son of man coming with the clouds of heaven, presented before God, and given dominion and glory and a kingdom, so that all peoples and nations should serve him, an everlasting dominion that shall not pass away (Daniel 7:13–14). In the Old Testament the one who rides the clouds is God. Daniel sees a figure who is truly human and is given what belongs to God, and Jesus puts that figure on. Before Mark is finished, this name will carry both his throne and his cross: the Son of Man came not to be served but to serve, and to give his life as a ransom for many (10:45).

On earth. Two small words, and they relocate the whole apparatus of pardon. Not in heaven, at some judgment after you die, where you will find out how it went. Not ninety miles south in Jerusalem, through a priest and a lamb and a curtain and a fee. Here, on the ground, in a fishing village, in a room with mud on the floor, from the mouth of a man you could touch, to somebody who had brought no sacrifice and could not have carried one if he had. God’s heavenly authority to forgive is now exercised on earth, in person, by Jesus.

I say to you, rise, pick up your bed, and go home. Three commands, all impossible for a paralysed man. Carrying his own mat would show the healing was complete. And the third command is the tender one. He is not sent to the temple, or to a rabbi, or on a lap of the town to prove it. He is sent home, and somebody there, a wife, a mother, children who had learned to step around a mat on the floor, is about to look up and see him standing in the doorway on his own legs, carrying the thing that carried him. That is the shape of everything this Man does. He does not merely repair you and leave you standing in the road. He sends you home.

What it does not mean. Not that church leaders today have authority in themselves to forgive sins. They declare Christ’s forgiveness to those who repent and believe (John 20:23; 2 Corinthians 5:18–20), but the authority is his.

Should I confess my sins to a pastor or priest to be forgiven? You do not need anyone but Christ to stand between you and God. There is one mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus (1 Timothy 2:5), and you may go to him directly, any time, and be forgiven. Scripture does also tell believers to confess their sins to one another and pray for one another (James 5:16), and there is great help in telling a trusted, mature Christian about a sin you are fighting. They cannot absolve you, but they can pray for you, hold you to account and remind you of the gospel. That is a mercy, not a requirement for forgiveness.

In a sentence. To prove he had authority on earth to forgive sins, Jesus commanded the paralysed man to get up, take his mat and go home.

On a Tuesday. Jesus has authority to forgive your sins. His word is as reliable as that man’s walking legs. If there is something you keep confessing because you do not believe it has really been forgiven, take this verse as the receipt. And think of the home he has sent you back to. Go into it today as someone forgiven, and let that change the way you speak to the people there.

For worship. The Son of Man of Daniel’s vision, given an everlasting kingdom by the Ancient of Days, used his authority on a Galilean afternoon to forgive a paralysed man and send him home. All authority in heaven and on earth is his, and he spends it on mercy. One day he will come on the clouds, and the nations will serve him. Today he forgives on earth, and the forgiven walk home under his authority as surely as they will one day stand before his throne.
verseByVerse.note: “Son of Man” is Jesus’ favourite title for himself.

parallels.desc: one like a son of man receives everlasting dominion

verseByVerse.quote: And he rose and immediately picked up his bed and went out before them all, so that they were all amazed and glorified God, saying, "We never saw anything like this!"
verseByVerse.commentary:
The man got up, immediately picked up his mat and walked out in front of them all. Everyone was amazed and glorified God, saying: we never saw anything like this!

And he rose and immediately picked up his bed and went out before them all. Immediately: no convalescence, no weeks of learning to walk. The command and the walking are the same instant, because the authority behind the command does not have to wait for nature to catch up. And before them all: the healing is not done quietly in a back room and reported afterwards. Jesus staked a claim on a public test, and the test is settled publicly, in front of the very scribes who had silently convicted him.
