The crowd that had blocked his way in now parted to let him walk out, carrying the mat that had carried him. What had been the emblem of his helplessness went home over his shoulder as evidence.

So that they were all amazed and glorified God. Praise to God, the right response, and better than the scribes managed.

We never saw anything like this! So the crowd said, and something new had come: God’s forgiveness and God’s healing power, present in a man. But weigh the crowd’s verdict carefully, because Mark has put it there for weighing. Read what they say, and then read what they do not say. Not one person in that room says: then the other thing he said must be true as well. Nobody says, if he can do that to a man’s legs with a word, what has he just done to a man’s guilt, and could he do it for me? They had been handed the proof, in the terms Jesus himself set, and their astonishment stopped at the miracle and never reached the thing the miracle was for.

Is it wrong to pray about my circumstances rather than my soul? No. The four friends asked about the legs, and Jesus did not scold them. God invites us to bring him everything, including health, money, work and family (Philippians 4:6). The danger is only when the whole list is legs: when we want him for what he might fix and never once come to him for what he came to forgive. A great deal of modern praying is exactly this. We ask him about the legs. He is waiting to talk about the sins. Ask for both, and put them in his order.

In a sentence. The healed man walked out carrying his mat, and the crowd praised God, saying they had never seen anything like it.

On a Tuesday. Run the honest inventory. Think of the last five things you asked God for. How many were about circumstances, and how many were about your soul: your sin, your love for him, your holiness, your usefulness? If the whole list is legs, you have understood him about as well as the crowd did, and they went home amazed and unforgiven. The man on the mat got both, and only one of them was still with him fifty years later.

For worship. Nobody had seen anything like it, because nothing like him had ever walked the earth. In one afternoon he spoke a pardon no one could see and backed it with legs everyone could, and a paralysed sinner went out through the parted crowd pardoned and whole. Glory to God, who in Jesus forgives all our iniquity and heals all our diseases, redeems our life from the pit and crowns us with steadfast love and mercy. The man had his legs for forty or fifty years. The pardon he walked out with, he has still.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 13–22 — Levi, Sinners, and New Wine
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Out again (vv. 13–14). Jesus leaves the house, teaches by the lake, and walks past a customs post. Sitting in it is Levi son of Alphaeus, a Jew collecting money for the occupying power, and the two words Follow me end his career in the time it takes to say them.

The dinner (vv. 15–17). Levi's first recorded act as a disciple is to throw a party for his own disreputable network and put Jesus at the centre of it. The scribes of the Pharisees do not challenge Jesus; they go at him through his followers. His answer is one sentence about a doctor, and it sorts the human race into two categories with no third.

The fasting question (vv. 18–20). Why do John's disciples fast and yours do not? Jesus answers with a wedding, quietly takes for himself a role the Old Testament gives to God alone, and in the same breath drops the first shadow of the cross into the Gospel.

Cloth and wineskins (vv. 21–22). Two pictures from ordinary domestic life make one uncomfortable point: what he has brought cannot be sewn onto what you already have.
verseByVerse.theology:
The two little parables of vv. 21–22 are the theological hinge of the chapter, and they are more radical than they look. An unshrunk patch on an old garment does not merely fail; when it is first washed it shrinks, grips, and pulls away, and the tear is worse than it was before the repair. New wine still working gives off gas; a skin that has already stretched once and gone brittle will split. In both pictures the old thing is not attacked. It is simply asked to contain something it was never built to hold, and it fails.

Jesus is not offering a reformed Judaism, and he is not offering a reformed you. Religion, as everyone naturally practises it, is patchwork — an addition to a self that stays fundamentally in charge. That, he says, does not produce a better garment; it produces a worse tear, which is exactly why adding a little Christianity to an unchanged life so often makes a person more miserable rather than less.

And then the promise at the end, which is easy to read past: new wine is for fresh wineskins. He supplies the skin as well as the wine. I will give you a new heart, and a new spirit I will put within you (Ezek. 36:26); if anyone is in Christ, he is a new creation (2 Cor. 5:17). He did not come to mend you. That is worse news, and far better news, than mending.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Levi cannot yet explain a doctrine, so he cooks. He gathers the only people he knows — the ones no synagogue wanted — and gets them into a room with Jesus.

Now: the newest Christian in your church, six weeks old in the faith, still knows every person from the old life; the man who has been converted thirty years often knows nobody outside the church at all. Levi's method needs no training course. Buy the food, make the call, and be in the room.

The harder half of the example is the one people skip. Jesus went to that table as the physician, not as a patient, and nobody left it unchanged — Levi, who had already left his booth to follow him, did not go back, and the meal did not end with Jesus agreeing with the guests. Both errors are live. One keeps a safe distance and calls it holiness; the other sits down at every table, says nothing about Christ for fifteen years, and calls it grace. The Pharisees would not go in. Jesus went in, and went in as himself.

verseByVerse.quote: He went out again beside the sea, and all the crowd was coming to him, and he was teaching them. And as he passed by, he saw Levi the son of Alphaeus sitting at the tax booth, and he said to him, "Follow me." And he rose and followed him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus went out again beside the lake. The whole crowd came to him, and he taught them. As he passed by, he saw Levi the son of Alphaeus sitting at the tax booth, and said to him: follow me. And he rose and followed him.

He went out again beside the sea, and all the crowd was coming to him, and he was teaching them. Teaching remains his priority. He has just done the most spectacular thing yet seen in Capernaum, and his response to a full house is to go outside and walk along the shore. As he walks he passes a customs post, and the whole chapter turns.

And as he passed by, he saw Levi the son of Alphaeus sitting at the tax booth. Levi is called Matthew in the first Gospel (Matthew 9:9; 10:3), and it is a fair guess that Levi was the name he was born with and Matthew the name he carried afterwards. Mark, writing about him, uses the old name. Matthew, writing about himself, uses the new one and adds the words the tax collector to his own name in the list of apostles, which nobody else does. A forgiven man is not embarrassed by his file. His tax booth was probably on the main road near Capernaum, the road from Damascus to the Mediterranean, collecting customs on goods passing between the territories of Herod Antipas and Philip. A booth on a border like that was a licence to print money.

Tax collectors. Understand how the system worked and you understand the loathing. The collector bid for the contract, paid the authorities up front, and lived on whatever he could extract above that figure. What he said you owed, backed by soldiers, was what you owed. Tax collectors were despised for serving the ruling powers, for cheating, and for contact with Gentiles that made them ritually unclean. They were classed with sinners and prostitutes and could not serve as witnesses in court; rabbinic rules even forbade taking alms from their money. A tax collector was a thief with legal cover and a collaborator, a Jew making his living off the occupation of his own country.

Beyond repair. And there was worse, which the crowd would have felt without needing it explained. The road back for a thief ran through restitution: you repaid what you took, and added a fifth (Leviticus 6:5; Numbers 5:7). A tax collector could not do it. He had defrauded hundreds of people over years and kept no list of who they were. His repentance looked, to his own religion, impossible. He was in a class of men widely regarded as beyond saving. That is the man Jesus stops for.

The debt he could not pay. Levi’s religion could see no way home for him, and it was right that he could not pay his own way. But the one who stopped at the booth had come to settle an account no tax collector could ever settle. The debt Levi owed to God, larger than everything he had taken from his neighbours, would be met by the man now calling him, who came to give his life as a ransom for many (10:45). God has cancelled the record of debt that stood against us, setting it aside by nailing it to the cross (Colossians 2:14). Levi made out other men’s bills for a living. Christ came to pay his.

And he said to him, “Follow me”. The same call as to the fishermen (1:17). Two words. No interview, no probation, no conditions, no requirement that he first put anything right. Jesus calls a man everyone else despised.

And he rose and followed him. Weigh what it cost against what it cost the fishermen. Peter and Andrew left their nets, and the nets were still there; after the crucifixion they went straight back to them for a night (John 21:3). A fisherman could go back to fishing. Levi stood up from a booth that somebody else would be sitting in by the afternoon. There was no going back to that job, ever, and everyone in Capernaum knew it. He gave up a profitable career, and his was the one call in the Gospel that could not be reversed. He made it without asking a single question.

If I become a Christian, must I leave a job that is morally compromised? It depends on what makes it compromised. Collecting taxes was not itself sinful; John the Baptist told tax collectors to collect no more than they were authorised to (Luke 3:12–13), and Paul tells Christians to pay taxes (Romans 13:6–7). What had to stop was the fraud. When Zacchaeus met Jesus he gave half his goods to the poor and repaid fourfold anyone he had cheated (Luke 19:8). So if your work requires you to lie, cheat or sin, you must stop doing those things, even if it costs you the job. If the work is lawful but your practice in it has been crooked, change the practice, put right what you can, and serve Christ there. Ask a wise pastor to help you think it through.

In a sentence. Jesus called Levi, a despised tax collector, from his booth, and he got up and followed him.

On a Tuesday. No one is too compromised for Jesus to call. Who have you written off: a relative, a colleague, a public figure you despise? Pray for them by name this week. And if you have ever privately concluded that you yourself have gone too far, been at it too long, done the kind of damage that cannot be undone or repaid, look hard at who is sitting in that booth. The man Jesus chose for the apostolic band, and for the writing of a Gospel, was the one man in town whose religion had already given up on him.

For worship. The Lord walked past every respectable house in Capernaum and stopped at the one booth no one else would approach. He looked at a man his whole nation had written off and said, follow me, and made him an apostle and a Gospel writer. That is the grace of God in Christ: it does not wait for us to make ourselves acceptable; it calls us, and the call makes us new. The man who once wrote out other people’s debts now writes, in the first book of the New Testament, the record of the King who paid his.
verseByVerse.note: Tax collectors gathered tolls for the ruling authorities and were widely despised as collaborators and cheats.

verseByVerse.quote: And as he reclined at table in his house, many tax collectors and sinners were reclining with Jesus and his disciples, for there were many who followed him. And the scribes of the Pharisees, when they saw that he was eating with sinners and tax collectors, said to his disciples, "Why does he eat with tax collectors and sinners?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
As Jesus reclined at table in Levi’s house, many tax collectors and sinners were eating with him and his disciples, for there were many who followed him. When the scribes of the Pharisees saw him eating with sinners and tax collectors, they asked his disciples: why does he eat with tax collectors and sinners?

And as he reclined at table in his house. Levi’s house. Levi’s first act as a disciple is to give a party: Luke tells us he made him a great feast in his house (Luke 5:29). At a formal meal guests reclined on couches round a low table, leaning on one elbow in the posture of a banquet, which meant hours.

Many tax collectors and sinners were reclining with Jesus and his disciples. The room was full of the only people Levi knew. He invited his friends: other tax collectors and sinners. The second word was not a general remark about human nature; it was almost a technical term for people known for immoral lives, or whose trade or way of life put them outside the purity rules the Pharisees kept, everyone the religious establishment had written off. And they were already moving toward him, for there were many who followed him.

Why does he eat with tax collectors and sinners? The question comes from the scribes of the Pharisees, the separated ones, a movement devoted to strict keeping of the law and its traditions, including purity rules about food and who you ate with. A modern reader has to be told why this detonated, because we eat with anybody. In that world a shared table was not a neutral social event. It meant acceptance and friendship, peace between the people at it. You did not eat with a man you regarded as unclean, because you would be saying in the most public way available that there was nothing between you. The Pharisees avoided eating with sinners to keep themselves pure. Jesus ate with them, and everybody in Capernaum could read what that said.

Said to his disciples. Note the tactic, because it is ancient and still in use. The scribes do not put the question to Jesus. They take it to his followers, who are new, unsure of their ground and easier to unsettle. If you cannot get at the leader, get at the people who follow him and make them feel foolish about the company they are keeping.

This man receives sinners. The charge is meant as an accusation, and it is the gospel. Isaiah had promised that on God’s mountain the LORD would make for all peoples a feast of rich food and well-aged wine, and swallow up death for ever (Isaiah 25:6–8). At Levi’s couches is a foretaste of it, with the host of that feast already reclining among the guests. A shared table meant peace between the people at it, and the peace Jesus offered over Levi’s food was real, because he would make it real: he came to reconcile enemies to God by the blood of his cross (Colossians 1:20). The Pharisees saw the company he kept. They did not see whose table it truly was.

How do I keep real friendships with people far from God without condemning them or signing off on everything? Jesus gives the answer by being at the table rather than drawing a line around it. But look closely at how he is there. He is not blending in and hoping not to be noticed. He is not there as a fellow patient. The host had given up his career that day, and the evening does not end with Jesus agreeing with the room. So go, eat, listen, laugh and love; and go as yourself, a follower of Christ, unashamed of him. The Pharisees would not go in at all and called it holiness; others go in and say nothing about Christ for fifteen years and call it grace. Jesus went in, and went in as himself.

How far can I join in? Join in everything that is good: the food, the friendship, the conversation, the celebration. Do not join in what is sinful: drunkenness, crude talk, gossip, cruelty. Jesus was accused of being a drunkard (Matthew 11:19), but the accusation was false. If you find that time with certain friends regularly draws you into sin rather than giving you openings for Christ, you may need to change the setting: invite them to your home, meet over coffee, or take a Christian friend with you. Bad company ruins good morals (1 Corinthians 15:33), but holy company can be the best thing that ever happened to a sinner.

In a sentence. Jesus ate with tax collectors and sinners at Levi’s house, and the Pharisees’ scribes objected.

On a Tuesday. When did you last share a meal with someone others look down on? Think of the last evening you spent among people far from God, and answer two questions honestly. Did anything about the way you were there make Christ visible, or were you simply indistinguishable? And did you go home more like them, or did any of them go home having met something in you they could not account for? Then open your diary and plan one meal this month with someone outside the church.

For worship. The Holy One reclined at a sinners’ table, and his holiness did not shrink; it spread. He was not afraid of their company, because he was not there to be changed by them but to change them. The same Lord now invites sinners to his own table, and one day he will host the marriage supper of the Lamb, where the guests will be tax collectors, prostitutes, Pharisees and pagans, all forgiven, all washed, all his.
verseByVerse.note: At a formal meal guests lay on couches around a low table, leaning on one elbow — hence “reclined.” “Sinners” here means people known for ignoring the law.

verseByVerse.quote: And when Jesus heard it, he said to them, "Those who are well have no need of a physician, but those who are sick. I came not to call the righteous, but sinners."
verseByVerse.commentary:
When Jesus heard it, he said: those who are well have no need of a doctor, but those who are sick. I came not to call the righteous, but sinners.

Those who are well have no need of a physician, but those who are sick. One sentence, and it is the whole gospel with the bark still on it. A proverb: doctors go to the sick. Jesus came as a doctor for sin-sick souls, and his holiness is not contaminated by sinners; it heals them. And do not miss the irony. He is not agreeing that the Pharisees are spiritually healthy. He is taking their own self-assessment and following it to its end: very well, if you are well, you will not want a doctor, and you will not get one. It is the gentlest and most terrible sentence in the chapter. The man who will not admit he is ill does not take the treatment; he dies of something treatable, holding the position that there is nothing wrong with him.

I came. He has said something like this before (1:38), but here he states it of his whole mission, and the words carry more than they seem to. Nobody says I came about being born. A man who says he came was somewhere before, and had business here.

Not to call the righteous, but sinners. The righteous are those who think they are righteous, like the Pharisees, and so see no need of him. In truth no one is righteous (Romans 3:10). Jesus calls those who know they are sick. Luke adds: to repentance (Luke 5:32). This is not theory; the room is the evidence. And here is what makes it good news rather than merely fair-minded: the only qualification for Christ is the disqualification. Not progress, not a clean stretch, not having got the worst of it behind you. Sickness is the entry requirement, and the ticket is the thing you have been trying to hide.

It cuts two ways. If your fear is that you are too far gone, that if the people in your church knew what was actually in your history or your head that would be the end of it, then read the sentence again slowly. He did not come for the respectable and take the odd sinner as an exception. He came to call sinners. You are not the awkward case. You are the stated purpose of the visit. But if your quiet position is that you are basically all right, decent, churchgoing, never did anybody much harm, then this verse is not a comfort and is not meant to be. There is no third category. There are the sick who know it and the sick who do not, and only one of those groups ever sends for the doctor. The Pharisees went home from Levi’s house with their reputations intact and their sins intact.

What it does not mean. Not that Jesus approved of sin, or that Christians should join in it to reach people. Jesus went among sinners as a doctor, to call them to repentance. Nor were the Pharisees truly healthy; Jesus speaks with irony.

If Jesus came for sinners, why should I try to be good? Because the doctor does not come to the sick to leave them sick. He calls sinners to repentance, and those he heals begin to get well. You do not try to be good in order to qualify for him; you could never manage that, and you do not need to. You try to be good because he has taken you on as his patient, and the medicine is working. Sin is the disease, not the freedom. Anyone who wants Christ’s forgiveness but not his healing has not understood what kind of doctor he is.

In a sentence. Jesus answered that, like a doctor going to the sick, he came to call sinners, not those who think themselves righteous.

On a Tuesday. Do you know yourself to be one of the sick whom Jesus came to heal? That is the only qualification for his call. Here is a test that takes about a minute. When did you last tell God something specific and shameful about yourself, in plain words, without softening it? Not a general admission that we all fall short, but the actual thing. A person who cannot remember doing that has not yet gone to the physician, however long he has been sitting in the waiting room.

For worship. Consider what it cost the Physician to say it. Doctors keep their distance; they wash, they wear gloves, they go home. This one came into the ward, took the disease into his own body, and died of it, so that the patients would live. By his wounds we are healed. He was not being broad-minded at Levi’s table. He was starting the treatment, and he has never lost a patient who came to him.

parallels.desc: “to seek and to save the lost”

verseByVerse.quote: Now John's disciples and the Pharisees were fasting. And people came and said to him, "Why do John's disciples and the disciples of the Pharisees fast, but your disciples do not fast?" And Jesus said to them, "Can the wedding guests fast while the bridegroom is with them? As long as they have the bridegroom with them, they cannot fast. The days will come when the bridegroom is taken away from them, and then they will fast in that day.
verseByVerse.commentary:
John’s disciples and the Pharisees were fasting. People came and asked Jesus: why do John’s disciples and the disciples of the Pharisees fast, but your disciples do not? Jesus said: can the wedding guests fast while the bridegroom is with them? The days will come when the bridegroom is taken away from them, and then they will fast in that day.

Now John’s disciples and the Pharisees were fasting. An odd alliance: the disciples of a man in camel’s hair and the strictest religious party in the country, agreeing on little else, united in bewilderment, because everybody serious fasts. Perhaps it was one of the regular fast days. The only fast required by the law was on the Day of Atonement (Leviticus 16:29), but the Pharisees fasted twice a week; the man in Jesus’ parable says so with some pride (Luke 18:12).

Why do John’s disciples and the disciples of the Pharisees fast, but your disciples do not fast? Fasting was a sign of devotion and of mourning, and by any measure of the day a teacher whose followers did not fast was not a serious teacher. Jesus’ disciples seemed less devout. It was a fair question.

Can the wedding guests fast while the bridegroom is with them? Jesus does not defend his disciples. He changes the category entirely, with a picture every person listening had stood inside. A Jewish wedding lasted up to a week, a time of feasting and joy. The phrase behind wedding guests is literally the sons of the bridechamber, the groom’s closest friends, who ran the celebration, and the rabbis themselves excused them from certain religious duties for the week, because you cannot mourn and rejoice at once. Fasting then would not be devotion; it would be sitting in the corner of a wedding feast refusing the food, with the bridegroom in the room.

Who is the bridegroom? Notice what he has just said about himself while apparently talking about lunch. In the Old Testament that role belongs to one Person, and there is no second candidate. Your Maker is your husband, the LORD of hosts is his name (Isaiah 54:5). As the bridegroom rejoices over the bride, so shall your God rejoice over you (Isaiah 62:5). I will betroth you to me forever (Hosea 2:19–20). Jesus is the bridegroom. He takes God’s role without a word of explanation, in the middle of an answer about diet. It is the second enormous claim of the chapter, and unlike the first, nobody in the room seems to have noticed. And it tells you what he thinks his own presence is: not an inspection but a wedding, the happiest week in a village’s life, food and wine and noise and a groom who cannot stop smiling.

When the bridegroom is taken away. And then, in a single clause, the light goes out of the sentence. Bridegrooms are not removed from their own weddings. Taken away suggests violent removal: this is Jesus’ first hint in Mark of his death, dropped into a cheerful answer about fasting in chapter 2, before any opponent has laid a finger on him. He knew, this early, how it ended.

And then they will fast in that day. After his departure, his disciples will fast (Acts 13:2–3; 14:23). That settles the practical question a reader is entitled to ask: are Christians meant to fast now? Jesus plainly assumed so. He did not say fasting was abolished; he said its time was coming. And when he taught about it he did not say if you fast but when you fast (Matthew 6:16–17), which is not the language of an optional extra for specialists.

What fasting is for. It is not a way of getting God’s attention or paying something off. It is a way of making the body say what the heart means: deliberately going hungry for a few hours so that a real, insistent ache reminds you, every twenty minutes, that there is a deeper hunger you have been feeding with everything except God. The stomach becomes an alarm clock. And keep the order of the two halves. We fast because the Bridegroom has been taken away and we want him back. It is not gloom. It is homesickness with a date in it.

How do I start fasting, and who should not? Start absurdly small. Miss one meal this week, tell nobody (Matthew 6:17–18), and spend the time you would have spent eating with the Bible open, praying about one specific thing. Drink water. Expect to feel hungry and irritable; that is part of the lesson. If you are pregnant or nursing, diabetic, on medication that must be taken with food, elderly and frail, or have ever struggled with an eating disorder, do not fast from food without medical advice. You can fast instead from something else, a screen, a habit, a pleasure, for the same purpose. Fasting is never a measure of your standing with God, and no one should be pressured into it.

In a sentence. Jesus explained that his disciples did not fast because the bridegroom was with them, but they would fast when he was taken away.

On a Tuesday. Is your Christian life marked by joy in Christ’s presence? Fasting has its place, but the bridegroom has come. If you have never fasted, try one missed meal this week and let the hunger do its work of reminding you what you actually want. You will learn more about your own heart in ninety minutes of that than in a month of reading about it. And if your faith has become grim, remember what Jesus said it is like to be near him: a wedding.

For worship. The LORD who called himself Israel’s husband came in person, and called himself the bridegroom. He was taken away on a Friday, violently, from his own wedding, so that his bride could be washed and made his for ever. And the wedding feast that every Jewish wedding was rehearsing has been fixed for a day that has already been named: blessed are those who are invited to the marriage supper of the Lamb (Revelation 19:9). Until then we fast a little and long a great deal, and the Bridegroom is coming.
verseByVerse.note: A wedding lasted days and was no time for fasting.

parallels.desc: the one yearly fast the law commanded
a Pharisee who fasted twice a week

verseByVerse.quote: No one sews a piece of unshrunk cloth on an old garment. If he does, the patch tears away from it, the new from the old, and a worse tear is made. And no one puts new wine into old wineskins. If he does, the wine will burst the skins—and the wine is destroyed, and so are the skins. But new wine is for fresh wineskins."
verseByVerse.commentary:
No one sews a piece of unshrunk cloth on an old garment, or the patch tears away from it, new from old, and a worse tear is made. And no one puts new wine into old wineskins, or the wine will burst the skins and both are lost. New wine is for fresh wineskins.

No one sews a piece of unshrunk cloth on an old garment. Two pictures from ordinary domestic life, and both are about the same mistake. New cloth off the loom is unshrunk. Sew a piece of it onto a garment that has been washed a hundred times, and for a while it looks like a decent repair. Then it gets wet, and the new patch pulls tight while the worn cloth around it has no give left, and it rips away and takes the old fabric with it. Mark’s summary is bleak and exact: a worse tear is made, and the repair did it.

And no one puts new wine into old wineskins. Wine in that world was carried in whole goatskins. New wine is still fermenting; it gives off gas and swells hard against the container, which is why it went into a new skin with stretch left in it. An old skin has done its stretching and become stiff and brittle. Pour working wine into it and it bursts, and Jesus counts the cost twice: the wine is destroyed, and so are the skins. You do not merely fail to gain the new. You lose what you had.

Different in kind. Neither picture attacks the old thing; the skin was perfectly good in its day. They are simply asked to contain something they were never built to hold, and they fail. The new life Jesus brings cannot simply be patched onto the old system of Pharisaic religion, with its traditions, fasts and purity rules. What he has brought is not an improved version of what was there before. It is different in kind, and the joy and freedom of the kingdom need new forms.

Patchwork religion. And the way most of us instinctively approach religion is patchwork. We take the life we have, with the self firmly in charge of it, and sew something on: church on Sunday, a habit of prayer, a tidied-up vocabulary, a few things given up. The garment is the same garment; the patch is decoration. This is why a certain kind of half-Christianity makes people more miserable than before. They are not lacking sincerity; they are living out a new patch on an old coat, pulling at the seams every time life gets wet. Something in them keeps ripping, and they conclude that faith does not work, when what has failed is the repair job.

But new wine is for fresh wineskins. And there is the whole gospel in the last clause, which almost everybody reads past on the way out. He does not leave you holding a jar of wine and a ruined skin, told to go and find a better container. He gives the skin. I will give you a new heart, and a new spirit I will put within you (Ezekiel 36:26). Paul says that whoever is joined to Christ is a new creation, the old gone and the new come (2 Corinthians 5:17): the fresh wineskin, made by God. The making of a vessel that can hold what he pours is his work and not yours, which is exactly why it can be asked of you.

The wine he would pour. The new wine is not a new rule. It is the life of the kingdom that has arrived with Jesus, and before Mark is done he will show what it cost. At the last supper Jesus took the cup, called it his blood of the covenant, poured out for many, and said he would not drink of the fruit of the vine again until he drinks it new in the kingdom of God (14:24–25). The wine that bursts old skins was pressed out of him. That is why it can never be stitched onto anyone’s religion as an improvement: it is a covenant made in his blood, and it makes a people new.

What it does not mean. Not that the Old Testament is worthless. Jesus fulfils it (Matthew 5:17). The old garments and old wineskins are the human traditions of the religious system, not God’s word itself.

Does this mean new church styles are always better than old ones? No. Jesus is not contrasting old-fashioned with modern, or hymns with new songs, or liturgy with informality. He is contrasting the gospel of his kingdom with a religion of human effort and tradition. A brand-new church can be as much a patch on the old self as an ancient one, and many old forms, rooted in Scripture, are excellent wineskins for the new wine. The question to ask of any practice is not whether it is old or new but whether it serves the free grace of Christ or competes with it.

In a sentence. The new life Jesus brings cannot be patched onto the old religious system; it needs new forms.

On a Tuesday. Test yourself honestly. Is Christ an addition to your life, an important one, a costly one, but an addition to a self that still holds the deciding vote? Or has the self been handed over? The two look similar from outside for a long time, and they behave completely differently under strain. And ask whether there are human traditions you cling to, in your family, your church or your private habits, that hinder the new life of the gospel.

For worship. He did not come to mend you. That is worse news than you wanted and immeasurably better than you hoped. Mending would have left you with the old coat and the old rips and a lifetime of stitching. Instead he intends to make you new, and the wine he has to pour is so alive, so far beyond anything the old self could contain, that it would burst you as you are. So he makes the vessel too. The Spirit of the living God is poured into hearts the Lord himself has made new. Behold, he is making all things new.
verseByVerse.note: Wineskins were goatskins. New wine is still fermenting and expanding; an old skin has lost its stretch and splits.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The field (vv. 23–24). The disciples walk through standing grain on a Sabbath, pulling heads off as they go and rubbing them in their hands. The Law explicitly allowed this; the Pharisees are not accusing them of theft. They are counting it as harvesting, threshing and winnowing — three of the thirty-nine categories of forbidden work, in one mouthful of wheat. And somebody had to be out in that field, on a Sabbath, watching.

The precedent (vv. 25–26). Jesus answers with a story rather than a ruling: David, hungry and on the run, eating the consecrated bread that only priests were permitted to eat, and Scripture recording not a word against him. The parallel is not simply that need outranks regulation. It is that a king travelling in rejection with his men has been here before.

The verdict (vv. 27–28). Two sentences that reset everything. The Sabbath was made for man, not man for the Sabbath — the day is a gift, and they had turned it into a scoring system. And then: the Son of Man is lord even of the Sabbath. The Giver is standing in the cornfield being told off for letting hungry men eat.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Son of Man is lord even of the Sabbath (v. 28) is a claim of breathtaking scope, and it is easy to miss how far it reaches. The Sabbath is not a national custom that a rabbi might reinterpret. It is stitched into the fabric of creation — God rested on the seventh day and made it holy before there was an Israel, a Sinai or a Jew (Gen. 2:2–3) — and it was afterwards written into the covenant by the finger of God (Exod. 20:8–11). To be lord of it is to be lord of the created order and of the covenant together.

And the day was always pointing past itself. Israel entered the land and never really entered the rest; centuries later Scripture can still say there remains a Sabbath rest for the people of God (Heb. 4:9). Every seventh evening for fifteen hundred years the nation rehearsed a rest it did not yet possess.

Put Mark's two sentences side by side and see what has happened. The Sabbath was made for man — so it is a gift. And the Son of Man is lord of the Sabbath — so the Giver is standing in the field. The rest the day rehearsed turns out not to be a square on a calendar but a Person, and he is the one being scolded. They were defending the gift against the Giver.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: hungry men pulling grain on a walk, and religious experts who had positioned themselves in a cornfield on a Sabbath in order to observe an infringement.

Now: the same instinct wherever the keeping of a form has become more important than the person the form was given to serve — the church where a visitor's clothes are noticed before his face is, the family where the standard is enforced and the child is not enjoyed. The institution that crushes the person it was designed to serve has inverted its own purpose, and it usually does so while feeling unusually devout.

The practical half of the day is worth taking as seriously as the doctrine of it. A modern reader does not break the Sabbath by working in a field; he breaks it by never stopping — by carrying the office in his pocket to bed. Stopping for a day feels like negligence, and it exposes precisely what a man believes about who is holding the world together. It keeps turning without you. That is the humiliation, and it is also the rest.

verseByVerse.quote: One Sabbath he was going through the grainfields, and as they made their way, his disciples began to pluck heads of grain. And the Pharisees were saying to him, "Look, why are they doing what is not lawful on the Sabbath?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
One Sabbath Jesus was going through the grainfields, and as they made their way his disciples began to pick heads of grain. The Pharisees said to him: look, why are they doing what is not lawful on the Sabbath?

One Sabbath he was going through the grainfields. The Sabbath was the seventh day, Saturday, when God commanded rest from work, remembering creation and the exodus (Exodus 20:8–11; Deuteronomy 5:12–15). It was the sign of the covenant with Israel (Exodus 31:13). Get the picture right, because almost everybody reads this as a story about stealing, and it is not. The disciples are walking a path through standing grain; field boundaries were unfenced and paths ran between them.

And as they made their way, his disciples began to pluck heads of grain. As they go they pull off heads of wheat, rub them between their palms to loosen the husk, blow the chaff away and eat the grain. It is what a hungry man does on a walk, and the law of Moses expressly allowed it: travellers could pick grain by hand from a neighbour’s field, though not put a sickle to it (Deuteronomy 23:25). God had legislated for hungry travellers. So notice what the Pharisees do not say. They do not accuse anyone of theft. The issue was the day.

Why are they doing what is not lawful on the Sabbath? The Pharisees’ traditions listed thirty-nine kinds of forbidden work, and the disciples had touched three of them in a single mouthful. Pulling the head off was reaping. Rubbing it in the hands was threshing. Blowing away the husk was winnowing. A man could be a farm labourer for a whole harvest in the time it takes to eat a handful of wheat.

The charge is brought to the Master. The Pharisees accuse the disciples, but they bring the accusation to Jesus, and he takes it up as his own. A teacher answered for his disciples, and this one never leaves his people to face their accusers alone. He stands between them and the charge, makes their defence, and rests it in the end on his own authority over the day. It is a small scene of something far larger. Who shall bring any charge against God’s elect? Paul asks, and answers that Christ Jesus, who died and was raised and is at the right hand of God, is interceding for us (Romans 8:33–34).

How did the Pharisees see it? They were there. On a Sabbath, out along a path through the fields, close enough to watch a group of working men to see whether any of them would put a hand out. And their first word, look, is almost a shout. They had been waiting for this. It is worth sitting with, because the same energy is alive in every generation and it always dresses as faithfulness. It is possible to be scrupulous about a rule and hard as flint about a person, to notice everything out of place in somebody’s life and never notice that he is hungry. Their own Scriptures had told them what to look for: I desire steadfast love and not sacrifice (Hosea 6:6).

Is it wrong to have rules in a church or a family? No. Rules can be wise and loving: a family that eats together on Sundays, a church that asks its children’s workers to be checked, a habit of daily prayer. The trouble comes when human rules are treated as if they were God’s law, used to judge other believers, or kept in a way that crushes the people they were meant to serve. Ask of any rule: does Scripture command this, or did we decide it? If we decided it, hold it humbly and do not bind other consciences with it (Colossians 2:20–23). That includes the Lord’s Day itself: because the Sabbath is fulfilled in Christ, Christians gladly set Sunday apart for worship, fellowship and rest as a gift, out of joy and wisdom, not as a law with rules about work, and no one may bind another believer’s conscience over it (Romans 14:5). And never let a rule stop you from seeing the person in front of you.

In a sentence. The Pharisees accused Jesus’ disciples of breaking the Sabbath by picking grain as they walked.

On a Tuesday. Do you judge others by rules that are yours, not God’s? Think of the last time you were sharply critical of another Christian: how he brings up his children, how he spends, what he does with his Sundays. Did you know, at the time, what was actually going on in that house? Or were you standing at the edge of the field with a clear view of the rule and none at all of the man?

For worship. The Lord of the harvest walked through his own fields with his hungry friends, and when the accusers came he answered for them. He answers for them still. Every charge the law, the conscience and the enemy can bring against his people is brought to him, and he does not hand them over; he stands in front of them, having borne the sentence himself. He sees the hunger of his disciples before he sees their faults, and he feeds them from his own fields.
verseByVerse.note: The objection was that plucking counted as harvesting, which was work.

parallels.desc: picking grain by hand was allowed

verseByVerse.quote: And he said to them, "Have you never read what David did, when he was in need and was hungry, he and those who were with him: how he entered the house of God, in the time of Abiathar the high priest, and ate the bread of the Presence, which it is not lawful for any but the priests to eat, and also gave it to those who were with him?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus said: have you never read what David did when he was in need and hungry, he and those with him: how he entered the house of God in the time of Abiathar the high priest and ate the bread of the Presence, which only the priests may eat, and also gave it to those with him?

Have you never read what David did. Jesus does not answer with a ruling. He answers with a story, and the story is a deliberate choice: 1 Samuel 21:1–6. David is already anointed king and not yet on the throne. He is running from Saul with a few men, in need and hungry, and he comes to the tabernacle at Nob and is given the holy bread by the priest. Human need is the point.

In the time of Abiathar the high priest. An honest reader with a reference Bible will notice something, and it is better dealt with plainly than hurried past. 1 Samuel 21 names the priest as Ahimelech, Abiathar’s father. Abiathar was there (he escaped the massacre that followed, 1 Samuel 22:20) and later became the more famous high priest under David. There are good answers. In the time of Abiathar may mean in the days of Abiathar, who was a priest then and became the better-known high priest, as we might say in the days of King David about events before he was king. Or the phrase may mean at the passage about Abiathar: with no chapter numbers, a teacher located a text by its best-known figure, as Jesus does with the passage about the bush (12:26). On that reading Jesus is giving a reference, not a date. Or the names were sometimes interchanged (2 Samuel 8:17 and 1 Chronicles 18:16 have Ahimelech son of Abiathar). Verdict: no error; the phrase identifies the period or passage by its most famous priest. And nothing in the argument depends on it. Jesus is not resting his case on which priest was on duty, and the Pharisees, who knew that chapter far better than we do, did not raise the objection.

And ate the bread of the Presence, which it is not lawful for any but the priests to eat. Twelve loaves placed fresh before the LORD each Sabbath, and the old ones afterwards eaten by priests only, as a most holy portion (Leviticus 24:5–9).

The argument. David ate the holy bread and gave it to those who were with him, breaking a ceremonial law, and Scripture does not condemn him; neither God nor the narrator rebukes him. Human need takes priority over ceremonial rules. Where a genuine human need collided with a regulation about worship, the regulation gave way and heaven did not object. The rule was never the ultimate thing. But there is a second point in the choice of this story, and it is sharper. Jesus does not pick a case about hunger in general. He picks the anointed king, rejected, unrecognised, on the road with his men, being fed from the holy table. David was God’s anointed; Jesus is the greater Son of David. The disciples in that field are the men of a King the country has not enthroned. If David’s men could eat the holy bread because of who was with them, how much more the disciples of David’s greater Son.

Does this mean I may break any rule when I am in need? No. Jesus is speaking about ceremonial rules, like the bread of the Presence, and about the Pharisees’ additions to the Sabbath law. He never suggests that need excuses breaking God’s moral law. Hunger does not justify stealing, and loneliness does not justify adultery. God’s moral commands, to love him and our neighbour, are themselves the shape of mercy. The point is that God’s laws were given for our good, and a reading of them that leaves a hungry man unfed has misunderstood the God who gave them.

In a sentence. Jesus pointed to David eating the holy bread to show that ceremonial rules give way to need, especially for God’s anointed and his companions.

On a Tuesday. God’s laws are for our good. Rules that hurt people in need may show that we have misunderstood his purpose. Is there someone in need near you whom you have been ignoring because helping would be inconvenient, irregular or messy? The question is not whether you are allowed to help but whether love requires it.

For worship. The rejected king of 1 Samuel ate holy bread on the run, and his greater Son walked through the fields with men no one honoured, the anointed King whom the nation did not know. He is the true bread of the Presence, the bread of God come down from heaven, and he does not keep the holy things from his hungry people. He gives himself to them.
verseByVerse.note: On the name Abiathar (1 Samuel 21 names the priest Ahimelech), see the commentary.

parallels.desc: the bread of the Presence, eaten by priests

verseByVerse.quote: And he said to them, "The Sabbath was made for man, not man for the Sabbath. So the Son of Man is lord even of the Sabbath."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus said: the Sabbath was made for man, not man for the Sabbath. So the Son of Man is lord even of the Sabbath.

The Sabbath was made for man, not man for the Sabbath. Only Mark records this saying. The Sabbath was made: brought about, given. And it was given long before there was a Jew in the world to keep it. God rested on the seventh day, blessed it and made it holy at the end of the creation account (Genesis 2:2–3), centuries before Sinai. It is part of the architecture of the world, like marriage and work. Which means it was a kindness: rest for weary people, a day to delight in God (Isaiah 58:13–14; Exodus 23:12). A day when the ox is unhitched and the poorest labourer in Israel gets what only rich men could buy, a day that is his. The Egyptians had given Israel no such day, and in Deuteronomy the command is set out with the memory of slavery attached (Deuteronomy 5:15). And there is the inversion. The Pharisees had taken a day designed to lift a burden off a man’s back and turned it into a burden to carry, a day with thirty-nine categories to be tracked, a day you could fail, as if people existed to serve the rules. The gift had become an examination.

So the Son of Man is lord even of the Sabbath. The climax. The Sabbath was the LORD’s day (Exodus 20:10). Jesus claims authority over it: the right to say what it means and how it should be kept. Only God could make this claim. Follow the logic and it is stunning. If the day was made for man, then the Man in whom humanity is summed up, the one Daniel saw given dominion, is its lord. He is not proposing a relaxation of the rules. He is telling a group of experts, in a cornfield, that the day belongs to him.

The Sabbath and Christ. The Sabbath always pointed past itself, to the rest Jesus gives (Matthew 11:28; Hebrews 4:9–10). Israel came into the land and never fully came into the rest; looking back over the whole story, Hebrews says that there remains a Sabbath rest for the people of God. Every seventh evening for fifteen hundred years, a nation rehearsed something it did not yet have. And then, on an ordinary Sabbath, in a wheat field in Galilee, the rest itself walked through the standing grain with a handful of hungry men, and was told off for it by the people who had spent their lives guarding the rehearsal. They were defending the gift against the Giver. After his resurrection on the first day of the week, Christians gathered on that day, the Lord’s Day (Acts 20:7; Revelation 1:10).

Where Christians differ: the Sabbath today. Christians who love the Bible have not landed in the same place on this, and it is only fair to say so. Some keep Saturday as the Sabbath. Many Reformed Christians, with the Westminster Confession and the 1689 London Baptist Confession, keep Sunday as the Christian Sabbath, holding that the fourth commandment, rooted in creation and written into the Ten, still binds one day in seven, now observed on the day of the resurrection (Westminster 21.7–8); it is held by many godly brothers and deserves respect. Others hold that the Sabbath is fulfilled in Christ, so that no day is binding as a Sabbath, pointing to Paul: one person esteems one day as better than another, while another esteems all days alike (Romans 14:5–6), and let no one pass judgment on you with regard to a festival or a new moon or a Sabbath (Colossians 2:16–17); Sunday is then the Lord’s Day for gathering. Verdict: the Sabbath is fulfilled in Christ, our true rest. The Lord’s Day is a gift: Christians gladly set Sunday apart for worship, fellowship and rest, out of joy and wisdom, not as a binding law with rules about work, and no one may bind another’s conscience about it (Romans 14:5; Colossians 2:16–17). Believers who keep a stricter Sabbath should be honoured, not judged.

What it does not mean. Not that people may do whatever they like with God’s gifts. The Sabbath serves human good as God defines it, which includes worship and rest. Nor does made for man mean that our wishes override God’s commands.

What neither side disputes. The day is a gift and not a scoring system, and a person who never stops has not understood the God who did. So make it concrete. Do you stop? Not slow down; stop. Is there a stretch in your week when the work is genuinely down, the phone is put away, and you are not quietly earning your right to exist? Most of us now miss the gift of rest in a way the Pharisees would not have recognised: not by putting a hand to grain, but by never taking a hand off anything. And be honest about why stopping is frightening. If you stop, things carry on without you. You find out you were not holding the world up. That is the humiliation in it, and it is also precisely the rest in it. It is in vain that you rise up early and go late to rest, eating the bread of anxious toil; for he gives to his beloved sleep (Psalm 127:2). A day of rest is a weekly, physical confession that you are not God.

What if my job requires me to work on Sundays? Then you are in good company: doctors, nurses, carers, police, firefighters and many others do necessary and merciful work that cannot stop, and Jesus himself defended doing good on the Sabbath (3:4). Because the Sabbath is fulfilled in Christ and the Lord’s Day is a gift, not a law with rules about work, you are not breaking a commandment. Do your work as service to Christ. Then guard what you can: gather with God’s people whenever possible, perhaps at another service or a midweek meeting, and take a real day of rest at another point in your week. If you have a choice and Sunday work keeps you from the church week after week, take that seriously, and ask whether you could rearrange things. The aim is not a rule kept but a heart that gathers with God’s people, worships and rests.

In a sentence. God made the Sabbath as a gift for human good, and Jesus, the Son of Man, is Lord over it.

On a Tuesday. How do you use the Lord’s Day? As a gift for worship, rest and doing good, or as a day like any other? Plan next Sunday now: gathering with God’s people, unhurried time with family or friends, a walk, a meal shared, a visit to someone lonely, and real rest from the work that fills the other six days. And somewhere in this week, stop, and let the world carry on without you for a while.

For worship. He is still the rest. Not a square on the calendar, not a scheme for the well-organised, but the one who says, Come to me, all who labor and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest (Matthew 11:28). He is Lord of the Sabbath because he made it, and he gave its rest at the cost of a Friday on which he had no rest at all, and lay in the tomb through the Sabbath, and rose on the first day of a new week. Because he finished his work, we may cease from ours, and the rest he won is the one Sabbath that will never end.

2.theology:
Chapter 2 opens the conflict that ends at the cross. The scribes and Pharisees are not villains in a simple morality tale — they are serious people defending serious religious commitments, and on the doctrine of forgiveness they are exactly right. Their error is not that they take the law too seriously; it is that they have not recognised the one the law was pointing to. When the fulfilment arrives, the categories built to anticipate it can no longer contain it, which is precisely the burden of the new wine and the old skins.

Four demonstrations, then, of why Jesus could not simply be absorbed into the religious system as constituted: he forgives sins directly rather than through the temple; he receives the excluded at his own table rather than at the end of a purification process; he calls his own presence a wedding rather than a fast; and he claims lordship over the creation ordinance of the Sabbath itself. Not because he is lawless, but because he is the law's Lord.
2.examples:
The Pharisees' discomfort at Jesus eating with sinners deserves sympathetic treatment before it receives critique. Their instinct toward purity was not irrational; it was a serious attempt to guard the holiness God had commanded, in a land under pagan occupation where the pressure to blur every line was constant. Their error was a category error: they had equated association with endorsement. Jesus's presence among sinners was not approval of their sin but the physician's presence among the sick, and the cure requires proximity. The model is the incarnation itself — the holy God does not deal with human ruin from a safe distance but comes into it to heal from within, and finally takes the disease into his own body on a cross.

Then: Pharisees keeping a careful distance in order to stay clean, while the one man in Capernaum who actually was clean reclined at a tax collector's table. Now: any form of Christianity that has quietly confused holiness with non-exposure — and, on the other side, any form of it that sits down at every table and never says who it came with.

3.title: By Whose Power?
3.text: <sup>1</sup>Again he entered the synagogue, and a man was there with a withered hand. <sup>2</sup>And they watched Jesus, to see whether he would heal him on the Sabbath, so that they might accuse him. <sup>3</sup>And he said to the man with the withered hand, “Come here.” <sup>4</sup>And he said to them, “Is it lawful on the Sabbath to do good or to do harm, to save life or to kill?” But they were silent. <sup>5</sup>And he looked around at them with anger, grieved at their hardness of heart, and said to the man, “Stretch out your hand.” He stretched it out, and his hand was restored. <sup>6</sup>The Pharisees went out and immediately held counsel with the Herodians against him, how to destroy him. <sup>7</sup>Jesus withdrew with his disciples to the sea, and a great crowd followed, from Galilee and Judea <sup>8</sup>and Jerusalem and Idumea and from beyond the Jordan and from around Tyre and Sidon. When the great crowd heard all that he was doing, they came to him. <sup>9</sup>And he told his disciples to have a boat ready for him because of the crowd, lest they crush him, <sup>10</sup>for he had healed many, so that all who had diseases pressed around him to touch him. <sup>11</sup>And whenever the unclean spirits saw him, they fell down before him and cried out, “You are the Son of God.” <sup>12</sup>And he strictly ordered them not to make him known. <sup>13</sup>And he went up on the mountain and called to him those whom he desired, and they came to him. <sup>14</sup>And he appointed twelve (whom he also named apostles) so that they might be with him and he might send them out to preach <sup>15</sup>and have authority to cast out demons. <sup>16</sup>He appointed the twelve: Simon (to whom he gave the name Peter); <sup>17</sup>James the son of Zebedee and John the brother of James (to whom he gave the name Boanerges, that is, Sons of Thunder); <sup>18</sup>Andrew, and Philip, and Bartholomew, and Matthew, and Thomas, and James the son of Alphaeus, and Thaddaeus, and Simon the Zealot, <sup>19</sup>and Judas Iscariot, who betrayed him. <sup>20</sup>Then he went home, and the crowd gathered again, so that they could not even eat. <sup>21</sup>And when his family heard it, they went out to seize him, for they were saying, “He is out of his mind.” <sup>22</sup>And the scribes who came down from Jerusalem were saying, “He is possessed by Beelzebul,” and “by the prince of demons he casts out the demons.” <sup>23</sup>And he called them to him and said to them in parables, “How can Satan cast out Satan? <sup>24</sup>If a kingdom is divided against itself, that kingdom cannot stand. <sup>25</sup>And if a house is divided against itself, that house will not be able to stand. <sup>26</sup>And if Satan has risen up against himself and is divided, he cannot stand, but is coming to an end. <sup>27</sup>But no one can enter a strong man’s house and plunder his goods, unless he first binds the strong man. Then indeed he may plunder his house. <sup>28</sup>“Truly, I say to you, all sins will be forgiven the children of man, and whatever blasphemies they utter, <sup>29</sup>but whoever blasphemes against the Holy Spirit never has forgiveness, but is guilty of an eternal sin”— <sup>30</sup>for they were saying, “He has an unclean spirit.” <sup>31</sup>And his mother and his brothers came, and standing outside they sent to him and called him. <sup>32</sup>And a crowd was sitting around him, and they said to him, “Your mother and your brothers are outside, seeking you.” <sup>33</sup>And he answered them, “Who are my mother and my brothers?” <sup>34</sup>And looking about at those who sat around him, he said, “Here are my mother and my brothers! <sup>35</sup>For whoever does the will of God, he is my brother and sister and mother.”
3.overview:
Chapter 3 is where the opposition hardens into a decision and the alternative community is formed. It opens with a trap in a synagogue and closes with a redefinition of family, and between the two everything about Jesus is contested. The Pharisees and Herodians — parties who agreed on nothing — walk out of a Sabbath service together to plan his death (v. 6). His own family concludes he is out of his mind and comes to take him home (v. 21). A delegation of scribes travels ninety miles from Jerusalem and pronounces him possessed (v. 22). Three verdicts, and all of them wrong.

Against that, Jesus does two constructive things. He appoints twelve men — a number no Jew could hear innocently — so that they might be with him and be sent out (vv. 13–15); and he tells the room what the kingdom actually is: a break-in. A stronger man has entered the strong man's house, tied him up, and is carrying out his property (v. 27). Every healing and deliverance in this Gospel is loot from that raid. The chapter ends by naming who now belongs to him, and the criterion is neither blood nor pedigree but doing the will of God.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–12 — The Withered Hand and the Widening Response
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The trap (vv. 1–2). Jesus walks into a synagogue where two things are waiting for him: a man with a ruined hand, and a row of men watching to see whether he will touch it. They are not curious. They are collecting evidence.

The question nobody would answer (vv. 3–4). He puts the man in the middle of the room and asks whether the Sabbath is for doing good or doing harm, saving life or killing. It is unanswerable, and they know it, so they say nothing.

The anger (v. 5). The one place in Mark where Jesus is said to look on people with anger — and in the same breath, grieved. Then a command to a man who cannot obey it, and a hand made new.

The verdict (v. 6). Two parties who despised each other walk out together to plan a murder, and it is still the Sabbath.

The crowds (vv. 7–12). He withdraws, and a hundred-mile radius follows him to the shore. He asks for a boat to keep from being crushed, and silences the only voices in the crowd that know exactly who he is.
verseByVerse.theology:
Verses 11–12 raise a question every attentive reader hits sooner or later: the demons keep saying true things about Jesus, and he keeps shutting them up. Why refuse free advertising from witnesses who cannot be wrong?

Two reasons converge, and the second is the one that touches the reader. The first is timing. In Galilee in that decade, to be publicly proclaimed Son of God meant one thing to a crowd — a nationalist king who would clear out the Romans. Jesus refuses to be crowned before he is crucified, because a title accepted on those terms would have to be unlearned at the cross. He will let the word be said out loud when it can be defined by his death (15:39, on the lips of the officer at the foot of it).

The second is more searching. What the unclean spirits say is doctrinally perfect. You are the Son of God is exactly right, and it saves them from nothing. James makes the point without flinching: you believe that God is one; you do well. Even the demons believe — and shudder (Jas. 2:19). A creed can be entirely correct and entirely worthless. The spirits here fall down before him, which is more than the scribes did, and confess his identity, which is more than the disciples had managed — and they remain what they are. Right belief about Christ is not the same as belonging to him, and this chapter will end by saying who does belong.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: a man with a shrivelled hand told to stand up in the middle of a watched synagogue, before anything had been healed, in front of the men who had come to build a case.

Now: every act of obedience that makes a person visible and vulnerable before the outcome is assured — the first time you say in an office that you are a Christian; the apology you make with no guarantee it will be received; the sin confessed to one other believer when it could have stayed hidden for life. He was asked to be conspicuous first and healed second, and he had no way of knowing the order in advance.

And notice what the same scene did to the watchers. They had come to see whether a rule would be broken, and they saw a crippled man made whole, and it did not move them an inch. It is possible to sit in a room where God is plainly at work and be entirely occupied with whether it is being done properly.

verseByVerse.quote: Again he entered the synagogue, and a man was there with a withered hand. And they watched Jesus, to see whether he would heal him on the Sabbath, so that they might accuse him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Again Jesus went into the synagogue, and a man was there with a withered hand. They watched Jesus closely to see whether he would heal him on the Sabbath, so that they could accuse him.

Meaning first. Mark 3 shows the lines being drawn around Jesus. In a synagogue he heals a man’s withered hand on the Sabbath, and the Pharisees respond by joining their political enemies to plot his death. Crowds pour in from every region, Jew and Gentile, and demons fall before him crying that he is the Son of God. On a mountain he chooses twelve men to be with him and to be sent out, the beginning of a renewed Israel. Then come two verdicts on him from opposite sides: his own family says he is out of his mind, and the scribes from Jerusalem say he is in league with Satan. Jesus answers that he is the stronger one who has bound the strong man, warns of the one sin that is never forgiven, and looks round at those sitting at his feet and calls them his mother and his brothers. The chapter asks every reader where he stands: outside, or inside with him.

Again he entered the synagogue. The fifth of five conflict stories (2:1–3:6), and the second about the Sabbath. And again is doing real work. The last time Jesus was in a synagogue on a Sabbath in this Gospel, a demon screamed and the whole town talked about it for weeks (1:21–28). He knows what happens when he walks into these buildings. He goes in anyway. Picture the room. A Galilean synagogue was not large: stone benches around three or four walls, the congregation facing inward, everybody able to see everybody. There is no back row to hide in, and that detail decides the scene, because a man is about to be told to stand up in the middle of it.

And a man was there with a withered hand. Shrunken or paralysed: the word suggests a hand that has dried up, the muscle wasted, whether from injury, disease or a stroke. Luke, who was a doctor, notices it was his right hand (Luke 6:6), which in a world of manual labour is the difference between a tradesman and a beggar; he probably could not work. A second-century gospel quoted by Jerome remembers him saying: I was a mason, earning my living with my hands; I beg you, Jesus, give me back my health, that I need not beg my bread in shame. Whether or not those were his words, they were certainly his situation. His condition was not life-threatening. The rabbis allowed healing on the Sabbath only when life was in danger. Nobody could argue that this was an emergency that could not wait a day, and that is precisely why the case suited the Pharisees. A borderline case makes the better trap.

And they watched Jesus. Watched (paretēroun) means watched closely, spied on, kept under observation, the way you watch a man you have already decided about. They were not there to worship but to catch him.

To see whether he would heal him on the Sabbath, so that they might accuse him. They knew Jesus would heal. They had seen enough by chapter 3 to be in no doubt that he could. Their question was not whether he could but whether he would break their rules, so that they could bring a charge. This is the language of the courtroom. They are not gathering understanding; they are gathering evidence. They were using a disabled man as bait.

Religion detached from love. Stop there, because it is uglier than a quick reading allows. There is a human being in that room with a wasted hand and a wrecked livelihood, and the most religious men present have looked at him and seen an opportunity. He is not a person to them. He is a test case. That is what happens to religion when it comes away from love: not usually in some dramatic collapse into wickedness, since these men would have been horrified to be called wicked, but by degrees, until a suffering man in your own congregation registers chiefly as an issue to be handled. And hold the two halves of the verse together, because Mark has set them side by side. A man with a withered hand, and men with withered hearts. Only one of them knew he needed healing.

Why did Jesus heal on the Sabbath when he could have waited a day? Because waiting would have conceded that their rules were God’s, and that doing good to a suffering man was work God forbade. Jesus was not being provocative for its own sake. He was showing what the Sabbath was for. Every day the man waited was another day of shame and begging, and the Lord of the Sabbath saw no reason to make him wait. Mercy delayed for the sake of a human tradition is not holiness. He chose the day deliberately, so that everyone would learn what kind of rest God gives.

In a sentence. In the synagogue, Jesus’ opponents watched to see if he would heal a man’s withered hand on the Sabbath, so they could accuse him.

On a Tuesday. You can sit in a place of worship looking for others’ faults instead of looking for God. Examine your own heart when you gather. And if you have ever found yourself more interested in whether something was done correctly than in the person it was done to, you have felt the pull of that room. Next Sunday, look around the congregation and notice one person who is struggling, and go to them as a person, not a problem.

For worship. He walked into a room where he knew a trap had been laid, and he walked in for the sake of one man nobody else saw. He is the Shepherd who notices the person the religious professionals were using. No one is merely a case to him. The Lord who sees withered hands also sees withered hearts, and he came to heal both.
verseByVerse.note: A “withered” hand is shrunken or paralysed. Healing a condition that was not life-threatening could wait a day — which is why they watched.

verseByVerse.quote: And he said to the man with the withered hand, "Come here." And he said to them, "Is it lawful on the Sabbath to do good or to do harm, to save life or to kill?" But they were silent.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus said to the man with the withered hand: come here. And he said to them: is it lawful on the Sabbath to do good or to do harm, to save life or to kill? But they were silent.

And he said to the man with the withered hand, “Come here”. Literally rise into the middle: stand up, where the room can see you. Jesus brings him out in front of everyone. He does not heal secretly to avoid trouble. He could have. The man could have been healed on his way out, at the door, and the trap would have closed on nothing. Instead, if the healing is going to be treated as a crime, it will be committed in open court. Jesus is not caught breaking the Sabbath; he chooses the moment, the venue and the audience, and makes the question unavoidable. And spare a thought for the man, who has not asked for any of this. He came, presumably, as he had come for years, and hid the hand inside his cloak the way you do. Now he is standing in the middle of the floor with the bad hand on display, before neighbours who have known about it all his life and officials who are visibly hostile. He is exposed first and healed second, and at this point he has no way of knowing that the second part is coming.

Is it lawful on the Sabbath to do good or to do harm, to save life or to kill? Jesus reframes the question. They were braced for an argument about the category of work: whether healing counts, whether the case is urgent, which precedents apply. Jesus refuses the whole frame. Not what work is permitted, but what the Sabbath is for. And he leaves no third option. On any given Sabbath you are either doing good or doing harm, saving life or destroying it. To have the power to do good and to withhold it is itself a choice. To refuse to do good when you can is to do harm. James says it plainly: whoever knows the right thing to do and fails to do it, for him it is sin (James 4:17).

To save life or to kill. Then notice the second half of the question, because it is a blade. Who is killing anybody? Nobody, yet. But by the end of verse 6 the men in that room will have spent the Sabbath planning a death. The irony is sharp: Jesus is about to restore a life, while his opponents are already planning to kill. He has read what is in them, and he says it out loud before they have said it to each other. Which is lawful on the Sabbath? The Sabbath on which he restores a hand is the Sabbath on which they begin to plot a murder, and only one of those is work.

Was healing on the Sabbath forbidden in the law? No. Moses forbade work on the Sabbath but nowhere forbade healing. The ban came from the scribal rules built around the law, which allowed treatment only when life was in danger. Jesus was not breaking Moses; he was breaking the fence the teachers had built around Moses. As for Christians today, the Sabbath is fulfilled in Christ, the Lord of the Sabbath (2:28), and no day binds the conscience as the old Sabbath did (Colossians 2:16–17); but the question Jesus asks still stands over every day of the week.

But they were silent. They could not answer without condemning themselves. The silence is not ignorance. These men could argue any point of law in the Torah for an afternoon. They are silent because the question has only one honest answer, and that answer costs them the case. That kind of silence is worth recognising, because most of us have used it. It is the silence in which you do not deny what has just been said, and do not act on it either. It feels safer than being wrong. It is not. A man who says nothing has not stayed neutral; he has decided, and simply avoided the cost of saying so out loud. Two verses later that same silence walks out of the building and starts making arrangements.

In a sentence. Jesus brought the man forward and asked whether the Sabbath is for doing good or harm, saving life or killing, and his opponents had no answer.

On a Tuesday. Failing to do good when you can is not neutral. What good could you do today, on a day you might think of as ordinary: the visit you keep postponing, the help you could give, the word of encouragement you could send? And notice the last time a clear word from Scripture met you and you answered it with silence. Silence before God is not a hiding place. Answer him.

For worship. With one question the Lord laid bare every heart in the room. He is the light that exposes, and the light that heals. He did not hide his mercy to protect himself; he set the man in the middle and set his own life on the line for him. That is how he has always loved: openly, at cost, in the full view of his enemies.

verseByVerse.quote: And he looked around at them with anger, grieved at their hardness of heart, and said to the man, "Stretch out your hand." He stretched it out, and his hand was restored.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus looked around at them with anger, grieved at their hardness of heart, and said to the man: stretch out your hand. He stretched it out, and his hand was restored.

And he looked around at them with anger. Mark tells us something the other Gospels leave out: this is the one place in his Gospel where Jesus is said to look at a group with anger. Not a glance. He swept the room, face by face, and what was in his face was anger. Matthew and Luke both record the healing and both omit this; Mark, whose Gospel carries Peter’s memory, keeps it, and Peter, standing there, is the likely source. Jesus felt real emotions. This was righteous anger: anger at cruelty, at religion that used people instead of loving them, at hearts that cared more about rules than a suffering man. God is angry at such things (Psalm 7:11).

The picture that cannot fit. This needs saying carefully, because many people carry a picture of Jesus in which this verse cannot fit: endlessly mild, never provoked, incapable of a hard look. That picture is not from the Bible. The Jesus of the Gospels was angry here, made a whip and cleared the temple courts (John 2:15), and called men whitewashed tombs to their faces (Matthew 23:27). And he never sinned once. So it is possible to be angry and holy at the same time. Be angry and do not sin (Ephesians 4:26) is not a contradiction; it is a command with a boundary.

Grieved at their hardness of heart. His anger was mixed with grief, and they are one motion. He is not merely furious; he is cut to the heart over what these men have become. Hardness (pōrōsei) means a callus, or the way a broken bone heals over into something stony: tissue that was once soft, thickening at the point of injury until it can no longer feel. They were not merely mistaken; their hearts were closed. Jesus grieved over them even as he was angry with them. Righteous anger is never without sorrow for the sinner.

How can I tell righteous anger from sinful anger? Mark answers in the same sentence, and the answer is the word grieved. Sinful anger enjoys itself. It wants the other person diminished; it rehearses the argument in the shower; it would be quietly disappointed if they repented, because then there would be nothing to be right about. Righteous anger grieves. It hurts to feel it. It wants the wrong put right and the wrongdoer restored, and it would be delighted to be made unnecessary. Run that on the last thing you were angry about. Did you want the person changed, or did you want them beaten? You will know the answer in about four seconds.

And said to the man, “Stretch out your hand”. A command he could not obey in his own strength. That is the whole point of it. This is exactly what the man cannot do; if he could stretch out that hand, he would not have spent his life hiding it in his cloak. He has almost certainly tried a thousand times. Jesus’ word gave the power to obey.

He stretched it out, and his hand was restored. Healed by a word. Mark gives no interval: no warmth spreading, no gradual return of movement. He obeyed, and in the obeying the power was there.
