And Jesus did no physical work at all. He did not touch the man or lift a finger. There was nothing to accuse him of except the healing itself.

The order of obedience. Do not miss the order, because it is the order of the Christian life. He does not stretch out a hand that has already been healed. The stretching is where the healing happens. Faith is not a feeling of confidence you wait to receive before you move; faith is moving on his word while you still feel exactly as incapable as you did a minute ago. That answers a question many believers are quietly stuck on: I would obey if I had more faith. No. You will find you had the faith in the doing of it. Make the phone call. Say the sentence. Open the Bible in the morning when nothing in you wants to. The strength arrives in the stretching, and never before it.

What it does not mean. Not that all anger is righteous. Ours is usually mixed with pride, and the anger of man does not produce the righteousness of God (James 1:20). Jesus’ anger was pure: aimed at sin, mixed with grief, and followed by an act of mercy (see Ephesians 4:26).

In a sentence. Angry and grieved at their hard hearts, Jesus told the man to stretch out his hand, and it was restored.

On a Tuesday. When you are angry at sin, is your anger mixed with grief and followed by good, as Jesus’ was? Think of the person who has most angered you recently. Pray for them by name, and ask God to restore them, not merely to vindicate you. And find one command of Christ you have been waiting to feel able to obey. Stretch out your hand today.

For worship. Look, last, at what the two hands mean together. One hand withered and useless, held out at his command and made new. And his own hands, sound and strong, a workman’s hands, stretched out one Friday on a piece of wood and ruined, so that the ruined might be restored. He healed with a word what would cost him nails. His anger at sin and his grief over sinners met at the cross, and there he made us whole.
verseByVerse.note: Mark alone records Jesus’ anger and grief here; Matthew and Luke do not mention them.

verseByVerse.quote: The Pharisees went out and immediately held counsel with the Herodians against him, how to destroy him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Pharisees went out and immediately plotted with the Herodians against Jesus, how to destroy him.

The Pharisees went out. After the healing, not before. Read the verse slowly, because several things in it are worse than they look. There has just been an undeniable miracle, in a room they know, done to a man they have seen every week for years, and their response is to walk out of the service. Nothing is said about the hand. Nobody congratulates the man.

And immediately held counsel with the Herodians against him. Immediately: there is no interval of reflection, no going home to think and pray. And the alliance is the detail a first-century reader would have found almost unbelievable. The Herodians were supporters of the family of Herod and of Herod Antipas’ rule, cooperating with Rome: courtiers, worldly and political, invested in the arrangement that kept them comfortable. The Pharisees were the strict separatists, whose whole programme was the purity of Israel, who regarded collaboration with Rome as a filthy compromise and Herod’s family as half-Edomite puppets propped up by pagan soldiers. On religion, politics, money and nationhood they agreed on nothing. Normally they were enemies; now they unite against Jesus within minutes, as they will again (12:13). Shared hatred makes strange allies. Nothing on earth makes allies like a shared hatred of the light. Pilate and Herod, Luke notes drily, became friends with each other that same day, the day they both had a hand in trying Jesus (Luke 23:12).

How to destroy him. Not how to discredit him, out-argue him or have him disciplined. The word is destroy. This is the first plot to kill Jesus in Mark, early in his ministry, in chapter 3 of sixteen. And set it against the day it happened on. It is still the Sabbath. Jesus has been accused of violating the day by restoring a man’s hand with a sentence; his accusers spend the rest of the same holy day organising a killing. On the Sabbath, the day for saving life, they plot death (v. 4). They would not have carried a bed. They will carry a cross to the authorities. From here the shadow of the cross falls across the Gospel. Everything from here is a man walking, with his eyes open, toward a verdict that has already been reached, and he heals somebody in nearly every chapter on the way.

Correct theology is not a preservative. That is what a hardened heart looks like from the inside: entirely convinced it is defending God, with murder in the diary. Nobody in that consultation thought of himself as wicked. They thought of themselves as serious. And here is the sober word for anyone who takes doctrine seriously, as we should. These were the orthodox party. They believed in the resurrection, the authority of Scripture, the coming Messiah and the moral law, and they left a service in which God had visibly acted and went straight into a meeting about how to kill him. The safeguard was never the doctrine on its own. It was whether the doctrine was still attached to love for God and pity for people, and in these men it had come away.

How do I guard my heart against this kind of hardness? Hardness grows by small refusals: hearing God’s word and not doing it, seeing a need and looking away, being corrected and defending yourself. So the remedy is small obediences, made promptly. When Scripture convicts you, act on it the same day. When you are shown to be wrong, say so. Keep company with believers who will tell you the truth, and exhort one another every day, so that none of you is hardened by the deceitfulness of sin (Hebrews 3:13). Pray that God would keep your heart soft. And keep your doctrine close to your knees: truth that is not prayed and loved soon becomes a weapon.

In a sentence. The Pharisees immediately joined their political enemies, the Herodians, in plotting to kill Jesus.

On a Tuesday. Religion that loses love can become murderous. Guard your heart against religious pride. Notice whether there is anyone you are quietly allied with only because you dislike the same person. And ask whether your convictions, true as they may be, have lately made you more tender toward people or less.

For worship. They plotted his death on the day of rest, and he knew it, and he did not stop healing. The cross was decided in Galilee, and the Son of God set his face toward it anyway. Their counsel was to destroy him; God’s counsel was to give him up for us all. The plans of wicked men became the means of our salvation, and the one they plotted to destroy has destroyed death itself.
verseByVerse.note: The Herodians were supporters of the Herod family’s rule — unlikely allies for the Pharisees.

verseByVerse.quote: Jesus withdrew with his disciples to the sea, and a great crowd followed, from Galilee and Judea and Jerusalem and Idumea and from beyond the Jordan and from around Tyre and Sidon. When the great crowd heard all that he was doing, they came to him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus withdrew with his disciples to the lake, and a great crowd followed, from Galilee, Judea, Jerusalem, Idumea, beyond the Jordan, and from around Tyre and Sidon. When they heard everything he was doing, they came to him.

Jesus withdrew with his disciples to the sea. Away from the synagogue and the plot. He does not escalate. He does not go looking for the men who have just decided to kill him, and he does not stay in the synagogue to make a point. He leaves the building and goes down to the lake, and the ministry gets bigger. The opposition of the leaders did not thin the crowd; it thickened it. What was intended to shut him down pushed him out of a room that held eighty people onto a shoreline that could hold thousands.

And a great crowd followed, from Galilee and Judea and Jerusalem and Idumea and from beyond the Jordan and from around Tyre and Sidon. Mark rarely bothers with addresses, and here he lists six. The list is not padding; it is a map, worth reading with a finger on it. Galilee is home, the northern province. Judea and Jerusalem are the religious heartland eighty and ninety miles south, which means people have walked for the better part of a week. Idumea is the ancient Edom, down beyond the southern desert, the descendants of Esau, forcibly converted more than a century before and still regarded as barely Jewish; Herod’s own people. Beyond the Jordan is the east bank, Gentile-mixed. And Tyre and Sidon are not in Israel at all: they are Phoenician port cities on the coast to the north-west, pagan cities, the cities of Jezebel’s father. Almost the whole territory of ancient Israel, and beyond. Jews and Gentiles.

The shape of the list. It runs from the centre outward in every direction: north, south, east, west, Jew, half-Jew, Gentile. Mark is not just reporting attendance. He is showing you a crowd assembling that looks, in miniature, like the church that is coming: everyone from everywhere, drawn to one man, most of them nowhere near understanding him yet. It is a rehearsal of a promise older than any of them. To Abraham: in you all the families of the earth shall be blessed (Genesis 12:3). To the Servant: I will make you as a light for the nations, that my salvation may reach to the end of the earth (Isaiah 49:6). By the end of this Gospel a Roman soldier will say the true thing about Jesus that none of the crowd said (15:39), and by Acts the list will have kept going until it reaches Rome.

When the great crowd heard all that he was doing, they came to him. Many came for healing. Be honest about why they came. Not for the teaching: Mark says they had heard what he was doing. This is a crowd assembled by reports of power, and within a few chapters much of it will be gone, because the day comes when he says something hard, and many of his disciples turned back and no longer walked with him (John 6:66).

Is a large crowd a sign of God’s blessing? Not by itself. Crowds gathered around Jesus, and crowds also shouted for his crucifixion. Some of the people on that shoreline came because of what they had heard he could give; some because of who he was. The beach looked identical either way, and only one of the two survives a hard winter. A large church may be blessed, or merely popular; a small one may be faithful, or merely stuck. The measure Jesus uses is not attendance but whether people hear his word and do it (v. 35). Pray for crowds, but pray more for disciples.

In a sentence. Jesus withdrew to the lake, and great crowds came from every region, Jewish and Gentile, having heard of his works.

On a Tuesday. As the leaders plotted against Jesus, the crowds came to him. Opposition does not stop people coming to Christ. Ask yourself the question that shoreline asks. What brought you to Jesus? And, more to the point, what is keeping you? If the honest answer is only what he might give, ask him to show you himself.

For worship. They came from the north and the south, from Edom and from Tyre, and he received them all. The promise to Abraham was being kept on a Galilean beach: the families of the earth were coming to the Seed in whom they would be blessed. He is the light for the nations, and the crowd on that shore was only the first trickle of a river that has not stopped flowing, and will not stop until a multitude no one can number stands before his throne.
verseByVerse.note: Idumea (old Edom) lay south of Judea; Tyre and Sidon were Gentile port cities on the coast to the north. The crowd came from every direction.

verseByVerse.quote: And he told his disciples to have a boat ready for him because of the crowd, lest they crush him, for he had healed many, so that all who had diseases pressed around him to touch him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus told his disciples to have a small boat ready for him because of the crowd, so that they would not crush him. For he had healed many, so that all who had diseases pressed around him to touch him.

And he told his disciples to have a boat ready for him because of the crowd. Here is a detail nobody expects in a Gospel: Jesus arranges an escape route. A small fishing boat kept just offshore, a few yards out, so he could step off the shore if the crowd pressed too hard, and teach from it (4:1). Not to sail anywhere, but as a platform and a way out.

Lest they crush him. The crowd was dangerous. The verb is the one you would use of a mob pressing a man against a wall. Understand what was actually happening on that beach. This is not an audience. It is a crowd of desperate, sick, frightened people who have heard that touching this man works, and every one of them wants to get a hand on him. There were children in that crowd. People got hurt in crowds like that. And Jesus, who could have stilled them with a sentence, quietly asks his friends to get a boat.

He did not despise the means. Sit with that, because it is more pastoral than it looks. The Son of God, in a real human body with a real human back and real human exhaustion, took an ordinary practical precaution. He did not stand there and let himself be trampled to prove something about faith. Jesus did not meet every need that presented itself, and he did not stay available every hour that people wanted him. He withdrew (v. 7). He slept in boats (4:38). He got up before dawn and went where they could not find him (1:35). He let a crowd stand on a beach while he pushed out a few yards into the water.

Isn’t it selfish to set limits when people need me? No, it is creaturely. Being finite is not a character flaw; it is how you were made, and the Lord himself lived within it. The needs around you are genuinely infinite and you are genuinely not, and pretending otherwise is not devotion; it is a slow way of becoming useless to everybody. If you are the person everyone comes to, in a family, a church or a job, take the boat. Rest, sleep, say no to some things, let others help. The aim is not to protect your comfort but to stay able to serve for the long haul. And remember that you are not the Saviour. He is, and he is not finite.

For he had healed many, so that all who had diseases pressed around him to touch him. Mark gives the reason for the crush almost as an aside. Many: so many that the beach became dangerous. Diseases (mastigas) literally means whips or scourges: afflictions that had flogged people for years, and Mark does not tidy them up. They believed that touching him would heal them (5:27–29; 6:56). And notice that he heals them. This is a crowd with no theology, no invitation and no understanding of who he is; they are simply people in pain who have heard he helps, mobbing him so hard he needs an exit. He does not lecture them about their motives first. He heals them.

In a sentence. The crowd seeking healing pressed so hard that Jesus had a boat ready in case they crushed him.

On a Tuesday. Many came to Jesus for what he could give them. Do you come for his gifts, or for him? And yet remember the mercy here when you come to him yourself with mixed motives and a bad attitude, wanting relief far more than you want him. He has never yet turned away a person for coming to him badly. Come as the crowd came, and let him sort out your motives once you are near enough for him to reach. And if you are worn out, look at your week for the boat: the hour of rest, the help you have refused to ask for.

For worship. The whips of disease had scourged them for years, and they pressed on him to be free of them. One day the whips would fall on him, and he would bear the scourging that heals. With his wounds we are healed. He took a real body, with real limits, and he spent it on people who did not understand him, until there was nothing left to give but his life, and he gave that too.

verseByVerse.quote: And whenever the unclean spirits saw him, they fell down before him and cried out, "You are the Son of God." And he strictly ordered them not to make him known.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Whenever the unclean spirits saw him, they fell down before him and cried out: you are the Son of God. And he strictly ordered them not to make him known.

And whenever the unclean spirits saw him, they fell down before him. Not in worship but in terror, acknowledging his authority. In that whole heaving crowd, hundreds of people from six regions, apostles included, the only voices saying anything theologically exact belong to the demons. Mark’s word is the ordinary word for prostration, the posture of worship. They are not doing it willingly; they are doing it because in his presence they cannot do anything else. It is a small, involuntary rehearsal of a day that is coming, when at the name of Jesus every knee should bow, in heaven and on earth and under the earth (Philippians 2:10). Every knee, including these. The only question any creature gets to decide is whether it bows now in love or later in ruin.

And cried out, “You are the Son of God”. The demons know who he is (1:24, 34). It is the truth Mark announced in his first verse and the Father spoke at the Jordan (1:11). It is more than the disciples have managed to say, more than the crowd has understood, and more than the scribes will allow. The people and even the disciples do not yet see it clearly. And it does the demons no good at all.

A creed can be word-perfect and worthless. Take hold of that, because it dismantles something many people are resting on. James puts it without cushioning: you believe that God is one; you do well. Even the demons believe, and shudder (James 2:19). These spirits have better Christology than most of the crowd. They fall down, which is more than the Pharisees did. They confess his identity aloud, which is more than Peter has yet done. And they remain exactly what they are. The difference between the demons’ confession and a Christian’s is not accuracy. One says you are the Son of God and means keep away from me; the other says the same words and means have me. Mark will end this very chapter by showing you which you are: not by what you can recite, but by whether you do the will of God (v. 35).

And he strictly ordered them not to make him known. The order is forceful. Jesus would not accept testimony from demons. The truth about the Son of God is not going to be carried on the tongue of the father of lies; that commission belongs to a fisherman, a tax collector, a Zealot, and to you. And he would not have his identity broadcast before people understood that the Son of God must suffer (8:29–31). In Galilee in that decade, Son of God shouted over a crowd of thousands would have been heard as a call to arms, a king to drive out Rome. Jesus will not be crowned before he is crucified. The messianic secret runs through Mark: his full identity will be revealed at the cross, where a Roman officer says the words at the foot of it (15:39), and nobody can mistake what kind of King he is.

If every knee will bow, will everyone be saved in the end? No. Every knee will bow, but not every knee will bow in love. The demons here bow and remain his enemies. Paul’s words in Philippians 2 describe the universal acknowledgement of Christ’s lordship on the last day, willing or unwilling. Scripture is clear that those who reject Christ will go away into eternal punishment, and the righteous into eternal life (Matthew 25:46). That is why the invitation is so urgent now. Today you may bow willingly and be received as a child. One day you will bow regardless. Bow now.

In a sentence. The demons fell before Jesus and called him the Son of God, but he ordered them to be silent.

On a Tuesday. The demons knew the truth about Jesus and remained his enemies. Knowing is not enough; trust him. Could you tick every box on a statement of faith and still be, in your own heart, at a distance from the Person the statements are about? Take one true thing you believe about Christ and turn it into a prayer of trust and love today. Doctrine is meant to be prayed.

For worship. Hell itself falls on its face before him. The spirits that terrorised men across Galilee could not stand upright in his presence. He is the Son of God, and the powers of darkness know it and tremble. And the same Lord before whom demons cower calls sinners to come near and bow in love, and lifts them up as brothers and sisters. Every knee will bow to him. Blessed are those who bow now, gladly, and call him Lord.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 13–35 — The Twelve, the Accusation, and the True Family
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The mountain (vv. 13–19). Jesus goes up, calls whom he wants, and constitutes twelve men — a number nobody in Israel could hear innocently. The stated purpose comes in two halves in a deliberate order: that they might be with him, and that he might send them out. The list ends on a name that ruins it.

The two accusations (vv. 20–22). Back at the house the pressure is such that they cannot even eat, and two verdicts arrive from opposite directions. His family says he is out of his mind and comes to take him home. A delegation from Jerusalem says he is possessed and works by the prince of demons. Both agree something is badly wrong with him; they differ only on whether he is mad or evil.

The answer (vv. 23–27). Jesus takes the charge apart with cold logic and then turns it round: the reason demons are leaving is that a stronger man has broken into the house, tied up the owner, and is carrying out his property.

The warning and the family (vv. 28–35). The widest promise of forgiveness in the Gospel, with one terrible exception attached — and then his mother and brothers arrive outside, and he looks round at the people sitting on the floor and calls them his family.
verseByVerse.theology:
The strong man of v. 27 is the hinge of the chapter and of the Gospel. Jesus concedes the scribes' premise that there is a real kingdom of darkness with a real ruler and a securely held house. What he denies is which side of the door he is on. He is not an agent of the owner. He is the burglar.

And the order in the picture is exact: the binding comes first, the plundering after. You cannot carry off a strong man's goods while he is loose. Every exorcism in Mark, every healing, every sinner set free, is loot being carried out of a house whose owner has already been tied up. This is why the New Testament can speak of Christians as people delivered us from the domain of darkness and transferred us to the kingdom of his beloved Son (Col. 1:13) — transferred is a word for moving property.

Then ask when the binding happened, and the answer is the surprise at the centre of the faith. He bound the strong man by being bound himself. He disarmed the rulers and authorities and put them to open shame, triumphing over them in him — in the cross (Col. 2:15). The strong man was tied up by a stronger man who let himself be tied up first, so that through death he might destroy the one who has the power of death (Heb. 2:14).
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: twelve men appointed so that they might be with him — and only then be sent out. A long season of watching him pray, eat, weep, touch lepers, sleep in boats, before they were first sent out to preach (6:7-13).

Now: the order is still not negotiable, and it is still the thing we reverse. It is entirely possible to be extremely busy for God and scarcely ever with him — to run a rota, lead a group, defend the faith online, and go months without an unhurried hour in his company. The activity is not the problem; the sequence is. Ministry that does not flow out of being with Jesus becomes performance, and performance eventually becomes exhaustion or pride, and often both.

The plainest way to test it is the calendar. Look at last week honestly. How much of it was doing things for him, and how much was being with him? If the first number is large and the second is near zero, you have inverted verse 14, and no amount of usefulness will make up for it — because the sending was never meant to be the source of the strength.

And there is comfort in the same verse for the person who cannot do much at all: the first calling on every disciple is one that illness, age and obscurity cannot take away.

verseByVerse.quote: And he went up on the mountain and called to him those whom he desired, and they came to him. And he appointed twelve (whom he also named apostles) so that they might be with him and he might send them out to preach and have authority to cast out demons.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus went up on the mountain and called to him those he wanted, and they came to him. He appointed twelve, whom he also named apostles, to be with him, and to send them out to preach and to have authority to cast out demons.

And he went up on the mountain. Mountains are places of revelation and covenant in Scripture: Sinai, where God formed Israel. Mark does not name this one, and the vagueness is a signal. In the Bible, going up a mountain to constitute a people is not a neutral piece of travel. Moses went up and came down with a nation ordered around twelve tribes. Luke adds that Jesus spent the whole night there in prayer before he chose (Luke 6:12).

And called to him those whom he desired. Jesus’ choice, by his will. Sit on that phrase, because it decides who is in charge. Not those who volunteered, not those who qualified: those whom he wanted. They did not volunteer; he chose them. You did not choose me, but I chose you (John 15:16). If you belong to Christ today, that is the reason. Not that you were searching harder than your neighbour or that something in you recommended itself. He wanted you. There is nothing behind that but his own good pleasure, which is exactly why nothing can get behind it and undo it.

And they came to him. Four words that are easy to skip, and they are half the doctrine. He calls, and they come. His wanting produces their coming. The call is not an offer left on the table but a summons that creates the answer, the way the same voice once said let there be light, and there was light.

Does those whom he desired mean that God chooses who will be saved? Yes, and that is a comfort, not a threat. This verse is about the choice of the Twelve for their office, but it shows the pattern of all God’s saving work. Scripture teaches that God chose his people in Christ before the foundation of the world, not because of anything foreseen in them but in love, according to the purpose of his will (Ephesians 1:4–5), and that those he calls he effectually draws (John 6:44). This never makes anyone’s coming unreal: they truly came. And it never closes the door on anyone who wants to come, for whoever comes to Christ will never be cast out (John 6:37). If you have come, it is because he wanted you first, and he will not let you go.

And he appointed twelve. Literally he made twelve. Nobody in Israel could hear that number innocently. Twelve sons of Jacob, twelve tribes, twelve stones on the high priest’s breastplate, twelve pillars at the foot of Sinai. Ten of those tribes had been scattered for seven hundred years, and the prophets had promised they would be gathered again. Jesus does not preach a sermon about restoring Israel. He appoints twelve men, and every Jew watching understands that a claim has been made without a word of argument. This is Israel, beginning again, around him: the restored people of God.

Whom he also named apostles. Apostle means one who is sent, an envoy carrying the sender’s authority. Some manuscripts omit this phrase here; it is certainly in Luke 6:13.

So that they might be with him. The first purpose of the Twelve, and it is not what a modern reader expects. Not so that they might be trained, deployed or made useful. So that they might be with him. Their first job description is his company. Before they could be sent, they had to spend time with him, learning from him. Take the measure of that. These men are about to spend three years mostly watching: watching him pray before dawn, watching him handle a hostile room, watching what he does when he is tired and interrupted, watching him touch a leper and eat with the wrong people. Almost none of it will feel like ministry. All of it is the training. Ministry flows from relationship.

And he might send them out to preach. The second purpose: mission, proclaiming the kingdom. And the two are in an order that never reverses. Sent men are with-him men first. You cannot go out with his authority if you have not been in his company, and the moment a church or a Christian swaps those round, the work starts to hollow out from the inside. That is the diagnosis for a very common kind of Christian tiredness. Not too much work, but too much work fed from too little Christ: a rota, a group, an argument to win online, and months without an unhurried hour with him. Verse 14 is the cure, and it is very simple: go back and be with him.

And have authority to cast out demons. Sharing his power over evil (6:7, 13).

Do Christians have this authority today? Many Pentecostal and charismatic Christians believe they do, and practise deliverance ministry, and they are often sincere brothers and sisters. But this authority was given to the Twelve when Jesus sent them out, as part of the signs that marked the apostles (2 Corinthians 12:12). The New Testament letters never tell believers to cast out demons. They tell them to resist the devil (James 4:7), to put on God’s armour (Ephesians 6:10–18), and to pray. The devil is real and still works, but Christ has bound the strong man (3:27), and the believer facing evil fights with the word, prayer and the fellowship of the church.

In a sentence. On a mountain, Jesus chose twelve, to be with him and to be sent out to preach with authority over demons.

On a Tuesday. Before you serve Jesus, spend time with him. Service that does not flow from being with him runs dry. Look at your week: how much of it is for him, and how much of it is with him? And there is a mercy here for anyone who can no longer do much of anything: the elderly, the ill, the housebound, the one whose usefulness has been taken away. The first calling on every disciple is one no illness can revoke. You are called to be with him, and you can do that from a bed.

For worship. He went up the mountain and called those whom he desired, and they came. The Lord of the new Israel chose his people before they could choose him, and called them first of all to himself. He wants our company before our work. What a Master, who calls servants to be friends, and sends them out only after he has drawn them in.
verseByVerse.note: “Apostle” means one who is sent.

parallels.desc: the Twelve and the twelve tribes

verseByVerse.quote: He appointed the twelve: Simon (to whom he gave the name Peter); James the son of Zebedee and John the brother of James (to whom he gave the name Boanerges, that is, Sons of Thunder); Andrew, and Philip, and Bartholomew, and Matthew, and Thomas, and James the son of Alphaeus, and Thaddaeus, and Simon the Zealot,
verseByVerse.commentary:
He appointed the twelve: Simon, whom he named Peter; James son of Zebedee and his brother John, whom he named Boanerges, that is, sons of thunder; Andrew, Philip, Bartholomew, Matthew, Thomas, James son of Alphaeus, Thaddaeus, Simon the Zealot.

Simon (to whom he gave the name Peter). Mark writes out the names, and they are worth reading slowly, because a list is easy to skim and this one is an argument. Peter (Petros) means rock. A new name meant a new identity and calling: not a nickname but a verdict spoken in advance. When it was given, Simon was anything but a rock: impulsive, loud and less than three years from swearing in a courtyard that he had never met the man. Peter was impulsive and unstable at first; Jesus named him for what grace would make him, not for what he was. That is how the Lord speaks to his people. He calls into existence the things that do not exist.

James the son of Zebedee and John the brother of James (to whom he gave the name Boanerges, that is, Sons of Thunder). Only Mark records this nickname, from Aramaic. It is a name with a smile in it and an edge under the smile, and it probably described their fiery temperament. These are the brothers who wanted to call down fire on a Samaritan village that would not receive him (Luke 9:54), and who came privately to ask for the two best seats in the kingdom (10:35–40). Jesus knew their temperament on the day he chose them, gave it a name, and appointed them anyway. He was not recruiting finished men. And John, the son of thunder, became the apostle of love (1 John 4:7–21). Jesus transforms temperaments.

Andrew. Peter’s brother, who was there first (John 1:40–42), and who spends his whole New Testament career bringing people to Jesus and then disappearing: his brother, a boy with some bread and fish, some Greeks who asked to see him. He is the younger brother, never at the head of a list, and he never shows any sign of minding. If your service is small and nobody attaches your name to it, Andrew is your man.

And Philip, and Bartholomew, and Matthew, and Thomas, and James the son of Alphaeus, and Thaddaeus. Bartholomew is probably Nathanael (John 1:45). Matthew is Levi, the tax collector of chapter 2 (2:14), the collaborator whose repentance his own religion had judged impossible. Thaddaeus is probably the Judas son of James of Luke 6:16. Several of these men say little or nothing in the New Testament. There is no recorded sermon of Thaddaeus. We have not one line from James the son of Alphaeus. They were with him for three years and are known to history as a name in a list, and their names are written on the foundations of the city of God (Revelation 21:14). If it troubles you that your life will leave no trace anyone can point to, look hard at the middle of this list.

And Simon the Zealot. Literally the Cananaean, from the Aramaic for zealous. He may have belonged to the Zealots, who wanted to overthrow Rome by force; at the least the name points to burning zeal for Israel and the law, the mood in which a Jew who collected Rome’s money was a traitor who deserved a knife. Now do the arithmetic Mark expects you to do. In any other year of history, Simon the Zealot’s ambition would have been to kill a man like Matthew. Jesus placed a former Roman collaborator and a former anti-Roman revolutionary in the same group. They walked the same roads for three years, ate from the same bag and slept in the same fields. Nothing in the politics of the day could have reconciled them; nothing did, except the man in the middle. In his kingdom, enemies become brothers.

Can my temperament really change? Yes, though usually slowly and never by willpower alone. The Spirit does not turn you into someone else; he makes you more truly yourself, with the sin burned out of your strengths. Peter stayed bold, but his boldness became courage for Christ. John stayed intense, but his intensity became love. Bring your temperament honestly to Christ: the temper, the anxiety, the coldness, the need to control. Name it, confess its sinful expressions, ask for the fruit of the Spirit (Galatians 5:22–23), and stay close to him and to his people. Look back in ten years, not ten days.

In a sentence. Jesus appointed twelve very different men, giving Peter and the sons of Zebedee new names that described what he would make of them.

On a Tuesday. Jesus puts very different people together in his church, and transforms their temperaments. Who in your church is very different from you, in politics, background or personality? Love them as family. If the church you attend contains people you would never otherwise have chosen, it is working. Seek out one of them this Sunday.

For worship. That is the church from the first day it had members: people with nothing in common but Christ, which turned out to be more than everything they had against each other. He named a wavering fisherman a rock and made him one. He tamed thunder into love. He wrote unknown names into the foundations of the eternal city. The Lord who chose these men chooses still, and he finishes what he begins.
verseByVerse.note: Peter means “rock.” Thaddaeus is probably the “Judas the son of James” of Luke’s lists.

verseByVerse.quote: and Judas Iscariot, who betrayed him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And Judas Iscariot, who betrayed him.

And Judas Iscariot. Mark has been listing names in a plain, unhurried way, and then the sentence ends and the floor gives way. Judas is always last in the lists, and every list of the Twelve in the Gospels attaches a clause about the betrayal. Nobody could say the name afterwards without saying what he did. Iscariot is often taken to mean man of Kerioth, a town in southern Judea, which would make him the only one of the Twelve not from Galilee; but that is uncertain. Other suggestions link it to an Aramaic word for false one, or to a word for an assassin’s dagger.

Who betrayed him. Mark tells the reader from the start how the story will go. And Judas was appointed on the mountain with the rest. He was called by name. He was there to be with him for three years: at the feeding of the five thousand, at every private explanation of every parable. He was sent out with the others to preach and given authority to cast out demons (6:7, 13), and there is no hint that his mission failed or that the others suspected him. When Jesus said at the last supper that one of them would betray him, nobody turned and looked at Judas. They each asked whether it was themselves (14:19). Judas shared everything: the teaching, the miracles, the mission. And still he betrayed him. Being close to Jesus, and even serving in his name, is not the same as belonging to him.

Did Jesus know? Yes. Jesus chose Judas knowingly (John 6:70). John says it without qualification: Jesus knew from the beginning who those were who did not believe, and who it was who would betray him (John 6:64). The appointment of Judas was not an error later regretted. And there is a strange comfort in it for anyone who has been betrayed by someone close. Your Lord chose his betrayer with his eyes open, kept him at his own table, washed his feet, and called him friend in the garden. He was not caught out. Nothing that has been done to you has caught him out either.

What it does not mean. Not that Judas was forced to betray Jesus. God’s plan included the betrayal (Acts 2:23), and Judas acted freely and was responsible (14:21). Mark holds the two together without embarrassment: the Son of Man goes as it is written of him, but woe to that man by whom the Son of Man is betrayed. It was written, and he did it, and he is answerable for it. Both.

Can I fall away like Judas? This is the question that keeps sensitive people awake, so let it be answered plainly. Judas was never a believer who lost his salvation; he was a man who was near Christ without ever being in Christ, and John names the mechanism: he was a thief, and having charge of the moneybag he used to help himself to what was put into it (John 12:6). The rot was private, ordinary and financial, and it ran for years under a spotless public record. He did not fall in one night; he arrived at that night. So no, a true believer cannot be snatched out of the Father’s hand (John 10:28–29). But do not use that as a reason to skip the examination; use it as the reason you can bear to make it. The honest test is not whether you have ever sinned badly. Peter denied him with oaths that same week and was restored on a beach. The test is what you do afterwards. Judas felt remorse, threw the money into the temple and went out to a rope. Peter wept, and came back. Remorse looks at itself and despairs; repentance turns to Christ and lives. If you fear you are a Judas, that fear is not the mark of a Judas. Go to Christ with the thing you are afraid of. That is the one move Judas never made, and it was always open to him.

In a sentence. The last of the Twelve was Judas Iscariot, the one who would betray Jesus.

On a Tuesday. Judas warns us that outward closeness to Jesus is not enough. Examine your heart. Is there a private sin, small and ordinary, that you have been feeding for a long time under a respectable surface: money, lust, resentment? Bring it into the light this week, to God and to one trusted believer. Rot that is confessed cannot keep spreading in the dark.

For worship. He knew, and he chose him anyway, and loved him to the end, and washed his feet. The patience of Christ with Judas is beyond our understanding. And the betrayal that Judas planned in darkness God turned into the light of the world’s salvation: the Son of Man was handed over, as it was written, to be handed over for our trespasses and raised for our justification. No treachery has ever defeated his purpose, and none ever will.
verseByVerse.note: “Iscariot” is often taken to mean “man of Kerioth,” a town in Judea, but that is uncertain.

verseByVerse.quote: Then he went home, and the crowd gathered again, so that they could not even eat. And when his family heard it, they went out to seize him, for they were saying, "He is out of his mind."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then Jesus went home, and the crowd gathered again, so that they could not even eat. When his family heard it, they went out to seize him, for they were saying: he is out of his mind.

Then he went home. Probably to the house in Capernaum (2:1), presumably Peter’s.

And the crowd gathered again, so that they could not even eat. The demands were relentless. Mark keeps giving us these small physical details, and they are not decoration. Not that they could not rest, or could not talk: they could not eat. The Son of God missed meals because of the volume of human need at the door. That household was chaotic, exhausting and loud, and had been for weeks.

And when his family heard it, they went out to seize him. Word travels some twenty-five miles to Nazareth: the crowds, the missed meals, the confrontation with the authorities, the reports of demons and healings, the delegation on its way from Jerusalem. His family (literally those beside him) means his relatives. They came from Nazareth to take him home by force. Verse 31 shows that his mother and brothers were among them. The verb is strong and physical, to take hold of, to arrest, the same word used later of the mob that comes for him in the garden (14:46). They are not coming to encourage him. They intend to take him home before he embarrasses the family any further or gets himself killed.

For they were saying, “He is out of his mind”. Out of his mind (exestē) means beside himself, mad. His family thought he had lost his senses: neglecting food, provoking the authorities, claiming divine authority. They probably meant well, trying to protect him and the family’s reputation. But they did not understand him. His brothers did not believe in him until after the resurrection (John 7:5; Acts 1:14).

The structure. Mark tells this story in two parts, with the accusation of the scribes sandwiched in between (vv. 22–30). His family thinks he is mad; the scribes say he is demon-possessed. Both are wrong. The sandwich invites comparison: his family’s misunderstanding, though less hostile, is uncomfortably close to the scribes’ rejection.

Mary among them. Verse 31 names who came, and the first name on the list is his mother. Mary, who had heard the angel; who had said, let it be to me according to your word; who had been told her son would be called the Son of the Most High; who had treasured the shepherds’ words in her heart (Luke 1:26–38; 2:19). And here she is on the road to Capernaum with her other sons, to take this one home before it gets worse. Mary was not a woman of flawless, finished faith standing serenely above the confusion of ordinary disciples. She was a real disciple, and like every real disciple she had to grow, her understanding stretched, corrected and deepened, sometimes painfully. And that is an encouragement rather than a scandal, because of where her story goes. The Mary who stands outside here is the Mary who stands at the foot of the cross when nearly all the Twelve have run (John 19:25), and who is found praying with the believers after the resurrection (Acts 1:14). She moved from outside to inside, from misunderstanding to worship. So if your own coming to Christ has been uneven, with long stretches where you did not understand him at all, you are in the company of his mother.

What it does not mean. Not that Mary had lost all faith. But she too struggled to understand her son’s mission (Luke 2:50). Mark shows honestly that even Jesus’ family did not grasp who he was.

Should I neglect food and rest for ministry, as Jesus did here? Not as a rule. This was a season of extraordinary demand, and the same Gospel shows Jesus withdrawing, sleeping, and later telling his disciples to come away by themselves and rest a while, because they had no leisure even to eat (6:31). There are times when love means missing a meal or a night’s sleep for someone in crisis, and that is right. But a life that never eats, never rests and never stops is not more spiritual; it is usually less wise. Jesus’ family were wrong about his sanity, but your family may be right about your exhaustion. Listen to them.

In a sentence. When crowds kept Jesus from even eating, his family came to take him home, thinking he was out of his mind.

On a Tuesday. If your family thinks your devotion to Christ is excessive, remember that Jesus’ family thought the same about him. Keep loving them. Your Lord felt that wound first, and from the people who knew him best. He did not harden against them, and he did not let it turn him aside from the will of God. He kept doing what his Father sent him to do and stayed tender toward them while he did it. By the end, his brother James is writing to the church as a servant of God and of the Lord Jesus Christ (James 1:1), and his mother is in the prayer meeting. Pray for your family by name today, and do one kind thing for one of them.

For worship. They called him mad, the people who had watched him grow up, and he went on loving them. The Son of God bore the misunderstanding of his own household, as he would bear the rejection of his own nation, and he did not stop until they were brought in. His brother who thought him out of his mind became a pillar of his church; his mother became his disciple. He is patient beyond all our patience, and his love outlasts our blindness.
verseByVerse.note: “His family” means his relatives.

parallels.desc: even his brothers did not believe

verseByVerse.quote: And the scribes who came down from Jerusalem were saying, "He is possessed by Beelzebul," and "by the prince of demons he casts out the demons."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The scribes who came down from Jerusalem said: he is possessed by Beelzebul, and he casts out the demons by the prince of demons.

And the scribes who came down from Jerusalem. The second verdict arrives from the opposite direction, and this one has credentials. Not local critics but an official delegation from the religious capital, sent to investigate. Jerusalem is high in the hills; people went up to it and down from it, whatever the compass said. These are the professionals, the men whose judgment carries weight, and they have travelled ninety miles to give it.

What they cannot do. They cannot deny the exorcisms, and that is worth pausing over, because it is often assumed that Jesus’ opponents thought the miracles were tricks. They did not. The people best placed to expose a fraud, with every professional motive to do so, concede the events and dispute only the power behind them. The evidence was not in question in Galilee. The explanation was.

He is possessed by Beelzebul. Beelzebul is a name for Satan (v. 23). Behind it stands Baal-zebub, the god of the Philistine city of Ekron whom King Ahaziah sent to consult (2 Kings 1:2), meaning lord of the flies, or Baal-zebul, lord of the dwelling. By Jesus’ day it had settled as a title for the prince of demons. They accuse Jesus of being in league with the devil, and more: that the man himself is occupied by him.

And by the prince of demons he casts out the demons. They could not deny his exorcisms, so they explained them: he has Satan’s power, so he can command Satan’s underlings. It was the most serious charge possible, and a deliberate rejection of the evidence.

Three verdicts. Notice the two accusations Mark has set side by side. His family says he is mad; the theologians say he is evil. Between them they cover the ground people have covered ever since, because there have only ever been three verdicts available on Jesus of Nazareth, and the third one is expensive. He is deluded, or he is dangerous, or he is what he says he is. What is not on the menu, never was, in Capernaum or now, is the comfortable modern option of a wise and gentle teacher whom everyone can admire. Nobody who actually met him thought that. They loved him or they wanted him dead.

Why didn’t the miracles convince them, and would miracles convince people today? These scribes had the best religious education in the world. They had the Scriptures largely by memory. They had walked ninety miles and watched the power of God set human beings free before their eyes, and they went home and wrote it up as demonic. The problem was never the evidence. When a heart has decided, it will build a theology to house the decision, and the better educated it is, the better the theology it can build. Abraham said the same in Jesus’ parable: if they do not hear Moses and the Prophets, neither will they be convinced if someone should rise from the dead (Luke 16:31). Evidence matters, and Christianity rests on it, but only the Spirit opens closed hearts. So when you share the faith, give reasons, and pray.

In a sentence. Scribes from Jerusalem claimed that Jesus was possessed by Satan and cast out demons by his power.

On a Tuesday. People who refuse to accept Jesus will find explanations for the evidence. Do you look for reasons to believe, or reasons to dismiss? Notice where in your own life you have already decided against something Jesus says, and are now collecting arguments to support the decision. Bring that to him honestly.

For worship. The professionals of Jerusalem called the Holy One unclean, and he bore it. The Son of God, full of the Spirit beyond measure, was called the house of Beelzebul by men who had seen his mercy with their own eyes. He endured such hostility from sinners against himself, and he endured it for sinners. He is what he says he is: the Lord, the Son of God, and the Saviour of the people who slandered him.
verseByVerse.note: Beelzebul is a name for Satan (v. 23).

verseByVerse.quote: And he called them to him and said to them in parables, "How can Satan cast out Satan? If a kingdom is divided against itself, that kingdom cannot stand. And if a house is divided against itself, that house will not be able to stand. And if Satan has risen up against himself and is divided, he cannot stand, but is coming to an end.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus called them and spoke to them in parables: how can Satan cast out Satan? If a kingdom is divided against itself, that kingdom cannot stand. If a house is divided against itself, it will not be able to stand. And if Satan has risen up against himself and is divided, he cannot stand, but is coming to an end.

And he called them to him and said to them in parables. Before a word of the argument, notice this. They have just accused him of being possessed by the devil, and his response is to invite them closer. He does not shout it across the room or dismiss them behind their backs. He calls the men who have slandered him into conversation. Parables here means picture-sayings, comparisons. Jesus answers his accusers directly.

How can Satan cast out Satan? Then he takes the charge apart, with cold logic rather than outrage. The accusation is absurd. Why would Satan destroy his own work, freeing the people he has enslaved? When the most serious accusation in the Gospel is laid against him, Jesus reasons. There is a place for argument in the defence of the faith, and the Lord uses it.

If a kingdom is divided against itself, that kingdom cannot stand. Civil war destroys nations. Everyone in that room knew the history of a divided kingdom. Israel had split in two after Solomon and the northern half was gone for ever; and they lived in the aftermath of Rome’s own civil wars.

And if a house is divided against itself, that house will not be able to stand. Division destroys families. Smaller and closer: anyone who has watched a family tear itself apart over money or a grievance knows the proof without needing the argument.

And if Satan has risen up against himself and is divided, he cannot stand, but is coming to an end. There is the trap closing. The scribes’ theory requires that the devil has begun a public campaign of expelling his own troops from the people he had captured, dismantling his own operation with visible success. If that were true, their theory has just announced the end of the kingdom of darkness, which is exactly what they came to deny. Either the exorcisms are not from Satan, or Satan is finished. If Jesus were Satan’s agent, Satan would be destroying himself. But in fact Satan is coming to an end, not because he is divided, but because someone stronger has come (v. 27).

How Jesus argues. Two things to take from this. First, he grants them what is true. Jesus does not say there is no devil, no kingdom of darkness, no organised opposition. He concedes the framework and shows that it will not carry the weight they have put on it. That is how a Christian should handle an argument: take seriously what is right in it, and press the part that fails. Second, and more searchingly, an unanswerable argument changed nobody in that room. Jesus wins the exchange completely, and the scribes go home unmoved. Argument can clear away an obstacle, and it is worth making well. It has never yet, on its own, changed a heart. That work belongs to the Spirit, which is exactly the Person these men are about to be warned against resisting.

Does a house divided mean churches must never divide? Unity is precious, and most church splits come from pride, not principle; Paul begs believers to be eager to maintain the unity of the Spirit (Ephesians 4:3). So work hard for peace, forgive quickly, and do not leave over preferences. But Jesus’ point here is about Satan’s kingdom, not a rule that Christians must stay together whatever is taught. Where the gospel itself is denied, faithfulness may require separation (Galatians 1:8–9; 2 John 10–11). Even then, go with grief and humility, and never with contempt.

In a sentence. Jesus showed the accusation was absurd: if Satan cast out Satan, his kingdom would be destroying itself.

On a Tuesday. Division destroys. Guard the unity of your family and church. Is there a quarrel you are keeping alive, a grievance you are nursing, a person you have stopped speaking to? Take one step toward peace this week. And if you are burning to win an argument about the faith with someone you love, make your case well, gently, and then pray, because only the Spirit changes hearts.

For worship. He called his slanderers near and reasoned with them. The Lord of glory did not crush them with a word, though he could have. He answered them with patience and truth. And his kingdom is not divided: Father, Son and Spirit are one, perfectly at peace, working one salvation. The kingdom of darkness is coming to an end, and the kingdom of the Son will never end.

verseByVerse.quote: But no one can enter a strong man's house and plunder his goods, unless he first binds the strong man. Then indeed he may plunder his house.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But no one can enter a strong man’s house and plunder his goods unless he first binds the strong man. Then indeed he may plunder his house.

But no one can enter a strong man’s house and plunder his goods. Now Jesus stops defending and goes on the attack, with one picture that turns the accusation inside out. A house; a strong owner; goods stacked inside that are secure because he is strong enough to keep them; and a burglar who wants what is in there. The strong man is Satan. His house is the world, or the people he holds captive. His goods are the people under his power. Notice first what Jesus concedes. He does not deny that there is a strong man, or that the house has been securely held, or that the goods are really in his possession. The picture takes the kingdom of darkness seriously. And the goods are people: every possessed man in Galilee, every soul in the crowd on the beach, every reader of this page before Christ came for them.

Unless he first binds the strong man. To rob a strong man you must first overpower him and tie him up. Jesus is the one stronger than Satan. John the Baptist had called him the mightier one (1:7). Isaiah asks whether the prey can be taken from the mighty, and God answers that the captives of the mighty shall be taken and he himself will contend with the contender (Isaiah 49:24–25). Now the question the scribes have to answer: which man in this story is Jesus? They have said he is the owner’s agent. But nobody breaks into a house he already owns, and nobody carries off goods that are already his. Jesus is not in the house as the owner’s servant. He is in it as the raider, and the owner is on the floor with his hands tied. And the order is exact: binding first, plundering afterwards.

Then indeed he may plunder his house. Every exorcism, every healing, every sinner forgiven is Jesus plundering Satan’s house, freeing his captives. Every deliverance in this Gospel is not a skirmish but a removal van: furniture being carried out of a house whose owner has already been dealt with. The New Testament keeps the picture when it describes what happened to you: God delivered us from the domain of darkness and transferred us to the kingdom of his beloved Son (Colossians 1:13), and transferred is a word for moving property.

When was the strong man bound? The binding began in the wilderness (1:12–13) and was completed at the cross (Colossians 2:15; Hebrews 2:14–15). And here is the strangest and best turn in the faith. He was bound by a stronger man who let himself be bound first. In a garden, soldiers put their hands on Jesus and tied him, and he did not resist. They led him away bound to a high priest, bound to a governor, and fastened him to a cross with his arms open and immovable, the posture of a man who can plunder nothing. And that was the binding of Satan. He disarmed the rulers and authorities and put them to open shame, by triumphing over them in him (Colossians 2:15); through death he destroyed the one who has the power of death, that is, the devil (Hebrews 2:14). The strongest man who ever lived walked into the house, and instead of overpowering the owner he let the owner tie him up, and died, and that is how the ropes went onto the other pair of wrists.

What it does not mean. Not that Satan is now inactive. He still prowls like a roaring lion (1 Peter 5:8). But he cannot stop the gospel or hold those whom Christ frees. Revelation 20:1–3 pictures Satan bound so that he cannot deceive the nations; Reformed amillennialists see this binding as the present gospel age, begun at Christ’s first coming, during which the nations are being plundered by the gospel.

If Satan is bound, why is there still so much evil? Because a bound enemy can still do damage within the length of his chain. Satan is defeated but not yet destroyed; that final destruction comes at Christ’s return (Revelation 20:10). For now he cannot stop the spread of the gospel among the nations, or keep a single one of God’s elect in his house, or separate a believer from Christ. But he still tempts, accuses and deceives, and the world still groans under sin. Christians live between the binding and the end: the decisive battle won, the war not yet over. So we resist him firmly in the faith, knowing that the God of peace will soon crush Satan under our feet (Romans 16:20).

In a sentence. Jesus is the stronger one who has bound Satan and is now freeing his captives.

On a Tuesday. Whatever has bound you, Christ is stronger. Ask him to set you free. And if you are in Christ, understand what you are. You are not a volunteer who signed up. You are rescued property. You were in that house, and the owner had every claim on you, and you had no way out. Somebody broke in and carried you out over his shoulder, and the price of the raid was his life. Live today like someone who has been carried out.

For worship. Praise Christ, the stronger one, who walked into the strong man’s house and let himself be bound, and died, and in dying tied the hands of our captor. He plundered hell of its prisoners, and we are among the spoil. The Lord who was led away bound now holds the keys of death and Hades. Thanks be to God, who gives us the victory through our Lord Jesus Christ.

parallels.desc: the prey taken from the mighty

verseByVerse.quote: "Truly, I say to you, all sins will be forgiven the children of man, and whatever blasphemies they utter, but whoever blasphemes against the Holy Spirit never has forgiveness, but is guilty of an eternal sin"— for they were saying, "He has an unclean spirit."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Truly, all sins will be forgiven the children of man, and whatever blasphemies they utter, but whoever blasphemes against the Holy Spirit never has forgiveness, but is guilty of an eternal sin. For they were saying: he has an unclean spirit.

Truly, I say to you. A solemn statement of Jesus’ own authority. The word behind truly is amen, the formula Jesus uses to put his own authority behind a statement.

All sins will be forgiven the children of man, and whatever blasphemies they utter. A great promise. He begins with the widest promise in the Gospel, and it is important to take it at full strength before anything else is said. All of them. Not most. Not the respectable ones. All sins, and every blasphemy men speak: the things said in rage, the things said in a hospital corridor at three in the morning, the years spent mocking him, the words you would not repeat to another human being. No sin is too great to be forgiven if it is repented of. Paul was a blasphemer and was forgiven (1 Timothy 1:13). Do not hurry past this on the way to the exception. It is the most sweeping sentence about mercy Jesus ever spoke, and he spoke it to men who had just called the Holy Spirit a devil.

But whoever blasphemes against the Holy Spirit never has forgiveness, but is guilty of an eternal sin. Then the one exception, stated with the same solemnity, and there is no getting round how serious it is. What is it? Mark tells us in the next sentence, and that is the key that unlocks the whole passage.

For they were saying, “He has an unclean spirit”. Mark does not leave it floating as an abstract category. He anchors it in the specific thing happening in that room. The scribes saw the Holy Spirit’s work in Jesus clearly, and deliberately called it the work of Satan. They cannot deny the events; they have travelled ninety miles and seen them. And with full knowledge of what they are looking at, they call it the work of hell. This is blasphemy against the Spirit: not a careless word, not doubt, not confusion, but a settled, wilful rejection of the Spirit’s clear testimony to Christ, looking straight at the light and naming it darkness, and going on saying so. Mark’s tense is worth noting: they were saying it. It is not a slip but a position maintained. It is unforgivable not because God’s grace is too small, but because it rejects the only source of forgiveness. The Spirit is the one who convicts of sin and leads to Christ (John 16:8–11). A person who calls his work satanic has shut the door on the only way back. It is unforgivable because it is unrepented, and it is unrepented because the man committing it has no intention of repenting and no wish to be forgiven.

What it does not mean. Many anxious Christians fear they have committed this sin. If you are worried that you have, you have not. Those who commit it do not care; they are hardened. Anxiety about offending God is itself a sign of the Spirit at work in you. Nor is it a single doubt, or a terrible sin committed in weakness, even a sin of the tongue. It is a settled rejection of Christ in the face of the Spirit’s clear witness.

Have I committed it? Let the answer be given straight, because you may be living inside this question and you do not need a survey of opinions. If you are afraid you have committed the unforgivable sin, you have not committed it. That is not a comforting fiction. The sin is the final hardening of a heart against the Holy Spirit, a heart so calcified that it can see God at work and call it the devil without a tremor. Fear of this sin requires that you want to be forgiven, that you care what God thinks of you, that being cut off from him horrifies you. That does not come from a hardened heart. Hardened hearts do not lie awake worrying about their standing with God; they sleep very well. The scribes went home untroubled. Your distress is itself the evidence of a conscience still alive under the Spirit’s hand, and the Spirit does not trouble a man he has abandoned. The hardness that commits this sin does not tremble. It calculates.

A test you can run tonight. Can you say honestly that you want Christ, that if he would have you, you would come? Then come, because he has never once turned away anyone who did. Whoever comes to me I will never cast out (John 6:37), and there is no clause in that sentence excepting people who are afraid they have gone too far. A person who wants pardon is by definition not in the position of the scribes. Your fear is not your danger. It may well be the Spirit’s own work in you, drawing you toward the only place where fear is answered.

In a sentence. Every sin can be forgiven except deliberately calling the Spirit’s clear work in Jesus satanic, as the scribes were doing.

On a Tuesday. If you fear you have committed the unforgivable sin, your fear shows you have not. Come to Christ; he will not turn you away (John 6:37). If a friend is tormented by this question, read them verse 28 first, and then verse 30, and pray with them. And if your own heart has grown comfortable with resisting what you know God is showing you, do not wait. The way back is open today.

For worship. All sins, and whatever blasphemies: the mercy of God in Christ is wider than the worst we have done. He spoke that promise to the very men who were slandering him, and it still stands over every sinner who will come. The only door that is shut is the one a man bolts from the inside against the Spirit who would bring him home. For everyone who comes, the door stands open, and the Father runs to meet them.

verseByVerse.quote: And his mother and his brothers came, and standing outside they sent to him and called him. And a crowd was sitting around him, and they said to him, "Your mother and your brothers are outside, seeking you."
verseByVerse.commentary:
His mother and his brothers came, and standing outside they sent word to him and called him. A crowd was sitting around him, and they said to him: your mother and your brothers are outside, looking for you.

And his mother and his brothers came. The second half of the story begun in verse 21, and now, after all that, they arrive. Mark has been building to this since verse 21. The family set out to seize him; the delegation from Jerusalem accused him; the argument about Satan and the strong man has been made; the terrible warning has been given. And into that room, at that moment, a message comes from the door. They had come to take him home.

And standing outside they sent to him and called him. Outside: Mark says it twice (vv. 31, 32), and the word carries the whole scene. Physically and spiritually, they stood outside the circle around him. The house is packed with people sitting on the floor around him, close enough to touch him, and his own mother is in the street sending a message in. They do not come in. They send for him, which is what you do when you expect to be obeyed. It is the summons of family authority, a mother and her grown sons requiring the eldest to come out to them, and we know from verse 21 what they intend to do when he does.

And a crowd was sitting around him. Inside, listening to his teaching: the posture of disciples (Luke 10:39).

Your mother and your brothers are outside, seeking you. The crowd relays it, perhaps helpfully, perhaps enjoying the interruption. And here is the geography of the whole chapter in one sentence: nearness is not the same as belonging. You can be his mother and be outside. You can have carried him, fed him, watched him grow and known him better than anyone alive, and be in the street while a crowd of strangers sits at his feet.

Who were his brothers? Jesus’ brothers were James, Joses, Judas and Simon (6:3), most naturally Mary’s later children. Matthew names them and adds sisters (Matthew 13:55–56); John says that not even his brothers believed in him (John 7:5); and Acts sets them beside Mary but apart from the apostles (Acts 1:14). Two other views arose in the early church, both to protect the belief that Mary remained a virgin all her life: that they were Joseph’s sons by an earlier marriage, or that they were cousins. But Scripture never says either, and Matthew says that Joseph knew her not until she had given birth to a son (Matthew 1:25), which most naturally implies that afterwards they lived as husband and wife. The more likely reading is that these were Jesus’ younger brothers. It does not lessen Mary’s honour as the mother of our Lord.

In the room, or at the door? This is the most searching thing in the passage for religious people, and it is not really about Mary. It is about anyone whose connection to Christ is a matter of nearness rather than surrender. Raised in it, related to it, married into it, employed by it, on the rota, in the building, known by name to everyone in the congregation, and still functionally outside, sending messages in, wanting Christ to come out and fit into a life that has been organised without him. So ask, without panic but without dodging it: am I in the room, or at the door? Not, have I been around this a long time; the family had been around him for thirty years. The question is whether you have sat down in front of him as one of the people who wants what he says more than you want him manageable.

In a sentence. Jesus’ mother and brothers stood outside and sent for him, while the crowd sat around him inside.

On a Tuesday. It is possible to be close to Jesus by family or background and still stand outside. Come in and sit at his feet. Notice where you are trying to summon Christ out to fit your plans, rather than going in to hear what he says. And if someone you love is still outside, take heart from this family: nobody in that street was beyond the reach of the man in that house.

For worship. There is real hope in the fact that Mark names them, because they did not stay outside. The woman in the street in Capernaum stood at the cross when the disciples had scattered, and prayed with the church after the resurrection. The brothers who did not believe at all became believers; one of them led the church in Jerusalem and wrote the letter of James, calling himself the servant of the Lord Jesus Christ, and another wrote Jude. It took them a resurrection, but they came in. The risen Lord appeared to his brother James (1 Corinthians 15:7) and brought him home. No one is outside his reach.

verseByVerse.quote: And he answered them, "Who are my mother and my brothers?" And looking about at those who sat around him, he said, "Here are my mother and my brothers! For whoever does the will of God, he is my brother and sister and mother."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus answered: who are my mother and my brothers? Looking at those who sat around him, he said: here are my mother and my brothers! Whoever does the will of God, he is my brother and sister and mother.

Who are my mother and my brothers? A startling question in a culture where family was everything. Read as a snub, it is shocking. It is not a snub. It is a question asked in order to be answered, and the answer is one of the most extraordinary things Jesus ever said about ordinary people.

And looking about at those who sat around him. Only Mark mentions the look. Mark keeps giving us the eyes of Jesus in this chapter. In verse 5 he looked around at hard men with anger and grief. Here he looks around at a floor full of nobodies, fishermen, a reformed tax collector, a former Zealot, and whoever else had got into the house that morning, and he takes his time. Jesus looked around the circle, at each face, before he said the words.

Here are my mother and my brothers! Those who sit at his feet and listen are his true family. He said it while his actual mother was standing in the street. He was not making a point at her expense; the whole New Testament forbids that reading. This is not the demotion of the natural family. It is the announcement of a second one.

For whoever does the will of God, he is my brother and sister and mother. Take the sentence apart slowly, because every word is doing work. Whoever: no pedigree. Not whoever is descended from Abraham, not whoever has the education, the record, the family, the reputation. Whoever. Anyone may join. Does the will of God: membership in Jesus’ family is not by birth but by doing God’s will, hearing his word, repenting, believing and obeying (1:15). Not whoever admires it, or believes the correct things about it; the demons on the beach had the doctrine right and were no relation of his. And lest anyone make that into a performance to be earned, John records the Lord’s own definition of the work God requires: this is the work of God, that you believe in him whom he has sent (John 6:29). My brother and sister and mother: he reaches for the closest words the language has. He does not say my followers or my servants, though he says that elsewhere. And he says sister, in a room where a rabbi’s disciples were men, which is not an accident. Women are explicitly included. The church is a family.

What it does not mean. Not that Jesus rejected his mother or family. He provided for his mother from the cross, arranging her care with almost his last breath (John 19:26–27), and he is the one who said that setting aside duty to parents for a religious excuse makes void the word of God (7:11–13). His brothers later came to faith. But blood ties are not the deepest ties. And this passage gives no support to devotion to Mary as an intercessor. Jesus pointed away from family to faith.

Does this mean I should put church above my family? Not in the sense of neglecting them. Scripture is fierce that anyone who does not provide for his own household has denied the faith (1 Timothy 5:8), and your husband or wife, children and parents are people God has given you to love first and most practically. What this passage does is set the order of loyalties: Christ above all, and his family as a real family, not a club. Where your natural family and your church family both need you, you will usually serve them in different ways at once. Where your natural family opposes Christ, you follow him while still loving them. And where you have no natural family, or have lost them, the church is meant to be home.

In a sentence. Jesus declared that those who do God’s will are his true family: his brothers, sisters and mother.

On a Tuesday. If you do God’s will, you are Jesus’ brother or sister. Who in your church family needs your care this week? Think of the person who sits alone, the widow, the student far from home, the believer whose relatives have cut them off since they came to Christ, the one with no family left alive. Invite one of them to a meal. The awkward, mismatched congregation you sit among on a Sunday is not a social arrangement you could improve on by finding people more like yourself. It is your family, given to you by Christ, and he named them before you did.

For worship. Some reading this had a father who was never satisfied. Some have a family that has gone quiet since they became Christians, the empty chair at Christmas, the brother who does not call. Some have no family left at all, and no one who remembers them as a child. To all of them the Lord Jesus Christ looks round a room and says: here. These are mine, and if you do the will of God, so are you. He is not ashamed to call them brothers (Hebrews 2:11). This is the man who said it: called mad by his own family and demonic by the theologians on the same afternoon, on his way to being deserted by every man in that room, going to the cross to make a family out of people who had none, so that a room of strangers on a dirt floor in Capernaum could be looked at, one face at a time, by the Son of God, and called his mother and his brothers.

3.theology:
Two of the most-asked questions in Mark sit in this chapter, and both deserve a straight answer.

Was Jesus's anger sinful? No — and v. 5 shows how to tell, because it gives the anger and the grief in one breath. He looked around at them with anger, grieved at their hardness of heart. Sinful anger wants the other person diminished and would be quietly disappointed by their repentance; righteous anger grieves, wants the wrong put right and the wrongdoer restored, and would be glad to be made unnecessary. Be angry and do not sin (Eph. 4:26) is a command with a boundary, not a contradiction.

What is the unforgivable sin? Mark answers it himself in v. 30 and the answer is anchored, not abstract: for they were saying, He has an unclean spirit. It is the settled, informed, deliberate attribution of the Holy Spirit's unmistakable work to Satan by men who have seen it with their own eyes and chosen their verdict. It is not a slip, a doubt, or a season of confusion. And the pastoral corollary is firm: the person terrified of having committed it has not, because the fear itself requires a conscience still responsive to the Spirit, and that is precisely what this sin destroys. The hardness that commits it does not tremble; it calculates.
3.examples:
The chapter's two great alliances are worth setting side by side, because they explain a great deal about churches.

Then: Pharisees and Herodians — strict separatists and worldly courtiers, men who despised each other on religion, politics and money — in a room together within minutes, agreeing perfectly on one thing: how to destroy him. Nothing on earth unites people like a shared hatred of the light. Pilate and Herod became friends the day Jesus was sent back and forth between them (Luke 23:12).

And then: Matthew the tax collector and Simon the Zealot on the same list of twelve, walking the same roads for three years. In any other year of the world, Simon's politics would have called for a knife in Matthew's ribs. Nothing reconciled them except the man in the middle.

Now: both are still in operation. A congregation can be welded together by what it is against, and it will feel like unity and it will not be. Or it can be a collection of people with nothing whatever in common except Christ — which is more than everything they had against each other. If your church contains people you would never otherwise have chosen, that is not a defect to be managed. It is the evidence.

4.title: Seed, Soil, and the Sleeping Lord
