4.text: <sup>1</sup>Again he began to teach beside the sea. And a very large crowd gathered about him, so that he got into a boat and sat in it on the sea, and the whole crowd was beside the sea on the land. <sup>2</sup>And he was teaching them many things in parables, and in his teaching he said to them: <sup>3</sup>“Listen! Behold, a sower went out to sow. <sup>4</sup>And as he sowed, some seed fell along the path, and the birds came and devoured it. <sup>5</sup>Other seed fell on rocky ground, where it did not have much soil, and immediately it sprang up, since it had no depth of soil. <sup>6</sup>And when the sun rose, it was scorched, and since it had no root, it withered away. <sup>7</sup>Other seed fell among thorns, and the thorns grew up and choked it, and it yielded no grain. <sup>8</sup>And other seeds fell into good soil and produced grain, growing up and increasing and yielding thirtyfold and sixtyfold and a hundredfold.” <sup>9</sup>And he said, “He who has ears to hear, let him hear.” <sup>10</sup>And when he was alone, those around him with the twelve asked him about the parables. <sup>11</sup>And he said to them, “To you has been given the secret of the kingdom of God, but for those outside everything is in parables, <sup>12</sup>so that they may indeed see but not perceive, and may indeed hear but not understand, lest they should turn and be forgiven.” <sup>13</sup>And he said to them, “Do you not understand this parable? How then will you understand all the parables? <sup>14</sup>The sower sows the word. <sup>15</sup>And these are the ones along the path, where the word is sown: when they hear, Satan immediately comes and takes away the word that is sown in them. <sup>16</sup>And these are the ones sown on rocky ground: the ones who, when they hear the word, immediately receive it with joy. <sup>17</sup>And they have no root in themselves, but endure for a while; then, when tribulation or persecution arises on account of the word, immediately they fall away. <sup>18</sup>And others are the ones sown among thorns. They are those who hear the word, <sup>19</sup>but the cares of the world and the deceitfulness of riches and the desires for other things enter in and choke the word, and it proves unfruitful. <sup>20</sup>But those that were sown on the good soil are the ones who hear the word and accept it and bear fruit, thirtyfold and sixtyfold and a hundredfold.” <sup>21</sup>And he said to them, “Is a lamp brought in to be put under a basket, or under a bed, and not on a stand? <sup>22</sup>For nothing is hidden except to be made manifest; nor is anything secret except to come to light. <sup>23</sup>If anyone has ears to hear, let him hear.” <sup>24</sup>And he said to them, “Pay attention to what you hear: with the measure you use, it will be measured to you, and still more will be added to you. <sup>25</sup>For to the one who has, more will be given, and from the one who has not, even what he has will be taken away.” <sup>26</sup>And he said, “The kingdom of God is as if a man should scatter seed on the ground. <sup>27</sup>He sleeps and rises night and day, and the seed sprouts and grows; he knows not how. <sup>28</sup>The earth produces by itself, first the blade, then the ear, then the full grain in the ear. <sup>29</sup>But when the grain is ripe, at once he puts in the sickle, because the harvest has come.” <sup>30</sup>And he said, “With what can we compare the kingdom of God, or what parable shall we use for it? <sup>31</sup>It is like a grain of mustard seed, which, when sown on the ground, is the smallest of all the seeds on earth, <sup>32</sup>yet when it is sown it grows up and becomes larger than all the garden plants and puts out large branches, so that the birds of the air can make nests in its shade.” <sup>33</sup>With many such parables he spoke the word to them, as they were able to hear it. <sup>34</sup>He did not speak to them without a parable, but privately to his own disciples he explained everything. <sup>35</sup>On that day, when evening had come, he said to them, “Let us go across to the other side.” <sup>36</sup>And leaving the crowd, they took him with them in the boat, just as he was. And other boats were with him. <sup>37</sup>And a great windstorm arose, and the waves were breaking into the boat, so that the boat was already filling. <sup>38</sup>But he was in the stern, asleep on the cushion. And they woke him and said to him, “Teacher, do you not care that we are perishing?” <sup>39</sup>And he awoke and rebuked the wind and said to the sea, “Peace! Be still!” And the wind ceased, and there was a great calm. <sup>40</sup>He said to them, “Why are you so afraid? Have you still no faith?” <sup>41</sup>And they were filled with great fear and said to one another, “Who then is this, that even the wind and the sea obey him?”
4.overview:
Chapter 4 is Mark's great block of teaching, and it is built to answer one question the previous chapter forced: if Jesus really is the King, why does this look so small and go so badly? The professionals have called him demonic, his family thinks he is unwell, and the kingdom of God at this point consists of a preacher in a borrowed boat and twelve unimpressive men.

The answer comes in seed. A sower broadcasts across ground he cannot see into, and three-quarters of it appears wasted — and the harvest is still thirty, sixty, a hundredfold, when a Galilean farmer expected five or ten (vv. 3–20). A man scatters seed and goes to bed, and it grows while he sleeps and he does not know how (vv. 26–29). The smallest speck in the garden becomes the largest plant in it, with room in its branches for the birds of the air — which in Ezekiel and Daniel means the nations (vv. 30–32).

Then the teaching stops and the test begins. He says let us go across, and the crossing nearly kills them. The chapter that has been about hearing the word ends with the word spoken to a hurricane, and with a question left deliberately unanswered: Who then is this, that even the wind and the sea obey him?

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–25 — The Sower and the Purpose of Parables
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The pulpit (vv. 1–2). The crowd is so large that Jesus pushes a boat out a few yards and preaches from the water, with the people banked up the shore. The setting is itself a picture: one voice, one seed, going out over a great many different kinds of ground.

The parable (vv. 3–9). A sower walks a field and the seed lands in four places — a trodden path, a shelf of rock under thin soil, a patch of thorn roots, and open ground. Three losses and one harvest so large it would have made a Galilean farmer laugh.

Why parables at all (vv. 10–12). The hardest paragraph in the chapter, and Jesus does not soften it. He quotes Isaiah's commission to a nation that had already shut its eyes, and says the stories both shelter the seeker and confirm the scorner.

The explanation (vv. 13–20). The only parable Jesus takes apart line by line in this Gospel. Four soils, four fates, and the third one is the one most of us are living in.

The lamp and the measure (vv. 21–25). The hiding is temporary — a lamp goes under a basket for a moment, not for a life. And what you do with what you have heard determines what you will be given next.
verseByVerse.theology:
Verses 11–12 are the hardest words in the chapter, and they should not be smoothed over. Matthew's version says Jesus speaks in parables because people do not see (Matt. 13:13); Mark's says he speaks so that they may not see, lest they should turn and be forgiven. Read flatly, that sounds as though the Lord veils truth deliberately to stop people repenting.

Three things dissolve the difficulty. First, the words are a direct quotation of Isaiah 6:9–10 — God's charge to a prophet sent to a nation that had already, for generations, shut its own eyes. This is not fresh cruelty; it is the settled judgement of God on hardened refusal. Second, the so that carries the weight of fulfilment as much as bare purpose: the parables come to a people who have chosen blindness and confirm the choice, which is how God deals with those who insist — he gives them over to the dark they preferred (cf. Rom. 1:24). Third, and decisively, the door is never bolted. Those around him with the twelve understood nothing either. The difference between them and the outsiders is one thing only: they asked.

So the same parable is judgement and mercy at once. It hardens the scornful and shelters the seeker — hiding the truth from the mouth that would only spit on it, while keeping it within arm's reach of anyone who will turn and ask.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: a farmer broadcasting seed by hand across ground he has not sorted in advance, some of it landing where it has no chance at all.

Now: every faithful preacher, parent and friend who keeps sowing without being able to see the soil. The sower in the parable does not test the ground first, and he is not blamed for the path, the rock or the thorns. That is a real relief for anyone who has taught a class for years, or raised children in the faith, and cannot see a harvest. Your job was the sowing.

And a hundredfold is not a rounded-up figure. Ordinary yields in that country ran five- or tenfold, and a farmer who got thirty would have talked about it for the rest of his life. Jesus names thirty as the lowest of the three good outcomes. Three-quarters of the field appears to fail, and the harvest is still absurd. Whatever the losses look like from where you are standing, the ledger at the end is not in doubt.

verseByVerse.quote: Again he began to teach beside the sea. And a very large crowd gathered about him, so that he got into a boat and sat in it on the sea, and the whole crowd was beside the sea on the land. And he was teaching them many things in parables, and in his teaching he said to them:
verseByVerse.commentary:
Again Jesus began to teach by the lake. The crowd was so large that he got into a boat on the water and sat down, while the whole crowd stood on the shore. He taught them many things in parables.

Meaning first. Mark 4 is Jesus’ great chapter of parables, ending with a storm. In chapter 3 the religious leaders rejected him and his family misunderstood him, while a circle of disciples sat at his feet. Why do some receive him and others reject him? Jesus answers with a story about a sower: the same seed, the word of the kingdom, falls on four kinds of ground, and only one bears fruit, but that fruit is an astonishing harvest. Then come short parables about a lamp that must shine, a measure that is filled to overflowing, seed that grows while the farmer sleeps, and a tiny mustard seed that becomes a great plant sheltering the birds. The kingdom is hidden and small now, growing by God’s power, and certain to come to harvest. The chapter ends on the lake at night, where Jesus sleeps through a storm, wakes, and silences the wind and the sea with a word, and his terrified disciples ask the question of the whole Gospel: who then is this?

The connection. In chapter 3 the religious leaders rejected Jesus and his family misunderstood him, while a circle of disciples gathered around him. Chapter 4 explains, in parables, what is happening: the word of the kingdom is like seed, received differently by different soils, small and hidden at first, but certain to produce a great harvest.

So that he got into a boat and sat in it on the sea. The boat prepared in 3:9. Picture the arrangement, because Mark has gone to the trouble of describing it. The crowd is too large for the shore, so Jesus gets into the boat, has it pushed out a few yards, and sits down in it. Sitting is the posture of a teacher in that world; a rabbi sat and the class stood. And the whole crowd is beside the sea on the land, packed along the beach and up the slope behind it. Anyone who has stood on the shore near Capernaum knows what that means. The ground rises from the water in a natural curve, and the water carries sound. A man in a boat can be heard by thousands on that hillside without shouting. He is using the shape of the world his Father made as a sound system.

The setting is the sermon. One voice, from one fixed point, going out across a very large crowd, landing on farmers and fishermen, on Pharisees who came to listen for errors, on women at the back with children pulling at them, on people who had walked from Judea and people who wandered down from the village because there was a commotion. One seed. Many kinds of ground.

And he was teaching them many things in parables. Mark keeps saying he taught, because it keeps needing to be said. We remember the miracles; Mark records that the bulk of the Lord’s time went on teaching. A parable (parabolē) is a story or picture from ordinary life placed beside a spiritual truth to illuminate it: farming, lamps, measures, seeds. It is not a children’s illustration, and it is not a code with a decoder ring. Parables usually make one main point, though Jesus explains some details. They invite hearers to think and respond, and they make you work.

Why stories? A straight statement, such as people respond differently to the word of God, is easy to agree with and easier to forget; you can nod at it without a flicker of self-suspicion. But hand a man a picture of a field with four kinds of ground in it, and he will find himself walking round the edge of it wondering which patch he is standing on. He has to enter the story to understand it, and once he is inside it, it has him. A story gets under the guard that an argument goes straight into. Nathan did not open by telling David that he was the man. He told him about a poor man and one little ewe lamb, and let David pass sentence on himself first (2 Samuel 12:1–7). So read this chapter expecting to be handled the same way. Jesus is not about to give you information about four types of hearer. He is about to walk you out into a field and ask you where you are standing.

How should I read a parable? Start with the setting: who Jesus is speaking to and what question is in the air. Look for the main point, often found in the surprise or the ending, such as the enormous harvest or the mustard plant that shelters birds. Where Jesus explains a parable, as he does with the sower, let his explanation govern yours. Do not press every small detail for a hidden meaning; a story needs scenery. And always ask the question a parable is designed to make you ask: where am I in this? Then come to Jesus with what you do not understand, as the disciples did (v. 10).

In a sentence. Jesus taught the huge crowd from a boat on the lake, using parables.

On a Tuesday. Jesus used ordinary things to teach eternal truths: seed, soil, lamps, baskets, weather. Look for God’s lessons in the ordinary things of your day: the bread you buy, the plant on the windowsill, the light you switch on. His world is full of pictures of his kingdom for those with eyes to see.

For worship. The Word through whom the world was made sat in a fishing boat and spoke of seeds and soil. The Creator used his own creation as his pulpit and his illustrations, and he spoke so that farmers and fishermen could understand. He is the wisest teacher who ever lived, and the humblest, and he still speaks to us through his word in pictures we can carry home.
verseByVerse.note: Teaching from a boat let the whole crowd on the shore see and hear him.

verseByVerse.quote: "Listen! Behold, a sower went out to sow. And as he sowed, some seed fell along the path, and the birds came and devoured it.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Listen! A farmer went out to sow. As he sowed, some seed fell along the path, and the birds came and ate it up.

Listen! He opens with a command, the first word out of his mouth. Not consider, or imagine, but listen; and he will end the same parable with he who has ears to hear, let him hear (v. 9). The story is bracketed by calls to hear, which is a fair sign of what it is about. The great issue of the chapter is how we listen.

Behold, a sower went out to sow. It helps enormously to know how it was actually done, because a modern reader imagines neat drills and a man walking a straight line. A Galilean farmer carried the seed in a fold of his cloak or a bag at his hip and threw it in a wide arc as he walked, broadcasting it across the whole field, often before ploughing, so it fell everywhere. In much of that country the ploughing came after the sowing: you scattered the grain and then turned it in. And the field was not fenced. Paths ran across it where people had walked for generations; limestone lay a few inches under the surface in places; last year’s thorn roots were still in the ground at the edges. So the sower is not careless. This is simply what sowing looked like. He throws it everywhere because he cannot see, from up there with a bag on his hip, what is six inches under the surface of any given yard of his field.

The first comfort. Hold on to that, because it is the first comfort in the chapter, and it is for anyone who has ever taught, preached, raised children in the faith, or talked about Christ to a friend and watched nothing happen. You are not asked to survey the soil first. You could not do it if you tried; you cannot see into another human being. Sow. The results were never the part assigned to you.

Some seed fell along the path. The hard-trodden footpaths between fields. The seed lay on the surface. The path is not bad soil by nature. It is ground that has been walked on so often that it has set like a floor. Nobody decided to make it hard. It was made hard by traffic, by the same feet going over it, day after day, until nothing could get in.

And the birds came and devoured it. At once. The seed does not even get the dignity of failing slowly. It lies on a surface it cannot penetrate, in plain view, and it is gone before the sower has reached the end of the row. Jesus will tell us in verse 15 who the birds are: Satan comes at once and takes the word away. So the most ordinary religious experience in the world, sitting through a sermon and remembering none of it by lunchtime, is not always a neutral failure of concentration. Something can be at work in it. And the path is the soil nobody worries about being, which is its danger. The rocky-ground hearer has a crisis; the thorny-ground hearer feels the squeeze. The path feels nothing at all. The word arrives, lies there and is carried off, and the man goes home to his lunch entirely undisturbed and slightly bored.

I forget sermons by lunchtime. What can I do? Several simple things help the seed go in before the birds arrive. Pray before the service that God would open your heart to his word. Read the passage beforehand if you know it. Listen with a pen: write down one sentence you want to remember. Talk about the sermon over lunch with your family or friends, and ask each other what struck you. Come back to it during the week, perhaps reading the passage again on Monday. And above all, act on one thing it said. Truth that is obeyed is not easily stolen.

In a sentence. A farmer scattered seed, and some fell on a hard path, where birds ate it.

On a Tuesday. How do you listen to God’s word? The parable is a mirror. Think back to last Sunday’s sermon. Can you remember what the passage was, and one thing it called you to do? If not, do not despair, but take it as information, and try one of the habits above this week.

For worship. The Sower scatters his seed with an open hand, on every kind of ground, without first demanding to see the soil. That is the generosity of God in the gospel: the word of life thrown wide, to the hard and the shallow and the crowded as well as the good. He does not ration his mercy to the promising. He sows it everywhere, and he is the Lord of the harvest.
verseByVerse.note: Seed was scattered by hand, and some fell on the hard footpaths between fields.

verseByVerse.quote: Other seed fell on rocky ground, where it did not have much soil, and immediately it sprang up, since it had no depth of soil. And when the sun rose, it was scorched, and since it had no root, it withered away.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Other seed fell on rocky ground, where it did not have much soil. It sprang up quickly, because the soil was shallow. But when the sun rose it was scorched, and because it had no root it withered away.

Other seed fell on rocky ground. Not soil full of stones, which would be a nuisance rather than a death sentence, but a thin layer of soil over limestone bedrock, common in Galilee: a shelf of rock a few inches beneath the surface with a skin of earth over the top. From above, standing in the field, it looks exactly like the rest. And here is the cruelty of it: this is the ground that performs best at first.

And immediately it sprang up, since it had no depth of soil. Read the logic, because it is the opposite of what you would expect. It came up fast because the soil was shallow. The shallow soil warmed quickly; the seed could not go down, so everything it had went up. It looked promising. The fastest, greenest, most impressive growth in the whole field is the growth that is going to die. Anyone who has been in church life for twenty years has watched this: the new convert whose enthusiasm makes everyone else feel lukewarm, who is at everything, telling everyone, radiant, and who is not there in three years, and nobody can quite say when they stopped coming. The rate of early growth told you nothing.

And when the sun rose, it was scorched, and since it had no root, it withered away. The roots could not reach water. The same sun that made it sprout killed it. Notice that the sun is not an enemy. The sun is what ripens the harvest in the good soil in the same field. The identical heat that kills one plant matures another, and the only difference is what is happening underground, where nobody can see. That reframes the hard seasons of a Christian life. Trouble is not sent to destroy you; it is the weather in which real growth is finished and shallow growth is exposed. The same bereavement, the same diagnosis, the same run of humiliating years will make one believer and break another, and the difference was decided long before the heat arrived. And the verdict is in a single clause: not attacked, not argued out of it, but withered, dried up from underneath, from a place nobody was looking.

Roots are grown in private. So the practical question is not how green you look this month but what is happening in the dark. Roots go down in the unglamorous stretches: the half-hour with a Bible on a wet Tuesday when nothing in you wants it; the prayers that feel like talking to the ceiling; the Sundays you attend when you would rather not; the doctrine you take the trouble to understand before you need it. None of that shows. That is precisely the point of it.

How can I tell whether my faith has roots, or whether I am rocky ground? Look below the feelings. Rooted faith keeps going when the feelings go: you still pray when prayer is dry, still trust when God seems silent, still belong to his people when church is disappointing. It rests on Christ and his word, not on an atmosphere. It has survived some heat already, a loss, a temptation resisted, a cost paid for being a Christian, and come out clinging to Christ rather than resenting him. If you are unsure, do not torment yourself with introspection. Go to Christ, ask him to root you, and start digging: Scripture, prayer, church, obedience, day after ordinary day.

In a sentence. Seed on shallow, rocky soil sprouted quickly but withered in the heat for lack of roots.

On a Tuesday. Quick enthusiasm is not deep roots. How deep do yours go? Here is the honest test: if the heat came this year, if the illness, the redundancy, the public embarrassment for being a Christian arrived in March, what exactly would you be drawing on? If the answer is a feeling you had at a conference, you have been told in advance, kindly, while there is still time to dig.

For worship. The Lord who tells us about the scorching sun is the one who bore its full heat himself. He was rooted in his Father through every trial, and when the fire of God’s judgment fell on him at the cross, he did not wither. Because his roots held, ours can. He is the root of David, and those who are grafted into him draw on a life that no drought can dry up. Blessed is the one who trusts in the LORD; he is like a tree planted by water, which does not fear when heat comes.
verseByVerse.note: Much of Galilee has limestone bedrock just under a thin layer of soil.

verseByVerse.quote: Other seed fell among thorns, and the thorns grew up and choked it, and it yielded no grain.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Other seed fell among thorns, and the thorns grew up and choked it, and it produced no grain.

Other seed fell among thorns. This is the soil many readers of this page are standing in, so read it slowly. Understand what the field actually looked like. Ground where thorn roots remained, not yet visible. The thorns are not visible when the sowing happens. What is in the ground is a root system: last season’s thorn bushes, cut down or burned off at the surface, entirely dormant, with the earth above them looking as good as any other part of the field. A man could walk it and see nothing wrong.

And the thorns grew up and choked it. Then the rains come, and both things grow at once. That is the whole picture: not a field of thorns with a bit of wheat in it, but wheat and thorns coming up together in the same soil, drawing on the same water, the same light, the same few inches of earth. The thorns grew faster and took the light, water and nutrients. Choking is silent, but it is total. There is no moment of decision. Nobody digs up the wheat. It is simply crowded, shaded and starved by things that are also alive, also growing, also using the ground.

And it yielded no grain. Only Mark adds this. The plant survived, but was fruitless. And that is the outcome that ought to stop us. The plant is still there. It is green, it is standing, it has leaves. Walk past that corner of the field in June and you would say the wheat is doing fine. It simply never produces anything.

The thorns are not sins. Here is what makes this the most searching of the three failures, and Jesus will spell it out in verse 19: the thorns are the cares of the world, the deceitfulness of riches and the desires for other things. Not adultery, theft or blasphemy, but worry, money and the wanting of ordinary things. Which means this soil cannot be diagnosed by examining your conduct. A man in this field is not doing anything he would need to confess to his minister. He is doing what everyone does: worrying about the mortgage, working hard for a promotion he does not really need, extending the house, taxiing children between activities, watching the pension, keeping up with the news and the group chat and the series everyone is talking about. None of it is wicked. All of it is alive, and all of it drinks. And the sign is not a sin you have committed but a fruit you cannot find: the prayer that has quietly stopped happening, the Bible opened on Sunday because someone else opens it, the conversation about Christ you have not had with anyone in a year, not because you decided against it, but because there has been no room.

Is it wrong to plan, work hard and provide for my family? No. Scripture commands it: work with your hands (1 Thessalonians 4:11), provide for your household (1 Timothy 5:8), learn from the ant (Proverbs 6:6–8). The problem is not that these things exist but that they take first place and leave no room. A good test is not whether you work hard but whether your work and plans are done before God, with prayer, and whether they leave room for him: for worship, for his word, for his people, for generosity. Seek first the kingdom of God and his righteousness, and all these things will be added to you (Matthew 6:33). Thorns grow where good things are allowed to grow unweeded.

In a sentence. Seed among thorns grew but was choked and produced nothing.

On a Tuesday. What thorns are growing beside God’s word in your life? Try the honest version of the question. Not, is there anything bad in my life? There may well not be. Ask instead: what has crowded out what? If you laid your week beside your Bible, which of the two would look like the thing you actually organise your life around? The wheat and the thorns are still growing in the same field, and only one of them is going to yield anything at harvest.

For worship. The ground was cursed with thorns and thistles when Adam fell, and the Son of God wore a crown of them. He took the curse of the thorns on his own head, so that the ground of our hearts could be made good. He does not leave us to clear our fields alone. He is the gardener of our souls, and what he plants he tends, and what he tends will bear fruit.

verseByVerse.quote: And other seeds fell into good soil and produced grain, growing up and increasing and yielding thirtyfold and sixtyfold and a hundredfold." And he said, "He who has ears to hear, let him hear."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Other seeds fell into good soil and produced grain, growing up and increasing, yielding thirtyfold, sixtyfold and a hundredfold. And Jesus said: whoever has ears to hear, let him hear.

And other seeds fell into good soil and produced grain, growing up and increasing. Three failures, and now the harvest. Deep, soft, clean soil, and the seed grows steadily. Note that the good soil does nothing to become good. It does not clear itself of stones or grub out its own thorn roots. It simply receives what falls on it and lets it go down. Whatever this parable asks of you, it is not asking you to manufacture your own fertility; the field is worked on, not self-improving. And Mark alone gives the process in stages, growing up and increasing, the quiet answer to the shallow soil. That plant sprang up immediately; this one takes its time. Fast is not the same as fruitful, and slow is not the same as dead.

And yielding thirtyfold and sixtyfold and a hundredfold. A Galilean farmer on that beach heard these numbers very differently from the way we do. A normal harvest was perhaps seven to tenfold: you sowed a measure and harvested seven, out of which next year’s seed had to come. A man who brought in thirtyfold would have talked about it for the rest of his life, and the village would have remembered the season. Thirty was excellent; a hundred was astonishing, the kind of blessing Isaac received in the year God prospered him (Genesis 26:12). Jesus names thirty as the lowest of his three good outcomes. So do the sum the parable wants you to do. Three-quarters of the field appears to be a total loss: seed gone to birds, seed withered on rock, seed strangled in thorns. And the harvest is still extravagant, the kind that fills every barn in the village and leaves the farmer standing in the yard laughing. Despite all the losses, the harvest is abundant. God’s word will not fail.

The accounts at the end. That was a live question for the twelve men listening. It looked, in Galilee that year, as though this was going badly. The professionals had declared him demonic, his family thought he was mad, the crowds wanted healings and not much else, and the kingdom of God consisted of a preacher in a borrowed boat and a dozen unimpressive men. Jesus tells them what the accounts will say at the end, and they are not close. Hold that when you look at your own field and see mostly loss: the children who are not walking with God, the years of teaching that seemed to change nobody, the church that is smaller than it was. The losses in this parable are real and named honestly. They are also not the story. He who supplies seed to the sower will supply and multiply your seed for sowing and increase the harvest of your righteousness (2 Corinthians 9:10).

He who has ears to hear, let him hear. Everyone has ears; not everyone listens. A call to hear with understanding and respond. The refrain will sound again over the seven churches in Revelation (Revelation 2–3). Everyone on that beach had ears, which is exactly why the sentence is not a truism but a warning: the hearing that saves is not the hearing that everybody in the crowd was already doing. Physical hearing is universal. Spiritual hearing is a gift, and the man who wants it has only to ask the one in the boat for it.

What is the fruit, exactly? Not only converts, though bringing others to Christ is part of it. The fruit is a life changed by the word: the fruit of the Spirit, love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faithfulness, gentleness, self-control (Galatians 5:22–23); good works done for God’s glory (Colossians 1:10); repentance that shows in what you do (Matthew 3:8); praise to God (Hebrews 13:15); and generosity (Philippians 4:17). Fruit grows slowly and is often seen more clearly by others than by yourself. Ask someone who knows you well whether they see Christ in you more than they did five years ago.

In a sentence. Seed in good soil produced an extraordinary harvest, and Jesus called everyone to listen carefully.

On a Tuesday. Ask God to make your heart good soil today. Then, if you teach Sunday school, lead a group, raise children or speak of Christ to friends, write down one name you have been sowing into for a long time with little to show for it, and pray for them, trusting the harvest to the one who promised it.

For worship. The God of the harvest is not stingy. He takes a field that looks three-quarters lost and fills the barns to overflowing. He brought a worldwide church out of twelve men and a borrowed boat. His word does not return to him empty, but accomplishes what he purposes and succeeds in the thing for which he sent it. The harvest is his, and it will be beyond counting.
verseByVerse.note: A hundredfold would be an extraordinary harvest.

verseByVerse.quote: And when he was alone, those around him with the twelve asked him about the parables. And he said to them, "To you has been given the secret of the kingdom of God, but for those outside everything is in parables, so that they may indeed see but not perceive, and may indeed hear but not understand, lest they should turn and be forgiven."
verseByVerse.commentary:
When Jesus was alone, those around him with the Twelve asked him about the parables. He said: to you has been given the secret of the kingdom of God, but for those outside everything is in parables, so that they may indeed see but not perceive, and indeed hear but not understand, lest they should turn and be forgiven.

And when he was alone, those around him with the twelve asked him about the parables. Disciples ask. The crowd goes home, the beach empties, and a smaller group stays behind and asks what he meant. Hold on to that, because it turns out to be the hinge of the passage. The insiders are not insiders because they understood. They did not understand a word of it, as verse 13 makes painfully clear. They are insiders because when the sermon was over they did not go home. They stayed and asked. Those who seek understanding come to Jesus.

To you has been given the secret of the kingdom of God. Secret (mystērion) in the Bible never means a puzzle to be cracked by clever people. It means a truth once hidden, now revealed by God. The secret is that the kingdom has come in Jesus, but in a hidden, unexpected way: like seed, not like a conquering army; in a carpenter from Nazareth who is going to a cross. Has been given: the verb is passive, and there is only one person doing the giving. Understanding is God’s gift (Matthew 16:17). Nobody works this out. It is handed over.

But for those outside everything is in parables. Those outside are those who have rejected Jesus, the word that described his family standing outside in 3:31–32.

So that they may indeed see but not perceive, and may indeed hear but not understand. Now the hardest sentence in the chapter, and it must not be smoothed over. It sounds as though Jesus speaks in stories so that people will not repent and be saved. Three things open it up. First, these are not new words. They quote Isaiah 6:9–10: God sent Isaiah to preach to a people who had already, for generations, shut their own eyes, and his preaching would harden them. Isaiah was not sent to a curious people wrongly denied the truth, but to a people who had refused it so long that the preaching itself would confirm them in it. Jesus’ parables have the same effect on those who have already rejected him: the truth is there, but they do not grasp it. It is a judgment on hearts already closed, and it is the passage the New Testament reaches for again and again to explain unbelief (Matthew 13:14–15; John 12:40; Acts 28:26–27). Second, so that is the language of fulfilment: this happens, and in it Isaiah’s word comes true. It is the pattern Paul describes when God gives people over to what they have already chosen (Romans 1:24, 26, 28), the darkness they preferred, finally granted.

Lest they should turn and be forgiven. Turn is repentance. The hardening confirms the choice they have made. And third, decisively, the door is never bolted against anyone who knocks. The proof is sitting in the room. The men who received the secret had understood nothing thirty seconds earlier. The only thing separating them from the crowd walking home along the shore is that they asked. Ask, and it will be given to you; seek, and you will find (Matthew 7:7).

What it does not mean. Not that Jesus wanted to prevent willing people from being saved. Those who wanted to understand came and asked, and he explained (v. 34). The hardening falls on those who refuse. And Jesus’ purpose in parables is also to reveal: a lamp is meant to be seen (v. 21). God is sovereign in revealing and hiding (Matthew 11:25–26), and people are responsible for refusing.

Judgment and mercy in one breath. So the parable works two ways at once. To the man who has already decided, it is one more story he can shrug at, and every shrug sets the ground harder. To the man who is troubled by it, it is a door left open, a truth kept just out of reach so that he has to come and ask for it, and the asking is the beginning of everything.

Am I one of those outside if I do not understand much of the Bible? No. The disciples did not understand either; Jesus had to explain everything to them, and they were still slow years later. Being inside is not about how much you understand but about whether you have come to Jesus and keep coming. If you love him, want to know him better, and bring him your questions, you are among those to whom the secret has been given. Understanding grows over a lifetime. Keep reading, keep asking, keep listening to faithful preaching, and be patient with yourself.

In a sentence. Jesus told his disciples that the secret of the kingdom had been given to them, while for those outside, parables confirmed their refusal to understand.

On a Tuesday. When you do not understand Scripture, do what the disciples did: come to Jesus and ask. This chapter has been strange to you in places. Did you notice, and go and ask him about it? Or did you read it, find it obscure, and get on with the day? The people who stayed behind on that beach did not have better minds. They had a habit of not leaving. Everything they eventually understood came out of that.

For worship. To you has been given: the deepest truth in the universe, kept hidden for ages, handed as a gift to fishermen who stayed behind to ask. God does not reveal his secret to the wise and understanding of this world, but to little children, and he is glad to do it. Yes, Father, for such was your gracious will. The kingdom is a gift, and so is the understanding of it, and so is the faith that receives it. Blessed be the God who gives.
verseByVerse.note: A “secret” (mystery) in the New Testament is something once hidden and now revealed by God.

verseByVerse.quote: And he said to them, "Do you not understand this parable? How then will you understand all the parables? The sower sows the word. And these are the ones along the path, where the word is sown: when they hear, Satan immediately comes and takes away the word that is sown in them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus said: do you not understand this parable? How then will you understand all the parables? The farmer sows the word. Those along the path are the ones in whom the word is sown, but when they hear, Satan comes immediately and takes away the word sown in them.

Do you not understand this parable? How then will you understand all the parables? There is a sigh in that, and Mark is not embarrassed to record it. But notice what kind of rebuke it is: not a refusal to explain, but a remark made in the middle of explaining. He says, do you not understand? and then tells them. That is a mercy for slow disciples, which is all of us. The men who were with him three years were, by any honest reading of this Gospel, consistently baffled, and the Lord kept teaching them. This parable is the key to the rest. If you understand how the word is received, you can understand everything else.

The sower sows the word. Five words, and they set the terms for everything that follows. The seed is the word: the message of the kingdom, God’s word. Not a general religious influence, an experience or a mood, but a message in sentences that can be spoken and heard. The sower is Jesus, and all who preach his word after him. That matters more than it seems. It means the kingdom of God comes to human beings by an ordinary means that anyone can use. Faith comes from hearing, and hearing through the word of Christ (Romans 10:17); we are born again through the living and abiding word of God (1 Peter 1:23). This is why an unremarkable sermon in a half-empty building on a wet Sunday is not a low-grade activity. It is the sowing. The one thing that has ever produced a harvest is being done.

And these are the ones along the path, where the word is sown: when they hear, Satan immediately comes and takes away the word that is sown in them. The first soil: hard hearts. The word lies on the surface and never sinks in. And Jesus takes the birds and names them. Satan: he attributes it to a person, not a process. He does not say the word evaporates or that people are naturally forgetful. Someone comes and takes it, by distraction, mockery, doubt or simple forgetfulness. The god of this world has blinded the minds of the unbelievers, to keep them from seeing the light of the gospel of the glory of Christ (2 Corinthians 4:4). Immediately: the theft is not a slow leak over months. It happens at once, in the car park, on the walk home, in the first conversation afterwards. Takes away: the loss is a theft rather than a verdict on the seed. The word did not fail to be good; it was removed before it could get in.

How a heart hardens. Remember what made the path hard. Nobody chose it. It was traffic, the same feet crossing the same ground until it set like a floor. That is how a heart hardens in real life: not usually by a decision to reject God, but by years of the same routines going over the same ground, until the sound of the gospel is simply a sound you have heard before.

If Satan takes the word away, are people who reject the gospel still responsible? Yes. Satan blinds, but he blinds people who prefer the dark (John 3:19). The path was hardened by traffic it allowed, and the hearer is not a passive victim but a willing participant in his own forgetting. Scripture never lets us blame the devil for our unbelief, any more than Eve could (Genesis 3:13). And the remedy is offered to every hearer: God is able to break up hard ground and to open blind eyes, and he invites everyone to ask. Responsibility and the need for grace stand together.

In a sentence. The seed is God’s word, and in hard-hearted hearers Satan snatches it away at once.

On a Tuesday. After you hear God’s word, take time to reflect on it before the birds come. And if you have started to find it dull, take that seriously and take it to God tonight, in exactly those words. He has never once refused a man who asked him to break up his own hard ground: I will remove the heart of stone from your flesh and give you a heart of flesh (Ezekiel 36:26). The path cannot plough itself. It does not have to.

For worship. The Lord did not lose patience with slow disciples; he sighed, and then explained. He keeps teaching people who are not quick. And the word he sows is stronger than the one who snatches it, for where the Spirit opens a heart, no bird can steal the seed. Thanks be to God, who breaks the hardest ground and makes his word take root in hearts that once felt nothing.

parallels.desc: the god of this world has blinded the minds

verseByVerse.quote: And these are the ones sown on rocky ground: the ones who, when they hear the word, immediately receive it with joy. And they have no root in themselves, but endure for a while; then, when tribulation or persecution arises on account of the word, immediately they fall away.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Those sown on rocky ground are the ones who, when they hear the word, immediately receive it with joy. But they have no root in themselves; they endure for a while, and when tribulation or persecution arises because of the word, they immediately fall away.

Immediately receive it with joy. An enthusiastic, emotional response. It looks like conversion. And there is nothing wrong with the joy, which is the first thing to say, because this soil frightens sensitive people and is often misread. Real conversion is glad: the man who found treasure in a field sold everything in his joy (Matthew 13:44). The problem is not that they were happy. It is that happiness was all there was.

And they have no root in themselves, but endure for a while. The response is shallow. It has not gone down into the heart and will. Look at the words in themselves, because they are the diagnosis. Not no root in the church, or no root in good teaching, but no root in themselves. Something was never made their own. The faith was held at the level of atmosphere, the music, the friendships, the feeling in the room, a preacher they admired, and never went down into the private ground where nobody could see it. And they endure for a while: that is why it takes time to tell. This soil looks identical to good soil, and better at first, for a season. Mark gives no timescale. It might be two years.

Then, when tribulation or persecution arises on account of the word. The scorching sun. Following Christ costs something. And notice exactly what the heat is. Jesus does not say when trouble comes; he specifies trouble that arrives on account of the word, the cost of the faith itself: the friendships that cool once you are known as a Christian, the joke at work you are now on the wrong side of, the family that has become careful with you, the promotion that goes elsewhere, and in much of the world today far worse. Mark’s first readers in Rome were facing exactly this. This is the soil that discovers Christianity is expensive, and had assumed it was free.

Immediately they fall away. Fall away (skandalizontai) means stumble, be offended, be tripped up; the same root names the offence the cross itself gives (1 Corinthians 1:23). As quickly as they came, they go. Mark uses immediately three times in three verses: fast in, fast up, fast out. The whole story of this soil is speed.

What it does not mean. Not that joy is suspicious; good soil also receives the word with joy (1 Thessalonians 1:6). The problem is the lack of root. Nor do true believers finally fall away. Those who do show that their faith was never rooted (1 John 2:19).

Were these true believers who lost their salvation? Arminian Christians read the parable that way: the rocky soil received the word with joy, so it must have been real faith, which was then lost (compare Hebrews 6:4–6). But Jesus says they have no root in themselves; something was missing from the start. The joy was real, but it was not the life of a new heart. John says of such people that they went out from us, but they were not of us (1 John 2:19). The more likely reading is that the fruitless soils describe profession without possession. A true believer may stumble and struggle, but the word that has truly taken root goes on to bear fruit, because God who began a good work will bring it to completion (Philippians 1:6).

How do I help a new believer put down roots? Do not dampen their joy; build under it. Read the Bible with them regularly, perhaps a Gospel, a chapter at a time, and show them how to pray from it. Bring them into the life of a church where people will know them, not just greet them. Teach them the basics of the faith, so they know why they believe. Warn them honestly that following Christ will cost something, so the heat does not take them by surprise. And keep in touch when they go quiet. Roots grow best in company.

In a sentence. Shallow hearers receive the word with quick joy, but without roots they fall away when trouble comes.

On a Tuesday. Pray for believers facing persecution, that their roots will hold. Then ask the question that has to be asked while the weather is fine: what are you doing this month that will still be holding you in ten years? Roots go down in the unglamorous places: the Bible opened with no appetite, the doctrine understood before the diagnosis comes, the prayer offered when it feels like talking to the ceiling, belonging properly to a church rather than attending one, so that other people know you well enough to hold you. And here is the encouragement. Rocky ground in a field cannot do anything about the rock. You can go to the Farmer and say: there is something hard underneath me, and I cannot shift it. That prayer has never once been declined.

For worship. The Lord knows the cost of following him, because he paid it all. When tribulation came on account of the word, he did not fall away; he set his face like flint and went to the cross. And those whom he roots in himself he keeps. No one will snatch them out of his hand. The joy he gives is not a passing flush but the beginning of a life that cannot die.

verseByVerse.quote: And others are the ones sown among thorns. They are those who hear the word, but the cares of the world and the deceitfulness of riches and the desires for other things enter in and choke the word, and it proves unfruitful.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Others are sown among thorns. They hear the word, but the cares of the world, the deceitfulness of riches and the desires for other things enter in and choke the word, and it proves unfruitful.

They are those who hear the word. They go further. The word takes root and grows. Here is the soil that describes most Christians in a comfortable country, and Jesus names its three weeds precisely.

But the cares of the world. Worries about life: money, health, family, work. Not open sin, but ordinary preoccupations that crowd God out. The word is the ordinary one for anxiety, the same one Peter uses when he says to cast all your anxieties on him, because he cares for you (1 Peter 5:7). The mortgage. The scan result. The child who is not doing well. The parents who are getting frail and the decisions that are coming. The news, checked six times a day, about disasters you cannot affect. These are not sins; most of them are duties. And they will strangle the word, because worry is not passive. It works. It takes the time and the mental room that hearing God requires, and it does it while you are asleep.

And the deceitfulness of riches. Wealth deceives. Not riches, but the deceitfulness of them: the lie money tells, and the lie is always the same, that a little more will make you safe. It promises security and satisfaction and does not deliver. It makes people feel they do not need God (10:23–25; 1 Timothy 6:9–10). That lie is told to the man with very little as loudly as to the man with a great deal, which is why this weed grows in every income bracket. Money is dishonest company. It promises a security it has never once delivered to anybody, and the promise is enough to organise a whole life around.

And the desires for other things. Only Mark adds this: all the other wants that compete with God. It is the most disarming phrase of the three, because it is so casual. Jesus does not even bother to name them. The other things. The extension, the bike, the holiday you are researching in the evenings, the series everybody is watching, the hobby that has quietly become the thing you think about while other people are talking. None of it is wrong, which is the point of this soil and why it is so hard to see from inside. Good things can become thorns when they take first place.

Enter in and choke the word, and it proves unfruitful. Notice the direction of travel: they enter in. Nothing was pushed out. Things were let in, one reasonable thing at a time, and the word was crowded to the edge of a life it had once been the centre of. And it proves unfruitful: not dead, not renounced. The plant survives, but bears nothing. A person may stay in church for years with no real fruit.

Is this hearer a Christian at all? Some teach that he is a carnal Christian, saved but fruitless and unrewarded (compare 1 Corinthians 3:15). But in the parable only the good soil yields a harvest, and Jesus says elsewhere that every tree that does not bear good fruit is cut down (Matthew 7:19). The more likely reading is that a life that bears nothing at the harvest shows a faith that never truly lived. A believer may go through seasons of little fruit and be pruned (John 15:2); but the word that is truly received does not stay barren for good.

Is it wrong to be wealthy? Not in itself. Abraham, Job and Joseph of Arimathea were rich and godly. But Jesus warns that wealth is unusually dangerous, because it deceives (10:23–25). Paul tells the rich not to be haughty or to set their hopes on the uncertainty of riches, but on God, and to be rich in good works, generous and ready to share (1 Timothy 6:17–18). So if God has given you money, hold it with an open hand: give regularly and generously, live below your means, and ask honestly whether your security is in your savings or in your Saviour. The test is not how much you have but how easily you could give it away.

In a sentence. In preoccupied hearers, worry, wealth and other desires choke the word until it bears no fruit.

On a Tuesday. Name the thorns in your life: anxieties, money, other desires. Root one out this week. Ask two hard questions. First: what has been crowded out? Name what used to happen and has quietly stopped: the praying, the reading, the hospitality, the conversation about Christ. Second: where does the overflow go? When your week has a spare hour and your mind a spare half-hour, where do they go without a decision being made? Whatever answers that is what is actually growing in your field. Then do the only thing that works with thorns, which is not to feel bad about them but to cut them, one at a time, with a name attached: the specific anxiety handed over in specific words, the specific spending stopped, the specific evening given back.

For worship. He who had nothing, not even a place to lay his head, was rich toward God, and for our sake he became poor, so that we by his poverty might become rich. Our anxieties he invites us to cast on him, because he cares for us. He is better than every other thing we desire, and the one who has him has all things. The thorns promise much and give nothing; he promises everything and gives himself.

verseByVerse.quote: But those that were sown on the good soil are the ones who hear the word and accept it and bear fruit, thirtyfold and sixtyfold and a hundredfold."
verseByVerse.commentary:
But those sown on the good soil are the ones who hear the word and accept it and bear fruit, thirtyfold, sixtyfold and a hundredfold.

The ones who hear the word and accept it. Three verbs, in an order that cannot be rearranged: hear, accept, bear fruit. Hear: the path heard it too; hearing is where everyone starts and where three of the four stop. Accept (paradechontai) means welcome, receive it fully, take it in as your own, the way you receive a guest rather than a leaflet. The good soil hears, welcomes the word into the heart, and holds it fast (Luke 8:15). It is the difference between a man who takes a letter at the door and a man who opens it, reads it and does what it says. And accepting is not merely agreeing that the sermon was true. It means letting the word in with authority: allowing it to contradict you and change what you do on Monday.

And bear fruit. The mark of good soil: a changed life, the fruit of the Spirit (Galatians 5:22–23), good works, and others brought to Christ. And the order is enormously important, because it is constantly reversed. Fruit is not the price of acceptance. It is the result of it. No plant produces grain by straining to produce grain. It receives light and water, and the fruit is what comes out of that. Abide in me, and I in you. As the branch cannot bear fruit by itself, unless it abides in the vine, neither can you, unless you abide in me (John 15:4). That is the answer to a way of living that exhausts many sincere Christians: trying to squeeze fruit out of themselves by effort, and concluding they are failures when they cannot. You are not asked to manufacture. You are asked to receive, and keep receiving, and let it go down.

Thirtyfold and sixtyfold and a hundredfold. Different amounts; every true believer bears some. And here is the kindness in the last clause: the yields are different, and all three are good soil. Jesus could have said a hundredfold and left it there. He put thirty in the same category as a hundred. There is no suggestion that the thirtyfold Christian is second-class.

Where does good soil come from? Every heart is hard by nature. God makes the soil good: he gives a new heart (Ezekiel 36:26), he opens hearts, as he opened Lydia’s (Acts 16:14), and he gives the growth (1 Corinthians 3:6–7). Our part is to receive the word humbly (James 1:21). The Sower who scattered his seed across your life knew exactly what was under the surface when he threw it, and threw it anyway, and he is the one who breaks up the ground.

The lessons. For hearers: what kind of soil are you? For witnesses and preachers: do not be discouraged when many do not respond. The sower sows widely, and the harvest will come. The problem is never the seed.

What if I see very little fruit in my life? First, be careful of measuring yourself by others. Some believers are given health, gifts, years and opportunity, and their lives are visibly fruitful. Some are ill, or poor, or obscure, or worn down by circumstances they did not choose, and what they produce is thirty: a marriage held together, a few people prayed for by name for decades, a faith kept in a hard place where nobody applauded. Both are in this verse, and the barn does not sort them. Second, fruit is often invisible to the tree. Ask a mature friend what they see. Third, if there really is nothing, go back to the root: are you abiding in Christ, in his word, in prayer, among his people? Fruit comes from there, not from trying harder.

In a sentence. Good-soil hearers welcome the word and bear abundant fruit.

On a Tuesday. Keep sowing God’s word, whatever response you see. The harvest is God’s. And do not spend your life comparing your field with someone else’s. What God asks of a field is not that it should be the best field, but honest ground, taking in what falls on it. Take in one word from Scripture today, and let it change one thing you do.

For worship. Thank God for making your heart receptive to his word. It was hard ground once, and he broke it. It was stony, and he gave a heart of flesh. It was choked, and he cleared it. Every fruit in your life is his, from the seed to the sun to the growth. The Lord of the harvest makes his fields good and then rejoices over what they bear, thirty or sixty or a hundred, and calls it all his.

parallels.desc: whoever abides in me bears much fruit

verseByVerse.quote: And he said to them, "Is a lamp brought in to be put under a basket, or under a bed, and not on a stand? For nothing is hidden except to be made manifest; nor is anything secret except to come to light. If anyone has ears to hear, let him hear."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus said: is a lamp brought in to be put under a basket or under a bed, and not on a stand? For nothing is hidden except to be made manifest, nor is anything secret except to come to light. If anyone has ears to hear, let him hear.

Is a lamp brought in to be put under a basket, or under a bed, and not on a stand? The tone changes, and the change is a relief. After a paragraph about seeing and not perceiving, Jesus picks up a household object and asks a question a child could answer. A household lamp was a small clay bowl of olive oil with a wick, giving about as much light as a candle. The basket (modios) was a grain measure, a bushel bowl. The bed was a low couch. And the question is faintly comic on purpose: no one lights a lamp to hide it. You would put it out and save the oil. Literally the Greek says, does the lamp come? and some see Jesus himself as the lamp who has come into the world.

For nothing is hidden except to be made manifest. This answers the worry the last paragraph raised. If the parables conceal, has God gone into the business of hiding things? No. The kingdom is now hidden, spoken in parables, understood by few (vv. 10–12). But it is hidden in order to be revealed. It does not say that hidden things sometimes come out; it says that the whole purpose of the hiding was the eventual showing. A lamp goes under a basket for a moment while somebody carries it across a room. It does not live there. The light will shine, and one day everything will be made plain.

Nor is anything secret except to come to light. The secret of the kingdom will be proclaimed to all after the resurrection (9:9). That is precisely what happens in this Gospel. Jesus silences demons, hushes the healed, tells the disciples to say nothing, and then dies in public on a hill outside a city wall in the busiest week of the year, and a Roman officer says aloud what nobody was allowed to say (15:39). The secret was always going to be shouted. It was being protected until it could be understood, the way you shield a flame with your hand while carrying it, not because you want the room dark but because you want it lit.

The dark parts of your own story. This is a real comfort for the parts of your life that make no sense yet. A great deal of what God is doing is in the dark at the moment, in you, and in situations you have prayed about for years with nothing to show for it. This verse does not promise an explanation next Tuesday. It promises that the darkness is not the point. Nothing in the hands of God is hidden for the sake of being hidden. Now we see in a mirror dimly, but then face to face (1 Corinthians 13:12).

If anyone has ears to hear, let him hear. The refrain returns, and by now it has an edge. He has just said that everything hidden is destined to be revealed. The only question left is whether you are the kind of person who goes and asks.

Will my secret sins be exposed on the day of judgment if I am a Christian? The New Testament does say that nothing is covered up that will not be revealed (Luke 12:2), and that we must all appear before the judgment seat of Christ (2 Corinthians 5:10). But for those in Christ, the judgment is not condemnation (Romans 8:1). Your sins were brought into the light at the cross, judged there, and removed as far as the east is from the west (Psalm 103:12). Whatever is shown on that day will be shown as forgiven, and will magnify his grace. So you do not need to live in dread of exposure. You can bring your secrets into the light now, to God and, where wise, to a trusted friend, and walk in the light (1 John 1:7).

In a sentence. The kingdom is hidden now only so that it may be revealed, as a lamp is lit to be seen.

On a Tuesday. The light of Christ in you is not meant to be hidden. Let it be seen today: in a kindness done without fuss, in a word about him to a friend, in honesty at work when a lie would be easier. And name one thing in your life you are keeping in the dark. Bring it to the light before God this week.

For worship. He is the light of the world, and he did not come to be hidden. He was shielded for a while, his glory veiled in flesh and his name hushed, and then he was lifted up in the sight of all, and the light broke out over the nations. One day every hidden thing will be revealed, and the brightest thing revealed will be the glory of the Lamb. In his light we see light.
verseByVerse.note: A household lamp was a small clay bowl of oil with a wick; the “basket” was a grain measure.

verseByVerse.quote: And he said to them, "Pay attention to what you hear: with the measure you use, it will be measured to you, and still more will be added to you. For to the one who has, more will be given, and from the one who has not, even what he has will be taken away."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus said: pay attention to what you hear. With the measure you use, it will be measured to you, and still more will be added to you. For to the one who has, more will be given, and from the one who has not, even what he has will be taken away.

Pay attention to what you hear. Literally see what you hear. Listen carefully. Luke records it as take care then how you hear (Luke 8:18). It turns out that listening is not a passive activity you succeed or fail at by accident. It is something you do, and can do well or badly, and will be held responsible for.

With the measure you use, it will be measured to you. A merchant’s picture. A man brings his own container to be filled, and what he gets depends on the size of the vessel he brought. Bring a thimble to the merchant and you will carry home a thimbleful, however generous he is. Here it applies to listening: the attention and response you give to God’s word determines how much understanding you receive.

And still more will be added to you. God is generous. Then Jesus breaks the picture open, and this is the part people miss. The merchant does not merely fill your container level. He heaps it over. This is God, not a shopkeeper, and the arrangement is not strict exchange; it is a generosity that outruns the vessel. Those who listen well receive more than they give.

For to the one who has, more will be given. Those who receive and respond to the truth receive more. It sounds at first like the worst thing about the world, the rich getting richer. But Jesus is not describing money. He is describing spiritual capacity, and there it is simply how understanding works. Everything you take in and act on enlarges the vessel you bring back next time. You know this from ordinary life. The man who learns a little music hears more in the next piece; the man who learns a little of a language hears words where he used to hear only noise. Use expands the organ.

And from the one who has not, even what he has will be taken away. Those who neglect the truth lose even what they had. Spiritual understanding not used is lost. A truth heard and never obeyed does not sit patiently waiting to be obeyed later; it hardens, and next time it comes past it will be a little easier to ignore. That is not a punishment arbitrarily imposed. It is the path of verse 15 described from the inside. The ground got hard by traffic.

Does this mean God gives more to clever people? No. The measure is not intelligence but obedience. A child who believes and obeys a simple truth receives more from God than a scholar who studies Scripture and does nothing with it. Some of the most spiritually wise people in any church have little formal education; they have simply spent decades doing what God says. The container that grows is a heart that hears and obeys, and anyone can bring that.

In a sentence. Listen carefully, because those who respond to God’s word receive more, and those who neglect it lose what they had.

On a Tuesday. How carefully do you listen to sermons and read your Bible? The measure you give is the measure you get. Think of the last clear thing God said to you through Scripture or a sermon: not the last interesting thing, the last thing you knew you were meant to do. The conversation to have, the habit to stop, the person to forgive, the money to give. Did you do it? If yes, expect more; that is the promise. If no, understand what is at stake: not that God is annoyed with you, but that the next thing he says will be fainter, and one day you may sit through the very words that once moved you and feel nothing. He is not asking for concentration. He is asking for obedience, because obedience is the only container that ever gets bigger.

For worship. The God we deal with is not a careful merchant but an overflowing giver. He heaps the measure, pressed down, shaken together, running over. Every truth we receive and obey opens room for more, and there is no end to what he has to give, because there is no end to him. From his fullness we have all received, grace upon grace.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 26–41 — The Growing Seed, the Mustard Seed, and the Storm
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The seed that grows while you sleep (vv. 26–29). A parable found only in Mark, and it is the most relaxing thing in the chapter. A man scatters seed and then goes to bed, gets up, goes to bed, gets up — and the seed grows, and he knows not how. The growth is not his doing and never was.

The mustard seed (vv. 30–32). The proverbially smallest thing in the garden becomes the largest plant in it, with branches enough for birds to nest in. Spoken to twelve unimpressive men whose movement looked like nothing at all.

As they were able to hear it (vv. 33–34). Mark tells us the teaching was calibrated: parables to the crowd, everything explained in private to the disciples. God gives truth at the rate a person can take it.

The storm (vv. 35–41). And then the chapter stops talking about the word and puts them in a boat. It was his idea to cross. The storm was not an interruption of obedience but the road it went down. He is asleep on a cushion; they are bailing; and the question they ask at the end — who then is this? — is the question the whole Gospel has been walking toward.
verseByVerse.theology:
The stilling of the storm is not a nature miracle among others; it is a disclosure of who is in the boat, and the disciples' own Scriptures gave them the answer to their question the moment they asked it.

In the Old Testament, mastery of the sea belongs to God and to nobody else. You rule the raging of the sea; when its waves rise, you still them (Ps. 89:9). He made the storm be still, and the waves of the sea were hushed (Ps. 107:29) — in a psalm about sailors at their wits' end who cried to the LORD in their trouble. It was God who shut in the sea with doors and said thus far shall you come, and no farther, and here shall your proud waves be stayed (Job 38:8–11). To the ancient mind the sea was chaos itself, the one thing no king could command.

So who then is this, that even the wind and the sea obey him? has exactly one possible answer, and it should have frightened them more than the weather did.

And hold the two halves of the scene together, because the chapter will not let you have one without the other. He was asleep because he was exhausted — a real man, worn out, on a boat cushion, so tired that a storm did not wake him. And he silenced the sea with a word. Fully man in his exhaustion, fully God in his voice, in the same four feet of a fishing boat.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: experienced fishermen, on their own lake, in their own boat, bailing with their hands and certain they were about to die — while the Lord of wind and wave slept four feet away.

Now: the same accusation, in the same words, from every believer in a storm — do you not care? And it is worth noticing that Mark preserved the accusation. The Gospel does not tidy up the prayer of frightened men into something more reverent. There is a place in Scripture for saying exactly that to God, and the Psalms are full of it: Awake! Why are you sleeping, O Lord? (Ps. 44:23).

Two things follow. First, he answered the panicked prayer before he corrected the panic — the storm was stilled, and then the question about faith was asked. He is not waiting for you to pray well before he acts. Second, their fear did not end when the danger did; Mark says they were filled with great fear after the calm. They were more frightened of the man in the boat than of the wind. That is not a failure. That is the beginning of knowing who he is.

verseByVerse.quote: And he said, "The kingdom of God is as if a man should scatter seed on the ground. He sleeps and rises night and day, and the seed sprouts and grows; he knows not how. The earth produces by itself, first the blade, then the ear, then the full grain in the ear. But when the grain is ripe, at once he puts in the sickle, because the harvest has come."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus said: the kingdom of God is like a man who scatters seed on the ground. He sleeps and rises night and day, and the seed sprouts and grows; he does not know how. The earth produces by itself, first the blade, then the ear, then the full grain in the ear. But when the grain is ripe, at once he puts in the sickle, because the harvest has come.

The kingdom of God is as if a man should scatter seed on the ground. Only Mark records this parable, and it is the most restful thing in the chapter. The farmer does his part: he sows. And then Jesus tells us what he does next, and it is the surprise of the story: nothing.

He sleeps and rises night and day. A few ordinary words for a man’s whole life. He goes to bed; he gets up; he goes to bed; he gets up. He gets on with ordinary life. There is no watching over the field at night, no anxious digging up of seed to see how it is doing. He cannot make the seed grow by worrying.

And the seed sprouts and grows; he knows not how. Growth is a mystery, beyond his control. Not that he does not control it: he does not even understand it. And his ignorance does not slow the crop by a single day. Now feel who this was spoken to: twelve men who had just been given a mission and were, on any reasonable assessment, unqualified for it. Soon they will be sent out two by two with no money and no spare tunic and told to preach. Everything in them will want to know how it works, whether they are doing it right, and what to do when it does not seem to be working. Jesus tells them: you scatter, and then you sleep. The power was never in the sower.

The earth produces by itself. By itself (automatē, from which we get automatic) means without visible cause. Not without God, obviously; this is a picture of how God works, not of his absence. But without the farmer. God makes it grow. I planted, Apollos watered, but God gave the growth (1 Corinthians 3:6–7).

First the blade, then the ear, then the full grain in the ear. Growth happens in stages, gradually, often unseen. This is the tenderest line for anyone worried about their own slowness, or somebody else’s. The stages cannot be skipped or hurried. A blade is not a failed ear; it is a blade, which is exactly what a healthy plant looks like in April. God is not disappointed with a young Christian for not being an old one, and he is not finished with an old one either.

But when the grain is ripe, at once he puts in the sickle, because the harvest has come. The words are lifted from Joel: put in the sickle, for the harvest is ripe (Joel 3:13), a text about the final judgment of the nations. The harvest pictures the end of the age and the final judgment (Matthew 13:39). So this is not merely a story about patience. There is a harvest, and it is fixed, and it comes not when the field is exhausted but when the grain is ripe. The long, quiet, unimpressive middle of history, the stretch you are living in, where the kingdom looks small and slow and nothing seems to happen, is not drift. It is growing season. The kingdom grows quietly now, and will come to its harvest at the end, and the man with the sickle knows the day.

The lesson. The kingdom grows by God’s power, not ours. We sow the word, and God gives the growth. This brings both relief and confidence: relief, because we do not have to make it grow; confidence, because God will bring it to harvest.

What it does not mean. Not that we should be passive. The farmer sows and reaps. But we cannot force growth: in our children, our friends, our church, or ourselves. You cannot argue a person into the kingdom, or engineer a revival, or produce growth in your own soul by force of will.

How should I pray for a child or friend who shows no sign of growth? Keep sowing and keep praying, and then actually go to bed. Pray specifically that God would open their heart, as he opened Lydia’s (Acts 16:14), and give them a new heart. Keep living out the faith in front of them with warmth rather than pressure, and keep the door open. Do not dig up the seed every week to see whether it has sprouted; nagging rarely helps. Many a believer looks back on years when parents or friends saw nothing, while the seed was quietly at work underground. And leave the timing to God. The harvest comes when the grain is ripe, not when we are ready.

In a sentence. The kingdom grows by God’s hidden power, like seed growing while the farmer sleeps, until the harvest comes.

On a Tuesday. Have you been sowing the word in someone’s life without seeing results? Keep sowing, sleep well, and trust God with the growth. Do your sowing honestly and generously: the conversation, the teaching, the years with your children, the invitation, the faithful ordinary Sunday. Then go to bed. The anxious sleeplessness that so often passes for spiritual seriousness is not in this parable at all, and the crop is not depending on it.

For worship. The God who makes the seed grow in the dark is the God who neither slumbers nor sleeps. While we sleep, he works. The life of the kingdom is his life, hidden in the soil of the world, rising in its seasons, unstoppable. He began it, he grows it, and he will bring in the harvest with joy. He gives to his beloved sleep, because the growth was always his.
verseByVerse.note: Only Mark records this parable of the seed growing by itself.

parallels.desc: put in the sickle, for the harvest is ripe
the farmer waits for the precious fruit

verseByVerse.quote: And he said, "With what can we compare the kingdom of God, or what parable shall we use for it? It is like a grain of mustard seed, which, when sown on the ground, is the smallest of all the seeds on earth, yet when it is sown it grows up and becomes larger than all the garden plants and puts out large branches, so that the birds of the air can make nests in its shade."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus said: with what can we compare the kingdom of God? It is like a grain of mustard seed, which when sown is the smallest of all seeds on earth, yet when it grows it becomes larger than all the garden plants and puts out large branches, so that the birds of the air can make nests in its shade.

With what can we compare the kingdom of God, or what parable shall we use for it? Jesus invites his hearers to think with him, asking aloud, as a teacher does when he wants the class leaning in. And the answer he reaches for is deliberately, almost comically, small.
