It is like a grain of mustard seed, which, when sown on the ground, is the smallest of all the seeds on earth. The black mustard seed was proverbially tiny, the smallest seed farmers in Galilee commonly sowed, and the rabbis used it as the standard picture of tininess, the way we say a grain of sand. Jesus speaks as people spoke. What matters is the size of the thing in the hand. It is a speck. You could lose it in the creases of your palm.

Was Jesus wrong that mustard is the smallest of all seeds? No. He was not giving a lecture in botany or making a claim about the seed catalogue of the world. He was using the everyday proverb of the people in front of him, about the seeds a Galilean farmer actually handled, exactly as we say the sun rises without being wrong about astronomy. Of all the seeds his hearers sowed in their fields and gardens, the mustard seed was the smallest, and everyone knew it. Speaking in the ordinary language of his hearers is not error; it is how all clear speech works.

Yet when it is sown it grows up and becomes larger than all the garden plants and puts out large branches. The mustard plant could grow up to three metres high in one season: tall enough to ride through, woody enough to hold weight. Nothing in the seed announces it.

So that the birds of the air can make nests in its shade. This is not decoration; it is a deliberate echo, and every Jew on that beach would have caught it. In the Old Testament, a great tree with birds in its branches pictures a great kingdom sheltering the nations (Ezekiel 17:23; 31:6; Daniel 4:12). In Ezekiel, God takes a sprig from the top of a cedar and plants it on the mountain height of Israel, and under it every kind of bird will nest. The birds are the nations. The kingdom of God, though tiny at first, will become great and shelter people from all nations.

The meaning. The kingdom began insignificantly: a carpenter from Nazareth, twelve ordinary men, rejected by the leaders. It looked like nothing. Hear who is listening: a dozen men and a handful of others on a beach in a provincial district of an occupied country, following a village carpenter whose family thinks he is unwell and whose national leaders have ruled him demonic. Rome has legions and roads and an emperor. This has a boat. And Jesus says: the kingdom of God is that speck in your hand. Yet it would grow into a worldwide kingdom, as it has. The distance between the speck and the shade is not covered by strategy or numbers. It is covered by the nature of the seed. Small is not the same as weak, and slow is not the same as failing, and it is only ever in the hand that a mustard seed looks like nothing.

What it does not mean. Not that the world will become Christian before Christ returns, as postmillennialists teach. The parables of growth stand alongside the parables of mixed fields and continuing evil (Matthew 13:24–30). Verdict: amillennial: the kingdom grows powerfully through the whole gospel age, and comes to its fullness when Christ returns.

In a sentence. The kingdom starts as small as a mustard seed but grows into a great plant that shelters the nations.

On a Tuesday. Do not despise small beginnings: a small church, a single conversation, a little faith. God’s kingdom grows from mustard seeds. If the part of the kingdom you can see is discouragingly small, the ageing congregation, the Sunday school class of four, the one believing member of a family, the years of prayer for a person who has not moved an inch, remember that you are not looking at the tree. You are looking at the seed, and you were never given the ability to tell the difference by looking.

For worship. Two thousand years after that afternoon, the speck has put out branches on every continent, and men and women of every language nest in its shade, and the seed has not finished growing. The kingdom that began with a carpenter and twelve fishermen will fill the earth, and the King who was planted in the ground like a seed on a Friday rose on the Sunday as the firstfruits of a harvest without end. Of the increase of his government and of peace there will be no end.
verseByVerse.note: Mustard seed was proverbially tiny; the plant can grow taller than a man.

verseByVerse.quote: With many such parables he spoke the word to them, as they were able to hear it. He did not speak to them without a parable, but privately to his own disciples he explained everything.
verseByVerse.commentary:
With many such parables Jesus spoke the word to them, as they were able to hear it. He did not speak to them without a parable, but privately to his own disciples he explained everything.

With many such parables he spoke the word to them. Mark records only a few. Mark steps back from the scene for two verses and tells us how the Lord taught, and both halves are worth having.

As they were able to hear it. Jesus adapted his teaching to his hearers’ capacity. Stop on that clause, because it is one of the kindest sentences in the Gospel. He measured what he said to what they could take. Not to what he could have said, nor to what was true, since all of it was true, but to what they could bear. He does that all the way through. In the upper room he says it in so many words: I still have many things to say to you, but you cannot bear them now (John 16:12). Parables were both a mercy, making truth memorable and accessible, and a test, concealing it from the unwilling.

He did not speak to them without a parable. To the crowds.

But privately to his own disciples he explained everything. Those who came to him and asked received full understanding (v. 10). Two audiences, two levels, and the difference between them is not intelligence but willingness to come to Jesus. The explanation happens privately, to those who stayed. Everything in this chapter keeps coming back to that: the crowd got the story, the ones who did not go home got the meaning, and the only qualification was that they were still there when the beach emptied. He explained everything. He did not leave his own people with a riddle, and the door into the private room was never locked.

Two lessons. To yourself, if you are impatient with your own understanding: there is a way of reading the Bible that turns into anxiety, the sense that you ought to have grasped more by now and that your slowness is a mark against you. He is not withholding out of displeasure. He gives at the rate a person can receive. And to how you handle other people: if the Lord matched what he said to his hearers, so should we. There is a kind of zeal that unloads everything it knows onto a new believer, a struggling one or a person just bereaved, every doctrine, every implication, every hard edge, and calls it faithfulness. It is a failure to notice who is in the room. Say what they can hear. There will be more Tuesdays.

How do I ask Jesus to explain Scripture today? He explains his word by his Spirit through his word, so the ordinary means are the way. Pray before you read, asking him to open your eyes (Psalm 119:18). Read slowly, and read the surrounding chapters, since Scripture interprets Scripture. Bring your questions to faithful preaching and to mature Christians, and use a good study Bible or commentary. Discuss passages in a small group. And obey what you do understand, because understanding grows through obedience (John 7:17). He does not give new revelation, but he does give light on what he has already said.

In a sentence. Jesus taught the crowds in parables as they could hear, and explained everything privately to his disciples.

On a Tuesday. Jesus explains his word to those who come close. Spend time with him in his word and prayer. The difference between a Christian who understands his Bible and one who does not is very rarely ability, and very often simply this: one keeps coming back to Christ with the bits he did not follow, and the other closes the book. Stay behind. Ask. And this week, with someone younger in the faith, say one thing they can hear rather than everything you know.

For worship. The Son of God, with all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge hidden in him, stooped to the measure of fishermen. He did not overwhelm them; he fed them as they could eat. He is gentle and lowly in heart, and he teaches like that still. And to his own he explains everything, in time, until the day we know fully, even as we have been fully known.

verseByVerse.quote: On that day, when evening had come, he said to them, "Let us go across to the other side." And leaving the crowd, they took him with them in the boat, just as he was. And other boats were with him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
That day, when evening had come, Jesus said: let us go across to the other side. Leaving the crowd, they took him with them in the boat, just as he was. And other boats were with him.

On that day, when evening had come. After a long day of teaching. Jesus was exhausted. Mark ties it to the day in the boat with the crowd on the shore. He has been preaching since morning. He is finished, and it is getting dark.

He said to them, “Let us go across to the other side”. To the eastern shore, Gentile territory (5:1). And here is the detail that changes how the whole storm is read: going out onto that lake was his idea. Not theirs. They were not running away from anything or making a poor decision he then had to rescue them from. The Son of God said cross, and they crossed, and the storm that nearly killed them was met in the middle of doing exactly what he told them. Notice too: Jesus said they would go to the other side. His word was a promise that they would arrive.

Does a storm in my life mean I have disobeyed God? Not necessarily. A great deal of Christian thinking assumes it: when trouble comes we search backwards for the wrong turn, what did I miss, where did I disobey, is this because I stopped praying. Sometimes there is a wrong turn, and it should be found and repented of. But this boat is in this storm because Jesus put it there, and obedience was the route in. Job did not suffer because he had drifted; the book opens by insisting he was blameless. Paul was in the will of God on the ship that broke up under him (Acts 27). The storm you are in may not be evidence of anything having gone wrong at all. It may simply be what the other side costs.

And leaving the crowd, they took him with them in the boat, just as he was. He was already in the boat, from which he had been teaching (v. 1). Just as he was: no going ashore, no meal, no change of clothes. They simply pushed off with him still in it, exhausted where he sat. It is a vivid detail, from an eyewitness like Peter. Keep hold of it when you reach verse 38 and find him asleep. Mark has already told you why.

And other boats were with him. Only Mark mentions this, another eyewitness detail, easy to skip. It means the storm did not fall on one boat. There were other people out on that water in the dark, in other boats, with no one aboard who could still a wave. Mark says nothing about what happened to them, and the silence is its own comfort: when the calm came, it came over the whole lake. Some who benefited from the miracle may never have known who had done it. Some of what God does in answer to the church’s terrified praying spills a long way past the church, and is never traced back.

In a sentence. At evening, Jesus told the disciples to cross the lake, and they set off with him in the boat.

On a Tuesday. When Jesus says let us go to the other side, he will get you there, whatever storms come. If you are in a hard place that you entered by doing what he asked, do not let the storm persuade you that you misheard him. Hold on to what he said at the shore.

For worship. He said, let us go over, and he went with them. The Lord who sends his people into the storm goes into it with them, in the same boat, under the same sky. He never sends us anywhere he does not come himself, and his word of promise at the shore is stronger than every wave on the way across.

verseByVerse.quote: And a great windstorm arose, and the waves were breaking into the boat, so that the boat was already filling. But he was in the stern, asleep on the cushion. And they woke him and said to him, "Teacher, do you not care that we are perishing?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
A great windstorm arose, and the waves were breaking into the boat, so that it was already filling. But Jesus was in the stern, asleep on the cushion. They woke him and said: Teacher, do you not care that we are perishing?

And a great windstorm arose. The word (lailaps) means a furious squall that hits without warning. The geography explains it, and these men knew it better than we do. The Sea of Galilee lies about 700 feet below sea level, in a bowl surrounded by hills, with the Golan heights rising steeply to the east and gullies running down to the water. Cold air rushing down from the heights onto the warm air over the lake can create sudden violent storms, and the surface can go from glass to breaking waves in minutes. It is still notorious.

And the waves were breaking into the boat, so that the boat was already filling. Not spray, but waves coming in over the side, one after another. The boat was sinking. And take seriously who these men are. At least four of them are professional fishermen who have worked this lake since boyhood, on water they know as well as their own street. Experienced fishermen were terrified, so this was no ordinary storm. When men like that conclude they are about to drown, they are almost certainly right.

But he was in the stern, asleep on the cushion. Mark gives three details nobody would invent: the stern, the cushion and the sleep. Only Mark mentions the cushion, perhaps a sandbag kept for ballast, or a leather pillow for the steersman; he writes the cushion, the way a man remembers the exact object. And hold what that sleep means, because it is a window onto who Jesus is. He is asleep because he is worn out. Jesus was truly human and truly exhausted. The Son of God got tired, properly, physically tired, the tiredness that will not wake for a squall and freezing water breaking over you. He was hungry (11:12), he was thirsty (John 19:28), he wept at a graveside (John 11:35). Whatever else the incarnation means, it means there is a man in that boat, and he is exhausted. And his sleep showed complete trust in his Father: in peace I will both lie down and sleep; for you alone, O LORD, make me dwell in safety (Psalm 4:8). He can sleep in a storm on a lake he made.

And they woke him and said to him, “Teacher, do you not care that we are perishing”? Only Mark records this accusing question, and he did not tidy it up. It is not a prayer request; it is an accusation. They do not ask him to do anything. They do not say save us; they say, do you not care? That is what fear does to us. It goes past the danger and attacks the character of God. The real terror in that boat was not only the water but the sudden conviction that the one in charge had gone quiet and might not be bothered. The disciples thought he did not care. In storms we often feel the same: God, do you not care? But he did care. He was with them in the boat.

Is it wrong to complain to God like that? Scripture is full of honest complaint, and it preserves this sentence rather than hiding it. Awake! Why are you sleeping, O Lord? (Psalm 44:23). How long, O LORD? Will you forget me forever? (Psalm 13:1). God would rather have that cried out to him from four feet away than have you drown politely at the other end of the boat. What is wrong is not bringing your fear to him but accusing him and walking away. These men got one thing right in the middle of getting everything else wrong: when they were sure they were dying, they went to him. So pour out your heart, and then, as the psalmists did, remind yourself of his steadfast love.

In a sentence. A violent storm swamped the boat while Jesus slept, and the terrified disciples woke him, asking if he did not care that they were perishing.

On a Tuesday. If you feel that God does not care in your storm, tell him so honestly, as the disciples did. He is in the boat with you. And if you have said something to God in a hospital corridor or at two in the morning that you would be ashamed to repeat in church, know that he heard it, and did not throw you overboard.

For worship. The Lord of the storm lay asleep on a cushion because he had taken a body that could be tired. He emptied himself so far that the wind could rage over his head while he slept. And he cared. He cared enough to come into the boat at all, and he cared enough to go, at the last, into a storm far worse than this one, so that his frightened friends would never perish.
verseByVerse.note: The Sea of Galilee lies low and ringed by hills; sudden violent storms are common. The cushion was probably the helmsman’s seat or a sandbag in the stern.

parallels.desc: the sleeping prophet in the storm
awake! why are you sleeping, O Lord?

verseByVerse.quote: And he awoke and rebuked the wind and said to the sea, "Peace! Be still!" And the wind ceased, and there was a great calm.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus woke up, rebuked the wind and said to the sea: peace! Be still! And the wind ceased, and there was a great calm.

And he awoke and rebuked the wind. No preparation. He does not take the helm, or tell them to bail harder, or pray to his Father for deliverance. He wakes in a swamped boat and speaks to the weather as though it had been misbehaving. Rebuked is the word used for silencing demons (1:25). He addresses the wind as one rebukes a disobedient servant, as a hostile thing that has no business being there.

And said to the sea, “Peace! Be still!” The English is gentler than the Greek. The first word means be silent; the second (pephimōso) literally means be muzzled, the very word used to the demon in 1:25. The sea is told to shut its mouth and stay shut. Hear that against everything an ancient reader believed about the sea. To Israel the sea was not a beauty spot; it was chaos, the old enemy, the thing that swallows men and gives nothing back. In the Old Testament the sea often pictures chaos and evil, and only God can rule it. You rule the raging of the sea; when its waves rise, you still them (Psalm 89:9; 65:7). He made the storm be still, and the waves of the sea were hushed (Psalm 107:23–30). Thus far shall you come, and no farther, and here shall your proud waves be stayed (Job 38:8–11). And this is a carpenter, standing in a fishing boat, wet through, speaking to a storm in the dark.

And the wind ceased, and there was a great calm. Do not let familiarity flatten that. Normally the waves continue long after the wind stops; anyone who has been at sea knows that the swell outlives the storm. Here, instant calm. Wind gone, water flat, as though the lake had never moved. Mark sets the two greats side by side: a great storm (v. 37), a great calm, and one sentence between them. And there is the difference between him and every other help you have ever had. Everything else that assists you works with the situation, manages it, gets you through it. He speaks to it.

If Jesus rules the wind and the sea, why does he allow storms and disasters? Scripture does not give us a full explanation, but it gives us enough to trust him. Natural disasters belong to a creation subjected to futility because of human sin, groaning as it waits to be set free (Romans 8:20–22). God rules them still: not one storm escapes his hand, and he works through all things for the good of those who love him (Romans 8:28). Sometimes disasters are warnings to a careless world to repent (Luke 13:4–5). And this story shows us his heart and his future: the one who stilled one storm on one lake will one day remove every storm from a renewed creation, where there is no more sea of chaos (Revelation 21:1). Until then, we bring our fears to the one who rules the waves.

In a sentence. Jesus rebuked the wind and commanded the sea to be still, and there was instant and great calm.

On a Tuesday. Name the storm you are in today, and speak it to the one who speaks to storms. You may not see the calm at once. But the same voice that silenced Galilee is the voice that intercedes for you, and nothing that rages against you is outside his rule.

For worship. Worship Jesus, whom the wind and the sea obey. And hold this alongside the only other moment in Mark when the world goes dark and then quiet. On a hill outside Jerusalem the sky turns black at noon for three hours, and a man cries out that God has forsaken him, and then he dies (15:33–37), and it goes quiet. That day nobody rebuked the storm. He went into it and let it break over him with nothing held back, and it was not muzzled, and it did not stop until it had finished with him. The voice that could have silenced anything said nothing at all, so that when the storms come for us they come as weather and not as wrath.

parallels.desc: you rule the raging of the sea
he made the storm be still

verseByVerse.quote: He said to them, "Why are you so afraid? Have you still no faith?" And they were filled with great fear and said to one another, "Who then is this, that even the wind and the sea obey him?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus said to them: why are you so afraid? Have you still no faith? And they were filled with great fear and said to one another: who then is this, that even the wind and the sea obey him?

Why are you so afraid? Have you still no faith? It sounds hard, and a nervous reader flinches. Two things take the sting out of it without taking away the point. First, look at the order of events. He stilled the storm and then asked the question. He did not require a better standard of praying before he would act. He dealt with the water first, because they needed it dealt with, and only afterwards turned to what was wrong inside the boat. Remember that the next time you are ashamed of how badly you prayed in a crisis. He is not waiting for you to pray well. Second, hear what the question asks. The word (deiloi) means timid, cowardly, and the issue is not the fear but its object. They had every reason to be afraid of the lake and no reason at all to be afraid with him in the boat. The rebuke is not, you felt something. It is, you forgot who was aboard.

Still no faith. Still is the sad word: after all they had seen, a leper made clean, a paralytic walking, a withered hand restored, demons obeying him in public. Their fear showed they did not yet trust him. Faith here means trusting Jesus to keep his word (they would go to the other side, v. 35) and to care for them. What they had not yet done is take any of it into the one place where it would cost them something: the place where they thought they were dying. That is a familiar distance, the gap between what you believe on a Sunday and what you can lay hold of at three in the morning. Faith is not tested by whether you can affirm a doctrine. It is tested by whether the doctrine bears weight when the water comes over the side.

Is fear always a lack of faith? No. Fear is a natural response to real danger, and Jesus himself was greatly distressed in Gethsemane (14:33). Scripture does not command us never to feel fear; it tells us what to do with it: when I am afraid, I put my trust in you (Psalm 56:3). The disciples’ problem was not that they felt afraid in a sinking boat, but that their fear made them doubt his care and forget his power. So when fear comes, do not add guilt to it. Take it to Christ, tell him plainly, and remind yourself who is in the boat.

And they were filled with great fear. Literally they feared a great fear. And now the strangest thing in the chapter. The danger is over. The lake is like glass. And the disciples are more frightened than they were during the storm. Their fear of the storm became a greater fear: awe at Jesus himself. The storm had frightened them; the one who stopped it frightened them more. They had been afraid of drowning. Now they are afraid of the man standing in the boat with them, dripping wet, four feet away. This is not a failure of faith; it is the beginning of understanding. This is the fear of God, as the sailors in Jonah’s storm feared the LORD exceedingly when the sea grew calm (Jonah 1:16). When Isaiah saw the Lord he said, Woe is me! For I am lost (Isaiah 6:5). The fear of the LORD is the beginning of knowledge, and it has to begin somewhere.

And said to one another, “Who then is this, that even the wind and the sea obey him”? The question of the whole Gospel. They ask it of each other, in the dark, on flat water, and they do not answer it. Mark leaves it hanging at the end of the chapter, because the whole Gospel is the answer, and it will not be complete until a Roman soldier says it at the foot of a cross (15:39). But their own Scriptures had already answered it, and they knew those Scriptures by heart. Psalm 107:29 says of the LORD that he made the storm be still, and the waves of the sea were hushed. Jesus has done what only God does. There is one name in the whole Old Testament that fits, and no second candidate. The answer to their question is in Mark’s first verse: the Son of God.

What it does not mean. Not that Jesus always removes the storms of life when we ask. Sometimes he calms the storm; sometimes he calms us in it. The story is first about who he is.

In a sentence. Jesus asked why they still had no faith, and they were filled with awe, asking who he could be, that wind and sea obey him.

On a Tuesday. Let the question who is this? grow your faith. The one in your boat commands the storm. Take one fear you are carrying this week and set it beside what this chapter has shown you of him. Then say aloud, if only to yourself, who it is that is with you.

For worship. The man asleep on the helmsman’s cushion, so worn out by a day’s preaching that a squall could not wake him, is the one who said to the ocean, thus far shall you come, and no farther, before there was a man alive to see it. That is who was in the boat. Not a good teacher who happened to be useful in an emergency, but the Lord of the wind and the sea, tired out in the stern, having chosen to be there, in a body he took so that he could sleep, and thirst, and bleed, and die, for the men bailing water round his feet. Who then is this? He is the Son of God, and he is ours.

parallels.desc: who stills the roaring of the seas

4.theology:
Why parables? Verses 11–12 are the hardest words in the chapter and they should not be softened. Matthew says Jesus speaks in parables because people do not see (Matt. 13:13); Mark says so that they may not see, lest they should turn and be forgiven. Three things resolve it. The words are a quotation of Isaiah 6:9–10, God's charge to a prophet sent to a nation that had already shut its eyes for generations — settled judgement on hardened refusal, not fresh cruelty. The so that carries fulfilment as much as bare purpose: the parables meet a people who have chosen blindness and confirm the choice, which is how God deals with those who insist (cf. Rom. 1:24). And the door is never bolted — those around him with the twelve understood nothing either, and the one thing that separated them from the crowd walking home was that they stayed and asked.

Who is in the boat? In the Old Testament, command of the sea belongs to God alone: you rule the raging of the sea; when its waves rise, you still them (Ps. 89:9); he made the storm be still, and the waves of the sea were hushed (Ps. 107:29); thus far shall you come, and no farther (Job 38:11). So the disciples' closing question has exactly one possible answer. And Mark holds the two natures within four feet of each other: asleep from sheer exhaustion on the helmsman's cushion, and muzzling a hurricane with a word.
4.examples:
The four soils are not four historical types but four live possibilities in any congregation on any Sunday, and the third is the one that describes most Christians in a comfortable country.

The path was not made hard by a decision; it was made hard by traffic — the same feet over the same ground until nothing could get in. That is how hearts harden in real life: not by rejecting God but by hearing about him so often that the sound becomes familiar.

The rocky ground grows fastest, and grows fastest because the soil is shallow. The heat that kills it is the same sun that ripens the harvest in the next furrow. Roots are grown in private, in the boring stretches, and the test is simple: if the trial came this year, what exactly would you be drawing on?

The thorns are not sins. Jesus names them — cares, riches, and the desires for other things. Worry, money, and the ordinary wanting of ordinary stuff. This soil cannot be diagnosed by examining your conduct, because there may be nothing in it to confess. It is diagnosed by what has quietly stopped: the praying, the reading, the conversation about Christ you have not had in a year — not refused, just crowded out.

And the good soil yields thirty, sixty, or a hundred — and all three are good soil. Jesus put thirty in the same category as a hundred. Some believers are given health and years and visible fruitfulness; some produce a marriage held together and a few names prayed for over decades in a hard place where nobody applauded. Both are in verse 20, and the barn does not sort them.

5.title: Legion, Daughter, and the Hand That Takes Hold
5.text: <sup>1</sup>They came to the other side of the sea, to the country of the Gerasenes. <sup>2</sup>And when Jesus had stepped out of the boat, immediately there met him out of the tombs a man with an unclean spirit. <sup>3</sup>He lived among the tombs. And no one could bind him anymore, not even with a chain, <sup>4</sup>for he had often been bound with shackles and chains, but he wrenched the chains apart, and he broke the shackles in pieces. No one had the strength to subdue him. <sup>5</sup>Night and day among the tombs and on the mountains he was always crying out and cutting himself with stones. <sup>6</sup>And when he saw Jesus from afar, he ran and fell down before him. <sup>7</sup>And crying out with a loud voice, he said, “What have you to do with me, Jesus, Son of the Most High God? I adjure you by God, do not torment me.” <sup>8</sup>For he was saying to him, “Come out of the man, you unclean spirit!” <sup>9</sup>And Jesus asked him, “What is your name?” He replied, “My name is Legion, for we are many.” <sup>10</sup>And he begged him earnestly not to send them out of the country. <sup>11</sup>Now a great herd of pigs was feeding there on the hillside, <sup>12</sup>and they begged him, saying, “Send us to the pigs; let us enter them.” <sup>13</sup>So he gave them permission. And the unclean spirits came out and entered the pigs; and the herd, numbering about two thousand, rushed down the steep bank into the sea and drowned in the sea. <sup>14</sup>The herdsmen fled and told it in the city and in the country. And people came to see what it was that had happened. <sup>15</sup>And they came to Jesus and saw the demon-possessed man, the one who had had the legion, sitting there, clothed and in his right mind, and they were afraid. <sup>16</sup>And those who had seen it described to them what had happened to the demon-possessed man and to the pigs. <sup>17</sup>And they began to beg Jesus to depart from their region. <sup>18</sup>As he was getting into the boat, the man who had been possessed with demons begged him that he might be with him. <sup>19</sup>And he did not permit him but said to him, “Go home to your friends and tell them how much the Lord has done for you, and how he has had mercy on you.” <sup>20</sup>And he went away and began to proclaim in the Decapolis how much Jesus had done for him, and everyone marveled. <sup>21</sup>And when Jesus had crossed again in the boat to the other side, a great crowd gathered about him, and he was beside the sea. <sup>22</sup>Then came one of the rulers of the synagogue, Jairus by name, and seeing him, he fell at his feet <sup>23</sup>and implored him earnestly, saying, “My little daughter is at the point of death. Come and lay your hands on her, so that she may be made well and live.” <sup>24</sup>And he went with him. And a great crowd followed him and thronged about him. <sup>25</sup>And there was a woman who had had a discharge of blood for twelve years, <sup>26</sup>and who had suffered much under many physicians, and had spent all that she had, and was no better but rather grew worse. <sup>27</sup>She had heard the reports about Jesus and came up behind him in the crowd and touched his garment. <sup>28</sup>For she said, “If I touch even his garments, I will be made well.” <sup>29</sup>And immediately the flow of blood dried up, and she felt in her body that she was healed of her disease. <sup>30</sup>And Jesus, perceiving in himself that power had gone out from him, immediately turned about in the crowd and said, “Who touched my garments?” <sup>31</sup>And his disciples said to him, “You see the crowd pressing around you, and yet you say, ‘Who touched me?’” <sup>32</sup>And he looked around to see who had done it. <sup>33</sup>But the woman, knowing what had happened to her, came in fear and trembling and fell down before him and told him the whole truth. <sup>34</sup>And he said to her, “Daughter, your faith has made you well; go in peace, and be healed of your disease.” <sup>35</sup>While he was still speaking, there came from the ruler’s house some who said, “Your daughter is dead. Why trouble the Teacher any further?” <sup>36</sup>But overhearing what they said, Jesus said to the ruler of the synagogue, “Do not fear, only believe.” <sup>37</sup>And he allowed no one to follow him except Peter and James and John the brother of James. <sup>38</sup>They came to the house of the ruler of the synagogue, and Jesus saw a commotion, people weeping and wailing loudly. <sup>39</sup>And when he had entered, he said to them, “Why are you making a commotion and weeping? The child is not dead but sleeping.” <sup>40</sup>And they laughed at him. But he put them all outside and took the child’s father and mother and those who were with him and went in where the child was. <sup>41</sup>Taking her by the hand he said to her, “Talitha cumi,” which means, “Little girl, I say to you, arise.” <sup>42</sup>And immediately the girl got up and began walking (for she was twelve years of age), and they were immediately overcome with amazement. <sup>43</sup>And he strictly charged them that no one should know this, and told them to give her something to eat.
5.overview:
Chapter 5 is three impossible cases in a row, and the arrangement is deliberate. A man no one could restrain, a woman no one could cure, and a child who has already died — the whole range of human helplessness, met in one day and a boat ride.

It is also a chapter about uncleanness, and a modern reader misses most of it without knowing that. Under the Law three things defiled by contact: a grave, a discharge of blood, and a pig. Mark has put all three in one chapter. Jesus lands in a graveyard among pigs to save a man who lives in the tombs; an untouchable woman takes hold of his clothes in a crowd; and he ends the day taking a corpse by the hand. Every one of those contacts should have made him unclean under the system he himself gave. Every one of them runs the other way instead.

The two halves are held together by twelve years — the length of the woman's suffering and the whole life of Jairus's daughter — and by one word. The father calls the girl his little daughter; Jesus calls the destitute, unclean woman in the street Daughter, the only time in the Gospels he addresses a woman that way. The chapter opens with a man nobody could chain and closes with a girl being handed something to eat.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The landing (vv. 1–5). The storm of chapter 4 was crossed to reach this beach, and the welcoming party is one man out of the tombs — chained, unchainable, screaming night and day, cutting himself with stones. Mark spends five verses establishing that this case is beyond every remedy human beings had.

The encounter (vv. 6–10). He runs and falls at Jesus's feet, and the voice that comes out of him tries to put Jesus under oath. Asked its name, it answers with the word for a Roman army: Legion.

The pigs (vv. 11–13). The demons beg to be sent into a herd, and are permitted — and the herd goes over the cliff. What they intended for the man is acted out on the hillside for everyone to see.

The town's verdict (vv. 14–17). The neighbours arrive, find the man dressed and talking sense, and are frightened. They do not ask Jesus to stay and do more. They ask him to leave, and he goes.

The commission (vv. 18–20). The one man who wants to come is told no — and given a district instead of a boat. He becomes the first missionary to the Gentiles, and his whole training was what had happened to him.
verseByVerse.theology:
This chapter turns on ceremonial uncleanness, and a modern reader misses most of its force without knowing that. Under the Law, three things made a person unclean by contact: a corpse or a grave (Num. 19:11–16), a discharge of blood (Lev. 15:25–27), and a pig (Lev. 11:7). Mark has put all three in one chapter, and the man in this scene is standing in all of them at once — living among tombs, on a hillside where pigs are grazing, in Gentile country.

The whole logic of the purity system ran one way: uncleanness is contagious and holiness is not. Touch a corpse and you are defiled; the corpse does not become clean. Which is why what happens next in this chapter is so startling. A woman whose bleeding has made her untouchable for twelve years puts her hand on Jesus, and she is healed rather than he defiled. He takes a dead girl by the hand, and she gets up. The current runs backwards.

That is not Jesus ignoring the Law. It is the Law's purpose arriving. The system taught Israel for centuries that sin and death spread and cleanness does not — so that when a man walked into Israel whose holiness was catching, they would know exactly what they were looking at. He is the one clean thing in the world that cannot be contaminated, and everything he touches is what changes.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: a Gentile town given a neighbour back — sane, dressed, sitting down — and a hillside of dead livestock, and it grieves the livestock and asks the Healer to go.

Now: the same trade is still on offer, and it is not usually made by wicked people. It is made by people who have counted the cost of Christ disrupting an arrangement that works — the business practice, the relationship, the private habit, the plans — and quietly concluded they would rather keep the pigs. Nobody in that town denied the miracle. They simply decided it was too expensive.

And note what he does when they ask. He does not argue, and he does not stay. He gets into the boat. That is one of the most sobering sentences in the Gospel: Jesus goes where he is asked to go, including away.

But he does not leave them without a witness. The man they had chained and could not hold is left behind in the district with nothing to offer but what had been done to him — and by chapter 7 the crowds on that side of the lake will come out to meet Jesus. One restored man, telling one town, and the ground was ready.

verseByVerse.quote: They came to the other side of the sea, to the country of the Gerasenes. And when Jesus had stepped out of the boat, immediately there met him out of the tombs a man with an unclean spirit.
verseByVerse.commentary:
They came to the other side of the lake, to the region of the Gerasenes. As soon as Jesus stepped out of the boat, a man with an unclean spirit came out of the tombs to meet him.

Meaning first. Mark 5 is a chapter of three rescues, each harder than the last. On the eastern shore Jesus sends a legion of demons out of a man who lives among the tombs, and the town, counting its drowned pigs, begs him to leave. On the western shore a woman who has bled for twelve years touches his cloak and is healed, and Jairus’ dead daughter is taken by the hand and told to get up. In every scene the same thing happens: what is unclean and dead does not defile him. His holiness and his life flow out to it.

The connection. Chapters 4:35–5:43 show Jesus’ authority over four enemies: the storm (nature), a legion of demons (the spiritual powers), chronic disease, and death itself. Each is a power no human can defeat. Mark sets them one after another so that by the end of the chapter there is nothing left in the list of what frightens human beings that has not been made to obey him.

They came to the other side of the sea. As Jesus had said they would (4:35), through a hurricane at night and a boat filling with water. Everything that happened on the lake happened on the way to this man. Jesus said, let us go across to the other side, and the other side had one person on it who needed him. If the price of the crossing was a night that nearly killed twelve experienced sailors, he paid it, and he paid it for a man whose own town had given up on him.

To the country of the Gerasenes. Gentile territory on the eastern shore of the lake: the region of the Decapolis, ten Greek cities, pagan country with pig farms on the hillsides. It is the first time in this Gospel that Jesus sets foot outside Jewish land, and he goes there to fight.

Gerasenes, Gadarenes or Gergesenes? A reader with a map will notice a real puzzle. Manuscripts vary between Gerasenes, Gadarenes (Matthew 8:28) and Gergesenes. Gerasa was a large city about thirty miles southeast, far too far for a herd to run down a steep bank into the sea; Gadara was closer, about six miles off, but still not on the shore; Gergesa (perhaps modern Kursi) was on the shore itself, where steep slopes come down to the water. The likeliest answer is that the names refer to regions: Gerasa and Gadara were the well-known cities whose districts reached down to that shore, and each writer named the region by the city his readers would recognise, as one might say a village lies in greater London. The place was probably near Kursi, where the steep bank is still there.

One man or two? Matthew says there were two men (Matthew 8:28); Mark and Luke tell of one. That is no contradiction. Mark and Luke follow the one who spoke, begged to go with Jesus and was sent home to tell his story, and neither of them says there was only one. A reporter who tells you about the survivor who gave the interview has not denied that there was another.

And when Jesus had stepped out of the boat, immediately there met him out of the tombs a man with an unclean spirit. He has one foot on the beach. The boat grounds and the man is coming down at them out of the rocks. And picture where he comes from. Tombs were caves cut in the hillside, and the limestone hills on that shore are full of them, some big enough to stand in. That is his address. A man is living in a graveyard, and the town knows it, and nobody has come to get him.

Unclean three times over. Under the law a grave defiled anyone who touched it for seven days (Numbers 19:16). This man is unclean three times over: demon-possessed, living among the dead, in a Gentile land near pigs. He is outside the town, outside worship, outside every category human beings use to organise the living.

The Holy One walks into the graveyard. Under the law uncleanness was catching: touch the dead and you became unclean. With Jesus the current runs the other way. The Holy One of God (1:24) walks into a cemetery and the cemetery is cleansed. And this beach is a preview of his whole errand. He would be counted among the transgressors, led out of the city to die where the unclean were sent (Hebrews 13:12), and laid in a tomb cut in the rock like the caves on this hillside. He went into our graveyard, not to be held by it, but to empty it from the inside. The man coming down out of the tombs is running towards the one who will walk out of a tomb himself.

Does demon possession happen today? The New Testament treats it as real, and nothing in it says the devil’s work ended with the apostles. Missionaries in places of open idolatry have often met things they could only describe this way. But Scripture also distinguishes the possessed from the sick (1:32–34), and most suffering of mind and body has ordinary causes and needs ordinary care. Two errors are to be avoided: seeing demons behind every illness, and denying that the devil works at all. And what drives out evil is not a technique, a ritual or a gifted specialist, but Christ himself, sought in prayer and trusted through his word (Ephesians 6:10–18; James 4:7).

Can a Christian be possessed by a demon? No. A believer is indwelt by the Holy Spirit (1 Corinthians 6:19), sealed by him (Ephesians 1:13), and has been delivered from the domain of darkness and transferred to the kingdom of God’s beloved Son (Colossians 1:13). A house cannot have two owners. Christians can be tempted, attacked and deceived, and they are told to resist the devil (1 Peter 5:8–9), but they are never told to fear being taken over by him. John’s word to anxious believers was that the one living in them is greater than the one in the world (1 John 4:4), and the Legion on this beach is the proof. If you belong to Christ and are troubled, the answer is not to look for something living in you but to look to the one who lives in you.

So Mark has arranged the meeting with great care. On one side of the beach is a man out of the tombs, unclean, unreachable, the property of something that hates him. On the other is a man stepping out of a boat, wet through, who has just been asleep on a cushion in a hurricane. Nothing in the scene says which of them is stronger. The rest of the story is about that.

In a sentence. As soon as Jesus landed in Gentile territory, a demon-possessed man came out of the tombs to meet him.

On a Tuesday. Think of the person you know who is furthest from God: furthest by background, by behaviour, by the sheer improbability of him ever darkening a church door. Jesus crossed a storm to reach a man like that, and no one is beyond his reach or his concern. Pray for that person by name this week, and be ready to cross some small storm of your own (an awkward conversation, an inconvenient visit) on his account. And if you are the one who feels furthest away, notice who stepped out of the boat first.

For worship. The Son of God did not wait on the clean shore for the unclean to make their way to him. He set out across the dark water, slept through the storm, and stepped out onto a graveyard beach in pagan country because one ruined man was there. That is how he has always come: not to the healthy but to the sick, not to the places where he is welcome but to the places where he is needed. Before this man had asked for anything, the Lord of the sea had already crossed the sea for him.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that some manuscripts read Gergesenes, some Gadarenes. The region lay on the east side of the lake, Gentile country. Tombs were unclean places.

verseByVerse.quote: He lived among the tombs. And no one could bind him anymore, not even with a chain, for he had often been bound with shackles and chains, but he wrenched the chains apart, and he broke the shackles in pieces. No one had the strength to subdue him. Night and day among the tombs and on the mountains he was always crying out and cutting himself with stones.
verseByVerse.commentary:
He lived among the tombs, and no one could bind him any more, not even with a chain. He had often been bound with shackles and chains, but he tore the chains apart and broke the shackles; no one had the strength to subdue him. Night and day among the tombs and on the mountains he was always crying out and cutting himself with stones.

He lived among the tombs. Mark now slows right down. Three verses of pure description come before a word is spoken, and every clause establishes that this man was past help. He lived there. Driven out of society, he made a graveyard his home, and the dead were his company.

And no one could bind him anymore, not even with a chain. The word anymore tells the whole history. People had tried to control him with force, repeatedly. There had been a time when the town still attempted something, and it had stopped. Human strength cannot defeat demonic power.

He wrenched the chains apart, and he broke the shackles in pieces. Superhuman strength (compare Acts 19:16): iron chains torn apart, and the metal cuffs on wrists and ankles smashed. Mark, who has this from Peter, gives the detail like a man describing physical evidence he has seen.

No one had the strength to subdue him. There is the town’s final verdict. The word means to tame, the word you would use of an animal. They had tried to tame a man, and failed at that too. He was written off, and the writing off had been going on for years.

The stronger man has come. Mark has already handed us the key to this scene. Jesus said that no one can enter a strong man’s house and plunder his goods unless he first binds the strong man (3:27). Here is the strong man’s house, a graveyard, and here are his goods, a human being. The town tried to bind the man and could not. Jesus binds the power that owns him, and he does it with a word. And this is a foretaste of the greater binding: at the cross he disarmed the rulers and authorities and triumphed over them (Colossians 2:15), so that the devil’s captives, chained far more deeply than this man, could walk free.

Night and day among the tombs and on the mountains he was always crying out. The screaming never stopped, on the hillsides where the sound carried down to the town. The people of that district went to sleep hearing him.

And cutting himself with stones. Here Mark says the thing that will land hardest on a modern reader, and it should be handled gently, because a great many people know exactly what this verse is describing. Understand first what it tells us about the power in him. Everything the demons do to this man is aimed at his destruction. They have taken him out of his home, out of his town, out of human company, out of clothing, out of his own mind, and now they are using his own hands against his own body. That is the settled programme of the enemy wherever he is given room: not pleasure, not power, but ruin, and ruin worked where possible through the victim’s own hands. The thief comes only to steal and kill and destroy (John 10:10).

What it does not mean. Not that people who harm themselves or suffer mental illness are possessed. The Gospels distinguish illness from possession (1:32–34), and pain, shame and illness are enough to explain most of what human beings do to themselves. Those who self-harm need compassion, safety and care, medical and spiritual. Going to a doctor is an ordinary mercy from God and not a failure of faith. But this man’s torment was demonic, and only Jesus could free him.

How can I tell whether a struggle is spiritual or medical? Usually you do not need to choose, because every human trouble is both: we are bodies and souls together, living in a fallen world with a real enemy. So do both things. See a doctor, and if a counsellor or medication is advised, accept it with thanks, as you would for a broken leg. And bring the whole thing to Christ in prayer, Scripture and the fellowship of his people, asking your pastor and elders to pray with you (James 5:14). Be wary of anyone who offers a quick spiritual diagnosis without knowing you well, and of anyone who tells you that faith means refusing treatment. The man in the tombs was beyond every remedy; most of us are not, and God normally heals through means.

The direction the story runs. If you are a person who hurts yourself, or you love one, take from this passage the direction the story runs. The man in the tombs, whom nobody could hold and nobody could help, is soon sitting quietly, dressed, talking, in his right mind, with the marks of the stones still on his arms. And the one who put him back together did not flinch at meeting him at his worst, in a graveyard, screaming, bleeding and out of control. He came to that beach on purpose.

In a sentence. The man lived among the tombs, too strong to be chained, crying out and cutting himself day and night.

On a Tuesday. If you or someone you love is self-harming, please tell someone and seek help today: a doctor, a trusted friend, your pastor, or an emergency line if you are in danger. That is not weakness; it is taking hold of the help God has put within reach. And if you know someone the people around them have quietly given up on, refuse to join the town’s verdict. Write their name down, pray for them, and look for one ordinary kindness you can do them this week.

For worship. The enemy works by ruin, and he is very good at it: he isolates, strips, torments, and turns a man’s own hands against him. But he is not the strongest power on that hillside. Christ is the one who looks at what everybody else has chained and abandoned and walks towards it. He is not repelled by our worst, because he came to bear it. The marks of the stones did not keep that man from him, and the marks of the nails are the proof that nothing in us will keep us from him either.

parallels.desc: who sit in tombs, who eat pig’s flesh

verseByVerse.quote: And when he saw Jesus from afar, he ran and fell down before him. And crying out with a loud voice, he said, "What have you to do with me, Jesus, Son of the Most High God? I adjure you by God, do not torment me."
verseByVerse.commentary:
When he saw Jesus from a distance, he ran and fell down before him. Crying out with a loud voice, he said: what have you to do with me, Jesus, Son of the Most High God? I adjure you by God, do not torment me.

And when he saw Jesus from afar, he ran and fell down before him. The whole tragedy of the man is in that sentence. He ran, across broken ground, from a distance, to get to Jesus, and then went down on his face in front of him. Who did the running? Mark does not tell us, and probably it cannot be separated. There is a man in there who has wanted help for years and has never once been able to get to it. And there is a power in there that has to come and bow before Jesus’ authority, because it cannot do anything else in the presence of the Son of God. Both are true, and they arrive at the same feet.

The posture of worship. It is not willing worship; it is the same involuntary prostration as by the lake in 3:11. But it is the rehearsal of a day when everything that has ever opposed him will do this: at the name of Jesus every knee should bow (Philippians 2:10). And crying out with a loud voice: the screaming that the district has heard for years is aimed now at one person.

What have you to do with me, Jesus, Son of the Most High God? The question means, leave me alone; what is there between us (1:24)? And the theology is flawless: not for the first time in Mark, the best confession in the district comes out of a demon (1:24; 3:11). “Most High God” was a title often used by or to Gentiles for the supreme God: it is Melchizedek’s name for him (Genesis 14:18–22), and Nebuchadnezzar’s (Daniel 3:26), and the slave girl’s spirit uses it in Philippi (Acts 16:17). On the pagan side of the lake even the demons use the local vocabulary, and they use it correctly. The demon knows exactly who Jesus is.

Right doctrine, no salvation. It still does them no good. That is the point Mark keeps making, and it will not go away: you can have the doctrine exactly right, use the right name, take the right posture, and be no nearer to being saved than you were before. The difference between this cry and a Christian’s is not accuracy. It is that this one means keep away from me.

I adjure you by God, do not torment me. Now look closely, because it is easily missed. To adjure someone is to put him under oath, and that was the standard technique of the professional exorcist in that world. You named a higher power and bound the spirit by it. The formula was the trade. So the demon is attempting an exorcism. It is trying to use the exorcist’s own tools on the exorcist, invoking God to bind the Son of God. The tormentor of the man begs not to be tormented. It is the last resort of something that has understood, in the first three seconds, that it is completely outmatched, and it does not work for even a moment.

Before the time. And there is the fear underneath. Matthew gives the sentence in full: Have you come here to torment us before the time? (Matthew 8:29). Demons know that judgment awaits them. They know there is a time. They know what is fixed for them, and they know who fixed it, and their only argument is about the schedule. The kingdom of darkness in this Gospel is not confidently opposing Christ. It is a defeated thing negotiating for a delay.

If demons believe the truth about Jesus, what makes my faith different? Saving faith is not only knowing who Jesus is; it is trusting him and coming to him to be saved. James says the demons believe, and shudder (James 2:19). They know he is the Son of God and they hate it; they want him to go away. A Christian knows the same truth and wants him to come nearer. So the test is not whether you can say the right words about Christ, but whether you rest on him, love him, and want to be with him. If you find in yourself even a weak longing for him, and grief that it is not stronger, that is not the faith of demons. It is the work of his Spirit.

In a sentence. The demon ran to Jesus, bowed, named him Son of the Most High God, and begged not to be tormented.

On a Tuesday. If the powers of evil frighten you, and there is no shame in that, notice who is on the ground and who is standing. The demons in Mark are never once calm in the presence of Jesus. They shout, they beg, they bargain, they go. He has not yet had to raise his voice. So when fear comes at night, or temptation presses, do not argue with it on its own terms. Go straight to Christ, speak his name in prayer, and stand on what he has already done.

For worship. There is no rival on the throne. The powers that hold men in chains cannot hold their ground before Jesus for a single moment; they fall on their faces, and they know his name better than his friends do. He is the Son of the Most High God, and every knee in heaven, on earth and under the earth is already bending in the direction of the day when it will bow. The darkness bargains for time, and he is the one who owns the time.
verseByVerse.note: “Most High God” is a title often used by or to Gentiles.

parallels.desc: even the demons believe — and shudder

verseByVerse.quote: For he was saying to him, "Come out of the man, you unclean spirit!" And Jesus asked him, "What is your name?" He replied, "My name is Legion, for we are many." And he begged him earnestly not to send them out of the country.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For Jesus had been saying to him: come out of the man, you unclean spirit! And Jesus asked him: what is your name? He replied: my name is Legion, for we are many. And he begged him earnestly not to send them out of the country.

For he was saying to him, Come out of the man, you unclean spirit. Mark drops the tense back a step to tell us what had already been happening: Jesus had already commanded it, and the whole exchange in verse 7 was the answer to that command. The screaming and the bargaining are what a thing does on its way out. And notice the command itself. No ritual, no formula, no invoking of a higher name, which is exactly what every exorcist in the ancient world needed, and precisely what the demon had just tried to use on him. Jesus does not appeal to an authority. He is one.

And Jesus asked him, What is your name? This is the only time in the Gospels that Jesus asks a demon its name, and he plainly does not need the information. He is not gaining power over it by learning its name, as the magicians of the day believed. Two things are being done. The first is for the man. Everything that has happened to him has happened in the dark, unnamed and unexplained, for years. The thing that owned him is about to be forced to identify itself out loud, in front of witnesses, before it is thrown out. What has been destroying you is made to say what it is. The second is for the record. Mark wants his readers to grasp the extent of the possession, the scale of what they are watching, and only the enemy can supply that figure.

My name is Legion, for we are many. The word lands like a boot. A Roman legion had about six thousand soldiers: not a metaphor to anybody in that district but the thing that had marched up their road. A legion arrives, occupies and stays. It cannot be resisted, cannot be negotiated with, and does not leave. The name suggests a vast number of demons, organised like an army, and it describes exactly what they had done to this man: moved in, taken possession, held territory. It also tells you why nothing had worked. The town had been trying to chain a man. The man was a garrison.

Two occupations. The man was occupied by a hostile force, as the land was occupied by Roman legions; the tenth legion, stationed in the region, had a boar as its emblem, which gives the pigs in the next verses a sharp edge. So Mark quietly sets two occupations side by side. There is the one everybody in that country could see, with soldiers on the road and taxes to Caesar. And there is the one nobody could do anything about at all. Jesus walks up the beach and evicts the second with a sentence. He will deal with the first in his own way and at his own cost, when Rome nails him to a cross outside Jerusalem and finds that it cannot hold him either.

And he begged him earnestly not to send them out of the country. Begged. The strongest power in the district has been reduced to asking, and it will beg again before it goes. Luke tells us what they were most afraid of: they begged him not to command them to depart into the abyss (Luke 8:31), the place of their confinement. Weigh the whole encounter as the man on the ground would have heard it. He had been held by thousands, and he was worth a storm and a crossing to the one who came for him, and the thousands spent the entire conversation pleading.

Should Christians name demons, or bind spirits over places? No. This scene is not a method to copy. Jesus asked the name for the man’s sake and for ours, not because naming gives power; the demon’s own attempt to use a formula failed. Nowhere does the New Testament tell believers to interrogate spirits, map territorial demons, or command the devil by special words. The apostles, with their unique authority, cast out demons in Jesus’ name (Acts 16:18), but the instructions given to every Christian are plainer: be sober and watchful, resist the devil, firm in your faith (1 Peter 5:8–9), take up the armour of God, which is truth, righteousness, the gospel, faith, salvation, the word of God and prayer (Ephesians 6:10–18). Our weapon is not a technique but the Lord himself.

In a sentence. Jesus commanded the spirit to leave and asked its name, and it called itself Legion, for there were many demons.

On a Tuesday. However many forces seem to be against you, they are not too many for Jesus. Name what you are up against honestly before him in prayer: the habit, the fear, the accusation that keeps returning. Bringing it out of the dark and into his presence is half the battle. Then remind yourself whose word has the last say over it.

For worship. Six thousand were not too many for him. The garrison that no chain could hold heard one voice and began to plead. Jesus is not one authority among many, needing a stronger name to call upon; he is the Name. What the legions of hell and the legions of Rome could not stand against was not a better formula but the Son of God himself, who at the end let the second kind of legion crucify him in order to break the first kind for ever (Colossians 2:15).
verseByVerse.note: A Roman legion numbered several thousand soldiers.

verseByVerse.quote: Now a great herd of pigs was feeding there on the hillside, and they begged him, saying, "Send us to the pigs; let us enter them." So he gave them permission. And the unclean spirits came out and entered the pigs; and the herd, numbering about two thousand, rushed down the steep bank into the sea and drowned in the sea.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A great herd of pigs was feeding on the hillside, and the demons begged him: send us to the pigs, let us enter them. So he gave them permission. The unclean spirits came out and entered the pigs, and the herd, about two thousand, rushed down the steep bank into the lake and drowned.

Now a great herd of pigs was feeding there on the hillside. Mark mentions them almost as scenery. Pigs were unclean under the law (Leviticus 11:7), and no Jewish district would have two thousand of them on a hillside. A herd that size shows this was Gentile country, and a valuable business: the pigs are somebody’s livelihood.

Send us to the pigs; let us enter them. The demons beg again. They have no power to resist Jesus; they can only plead. The Legion cannot go anywhere or do anything without permission, which tells you exactly how much of what happens in this world is unsupervised. Nothing. So he gave them permission: Jesus permits it, for his purposes.

And the herd, numbering about two thousand, rushed down the steep bank into the sea and drowned in the sea. Two thousand animals over a cliff. A reader who cares about God’s justice, and about somebody’s ruined business, is entitled to ask what this was for. Three things answer it, and none of them requires pretending the loss did not happen.

The demons did this. First, the demons drove the herd, not Jesus. He permitted their request, and in permitting it he let their intention show itself in the open. For five verses we have been told what they were doing to a man: the tombs, the chains, the screaming, the stones. Now the whole district gets to watch what that programme looks like when it runs unhindered: everything it enters goes straight over the edge and into the water. Demons destroy whatever they inhabit. The pigs are the man’s story acted out in a few seconds on a hillside. And it shows that the man was truly freed: everyone could see that the demons had gone.

The arithmetic of heaven. Second, one human being matters more to Jesus than two thousand pigs. One tormented man, restored to his mind, his clothes, his family and his town, and sent out as a herald of mercy, is worth more than any number of animals. Jesus had already said it in a synagogue argument: Of how much more value is a man than a sheep! (Matthew 12:12). And a man than a pig. God’s care for animals is real: he feeds the ravens, he counts the sparrows, and Proverbs says the righteous man has regard for the life of his beast (Proverbs 12:10). But when the two are set against each other, there is no contest, and there never was.

The real price of his freedom. Yet the pigs were not what this man’s freedom cost. The herd paid nothing; it only showed what had left him. The true price was paid on another hill. The Son of Man came to give his life as a ransom for many (10:45), and the man on this beach was set free on credit, as it were, against the blood that would be shed at Golgotha. You were ransomed, says Peter, not with silver or gold but with the precious blood of Christ (1 Peter 1:18–19). Two thousand pigs is the town’s figure. The figure in heaven’s books is the life of the Son of God.

The town’s reaction. Third, the reaction of the town settles the matter. Presented with a neighbour raised out of a living death and a hillside of dead livestock, they will grieve the livestock and ask the Healer to leave.

What it does not mean. Not that Jesus was careless with others’ property. He judged that a man’s freedom was worth more. And he is the Lord of all things: the cattle on a thousand hills are his (Psalm 50:10), and so were these pigs. The deeper question is the one the townspeople faced: what do you value more?

Why would Jesus grant a request from demons at all? Because their going into the pigs served his purposes, not theirs. It gave visible proof that the man was free, it exposed what the demons are, and it put the town’s heart to the test. Throughout Scripture God permits evil powers to act only within limits he sets, and he turns what they intend for harm into good (Job 1:12; 2:6; Genesis 50:20). The demons got what they asked for and lost everything: they wanted a home and ended in the sea. That is the pattern of every concession evil wins from God. It is never a defeat for him. It is always a rope by which it hangs itself.

In a sentence. Jesus let the demons enter a herd of two thousand pigs, which rushed down into the lake and drowned.

On a Tuesday. This scene puts an uncomfortable question to us, and it is not about pigs. There are still people who would rather keep their herd than lose their sins. The cost of Christ is always visible and always countable: the money, the relationship, the ambition, the private arrangement that works. What he gives is a man in his right mind, and that never appears in the accounts until later. Ask yourself where you have done the town’s sum this year, and come out against him, over something considerably less than two thousand pigs. And value people above possessions: the person who interrupts your plans is worth more than the plans.

For worship. The night before, the sea had obeyed him; this morning it receives the destroyers he sends into it. The Lord who stilled the waves is the Lord of the deep, and the deep is where his enemies go. The herd went down and the man stayed on the shore, and so it is with every sinner he saves: the powers that owned us go under, and we are left standing, clothed and free, beside him. He will tread our iniquities underfoot and cast all our sins into the depths of the sea (Micah 7:19), and not one of them will ever climb back up the bank.
verseByVerse.note: Pigs were unclean animals under the law; a herd of two thousand shows this was Gentile country.

verseByVerse.quote: The herdsmen fled and told it in the city and in the country. And people came to see what it was that had happened. And they came to Jesus and saw the demon-possessed man, the one who had had the legion, sitting there, clothed and in his right mind, and they were afraid.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The herdsmen fled and told it in the city and in the country, and people came to see what had happened. They came to Jesus and saw the man who had been possessed by the legion sitting there, clothed and in his right mind, and they were afraid.

The herdsmen fled and told it in the city and in the country. Of course they ran: two thousand animals at the bottom of a cliff, and somebody is going to want an explanation. Within an hour the whole district knows.

And people came to see what it was that had happened. They come out in numbers, and Mark lets us watch them arrive at the scene.

And they came to Jesus and saw the demon-possessed man, the one who had had the legion. Even now that is his name in this town: the demon-possessed man. Then Mark gives three details, and they are three of the loveliest words in the Gospel.

Sitting there. This man has not sat down in years. He has been running the hills, tearing at chains, roaming the tombs night and day; whatever was in him never let him be still. And now, in the middle of the whole town, he is no longer running wild but at rest. Luke adds where: sitting at the feet of Jesus (Luke 8:35), which is the posture of a disciple at his teacher’s feet.

Clothed. He had been naked; Luke says so plainly (Luke 8:27). Somebody has given him a garment, and his dignity is restored along with his mind.

The one who would be stripped. Mark’s readers knew how this Gospel ends. The man who gave this naked man back his dignity would himself be stripped, and soldiers would divide his garments among them, casting lots (15:24). He would hang uncovered under the shame that the tombs had put on this man and that our sin has put on us all. That is how clothing is given in the kingdom of God. The Lord God covered Adam and Eve with skins after the fall (Genesis 3:21), and Christ gives his people the robe of his own righteousness (Isaiah 61:10) because he went out naked to Golgotha in their place.

And in his right mind. The Greek is a single word meaning sound-minded, sane, self-possessed. He is no longer tormented. He can hold a conversation. He knows his own name, and he can hear his own thoughts for the first time in years.

A case everybody else had closed. No process, no gradual rehabilitation. He came down out of the rocks screaming and he is sitting on the ground with a borrowed coat on, listening. That is what Christ does with a case that everybody else has closed, and it is a picture of what he does for everyone he saves: peace, dignity and a renewed mind. And it is worth saying to anyone praying for a person who has been beyond reach for a long time, the addict, the one who is not in his right mind, the family member nobody knows how to help, that this town had reached the settled conclusion that nothing could be done. They were right about their own resources and wrong about the possibilities, and the difference arrived by boat.

And they were afraid. Not glad for him, but afraid. The man they had feared and chained was now calm, and the power that did it frightened them more. It is the same fear that filled the boat after the storm (4:41): the fear of a power you cannot classify or control. In itself it is not a wicked reaction; awe in the presence of God is right. But what this town does with it in the next two verses is another matter entirely.

Is the change always this sudden? The freeing was instant, and so is the new birth: God gives a new heart, and a person passes from death to life (John 5:24; Ephesians 2:4–5). But what follows is usually slow. This man had to learn to live in a town, rebuild trust, and face people who remembered him; the sitting, the clothing and the right mind were the beginning of a life, not the end of it. So when you pray for someone, ask boldly for the decisive work only Christ can do, and then be patient with the long recovery afterwards, in them and in yourself. Christians are being transformed by the renewal of the mind (Romans 12:2), and that is a lifetime’s work.

In a sentence. The townspeople came and found the former demoniac sitting, clothed and in his right mind, and they were afraid.

On a Tuesday. Think of a long-closed case on your prayer list, the person you stopped praying for because nothing ever changed. Open the file again today. And then look at your own life for the three marks of this man: is there rest at Jesus’ feet in it, or only running? Do you remember that you are clothed in a righteousness not your own? Are you letting his word renew your mind, or only the noise of the week?

For worship. The town came out expecting a disaster and found a man sitting still. That stillness is the signature of Jesus. He who commanded the wind, Peace, be still, has spoken the same peace into a human soul, and the soul obeyed like the sea. Years of running ended at his feet. There is no restlessness he cannot quiet and no ruin he cannot sit down and clothe and set right. The man the town could only chain, Christ could only love, and his love was stronger than all their iron.

verseByVerse.quote: And those who had seen it described to them what had happened to the demon-possessed man and to the pigs. And they began to beg Jesus to depart from their region.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Those who had seen it described what had happened to the demon-possessed man and to the pigs. And they began to beg Jesus to leave their region.

And those who had seen it described to them what had happened to the demon-possessed man and to the pigs. The eyewitnesses give their report, and Mark’s summary of it is quietly devastating: the man and the pigs. Both items, in one account, presented for the town to weigh.

And they began to beg Jesus to depart from their region. That is the third begging in this chapter, and it is the one that should stop us. The demons begged Jesus not to send them away; the townspeople beg Jesus to go away. Nobody in that district disputes what has happened. Nobody says it was a trick. They have the facts, they have the eyewitnesses, and they have their neighbour sitting in front of them in his right mind. And their considered, unanimous request is that the man who did it should get back in his boat.

Why did they want him gone? Mark does not explain, and he does not need to. They preferred their pigs and their comfort to the presence of the one who sets people free. His power threatened their way of life. They had understood something about Jesus that many who admire him never grasp: he is not safe, and he does not stay within the budget. A man who can do that to a herd of pigs might do it to anything. Better to have the misery you have priced than the mercy you cannot. So they chose the graveyard they knew, and the terrible thing is that the choice is not exotic. It is the most ordinary transaction in the world.

And Jesus left. Jesus does not force himself on those who do not want him, and this is the most frightening thing here. Mark states it without comment in the next verse: as he was getting into the boat. No argument, no second attempt. They asked him to leave and he left. Ephraim is joined to idols; leave him alone (Hosea 4:17) is a real sentence in the Bible, and it is the most terrifying kind of answered prayer there is.

The first of many who sent him away. This shore is a rehearsal for Jerusalem. He came to his own, and his own people did not receive him (John 1:11): his home town of Nazareth will take offence at him next (6:1–6), and at the last a crowd will be offered Jesus or Barabbas and choose the man of violence. Jerusalem will want him gone, and he will go, led out of the gate to be crucified. Yet that rejection is the very road of salvation. The stone the builders rejected has become the cornerstone (12:10). He let himself be sent away so that those who sent him away could be brought near.

Not the end of the account. Yet do not close the account there, because he does not. He leaves the district the one thing it cannot chain, cut or drive away: a man with a story. And when Jesus returns to that side of the lake, the crowds come out to meet him (7:31–37; 8:1–10).

If I have pushed Jesus away before, has he left me for good? Not if you want him now. The danger in this passage is a settled preference for life without him, not a single moment of fear or refusal. The Gerasenes sent him away, and by chapter 7 that same region is bringing him their sick. Peter denied him three times and was restored on a beach (John 21:15–19). The very fact that you are troubled by having pushed him away is a sign that he has not left you to yourself. Whoever comes to him he will never cast out (John 6:37). So do not wait to feel worthy: ask him back today, and he will come.

In a sentence. Hearing about the man and the pigs, the townspeople begged Jesus to leave, and he went.

On a Tuesday. Ask it plainly of yourself, because this is what the passage is for. Is there any part of your life where you would rather Jesus stayed away, because his presence might cost you something? Not in theory, in fact. The relationship you know he would not sanction. The way you make your money. The evening habit. The plan for the next ten years you have never once put in his hands.
