For many were coming and going, and they had no leisure even to eat. The demand is so constant that meals are being missed, as before (3:20): not a hard week, but a pattern. That is a test worth applying to your own life, because it is measurable rather than vague. Not, do I feel busy: everybody feels busy. Are the ordinary human things being squeezed out? Meals eaten standing up. Sleep treated as the flexible item. Days off that quietly became half days and then nothing. When the basics start going, something has gone wrong that no amount of fruitfulness justifies, and Jesus treated it as a reason to stop rather than a sign of seriousness.

And they went away in the boat to a desolate place by themselves. They actually go. The desolate place (erēmos) is the wilderness, where God fed Israel (Exodus 16), and what follows will recall that. And the rest was his idea, he arranged it, they obeyed it, and in a moment it will be completely ruined by the crowds. Planning rest is right, and it will still sometimes be taken from you; what matters is what you do when it is.

Is it selfish to rest when there is so much need? No. Jesus himself sent his apostles to rest while crowds were still coming. God built rest into creation and into his law (Genesis 2:2–3; Exodus 20:8–11). The Sabbath is fulfilled in Christ, and the Lord’s Day is his gift: Christians gladly set Sunday apart for worship, fellowship and rest, out of joy rather than as a law with rules about work, and no one may bind another’s conscience (Romans 14:5; Colossians 2:16–17). Many godly Reformed brothers keep it as the Christian Sabbath, and they are to be honoured. All agree that a weekly rhythm of worship and rest is God’s gift, and that you are not the Saviour of the world. The need will always be greater than your strength. Rest is an act of trust that God keeps the world running while you sleep (Psalm 127:2).

In a sentence. When the apostles returned and reported, Jesus invited them to come away to a quiet place and rest a while, because they had not even had time to eat.

On a Tuesday. Are you exhausted from serving? Hear Jesus’ invitation: come away and rest a while. Take time to be with him. Look at your diary for the next fortnight and find where rest has been squeezed out. Put back one meal eaten slowly, one evening with no obligations, one unhurried time of prayer, and keep it as an appointment with the Lord.

For worship. The Lord who commands his servants to work is the Lord who commands them to rest. The same hands that gave the Twelve authority over demons beckon them into a boat for a quiet day. He notices when we have not eaten, and he calls us away to himself before we break. That is the Good Shepherd: not a taskmaster driving his flock to exhaustion, but the one who makes them lie down in green pastures and restores their souls.

verseByVerse.quote: Now many saw them going and recognized them, and they ran there on foot from all the towns and got there ahead of them. When he went ashore he saw a great crowd, and he had compassion on them, because they were like sheep without a shepherd. And he began to teach them many things.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Many saw them going and recognised them, and ran there on foot from all the towns and got there ahead of them. When Jesus went ashore, he saw a great crowd, and he had compassion on them, because they were like sheep without a shepherd. And he began to teach them many things.

Now many saw them going and recognized them, and they ran there on foot from all the towns and got there ahead of them. The plan fails immediately. They are seen leaving. Somebody works out from the direction of the boat where they must be heading. Word goes out to the villages along the shore, and people set off round the head of the lake on foot, and they get there first. Picture the boat coming in. Twelve exhausted men who have been travelling and preaching for weeks, who were promised a quiet day, rowing towards an empty shore and seeing, as it comes into view, that the empty shore is covered with people. Thousands of them, already waiting. Anyone who has ever needed a day off knows what would rise in the chest at that moment.

When he went ashore he saw a great crowd. He is tired. His plan for the day is destroyed. The people on that beach are the reason he had to leave in the first place, and they have chased him round the lake.

And he had compassion on them. Not irritation, but deep, gut-level compassion (splanchnizomai), one of the strongest words in the language for pity, built on the word for the inward organs. It is not a decision to be nice. It is what happens inside him when he sees them.

Because they were like sheep without a shepherd. This phrase is not a general remark about how lost people are. It is a quotation, and it comes loaded. Moses prayed at the end of his life that the congregation of the LORD may not be as sheep that have no shepherd (Numbers 27:17). Micaiah saw Israel scattered on the mountains as sheep that have no shepherd after the death of a bad king (1 Kings 22:17). And behind both stands Ezekiel 34, where God condemns Israel’s shepherds, who fed themselves and not the flock, who did not strengthen the weak or heal the sick or bring back the strays, and promises that he himself will shepherd his people through a new David: I myself will search for my sheep and will seek them out; I myself will be the shepherd of my sheep (Ezekiel 34:11, 15).

The false shepherd and the true. Herod, the supposed king who had killed John the Baptist at a birthday feast for the powerful, was such a false shepherd: he fed his nobles and devoured the prophet. Jesus is the true Shepherd, who will now feed his flock in the wilderness. He is not merely feeling sorry for a crowd. He is looking at a nation and seeing the ancient failure, people with no one to feed them, and every one of those texts has an answer, and he is it.

And he began to teach them many things. Notice what the compassion produces first: not the loaves, not healing, but teaching, as Mark has shown before (2:2). The people’s first need was God’s word (Deuteronomy 8:3). Given a hungry, tired, spiritually starving crowd, the first thing he gives them is words, because the deepest thing wrong with sheep that have no shepherd is that nobody has been feeding them. He will get to their stomachs before the day is out. He starts with the thing they did not know they came for.

How do I find compassion when I am exhausted? Not by trying to feel it, but by looking at people the way Jesus did, and by drawing on his compassion rather than your own reserves. Ask him to show you what he sees: not interruptions, but sheep without a shepherd. Remember how he has had compassion on you when you came to him at inconvenient times. And be honest about your limits; Jesus’ compassion did not stop him from sending the crowds away that evening and going to pray. Compassion is not saying yes to every demand. It is meeting people with his heart, and then trusting him with what you cannot do.

In a sentence. When the crowd arrived ahead of them, Jesus had compassion on them as sheep without a shepherd, and taught them.

On a Tuesday. When others interrupt your rest with their needs, ask for Jesus’ compassion. And remember that people’s deepest need is the word of God. If you are a parent, a teacher, a small-group leader, do not neglect to feed those in your care from Scripture. And pray for your pastors, that they may be true shepherds and not hirelings.

For worship. Here is the Shepherd Israel had waited for. The kings of the earth feed themselves; this King steps out of a boat on his ruined day off and feeds his flock. A crowd that has chased him round a lake meets not a closed face but a heart moved to its depths. The LORD who promised to come and seek his own sheep has come in person, and he is standing on the shore, teaching. He is the Good Shepherd who lays down his life for the sheep (John 10:11), and his compassion on that beach was the same compassion that would take him to the cross.

parallels.desc: not as sheep without a shepherd

verseByVerse.quote: And when it grew late, his disciples came to him and said, "This is a desolate place, and the hour is now late. Send them away to go into the surrounding countryside and villages and buy themselves something to eat." But he answered them, "You give them something to eat." And they said to him, "Shall we go and buy two hundred denarii worth of bread and give it to them to eat?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
When it grew late, the disciples said: this is a desolate place, and the hour is late. Send them away to buy food in the surrounding countryside and villages. But Jesus answered: you give them something to eat. They said: shall we go and buy two hundred denarii worth of bread and give it to them to eat?

And when it grew late, his disciples came to him and said, This is a desolate place, and the hour is now late. The disciples see the problem, and they are being sensible. They are right about the facts: it is an empty place, it is getting dark, and there are thousands of people here with no arrangements made.

Send them away to go into the surrounding countryside and villages and buy themselves something to eat. A reasonable suggestion: disperse them while there is still light, and let everyone sort himself out. But it shows they did not yet think of Jesus as able to provide. It is the standard shape of religious problem-solving. The need is real, the resources are insufficient, therefore reduce the need. Send them away. It is not callous; they are trying to get people fed. It simply never occurs to them that the man standing next to them might be a factor in the calculation, and they have just come back from a mission on which they cast out demons.

But he answered them, You give them something to eat. The pronoun is emphatic: you. Jesus puts the responsibility on them, to show them their inadequacy and his sufficiency. He is handing twelve tired men a responsibility that is plainly, mathematically beyond them, and standing there while they work out what to do with it. He does this. It is one of his settled habits with his people: the command that cannot be obeyed out of your own resources. Stretch out your withered hand (3:5). Feed this crowd. Go and make disciples of all nations (Matthew 28:19). Every one of them is impossible, and every one of them is an invitation.

Shall we go and buy two hundred denarii worth of bread and give it to them to eat? And out comes the arithmetic. A denarius was a day’s wage for a labourer. Two hundred denarii was about eight months’ wages: far more than they had, and they could not have spent it in a village at dusk anyway. They have evidently done the sum on the spot. Their answer is half sarcastic. You can hear the tone: it is not quite rude and it is not quite faith. It is a man showing his working to prove the thing cannot be done.

Can God spread a table in the wilderness? Israel once asked that very question in unbelief, in the desert, with manna still on the ground: Can God spread a table in the wilderness? (Psalm 78:19). The disciples are asking it again with a calculation. And the answer is standing beside them. This is not a prophet who will ask God for bread; it is the God who fed Israel for forty years, come in the flesh to a desolate place to do it again. Every human sum about the wilderness leaves him out, and every time he is the whole of the answer. He would one day give a bread no money could buy, his own flesh for the life of the world (John 6:51).

A spreadsheet beside the Son of God. These are the men who, a few days before, were casting out demons in villages on borrowed authority. They have seen a paralytic walk, a leper cleansed, a girl raised from the dead and a hurricane muzzled. They are standing next to the person who did all of it, and their considered response to a catering problem is a spreadsheet. Before that is used as a stick, be honest: most of us pray about the things we already half expect to manage and quietly do arithmetic about the rest. We have a category for what God might do, and a much larger category for what is realistically going to happen, and the second one runs our week. The disciples’ sum was not wrong. Two hundred denarii really would not have been enough. That is the point. They were correct, and completely beside the point, because they had left out the only variable that mattered.

Is it wrong to plan and count costs? No. Jesus himself told his hearers to count the cost (Luke 14:28), and careful planning is part of good stewardship. The disciples’ fault was not that they counted but that they counted without him, as if the Lord of heaven and earth were not standing beside them. Plan, budget and prepare, and then bring the plan and the shortfall to him in prayer, expecting him to act according to his will. The question is not whether you do arithmetic, but whether Christ is in the sum.

In a sentence. The disciples wanted to send the crowd away to buy food, but Jesus told them to feed it, and they objected that it would cost eight months’ wages.

On a Tuesday. When need seems overwhelming, do you calculate what you lack, or bring what you have to Jesus? Think of the task in front of you that is plainly beyond you: the ministry with no volunteers, the family need with no money, the friend with problems too deep for you. Before you send it away, bring it to him.

For worship. Our Lord gives commands bigger than our resources because his resources are bigger than his commands. He is never caught by surprise at nightfall in a desolate place; he knew all along what he was going to do (John 6:6). He lets us do our arithmetic so that we may see, when the baskets come back full, that he was the answer the sum left out. Blessed be the God who asks of us what only he can supply.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that a denarius was a day’s wage for a labourer; two hundred denarii was most of a year’s wages.

verseByVerse.quote: And he said to them, "How many loaves do you have? Go and see." And when they had found out, they said, "Five, and two fish." Then he commanded them all to sit down in groups on the green grass. So they sat down in groups, by hundreds and by fifties.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus said: how many loaves do you have? Go and see. When they found out, they said: five, and two fish. Then he commanded them all to sit down in groups on the green grass. So they sat down in groups, by hundreds and by fifties.

How many loaves do you have? Go and see. He does not answer the objection; he asks a different, practical question. Not how much do you need: they have already worked that out and it paralysed them. How many have you got? And then, gently: go and count it. That is exactly what to do when a need is obviously beyond you. Stop calculating the gap. Go and find out precisely what is in your hands, however little that is, and bring it to him. The gap is his business; the inventory is yours.

Five, and two fish. John says they came from a boy in the crowd, and that they were barley loaves, the bread of the poor (John 6:9). The fish would have been small and salted, the relish you ate with bread rather than a meal. It is an embarrassing thing to say out loud in front of five thousand hungry people. Five, and two fish. Somebody had to walk back and report that. And it was the right answer. Christ has never once been hindered by the smallness of what was brought to him; he has often been hindered by its being kept back.

Then he commanded them all to sit down in groups on the green grass. Only Mark mentions that the grass was green, and that is Peter’s eye. The hills there are green for a few weeks in spring and brown the rest of the year, so it tells you the season, near Passover (John 6:4). And it puts a psalm into the scene without saying a word. The LORD is my shepherd; I shall not want. He makes me lie down in green pastures (Psalm 23:1–2). Mark has just called the crowd sheep without a shepherd. Now the Shepherd is making his sheep lie down in green pasture, in the wilderness, and will feed them.

So they sat down in groups, by hundreds and by fifties. Literally, in garden beds: the groups looked like rows of flowerbeds, perhaps in colourful clothes on the green grass. From the hillside above, the crowd would have looked like a garden laid out in plots. And the arrangement is not crowd control. Hundreds and fifties recalls how Moses organised Israel in the wilderness, with chiefs of thousands, of hundreds, of fifties and of tens (Exodus 18:21, 25; Deuteronomy 1:15). A crowd seated in hundreds and fifties in a desolate place, about to be given bread at the hands of a leader, is Israel in the wilderness all over again. Jesus is forming a new Israel in the wilderness, and feeding it like a new Moses. And he is greater than Moses, who never made a loaf in his life, and only ever announced that the manna had arrived.

What if what I have really is too little? Then bring it anyway, because the miracle did not begin with a large gift. A boy’s lunch was all it took for Jesus to feed thousands, and he chose to work through that lunch rather than without it. Your time, your small gift of money, your stumbling words to a friend, your weak prayers: none of them is impressive, and none of them is the point. He is the point. God chose what is weak in the world to shame the strong (1 Corinthians 1:27). The only gift he cannot use is the one we keep.

In a sentence. With only five loaves and two fish, Jesus had the crowd sit in organised groups on the green grass, like Israel in the wilderness and sheep in green pastures.

On a Tuesday. The Lord is your shepherd too. You shall not want for what you truly need. Take an honest inventory today of what is in your hands, your time, your money, your skills, your home, and offer one specific piece of it to him for someone else’s need this week.

For worship. Seen from the hillside, the desolate place had become a garden, rows of colour laid out on the green like flowerbeds. That is what happens wherever this Lord sits his people down. The wilderness and the dry land shall be glad; the desert shall rejoice and blossom (Isaiah 35:1), and the last Adam, who would be tested in another garden and laid in a garden tomb, plants his redeemed in beds of life where there should be nothing. Paradise begins again in rows of fifty and a hundred around his hands.
verseByVerse.note: The groups of hundreds and fifties recall the way Moses organised Israel in the wilderness.

verseByVerse.quote: And taking the five loaves and the two fish, he looked up to heaven and said a blessing and broke the loaves and gave them to the disciples to set before the people. And he divided the two fish among them all. And they all ate and were satisfied.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Taking the five loaves and the two fish, Jesus looked up to heaven, said a blessing and broke the loaves and gave them to the disciples to set before the people. And he divided the two fish among them all. And they all ate and were satisfied.

And taking the five loaves and the two fish, he looked up to heaven and said a blessing. Like the head of a Jewish household at a meal. The blessing was not said over the food but to God for it: blessed are you, O Lord our God, King of the universe, who brings forth bread from the earth. Looking up to heaven expressed dependence on the Father. He is not enchanting the loaves. He is thanking his Father, out loud, over food that is obviously not enough, before a single extra crumb exists. Gratitude offered before the provision arrives is one of the plainest marks of faith there is, and it is very easy to test in your own house: do you thank God for what is in front of you when you can see it is not going to stretch?

And broke the loaves and gave them to the disciples to set before the people. Four verbs, and every Christian reading this Gospel is meant to feel them land: he took, he blessed, he broke, he gave. The same four verbs as the Last Supper (14:22): he took bread, and after blessing it broke it and gave it to them, and said, Take; this is my body. And the two disciples on the Emmaus road will recognise a stranger at their own table by exactly this sequence: he took the bread and blessed and broke it and gave it to them. And their eyes were opened (Luke 24:30–31). So this is not the Lord’s Supper, but Mark has laid the two scenes on top of each other on purpose. The feeding looks forward to the Lord’s Supper and to the great banquet of the kingdom (Isaiah 25:6). The man who feeds a hillside with broken bread is going to be broken himself, and the church has been fed from that ever since.

The multiplication happened in their hands. Jesus works through his disciples: they distribute what he provides. He does not hand it out himself. He hands it to the Twelve, and they carry it out to the rows on the grass. Nobody records the moment; Mark does not describe bread swelling. Somewhere between the Lord’s hands and the hundredth row, there kept on being more, and the men doing the carrying were the men who, a little earlier, had proved by arithmetic that it could not be done. That is how he still works. He does not usually rain provision directly onto the people who need it. He gives it to his church to carry, and the carriers discover the sufficiency by handing it out. You will not find out whether there is enough by standing still and calculating. You find out on the fourth row.

And he divided the two fish among them all. Nothing was left out, not even the fish; each person had both.

And they all ate and were satisfied. A full meal, not a taste: they were filled, the word you would use of an animal fed to fullness. They had come out to that place with no food, chasing a man round a lake, and the day ended with every one of them full. In the wilderness God gave Israel manna, and they were satisfied (Exodus 16:12; Psalm 78:24–29). Elisha fed a hundred men with twenty loaves (2 Kings 4:42–44). Jesus feeds thousands with five. He is greater than Moses and Elisha. John records his explanation: I am the bread of life (John 6:35).

What it does not mean. Not that people simply shared hidden lunches, as some have suggested. The Gospels describe a miracle of creation. All four Gospels record it: the only miracle, apart from the resurrection, in all four. If it were a lesson in sharing, nobody would have tried to make him king that night (John 6:14–15), and nobody would have needed twelve baskets for the leftovers.

Should we give thanks before every meal? It is a good and biblical habit, though no rule requires a set form. Jesus gave thanks before eating here, at the Last Supper, and at Emmaus; Paul gave thanks for bread in front of a shipload of pagans in a storm (Acts 27:35), and says that everything created by God is good and is made holy by the word of God and prayer (1 Timothy 4:4–5). A few honest words before a meal remind us that our food comes from our Father’s hand, keep gratitude from going stale, and teach children where their daily bread comes from. Say it, and mean it.

In a sentence. Jesus blessed and broke the loaves, gave them through his disciples, and everyone ate and was satisfied.

On a Tuesday. Before your next meal, thank God out loud for it, even if it is modest, even if money is tight. And look for the place where Christ has put something into your hands to carry to others: a ministry, a family, a neighbour. Start handing it out, and see whether it runs out.

For worship. Praise to Jesus, the bread of life, who satisfies. He took, blessed, broke and gave on a hillside, and later in an upper room, and then on a cross, where his own body was broken so that a hungry world could be fed. He is the Lord who looks up to heaven before the provision comes and gives thanks, the Son who trusts his Father perfectly. He gave thanks for five loaves, and then he gave himself, and no one who feeds on him by faith has ever gone home hungry.

verseByVerse.quote: And they took up twelve baskets full of broken pieces and of the fish. And those who ate the loaves were five thousand men.
verseByVerse.commentary:
They picked up twelve baskets full of broken pieces and of the fish. Those who ate the loaves were five thousand men.

And they took up twelve baskets full of broken pieces and of the fish. John tells us the gathering up was commanded: Gather up the leftover fragments, that nothing may be lost (John 6:12). The one who has just created bread out of five loaves will not have scraps trodden into the grass. Abundance in the kingdom of God never licenses waste. There is no contradiction between believing that God’s supply is endless and refusing to be careless with a slice of bread, and the man who made the supply is the one who gave the order.

Twelve baskets. The number is not accidental. one for each disciple, or a sign of provision for the twelve tribes of Israel, and perhaps both. Each man who went out among the rows with an impossible task and a fraction of a loaf comes back at the end of the evening carrying a full basket. The baskets (kophinoi) were wicker baskets that Jews carried for food. Abundant provision: more left than they started with.

The arithmetic comes out backwards. Do the disciples’ sum and it comes out backwards: five loaves and two fish at the start, more food than that at the end, after feeding a multitude. That is the accounting of the kingdom, and it is why their two hundred denarii was the wrong question. Paul says the same thing in a sentence: God is able to make all grace abound to you, so that having all sufficiency in all things at all times, you may abound in every good work (2 Corinthians 9:8). And the widow of Zarephath, down to a handful of flour and a little oil and expecting to die after one last meal, found that the jar of flour was not spent (1 Kings 17:14–16).

And those who ate the loaves were five thousand men. Mark gives the number at the end, almost as a footnote. “Men” (andres) means adult males, not the general word for people. Matthew adds: besides women and children (Matthew 14:21). Perhaps fifteen to twenty thousand people altogether. That is considerably more than the population of any town in Galilee except perhaps Tiberias and Sepphoris: a whole district, sitting on the grass, fed. And it happened because a boy handed over his lunch and twelve men did what they were told with what they had.

What the crowd did not understand. John records that they tried to make him king by force that night and had to be dispersed (John 6:15). They had eaten from his hands and concluded that a man who can do that should be running the country. They were nearly right, and entirely wrong. He had not come to be the kind of king who keeps a nation fed. He had come to be the bread, and when he said so the next day, many of them left (John 6:66).

Does this mean God will always give me plenty? No. God promises to supply every need of his people according to his riches in glory in Christ Jesus (Philippians 4:19), but he does not promise wealth or comfort, and Paul learned to be content in hunger as well as plenty (Philippians 4:11–13). Many faithful Christians are poor, and some go hungry for Christ’s sake. What this miracle promises is that the Lord knows our needs, cares about our bodies, is never short of resources, and will give us everything we need to do his will and reach his kingdom. And it points beyond bread to himself: the abundance he guarantees without limit is grace.

In a sentence. Twelve baskets of leftovers were gathered after five thousand men had eaten.

On a Tuesday. God’s provision is never stingy. Trust him with needs that seem too large. And do not waste what he gives: food, money, time, opportunities. Look this week at what you throw away, and ask whether some of it could feed someone else.

For worship. With Christ there are always more fragments than there were loaves. His grace is never measured out grudgingly; he gives until all are satisfied and then fills twelve baskets for good measure. He is the bread from heaven that never runs out, and not a crumb of what he gives is lost. As he gathered the fragments from the grass, so he will lose nothing of all that the Father has given him, but raise it up on the last day (John 6:39).

verseByVerse.quote: Immediately he made his disciples get into the boat and go before him to the other side, to Bethsaida, while he dismissed the crowd. And after he had taken leave of them, he went up on the mountain to pray. And when evening came, the boat was out on the sea, and he was alone on the land.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Immediately Jesus made his disciples get into the boat and go ahead of him to the other side, to Bethsaida, while he dismissed the crowd. After he had taken leave of them, he went up on the mountain to pray.

Immediately he made his disciples get into the boat. “Made” (ēnankasen) means compelled. Something is being cut short in a hurry, and the disciples plainly did not want to go. Why the urgency? John tells us: the crowd wanted to take Jesus by force to make him king (John 6:14–15). Five thousand men on a hillside in an occupied country, well fed and enthusiastic, is a rebellion looking for a leader, and twelve disciples who had spent the evening handing out miraculous bread were in no state to resist that mood. One of them was a Zealot. Jesus sent the disciples away, ahead of him to Bethsaida, home of Peter, Andrew and Philip (John 1:44), before they were swept up in political excitement.

While he dismissed the crowd. He refused the crown they offered: a crown offered freely, by acclamation, without a cross. The shortest road to glory has been laid in front of him before, by the devil in the wilderness (1:13; Matthew 4:8–9). He will not take a kingdom on those terms, because a king who feeds you is not the same as a king who saves you. His kingdom would come by the cross.

And after he had taken leave of them, he went up on the mountain to pray. Here is the pattern of his life. He has had no rest. The retreat was ruined before it started. He has taught for hours, fed thousands, defused a political crisis, and dismissed a crowd of that size personally: after he had taken leave of them is a whole evening’s work in a subordinate clause. And what he does with the first free hour is climb a hill in the dark to pray.

Three nights of prayer. This is the second of three times Mark shows Jesus praying alone at night (1:35; 14:32–39), each at a moment of temptation or decision. Before dawn, at the height of his popularity in Capernaum. Here, on the night the crowd tried to crown him. And in Gethsemane, on the night they came to arrest him. Success, the offer of glory, and the approach of death, and he handles all three the same way. Most of us pray hardest at the third kind of moment and hardly at all at the first two. Prosperity is treated as a season that requires no prayer, and it is the season in which many are most easily lost (Deuteronomy 8:10–14).

And when evening came, the boat was out on the sea, and he was alone on the land. Mark paints the picture and leaves it there for a moment: a boat somewhere out in the dark, and a man by himself on the mountain. They are separated, and they cannot see him. He is on the land, they are on the water, and night has come down between them. That is exactly what a hard stretch feels like from inside the boat. But a man alone on a mountain at night, praying, is not absent from the boat. He is keeping watch over it.

Why did Jesus refuse to be made king? Because he was already King, and because the crown they offered was the wrong one. They wanted a ruler who would drive out Rome and keep the bread coming. He had come to deal with a deeper enemy, sin and death, and that could only be done by the cross. To accept their crown would have been to bypass the cross, which is exactly what Satan had offered in the wilderness. He would be crowned, but with thorns first, and then at the Father’s right hand (Philippians 2:8–11). His kingdom is not of this world (John 18:36); it comes by word and Spirit, not by force.

Should Christians then avoid politics? Not necessarily. Christians may serve as rulers, judges and officials, as Joseph and Daniel did, and should seek justice and the good of their city (Jeremiah 29:7). What this passage warns against is confusing Christ’s kingdom with any political cause, or trying to bring in his rule by force, popularity or votes. No party is the kingdom of God. Serve faithfully wherever you are placed, pray for those in authority, and keep your deepest hope fixed on the King who refused a crowd’s crown and will return in glory.

In a sentence. Jesus sent his disciples away by boat, dismissed the crowd who wanted to make him king, and went up the mountain to pray.

On a Tuesday. At moments of success or temptation, do what Jesus did: go and pray. When things go well this week, a promotion, a good report, praise from others, take it straight to God in thanks and in asking him to keep your heart humble. Success is not the time to stop praying; it is the time to pray most carefully.

For worship. The King of kings walked away from a crown that would have cost him nothing, because he had come to wear one that would cost him everything. He sent his friends away from the flattering crowd, dismissed the multitude himself, and climbed a mountain in the dark to be with his Father. That is our Saviour: unmoved by applause, unswerving in obedience, and praying for his people while the night comes down between them and him.

verseByVerse.quote: And he saw that they were making headway painfully, for the wind was against them. And about the fourth watch of the night he came to them, walking on the sea. He meant to pass by them,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus saw that they were straining at the oars, for the wind was against them. About the fourth watch of the night he came to them, walking on the sea. He meant to pass by them.

And he saw that they were making headway painfully, for the wind was against them. This may be the most comforting sentence in the chapter. He saw them. It is the middle of the night. He is up a mountain, on shore, and they are out on the lake in the dark, three or four miles out, John says (John 6:19). Whatever kind of seeing this was, he was watching them the whole time. They did not know that. From inside the boat there was nothing but wind, black water, and a horizon with nobody on it. Every fact available to them said they were alone.

Making headway painfully. “Painfully” (basanizomenous) means tormented, tortured: they were tormented in the rowing. This is not a storm that threatens to sink them, as in chapter 4. It is worse in a particular way: hours of grinding, exhausting, unrewarded effort. They row and the shore does not get closer.

For the wind was against them. They are out there because he sent them. He made them get into that boat. Obedience put them in the wind. So here is the shape of a great deal of Christian experience, laid out in one verse. You are where he put you. You are pulling as hard as you can. Nothing is moving. He appears to be somewhere else entirely, and it is dark. And the verse tells you the one thing you cannot possibly know from inside the boat: he is watching, and he was watching the whole night, and he was praying while he watched. He went up the mountain to pray, and from that mountain he saw them. Those two facts belong together, and they are still true: he always lives to make intercession for them (Hebrews 7:25).

And about the fourth watch of the night. Between about 3 and 6 a.m. Mark told us they set out in the evening; they have been rowing for hours against the wind, perhaps nine of them. He came: not at the first hour, when it started to get hard; not at midnight; but in the last watch of the night, when men have stopped talking and are simply pulling. He is never early, in the way we would arrange it. He has never yet been late.

He came to them, walking on the sea. In the Old Testament, only God walks on the sea. Job says that God alone stretched out the heavens and trampled the waves of the sea (Job 9:8); the psalmist says, Your way was through the sea, your path through the great waters (Psalm 77:19). Mark’s readers knew those books.

He meant to pass by them. A puzzling phrase, found only in Mark, which sounds as though he intended to leave them to it. He did not. In the Old Testament, God passing by is how he reveals his glory. He passed by Moses on the mountain, sheltering him in a cleft of the rock, and proclaimed his name (Exodus 33:19–22; 34:6). He passed by Elijah at Horeb: And behold, the LORD passed by (1 Kings 19:11). And most exactly of all, Job, describing the God who trampled the waves of the sea, says three verses later, Behold, he passes by me, and I see him not (Job 9:11). Trampling the waves and passing by, in the same passage, about God. So this is not a man taking a shortcut past a struggling boat. It is a self-disclosure. Jesus intended to reveal his divine glory to the disciples, as God did to Moses and Elijah. He was not passing them by. He was passing before them, so that they could see who had been watching from the mountain.

If Jesus sees me struggling, why does he wait so long? Because his timing serves purposes we cannot see from the boat. The disciples learned that night what they could not have learned at the first hour: that he watches, that he comes, and that he is the Lord of the sea. Delay is not neglect. The Lord is not slow as some count slowness (2 Peter 3:9), and his help comes at the hour he has fixed. Meanwhile he is not idle; he is interceding. Keep rowing where he has put you, keep praying, and expect him, not on your schedule, but certainly on his.

In a sentence. Seeing the disciples struggling against the wind, Jesus came to them walking on the sea before dawn, intending to pass by them as God passed by Moses and Elijah.

On a Tuesday. If you have been straining at the oars for a long time, Jesus sees you. He will come. Name the place where obedience has put you into a headwind: a hard marriage, a thankless job, a ministry that never grows. Tell him plainly that you are tired, and remind yourself that the One who sent you is watching and praying for you now.

For worship. The God who trampled the waves of the sea walked on them in the person of his Son. The Lord who passed by Moses in glory passed by a fishing boat at four in the morning, to show tired men who he was. He sees every boat in the dark, and none of his people rows unwatched. He prays for us on the mountain and comes to us across the water, and he comes in the last watch, which is always the right watch, because he is the Lord of the night as well as the day.
verseByVerse.note: The fourth watch was about 3 to 6 a.m. “Pass by” recalls God “passing by” Moses and Elijah to show his glory.

parallels.desc: I will make my goodness pass before you

verseByVerse.quote: but when they saw him walking on the sea they thought it was a ghost, and cried out, for they all saw him and were terrified. But immediately he spoke to them and said, "Take heart; it is I. Do not be afraid."
verseByVerse.commentary:
When they saw him walking on the sea, they thought it was a ghost and cried out, for they all saw him and were terrified. But immediately he spoke to them and said: take heart; it is I. Do not be afraid.

But when they saw him walking on the sea they thought it was a ghost. Of course they did. They have been rowing for hours into a headwind, and there is a figure moving on the surface of the water beside the boat. Mark’s word is phantasma: an apparition, a spirit, perhaps an evil sea spirit, in the dark before dawn. Every sailor on that lake would have grown up on such stories.

The Lord in the shape of their worst fear. The Lord of glory came to them in the exact form of their worst fear, and they did not recognise him. Their instinct was not stupid; it was human. The one thing that could actually save them looked, in the dark, like the thing most likely to kill them. God has a way of coming to his people wearing the shape of what they most dread. Job did not recognise mercy when it arrived in a whirlwind. Joseph’s brothers did not recognise their salvation in the man who had them arrested. The thing bearing down on you out of the dark this year may be the Lord at work, and you will not necessarily know it at the time.

And cried out, for they all saw him and were terrified. All of them. Mark closes off any possibility that this was one man’s imagination or a trick of the light on a wave. Twelve men, including four professional fishermen who had spent their lives on that water at night, all saw the same thing and all reacted the same way.

But immediately he spoke to them. He did not leave them in terror. The moment they cry out, he speaks, and notice what comes first. Not the calming of the wind, not getting into the boat, but his voice. Before anything about their circumstances changes, he tells them who he is. That is the order in which he deals with frightened people. Take heart: be of good courage, now, before anything changes.

It is I. In Greek egō eimi, literally I am. It can simply mean it is me; in everyday speech it is how you identify yourself in the dark. But it is also God’s name revealed to Moses at the burning bush, when Moses asked for his name (Exodus 3:14), and God’s words in Isaiah: I am he; before me no god was formed (Isaiah 43:10), and I, I am he who comforts you (Isaiah 51:12). And they are spoken here by a man standing on water in the middle of the night, having come out to them across a sea that the Scriptures say God alone tramples. Walking on the sea, passing by as God did, and saying I am, Jesus reveals himself as the LORD.

Do not be afraid. God’s words when he reveals himself (Genesis 15:1; Isaiah 41:10). And it follows, and only follows, from the middle phrase. Take the whole sentence in the order he gives it. Take heart: courage, now. It is I: and here is the reason, and the reason is not the weather but a Person, and the name he uses is the name from the bush. Do not be afraid. There is no argument in it. He does not tell them the wind will drop, or that they will reach the shore, or that the night is nearly over. He tells them who is with them, and treats that as sufficient. It is sufficient. That is the whole of Christian comfort in three phrases, and every one of them was spoken from the middle of the water they were afraid of.

Is Jesus really claiming to be God here? Yes, though he does it in the way Mark loves: by deeds and echoes rather than a lecture. Walking on the sea is what Scripture says God alone does; passing by is how God shows his glory; I am is God’s name. Any one of those might be a coincidence; all three together, in one scene, are a revelation. The same Jesus will say I am before the high priest and be condemned for blasphemy (14:62–64). The disciples would not grasp it fully until after the resurrection, but Mark wants his readers to grasp it now: the man in the boat is the LORD.

What do I do with fear that will not go away? Listen to the order of Jesus’ words. He does not first remove the storm; he first tells you who he is. So when fear grips you, do not only ask him to change your circumstances. Remind yourself who is with you: the Lord who made the sea, who walked on it, who died and rose and holds your life. Speak his promises aloud (Isaiah 41:10; Hebrews 13:5–6). Bring the fear to him in prayer as it is (Philippians 4:6–7). If anxiety is constant and crippling, seek help from a pastor or a doctor as well; that is not unbelief. And expect that faith may coexist with trembling for a while. Courage is not the absence of fear but trust in the One who is greater.

In a sentence. The disciples thought Jesus was a ghost, but he comforted them at once with words that echo God’s own name: take heart; it is I; do not be afraid.

On a Tuesday. In the dark and the storm, listen for Jesus: take heart; it is I; do not be afraid. Write those three phrases where you will see them this week. And when something frightening comes at you, before you ask what will happen, ask who is with you.

For worship. The great I AM walked on the water to frightened men and spoke his name into the dark. He did not rebuke their fear before he comforted it; he came close and said, it is I. The God who revealed himself to Moses in a burning bush revealed himself to fishermen on a heaving sea. He is the same yesterday and today and for ever (Hebrews 13:8), and his first word to his frightened people is still not an explanation but himself.
verseByVerse.note: “It is I” can also be heard as the divine name, “I am.”

verseByVerse.quote: And he got into the boat with them, and the wind ceased. And they were utterly astounded, for they did not understand about the loaves, but their hearts were hardened.
verseByVerse.commentary:
He got into the boat with them, and the wind ceased. They were utterly astounded, for they did not understand about the loaves, but their hearts were hardened.

And he got into the boat with them, and the wind ceased. His presence brought calm. After hours of rowing and a night of terror, the ending is almost domestic: a man climbs over the side and sits down with them, and the wind stops. Mark does not even say he rebuked it this time. It simply stops, because he is aboard. (Mark does not record Peter walking on the water; Matthew does, Matthew 14:28–31.)

And they were utterly astounded. Literally, beyond measure astonished within themselves, as in the room where the little girl got up (5:42). And then Mark says something about his own leaders that no church would ever have invented.

For they did not understand about the loaves. Only Mark adds this. It is the verdict of the Gospel on the twelve apostles, written by a man who got his information from the chief of them, and circulated in the church while most of them were still alive. And the connection is not the one we would expect. He does not say they failed to understand the walking on water. He says the walking on water astonished them because they had not understood the loaves. The feeding should have taught them who Jesus is: the Lord who provides, the Shepherd of Psalm 23, greater than Moses. That afternoon they had carried food out of his hands to thousands of people and come back with twelve baskets between them, and they had drawn no conclusion from it about who he was. If they had understood the loaves, they would not have been so astonished at the walking on water. Both revealed the same truth: Jesus is God with them.

God’s past dealings are meant to be evidence. The reason a new trouble knocks us flat is very often that we drew nothing from the last deliverance. We were relieved, and we were grateful for about a fortnight, and we filed it as something that happened rather than as something we learned about him.

But their hearts were hardened. A shocking statement about the disciples. The same word was used of the Pharisees in chapter 3, the men in the synagogue who watched a withered hand restored and walked out to plan a murder (3:5). These are not enemies. They are the apostles, mid-mission, fresh from casting out demons in his name, and their hearts are described with the vocabulary of his opponents. Not that they had rejected Jesus, but that their hearts were dull, slow and resistant to understanding. Hardness of heart is not only the sin of opponents; disciples suffer from it too (8:17). And it does not announce itself. It is not disbelief; the Twelve believed a great deal. It is the slow loss of the capacity to be affected: the state in which the same truths arrive and produce nothing, in which a man can carry the bread and never taste it. Mark is honest: Peter told this story against himself.

What it does not mean. Not that the disciples were unbelievers like the Pharisees. But it shows that even true followers need God to open their eyes again and again (8:22–26). The hardening was real and it was not final. He kept them, taught them, corrected them, was betrayed and denied by them, and after the resurrection he fed them breakfast on a beach and sent them out, and the man whose memory this Gospel preserves was the one who had denied him three times. He does not give up on hard-hearted disciples. He gets into the boat with them.

How can I stop forgetting what God has done? By deliberately remembering, which is what Scripture keeps telling God’s people to do. Israel was told to set up stones, keep feasts and tell their children (Joshua 4:6–7; Deuteronomy 6:12). So keep a record of answered prayers and deliverances, and read it back when trouble comes. Speak of God’s past mercies to others, at home and in church. Come to the Lord’s Supper as a feast of remembrance (1 Corinthians 11:24–25). And ask the Spirit to soften your heart, because remembering is not merely a technique; it is grace. Bless the LORD, O my soul, and forget not all his benefits (Psalm 103:2).

In a sentence. When Jesus got into the boat the wind stopped, and the disciples were utterly astonished, because they had not understood the loaves and their hearts were hardened.

On a Tuesday. What has God done in your life that you have not yet understood? Ask him to soften your heart and open your eyes. Sit down this week and write a list of five times God has helped you. Then look at the trouble in front of you in the light of that list.

For worship. How patient is our Lord with slow disciples. He fed them, and they did not understand; he walked on the sea, and they were terrified; he called their hearts hard, and then he climbed into the boat and sat down with them. He does not wait for us to understand before he comes aboard. His faithfulness does not depend on our perception, and he keeps softening hard hearts until the day we see him as he is.

verseByVerse.quote: When they had crossed over, they came to land at Gennesaret and moored to the shore. And when they got out of the boat, the people immediately recognized him and ran about the whole region and began to bring the sick people on their beds to wherever they heard he was. And wherever he came, in villages, cities, or countryside, they laid the sick in the marketplaces and implored him that they might touch even the fringe of his garment. And as many as touched it were made well.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When they had crossed over, they came to land at Gennesaret and moored the boat. When they got out, the people immediately recognised him and ran around the whole region and began to bring the sick on their beds to wherever they heard he was. Wherever he went, in villages, cities or countryside, they laid the sick in the marketplaces and begged him that they might touch even the fringe of his garment. And as many as touched it were made well.

When they had crossed over, they came to land at Gennesaret and moored to the shore. A fertile plain on the northwest shore, between Capernaum and Magdala: a few miles of unusually rich farmland, and Josephus was lyrical about it. The wind had blown them off course from Bethsaida, where he had sent them; the night has put them down somewhere else entirely.

The people immediately recognized him and ran about the whole region. His fame had spread everywhere. The boat touches the shore and it starts.

And began to bring the sick people on their beds to wherever they heard he was. Carried on mats, as the paralysed man had been (2:3). One of the most remarkable pictures in the Gospel goes by in a sentence. Word spreads across the plain, and people start carrying: not helping the sick to walk, but carrying them, on the pallets they lie on, in from the villages and the farms. And they are chasing a moving target: to wherever they heard he was. He is walking, so the beds are being carried from place to place after him, all day, by relays of neighbours and relatives.

They laid the sick in the marketplaces. The open public spaces: the square where everything happened, the shops, the courts, the gossip, the labourers waiting for work. And the sick are being laid out in rows in the middle of it, in public, in the way of everybody. These people have stopped caring how it looks. There is a certain kind of desperation that has burned through embarrassment entirely, and it is the only kind that ever gets anywhere with Christ.

And implored him that they might touch even the fringe of his garment. Like the woman who was healed (5:27–29). The fringe was the tassel on the corner of a Jewish man’s garment, commanded as a reminder of the commandments of the LORD (Numbers 15:38–40). The request has a history in this Gospel. A woman with twelve years of bleeding had said to herself, if I touch even his garments, I will be made well, and reached from behind in a crowd, and it worked. She had hoped to slip away unnoticed, and Jesus stopped everything and drew her out and called her daughter. Now a whole region is doing what she did. That is what one healed woman’s story did when it got out, and it is exactly what one healed madman’s story did on the other side of the lake (5:20). Mark keeps showing you the same mechanism: somebody tells what happened to them, and a district comes.

And as many as touched it were made well. Literally, were saved. All of them. Not one was turned away. Mark does not qualify it, and he does not tell us that anyone’s theology was corrected first. Their understanding was thin and probably half superstitious, as hers had been. He does not lecture them about the tassel. He heals them.

What it does not mean. Not that Jesus’ clothes had magical power. The power was his own, received by faith.

The contrast. The chapter began in Jesus’ hometown, which rejected him and saw few miracles. It ends with crowds who sought him eagerly and were healed. The difference is faith. Nazareth had every advantage and would not stretch out a hand. Gennesaret had almost no understanding and grabbed the hem of his coat. Between those two lies the whole difference, and it is not intelligence, and it is not opportunity, and it was never information. One town thought it already knew him. The other only knew it needed him.

Why does Jesus not heal everyone like this today? Because these mass healings were signs of who he is and of what his kingdom will finally bring, given in a unique moment as the King arrived. They were not a promise that every illness will be removed in this life. Christ still heals, in answer to prayer and through medicine, as he wills. But the full fulfilment of this scene is still ahead: on the last day, every one of his people will be raised with a body that no disease can touch, and there will be no more mourning, nor crying, nor pain (Revelation 21:4). Gennesaret was a preview. The resurrection is the whole picture.

In a sentence. At Gennesaret, people brought their sick from everywhere, and all who touched even the fringe of Jesus’ garment were healed.

On a Tuesday. Bring your needs, and the needs of others, to Jesus today. No one who comes to him is turned away. Who is the sick or burdened person you could carry to him this week, in prayer, by a visit, by bringing them to church? Be one of the neighbours who carry the beds.

For worship. The chapter that began with a village refusing him ends with a whole region running to him with its sick, and every one who touched him was made well. That is the Lord we worship: one who is despised by the proud and sought by the desperate, and who never turns away the hand that reaches for him. His power is undiminished by our ignorance, his mercy undeterred by our superstitions, and his welcome as wide as the marketplaces of Galilee. Whoever comes to him, he will never cast out.
verseByVerse.note: Gennesaret was a fertile plain on the north-west shore of the lake. The fringe was the tassel the law required on a garment.

6.theology:
Could he not, or would he not? Verse 5 should not be softened — Mark wrote he could do no mighty work there, where Matthew writes did not do many (Matt. 13:58). But the exception clause settles the sense: he healed a few sick people that afternoon, so it was no failure of power. The impossibility is moral. In a village that had already decided what he was, mighty works would have been spectacle, and he does not do spectacle — he refuses a sign to the Pharisees (8:11–12) and stands silent before Herod, who wanted to watch one (Luke 23:8–9). Faith is not a mechanism that generates miracles, as though God were a machine and belief the coin. It is the setting in which he ordinarily works, because he deals with persons. Unbelief does not disable God; it makes his help unwelcome, and he does not force it.

He meant to pass by them (v. 48) is not a shortcut past a struggling boat. Passing by is the Old Testament's own vocabulary for God making himself visible: while my glory passes by (Ex. 33:22), behold, the LORD passed by (1 Kgs. 19:11). Most exactly, Job says of God that he alone stretched out the heavens and trampled the waves of the sea, and three verses later, behold, he passes by me, and I see him not (Job 9:8, 11). Trampling the sea and passing by, in one passage, about God. And when they scream he answers with egō eimi — it is I, the ordinary words for identifying yourself in the dark, and the words from the burning bush (Ex. 3:14).

And their hearts were hardened (v. 52) is said of the apostles, in the very word used of the men in the synagogue who watched a hand restored and left to plan a murder (3:5). Hardness is not a disease of unbelievers only. It is not disbelief — the Twelve believed a great deal. It is the slow loss of the capacity to be affected, the state in which a man can carry the bread and never taste it.
6.examples:
Herod is the most searching portrait in the chapter, because he is not a scoffer. He feared John, knew he was a righteous and holy man, protected him from a wife who wanted him dead, was greatly perplexed by his preaching — and heard him gladly. He sent for him. He came back for more. He is the rocky ground of chapter 4 given a name and a palace: real interest, real feeling, real pleasure, and no root.

Everything was there except the one thing John was actually asking for. Herodias stayed. And a man who will not repent must eventually silence the voice that keeps asking him to — it took only a party, a dance and an audience to finish what had been decided long before.

Then: a king who kept his oath and killed a prophet, because of his oaths and his guests. Not conscience — he had already lost that argument. He could not bear to look foolish in front of people whose opinion he had spent his life courting.

Now: almost nobody does the worst thing they ever do because they wanted to. They do it because backing out in front of the people watching was unthinkable — the joke laughed at, the thing gone along with once the room had turned, the stand not taken because of who would have seen. Peter is eight chapters from exactly this, in a courtyard, in front of a servant girl. The fear of man lays a snare (Prov. 29:25), and it walked a king with an army into a murder he did not want to commit.

So the test is not whether you enjoy good preaching. Herod did. It is whether you can name one thing it has actually cost you this year.

7.title: What Really Defiles a Man
7.text: <sup>1</sup>Now when the Pharisees gathered to him, with some of the scribes who had come from Jerusalem, <sup>2</sup>they saw that some of his disciples ate with hands that were defiled, that is, unwashed. <sup>3</sup>(For the Pharisees and all the Jews do not eat unless they wash their hands properly, holding to the tradition of the elders, <sup>4</sup>and when they come from the marketplace, they do not eat unless they wash. And there are many other traditions that they observe, such as the washing of cups and pots and copper vessels and dining couches.) <sup>5</sup>And the Pharisees and the scribes asked him, “Why do your disciples not walk according to the tradition of the elders, but eat with defiled hands?” <sup>6</sup>And he said to them, “Well did Isaiah prophesy of you hypocrites, as it is written, ‘This people honors me with their lips, but their heart is far from me; <sup>7</sup>in vain do they worship me, teaching as doctrines the commandments of men.’ <sup>8</sup>You leave the commandment of God and hold to the tradition of men.” <sup>9</sup>And he said to them, “You have a fine way of rejecting the commandment of God in order to establish your tradition! <sup>10</sup>For Moses said, ‘Honor your father and your mother’; and, ‘Whoever reviles father or mother must surely die.’ <sup>11</sup>But you say, ‘If a man tells his father or his mother, “Whatever you would have gained from me is Corban”’ (that is, given to God)— <sup>12</sup>then you no longer permit him to do anything for his father or mother, <sup>13</sup>thus making void the word of God by your tradition that you have handed down. And many such things you do.” <sup>14</sup>And he called the people to him again and said to them, “Hear me, all of you, and understand: <sup>15</sup>There is nothing outside a person that by going into him can defile him, but the things that come out of a person are what defile him.” <sup>17</sup>And when he had entered the house and left the people, his disciples asked him about the parable. <sup>18</sup>And he said to them, “Then are you also without understanding? Do you not see that whatever goes into a person from outside cannot defile him, <sup>19</sup>since it enters not his heart but his stomach, and is expelled?” (Thus he declared all foods clean.) <sup>20</sup>And he said, “What comes out of a person is what defiles him. <sup>21</sup>For from within, out of the heart of man, come evil thoughts, sexual immorality, theft, murder, adultery, <sup>22</sup>coveting, wickedness, deceit, sensuality, envy, slander, pride, foolishness. <sup>23</sup>All these evil things come from within, and they defile a person.” <sup>24</sup>And from there he arose and went away to the region of Tyre and Sidon. And he entered a house and did not want anyone to know, yet he could not be hidden. <sup>25</sup>But immediately a woman whose little daughter had an unclean spirit heard of him and came and fell down at his feet. <sup>26</sup>Now the woman was a Gentile, a Syrophoenician by birth. And she begged him to cast the demon out of her daughter. <sup>27</sup>And he said to her, “Let the children be fed first, for it is not right to take the children’s bread and throw it to the dogs.” <sup>28</sup>But she answered him, “Yes, Lord; yet even the dogs under the table eat the children’s crumbs.” <sup>29</sup>And he said to her, “For this statement you may go your way; the demon has left your daughter.” <sup>30</sup>And she went home and found the child lying in bed and the demon gone. <sup>31</sup>Then he returned from the region of Tyre and went through Sidon to the Sea of Galilee, in the region of the Decapolis. <sup>32</sup>And they brought to him a man who was deaf and had a speech impediment, and they begged him to lay his hand on him. <sup>33</sup>And taking him aside from the crowd privately, he put his fingers into his ears, and after spitting touched his tongue. <sup>34</sup>And looking up to heaven, he sighed and said to him, “Ephphatha,” that is, “Be opened.” <sup>35</sup>And his ears were opened, his tongue was released, and he spoke plainly. <sup>36</sup>And Jesus charged them to tell no one. But the more he charged them, the more zealously they proclaimed it. <sup>37</sup>And they were astonished beyond measure, saying, “He has done all things well. He even makes the deaf hear and the mute speak.”
7.overview:
Chapter 7 takes down a wall, and then walks through the gap.

It opens with a delegation from Jerusalem who have travelled ninety miles to raise the matter of unwashed hands. Jesus does not defend his disciples; he quotes Isaiah at the delegation, and then proves the charge with a single devastating example. Corban was a vow that could put a man's money beyond his parents' reach by declaring it dedicated to God — and the tradition would not merely permit it but forbid him to change his mind. A rule invented to honour God had become a device for robbing your father, with a straight face and in God's name.

Then he calls the crowd over and says the thing that changed everything: there is nothing outside a person that by going into him can defile him. Mark, writing down Peter's preaching years later, adds six words in a bracket — thus he declared all foods clean — and the boundary between clean and unclean peoples, kept for fifteen centuries, is gone.

And having dissolved it, he crosses it. The second half of the chapter is two healings on Gentile ground: a Phoenician mother who takes his own hard word and finds the door in it, and a deaf man in the Decapolis brought by friends, taken quietly aside, and given his hearing with one Aramaic word. The crowd's verdict is bigger than they know — he has done all things well is the sentence pronounced over the finished creation.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–23 — Tradition, the Word of God, and the Human Heart
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The complaint (vv. 1–5). A delegation arrives from Jerusalem — the second one in this Gospel — and what they have come ninety miles to raise is that the disciples do not wash their hands before eating. Mark stops to explain the custom, which tells you he is writing for people who have never heard of it.

The answer (vv. 6–8). Jesus does not defend his men. He quotes Isaiah at the delegation and calls them hypocrites: lips near, heart far, and human rules taught as though God had given them.

The example (vv. 9–13). Then he makes it concrete with a case anyone can follow. A man could put the money owed to his aged parents beyond their reach by pronouncing one word over it — and the tradition would back him. That is not a lapse in the system. That is the system working.

The principle (vv. 14–23). He calls the crowd over and says the most subversive thing in the chapter: nothing that goes into a man can defile him. Mark, writing years later with Peter's memory in his hand, adds a parenthesis that changed the church — thus he declared all foods clean — and then Jesus tells the disciples in private where defilement actually comes from, and lists thirteen of them.
verseByVerse.theology:
Why does your Bible skip verse 16? Look down the page and the numbers run 15, 17. Nothing has been lost and nothing has been hidden.

The oldest and best manuscripts of Mark do not have a verse 16. Later copies add the familiar refrain if anyone has ears to hear, let him hear — a sentence Jesus certainly said, and which Mark records elsewhere (4:9, 4:23). What almost certainly happened is that a scribe, copying by hand, felt the sentence belonged after v. 15 and wrote it in the margin, and a later copyist took the margin note for part of the text.

The verse numbering itself is not ancient — it was added in the sixteenth century, long after the manuscripts. So when translators went back to the earliest copies and found the sentence absent, they could not renumber the whole New Testament; they simply left the number empty and put the words in a footnote.

That is worth a plain word of reassurance to any reader who finds a gap like this unsettling. Nothing has been taken out of your Bible. The opposite has happened: we now have older and better copies than were available in 1611, and where those copies show that a sentence crept in later, honest translators tell you so in the margin rather than quietly leaving it in. A faith that will not look at its own manuscripts has something to hide. This one publishes the workings.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Corban — a rule invented to honour God, turned into a device for robbing your parents, with a straight face and in God's name.

Now: the shape survives perfectly, and it is almost never dishonest. It is the man so committed at church that his mother has not had a visit in four months. It is the giving that goes to the building fund while a brother in the same congregation cannot pay his heating bill. It is any arrangement in which something genuinely religious has been placed in front of a plain duty God commanded, so that the duty can be quietly dropped without anybody feeling wicked.

So here is a test you can actually run, and it is the one this passage supplies. Take any tradition you hold — a practice, a standard, a way of doing things — and ask whether keeping it is currently costing somebody else something God told you to give them. Not whether it is in the Bible; a good many decent traditions are not, and need not be. Whether it has begun to displace a commandment.

Jesus does not attack tradition as such. He attacks tradition that has been promoted — set level with Scripture, and then used against it.

verseByVerse.quote: Now when the Pharisees gathered to him, with some of the scribes who had come from Jerusalem, they saw that some of his disciples ate with hands that were defiled, that is, unwashed.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Pharisees and some scribes who had come down from Jerusalem gathered around Jesus, and they noticed that some of his disciples were eating with defiled hands, that is, without washing them in the ritual way.

Meaning first. Mark 7 asks where uncleanness really lives. A delegation from Jerusalem complains that Jesus’ disciples eat without the ritual hand-washing of the elders’ tradition, and Jesus answers with Isaiah: they honour God with their lips while their hearts are far from him, and they set aside God’s commandment to keep their own tradition, as in the Corban rule that let a son withhold support from his parents. Then he tells the crowd that nothing going into a person can defile him; defilement comes out of the heart, and Mark adds that Jesus thereby declared all foods clean. At once Jesus walks into Gentile country, where a Syrophoenician mother asks for the crumbs from the children’s table and her daughter is freed by his word, and in the Decapolis he opens the ears and loosens the tongue of a deaf man. The religious experts go home unmoved; the outsiders receive the bread. And the crowd’s cry, he has done all things well, announces that the God of Isaiah 35 has come to make his broken creation new.

Setting. This is the second delegation from Jerusalem in this Gospel. The first decided that Jesus cast out demons by Beelzebul (3:22). Jerusalem was the centre of religious authority, and these men came as inspectors, having made the journey of some ninety miles, four or five days on the road; they are not here to learn. The scene follows straight on from the feeding of the five thousand and the healings at Gennesaret (6:30–56): the crowds are being fed, healed and taught, and the experts’ concern is how the disciples hold their bread.

Now when the Pharisees gathered to him, with some of the scribes who had come from Jerusalem. Note the word gathered: they collect around him, the way a committee collects. The Pharisees were a lay movement devoted to strict keeping of the law, including the purity rules that the Old Testament gave to priests, which they applied to ordinary daily life. The scribes were the professional experts in the law, many of them Pharisees.

They saw that some of his disciples ate with hands that were defiled. And this is what they came for. Sit with the disproportion for a moment, because it is the point of the whole passage. Trained theologians have travelled from Jerusalem to Galilee, at real expense, and what they have found and what they will raise is that some of the men in this group did not rinse their hands before a meal. They are standing in front of a man who has cleansed a leper, raised a dead girl, fed a district on five loaves and stilled a storm. They have taken notes on his catering. “Defiled” (koinais) literally means common: ordinary, not set apart as holy, and therefore ritually unclean, the opposite of holy. The issue is not dirt. It is a ceremony of purity.

That is, unwashed. Mark explains the term for his Gentile readers, probably in Rome, who would not know what common hands meant.

What it does not mean. Not that Jesus was careless about hygiene, or that his disciples were slovenly. The washing in question had nothing to do with germs. It was a religious rite that the law of Moses did not command for ordinary people.

An honourable intention. Two things need saying so that we are fair to them, and then one thing that is not fair to them at all. Their intention was honourable. The law required priests to wash before handling holy things (Exodus 30:19–21). The Pharisees, wanting the whole nation to be what God had called it, a kingdom of priests and a holy nation (Exodus 19:6), extended the priestly rule to every Jew and every meal. Every table becomes an altar; every family becomes a priesthood. As an idea it is not contemptible; it is devout. And here is what is not fair: God never asked for it. The washing of hands before ordinary food is nowhere in the law of Moses. It was a good idea that men had, and by this point it had hardened into an obligation with the force of a commandment, and men were being judged by it.

How it always happens. It is worth naming carefully, because it is not a first-century disease. Nobody sets out to replace Scripture. A wise practice is adopted for good reasons. In a generation it is the way we do things. In two it is the way serious Christians do things. In three, a man who does not do it is regarded as unsound, and nobody can any longer say which chapter and verse required it. The Pharisees did not steal the Bible. They buried it under good ideas.

Were the Pharisees simply bad people? No, and that is what makes them a warning rather than a cartoon. Many were sincere, devout and disciplined; they prayed, fasted, tithed and knew their Bibles thoroughly. Paul was one, and he says he was blameless by their standard (Philippians 3:5–6). Their danger was not that they did not care about God, but that they had come to trust in their own carefulness and to judge others by rules God had not given. That is a temptation for every earnest believer, and the more serious you are, the more you need to watch for it.

In a sentence. Religious inspectors from Jerusalem noticed that Jesus’ disciples did not perform the ritual hand-washing before meals.

On a Tuesday. It is easy to notice what others do with their hands and miss what God is doing in front of you. Watch for that in yourself. Next time you find yourself irritated by how another Christian does something, ask whether what bothers you is a command of God or a preference of yours, and whether you have noticed the grace at work in him while you were noticing his hands.

For worship. While the inspectors examined the disciples’ hands, the Lord of glory had just fed thousands in the wilderness and healed every sick person who touched him. He is not the God of small scrutiny but of overflowing mercy. He does not come to measure our rinsing but to make us clean from the inside, and his patience with men who travelled ninety miles to find fault is itself a wonder. He answers them not with contempt but with the word of God.
verseByVerse.note: The washing in question was a ritual of purity, not hygiene.

parallels.desc: the Pharisee astonished that Jesus did not wash

verseByVerse.quote: (For the Pharisees and all the Jews do not eat unless they wash their hands properly, holding to the tradition of the elders, and when they come from the marketplace, they do not eat unless they wash. And there are many other traditions that they observe, such as the washing of cups and pots and copper vessels and dining couches.) And the Pharisees and the scribes asked him, "Why do your disciples not walk according to the tradition of the elders, but eat with defiled hands?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Mark pauses to explain. The Pharisees, and the Jews generally, do not eat without carefully washing their hands, holding to the tradition of the elders. Coming from the market, they do not eat without washing, and they keep many other traditions, such as washing cups, pots, copper vessels and dining couches. So the Pharisees and scribes asked Jesus why his disciples did not walk by the tradition of the elders but ate with defiled hands.

For the Pharisees and all the Jews. A generalisation: the Pharisees’ practice had spread widely and was respected by ordinary Jews, even if not all kept it strictly. And notice that Mark stops the narrative and explains the custom, in a bracket, for two whole verses. That tells you who this Gospel was written for. A Jewish reader would need none of this; it would be like explaining a kettle to an Englishman. Mark is writing for Gentiles, almost certainly for the church in Rome, and he keeps doing this: translating Aramaic phrases, converting money into Roman coinage, using Latin loan-words. The oldest Gospel we have was written for people outside the covenant, and that is quietly relevant to a chapter that ends with a Gentile woman and a Gentile deaf man.

Wash their hands properly. Literally, with a fist (pygmē). The exact meaning is uncertain. It may mean cupping one hand to pour water over the other, washing up to the wrist, or rubbing the fist in the palm. Whatever the gesture, it was a precise ritual.

Holding to the tradition of the elders. The key phrase, and everything in the passage turns on it. The tradition (paradosis, what is handed down) was the body of oral rules that the rabbis had built around the written law of Moses, to apply it to every situation and, as they said, to build a fence around the law so that no one would come near breaking it. It was later written down in the Mishnah (about AD 200), and it runs to a substantial book; there is a whole tractate on hand-washing, specifying the quantity of water, the position of the hands and the number of rinses. And the Pharisees believed, and this is the crucial point, that this oral tradition had been given to Moses on Sinai alongside the written law and was equally binding. Jesus will deny that flatly.

And when they come from the marketplace, they do not eat unless they wash. In the market you might brush against a Gentile, or a Jew who was unclean, or touch something unclean. So you washed, or even immersed yourself (the Greek is literally baptise themselves), before eating.

The washing of cups and pots and copper vessels and dining couches. Vessels could become unclean (Leviticus 11:32–35), and the tradition multiplied the rules. Mark’s list is faintly comic and probably meant to be: cups, pots, bronze vessels, the furniture you eat on. There were rules for all of it, and men had spent their lives mastering them. Some manuscripts lack and dining couches, which was probably added later; the meaning is unaffected.

Why do your disciples not walk according to the tradition of the elders? To walk is the Jewish way of speaking of how you live (the rabbis called their rules halakah, from the word for walking). The question is an accusation: your disciples are disobeying the recognised authorities, and you as their teacher are responsible. Now look hard at how they frame it, because the framing gives the whole game away. They do not ask why the disciples break the law of God. They ask why they do not walk according to the tradition of the elders. They know exactly which authority is being contravened, and they name it accurately, and they are perfectly confident that it settles the matter.
