His tongue was released. Literally, the bond of his tongue was loosed. The picture is of something tied up being set free. Ancient people sometimes spoke of a demon binding the tongue, though Mark does not say this man was possessed. Either way, he was in bondage, and Jesus set him free.

And he spoke plainly. “Plainly” (orthōs): correctly, normally. Not only could he hear; he could speak properly at once, without having to learn. That is, in human terms, the strangest part. You learn to speak by hearing. This man opens his mouth and talks properly, at once, with no learning at all, which tells you that what happened here was not a repair. It was a creation.

And Jesus charged them to tell no one. The messianic secret again (1:44; 5:43). Jesus did not want to be known chiefly as a miracle-worker. Crowds seeking signs would hinder his teaching, and popular messianic excitement could provoke the authorities before his time. We are in Gentile territory, far from the Galilean crowds who wanted to crown him, but the same logic holds wherever he is. He will not have a following built on what he can do to a body. A reputation as a healer is not the truth about him; it is a fragment of the truth that can be believed enthusiastically by people who have understood nothing. His true identity could only be understood in the light of the cross.

But the more he charged them, the more zealously they proclaimed it. “Proclaimed” (ekēryssen) is the word for preaching. Their disobedience was understandable but still disobedience. The sentence is a see-saw: the more he told them to be quiet, the more they told everybody. It happened before: he told the cleansed leper to say nothing, and the man went out and began to talk freely about it, so that Jesus could no longer openly enter a town (1:45). The irony is that in Mark, people told to keep silent proclaim, while the disciples later told to proclaim (16:15) were slow to understand.

Why the news travels among the astonished. There is something worth turning over in that. These were people with no theology, no covenant, no Scriptures and no commission, the very opposite of the twelve trained men who had been explicitly sent out to preach. And they could not stop talking. It is a fair question why the news travels so much more easily among people who have just been astonished by Christ than among people who have known about him for thirty years. The difference is not information. Nobody has to be persuaded to talk about something that has just happened to them.

How can I get back the wonder of a new believer? Not by manufacturing excitement, but by looking again at what Christ has actually done for you. Wonder fades when grace becomes familiar. So remember what you were without him (Ephesians 2:1–5), read the Gospels slowly enough to be surprised, spend time with new Christians and hear their stories, and ask God to restore the joy of your salvation (Psalm 51:12). The more clearly you see your own deafness and his voice that opened your ears, the less you will need to be pushed to speak of him.

In a sentence. The man was healed at once and spoke clearly; Jesus told the people to tell no one, but they spread it all the more.

On a Tuesday. Zeal is good, but obedience is better. Tell Christ’s works when and how he wants them told. We are not under his command to silence but under his command to go and tell (Matthew 28:19). So tell one person this week, simply, something Jesus has done for you.

For worship. With one word the Creator gave a man ears that worked and a tongue that could speak perfectly at once. That is not a doctor’s cure but a Maker’s act. And the Lord who commanded silence because the cross was not yet complete is the Lord who, after the cross, sends his church to shout it from the housetops. The tongue he loosed that day was the first of countless tongues he has loosed since, to sing the praise of the God who opens the ears of the deaf.

verseByVerse.quote: And they were astonished beyond measure, saying, "He has done all things well. He even makes the deaf hear and the mute speak."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The people were astonished beyond all measure. They said: he has done all things well. He even makes the deaf hear and the mute speak.

And they were astonished beyond measure. A double strengthening in the Greek, used only here in the New Testament: they were overwhelmed, beyond the beyond. Mark has run out of ordinary words. And then he gives us what the crowd actually said, and they said more than they knew. Both halves of their sentence are quotations they did not realise they were making.

He has done all things well. An echo of Genesis 1:31: God saw everything that he had made, and behold, it was very good. The crowd means something quite modest: this healer is impressive; everything he touches turns out right. What they have in fact said is the sentence pronounced over the finished creation, at the close of the sixth day, when God looked at a world with nothing wrong in it. Jesus’ works are works of new creation, restoring what was broken. The one who made ears has repaired a pair of them. The one who gave the tongue its power of speech has given it back. This is not a rescue operation bolted on to a ruined world; it is the Creator returning to his own marred work and beginning, one man at a time, to make it good again. The crowd may not have meant this, but Mark’s readers would hear it.

He even makes the deaf hear and the mute speak. Mark’s point is Isaiah 35:4–6: Behold, your God will come… He will come and save you. Then the eyes of the blind shall be opened, and the ears of the deaf unstopped; then shall the lame man leap like a deer, and the tongue of the mute sing for joy. The rare word in verse 32 pointed here. Isaiah 35 is not a general promise of better days. It is the description of what will happen when God himself comes to save his people. Isaiah said these signs would mark the coming of God himself to save. In Jesus, God has come. And these Gentiles of the Decapolis, who had no part in the promises, are the ones who see it, in front of a crowd that could not have quoted Isaiah if you had paid them.

The wider meaning. In Mark’s structure, this healing of a deaf man stands next to the disciples’ spiritual deafness: Having ears do you not hear? (8:18). The man is a picture of what the disciples need, and of what every person needs. We cannot open our own ears to God’s word. Only Christ can say to us, Be opened.

How it ends. That is how he works, from one end of this Gospel to the other. The scholars came ninety miles from Jerusalem to raise the matter of unwashed hands, and went home unmoved. A pagan mother took hold of one word and got her daughter back. A deaf man was carried to him by friends and heard his own voice. The chapter began with men measuring the cleanness of cups. It ends with the Creator of the world groaning over one broken body and then saying, be opened.

How can I say he has done all things well when my life is going badly? Because the sentence is about him, not about your circumstances this week. It does not mean that everything that happens is pleasant, but that everything he does is right, wise and good, even when we cannot yet see how (Romans 8:28; Genesis 50:20). The deaf man had lived years in silence before that day; the crowd’s cry came at the end of a long wait. So say it by faith now, and you will say it by sight later. Many Christians have written that sentence over the hardest chapters of their lives, looking back. The cross itself looked like the worst thing ever done, and it was the best.

In a sentence. Overwhelmed, the people declared that Jesus did all things well, unknowingly confirming that the God who promised to open deaf ears had come.

On a Tuesday. He has done all things well is a confession for every Christian, in joy and in trial. Say it at the end of today, and name one thing he has done well in it. And pray for the Lord to open the ears of those you love who cannot yet hear him, and your own ears, to hear him more clearly.

For worship. Behold, your God has come. The Lord of Isaiah 35 has walked through the Decapolis, and the deaf hear and the mute speak. He has done all things well: at creation, at the cross, in the opening of every deaf heart, and he will do all things well at the end. One day he will say be opened over every grave that has ever been dug, and the redeemed will rise with ears to hear and tongues to sing, and once again the verdict of heaven over his finished work will be: very good.

parallels.desc: the ears of the deaf unstopped, the tongue of the mute sings

7.theology:
Why does your Bible skip verse 16? The numbers run 15, then 17, and nothing has been lost. The oldest and best manuscripts of Mark have no verse 16; later copies add the familiar refrain if anyone has ears to hear, let him hear — a sentence Jesus certainly said and which Mark records elsewhere (4:9, 4:23) — almost certainly written first in a margin and then mistaken for text. The verse numbers themselves date only from the sixteenth century, so translators could not renumber the New Testament; they left the number empty and put the words in a footnote. Nothing has been removed from your Bible. We simply have older copies than were available in 1611, and honest translators tell you in the margin rather than quietly leaving something in.

Was Jesus cruel to the Syrophoenician woman? Three things settle it without softening the difficulty. The word first is a door standing open — let the children be fed first implies a second course, and Paul states the same order plainly (Rom. 1:16). And the dogs in the picture are under the table (v. 28): not the scavengers of the street but the household pets, already inside the house. And the outcome is the loudest commentary of all — he grants her request at once, at a distance, and Matthew records him saying O woman, great is your faith! (Matt. 15:28). He handed her a picture with a door in it to see whether she would find the door, and she found it in one sentence.

And the crowd at the end echoes two texts without knowing it. He has done all things well sounds like the verdict over the finished creation — God saw everything he had made, and it was very good (Gen. 1:31). He even makes the deaf hear and the mute speak is Isaiah 35:5–6, the sign of the day when God himself comes to save.
7.examples:
Then: Corban — the money owed to an old man, put beyond his reach by a holy word, while his son kept the use of it and his reputation.

Now: the shape survives perfectly, and it is almost never dishonest. The man so committed at church four nights a week that his mother has not had a visit since March. The giving that goes to a fund while a brother in the same congregation cannot pay his heating bill. Any arrangement in which something genuinely religious has been set in front of a plain duty God commanded, so that the duty can be dropped without anybody feeling wicked.

So take the test the passage supplies, in one sentence: is anything I do for God currently costing somebody else something God told me to give them?

Note that Jesus does not attack tradition as such — every church has customs and must. He attacks tradition that has been promoted: set level with Scripture, and then used against it. And note what he reaches for when he wants a case anybody can measure. Not prayer, not fasting, not the temple. Whether the old people in your family are being looked after — which is exactly where the New Testament keeps landing (Jas. 1:27; 1 Tim. 5:8).

And one more, from the parenthesis in v. 19. Peter was in that house and heard the explanation with his own ears — and years later needed a sheet let down from heaven three times before he would eat with a Gentile (Acts 10:9–16), and a public rebuke from Paul after that (Gal. 2:11–14). It is possible to be taught a truth plainly by Christ himself and go years before it lands. That is not proof you were never taught. It is what learning looks like in creatures like us — and Peter is the one who tells us he had been told all along.

8.title: Who Do You Say That I Am?
8.text: <sup>1</sup>In those days, when again a great crowd had gathered, and they had nothing to eat, he called his disciples to him and said to them, <sup>2</sup>“I have compassion on the crowd, because they have been with me now three days and have nothing to eat. <sup>3</sup>And if I send them away hungry to their homes, they will faint on the way. And some of them have come from far away.” <sup>4</sup>And his disciples answered him, “How can one feed these people with bread here in this desolate place?” <sup>5</sup>And he asked them, “How many loaves do you have?” They said, “Seven.” <sup>6</sup>And he directed the crowd to sit down on the ground. And he took the seven loaves, and having given thanks, he broke them and gave them to his disciples to set before the people; and they set them before the crowd. <sup>7</sup>And they had a few small fish. And having blessed them, he said that these also should be set before them. <sup>8</sup>And they ate and were satisfied. And they took up the broken pieces left over, seven baskets full. <sup>9</sup>And there were about four thousand people. And he sent them away. <sup>10</sup>And immediately he got into the boat with his disciples and went to the district of Dalmanutha. <sup>11</sup>The Pharisees came and began to argue with him, seeking from him a sign from heaven to test him. <sup>12</sup>And he sighed deeply in his spirit and said, “Why does this generation seek a sign? Truly, I say to you, no sign will be given to this generation.” <sup>13</sup>And he left them, got into the boat again, and went to the other side. <sup>14</sup>Now they had forgotten to bring bread, and they had only one loaf with them in the boat. <sup>15</sup>And he cautioned them, saying, “Watch out; beware of the leaven of the Pharisees and the leaven of Herod.” <sup>16</sup>And they began discussing with one another the fact that they had no bread. <sup>17</sup>And Jesus, aware of this, said to them, “Why are you discussing the fact that you have no bread? Do you not yet perceive or understand? Are your hearts hardened? <sup>18</sup>Having eyes do you not see, and having ears do you not hear? And do you not remember? <sup>19</sup>When I broke the five loaves for the five thousand, how many baskets full of broken pieces did you take up?” They said to him, “Twelve.” <sup>20</sup>“And the seven for the four thousand, how many baskets full of broken pieces did you take up?” And they said to him, “Seven.” <sup>21</sup>And he said to them, “Do you not yet understand?” <sup>22</sup>And they came to Bethsaida. And some people brought to him a blind man and begged him to touch him. <sup>23</sup>And he took the blind man by the hand and led him out of the village, and when he had spit on his eyes and laid his hands on him, he asked him, “Do you see anything?” <sup>24</sup>And he looked up and said, “I see people, but they look like trees, walking.” <sup>25</sup>Then Jesus laid his hands on his eyes again; and he opened his eyes, his sight was restored, and he saw everything clearly. <sup>26</sup>And he sent him to his home, saying, “Do not even enter the village.” <sup>27</sup>And Jesus went on with his disciples to the villages of Caesarea Philippi. And on the way he asked his disciples, “Who do people say that I am?” <sup>28</sup>And they told him, “John the Baptist; and others say, Elijah; and others, one of the prophets.” <sup>29</sup>And he asked them, “But who do you say that I am?” Peter answered him, “You are the Christ.” <sup>30</sup>And he strictly charged them to tell no one about him. <sup>31</sup>And he began to teach them that the Son of Man must suffer many things and be rejected by the elders and the chief priests and the scribes and be killed, and after three days rise again. <sup>32</sup>And he said this plainly. And Peter took him aside and began to rebuke him. <sup>33</sup>But turning and seeing his disciples, he rebuked Peter and said, “Get behind me, Satan! For you are not setting your mind on the things of God, but on the things of man.” <sup>34</sup>And calling the crowd to him with his disciples, he said to them, “If anyone would come after me, let him deny himself and take up his cross and follow me. <sup>35</sup>For whoever would save his life will lose it, but whoever loses his life for my sake and the gospel’s will save it. <sup>36</sup>For what does it profit a man to gain the whole world and forfeit his soul? <sup>37</sup>For what can a man give in return for his soul? <sup>38</sup>For whoever is ashamed of me and of my words in this adulterous and sinful generation, of him will the Son of Man also be ashamed when he comes in the glory of his Father with the holy angels.”
8.overview:
Chapter 8 is the hinge of Mark, and everything in the book turns on it. The first half asks who Jesus is; the second half walks to Jerusalem to die.

It is built around sight. Four thousand Gentiles are fed on a hillside and the disciples learn nothing from it. The Pharisees, days after a district was fed from seven loaves, ask for a sign — and he groans, refuses flatly, and gets back in the boat. Then twelve men who have twice carried the surplus away in baskets sit worrying about having one loaf between them, and Jesus asks eight questions in five verses, ending with do you not yet understand?

So Mark puts a blind man next, and has him healed in two stages — the only such healing in the Gospels. I see people, but they look like trees, walking. Not blind. Genuinely seeing. Seeing wrong shapes. It is a picture of exactly what happens next.

At Caesarea Philippi — beneath a cliff of pagan shrines, in a city named for Caesar — Peter gets it right: You are the Christ. And immediately Jesus begins to teach that the Son of Man must suffer, be rejected, be killed, and rise, and Mark notes that he said it plainly, the first plain speech in the book. Peter takes him aside to correct him and is called Satan. Then the crowd is called over and told the terms: deny yourself, take up your cross, follow me.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–21 — Four Thousand Fed, a Sign Refused, and the Leaven
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The second hillside (vv. 1–10). A crowd of four thousand has been with him three days in an empty place, and some of them have a long walk home. Seven loaves, a few small fish, and seven hampers of scraps at the end. It is not a retelling of chapter 6 — Jesus himself will insist on the difference in verse 19.

The demand (vv. 11–13). The Pharisees arrive and ask for a sign from heaven, days after a hillside was fed from a basket. He groans, refuses flatly, gets back in the boat and leaves them.

The boat (vv. 14–21). A warning about leaven is heard as a comment about catering, and Jesus asks eight questions in five verses. The list of what they have seen is read back to them, with the numbers, and it changes nothing.

Everything in this half of the chapter is about seeing — a crowd fed and not understood, a sign demanded by men who have had a hundred, and twelve men in a boat with the bread-maker, worrying about bread. Which is exactly why the next thing Mark records is a man who could not see at all.
verseByVerse.theology:
Are the two feedings one story told twice? It is the standard suggestion, and Mark closes it off himself. In vv. 19–20 Jesus makes the disciples recite both, with the figures — five loaves and five thousand and twelve baskets; seven loaves and four thousand and seven baskets — as two separate events they were present at.

The settings differ too. The five thousand were Jews on the green grass of Galilee, seated in ranks of hundreds and fifties like Israel in the wilderness, with twelve baskets over. The four thousand are in the Decapolis, on Gentile ground, with seven — and some of them have come from far away, which is how the Old Testament speaks of the nations (Isa. 60:4; Josh. 9:6). Twelve is the number of the tribes. Seven is the number of fullness. He fed Israel and had a basket for every tribe; he fed the nations and there was more than enough.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: twelve men in a boat, worrying about having one loaf between them, having twice watched thousands fed out of nothing.

Now: exactly the same, and the comedy of it is uncomfortable rather than funny. We have documented evidence of God's provision — the job that came, the diagnosis that was not what we feared, the money that arrived, the marriage that held — and the next shortage finds us doing arithmetic as though none of it had happened.

Note where Jesus locates the failure. Not in their circumstances and not even in their fear. Do you not remember? The problem is memory. They had the facts; they had carried the baskets themselves; and the facts had not been converted into knowledge of the Person who supplied them.

So the practical remedy is unglamorous and it works. Keep a record. Write down what God has actually done, with dates, so that the next crisis meets a list rather than a mood. The disciples could still produce the numbers when they were asked — twelve, seven — and had drawn nothing from them. Israel was commanded to build cairns of stones in the Jordan so that children would ask what they meant (Josh. 4:6–7). We are people who forget, and God has never treated that as a small problem.

verseByVerse.quote: In those days, when again a great crowd had gathered, and they had nothing to eat, he called his disciples to him and said to them, "I have compassion on the crowd, because they have been with me now three days and have nothing to eat. And if I send them away hungry to their homes, they will faint on the way. And some of them have come from far away."
verseByVerse.commentary:
In those days a great crowd had gathered again, and they had nothing to eat. Jesus called his disciples and said: I have compassion on the crowd, because they have been with me three days now and have nothing to eat. If I send them home hungry, they will collapse on the way, and some of them have come a long way.

Meaning first. Mark 8 is the hinge of the Gospel. It opens in Gentile country, where Jesus has compassion on a crowd that has been with him three days and feeds four thousand from seven loaves. Back on the Jewish side, the Pharisees demand a sign from heaven and he refuses, warning his disciples against the leaven of the Pharisees and of Herod; but the disciples, worried about having one loaf, have still not understood the loaves, and he presses them with question after question: do you not yet understand? Then at Bethsaida he heals a blind man in two stages, a picture of the disciples’ half-sight. At Caesarea Philippi, among pagan shrines, Peter confesses, You are the Christ, and for the first time Jesus tells them plainly that the Son of Man must suffer, be killed and rise again. Peter rebukes him and is rebuked in turn: Get behind me, Satan. And Jesus calls everyone who would follow him to deny himself, take up his cross and follow, because whoever loses his life for Christ and the gospel will save it. The whole chapter turns on one question: who is Jesus, and what kind of Christ is he?

Setting. Jesus is still in the Decapolis, on the eastern, largely Gentile side of the lake (7:31). The feeding of the five thousand (6:30–44) was on the Jewish side. Chapter 7 has taken Jesus on a long loop through pagan country, and there is nothing in this account to bring him home. Now, having declared all foods clean (7:19) and given the crumbs to a Gentile woman (7:28), he feeds a Gentile crowd. The children were fed first; now the bread is given to the others too, and not as crumbs.

In those days, when again a great crowd had gathered. The word again is Mark’s own signal that we have been somewhere like this before, and he expects the reader to remember it. The man freed from Legion and the healed deaf man had spread the news in this region (5:20; 7:36). The crowd is the fruit.

I have compassion on the crowd. He speaks first, before anybody asks. “Compassion” (splanchnizomai) is a gut-deep word: moved in the inner parts. At the first feeding, Jesus had compassion because they were like sheep without a shepherd (6:34); here the compassion is for their hunger. He cares for bodies as well as souls. And it is the same compassion as before. This is not a policy. It is what happens inside him when he looks at people.

Because they have been with me now three days. Take that in, because it changes the picture entirely. These people have not come out for an afternoon. They have stayed in a desolate place for three days, sleeping rough, listening to a Jewish teacher whose language and religion were not their own, long enough for any food they brought to run out. Their hunger for his word was greater than their concern for their stomachs. And he has noticed. In the middle of teaching thousands of people, he has been keeping track of how long they have been there and what they have had to eat.

They will faint on the way. Jesus anticipates their need before anyone asks. At the first feeding, the disciples raised the problem (6:35); here Jesus does. And watch what he is actually thinking about. Not the sermon, not the crowd’s response, but the walk home: people going light-headed on a hot road with miles still to go, and children, and the old. He is picturing it.

And some of them have come from far away. A clause almost everybody reads past, and it is doing two things at once. At the plain level it is pure pastoral care: some of these people have the furthest to travel, and he has taken that into account. He is not calculating an average; he is thinking about the ones with the longest road. And underneath it, for a reader with the Old Testament open, “from far away” (apo makrothen) is the phrase the Old Testament and the apostles use for the Gentiles: those who were far off (Joshua 9:6; Isaiah 60:4; Acts 2:39; Ephesians 2:13, 17). You who once were far off have been brought near by the blood of Christ. Mark’s first readers may well have heard it that way. So the sentence works in both directions. He is worried about their legs, and Mark is telling you who they are.

Where Christians differ: one feeding or two? Some critical scholars argue that the feedings of the five thousand and the four thousand are two versions of one event. Verdict: Mark and Matthew record both, and Jesus himself refers to both separately, with different numbers and different baskets (vv. 19–20). The differences in place, crowd, numbers, loaves, baskets and timing are real. There were two feedings.

Does Jesus care about my body, or only my soul? Both, and this verse proves it. He had spent three days feeding their souls with his word, and then he would not send them home hungry. God made us bodies and souls together, and he will raise our bodies at the last (1 Corinthians 15:42–44). So you may pray about food, rent, health and sleep without embarrassment; your Father knows you need these things (Matthew 6:32). And Christians should care for the bodily needs of others too, not as a substitute for the gospel but alongside it, as Jesus did (James 2:15–16).

In a sentence. In Gentile territory, Jesus had compassion on a crowd that had stayed with him three days without food, some from far away.

On a Tuesday. Jesus notices needs before they are spoken. Bring him yours, and notice the needs of others before they ask. Who in your church or street has a long road home: the elderly widow, the family under strain, the newcomer from far away? Think what it would take for them not to faint on the way, and do one part of it.

For worship. If you are a Gentile reading this, and most of us are, take it personally. The first thing recorded of Jesus on the day the nations were fed is that he had noticed how far they had come and did not want them to collapse on the way home. He is the Lord who counts the days his people have waited, who knows the length of every road, and who brings near those who were far off. His compassion is not a policy but a heart, and it beats for the ones at the back of the crowd.
verseByVerse.note: This crowd, in the Decapolis, was probably largely Gentile.

verseByVerse.quote: And his disciples answered him, "How can one feed these people with bread here in this desolate place?" And he asked them, "How many loaves do you have?" They said, "Seven."
verseByVerse.commentary:
His disciples answered: how can anyone feed these people with bread here in this desolate place? He asked them: how many loaves do you have? They said: seven.

How can one feed these people with bread here in this desolate place? It is the same objection as in chapter 6, and it is worse this time, because last time they had not seen it done. An astonishing question, after the five thousand. They had seen him do exactly this, perhaps only weeks before, and had gathered twelve baskets of leftovers. Yet they react as if it had never happened. This is the point Jesus will press in verses 17–21: they did not understand about the loaves (6:52). Their forgetfulness is ours. Each new difficulty can make us forget all God has already done.

The shape of the sentence. Do not rush to enjoy their failure. Look first at the exact shape of the sentence, because it is remarkably familiar. How can one feed these people? The question is impersonal, and that is its trouble. Not how can you feed them, which would at least have put the problem where it belonged. They are surveying a situation and reporting that the resources are inadequate, and they are entirely right, and the Person standing beside them does not appear in the calculation at all.

Desolate place. Erēmia, a wilderness. The setting recalls Israel in the wilderness, where God fed his people with manna. And it is a very old sentence. When Israel wanted meat in the wilderness, Moses said to the LORD, Where am I to get meat to give to all this people? (Numbers 11:13), and asked the same despairing question: Shall flocks and herds be slaughtered for them, and be enough for them? (Numbers 11:22). And God answered him with a question that could be printed over this whole chapter: Is the LORD’s hand shortened? Now you shall see whether my word will come true for you or not (Numbers 11:23). So the disciples are standing in a wilderness, in front of a hungry multitude, saying what Moses said. Mark’s readers were meant to hear it.

How many loaves do you have? The same question as before (6:38), and the same method. Jesus begins with what they have. He does not argue with their arithmetic and he does not lecture them about faith. He asks what is actually in their hands. He does not create from nothing here, but multiplies what is offered. That is worth taking as a habit, because it is the practical antidote to being overwhelmed. The mind, faced with something too big, produces a paralysing survey of the gap. He turns it round: never mind the gap, what have you got? Count it. Bring it.

Seven. More than the five loaves of the first feeding, for fewer people. Some see symbolism (seven as the number of completeness, or of the nations: the seven nations of Canaan, or the seventy nations of Genesis 10). Mark does not draw it out, but Jesus does make the numbers count (vv. 19–21). And notice what is missing from the exchange. Nobody says: Lord, last time you did this with five. Nobody looks up. They produce the number the way a man produces a stock figure, and wait. They are not being obstructive; they are being ordinary. And that is precisely what Mark wants you to see, because the whole first half of this chapter is about people who have all the evidence and none of the sight, and it is about to end with a man who cannot see at all being led out of a village by the hand.

Is it a lack of faith to feel overwhelmed? Not in itself. Feeling the size of a need honestly is not unbelief; Moses felt it, and so did Paul (2 Corinthians 1:8–9). The fault comes when we leave Christ out of the sum, as though the problem and our resources were all there is. So when you are overwhelmed, say so to God plainly, as the psalmists do. Then do the two things Jesus asks here: look at what you actually have, and bring it to him. Feelings may lag behind faith for a while. Faith is not the absence of the feeling but the decision to count him in.

In a sentence. The disciples, forgetting the five thousand, asked how anyone could feed such a crowd in the wilderness; Jesus asked what they had, and they had seven loaves.

On a Tuesday. Remember what God has done for you before. Yesterday’s faithfulness is the answer to today’s how can? When you next catch yourself saying, how can this possibly work out, finish the sentence with a specific memory of a time God provided, and then bring what you have to him.

For worship. The LORD’s hand is not shortened. He fed Israel in the wilderness, he fed five thousand on a Galilean hillside, and here he spreads a table for Gentiles in a desolate place. Our forgetfulness does not exhaust his faithfulness; he asks the same patient question again, how many loaves do you have, and starts once more from the little in our hands. Blessed be the God who answers our impersonal despair with his personal care.

parallels.desc: Moses asks how so many can be fed

verseByVerse.quote: And he directed the crowd to sit down on the ground. And he took the seven loaves, and having given thanks, he broke them and gave them to his disciples to set before the people; and they set them before the crowd. And they had a few small fish. And having blessed them, he said that these also should be set before them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
He told the crowd to sit down on the ground. He took the seven loaves, gave thanks, broke them and gave them to his disciples to set before the people, and they served the crowd. They also had a few small fish; he blessed them and told them to serve these too.

And he directed the crowd to sit down on the ground. No green grass this time (6:39). It is a later season, or a drier place. A small difference from chapter 6, and Mark, drawing on Peter’s memory, keeps it. Different place, different season, different crowd. And there is no seating in ranks of hundreds and fifties this time. That arrangement was Israel in the wilderness, drawn up as Moses drew them up. These are Gentiles, and Mark does not impose the pattern on them.

And having given thanks. Eucharistēsas, from which comes Eucharist. At the first feeding Mark used blessed (6:41), the Jewish form; here gave thanks, the word that Paul uses for the Lord’s Supper (1 Corinthians 11:24). The two words mean the same thing: a Jewish blessing before meals was thanks to God. Mark uses both of the same action, which is its own small lesson: the thing being described is not a formula but a man thanking his Father for food that is plainly not enough. Jesus thanks the Father for the little there is.

He broke them and gave them to his disciples to set before the people. The same sequence as before (6:41) and at the Last Supper (14:22): took, gave thanks, broke, gave. By now the reader of this Gospel should be feeling the shape of those verbs. They will be done once more in an upstairs room in Jerusalem, over bread that he will call his body. The disciples are the servers, distributing what comes from his hands, as ministers of the gospel do. And Mark is emphatic about the mechanism; he says it twice in one verse. He gives it to the disciples; the disciples give it to the crowd. The multiplication happens in their hands, out among the people, exactly as it did before. These are the men who have just said it could not be done, and they are the ones who will find out that it can, by carrying it.

You settle it on the fourth row. That is how he has always worked with his church. He does not usually rain provision directly onto the people who need it; he gives it to ordinary and unconvinced servants to distribute, and the sufficiency is discovered in the distributing. You will never settle the question of whether there is enough by standing at the front doing sums. You settle it on the fourth row.

And they had a few small fish. Ichthydia, little fish, probably dried or salted. Mark handles the fish as an afterthought, almost apologetically: a few small fish, dealt with in a separate sentence. It is a very human detail. Somebody remembered, halfway through, that there were also some fish. Nobody composing a legend includes that.

And having blessed them. A separate blessing for the fish. And it says something quietly about him. He blesses the few small fish too. The scraps are not beneath his notice, and nothing brought to him is handled carelessly, which is the same care that will send men out afterwards to pick up the broken pieces so that nothing is lost.

What it does not mean. The feeding is not itself the Lord’s Supper, though the words point towards it. It is a real meal, for hungry people, that also shows who Jesus is: the one who provides bread from heaven.

What then happens at the Lord’s Supper? The bread and wine do not change into Christ’s body and blood, and Christ is not sacrificed again (Hebrews 10:10–14). But the Supper is far more than a bare reminder. Believers who receive it in faith feed on Christ spiritually, receiving and being nourished by all the benefits of his death, as truly as the crowd was fed on that hillside (1 Corinthians 10:16; 1689 London Baptist Confession 30.7). So come to the Table as hungry people come to a meal: not because you are worthy, but because you need him, and because he gives himself to those who trust him.

In a sentence. Jesus seated the crowd, gave thanks for the loaves and the few fish, broke them, and gave them to his disciples to distribute.

On a Tuesday. Give thanks before you eat, as Jesus did, even when you have little. Thanksgiving is the beginning of every gift being multiplied. And if Christ has put something into your hands to pass on, a class to teach, a family to feed, a friend to help, do not wait until you are sure there is enough. Start handing it out.

For worship. Here is the Son giving thanks to the Father over seven loaves in a desolate place, and then giving with both hands until thousands are fed. He took, gave thanks, broke and gave, and one night in Jerusalem he would do it again over bread that was his own body, given for us. He is the host of the nations’ table, and he does not despise the few small fish. Every gift offered to him is blessed, and every hungry soul who comes to him is filled.

verseByVerse.quote: And they ate and were satisfied. And they took up the broken pieces left over, seven baskets full. And there were about four thousand people. And he sent them away. And immediately he got into the boat with his disciples and went to the district of Dalmanutha.
verseByVerse.commentary:
They ate and were satisfied, and they took up the leftover pieces, seven baskets full. There were about four thousand people. He sent them away, and immediately got into the boat with his disciples and went to the district of Dalmanutha.

And they ate and were satisfied. Everyone, fully. The same emphatic word as in chapter 6 (6:42): filled, fed to the point of stopping. Not a token, not a taste. Four thousand people ate until they had had enough. God’s provision is not a token; it fills.

Seven baskets full. Twelve baskets last time, seven now, from seven loaves rather than five, for four thousand rather than five. And the basket here (spyris) is different from the one at the feeding of the five thousand (kophinos, a small wicker basket a Jew might carry). The spyris could be large: Paul was lowered from the wall of Damascus in one (Acts 9:25). Fewer baskets this time, but perhaps more bread. Jesus himself will remind the disciples of the distinction (vv. 19–20), keeping every figure of each event apart. That is not the behaviour of a story told twice and mistakenly recorded as two. Mark has two events because there were two.

Twelve and seven. The numbers may well be doing work. Twelve is the number of the tribes: he fed Israel and there was a basket for every tribe. Seven is the Bible’s number for fullness and completion: the days of the week, the finished creation. He has fed the nations, and there was more than enough.

And there were about four thousand people. Given last, as before, almost as a footnote. Matthew adds: besides women and children (Matthew 15:38).

And he sent them away. Unlike the first feeding, there is no attempt to make him king (John 6:15). These are Gentiles, without the Jewish political hopes of a Messiah.

The district of Dalmanutha. An unknown place, mentioned nowhere else in ancient literature, and copyists were already substituting more familiar places for it. Matthew has Magadan (Matthew 15:39), also unknown, though some manuscripts there read Magdala, the home of Mary Magdalene on the western shore. It must have been somewhere on the western, Jewish side of the lake, because the Pharisees meet him there (v. 11). Which is, in its own way, a small argument for the account: an inventor puts his story somewhere the reader has heard of. What matters is the direction. He is crossing back to the Jewish side of the lake, having fed the Gentiles on the far shore, and the first thing waiting for him at home is a delegation asking him to prove himself.

Should we look for hidden meanings in the Bible’s numbers? Cautiously. Some numbers clearly carry meaning in Scripture: twelve for the tribes and apostles, seven for completeness, forty for testing. But the Bible never asks us to build doctrines on number codes, and readers who do so usually end up reading their own ideas into the text. Take a number’s meaning where Scripture itself makes it plain, hold suggested meanings lightly, and keep your eyes on the main point the passage makes. Here the main point is unmistakable: Jesus gave more than enough, to Israel and to the nations.

In a sentence. Four thousand people ate their fill from seven loaves, with seven large baskets left over, and Jesus crossed back to the Jewish side of the lake.

On a Tuesday. Christ gives more than enough. Whatever you lack, he is not short of supply. Name one need you are carrying today, and tell him plainly that you trust him to be enough for it, whatever form his answer takes.

For worship. There is always something left over with Christ. Twelve baskets for Israel, seven for the nations, and still the supply is not exhausted. He fills the hungry with good things (Luke 1:53), and he has bread enough for every tribe and every people. The table he spread in the Decapolis is a foretaste of the feast at the end of the age, when people will come from east and west and north and south and recline in the kingdom of God (Luke 13:29).
verseByVerse.note: The word for these baskets differs from the one used at the feeding of the five thousand and could mean a large hamper. Dalmanutha’s location is unknown; Matthew says Magadan.

parallels.desc: Paul let down in such a basket

verseByVerse.quote: The Pharisees came and began to argue with him, seeking from him a sign from heaven to test him. And he sighed deeply in his spirit and said, "Why does this generation seek a sign? Truly, I say to you, no sign will be given to this generation." And he left them, got into the boat again, and went to the other side.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Pharisees came and began to argue with him, demanding a sign from heaven, to test him. He sighed deeply in his spirit and said: why does this generation seek a sign? Truly, I tell you, no sign will be given to this generation. And he left them, got into the boat again and went to the other side.

The contrast. Gentiles have just been fed by a miracle. Now, back on the Jewish side, the religious leaders demand a sign. They had heard of the healings, the exorcisms, the feedings. It was not evidence they lacked. The boat has barely touched the shore. He has been away in Gentile country for weeks, and this is the reception committee.

Seeking from him a sign from heaven. Note the phrase, because it is a specific request. A sign from heaven meant a spectacular proof directly from God, beyond any possibility of doubt: fire from the sky like Elijah on Carmel, or the sun standing still like Joshua, or manna like Moses, or thunder in the wheat harvest like Samuel. They are not asking whether he can heal; that has been settled for chapters. Exorcisms could be explained away as Satan’s work (3:22). They wanted something undeniable, on their terms.

To test him. Peirazontes, the same word used of Satan testing him in the wilderness (1:13). Mark tells us the motive and does not leave it for us to infer. The demand was not sincere inquiry but a trap. If he refused, they could say he had no credentials; if he tried and failed, he was discredited. It is an examination set by men who have already marked the paper. And consider the timing. Somewhere behind him on the eastern shore, four thousand people are walking home fed. Before that, five thousand. Before that, a leper, a paralytic, a withered hand, a legion, a dead girl, a hurricane. They want a sign.

And he sighed deeply in his spirit. A stronger word than the sigh of 7:34 (anastenaxas), a groan from the depths; the intensified form occurs nowhere else in the New Testament. So the same sound is drawn out of him twice, and the two occasions are worth putting side by side. He groans over a body that cannot hear. And he groans over men who will not see. The second one is deeper. This is not irritation. It is grief and indignation at their hardness, and it comes up from somewhere.

Why does this generation seek a sign? This generation in the Gospels is a phrase loaded with Old Testament echoes: the wilderness generation that saw God’s works for forty years and still tested him (Psalm 95:8–10; Deuteronomy 32:5, 20). The Pharisees are repeating Israel’s ancient sin.

Truly, I say to you, no sign will be given to this generation. The Greek uses a Hebrew oath form: literally, if a sign shall be given, with the unspoken ending, may God punish me. It is the most emphatic refusal he ever makes. Matthew adds: except the sign of Jonah (Matthew 12:39; 16:4), meaning his resurrection, three days and three nights in the heart of the earth (Matthew 12:40). There is no contradiction. Mark records the flat refusal: no sign of the kind they demand, no proof on request. The one sign he will give is his death and resurrection, and Mark is about to have Jesus announce it plainly (v. 31).

What it does not mean. Not that Jesus gave no evidence. His whole ministry was full of signs. But he would not perform to order for those who had already decided against him. What he refuses is a miracle produced on demand as a condition of belief, because faith manufactured that way is not faith at all but a calculated response to a demonstration. Signs confirm faith; they do not compel the unwilling. If they do not hear Moses and the Prophets, neither will they be convinced if someone should rise from the dead (Luke 16:31). Which turned out to be exactly right. Somebody did rise from the dead, and the men who had the report first paid soldiers to say the body was stolen (Matthew 28:12–15).

The problem was never the evidence. If you have ever wished God would do something undeniable, settle it once and for all, in the sky, where nobody could argue, this passage is a kindness, though it does not feel like one. The problem was never the quantity of evidence. Every one of the men in this conversation had watched things that could not be explained, and it moved them not an inch, because the trouble was never in their eyes.

And he left them. A solemn act of judgment. He turned his back, got into the boat again, and went to the other side. He does not argue. He does not stay to win. It is the third time in this Gospel he has walked away from people who did not want him: the Gerasene town that asked him to leave (5:17), the Nazareth synagogue (6:6), and now the Pharisees at Dalmanutha. He never forces himself on anybody, and there is no more frightening fact about him than that.

Is it wrong to ask God for a sign? It depends on what you are asking and why. It is never wrong to ask God for wisdom (James 1:5), or to pray for him to make his will clear and to act. But demanding a miracle before you will believe or obey what he has already said is testing God, and that is what Jesus refuses here. God has given us his complete and sufficient word in Scripture (2 Timothy 3:16–17), and the great sign of the risen Christ. When you face a decision, search the Scriptures, pray, seek wise counsel, and then act in faith. Do not wait for fleeces and coincidences to do the work that obedience to his written word should do.

In a sentence. When the Pharisees demanded a sign from heaven to test him, Jesus, groaning in spirit, refused outright and left them.

On a Tuesday. Do not demand that God prove himself on your terms. He has given enough evidence in Christ, crucified and risen. If there is something you are refusing to obey until God gives you one more sign, recognise that for what it is, and obey what he has already said.

For worship. The Lord of glory will not be put on trial by his creatures. He groans over hardness, he refuses to perform, and he walks away from those who will not have him, and all of that is the dignity of the true God. Yet he gave the one sign that matters: the Son of Man three days in the heart of the earth and then risen. The resurrection is God’s sign from heaven, written not in the sky but in an empty tomb, and it is enough for every heart he opens.

verseByVerse.quote: Now they had forgotten to bring bread, and they had only one loaf with them in the boat. And he cautioned them, saying, "Watch out; beware of the leaven of the Pharisees and the leaven of Herod." And they began discussing with one another the fact that they had no bread.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The disciples had forgotten to bring bread and had only one loaf with them in the boat. Jesus warned them: watch out; beware of the leaven of the Pharisees and the leaven of Herod. And they began discussing with one another that they had no bread.

Now they had forgotten to bring bread. After the seven basketfuls! In the hurry to leave, the leftovers were left behind. Mark’s detail is precise and slightly comic, and he sets it up deliberately. They pushed off in a hurry and nobody did the shopping.

And they had only one loaf with them in the boat. A detail only Mark records. One loaf and thirteen men. Hold on to that phrase, because Mark has placed it with great care. There is one loaf in that boat, and the disciples are worried about it. There is also one Person in that boat who has twice in recent weeks fed a multitude out of a basket. Some see a deeper meaning: the one loaf they did have was Jesus himself, the bread of life (John 6:35). Mark does not say so, but the conversation that follows suggests he expects readers to think it: they were worried about bread with the Lord of the loaves in the boat.

Watch out; beware. Two words of warning together, for emphasis, both about vigilance. The tense means: keep on watching. And then a metaphor which they are about to get spectacularly wrong.

The leaven of the Pharisees. Leaven in that world was not a sachet of yeast. It was a piece of old fermented dough kept back to start the next batch, going sour, worked into the new lump, and it works invisibly through the whole lump (1 Corinthians 5:6–8; Galatians 5:9). A little leaven leavens the whole lump: the point of the image everywhere in Scripture is that a very small quantity changes the whole mass, silently, from inside. In Scripture it nearly always pictures a corrupting influence. Luke says the leaven of the Pharisees is hypocrisy (Luke 12:1); Matthew, their teaching (Matthew 16:12). In context, it is their unbelief that demanded signs while refusing to see the ones in front of them. He has just walked away from them, and their disease is fresh in the mind: the demand for evidence from men who have all the evidence they will ever get. It is unbelief dressed as rigour, the settled habit of a mind that keeps asking for one more proof because it has no intention of yielding to any.

And the leaven of Herod. Herod Antipas, ruler of Galilee, who had killed John the Baptist (6:14–29). Mark has given us sixteen verses on Herod so that we will know exactly what this means. Herod feared John, knew he was righteous, protected him, heard him gladly, and killed him because of his oaths and his guests. His leaven was worldliness, political scheming, and the same unbelief: he wanted to see Jesus do a miracle too (Luke 23:8). That leaven is the accommodation of power: religion kept as an interest, and conscience overruled every time it collides with what the room expects. The Pharisees and Herod’s supporters had already plotted together to destroy Jesus (3:6). Religious hypocrisy and worldly power are different leavens, with the same effect: hardness towards Jesus.

Two ways to be lost. Set the two side by side and they cover most of the ways a person is lost. One is too clever to believe. The other believes well enough and will not pay. And Jesus warns his own disciples about both, which means neither is a danger only to outsiders.

And they began discussing with one another the fact that they had no bread. They missed the point entirely. Jesus speaks of spiritual danger; they think he is scolding them for forgetting lunch. You can imagine the muttering: he is talking about bread because somebody was supposed to bring bread. They have taken the deepest warning of the chapter and turned it into a domestic grievance. Before that is laughed at, notice how easily it is done. It is entirely possible to sit under a sermon that names the thing quietly killing you, and to spend the drive home discussing the length of the service, the temperature of the building, or whether that illustration was quite fair. The mind will reach for the manageable subject every time, and the smaller subject is always the more comfortable one.

How do I watch out for leaven in my own life? Look for the small, quiet influences rather than the obvious ones. Notice what you are absorbing day by day: the cynicism of the commentators you follow, the habit of asking for one more reason before you obey, the instinct to keep faith as a private interest that never costs you at work or with friends. Ask a trusted Christian friend where they see these things in you. Feed on Scripture daily, because a heart full of God’s word has less room for the old dough (Colossians 3:16). And when a warning lands in a sermon, resist the urge to change the subject; stay with it and ask what it means for you.

In a sentence. With only one loaf in the boat, Jesus warned his disciples against the corrupting influence of the Pharisees and Herod, but they thought only of their bread.

On a Tuesday. Watch for the small influences that slowly spread through a life: cynicism, hypocrisy, the worldly mind. They work like yeast, unseen. Choose one influence in your week, a feed, a programme, a friendship, a habit of thought, and ask honestly which way it is working in you.

For worship. The Lord who warns us is the Lord who loves us. He sees the leaven before we notice the dough rising, and he speaks while there is still time. He is himself the one loaf in the boat, the bread of life, unleavened by any sin, broken for us so that we might be a new lump (1 Corinthians 5:7). Christ our Passover lamb has been sacrificed, and with him in the boat no disciple of his will starve.
verseByVerse.note: Leaven (yeast) works invisibly through a whole lump; it pictures a corrupting influence. Herod stands for worldly power and its politics.

verseByVerse.quote: And Jesus, aware of this, said to them, "Why are you discussing the fact that you have no bread? Do you not yet perceive or understand? Are your hearts hardened? Having eyes do you not see, and having ears do you not hear? And do you not remember?
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus knew what they were saying and said: why are you discussing having no bread? Do you not yet perceive or understand? Are your hearts hardened? Having eyes, do you not see, and having ears, do you not hear? And do you not remember?

And Jesus, aware of this. He is not told. Mark keeps quietly noting that he knows what is going on inside people (2:8), and this time it is his own men.

Five questions. Jesus presses them with a rapid series of rebukes, the sharpest he gives the disciples in Mark: question after question, one after another, with no pause for answers until the very end. Why are you discussing the fact that you have no bread? The first question simply holds the absurdity up. You are in a boat, with me, discussing a shortage of bread.

Do you not yet perceive or understand? “Yet”: after all they had seen. The word yet is the painful one. They have had more time with him than anyone, and still they miss it. It has been eight chapters. There has been a leper, a paralytic, a hurricane, a legion, a dead girl raised, five thousand fed, a man walking on water, four thousand fed. Yet.

Are your hearts hardened? The very charge made against the Pharisees (3:5), and the one Mark made about the disciples after the walking on the water (6:52). And here is the sentence that should stop any Christian reading comfortably. It is the third time Mark has used this word. In chapter 3 it described the men in the synagogue who watched a withered hand restored and went out to plot a murder. In chapter 6 it was said of the disciples. And now Jesus says it to their faces, as a question. A hardened heart is not just slow; it is resistant, insensitive to God’s work. The word is related to a callus: tissue that thickens at the point of injury until it can no longer feel. It is not disbelief; these men believed a great deal, had left everything, and had just been out casting out demons in his name. It is the loss of the capacity to be affected. A hardened heart can carry the bread and never taste it. And it is put as a question rather than a verdict, which is the mercy in it. He is asking them to check. It is a sobering thing that Jesus asks this of his own chosen followers. Hardness is not only a problem for enemies.

Having eyes do you not see, and having ears do you not hear? The language of Jeremiah 5:21 and Ezekiel 12:2, about rebellious Israel, and of Isaiah 6:9–10, which Jesus quoted about outsiders (4:12). It lands like a slap. He is applying the outsiders’ text to the inner circle. The men who were given the secret of the kingdom are being described in the language of those who were not. The disciples were in danger of being like those outside. And the words point to the healings on either side: the deaf man (7:31–37) and the blind man (8:22–26). The disciples need the same miracle in their hearts.

Proximity is not immunity. That is the warning of this passage, and it is not for the world. It is for people who have been near Christ a long time. It is entirely possible to hold the correct doctrine, attend the right church, do genuine work in his name, and be steadily losing the ability to be moved by him, and the loss is undetectable from inside, which is why he has to ask.

And do you not remember? Memory is essential to faith. Israel was always told to remember what God had done (Deuteronomy 8:2–3), and failed. Forgetfulness of God’s past works leads to anxiety in the present. And with this question he turns the corner, because this one has an answer, and the answer is going to be their own. He does not tell them what they have forgotten. He is about to make them say it.

What it does not mean. Not that the disciples were reprobate. Jesus rebukes them because he loves them and is teaching them. Hardness in a believer is real and dangerous, but Christ does not abandon his own. Their eyes will be opened, slowly, like the blind man’s (vv. 22–26).

How do I know if my heart is hardening? Watch for the loss of feeling rather than the loss of belief. Signs include: Scripture that once moved you now passes without effect; you can hear about sin, including your own, without grief; prayer has become a formality; you are more irritated by sermons than searched by them; God’s past kindness to you no longer produces thanks. If you recognise these, do not despair, because the fact that you are concerned is itself a sign of life. Confess it honestly, return to the means of grace, and ask God to do what Ezekiel promised: to take away the heart of stone and give a heart of flesh (Ezekiel 36:26). Today, if you hear his voice, do not harden your hearts (Hebrews 3:7–8).

In a sentence. Jesus rebuked his disciples for their spiritual blindness, deafness, forgetfulness and hardened hearts, which left them anxious about bread.

On a Tuesday. When you worry about provision, ask: do I not remember? Make a list of God’s past faithfulness and read it. And ask a trusted friend whether they have noticed any hardening in you that you cannot see from the inside.

For worship. How tender are the rebukes of Christ. He fires question after question at slow disciples, not to drive them out of the boat but to wake them up. He knows the hardness of our hearts better than we do, and he does not leave it untouched. The Lord who opened deaf ears and blind eyes is the Lord who opens hardened hearts, and he will not give up on those the Father has given him (John 6:37–39).

verseByVerse.quote: When I broke the five loaves for the five thousand, how many baskets full of broken pieces did you take up?" They said to him, "Twelve." "And the seven for the four thousand, how many baskets full of broken pieces did you take up?" And they said to him, "Seven." And he said to them, "Do you not yet understand?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
When I broke the five loaves for the five thousand, how many baskets full of pieces did you take up? They said: twelve. And the seven for the four thousand, how many large baskets full? They said: seven. And he said to them: do you not yet understand?

A lesson in arithmetic. He does not preach at them. He examines them, and the examination consists of making them recite facts they already know. They know the numbers. They had been there and carried the baskets.

When I broke the five loaves for the five thousand, how many baskets full of broken pieces did you take up? They said to him, Twelve. Straight away. No hesitation. They have the number at their fingertips, because each of them carried one.

And the seven for the four thousand? And they said to him, Seven. Again, instantly. The data is intact. The filing system is perfect.

Twelve and seven. Jesus carefully uses the two different words for basket: kophinous for the twelve, spyridōn for the seven. He remembers precisely. And note in passing what this exchange does to the suggestion that the two feedings are one event told twice. Jesus makes them recite both, with different loaves, different crowds, different baskets, and the men in that boat were at both.

What should they have understood? At the least, that bread was no problem with Jesus in the boat. He could supply from one loaf, or none. Their worry was needless. But more: the feedings revealed who he is. He is the one who feeds his people in the wilderness, as God did with manna, the shepherd of Psalm 23 and Ezekiel 34, the giver of the messianic banquet (Isaiah 25:6). And with twelve baskets on the Jewish side and seven on the Gentile side, perhaps also that his bread was enough for Israel and the nations. Mark leaves the question open, so that the reader too must answer it.

Do you not yet understand? The last word of the scene, a question left hanging, and Mark records no answer. It is the question of the whole first half of Mark: who is this? The answer will come at Caesarea Philippi (v. 29), after the healing of the blind man.

They remembered everything and understood nothing. Now see exactly what he has proved, because it is not what we would expect and it is the most useful thing in the chapter. The facts were not missing. They could produce the figures on demand. The problem was not their information but what they made of it. What had never happened was the step from the figures to the Person: from twelve baskets to, therefore the man in this boat will not be defeated by a bread shortage. That is the disease, and it is extremely common among people who have been Christians for years. We are not usually short of information. Most of us could give an account of God’s dealings with us: the provision that came, the door that opened, the illness that turned, the year we could not have got through and did. And the next difficulty arrives and finds us exactly where the disciples were, doing sums in a boat.

Make yourself recite it. Take the remedy, which is plain and practical and is more or less what he does here. Not vaguely, but with numbers and dates, the way they answered him. Write down what God has actually done for you, and keep the list where you will see it when the next thing comes. That is not sentiment; it is a command running right through Scripture. Israel was told to pile twelve stones out of the Jordan so that when the children asked what they meant, the fathers would have to tell the story (Joshua 4:6–7). Bless the LORD, O my soul, and forget not all his benefits (Psalm 103:2) is a man giving orders to his own memory, because he knows it will not do it by itself.

He did not put them out of the boat. And notice what Jesus does not do at the end of this. He asks the question, gets no answer, and takes them on to Bethsaida, where the very next thing that happens is a blind man being led out of a village by the hand and given his sight in two stages. Mark has put that story exactly there on purpose.

Why does Jesus ask questions instead of simply telling them? Because understanding that is drawn out of us goes deeper than understanding that is handed to us. Jesus does this throughout the Gospels: who do you say that I am, what do you want me to do for you, do you love me. Questions make us look at what we already know and draw the conclusion ourselves. They also show us where our hearts are. When you read Scripture, notice the questions God asks and answer them honestly, aloud if it helps. They are not rhetorical. He is still asking.

In a sentence. Jesus made the disciples recite the leftovers from both feedings, and left them with the question: do you not yet understand who I am?

On a Tuesday. Knowing the facts of the gospel is not the same as understanding them. Ask God to show you what the facts mean for today. Take one thing you have known about Christ for years, that he provides, forgives, is with you, and ask what difference it should make to the particular worry in front of you now.

For worship. The Lord is a patient teacher. He feeds his people twice, asks them to count the baskets, and waits for the penny to drop. He does not despise slow learners; he leads them on to the next lesson, even if it is a blind man by the hand. He remembers every basket and every crumb, and he remembers us. The God who never forgets his people keeps asking until they remember him.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 22–38 — Two-Stage Sight and the Great Confession
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The blind man (vv. 22–26). The only healing in the Gospels that happens in two stages, and it is placed here on purpose. A man is led out of the village by the hand, sees people like walking trees, is touched again, and sees clearly. It is a picture of what is about to happen to the men in the boat.

The question (vv. 27–30). At Caesarea Philippi — at the foot of a mountain, beside a cave sacred to Pan, in a city named for Caesar — Jesus asks the question the whole Gospel has been building to, and Peter answers it: You are the Christ.

The correction (vv. 31–33). And immediately Jesus starts teaching them something they cannot bear: that the Son of Man must suffer, be rejected, be killed, and rise. Mark says he said it plainly — the first plain speech in the book. Peter takes him aside to put him right, and gets the hardest sentence any disciple ever heard.

The terms (vv. 34–38). Then he calls the crowd over, so that nobody can say the terms were for professionals only, and states them: deny yourself, take up your cross, follow me.

This is the hinge of the Gospel. Everything before it asks who he is. Everything after it walks to Jerusalem.
verseByVerse.theology:
Why two touches? Not because the first failed. Mark places this healing between the disciples who have eyes and do not see (v. 18) and Peter's half-sighted confession, and it is an enacted parable of exactly that. I see people, but they look like trees, walking is a precise description of where the Twelve now stand: no longer blind, genuinely seeing, and seeing wrong shapes. Peter will name him Christ in verse 29 and rebuke him in verse 32.

And why "after three days"? Mark writes after three days (v. 31; also 9:31; 10:34) where Matthew and Luke have on the third day, and honest readers have wondered whether that requires a fourth day and breaks the Friday-to-Sunday timeline. It does not; it is simply the Jewish way of counting, in which any part of a day counted as a whole day. Scripture proves it on the spot: the chief priests remember this very prediction as After three days I will rise, and in the same breath ask Pilate for a guard until the third day (Matt. 27:63–64) — both phrases, of one morning, without a flicker of contradiction.

And why "Get behind me, Satan"? Not because Peter was demonic. Because the content of his objection was the wilderness temptation returning through the mouth of a friend: a kingdom without a cross. Jesus had heard it before (1:13), and he will hear it again from passers-by at the foot of the cross itself — save yourself, and come down (15:30). Peter meant it lovingly, which is precisely what made it dangerous.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: a crowd in Galilee hearing the words take up his cross, in a country where Varus had crucified two thousand men within living memory. Nobody in that crowd thought of a metaphor. They had seen men carrying the crossbeam through the streets, stripped, jeered at, on a walk with one destination.

Now: we have worn the phrase smooth. A cross has become a difficulty — a hard marriage, an illness, a colleague. That is not what it meant. A man carrying a cross was not a man with a burden; he was a man already condemned, publicly, walking away from everything he had.

And note who is being addressed. Mark says he called the crowd — not just the Twelve. This is not a higher path for the heroic few. It is the entry requirement, stated to the general public, by a man who knew exactly what he was asking because he was going to do it first.

So make it concrete rather than admiring it in the abstract. Deny himself is not going without sugar; it is the removal of the self from the throne — the decision, in a specific matter this week, that what you want is no longer the deciding vote. Name the matter. If you cannot name one, the denial is theoretical.

verseByVerse.quote: And they came to Bethsaida. And some people brought to him a blind man and begged him to touch him. And he took the blind man by the hand and led him out of the village, and when he had spit on his eyes and laid his hands on him, he asked him, "Do you see anything?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
They came to Bethsaida. Some people brought a blind man to Jesus and begged him to touch him. He took the blind man by the hand and led him out of the village. When he had spat on his eyes and laid his hands on him, he asked: do you see anything?

The placing of the story. Mark has placed this healing, which only he records, at the hinge of his Gospel. Just before it, the disciples were told that they had eyes but did not see (v. 18). Just after it, Peter will confess Jesus as the Christ (v. 29), and yet will not understand what that means (v. 32). The blind man is a picture of the disciples. A matching healing of blind Bartimaeus closes the next section (10:46–52). Between the two blind men, Jesus teaches about the cross.

And they came to Bethsaida. A fishing town at the north end of the lake, where the Jordan flows in, home of Peter, Andrew and Philip (John 1:44). Jesus had pronounced woe on it for its unbelief despite his mighty works (Matthew 11:21), which gives the last verse of this little account its edge.

And some people brought to him a blind man and begged him to touch him. Again the pattern: the man is brought. He did not find his way here; somebody led him. It is the pattern of this Gospel that a person who could not get to Christ is carried by people who could: the paralytic through the roof, the deaf man in the Decapolis, the little girl’s father, and now this.

And he took the blind man by the hand and led him out of the village. Personal and gentle, and one of the tenderest sentences in Mark. A blind man needs a guide, and Jesus himself becomes his guide. The Lord of glory takes a blind man’s hand and walks him out of town. Not a word is recorded: just a man in the dark, holding on, going somewhere he cannot see, led by somebody he has never met. It takes as long as it takes; nobody hurries a blind man over rough ground. And Mark keeps this detail because it is the whole disposition of Christ towards people who cannot see: he does not shout instructions from a distance. He comes and takes the hand. As with the deaf man (7:33), he takes him away from the crowd that stares. At the hinge of the Gospel, the two great healings are done quietly, off to one side, for one man at a time.

And when he had spit on his eyes and laid his hands on him. Again, touch that the man could feel, telling him what Jesus was doing, since he could not see. The saliva again, as in chapter 7: widely regarded as having healing properties, so the gesture would have registered with the man as treatment. And there is nothing fastidious about it. He touches the man’s eyes with his own hands and his own saliva. This is a very physical Saviour.

Do you see anything? The only time in the Gospels that Jesus asks about the progress of a healing, and the reason people have always found this account difficult. He asks as though the outcome were not certain. He was not checking. Nothing in this Gospel suggests he ever needed a second attempt at anything; he had just fed four thousand people and silenced a hurricane with a word. He is doing something deliberate, and it prepares for what follows.

Does Jesus still lead people by the hand? Yes, though now by his word and Spirit rather than in the flesh. He promised: I will lead the blind in a way that they do not know, in paths that they have not known I will guide them (Isaiah 42:16). He is the Good Shepherd who goes before his sheep (John 10:4), and the Spirit guides his people into the truth (John 16:13). Often we do not see the road ahead, only the next step. That is not a sign he has let go. Hold on to him through Scripture, prayer and the counsel of his people, and trust that the hand holding yours knows where it is going.

In a sentence. At Bethsaida, Jesus led a blind man by the hand out of the village, touched his eyes, and asked if he could see anything.

On a Tuesday. Let Jesus take you by the hand. He leads the blind on paths they do not know (Isaiah 42:16). If you are in a season where you cannot see the way, tell him so, and take one step of obedience you can see. And look for someone you could lead by the hand towards him.

For worship. The Light of the world walked a blind man out of a village holding his hand. He did not shout directions from far off; he came near and touched. That is our Lord: the Creator of eyes stooping to lead the sightless, slow enough for the blind, gentle enough for the frightened, physical enough to spit and touch. He has never once let go of a hand he has taken.
verseByVerse.note: Bethsaida was a fishing town at the north end of the lake, home of Peter, Andrew and Philip.

parallels.desc: Bethsaida, the city of Andrew and Peter

verseByVerse.quote: And he looked up and said, "I see people, but they look like trees, walking." Then Jesus laid his hands on his eyes again; and he opened his eyes, his sight was restored, and he saw everything clearly. And he sent him to his home, saying, "Do not even enter the village."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The man looked up and said: I see people, but they look like trees, walking. Then Jesus laid his hands on his eyes again; the man looked intently, his sight was restored, and he saw everything clearly. Jesus sent him home, saying: do not even go into the village.

I see people, but they look like trees, walking. A partial healing, and one of the most vivid sentences in the New Testament; it can only have come from the man himself. He can see shapes moving, but blurred: upright, tall, vague, like tree trunks. He can tell they are people because they are moving; without the movement they would be a wood. The detail suggests he had once had sight and knew what trees looked like. Two things follow. He is genuinely seeing: this is not blindness. And he is genuinely not seeing properly: he could not have crossed a street.

Then Jesus laid his hands on his eyes again. The only healing in the Gospels done in two stages.

And he opened his eyes. Literally, he looked intently, or stared: he focused.

His sight was restored, and he saw everything clearly. Three descriptions of complete healing, piled up where one would do, as though Mark were determined that nobody should be left wondering whether the work was finished. “Clearly” (tēlaugōs) means far-shining: he could see clearly at a distance. Nothing blurred.

Why two stages? Not because Jesus’ power was weak, or because the man’s faith was lacking; the text says nothing of his faith. Jesus is in complete control, and chooses to do it this way. The healing is an acted parable. Look where Mark has put it. Six verses ago Jesus said to the Twelve, having eyes do you not see? Five verses later Peter will say, You are the Christ, and three verses after that he will take Jesus aside and try to correct him about the cross. That is a man seeing people like trees walking: not blind, genuinely seeing, but seeing wrong shapes. The disciples are at stage one: they see something, but not clearly. Peter will see that Jesus is the Christ (v. 29), but see him blurred, a Christ without a cross (v. 32). They need a second touch. Full sight will come only after the cross and resurrection, and the gift of the Spirit.

The man many believers are. But take it first as it stands, because a great many honest believers are the man in this story. He was not blind any longer; he genuinely saw. But he did not yet see clearly. A great many Christians live at exactly that stage. They see enough to know that Jesus is real, that the gospel is true, that they belong to him, and so much is still blurred. Prayers that feel like talking to a ceiling. Promises believed and not felt. A grasp of who he is that is more outline than face. If that is you, hear what this healing says. The same hand that gave the first touch gave the second. Jesus did not lead him out of the village, open his eyes halfway, and walk off satisfied. He stayed, and laid his hands on him again, and did not stop until the man saw everything clearly.

Do not despise dim sight, and do not settle for it. Do not despise a dim sight of Christ, and do not conclude from its dimness that you do not truly see him.
