Partial sight is real sight; the man who saw walking trees was no longer blind. But do not settle there either, as though blurred vision were all this life allows. Keep coming for the second touch, in the word, at the Table, on your knees, among his people, and know that the clearing of your sight is finally his work and not yours. He who began a good work in you will bring it to completion at the day of Jesus Christ (Philippians 1:6). And the day is coming when everyone who now sees in a mirror dimly will see him face to face (1 Corinthians 13:12). He has never yet left a work of his half-finished.

Does conversion happen in stages then? The new birth itself is a single act of God: a person is either dead in sin or made alive in Christ, and there is no halfway (John 3:3–8; Ephesians 2:4–5). But a person’s understanding and awareness of what has happened often grows slowly, and some people cannot name the day it began. After that, sanctification is a lifelong process of seeing more clearly and growing more like Christ (2 Corinthians 3:18). So do not demand of yourself or others a dramatic moment, and do not mistake slow growth for no life. The question is not how sharp your sight is, but whether you are looking at Jesus.

Do not even enter the village. Another command to avoid publicity. Go home, not back to the crowds. Given what Jesus says elsewhere about that town’s unbelief (Matthew 11:21), the instruction reads like mercy: a man with new eyes is not to be turned into a spectacle for people who will not be changed by him anyway.

In a sentence. After a first touch the man saw blurred shapes; after a second, he saw everything clearly, an acted picture of the disciples’ partial sight.

On a Tuesday. If you see Christ only dimly, keep coming to him. He finishes what he begins (Philippians 1:6). Pick one Gospel passage this week and read it slowly each day, asking him to show you one thing about himself you have not seen clearly before.

For worship. Christ does not do half a work. He laid his hands on blind eyes twice, until all was clear, and he will lay his hands on our dim hearts as often as it takes. Now we see in a mirror dimly, but then face to face. The Lord who began to open our eyes will not stop until we behold the King in his beauty (Isaiah 33:17), and see him as he is.
verseByVerse.note: Only Mark records this two-stage healing; it sits just before the disciples see who Jesus is — but only in part.

parallels.desc: the eyes of the blind opened

verseByVerse.quote: And Jesus went on with his disciples to the villages of Caesarea Philippi. And on the way he asked his disciples, "Who do people say that I am?" And they told him, "John the Baptist; and others say, Elijah; and others, one of the prophets."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus went on with his disciples to the villages of Caesarea Philippi. On the way he asked them: who do people say that I am? They told him: John the Baptist; others say Elijah; and others, one of the prophets.

The turning point. This is the hinge of Mark’s Gospel. The first half (1:1–8:26) asks: who is Jesus? The second half (8:31–16:8) answers: what kind of Messiah is he, and where is he going? He is going to the cross.

The villages of Caesarea Philippi. The location is chosen, and the setting is part of the sermon. Caesarea Philippi was about 25 miles (40 km) north of the Sea of Galilee, at the foot of Mount Hermon, at a spring that is one of the sources of the Jordan. It was a Gentile city, rebuilt by Herod’s son Philip and named in honour of Caesar (and himself). There was a shrine to the god Pan in a cave there, with niches cut into the cliff face for idols, and the place was called Paneas; Herod the Great had built a temple of white marble to Augustus as a god. A cliff full of pagan shrines, a temple to a man who called himself a god, and a city named for the emperor of the world. In this place of pagan gods and a divine emperor, Jesus asks who he is.

And on the way. It happens on the road, walking. “The way” (hodos) becomes a key word in this section (8:27; 9:33–34; 10:17, 32, 46, 52). Jesus is on the way to Jerusalem and the cross, and disciples are those who follow him on it.

Who do people say that I am? Jesus is not seeking information for himself. He is preparing them to state what they believe. He starts with the safe question. It is the one anybody can answer, because it requires nothing of the person answering: report the opinions.

John the Baptist; and others say, Elijah; and others, one of the prophets. The same opinions reported to Herod (6:14–15). Nothing has moved. Months of ministry, thousands fed, a district full of healings, and the public verdict is exactly where it was. And look at the quality of the answers, because they are not insults. Every one is a compliment. All of them high. People thought Jesus was a great prophet, a messenger from God, even a figure raised from the dead. John the Baptist: the greatest man born of women, come back. Elijah: expected to return before the day of the Lord (Malachi 4:5). One of the prophets: a man who speaks for God. But all of them fall short. They see him as a forerunner or a messenger, not the one to whom the prophets pointed. These are the largest categories available, and every one is far too small. The crowd is doing what crowds always do: reaching for the biggest box it already owns, rather than admitting that a new one is required.

The modern versions. The modern versions are the same shape at a lower altitude: a great moral teacher, a revolutionary, a mystic, a good man. All respectful, all inadequate, and all of them costing nothing, which is precisely their appeal. You can admire a prophet from a distance. You cannot admire the Son of God; you either fall down or walk away.

What do I say to someone who calls Jesus a good teacher? Agree that he was a teacher, and then gently show what he taught about himself. He forgave sins against others as though he were the one offended (2:5–7). He claimed to be Lord of the Sabbath (2:28), to give his life as a ransom for many (10:45), and to return in his Father’s glory to judge (8:38). A merely good teacher would not say such things. Either he was who he said, or he was badly mistaken or worse. Then invite your friend to read one of the Gospels and meet him for himself. Arguments help, but it is Christ himself, speaking in his word, who opens eyes.

In a sentence. Near the pagan shrines of Caesarea Philippi, Jesus asked who people thought he was, and heard that they saw him as a great prophet.

On a Tuesday. Many today still think well of Jesus: a great teacher, a prophet, a good man. That is not enough, and it is not true to who he is. Listen this week for how people around you speak of Jesus, and pray for an opening to ask one of them what they think he claimed.

For worship. Among the idols of Pan and the temple of the emperor-god, the true King stood on a dusty road and asked who he was. Every god in that cliff was dead stone, and the man who called himself divine would die like any other. The one asking the question is the living God in human flesh, too great for every category the world can offer. Prophets pointed to him; kings were shadows of him; and he is not one of the great men of history but the Lord of it.
verseByVerse.note: Caesarea Philippi was a Gentile city at the foot of Mount Hermon, north of the Sea of Galilee.

verseByVerse.quote: And he asked them, "But who do you say that I am?" Peter answered him, "You are the Christ." And he strictly charged them to tell no one about him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
He asked them: but who do you say that I am? Peter answered: you are the Christ. And he strictly ordered them to tell no one about him.

But who do you say that I am? The but is a hinge, and the weight falls on the pronoun. “You” is emphatic and plural: but you, all of you, what about you? This is the question the whole Gospel has been walking towards, and it is put to them personally after they have safely reported what everyone else thinks. The question everyone must answer. Public opinion is not enough; Jesus asks for personal confession. It is perfectly possible to spend years discussing what people say about Jesus: what the church teaches, what your parents believed, what the current arguments are. All of it can be conducted at a comfortable distance, and none of it commits you to anything. Then a moment comes when the question is asked in the second person, and nobody can answer it on your behalf: not a godly mother, not a good church, not a tradition you were raised in and still respect. If you have never answered it in your own words, you have not yet been asked anything by Christianity. You have only been informed.

Peter answered him. Peter, as usual, gets there first and speaks for the Twelve.

You are the Christ. The key word. “Christ” (Christos) translates the Hebrew Messiah: the Anointed One. It is not a surname; it is a title, and it carried the whole weight of Israel’s hope. In the Old Testament, kings, priests and prophets were anointed with oil to set them apart for their office. The Messiah was the promised King, the son of David, who would bring in God’s kingdom (2 Samuel 7:12–16; Psalm 2; Isaiah 9:6–7; 11:1–10). Mark’s first line called Jesus Christ (1:1); now, for the first time, a human being says it. Peter sees what the crowd did not: Jesus is not a forerunner but the one himself. And it is correct. Jesus does not qualify it, correct it or deny it.

What Mark leaves out. Matthew records the fuller confession (the Son of the living God) and Jesus’ blessing on Peter: Blessed are you, Simon Bar-Jonah! For flesh and blood has not revealed this to you, but my Father who is in heaven, with the promise about the rock and the keys (Matthew 16:16–19). Mark has none of it. Writing probably from Peter’s own preaching, he records the bare confession and moves straight to Peter’s failure, as if Peter himself told it that way. This Gospel gives Peter’s finest hour in four words and his worst moment in full. The man remembered the rebuke and let the commendation go.

Where Christians differ: the rock in Matthew 16. Roman Catholic teaching takes the rock to be Peter and his successors, the popes, with authority over the whole church. Others have taken it as Peter’s confession, or as Christ himself. Verdict: the most natural reading is that Peter, as the first to confess Christ, is the rock in the sense that the apostles are the church’s foundation (Ephesians 2:20). But nothing in the text speaks of successors, and a foundation is laid once, not handed down. It gives no ground for a papacy. Christ alone is the head of the church (Colossians 1:18).

And he strictly charged them to tell no one about him. The right answer, and immediately silenced. “Strictly charged” (epetimēsen) is the word for rebuke, the same word used for silencing demons (1:25; 3:12). Why silence? Because the title Messiah was explosive; it was a word with a national programme attached, and the programme was wrong. Popular hopes imagined a political and military deliverer who would drive out the Romans. Proclaimed now, the title would provoke a revolt or a premature arrest, and would be misunderstood. Peter has said the true word with a false picture behind it, and the next verses are going to show just how false. The disciples themselves did not yet know what kind of Messiah he was. Only after the cross and the resurrection could the title be preached rightly (9:9). Jesus will accept it openly before the high priest, on the night it condemns him (14:61–62), when there is no possibility of misunderstanding what kind of king he is.

What if I am not sure what I say about Jesus? Then take the question seriously, and do not settle for borrowed answers. Read one of the Gospels, Mark is short, asking at each page who this man is. Ask God honestly to show you the truth. Talk with a Christian you trust, and bring your doubts into the open. Peter did not reach his answer by debate but by following Jesus and watching him; and flesh and blood did not reveal it to him but the Father (Matthew 16:17). So ask the Father. And if you find that you believe he is the Christ, say so, to him first and then to others. Faith that is confessed grows stronger (Romans 10:9–10).

In a sentence. Peter confessed that Jesus is the Christ, the promised King, and Jesus ordered them to tell no one until they understood what that meant.

On a Tuesday. Jesus asks you, personally: who do you say I am? Your answer shapes everything. Write your answer in one sentence, in your own words, and then ask what that sentence requires of you today.

For worship. You are the Christ: the King Israel waited for, the Anointed One of every prophecy, the son of David who reigns for ever. Peter said it in four words on a road near the idols, and heaven had revealed it to him. Blessed be the Father who opens the eyes of fishermen to see his Son, and blessed be the Son who accepts the confession of weak men and builds his church on the truth they confess.
verseByVerse.note: “Christ” means anointed one, the Messiah — the promised king. Popular hopes for a political Messiah may explain the command to silence.

verseByVerse.quote: And he began to teach them that the Son of Man must suffer many things and be rejected by the elders and the chief priests and the scribes and be killed, and after three days rise again. And he said this plainly. And Peter took him aside and began to rebuke him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
He began to teach them that the Son of Man must suffer many things, be rejected by the elders, the chief priests and the scribes, be killed, and after three days rise again. He said this plainly. And Peter took him aside and began to rebuke him.

And he began to teach them. A new beginning. Mark’s word began marks a turn: something starts here that had not been said before, and from now on it is the burden of everything. From now on, Jesus repeatedly teaches about his death (9:31; 10:33–34), the three passion predictions that structure this section of Mark.

The Son of Man. Jesus’ favourite title for himself, the one he chose above all others. It comes from Daniel 7:13–14: one like a son of man, coming with the clouds of heaven, to whom the Ancient of Days gives everlasting dominion over all peoples. It is a title of glory. But it was less politically loaded than Messiah, and Jesus fills it with new content. Here he does something no one had done: he puts the glorious figure of Daniel together with suffering and rejection. The Son of Man suffers before he reigns.

Must suffer many things. “Must” (dei): divine necessity, one of the great words of the New Testament. It is not the language of resignation but of a plan. This is the point to be clear about, because everything about the cross depends on it. What is coming is not a tragic accident, a defeat, a miscalculation, or a good movement overtaken by its enemies. It is God’s plan, written in Scripture (Isaiah 53; Psalm 22; Zechariah 13:7): delivered up according to the definite plan and foreknowledge of God (Acts 2:23). Jesus goes to the cross because the Father has willed it and he has embraced it (10:45).

Why must he die? Because of sin. The Son of Man came to give his life as a ransom for many (10:45), to die in the place of sinners, bearing the punishment their sins deserved, as the Servant of Isaiah 53 was pierced for our transgressions and crushed for our iniquities, with the LORD laying on him the iniquity of us all (Isaiah 53:5–6). He who knew no sin was made sin for us, so that in him we might become the righteousness of God (2 Corinthians 5:21). The must is God’s way, foretold in the Scriptures, to save the guilty without denying his justice: the Judge himself takes the sentence. There was no other way for sinners to be forgiven and God to remain just (Romans 3:25–26).

And be rejected by the elders and the chief priests and the scribes. The three groups that made up the Sanhedrin, the supreme Jewish council in Jerusalem, all three named separately. Not rejected by the mob or the Romans first, but by the official leadership of the people of God. The leaders of God’s people will reject God’s Messiah, the stone the builders rejected (Psalm 118:22, quoted in 12:10).

And be killed. Flat, unadorned, no euphemism. Unthinkable for a Messiah, in Jewish expectation.

And after three days rise again. Jewish idiom for on the third day (compare Matthew 16:21). The resurrection is part of the prediction from the start. He told them the resurrection at the same time as the death, in the same sentence, the first time he ever mentioned either. The disciples seem not to have heard it at all; when he mentions rising again after the transfiguration, they are left questioning what it could mean (9:10). But he said it, from the very first telling.

Does after three days contradict on the third day? No. Mark writes after three days here and twice more (9:31; 10:34), where Matthew and Luke say on the third day, and honest readers have wondered whether that demands a fourth day. It is simply the Jewish way of counting, in which any part of a day counted as a whole day, so Friday, Saturday and Sunday are three days. And Scripture settles it: the chief priests, remembering this very prediction, tell Pilate that Jesus said, After three days I will rise, and in the same breath ask for a guard until the third day (Matthew 27:63–64). Both phrases, of one and the same morning, from men who had every motive to be exact. There is no discrepancy, only two idioms for one promise.

And he said this plainly. “Plainly” (parrēsia): openly, no longer in riddles. Only Mark records this, and it is a landmark in this Gospel. Up to now Jesus had taught in parables, and everything had been managed: demons silenced, healed men told to say nothing, crowds taught in parables with private explanations for those who stayed. Now he speaks of the cross directly. The moment they get the title right, the lid comes off, and the first plain, unveiled thing he says to them is that he is going to be killed. Which tells you what the secret was protecting. It was never only that he was the Christ. It was what kind.

And Peter took him aside and began to rebuke him. Astonishing, and worth reading slowly. Took him aside: a private word, man to man, kindly meant, out of earshot of the others. And then the verb: rebuke, the same word as in verse 30, the word used of Jesus rebuking demons and the wind. Jesus rebuked them to silence, and now Peter rebukes Jesus. Three verses after confessing him as the Christ, Peter takes the Christ to one side to correct him. Peter, who has just confessed him as Messiah, cannot accept a suffering Messiah. To him the idea was a contradiction. The Messiah was supposed to conquer, not die. Matthew records his words: Far be it from you, Lord! This shall never happen to you (Matthew 16:22). And he is doing it out of love. He has just seen who this is, and he cannot bear what he has heard, and everything decent in him wants to stop it. It is the most affectionate sentence in the chapter, and it gets the hardest answer in the book.

In a sentence. Jesus began to teach plainly that he must suffer, be rejected, be killed and rise again, and Peter, appalled, took him aside to rebuke him.

On a Tuesday. We, like Peter, want a Christ who fits our expectations. Let the cross reshape what you think Christ is for. Ask yourself what you most want Jesus to do for you this year, and then ask whether it fits a Lord who went to a cross. If it does not, bring the want to him, and let him reshape it.

For worship. The Son of Man must suffer. Before the world began, the Father and the Son had agreed this road, and the Lamb was slain in the purpose of God from the foundation of the world (Revelation 13:8; 1 Peter 1:19–20). He went to the cross not as a victim of events but as the willing Saviour, bearing in his body the punishment we deserved, so that God could be just and the justifier of the one who has faith in Jesus. And in the same breath he spoke of rising again. The must of the cross is followed by the must of the empty tomb, and both are for us.

verseByVerse.quote: But turning and seeing his disciples, he rebuked Peter and said, "Get behind me, Satan! For you are not setting your mind on the things of God, but on the things of man."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus turned, looked at his disciples, and rebuked Peter: get behind me, Satan! For you are not setting your mind on the things of God, but on the things of man.

But turning and seeing his disciples. Only Mark records this, and the choreography matters. Peter has taken him aside for a private conversation. Jesus turns round, away from Peter, towards the others, and looks at them, and only then speaks. Peter’s thought was theirs too, and they needed to hear the answer. The rebuke is public, because the error is dangerous. Peter said it quietly; the answer is given in front of everybody, because every man there is thinking it and the correction is for all of them.

He rebuked Peter. The third use of the word in the scene. Peter rebuked Jesus; Jesus rebukes Peter.

Get behind me. Literally, go behind me. Back to your place, as a follower. The same words, behind me, appear in Jesus’ call: Follow me (literally come behind me, 1:17). It is not get away from me. It is the language of position: get back where a disciple stands, which is behind. Peter had stepped in front of Jesus, trying to lead and starting to give directions; he must go back behind and follow.

Satan! A shocking word to use of his chief disciple, the hardest sentence any disciple ever heard, spoken to the man who moments earlier had given the best answer in the Gospel. But look at the content of what Peter said, and it is instantly recognisable: this shall never happen to you. A Messiah without a cross, a crown without a death, glory by a shorter road. Peter was doing what Satan did in the wilderness: tempting Jesus to reach the kingdom without the cross (Matthew 4:8–10). Jesus has heard that before, and he will hear it again at the end, from passers-by at the foot of the cross: save yourself, and come down from the cross (15:30). The same offer three times: in a wilderness, from a friend, and from a crowd at an execution. Satan was using Peter’s love and ignorance. The temptation was real for Jesus, which is why the answer is so sharp. Peter was not possessed; he was being Satan’s mouthpiece.

For you are not setting your mind on the things of God, but on the things of man. “Setting your mind” (phroneis) means thinking, having an outlook, a mindset (Philippians 2:5; Romans 8:5). And there is the diagnosis, and it is the most useful sentence here for ordinary people, because it names a category rather than a crime. Peter was not being wicked. He was thinking like a man, as people naturally think: power, success, avoiding suffering. Every human instinct says that suffering is to be avoided, that a good plan does not end in a grave, that if you love somebody you get them out of danger. All of that is decent, and all of it is the things of man, and when it is set against the declared purpose of God it becomes, whatever the intention, the devil’s argument. God’s way is the way of the cross. This is the great clash of the Gospel: human thinking against divine thinking about what the Messiah is and does (1 Corinthians 1:18–25).

Opposition from those who love you. That is the warning to take away, and it is not what we expect from a passage with Satan in it. The most dangerous opposition to the will of God in your life may not come from your enemies. It may come from people who love you, meaning it kindly, taking you aside for a quiet word, and from the reasonable, protective, entirely natural voice in your own head that says: surely not this; surely there is another way. Peter’s motives were good. Peter was wrong. And the two facts sat together in one man, moments after the best confession in the Gospel.

What it does not mean. Not that Peter was rejected. It is not a verdict on Peter’s soul. Jesus still loved him, kept him, took him up the mountain in the very next chapter, and later restored him on a beach (John 21:15–19). What is being identified is the source of the objection, not the state of the man. But even a sincere believer can speak for Satan when he puts human comfort above God’s purposes.

How do I tell whether advice is from God or only from man? Test it by the cross and by Scripture. Advice that always steers you away from cost, sacrifice and obedience, and towards comfort, safety and reputation, should be examined carefully, however kindly it is meant. Ask: does this fit what God has plainly said? Does it ask me to step in front of Christ or to follow him? Would it have kept Jesus from the cross? Godly counsel can certainly warn against foolish risks; wisdom is not recklessness. But when the clear will of God is costly, beware of the friend, and the inner voice, that says: surely not this. And when you give advice, check whose thoughts you are thinking.

In a sentence. Jesus rebuked Peter as Satan for trying to turn him from the cross, because Peter was thinking in human terms, not God’s.

On a Tuesday. When you advise a fellow Christian to avoid costly obedience, check whose thoughts you are thinking. And when someone you love advises you to take the easier road, listen with respect, and then weigh it by Scripture before you decide.

For worship. The Son of God would not be turned from the cross, not by the devil in the wilderness, not by his dearest friend on the road, not by the mockers at Golgotha. He set his face like flint (Isaiah 50:7). Every soft voice that said surely not this he answered with obedience, because he loved the Father and he loved us. And he did not cast Peter off for the error; he put him back behind him and kept leading. Blessed be the Saviour who would not save himself, so that he could save us.

verseByVerse.quote: And calling the crowd to him with his disciples, he said to them, "If anyone would come after me, let him deny himself and take up his cross and follow me.
verseByVerse.commentary:
He called the crowd to him with his disciples and said: if anyone would come after me, let him deny himself, take up his cross, and follow me.

And calling the crowd to him with his disciples. Before a word of it, notice the audience. What follows is not only for the Twelve, or for a spiritual elite. It is for everyone who would follow Jesus. He could have said this to the Twelve alone. What follows is the most demanding thing in the Gospel, and every instinct of religious management would keep it for the committed. Instead he gathers the general public and states the terms out loud. That settles a question permanently. Cross-bearing is not an advanced course for the heroic few, a special vocation for missionaries and martyrs while ordinary believers get an easier arrangement. It is the entry requirement, published, to anyone considering him. Mark’s readers in Rome, who may already have been facing persecution under Nero, would hear it as addressed to them.

The logic. The way of the Messiah is the way of the cross; therefore the way of his followers is the way of the cross. As the master, so the disciple.

If anyone would come after me. “Would” (thelei): wants to, wills to. Discipleship is a choice, and Jesus sets out its terms honestly before anyone makes it. Anyone. And the phrase is the ordinary one for discipleship: to come after somebody is to walk behind him, which is exactly where Peter has just been told to get back to. Then three things, in an order that cannot be rearranged.

Let him deny himself. To deny yourself (aparnēsasthō heauton) is not to deny yourself things, like giving up chocolate for Lent. It is to say no to self as the centre and master of your life. The same word is used of Peter denying Jesus (14:30, 72): to disown, to say, I do not know him; I have no connection with him. That is the force of it, and it is much stronger than we usually allow. To deny yourself is to say about yourself what Peter said about Christ: I do not know this man; his claims have no authority over me; he does not get the deciding vote. The disciple says that of his own self-will: I no longer belong to myself. It is not self-improvement, and it is not self-hatred; the Bible never asks you to despise a creature God made and Christ died for. It is the removal of the self from the throne. The question, what do I want, stops being the question that decides.

And take up his cross. We have worn this phrase completely smooth, and it needs its edge back. Everyone in the Roman world knew what this meant. Nobody in that crowd heard a metaphor. Crucifixion was local and recent: when revolt broke out after Herod the Great died, the governor Varus crucified two thousand Jews, within living memory of the older people standing there. A condemned man carried the crossbeam of his own cross to the place of execution, through jeering crowds. It was the walk of a man who had already lost everything and was going to die, walking in one direction only. To take up the cross is to accept rejection, shame and death, if need be, for Jesus’ sake. Not a metaphor for ordinary troubles (an illness, a difficult relative), but the costly path of loyalty to Jesus in a world that rejects him. It means accepting that the old self is under sentence, that the sentence is public, and that the walk goes one way. I have been crucified with Christ (Galatians 2:20) is not poetry; it is Paul taking this call as his own. Luke adds daily (Luke 9:23).

And follow me. Where? To Jerusalem, where he will be crucified. The present tense means keep on following. And the third command is what turns the first two from grim heroism into something else entirely. You are not asked to carry a cross into the dark by yourself. You are asked to walk behind someone, and he is going first, and he is not asking anything he has not already accepted. Within months he will be in Gethsemane, and then he will carry the actual beam up an actual road. The whole difference between Christian self-denial and mere religious severity is in that last word. It is not a discipline. It is a Person, walking ahead, whose back you can see.

What it does not mean. Not that we save ourselves by self-denial, or earn salvation by suffering. Jesus alone bears the cross that atones for sin (10:45). The disciple’s cross is not redemptive; it is the shape of a life that belongs to the one who was crucified. Nor is it a call to seek suffering for its own sake.

What does taking up my cross look like on an ordinary day? Usually it is quieter than martyrdom, but it is the same shape. It is choosing obedience to Christ when it costs you: telling the truth at work when a lie would be easier, refusing the sexual relationship he forbids, giving money you would rather keep, forgiving someone who has not apologised, being known as a Christian in a room where that will lower you. It is accepting the mockery or loss that comes from being his. And in many parts of the world today it is literally risking prison or death. Name the place in your week where loyalty to Jesus costs you something. If you cannot name one, ask whether you are following him or only admiring him.

Does self-denial mean I can never enjoy anything? No. God gives us richly all things to enjoy (1 Timothy 6:17), and the Christian life is full of joy, food, friendship, marriage, beauty and rest received with thanks. Self-denial is not rejecting God’s gifts but dethroning self as the one who decides. A person who has denied himself can enjoy a good meal more, not less, because he receives it as a gift rather than demanding it as a right. What he gives up is not pleasure but the claim to run his own life. And Jesus promises that those who lose for his sake receive a hundredfold, now and in the age to come (10:29–30).

In a sentence. Whoever would follow Jesus must say no to self, accept the shame and cost of loyalty to him even to death, and keep on following.

On a Tuesday. Where today does following Jesus mean saying no to yourself? Name it, and take it up. Name the matter this week where what you want and what he wants are pulling in different directions: the money, the relationship, the grudge, the ambition, the hour of the day. If you cannot name one, the denial is theoretical, and theoretical self-denial has never cost anybody anything.

For worship. He does not ask us to walk any road he has not walked first. The Lord who calls us to take up a cross took up his own, and carried it to Golgotha for us. Our self-denial follows his self-giving; our crosses are light because his was heavy enough to bear our sins. And the one who says follow me is not a slave-driver behind us but a Shepherd ahead of us, whose wounded back we can see, leading us through death to life.
verseByVerse.note: Condemned men carried their own crossbeam to the place of execution.

verseByVerse.quote: For whoever would save his life will lose it, but whoever loses his life for my sake and the gospel's will save it. For what does it profit a man to gain the whole world and forfeit his soul? For what can a man give in return for his soul?
verseByVerse.commentary:
For whoever wants to save his life will lose it, but whoever loses his life for my sake and the gospel’s will save it. For what does it profit a man to gain the whole world and lose his soul? What can a man give in exchange for his soul?

For whoever would save his life will lose it. This is the reason for the demand, and it is worth noticing that it is an argument. He does not say, because I say so. He gives a for, three of them in a row, and every one is an appeal to self-interest properly understood. “Life” (psychē) means the self, the whole person, both life now and life eternal. The same word is translated soul in the next verse. English has to use two words; Mark uses one, and the play on it is the whole point: your life, your self, your soul, the thing that is you. A paradox: hold on to your life, protecting it from the cost of following Jesus, and you lose it, eternally.

But whoever loses his life for my sake and the gospel’s will save it. Give your life up, even to death, for Jesus, and you gain it, eternally. And the gospel’s: only Mark adds this. To be loyal to Jesus is to be loyal to the message about him. Mark’s readers might lose their lives for preaching it.

The most easily verified thing in the passage. This is not a religious paradox invented to sound deep. Look at the people you know. The ones who have organised their lives around protecting themselves, their comfort, their reputation, their options, their feelings, have they become larger or smaller? A life curved in on itself gets steadily narrower; the range of what can be enjoyed shrinks, the tolerance for inconvenience drops, and the person ends up with very little that is not about him. Everyone has watched this happen to somebody. And the people you know who have genuinely spent themselves, on their children, on the sick, on a church, on the work of God in some obscure place, are almost always the ones with the most life in them. They are not depleted. They are the ones you go to when you are in trouble. Jesus is not asking for a sacrifice that leaves you poorer. He is telling you where the arithmetic actually comes out.

Is this salvation by self-sacrifice? No. Losing one’s life for Christ is not the price of salvation; it is the shape of the life that faith produces. We are saved by grace through faith, and created for good works (Ephesians 2:8–10). But the faith that saves is the faith that follows Christ, and following him costs everything (Luke 14:26–33). The verse is not only for martyrs. It is for every disciple who gives up the right to his own life.

For what does it profit a man to gain the whole world and forfeit his soul? The language of a business deal, and one of the most quoted sentences in this Gospel, worn as smooth as the cross was. Give it back its teeth by taking the two halves seriously. Gain the whole world: not a good career or a comfortable house, but the whole thing, all its wealth, pleasure and power, with nothing left over for anyone else. He is being deliberately extravagant, because he wants the best possible case for the other side. Suppose you won completely. And forfeit his soul. “Forfeit” (zēmiōthēnai) means suffer the loss of, be fined. Assets acquired, price paid. And the sum does not work even at the maximum. You would be bankrupt. Even if you got everything, you would have paid too much, because the thing paid over is the thing that would have enjoyed it.

The smaller prices. That is what makes this verse useful rather than merely solemn, because almost nobody is actually offered the whole world. What people trade their souls for is invariably smaller. A promotion. A house in the right street. A relationship that could not survive their being a Christian. The good opinion of a particular set of people. Twenty more years of being left alone. If the whole world is a bad price, what is the price you are quietly considering?

For what can a man give in return for his soul? Nothing can buy it back once lost. The last question closes the door, and it is about redemption, the price of a life. What could you produce, if you had lost it, to get it back? The question echoes Psalm 49:7–8: no man can ransom another, or give to God the price of his life, for the ransom of their life is costly and can never suffice. Never suffice. No human price can redeem a soul. There is nothing in the world large enough. Only one ransom can, and Jesus will give it: he came to give his life as a ransom for many (10:45). The price no man could pay was paid, not by the world, which was never worth it, but by him.

What it does not mean. Not that every Christian will be martyred, or that only martyrs are saved. But every Christian must be willing, and in a thousand smaller ways each day, the principle holds: what you hold back for yourself you lose; what you give to Christ you keep.

What if I am afraid I would not stand firm if I were persecuted? Most Christians have felt that fear, and it is not a sign that you lack faith. Peter boasted he would never fall, and fell; later, strengthened by the Spirit, he stood before the council and, the early church tells us, died for Christ (Acts 4:13, 19–20; John 21:18–19). Grace for martyrdom is given when it is needed, not in advance. God will not let you be tested beyond what you can bear (1 Corinthians 10:13), and the one who keeps you is Christ, not your own courage (John 10:28–29). So do not try to feel brave about tomorrow. Be faithful in today’s small costs, and trust him for the large ones.

In a sentence. To cling to your life is to lose it, and to lose it for Christ and the gospel is to save it, since nothing in the world is worth a soul.

On a Tuesday. Weigh today’s choices on Jesus’ scales. What gain would you trade your soul for? Nothing is worth it. Look at the one thing you are most tempted to protect from Christ, and ask honestly what it would profit you if you kept it and lost him.

For worship. No man can ransom his own soul, and so the Son of Man ransomed it for us. He lost his life that we might save ours; he was stripped of everything so that we might be given everything. He gained no worldly kingdom, refused every shortcut, and gave his soul as an offering for sin (Isaiah 53:10). And because he did, the soul that is his can never be forfeited. Whoever loses his life for him finds that it was safe in his hands all along.

parallels.desc: the ransom of a life is costly

verseByVerse.quote: For whoever is ashamed of me and of my words in this adulterous and sinful generation, of him will the Son of Man also be ashamed when he comes in the glory of his Father with the holy angels."
verseByVerse.commentary:
For whoever is ashamed of me and of my words in this adulterous and sinful generation, of him the Son of Man will also be ashamed when he comes in the glory of his Father with the holy angels.

For whoever is ashamed of me and of my words. The last for, and it moves from the sums to something far more ordinary and far more likely. Notice that he does not say, whoever denies me, though Peter will do that within months, or whoever renounces me. He says ashamed, which is not a decision, not a denial, and not usually a moment at all. It is a temperature. The pressure to deny Christ was not usually a sword but a sneer. To follow a crucified man was shameful in the Roman world, foolishness and scandal (1 Corinthians 1:23). Being ashamed of Jesus means hiding your allegiance to avoid contempt. And of my words: his teaching, including the teaching about the cross just given. A man can be quite content to be associated with Jesus in general and thoroughly embarrassed by particular things he said. Most of us find some of his words easy to quote and others we would rather were not there.

In this adulterous and sinful generation. Adulterous is not primarily about sexual sin. It is the prophets’ word for Israel’s unfaithfulness to God, like a wife who leaves her husband and goes after other lovers (Hosea 1–3; Jeremiah 3; Ezekiel 16). The generation that rejects Jesus is unfaithful to God. It is in front of this kind of audience that the disciple is tempted to be ashamed: the atmosphere in which being ashamed of him feels like good manners.

How it operates. That is exactly how it works. Very few Christians in a comfortable country ever face a moment of open denial. What we face is a thousand small pressures towards silence, and every one of them can be given a respectable name. It is the conversation at work that turns, and the sentence you do not say. It is the qualifying phrase, I mean, I am not one of those Christians, offered to buy a little distance. It is the dinner party where you let it be assumed you agree, and tell yourself it was not the moment. It is the grace not said in a restaurant, the belief not mentioned to the colleague after four years, the Bible turned face down when somebody comes in. None of it feels like betrayal. All of it is what this verse is about.

Of him will the Son of Man also be ashamed. Measure for measure: shame now, shame then. Jesus will not acknowledge, at the judgment, those who would not acknowledge him now (Matthew 10:32–33). To be disowned by him then is the ultimate loss. Do not soften it, but do understand what it is measuring. He is not threatening people for a failure of nerve in a hard moment. The man whose preaching lies behind this sentence had failed exactly that, in a courtyard, three times, with oaths, and was forgiven on a beach and made a leader of the church. Settled shame is not the same as a moment of cowardice, and the difference is what you do afterwards. What he is describing is a life in which he was quietly kept out of sight because the cost of being known with him was judged too high.

When he comes in the glory of his Father with the holy angels. The Son of Man of Daniel 7 again, now in full glory: one like a son of man coming with the clouds of heaven, given dominion and glory and a kingdom, that all peoples should serve him (Daniel 7:13–14). The one who is about to be rejected and killed will return as judge of all. Notice the claims: the glory is his Father’s, so he is the Son of God; the angels accompany him, so they are his servants. The suffering Messiah and the glorious Judge are the same person. And consider who is speaking: a Galilean carpenter, standing on a road near a pagan shrine, in an occupied province, with twelve men around him who have just shown they do not understand, who has told them he is going to be arrested by the leadership of his own nation and executed. And he says: when I come in the glory of my Father, with the holy angels.

The structure. Note how the whole passage moves: the cross for Jesus (v. 31), the cross for the disciple (v. 34), and the glory for both (v. 38; 9:1). Suffering now, glory later. That is the pattern of the Christian life: if we suffer with him, we will also be glorified with him (Romans 8:17–18).

A question of timing. So the whole question of shame is finally a question of timing. There is a case for being embarrassed by him now: he is a provincial nobody with a crucifixion in front of him, and the world’s opinion of him has not improved much since. And there is a day coming when the sky opens and the Son of Man arrives in his Father’s glory with the armies of heaven, and every one of the people you were afraid of is looking at him. Nobody will be ashamed of him then. The only question is whether you were ashamed of him now, when it cost something, and whether, on that day, the one thing you want is to hear him say your name in front of the holy angels and not look away.

I have been ashamed of Christ. Is there any hope for me? Yes, the same hope Peter had. He denied Jesus three times with curses, and the risen Lord sought him out, asked him three times if he loved him, and gave him work to do (John 21:15–17). The warning is against a settled life of shame, not against the believer who has failed and grieves over it. Confess it to the Lord plainly, receive his forgiveness (1 John 1:9), and then take the next opportunity, however small, to own him: a sentence at work, a grace at a meal, an honest answer to a question. He is not ashamed to call his people brothers (Hebrews 2:11), even those who once were ashamed of him.

Must I talk about Jesus in every conversation? No. Not being ashamed of Christ does not mean forcing him into every sentence or being tactless. There is a time to keep silence and a time to speak (Ecclesiastes 3:7), and speech should be gracious and wise (Colossians 4:5–6). It means not hiding that you belong to him, not denying him when asked, not pretending to agree with what dishonours him, and being willing to speak when the moment comes, even if it costs you. Live openly as his, and you will find that opportunities come more often than you expected.

In a sentence. Whoever is ashamed of Jesus and his words before an unfaithful world will be disowned by him when he returns in his Father’s glory.

On a Tuesday. Where are you tempted to hide that you belong to Jesus: at work, with friends, online? Remember the day when he will either own you or not. This week, take one small step of being known as his where you have been quiet, and leave the result with him.

For worship. The Lord who was despised and rejected will come in the glory of his Father with the holy angels. Every knee will bow, and those who were ashamed of him will be ashamed indeed. But for his people that day will be the day he is not ashamed of them. He bore our shame on the cross, despising it for the joy set before him (Hebrews 12:2), so that he might present us before his Father with great joy. To be owned by him in front of heaven is worth every sneer on earth, and he will own every one who is his.
verseByVerse.note: “Adulterous” is the prophets’ word for Israel’s unfaithfulness to God.

8.theology:
Two feedings, not one story told twice. Jesus makes the disciples recite both with the figures (vv. 19–20): five loaves, five thousand, twelve baskets; seven loaves, four thousand, seven baskets. Twelve baskets for Israel, one for each tribe; seven for the nations, the number of fullness. And some of them have come from far away is how Scripture speaks of the Gentiles coming in (Isa. 60:4; Eph. 2:13).

Why no sign? Not because evidence is illegitimate — he had given a great deal and would give more. What he refuses is a miracle produced on demand as the price of belief, from men who have already shown what they do with the evidence they have. If they do not hear Moses and the Prophets, neither will they be convinced if someone should rise from the dead (Luke 16:31) — which proved exactly right, since somebody did, and the men who got the report first paid soldiers to say the body was stolen (Matt. 28:12–13).

After three days. Mark's phrase (v. 31; 9:31; 10:34) against Matthew's and Luke's on the third day is not a discrepancy but the Jewish reckoning, in which any part of a day counts as a day. Scripture settles it: the chief priests recall this prediction as After three days I will rise and in the same breath ask Pilate for a guard until the third day (Matt. 27:63–64).

Get behind me, Satan. Not a verdict on Peter — Jesus takes him up the mountain in the next chapter and restores him on a beach at the end. It names the source of the objection. This shall never happen to you (Matt. 16:22) is a kingdom without a cross, which is the wilderness offer (1:13) returning through the mouth of a friend, and it will come a third time from passers-by at the foot of the cross — save yourself, and come down (15:30).
8.examples:
Then: a crowd in Galilee hearing take up his cross in a country where the governor Varus had crucified two thousand men within living memory. Nobody heard a metaphor. They had watched condemned men carry the crossbeam out through the streets, stripped and jeered at, walking in one direction only.

Now: we have worn the phrase smooth and made a cross into a difficulty — a hard marriage, an illness, a colleague. That is not what it meant. A man carrying a cross was not a man with a burden; he was a man already condemned, publicly, on his way out of his own life.

And deny himself is the verb used of Peter in the courtyard: I do not know the man, he is nothing to do with me. That is what you are asked to say about yourself — not self-hatred, and not going without sugar, but the removal of the self from the throne, so that what do I want? stops being the question that decides. Name the specific matter this week where that is in play. If you cannot name one, the denial is theoretical.

And the third word is what keeps this from being grim heroism: follow me. You are not asked to carry a cross into the dark alone. You are asked to walk behind somebody whose back you can see, who is going first, and who within months will carry an actual beam up an actual road.

One more, from v. 38. He does not say whoever denies me — he says ashamed, which is not a decision or a moment but a temperature. Very few Christians in a comfortable country face a moment of denial. What we face is a thousand small pressures toward silence, each with a respectable name: the sentence not said when the conversation turned, the qualifying phrase offered up to buy distance (I'm not one of those Christians), the belief not mentioned to a colleague in four years. None of it feels like betrayal. All of it is what the verse is about.

9.title: Glory on the Mountain, Failure in the Valley
9.text: <sup>1</sup>And he said to them, “Truly, I say to you, there are some standing here who will not taste death until they see the kingdom of God after it has come with power.” <sup>2</sup>And after six days Jesus took with him Peter and James and John, and led them up a high mountain by themselves. And he was transfigured before them, <sup>3</sup>and his clothes became radiant, intensely white, as no one on earth could bleach them. <sup>4</sup>And there appeared to them Elijah with Moses, and they were talking with Jesus. <sup>5</sup>And Peter said to Jesus, “Rabbi, it is good that we are here. Let us make three tents, one for you and one for Moses and one for Elijah.” <sup>6</sup>For he did not know what to say, for they were terrified. <sup>7</sup>And a cloud overshadowed them, and a voice came out of the cloud, “This is my beloved Son; listen to him.” <sup>8</sup>And suddenly, looking around, they no longer saw anyone with them but Jesus only. <sup>9</sup>And as they were coming down the mountain, he charged them to tell no one what they had seen, until the Son of Man had risen from the dead. <sup>10</sup>So they kept the matter to themselves, questioning what this rising from the dead might mean. <sup>11</sup>And they asked him, “Why do the scribes say that first Elijah must come?” <sup>12</sup>And he said to them, “Elijah does come first to restore all things. And how is it written of the Son of Man that he should suffer many things and be treated with contempt? <sup>13</sup>But I tell you that Elijah has come, and they did to him whatever they pleased, as it is written of him.” <sup>14</sup>And when they came to the disciples, they saw a great crowd around them, and scribes arguing with them. <sup>15</sup>And immediately all the crowd, when they saw him, were greatly amazed and ran up to him and greeted him. <sup>16</sup>And he asked them, “What are you arguing about with them?” <sup>17</sup>And someone from the crowd answered him, “Teacher, I brought my son to you, for he has a spirit that makes him mute. <sup>18</sup>And whenever it seizes him, it throws him down, and he foams and grinds his teeth and becomes rigid. So I asked your disciples to cast it out, and they were not able.” <sup>19</sup>And he answered them, “O faithless generation, how long am I to be with you? How long am I to bear with you? Bring him to me.” <sup>20</sup>And they brought the boy to him. And when the spirit saw him, immediately it convulsed the boy, and he fell on the ground and rolled about, foaming at the mouth. <sup>21</sup>And Jesus asked his father, “How long has this been happening to him?” And he said, “From childhood. <sup>22</sup>And it has often cast him into fire and into water, to destroy him. But if you can do anything, have compassion on us and help us.” <sup>23</sup>And Jesus said to him, “‘If you can’! All things are possible for one who believes.” <sup>24</sup>Immediately the father of the child cried out and said, “I believe; help my unbelief!” <sup>25</sup>And when Jesus saw that a crowd came running together, he rebuked the unclean spirit, saying to it, “You mute and deaf spirit, I command you, come out of him and never enter him again.” <sup>26</sup>And after crying out and convulsing him terribly, it came out, and the boy was like a corpse, so that most of them said, “He is dead.” <sup>27</sup>But Jesus took him by the hand and lifted him up, and he arose. <sup>28</sup>And when he had entered the house, his disciples asked him privately, “Why could we not cast it out?” <sup>29</sup>And he said to them, “This kind cannot be driven out by anything but prayer.” <sup>30</sup>They went on from there and passed through Galilee. And he did not want anyone to know, <sup>31</sup>for he was teaching his disciples, saying to them, “The Son of Man is going to be delivered into the hands of men, and they will kill him. And when he is killed, after three days he will rise.” <sup>32</sup>But they did not understand the saying, and were afraid to ask him. <sup>33</sup>And they came to Capernaum. And when he was in the house he asked them, “What were you discussing on the way?” <sup>34</sup>But they kept silent, for on the way they had argued with one another about who was the greatest. <sup>35</sup>And he sat down and called the twelve. And he said to them, “If anyone would be first, he must be last of all and servant of all.” <sup>36</sup>And he took a child and put him in the midst of them, and taking him in his arms, he said to them, <sup>37</sup>“Whoever receives one such child in my name receives me, and whoever receives me, receives not me but him who sent me.” <sup>38</sup>John said to him, “Teacher, we saw someone casting out demons in your name, and we tried to stop him, because he was not following us.” <sup>39</sup>But Jesus said, “Do not stop him, for no one who does a mighty work in my name will be able soon afterward to speak evil of me. <sup>40</sup>For the one who is not against us is for us. <sup>41</sup>For truly, I say to you, whoever gives you a cup of water to drink because you belong to Christ will by no means lose his reward. <sup>42</sup>“Whoever causes one of these little ones who believe in me to sin, it would be better for him if a great millstone were hung around his neck and he were thrown into the sea. <sup>43</sup>And if your hand causes you to sin, cut it off. It is better for you to enter life crippled than with two hands to go to hell, to the unquenchable fire. <sup>45</sup>And if your foot causes you to sin, cut it off. It is better for you to enter life lame than with two feet to be thrown into hell. <sup>47</sup>And if your eye causes you to sin, tear it out. It is better for you to enter the kingdom of God with one eye than with two eyes to be thrown into hell, <sup>48</sup>‘where their worm does not die and the fire is not quenched.’ <sup>49</sup>For everyone will be salted with fire. <sup>50</sup>Salt is good, but if the salt has lost its saltiness, how will you make it salty again? Have salt in yourselves, and be at peace with one another.”
9.overview:
Mark puts the brightest and the bleakest scenes in his Gospel back to back, and the join is the point.

Six days after telling his disciples he must be killed, Jesus takes three of them up a mountain and stops holding the veil in place. Moses and Elijah stand with him and — Luke tells us — discuss his exodus, which he is about to accomplish at Jerusalem. Peter, terrified, offers to build shelters. A cloud comes down and the Father says the only thing he commands in this Gospel: listen to him. Then the light goes, and they see Jesus only.

And they walk down into a shouting crowd, an argument with the scribes, nine defeated colleagues, and a boy convulsing on the ground. The father has been watching this since the child was small, has pulled him out of fires and out of water, and has just been let down by the disciples — which is where the if you can in his prayer came from. Out of him comes the most honest sentence anybody says to Jesus in the Gospels.

The rest of the chapter is a road and a house. Jesus tells them a second time that he will be handed over and killed; they do not understand and are afraid to ask; and they fill the silence by arguing about which of them is the greatest. So he sits down, picks up a child, and redefines greatness — then warns them, in the most violent language he ever uses, about tripping up the little ones and about keeping anything that is taking them to Gehenna. The chapter ends: be at peace with one another.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–29 — The Transfiguration and the Failure in the Valley
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The mountain (vv. 2–8). Six days after telling them he must be killed, Jesus takes three men up a high mountain and, for a few minutes, stops holding the veil in place. Moses and Elijah stand with him. Peter, terrified, starts talking. A cloud comes down, and a voice says the one thing heaven has ever commanded about him: listen to him.

The descent (vv. 9–13). Coming down, he tells them to keep it quiet until the resurrection — and they go on down the hill privately trying to work out what rising from the dead could possibly mean.

The valley (vv. 14–29). And at the bottom: a crowd, an argument, scribes pressing their advantage, nine defeated disciples, and a father whose son has been convulsing since childhood and who has just watched the professionals fail. Out of his mouth comes the most honest sentence anybody says to Jesus in the Gospels.

Mark has put the brightest and the bleakest scenes in his book back to back on purpose. The glory on the mountain is real. The failure in the valley is real. And the same Christ is in both.
verseByVerse.theology:
What actually happened on the mountain? The word is metamorphōthē — he was transformed, changed in form. And the point is not that something was added to Jesus but that something was, for a moment, no longer withheld.

Set it beside Moses. When Moses came down Sinai his face shone (Ex. 34:29–35), and he had to veil it — but that light was borrowed, reflected off a glory he had stood near, and it faded, which Paul says is exactly why he veiled it (2 Cor. 3:13). Here the light comes out from inside. His clothes go white because of what is underneath them.

So this is not a miracle done to Jesus. It is a brief withdrawal of the ordinariness he had been wearing since Bethlehem — three men allowed to see, for a few minutes, what was true of him every day they had walked beside him without noticing.

And why these two men? Moses is the Law and Elijah the Prophets; between them they are the whole Old Testament, standing on that mountain not to be admired alongside Jesus but to attend on him. Luke tells us what they were discussing: his departure — the word is exodus — which he was about to accomplish at Jerusalem (Luke 9:31). Moses, who led the first one out of Egypt, is talking about the greater one with the man who will lead it, and the road out runs through a cross.

Then they are gone, and Mark writes the sentence the whole scene exists for: they no longer saw anyone with them but Jesus only.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: three men who had seen the glory of God on a mountaintop, walking down into a shouting crowd, a public argument, and nine colleagues who had just failed in front of everybody.

Now: the come-down is the most ordinary experience in the Christian life, and Mark has built the chapter to prepare you for it. The conference ends. The retreat finishes. The Sunday that lifted you is followed by a Monday. And what is waiting at the bottom of the hill is usually not glory but a mess — the same marriage, the same diagnosis, the same argument, the same failure.

Two things to take from how Mark has arranged this. First, the mountain is not the point. Peter wanted to build shelters and stay, and he was told to come down and listen. The vision was given so that three men could go into the valley knowing who was walking beside them.

Second, Jesus goes down. He does not stay in the light. He walks into the shouting, asks what the argument is about, and takes charge of it — and the boy he lifts up off the ground is lifted by the same hands that had shone on the mountain.

verseByVerse.quote: And he said to them, "Truly, I say to you, there are some standing here who will not taste death until they see the kingdom of God after it has come with power."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus said to them: truly, I tell you, some of those standing here will not taste death until they see the kingdom of God having come with power.

Meaning first. Mark 9 climbs a mountain and comes down into a valley. Six days after Jesus first spoke plainly of his death, he takes Peter, James and John up a high mountain, where his glory shines out through his humanity, Moses and Elijah talk with him, and the Father says, This is my beloved Son; listen to him. Below, the nine have failed to free a tormented boy; Jesus delivers him and teaches that such power works only through prayer. On the road he speaks again of his death, and the disciples argue about who is greatest. So he teaches greatness: serve all, welcome the child, do not despise those outside your circle, never trip up a little one, deal ruthlessly with your own sin, and be at peace. The glory of the Son is real, and the road to it runs through the cross.

The setting. This verse belongs with the end of chapter 8. Six days earlier, at Caesarea Philippi, Peter had confessed that Jesus is the Christ. Jesus had then told them for the first time that the Son of Man must be rejected, killed and raised; Peter had tried to talk him out of it and been called Satan; and the whole company had been told to deny themselves and take up a cross. The last thing Jesus said before this verse was that he would come in the glory of his Father with the holy angels (8:38). Now, into that heavy week, he makes a promise.

Truly, I say to you. “Truly” (amēn) at the start of a sentence was Jesus’ own way of speaking, with no real parallel among the rabbis. Others said amen at the end, to agree with what had been said. He says it at the beginning, because what follows needs no one’s agreement to be true.

There are some standing here who will not taste death. Not all; some, a few. To taste death is a Hebrew idiom for dying, a vivid picture of death as a bitter cup that every person must drink. Some of these men will see something before they drink it.

Until they see the kingdom of God after it has come with power. The tense (a perfect participle, elēlythuian) means they will see it as already having come: established, a present reality, not a rumour. And “with power”: not in weakness, as now, hidden like a seed in the ground (4:30–32), but in open demonstration.

Did Jesus promise something that failed? This verse has troubled readers for centuries, and it deserves a straight answer rather than a shrug, because at first glance it looks like a broken promise. Every person standing there has been dead for nearly two thousand years. But the answer lies largely in reading the next sentence. Mark almost never gives precise intervals, and he gives one here: after six days. Then three of the men standing there are taken up a mountain and see the Son of God in unveiled glory. Some standing here will see it, and six days later three of them did.

Where Christians differ: what did they see? Some take it as a promise of the second coming, and conclude Jesus was mistaken about its timing. Others see the fall of Jerusalem in AD 70, or Pentecost. Verdict: Mark places the transfiguration immediately after, six days later (v. 2), where three of those standing there, Peter, James and John, saw the kingdom in power, Jesus in his glory. That is the first and clearest fulfilment, and Peter himself understood it so: he called himself an eyewitness of Christ’s majesty on the holy mountain, and offered it as evidence of the power and coming of the Lord Jesus (2 Peter 1:16–18). But the transfiguration was a preview of something larger. The kingdom came with power in the resurrection, by which Jesus was declared Son of God in power (Romans 1:4), at the ascension, and at Pentecost, all within the lifetime of those standing there. The transfiguration was the foretaste of all of it. Jesus was not mistaken.

What is the kingdom of God? It is God’s rule, his royal reign, arriving in the person of his King. It is not first a place on a map but a reign over people: where Jesus is obeyed as Lord, the kingdom has come. It came in hiddenness when Jesus began to preach (1:15), it came with power at his resurrection and the giving of the Spirit, it grows now as the gospel goes out, and it will come in fullness when he returns and every enemy is put under his feet. So the kingdom is both now and not yet. You enter it now by repentance and faith, and you wait for it to be revealed in glory.

Why make this promise at that moment? Think about the week it was made in. They had been told he would be rejected and killed. Peter had been rebuked in front of them all. They had been told to take up a cross. Into that, Jesus promises that some of them will see the kingdom before they die, and then, within a week, he keeps it. He gave three exhausted, frightened men a sight of the end of the story to carry them through the middle of it. And one of them was still writing about it as an old man facing his own execution.

In a sentence. Jesus promised that some of those with him would live to see the kingdom of God come in power, as three of them did six days later on the mountain.

On a Tuesday. When the promises of God feel a long way off and you have been told to expect a cross, remember that he is not vague about the future because he is unsure of it. Name one thing you are carrying this week because you follow him: a cost at work, a loss, a decision that made life harder. Then set beside it what he has shown you of the end: a risen King, a coming kingdom, an inheritance kept in heaven. The cross is not the end. Glory is promised. Take up the cross (8:34) knowing the kingdom has come in power.

For worship. The Lord who told his friends they must carry a cross did not leave them in the dark about where the road ended. He showed them. He never asks his people to walk by a promise he has not already begun to keep, and he kept this one in six days. The King whose reign was hidden like a seed has risen in power, and the glory three men glimpsed on a mountain is the glory he now wears at the Father’s right hand.

verseByVerse.quote: And after six days Jesus took with him Peter and James and John, and led them up a high mountain by themselves. And he was transfigured before them, and his clothes became radiant, intensely white, as no one on earth could bleach them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Six days later Jesus took Peter, James and John and led them up a high mountain by themselves. He was transfigured before them, and his clothes became dazzling, intensely white, whiter than any bleacher on earth could make them.

And after six days. Mark rarely dates anything, and he dates this. Six days after Caesarea Philippi: six days after Peter’s confession, the first plain word about the cross, and the hardest rebuke in the Gospel. And any Jew reading it would hear a second thing. When Moses went up Sinai, the glory of the LORD dwelt on the mountain and the cloud covered it six days, and on the seventh day God called to Moses out of the midst of the cloud (Exodus 24:16). Six days of waiting, then the voice from the cloud. Mark is telling you what kind of scene this is before it starts. The whole passage is full of Sinai.

Peter and James and John. The inner circle again: the same three who were in the room when the little girl was raised (5:37), and the same three who will be taken further into the garden at Gethsemane (14:33). Moses too took named companions up his mountain (Exodus 24:1, 9). But notice the syllabus. The men chosen to see him in glory are the men chosen to see him in agony. Neither sight is complete without the other, and the Lord does not give the first without eventually asking them to watch the second.

Why did Jesus take only three? Not because he loved the others less or because the three were better men. Peter would deny him and James and John would ask for the best seats. It was his free choice, and Scripture never explains it except by the purposes it served: these three would be witnesses, and the law required two or three witnesses to establish a matter (Deuteronomy 19:15). If you are not given the experiences others seem to have, the remedy is not envy. Their testimony was given for you too. Peter wrote it down so that you would have it (2 Peter 1:15–16).

And led them up a high mountain by themselves. Mark does not name it. Tradition since the fourth century has said Mount Tabor in Galilee, but Tabor is not high (about 1,900 feet, 575 m) and probably had a fortress on its summit in Jesus’ day. Mount Hermon, about 9,200 feet (2,800 m), snow-covered much of the year and near Caesarea Philippi where they had just been, fits better. Either way the point is the isolation: up, and away, and alone. Mountains in Scripture are places of revelation: Sinai, Carmel, Zion.

And he was transfigured before them. The word is metemorphōthē, from which comes our “metamorphosis”: changed in form. Luke says the appearance of his face was altered (Luke 9:29); Matthew, that his face shone like the sun (Matthew 17:2). And the crucial thing to grasp is that nothing was added. This is not a miracle performed on Jesus, as though heaven had turned a light on him. It is a withdrawal: for a few minutes the ordinariness he had worn since Bethlehem stopped being held in place, and the disciples saw the glory he had with the Father before the world existed (John 17:5), and the glory he would wear after his resurrection. John, who was there, would later write: we have seen his glory (John 1:14).

Borrowed light and native light. Set it beside Moses, because Mark expects you to. When Moses came down Sinai his face shone, and he had to put a veil over it (Exodus 34:29–35). But that light was borrowed. He had stood near a glory and carried some of it away, and it faded, which Paul says is exactly why he covered it (2 Corinthians 3:7–13). Here the veil is the flesh, and the glory is inside it. Jesus’ glory was not reflected. It shone from within. They had walked beside this man for months, eaten with him, watched him sleep in a boat, seen him tired, and the whole time this was what was underneath.

Was Jesus less divine when he was not shining? No. He was fully God and fully man the whole time, in the carpenter’s shop and asleep in the boat as much as on the mountain. When the Son took our nature he did not lay aside his deity; he veiled its glory. Paul says he emptied himself by taking the form of a servant (Philippians 2:7), not by subtracting anything from what he was but by adding what he was not. The transfiguration did not make him more divine for a few minutes. It let three men see what had been true all along. That is why the ordinary-looking Jesus of the rest of the Gospel can be trusted and worshipped: the one who wept and hungered is the same one who shone.

And his clothes became radiant, intensely white. “Radiant” (stilbonta) means glistening, gleaming like polished metal. White is the colour of heaven, of purity and of divine glory: the Ancient of Days had clothing white as snow (Daniel 7:9). Mark keeps his eye where a frightened man’s would go, on the garment, and the light was coming through it from underneath.

As no one on earth could bleach them. A homely detail, very probably Peter’s own. The word for bleaching is the technical term for the fuller’s trade: the cloth-dresser who washed and whitened wool, the best whitener anyone in that village knew. And Mark says: not like that. He reaches for the only comparison a fisherman had and admits it will not do. Nothing on earth does this. It was not of this world.

What does this mean for me? Paul uses the very same verb for what happens to Christians. Be transformed by the renewal of your mind (Romans 12:2); we all, beholding the glory of the Lord, are being transformed into the same image from one degree of glory to another (2 Corinthians 3:18). What broke out of him on that mountain is what is being worked into us, slowly, all our lives, as we look at him in his word. And at his appearing it will be finished: we shall be like him, because we shall see him as he is (1 John 3:2). The change in you is real even when it is slow, and it has a destination.

In a sentence. On a high mountain, Jesus was changed before Peter, James and John, his divine glory shining out so that even his clothes became a heavenly white.

On a Tuesday. You will not see this sight this week. But you can do what Paul says changes us: behold him. Before the day fills, read one Gospel scene slowly and ask, who is this, and what does it show me of his glory? Then carry that picture into the ordinary hours, because the man who shone is the man who walks with you through them. And when you feel how little you have changed, remember that glory is being worked in by degrees, and that he who began it will finish it.

For worship. The Jesus you pray to is this glorious Lord. The one who washed feet and slept in a boat and was nailed to a beam is the one whose garments outshone the sun, and the glory was his own, not lent. He hid it so that he could reach us, and he will not hide it for ever. One day believers will be changed into his likeness, by the same word Mark uses here, and will see without a veil the face that three fishermen saw for a few minutes on a mountain.
verseByVerse.note: The mountain is unnamed; tradition says Tabor, but Hermon, near Caesarea Philippi, is also suggested. A fuller bleached and whitened cloth.

verseByVerse.quote: And there appeared to them Elijah with Moses, and they were talking with Jesus.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Elijah appeared to them with Moses, and they were talking with Jesus.

And there appeared to them Elijah with Moses. Two men, dead or departed for centuries, standing on a mountainside in Galilee, in conversation. Mark names Elijah first, perhaps because Elijah is the subject of the conversation that follows (vv. 11–13). Together they represent the whole Old Testament: Moses the giver of the Law, and Elijah the greatest of the prophets. The Law and the Prophets bear witness to Jesus (Luke 24:27; Romans 3:21), and here they do it in person.

What this says about death. Take the fact before the symbolism, because it is easy to move to the meaning and miss what is being said about the dead. Moses died on Nebo and God buried him (Deuteronomy 34:5–6). Elijah went up in a whirlwind and did not die at all (2 Kings 2:11). Both of them are here, alive, recognisable, and busy. Whatever happens to the people of God when they leave this world, it is not extinction and it is not an unconscious sleep. They are alive to God (12:26–27), and they have things to discuss.

Why these two? Both met God on Sinai, also called Horeb (Exodus 24; 1 Kings 19:8), and both had unusual ends, one buried by God in a grave no one knows, the other taken up alive. Both were expected, in Jewish hope, to have a role at the end: the prophet like Moses (Deuteronomy 18:15), and Elijah before the day of the Lord (Malachi 4:4–5, named together on the last page of the Old Testament). Moses asked to see God’s glory and was hidden in a cleft of the rock while the glory passed by (Exodus 33:18–23). Elijah, fleeing for his life, stood at the mouth of a cave on the same mountain while the LORD passed by (1 Kings 19:8–13). The two men in all Scripture who had asked to see the glory of God and been given a glimpse of it are standing on another mountain, looking straight at it. They asked to see. Now they see, and it has a face and a name and is going to Jerusalem to die.

And they were talking with Jesus. Mark leaves the conversation unreported. Luke does not: they spoke of his departure, which he was about to accomplish at Jerusalem (Luke 9:31), and the word Luke uses is exodos. Sit with that. Moses led the first exodus: the blood on the doorposts, the sea opened, a nation walking out of slavery. And here he is, discussing the greater one with the man who will lead it, and this exodus will be accomplished not by a sea but by a cross, and the blood will not be a lamb’s. Six days ago Peter tried to talk Jesus out of the cross. Now the Law and the Prophets appear in glory and talk about nothing else.

What it does not mean. Not that the dead can be consulted. Scripture forbids it absolutely (Deuteronomy 18:10–12), and this was God’s act, not a séance; no one on the mountain summoned anyone. Nor that Moses and Elijah were equal to Jesus, as the next verses make clear. They have not come to be admired alongside him. They have come to attend on him. But it does show that the faithful dead are alive to God now, before the resurrection.

Will I know my loved ones in heaven? This scene gives real grounds for hope that you will. Moses and Elijah were themselves, recognisable, and the disciples knew who they were without being introduced. Death does not dissolve the person God made. The believer who dies is with Christ, which is far better (Philippians 1:23), awaiting the resurrection of the body. Scripture does not answer every question about what that life is like, but it never suggests that we become strangers to one another. What it promises above all is that we will know him, and in knowing him we will not lose those who are his.

In a sentence. Moses and Elijah, representing the Law and the Prophets, appeared and talked with Jesus about the death he was about to accomplish.

On a Tuesday. Read your Old Testament as Moses and Elijah spoke on the mountain: it is all about Jesus.
