When you read a law, a sacrifice, a prophet’s cry, ask where it points, and you will find it points to a cross. And if you have buried a believer you love, let this verse sit beside the grave. They are not gone into nothing. They are alive to God, and the conversation they are part of is about the Lamb.

For worship. The whole of the Old Testament came to that mountain to bow. The lawgiver who could not enter the land and the prophet who thought he was the only faithful man left stood beside the One they had both been waiting for, and the subject they chose was his death. Heaven’s greatest saints are not interested in themselves. They are absorbed in the exodus he accomplished at Jerusalem, and the song of Moses has become the song of the Lamb.
verseByVerse.note: Moses and Elijah stand for the Law and the Prophets.

verseByVerse.quote: And Peter said to Jesus, "Rabbi, it is good that we are here. Let us make three tents, one for you and one for Moses and one for Elijah." For he did not know what to say, for they were terrified.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Peter said to Jesus: Rabbi, it is good that we are here. Let us make three tents, one for you, one for Moses and one for Elijah. He did not know what to say, for they were terrified.

Rabbi, it is good that we are here. Peter is not wrong about that. It is good that they are there, and there is nothing to criticise in the gladness. But “Rabbi”, teacher, falls far short of what he has just seen. And then he keeps going.

Let us make three tents. The word is skēnas: booths, shelters of branches. It also means tabernacles, like the tabernacle in the wilderness where God’s glory dwelt among Israel (Exodus 40:34). Peter very likely had the Feast of Booths in mind, when Israel lived in leafy shelters for a week to remember the wilderness, and which the prophets had made a picture of the age to come, when God would dwell with his people at last (Zechariah 14:16–19). So Peter is thinking: this is it. The glory has come, the great ones have arrived, the age of God dwelling with men is beginning. Let us set up and stay.

One for you and one for Moses and one for Elijah. Three things are wrong with it. He wants to stay: six days ago he heard that the Son of Man must suffer and be killed, and he objected; now, on a mountain full of light, his instinct is to make the moment permanent. It is the same instinct in a nicer form: anything but the road down. He wants to build something: faced with the unveiled glory of God, his impulse is to get busy, to organise, to be useful, when the moment called him simply to stand still and behold. And he makes it three: equal accommodation, equal honour. It is the kindest possible mistake and it is still a mistake, and the voice from the cloud is about to correct precisely that.

Jesus in a row of great men. Notice that Peter’s error is not disbelief. He is being warm, reverent, hospitable and enthusiastic. He is also arranging the Son of God as one of three, and that is a thing people still do: Jesus placed respectfully in a line of great teachers, given his own shelter, honoured among the founders of the world’s religions. He fits nowhere in such a row. He is not the best of the prophets. He is the one the prophets came to see.

For he did not know what to say, for they were terrified. Mark’s editorial note is one of the most human sentences in the Gospel, and remember whose memory this is. Peter is the source. This is a man, thirty years later, telling the church: I had no idea what to say, so I said something. “Terrified” (ekphoboi) means overcome with fear, the natural response of sinners in the presence of divine glory (Isaiah 6:5). He was standing in undisguised glory, the silence was unbearable, and words came out.

Filling the silence. It is one of our most reliable failures. In the presence of something too large, real glory, real grief, real suffering, the impulse is to fill the space. Job’s friends were faultless for seven days while they said nothing, and ruined it the moment they opened their mouths. At a graveside, at a hospital bed, in the presence of God himself, the pressure to produce a sentence is enormous and it is almost always better resisted. Be still, and know that I am God (Psalm 46:10). Peter could not be still, and Mark did not hide it.

Is it wrong to want to stay on the mountain? Not to love it. The longing to remain in God’s presence is holy, and it will be fully satisfied in the age to come, when God will dwell with his people and the tabernacle will be permanent (Revelation 21:3). Peter’s mistake was timing. He wanted the glory without the cross, and the end before the road. So treasure the moments of nearness God gives you, in worship, in Scripture, at the Lord’s Table, and do not despise them. But do not try to live in them. They are given to strengthen you for the valley, not to excuse you from it.

In a sentence. Terrified and not knowing what to say, Peter proposed making three shelters, putting Jesus alongside Moses and Elijah and wanting to keep the glory without the cross.

On a Tuesday. When God’s presence is overwhelming, it is better to be silent than to fill the silence with nonsense (Ecclesiastes 5:2), and the same is true at a friend’s sickbed. And watch for the quiet temptation to keep Jesus as one honoured figure among several in your life, alongside your career, your family, your causes. He will not share a row.

For worship. Peter wanted to build the Lord a shelter, and the Lord was about to build Peter one: not of branches but of his own body, broken and raised, the true tabernacle in which God dwells with men for ever. The Son of God bore with a frightened fisherman’s nonsense in the very hour of his glory, and did not withdraw. He has always been patient with the foolish words of people who love him.
verseByVerse.note: The tents may recall the Feast of Booths.

verseByVerse.quote: And a cloud overshadowed them, and a voice came out of the cloud, "This is my beloved Son; listen to him." And suddenly, looking around, they no longer saw anyone with them but Jesus only.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A cloud overshadowed them, and a voice came from the cloud: This is my beloved Son; listen to him. Suddenly, looking around, they no longer saw anyone with them but Jesus only.

And a cloud overshadowed them. The cloud is not weather. Any reader of the Old Testament knows this cloud. It went before Israel out of Egypt (Exodus 13:21), settled on Sinai (Exodus 24:15–18), filled the tabernacle so that Moses could not enter, and came down on Solomon’s temple so that the priests could not stand to minister (Exodus 40:34–35; 1 Kings 8:10–11). It is the visible sign that God himself has come down, what later Jewish writers called the Shekinah, the dwelling. And “overshadowed” (episkiazousa) is the word used in the Greek Old Testament of the cloud settling on the tabernacle (Exodus 40:35), and the very word the angel used to Mary: the power of the Most High will overshadow you (Luke 1:35). So Peter, who wanted to build three shelters, is enveloped in the real one. God does not need his branches. He has brought his own dwelling, and it has covered them.

And a voice came out of the cloud. The Father speaks, as at the baptism (1:11). They are the only two times in Mark that God speaks from heaven, and the words are almost the same. At the Jordan the voice spoke to Jesus: You are my beloved Son. Here it is: This is. The same testimony, turned outward, addressed to three men standing there. God is telling somebody else who this is.

This is my beloved Son. This answers Peter’s mistake. Jesus is not one of three equals; he is the Son. Moses was faithful in all God’s house as a servant; Christ is faithful over God’s house as a son (Hebrews 3:5–6). “Beloved” may also carry the sense of only, as with Abraham’s only son Isaac, whom he loved and was told to offer on a mountain (Genesis 22:2). And consider the timing. The Father’s public endorsement comes six days after the Son announced that he was going to be rejected and killed, precisely at the point where the plan looks like failure, as if to say: this is the one I love, and the road he has just described is the road I sent him down.

Listen to him. Three words, and they are the only command God the Father gives in the whole Gospel of Mark. Everything the Almighty has to say to these men, at the height of the greatest vision they will ever be given, is: listen to him. Not build for him, which is what Peter proposed. Not feel something, which is what the moment was producing. Not stay here. Listen. There is an echo underneath it that Moses would have recognised, since he is standing there: God would raise up a prophet like him, and to him you shall listen (Deuteronomy 18:15). The voice from the cloud is telling three Jewish fishermen that the promise has arrived.

Listen to him about what? About the last thing he said, which they had refused to accept. The command is aimed straight at the argument at Caesarea Philippi. Jesus had said he must suffer and die (8:31), and that they must take up their cross (8:34), and Peter had rebuked him for it. The Father says: do not correct him; hear him. Whatever else God wants from you, this is what he has said out loud: listen to his Son. Not to your instincts about what the Christian life ought to look like. Not to the version of Jesus you find manageable. To him, including the parts you would rather he had not said.

How do I listen to Jesus today? Through his word. The Son spoke in the days of his flesh, and he speaks now by the Spirit through the Scriptures he gave, the Old Testament that bears witness to him and the New Testament written by the apostles he sent. You do not need a voice from a cloud, and you should not wait for one or trust a voice that contradicts what is written. God has spoken to us by his Son (Hebrews 1:1–2), and that word is complete. Listening means reading and hearing it preached with the intention of obeying, especially where it costs.

And suddenly, looking around, they no longer saw anyone with them but Jesus only. The cloud lifts. Moses is gone. Elijah is gone. The light is gone. And Mark writes the phrase the whole scene exists for: Jesus only. The Law has done its work and stepped back. The Prophets have done theirs and stepped back. Everything Israel had been given for fifteen hundred years was pointing at this man, and when he is fully in view the pointers are not needed. What is left standing is what was there before the vision began and will be there after every vision any Christian ever has: an ordinary-looking man from Nazareth, who is the Son of God, and no one else. And he is enough.

In a sentence. God’s presence came in the cloud and the Father declared Jesus his beloved Son and commanded the disciples to listen to him, and then they saw Jesus alone.

On a Tuesday. Above every other voice, even the greatest teachers and the best traditions, God says of Jesus: listen to him. Open his word today, and before you read, ask him to show you one thing to obey. Then notice where you are most tempted to argue with him: about money, about forgiveness, about suffering, about your plans. That is the place the Father’s command is aimed at.

For worship. The cloud that once filled the tabernacle came down on a mountain and wrapped itself around a man from Nazareth, and the Father could not keep his love to himself. Moses had begged to see the glory and been hidden in a rock while it passed; now the glory stood in the open with a human face, and the voice that once shook Sinai said only, hear him. The eternal delight of the Father rests on the Son, and everything God has to say to a lost world he has spoken in him.
verseByVerse.note: The cloud recalls the cloud of God’s presence at Sinai and over the tabernacle.

parallels.desc: it is to him you shall listen

verseByVerse.quote: And as they were coming down the mountain, he charged them to tell no one what they had seen, until the Son of Man had risen from the dead. So they kept the matter to themselves, questioning what this rising from the dead might mean.
verseByVerse.commentary:
As they were coming down the mountain, he ordered them to tell no one what they had seen until the Son of Man had risen from the dead. So they kept the matter to themselves, discussing what this rising from the dead might mean.

And as they were coming down the mountain. A phrase worth pausing on before its content. They came down. Peter wanted to stay; the shelters were never built; and within a paragraph the three of them are back in a shouting crowd. Nobody lives on the mountain. The vision is given for the valley.

He charged them to tell no one what they had seen. Not even the other nine. The silence again, but this is the first time in Mark that the ban has an expiry date, and that changes it entirely. Everything so far has been tell no one, full stop. Now it is tell no one until.

Until the Son of Man had risen from the dead. The only time Jesus sets a limit on the secret, and the limit is the resurrection. Which tells you what the secret was always for. It was never permanent concealment. It was timing: the truth about him kept back until there was a cross and an empty tomb to define it, because a glorious Christ preached without a crucified one produces exactly the kind of conquering Messiah Peter had in mind six days ago. Had those three gone down and told the crowds, the story would have been the wrong story, with no cross in it. After the resurrection the glory can be told, because then it will be understood. And Peter did tell it (2 Peter 1:16–18).

So they kept the matter to themselves. They obeyed, and for once in this Gospel an instruction to be quiet is kept, which nobody else in Mark manages. But they were puzzled.

Questioning what this rising from the dead might mean. These are the three. They have just watched the Son of God shining, heard the voice of the Father, and seen two prophets alive on a mountainside, and they walk down the hill arguing quietly about what he could possibly mean by rising from the dead. It is not that they disbelieved in resurrection as such. Jews who believed in it, as the Pharisees did, expected it at the end of the age, for all the righteous together (Daniel 12:2; John 11:24). What they could not fit together was a Messiah who dies and then, alone, in the middle of history, gets up. There was no category for it. And they could not grasp that the Messiah must die at all.

A story nobody invented. This is quietly one of the strongest arguments that the resurrection was not made up. Men do not fabricate a story they were manifestly not expecting, had no framework for, and did not understand when it was explained to them in advance. Mark records their bafflement without embarrassment, because it is what happened.

What if I have read something many times and still do not understand it? Then you are in good company, and it is not necessarily unbelief. These three heard the words plainly and could not take them in. Sometimes a truth is bigger than the categories you have, and it will not fit until something makes room for it. For them it was an empty tomb; for you it may be years of reading, a trial, or a sermon that suddenly joins two passages. Keep reading, keep asking, and read with the cross and resurrection in view, because they are the key that opens the rest.

In a sentence. Jesus ordered the three to keep the vision secret until he had risen from the dead, and they obeyed, puzzling over what rising from the dead could mean.

On a Tuesday. Some things in Scripture make sense only in the light of the cross and resurrection. When a passage puzzles you, ask how it looks from Easter morning. And if you came down from a Sunday or a retreat where God was near, expect the valley on Monday, and do not take the come-down as proof that the mountain was false.

For worship. The Son of Man knew exactly where the road went, and he spoke of his own rising as calmly as of his death. He was not guessing. He kept the glory quiet until the tomb was empty, because he would not have us know him as anything but the crucified and risen Lord. Every truth about him is now unlocked by that morning, and the slowest disciple can sing it.

verseByVerse.quote: And they asked him, "Why do the scribes say that first Elijah must come?" And he said to them, "Elijah does come first to restore all things. And how is it written of the Son of Man that he should suffer many things and be treated with contempt? But I tell you that Elijah has come, and they did to him whatever they pleased, as it is written of him."
verseByVerse.commentary:
They asked him: why do the scribes say that Elijah must come first? He said: Elijah does come first to restore all things. And how is it written of the Son of Man that he must suffer many things and be treated with contempt? But I tell you that Elijah has come, and they did to him whatever they pleased, as it is written of him.

Why do the scribes say that first Elijah must come? The question follows naturally: they have just seen Elijah. The scribes taught it from the last page of the Old Testament: Behold, I will send you Elijah the prophet before the great and awesome day of the LORD comes (Malachi 4:5). Elijah comes first, to turn hearts and prepare the people; then the Day. So if Elijah has only now appeared, to three men in private, where does that leave the timetable? And more sharply: if you are the Messiah, where was the forerunner? There was probably an objection buried in it, of the kind the scribes were no doubt already making: you cannot be the Christ, because Elijah has not come.

Elijah does come first to restore all things. Jesus grants the doctrine. The scribes are right about the sequence. Malachi was right: Elijah comes first, and his work is restoration, turning the hearts of fathers to their children and of children to their fathers (Malachi 4:6).

And how is it written of the Son of Man that he should suffer many things and be treated with contempt? Then, in the middle of answering, he turns a question back on them, and it is the more important one. Since you are so attentive to what is written about Elijah, what have you done with what is written about the Son of Man? “Treated with contempt” (exoudenēthē) means regarded as nothing. And he assumes they know where it is written. He was despised and rejected by men, a man of sorrows (Isaiah 53:3); all who see me mock me (Psalm 22:7); the stone the builders rejected (Psalm 118:22); they will look on him whom they have pierced (Zechariah 12:10). A nation had built a Messiah out of the conquering passages and quietly stepped over the suffering ones. Both are true. The forerunner’s restoration did not prevent the Messiah’s rejection.

The verses we skip. That is a permanent temptation, not an ancient one. We assemble a picture of God from the verses we like and treat the rest as background noise: the promises without the warnings, the comfort without the cost, the Jesus who accepts without the Jesus who commands. Jesus’ question is the corrective, and it is uncomfortable precisely because it appeals to Scripture they already had.

But I tell you that Elijah has come. The forerunner has already been and gone, and they missed him, because he did not look like Elijah returned in fire. He looked like a man in camel’s hair by a river, dressed like Elijah himself (1:6; 2 Kings 1:8). Matthew says the disciples understood that he was speaking of John the Baptist (Matthew 17:13), and the angel had said it before John was born: he would go before the Lord in the spirit and power of Elijah (Luke 1:17).

Was John the Baptist Elijah come back? Not in person. When asked directly, John said he was not Elijah (John 1:21), and he was right: he was not the Tishbite returned from heaven, and Scripture gives no support to the idea of souls returning in new bodies. But he came in Elijah’s spirit and power and did Elijah’s work. Malachi’s promise was fulfilled not by reappearance but by a new prophet in the old mould. So both statements are true: John was not Elijah, and Elijah has come.

And they did to him whatever they pleased, as it is written of him. Herod arrested and beheaded him, and his head was carried into a banquet on a dish because a girl danced well (6:17–29). As Jezebel had sought to kill the first Elijah (1 Kings 19:2), so Herodias destroyed the second. As it is written of him points not to a single prophecy of John’s death but to the pattern of Elijah’s life in Scripture: a prophet persecuted by a wicked king and queen.

The herald and the King. See what Jesus has actually done with this exchange, because it is not a lesson in prophetic chronology. He has said: the forerunner came, and they killed him. And in the same breath he has asked what is written about the Son of Man suffering. The pattern of the herald is the pattern of the King. They did to John whatever they pleased; they will do the same to me. He is walking down that mountain with the glory barely faded off him, telling three men that the road runs the same way it ran for John.

In a sentence. Jesus affirmed that Elijah must come first, explained that he had already come in John the Baptist and been killed, and said that the Son of Man must likewise suffer.

On a Tuesday. God’s plan often looks like failure: a murdered prophet, a crucified Messiah, a faithful Christian passed over or mocked. Trust Scripture’s pattern: suffering before glory. And when you read your Bible this week, read the parts you usually skip. Ask what you have done with the hard verses, and let them stand beside the sweet ones.

For worship. Every word written of the Son of Man came true, the contempt and the suffering as surely as the glory. He did not walk into his death by accident. He read it in his own Scriptures and walked toward it with open eyes, because those same Scriptures said it would bring many sons to glory. The Christ the scribes could not imagine, crowned with thorns, is the only Christ who could save us.
verseByVerse.note: Elijah, in Jesus’ words, is John the Baptist.

verseByVerse.quote: And when they came to the disciples, they saw a great crowd around them, and scribes arguing with them. And immediately all the crowd, when they saw him, were greatly amazed and ran up to him and greeted him. And he asked them, "What are you arguing about with them?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
When they came back to the other disciples, they saw a great crowd around them and scribes arguing with them. As soon as the crowd saw Jesus, they were greatly amazed, ran to him and greeted him. He asked: what are you arguing about with them?

From the mountain to the valley. Mark’s cut is deliberate and brutal. The previous verse has them on the mountainside with the light barely gone. This one has them at the bottom, walking into noise. Raphael’s last painting puts the transfigured Christ in the upper half of the canvas and this scene in the lower, the convulsing boy and the pointing hands, because the two belong in one frame. As Moses came down from Sinai to find Israel dancing round the golden calf (Exodus 32), Jesus comes down to find faithlessness (v. 19). The glory of the mountain does not take Jesus away from the misery of the world; it sends him into it.

They saw a great crowd around them, and scribes arguing with them. A great crowd: this is public. Scribes, the professional opponents, who have found the disciples in a failure and are pressing it in front of everybody, probably to discredit their master. Nine men are standing there having promised something and not delivered it, with a sick child on the ground and their critics in full voice. That is what was waiting at the bottom of the hill.

The come-down. It is such a common experience that it needs saying plainly: the come-down is not a sign that the mountain was false. Peter, James and John had genuinely seen the glory of God, and it did not exempt them from walking into a shouting match. The retreat ends and Monday arrives with nothing changed. That is not evidence that God was absent on the mountain. It is the shape of the Christian life, and Mark has arranged his Gospel to prepare you for it.

Were greatly amazed and ran up to him and greeted him. The whole crowd turns. Mark’s word (exethambēthēsan) is strong: utterly astonished, overwhelmed, a word only he uses, and from the same root as the women’s alarm at the empty tomb (16:5–6). Why so startled? Mark does not say. Some think something of the glory still lingered on him, as Moses’ face shone when he came down (Exodus 34:29–30), though here people ran toward him rather than away. It may simply be the shock of his arrival at the exact moment of a public humiliation. Either way, the argument stops and everybody runs.

What are you arguing about with them? With one question he takes possession of the scene. Notice what he does not do. He does not upbraid the nine in front of the crowd. He asks what the argument is about, and by asking he moves himself into the middle of it, and the scribes are now arguing with him. He steps between his failed disciples and the men attacking them, and that is the first act of the rescue. Whatever he has to say to the nine he will say inside a house, privately, at the end (v. 28).

In a sentence. Coming down from the mountain, Jesus found his disciples in an argument with the scribes before a crowd, and stepped in.

On a Tuesday. Mountaintop experiences are given to equip us for the valley. Expect to come down to ordinary need and difficulty, and go into it as he did, toward the trouble rather than away from it. And if you lead or correct others, learn from how he handled the nine: he defended them in public and dealt with them in private.

For worship. He came down. The Son who had just heard the Father’s voice and worn the glory of heaven walked straight into a crowd of critics and a child in torment, and he did not hold himself aloof. He took his disciples’ shame on himself and stood between them and their accusers. That is what he has always done for his people, and on a cross he did it finally.

verseByVerse.quote: And someone from the crowd answered him, "Teacher, I brought my son to you, for he has a spirit that makes him mute. And whenever it seizes him, it throws him down, and he foams and grinds his teeth and becomes rigid. So I asked your disciples to cast it out, and they were not able."
verseByVerse.commentary:
A man from the crowd answered: Teacher, I brought my son to you, because he has a spirit that makes him mute. Whenever it seizes him, it throws him down, and he foams at the mouth, grinds his teeth and goes rigid. I asked your disciples to cast it out, and they could not.

Someone from the crowd answered him. Not the scribes, though the question was addressed to them. Not the disciples. A man in the crowd, almost anonymous, the only person present who is not interested in the argument.

Teacher, I brought my son to you. Three things in that little sentence. Teacher: the smallest title in the chapter; he has no theology of who Jesus is. I brought my son: he has done the one thing available to him, and carried the boy here. Luke adds that he was his only child (Luke 9:38). And to you: this is the ache under everything he says. He came looking for Jesus, and Jesus was up a mountain, and he got the disciples instead.

For he has a spirit that makes him mute. The boy cannot speak, and verse 25 adds that he cannot hear either. He has never told his father what it is like.

It throws him down, and he foams and grinds his teeth and becomes rigid. The father describes it, and the detail is unbearable because it is a father’s detail. He has watched this many times. He knows the sequence: the seizure, the fall, the foam, the teeth, and then the body going rigid and spent. The symptoms resemble epilepsy, and Matthew uses a word for it, literally moonstruck (Matthew 17:15). But Mark is clear that the cause here was a demon, which Jesus addresses and casts out (v. 25). The two are not exclusive: a demon could cause physical symptoms. Not all illness is demonic, and the Gospels distinguish them, listing the sick and the demonised separately (1:32–34). But this case was.

Should seizures or mental illness be treated as possession? No, and it must not be made to follow from this passage. That inference has done immense harm to suffering people, and the Bible does not license it. Scripture routinely distinguishes ordinary illness from demonic affliction; this is a specific case in which the two were bound together, and Jesus knew it because he knows all things. We do not. If your child has epilepsy, this passage is not a diagnosis. Take them to a doctor, which is an ordinary mercy of God, and pray for them, which is another. Medicine and prayer are not rivals.

So I asked your disciples to cast it out, and they were not able. The last clause is said quietly and it is the hinge of everything that follows. There is no accusation in it. He simply reports the fact, and the fact has done its damage. It was a painful failure: Jesus had given them authority over unclean spirits (6:7), and they had cast out many demons (6:13). Now they could not. Jesus will give the reason in verses 19 and 29: unbelief, and prayerlessness.

To you, and not to them. The father’s little phrase holds the lesson of the valley. He came for Jesus and found only his followers, and the followers could not do what their Master does. Their authority had always been his, lent and never owned. That is why the story does not end with the nine. What the servants could not do, the Master will do with one sentence. The church can fail a sufferer; Christ never has, and the father’s to you was aimed at the right person all along.

What if I am caring for someone who cannot be fixed? Then this man is in your Bible on purpose. He has spent years watching his child thrown to the ground. He has never had a conversation with him. He has lifted him off floors, cleaned him up and lived with the sound of it, and Jesus is about to give him a great deal of time. Your long, unseen labour is known to the Lord, and he is not impatient with your weariness or your questions. Bring the one you care for to him, as this father did, again and again. And if the church has let you down, do not let that become your final word about Christ.

In a sentence. The father described his son’s violent possession by a mute spirit, and the disciples’ failure to cast it out.

On a Tuesday. Past success in ministry is no guarantee for today; every work depends freshly on God. Think of someone near you who is carrying a long burden, a sick child, a disabled spouse, an ageing parent, and do one concrete thing for them this week: a meal, an hour so they can sleep, a message that says you are praying. The church should not be the place that could not help.

For worship. A father brought his only son to the Son, and the Son had come down from the mountain to meet him. The beloved of the Father did not keep his glory on the heights. He carried it into a shouting crowd and spent it on a boy who had never spoken a word. He asks for no impressive case and no eloquent prayer; a man with no theology and a child on the ground were enough to stop the Lord of heaven. The compassion that met this father on a hillside meets every weary carer who calls on his name.

verseByVerse.quote: And he answered them, "O faithless generation, how long am I to be with you? How long am I to bear with you? Bring him to me."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus answered them: O faithless generation, how long am I to be with you? How long am I to bear with you? Bring him to me.

O faithless generation. This is one of the sharpest things Jesus says in the whole Gospel, and it needs handling carefully, because a hasty reading turns it into impatience with a suffering father, which it is not. “Faithless” (apistos) means without faith, unbelieving. Mark says he answered them, plural, and the address is to a generation, not a man. It takes in the nine who failed, the scribes who were arguing, and the crowd who came to watch. It is not aimed at the father, who is the one person there doing the right thing. The words echo God’s own complaint against Israel in the wilderness: a crooked generation, children in whom is no faithfulness (Deuteronomy 32:5, 20).

How long am I to be with you? How long am I to bear with you? And the tone is not irritation at inconvenience. It is God’s language. The LORD in the wilderness said: How long will this people despise me? And how long will they not believe in me, in spite of all the signs? (Numbers 14:11). It is the grief of a God who has done everything and been believed by almost nobody. “Bear with” (anexomai) means put up with, endure. It shows the real cost to Jesus of living among sinners, even his own disciples. And there is a shadow of the cross in it: he is not going to be with them much longer, and he knows it. A man measuring the time he has left against the slowness of the people he is leaving it with.

Bring him to me. Now notice what comes next, because it is the whole character of Christ in four words. The rebuke ends and the rescue begins in the same breath. He does not say: come back when you have more faith. He does not refuse to act in an atmosphere of unbelief, or make the healing conditional on an improvement in the general standard. Where the disciples failed, he does not. Whatever his grief, he does not turn the child away.

Does Jesus get tired of me? He feels the weight of unbelief; this verse proves it, and you should not make his patience cheap. But look at what his weariness does. It does not withdraw; it calls the boy over. His patience is not a fuse that will one day run out on a believer who keeps coming. It is the patience of the God who passed before Moses as merciful and gracious, slow to anger, abounding in steadfast love (Exodus 34:6). If you have hesitated to bring something to him because you were ashamed of the state of your faith, this chapter holds a hard word about unbelief and an immediate invitation, spoken by the same voice. The rebuke is real. It is not a refusal.

In a sentence. Grieved by the unbelief all around him, Jesus cried out at how long he must bear with them, and then called for the boy to be brought to him.

On a Tuesday. When others have failed to help, and you have failed too, there is still one word: bring him to me. Name the person or situation you have given up on, and bring it to him in prayer today, not when your faith is stronger. And when other people disappoint you, remember how much he bears with you, and bear with them.

For worship. The Holy One endured the unbelief of the people he came to save, felt every bit of it, and still said, bring him to me. He bore with them in Galilee, and at the cross he bore far more than their slowness: he bore their sin. His grief over our faithlessness has never once become a closed door. It is the sorrow of a love that will not let go.

parallels.desc: a perverse generation, children in whom is no faithfulness

verseByVerse.quote: And they brought the boy to him. And when the spirit saw him, immediately it convulsed the boy, and he fell on the ground and rolled about, foaming at the mouth. And Jesus asked his father, "How long has this been happening to him?" And he said, "From childhood. And it has often cast him into fire and into water, to destroy him. But if you can do anything, have compassion on us and help us."
verseByVerse.commentary:
They brought the boy to him. When the spirit saw Jesus, it immediately convulsed the boy, and he fell on the ground and rolled around, foaming at the mouth. Jesus asked the father: how long has this been happening to him? He said: from childhood. It has often thrown him into fire and into water, to destroy him. But if you can do anything, have compassion on us and help us.

And when the spirit saw him. The demon recognises Jesus and reacts with violence. It has been like this since chapter 1: demons know who he is (1:24; 3:11), nothing unclean can be near him and stay quiet, and in their last moments they rage. And there is a hard mercy in the timing, though it will not have felt like it to the father. The worst seizure the boy has, he has in front of Jesus. What had been happening in fields and houses where nobody could help is now happening in the one place where something can be done about it.

And he fell on the ground and rolled about, foaming at the mouth. Mark does not look away, and neither should we. This is a child on the ground in front of a crowd.

And Jesus asked his father, How long has this been happening to him? Now stop, because this question is the most surprising thing in the passage. There is a boy convulsing at his feet. Jesus has silenced a legion and a hurricane with fewer words than this. And he turns to the father and asks about the case history. He does not need the information. So what is the question for? It is for the father. Nobody has asked this man anything. He has carried this alone for years; he has just been let down in front of a crowd; and the Son of God stops the scene and asks him how long it has been going on. Faced with a crisis, we go straight to the problem. He goes to the person, and lets him talk.

From childhood. Two words, and there is a life in them. Not a recent illness. From when he was small. This is a hard case, long established. The father has never heard his son’s voice; the boy has never had a normal day.

It has often cast him into fire and into water, to destroy him. Now he tells the rest, because he has been asked. The open cooking fire in the floor of a village house. The well. The lake. Every hearth and every water jar in that man’s life has been a threat for years, and he has pulled his son out of them often. This father has not slept properly in a decade. And he understands what he is dealing with: to destroy him. He is not describing bad luck. There is an intention behind it. That is Satan’s purpose for every human being: the thief comes only to steal and kill and destroy (John 10:10), and the devil prowls around like a roaring lion, seeking someone to devour (1 Peter 5:8).

But if you can do anything. Read it slowly, because it is the honest condition of a great many people. He did not arrive with that clause. He came looking for the man everyone said could heal, and he found nine followers who could not, and a public argument about it, and now the doubt has got in through the crack their failure made. The disciples’ failure damaged this man’s faith in Christ. And it still works that way. People’s confidence in the Lord is regularly damaged by his people: the church that let them down, the Christian who wronged them, the leader who fell. They come to Christ afterwards with an if you can that was not there before.

Have compassion on us and help us. Not on him; on us. The father identifies himself completely with his son’s suffering. He has been ill for both of them. It is the whole family’s affliction, and he asks for the one thing he knows to ask for: compassion, the word used of Jesus’ own heart for the crowds (6:34).

Why does God allow a child to suffer for years? Scripture does not give us the whole answer, and we should not pretend it does. But this passage gives us what we most need. It names the evil for what it is: not God’s delight but an enemy’s work, aiming at destruction. It shows that the suffering is seen, in detail, by Jesus, who asks about it. And it shows him overthrowing it. God permits evil for a time for purposes he has not fully explained, but he is not its author in the way the destroyer is, and he has not left it unanswered. The final answer is a cross where he took the worst of it upon himself, and a resurrection that promises an end of it.

In a sentence. As the demon threw the boy into a fit, the father told Jesus it had tried for years to destroy him, and asked for help, if Jesus could do anything.

On a Tuesday. Satan’s aim is to destroy. Jesus’ aim is to save. Pray this week by name for someone whose life is being torn apart. And when you are with someone in trouble, copy the Lord’s question: ask them how long it has been, and listen to the answer before you offer anything else.

For worship. The Lord of glory stopped in the middle of a crisis to ask a tired father how long it had been. He knew already, and he asked anyway, because he cares for the whole person and not only the problem. The one who rules the winds also notices the man nobody noticed, and his compassion has room in it for every us that has been carrying a burden too long.

verseByVerse.quote: And Jesus said to him, "'If you can'! All things are possible for one who believes." Immediately the father of the child cried out and said, "I believe; help my unbelief!"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus said to him: “If you can”! All things are possible for one who believes. Immediately the boy’s father cried out: I believe; help my unbelief!

“If you can”! Jesus picks up the man’s own two words and hands them back. The Greek is abrupt: Jesus quotes the phrase and leaves it hanging, and the exclamation mark is right. It is not mockery. It is seizing on the one word in the sentence that does not belong there, and refusing to let it pass. Because the if is in the wrong place. The father has attached it to Jesus’ ability, and there is nothing wrong with Jesus’ ability. The question is not whether Jesus can. The question is whether the father will trust him. Some manuscripts read slightly differently here, but the meaning is the same.

All things are possible for one who believes. Here a note of caution is needed, because this sentence has been made to say something cruel that it does not say. It is not a formula: believe hard enough and you will get what you want. That doctrine has crushed a great many suffering people, who have been told that a diagnosis stands because their faith was insufficient. Faith is not a force that makes things happen. Faith is trust in God, and it is God for whom all things are possible (10:27; 14:36). Faith is empty hands held out to someone who has everything; it links us to his power. The believer does not set limits on what God can do.

Immediately the father of the child cried out. Not just spoke, but cried out, from the depths. This is not a considered theological formulation. It is a shout, from a man beside a convulsing child, with a crowd watching.

I believe; help my unbelief! One of the most honest prayers in the Bible, and only Mark records it. Take the two halves separately. I believe: he will not deny the faith he has. It is real; it is what brought him here. Help my unbelief: and he will not pretend it is more than it is. Instead of manufacturing a confidence he does not feel, he tells the truth: there is unbelief in me, and I am asking you to deal with that too. He does not ask for stronger faith so that he can then qualify. He asks Christ to help the very thing that disqualifies him. And Jesus accepts it.

Believing and doubting in the same hour. That is the reason this verse has been the lifeline of honest Christians for two thousand years. Most of us are not in one state or the other. We believe and we doubt, in the same hour, about the same thing. We can affirm every article of the creed and lie awake unable to feel a word of it. And the great temptation is to sort yourself out before you come, to work up the required confidence and then pray, as though faith were the entry fee. This man did the opposite. He brought both halves and laid them at Christ’s feet. And the boy was healed.

All things are possible for you. Mark records those words once more, on the lips of Jesus himself. In Gethsemane he will fall on the ground and pray, Abba, Father, all things are possible for you (14:36). There is the one man whose faith had no unbelief in it at all, and the cup was not removed. He trusted the Father perfectly and was handed over, so that people whose faith is half doubt might be heard for his sake. The father in the valley could bring his ragged prayer because the Son would bring a perfect one, and drink the cup anyway, in his place.

What it does not mean. Not that only perfect faith receives an answer. Weak faith in a strong Saviour is enough. The power is in the one believed, not in the strength of the believing. Faith as small as a mustard seed is enough (Matthew 17:20). Nor does it mean that every prayer offered in faith will be answered with exactly what was asked, as Gethsemane shows.

If my prayer is not answered, was my faith too weak? Not necessarily, and usually not. Paul prayed three times for his thorn to be removed and was told no, because God’s grace was sufficient and his power made perfect in weakness (2 Corinthians 12:7–9). Faith does not dictate outcomes to God; it trusts him with them. Sometimes he heals; sometimes he gives grace to bear what he does not remove; always he hears. Never let anyone tell you that a sickness persists because you did not believe hard enough. The father in this passage confessed that his faith was mixed with unbelief, and he was not turned away.

Is doubt a sin? Unbelief that refuses God’s word is sin, and Jesus has just grieved over it (v. 19). But the struggling faith of a believer who wants to trust and finds it hard is not the same thing. It is weakness, and the remedy for weakness is to bring it to Christ, exactly as this man did. Doubts are best fought not by staring at your faith but by looking at the one you trust: his word, his promises, his cross and empty tomb. Feed faith with Scripture, pray this prayer, stay among God’s people, and do not make major decisions to walk away in a dark hour.

In a sentence. Jesus told the father that everything is possible for one who believes, and the father cried out that he believed and asked Jesus to help his unbelief.

On a Tuesday. If your faith this morning is a mess, if you believe and cannot feel it, or feel it and cannot hold it, do not wait until it improves. Say this man’s sentence, out loud if you can. Then take one promise of God, write it where you will see it, and come back to it whenever the doubt returns.

For worship. A father brought a prayer that was half belief and half doubt, and Christ took it as if it were whole. That is his way with all his people. He does not wait for our faith to be finished before he acts; he takes the trembling hand and does the very thing the doubt said he could not do. Our salvation never rested on the strength of our grip, but on the Son who believed perfectly in our place and holds us with hands that will not let go.
verseByVerse.note: Only Mark records the father’s cry.

parallels.desc: without faith it is impossible to please him

verseByVerse.quote: And when Jesus saw that a crowd came running together, he rebuked the unclean spirit, saying to it, "You mute and deaf spirit, I command you, come out of him and never enter him again." And after crying out and convulsing him terribly, it came out, and the boy was like a corpse, so that most of them said, "He is dead." But Jesus took him by the hand and lifted him up, and he arose.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When Jesus saw a crowd running together, he rebuked the unclean spirit: you mute and deaf spirit, I command you, come out of him and never enter him again. Crying out and convulsing him terribly, it came out, and the boy was like a corpse, so that most of them said: he is dead. But Jesus took him by the hand and lifted him up, and he arose.

And when Jesus saw that a crowd came running together. He notices the crowd swelling and acts because of it. He wants this over before it becomes a spectacle. He has been avoiding that all Gospel: the healing that turns into a show.

You mute and deaf spirit, I command you. He names it precisely. The father said the boy could not speak; Jesus adds deaf. The thing has shut the child in, sealing off both the way words come out and the way they get in. And “I” is emphatic: I myself. No invocation, no formula, no appeal to a higher name. This is not what the exorcists of that world did, and it is not what the disciples had done. The master commands in his own authority.

Come out of him and never enter him again. Nowhere else in the Gospels does Jesus add this clause. Why here? Because the father has just told him it has been happening from childhood, and the fear in that household is not only that it might happen but that it will keep happening. Jesus is not simply ending an episode. He is closing the door and telling the father it is closed. The father need not fear its return. Jesus’ deliverance is complete (Matthew 12:43–45). He did the same for the woman with the bleeding: be healed of your disease (5:34), a word of permanence for someone who would otherwise have spent every morning waiting for it to come back.

And after crying out and convulsing him terribly, it came out. It does not go quietly. The last thing it does on the way out is hurt him as much as it can. The powers of darkness in this Gospel are malicious to the final second, and they always obey.

And the boy was like a corpse, so that most of them said, He is dead. Stillness after the violence. He is lying still, white, not breathing that anyone can see, and the crowd concludes that the healer has killed him. It looked as though the demon had achieved its purpose. Imagine the father in that half-minute. He has just prayed the truest prayer of his life, and his son is lying on the ground looking dead. The moment before deliverance can look exactly like the disaster you feared. Israel was never more trapped than with the sea in front and the chariots behind.

But Jesus took him by the hand and lifted him up, and he arose. Now look at the vocabulary, because it reads like a resurrection. Took him by the hand: the same gesture as with Peter’s mother-in-law (1:31) and the dead girl in Jairus’ house (5:41–42). Lifted him up (ēgeiren) and arose (anestē) are the two words used for Jesus’ own resurrection (16:6; 8:31). Mark could have written that the boy got up. He wrote the two words the church would use for Easter, in the same chapter where Jesus spoke of rising from the dead and nobody understood (vv. 9–10). Here, in front of a crowd that has pronounced the boy dead, the Son of Man takes a child’s hand and raises him: a small, dusty rehearsal of what he is walking to Jerusalem to do for the world.

Can Christians be possessed, and should we be casting out demons today? Christ’s victory here is the reason for confidence, not fear. A believer is indwelt by the Holy Spirit and belongs to Christ; Scripture never describes a Christian as possessed, and greater is he who is in you than he who is in the world (1 John 4:4). Believers are tempted and attacked, and we resist the devil by faith, prayer and the word (Ephesians 6:10–18; James 4:7). The extraordinary sign gifts that marked the apostles’ ministry served to confirm their message and have ceased (Hebrews 2:3–4), a conviction held charitably towards brothers who see it differently; but God still hears prayer for the afflicted, and Satan still flees from Christ. Where real spiritual oppression is suspected, the remedy is the ordinary means: the gospel, repentance, prayer by the elders, and patient care, without theatre and without neglecting medical help.

In a sentence. Jesus commanded the spirit to come out and never return; after a last convulsion the boy lay as if dead, but Jesus took his hand and raised him up.

On a Tuesday. When it looks as though evil has won, Jesus has the last word. He takes the hand and raises up. If you are in the half-minute where everything looks worse than before you prayed, hold on: that is not proof he has failed. And if a past sin or fear has been dealt with by Christ, believe him when he says it is finished, and stop living as though it will return to rule you.

For worship. He speaks, and the destroyer obeys. He commands, and the door is shut for good. And then the King of glory bends down, takes a limp hand, and raises the one everyone had given up for dead. That is the gospel in a valley: our Lord does not merely drive out the enemy; he lifts us up, and one day he will take every sleeping believer by the hand and say, arise.

parallels.desc: he took her by the hand

verseByVerse.quote: And when he had entered the house, his disciples asked him privately, "Why could we not cast it out?" And he said to them, "This kind cannot be driven out by anything but prayer."
verseByVerse.commentary:
When he had gone into the house, his disciples asked him privately: why could we not cast it out? He said to them: this kind cannot be driven out by anything but prayer.

Why could we not cast it out? Notice first where the conversation happens: indoors, afterwards, in private. He never humiliated them in the valley. The correction is real and it is coming, but it is not delivered in front of an audience. And their question is a fair one. They are not making excuses. They had been given authority over unclean spirits (3:15) and had cast out many (6:13). They are not amateurs, and they know something has gone wrong that they cannot account for.

This kind cannot be driven out by anything but prayer. “This kind”: some demons were more powerful or deeply entrenched. But notice what the answer is not. It is not a technique. He does not say they used the wrong formula, or commanded too weakly, or needed a different name. There is no method being withheld. It is not more authority, either: they had all the authority they needed, and he had never withdrawn it. It is prayer, and here you have to see that he is not prescribing a step they omitted on the day. He is diagnosing a life.

Prayer as the posture of a life. If prayer were a component of the procedure, the failure would be a slip. But that reading collapses at once, because Jesus himself does not pray in this passage. He arrives, asks a question, speaks a sentence, and it is done. What he does not do here is what he does very early in the morning in a desolate place (1:35), and all night on a mountain before choosing the Twelve (Luke 6:12), and he has just come down from a mountain of communion with the Father. The disciples had been arguing with scribes. So prayer here means the settled, daily, unspectacular dependence out of which authority actually operates.

The drift from dependence. Now the diagnosis becomes uncomfortably clear. These men had succeeded before. They had come back from that mission delighted. And somewhere between that success and this valley, the authority had quietly become a possession: something they had, something that worked, a capacity they carried about rather than a gift held moment by moment from the hand of the one who gave it. They did not stop believing. They stopped depending. And the two are almost impossible to tell apart from the inside, until a day comes when the thing does not work. Every generation of the church faces the same drift: preaching, counselling, leading and serving on accumulated competence, without the ongoing communion that gives them any power at all.

The Son who never drifted. Set beside the nine the one man who never once treated his power as a possession. The eternal Son, who shares the Father’s own might, chose to live as a man in moment-by-moment dependence: the Son can do nothing of his own accord, but only what he sees the Father doing (John 5:19). Every word he spoke in that valley came out of that communion. And his praying did not end with his earthly life. He lives now at the Father’s right hand to intercede for his people, so that what the disciples lacked in the valley, their Lord supplies from the throne.

Faith and prayer. Jesus said their problem was faithlessness (v. 19); here, lack of prayer. The two are the same thing from different sides. Prayer is faith expressing its dependence on God. Matthew records that Jesus said: Because of your little faith (Matthew 17:20). A prayerless believer is a person who has quietly concluded that he can manage.

Textual note. Some manuscripts add “and fasting”. The words are missing from the two earliest and most reliable manuscripts, and were probably added later as the church came to practise fasting more. The ESV puts them in a footnote. Fasting is good, and Jesus expected his disciples to fast (Matthew 6:16–18), but it is not the secret here. Jesus’ point is dependence on God in prayer.

What it does not mean. Not that prayer is a more powerful technique, a formula you add to make an exorcism work. The point is a life of dependent prayer, not a ritual.

How do I build a life of dependent prayer? Start small and real rather than large and short-lived. Set a fixed time each day, even ten minutes, with your Bible open, and pray back what you read. Pray before the things you think you can do, not only the things you know you cannot: before the meeting, the lesson, the hard conversation. Keep a short list of people and situations, and pray through it. Pray with others, in your church’s prayer meeting and with your household. And when you find you have gone days without real prayer, do not wait to feel spiritual again. Confess it and begin again today.

In a sentence. When the disciples asked why they had failed, Jesus told them that this kind of demon could only be driven out by prayer, that is, by dependence on God.

On a Tuesday. Is there a problem you have been trying to solve in your own strength? Have you prayed about it? Begin there. And ask honestly: how much of what I will do for God this week will have been prayed about beforehand, not with a sentence before I start, but as a man who knows he can do nothing without Christ?

For worship. Apart from Christ his people can do nothing, and the nine in that valley proved it. But the glory is that he does not hoard what they lack. The Lord who came down from communion with his Father on the mountain shares his strength with the weakest disciple who asks, and every faltering prayer of the smallest believer is received by a Master who delights to be needed. He has never yet grown tired of being depended on.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that some manuscripts add “and fasting.”

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 30–50 — The Second Prediction and the Argument on the Road
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The second telling (vv. 30–32). Walking quietly through Galilee, avoiding notice, Jesus tells them again that he will be delivered up, killed, and rise. Mark adds a devastating detail: they did not understand, and were afraid to ask.

The argument (vv. 33–37). And what they were talking about instead comes out at Capernaum. He asks what they were discussing on the road, and they go silent — because they had been arguing about which of them was the greatest. His answer is to sit down, state the rule (last of all and servant of all), and then pick up a child and hold him.

The complaint (vv. 38–41). John, apparently thinking this a good moment, reports that they stopped a man casting out demons in Jesus's name because he was not one of them. He is told to leave him alone — and that a cup of water given to a disciple will not be forgotten.

The warnings (vv. 42–50). Then the hardest words in the Gospel: a millstone for anyone who trips up a little one, and a hand, a foot and an eye better lost than kept.

The whole section hangs together. Men who have just been told about a cross are arguing about rank, policing the boundaries of their group, and in serious danger of tripping up people smaller than themselves — and it ends with be at peace with one another.
verseByVerse.theology:
"The one who is not against us is for us" (v. 40) seems to collide head-on with whoever is not with me is against me (Matt. 12:30; Luke 11:23), and a reader who notices it deserves an answer.

They are not answering the same question, and that is the whole key. Here the subject is a fellow worker — a man casting out demons in Jesus's name, plainly on Christ's side, who simply does not belong to the disciples' circle; and the lesson is generosity: do not treat an ally as an enemy merely because he is not of your party. There the subject is Christ himself, and the men in view are Pharisees who had just called his works the devil's — open opponents; and the lesson is that toward Jesus there is no neutral ground.

So the two sayings guard two different errors. Toward other Christians serving under a different banner from ours we are far too quick to say against us, and Jesus says: not so — if he is for me, he is for you. Toward the Lord himself we would love to imagine a comfortable middle ground of the undecided, and Jesus says there is none. Read together they are not a contradiction but a pair of fences: be generous about the boundaries of the movement, and uncompromising about the claims of the King.

And a word about the verses your Bible skips. A reader with a King James Bible will find the refrain of v. 48, about the undying worm and the unquenched fire, three times over, at verses 44, 46 and 48. Modern Bibles print it once, at v. 48, and leave 44 and 46 as footnotes. Those two repetitions are a copyist's echo of v. 48 and are not in the earliest manuscripts. Nothing is lost. The sentence stands once, in full force, exactly where Jesus quoted it from Isaiah 66:24.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: twelve men arguing on a road about which of them was the greatest, on the road after being told that their Master would be handed over and killed.

Now: the same argument, conducted with better manners. It runs under a great deal of church life — who was consulted, who was thanked from the front, whose name went on it, who got asked to do the thing you were not asked to do. Nobody says I am the greatest. Everybody knows exactly where they stand in the room.

And notice how Mark exposes it: they kept silent. They would not tell him. Which is the surest sign of all that they already knew it was wrong — you do not go quiet about a conversation you are comfortable with.

Then watch what Jesus does with it, because he does not abolish ambition; he reverses its direction. If anyone would be first — the wanting is allowed to stand — he must be last of all and servant of all. Not last of some. Not servant of the deserving. Of all.

And then he picks up a child, who in that world had no legal standing, no money, no influence and nothing whatever to offer in return — and says that receiving one such is receiving him. The test of greatness in the kingdom is not how you treat the people who can advance you. It is how you treat the ones who cannot do a thing for you, when nobody is watching.

verseByVerse.quote: They went on from there and passed through Galilee. And he did not want anyone to know, for he was teaching his disciples, saying to them, "The Son of Man is going to be delivered into the hands of men, and they will kill him. And when he is killed, after three days he will rise." But they did not understand the saying, and were afraid to ask him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
They left there and passed through Galilee. Jesus did not want anyone to know, because he was teaching his disciples. He told them: the Son of Man is going to be delivered into the hands of men, and they will kill him; and when he has been killed, after three days he will rise. But they did not understand the saying, and were afraid to ask him.

They went on from there and passed through Galilee. Quietly, heading south toward Capernaum and then Jerusalem. He is travelling incognito through his own province: the region where his ministry began, where the crowds first came, where a few chapters ago he could not enter a town openly. The public Galilean ministry is over. From here the Gospel narrows: fewer crowds, more instruction, and the road turns toward Jerusalem.

And he did not want anyone to know, for he was teaching his disciples. That is why he wants privacy. His priority now is to prepare the Twelve for what is coming. What he has left to do is with these men, and there is not much time.

The Son of Man is going to be delivered into the hands of men. The second passion prediction, shorter than the first (8:31), but it is not a repeat: there is a new word in it, and it is the darkest in the sentence. “Delivered” (paradidotai) means handed over, given up, betrayed. The same word is used of Judas’ betrayal (3:19; 14:10), of the Jewish leaders handing Jesus over to Pilate (15:1), of Pilate handing him over to be crucified (15:15), and of God giving up his Son for us all (Romans 8:32). And here it is in a form that does not say who is doing it. Somebody hands him over. Judas will, and the priests will, and Pilate will, and behind all of them stands the Father’s purpose. There is a play on words too: the Son of Man, into the hands of men, humanity in general, which is where the reader is standing.

If God handed him over, are the betrayers less guilty? No. Scripture holds both truths together without embarrassment. Peter preached that Jesus was delivered up according to the definite plan and foreknowledge of God, and in the same sentence that his hearers crucified and killed him by the hands of lawless men (Acts 2:23). God ordains what happens without being the author of the sin, and human beings act freely and are fully responsible for their wickedness (Westminster 3.1). Judas was not a puppet; he chose for silver. And God, in his wisdom, used the worst thing ever done to accomplish the best. That is why the cross is both the guilt of the world and the gift of God.

And they will kill him. And when he is killed, after three days he will rise. Flat, unadorned, and with the resurrection attached again, as it was the first time. He has never once mentioned the death without the rising.

But they did not understand the saying, and were afraid to ask him. Mark, as usual, tells the truth about his own leaders, and there are two failures. They did not understand: that is forgivable and by now familiar; it is the second time they have heard it plainly, and still it will not go in. And they were afraid to ask him: that is not ignorance; that is a choice. Perhaps because of what happened last time somebody raised it: Peter took him aside about this exact subject and was called Satan (8:33). Perhaps for a more ordinary reason: they suspected they would not like the answer. Sometimes we do not ask because we are afraid of the answer.

The questions we do not ask. There are questions Christians decline to ask God, not because they cannot be asked, for Scripture is full of people asking far bolder ones, but because we half-know the answer and the answer would require something. The passage you skip. The subject you never bring into prayer. The area of your life you have quietly agreed with yourself not to discuss with him. It is not doubt; doubt at least engages. It is avoidance. And look what the disciples do with the silence. They do not ask him about the cross, and then they fill the rest of the walk with an argument about which of them is the most important. The unasked question leaves a space, and something always moves into it.

In a sentence. Travelling quietly through Galilee, Jesus again told his disciples he would be betrayed, killed and raised, but they did not understand and were afraid to ask.

On a Tuesday. Don’t be afraid to ask Jesus your hard questions in prayer and in his word. He would rather you asked. Name the subject you avoid bringing to him, the one you suspect would cost you something, and bring it to him today with your Bible open.

For worship. He knew every hand that would pass him along: the friend’s, the priest’s, the governor’s, the soldier’s. And he walked toward them. The Son of Man was delivered into the hands of men because the Father had first given him up for us all, and he who did not spare his own Son will, with him, graciously give us all things. Every handing over was love going all the way down.

verseByVerse.quote: And they came to Capernaum. And when he was in the house he asked them, "What were you discussing on the way?" But they kept silent, for on the way they had argued with one another about who was the greatest. And he sat down and called the twelve. And he said to them, "If anyone would be first, he must be last of all and servant of all."
verseByVerse.commentary:
They came to Capernaum. When he was in the house, he asked them: what were you discussing on the way? They kept silent, because on the way they had argued with one another about who was the greatest. He sat down and called the Twelve, and said: if anyone would be first, he must be last of all and servant of all.

And they came to Capernaum. Jesus’ base in Galilee, and probably Peter’s house (1:29). It is the last time Mark mentions the town. And Jesus waits until they are indoors. Whatever he heard on the road, he says nothing about it until the door is shut, the same restraint he showed with the nine after the failure in the valley.

What were you discussing on the way? Jesus knew. The question is gentle; he does not accuse, he asks. And “on the way” is loaded in Mark: it is the way to the cross, where Jesus was going to give his life. That was the road on which they had been arguing about greatness.

But they kept silent. Three of the most eloquent words in the chapter. They will not tell him, and the silence is a confession, because you do not go quiet about a conversation you are comfortable with. They had been perfectly happy to have it among themselves on the road; asked to repeat it in front of him, not one of the twelve can get the sentence out. Would you be willing to repeat, out loud, to Christ, the last conversation you had about somebody else? Not the words only, but the tone, and the reason you said it. Most of us have a category of speech that dies instantly in his presence, and the dying is the verdict.

For on the way they had argued with one another about who was the greatest. Mark supplies what they would not, and the placing is the whole indictment. Jesus had just told them, for the second time, that he would be handed over and killed. The men walking behind him were arguing about rank. Perhaps the choosing of three for the mountain had stirred jealousy. And it was an argument, not a passing thought: there were positions, and cases were made. It kept coming back (10:35–45; Luke 22:24). Pride is the most persistent of sins, even in disciples.

The silent argument in church. Before that is treated as a first-century absurdity, be honest about how familiar it is. Nobody in a church says I am the greatest. But the argument runs anyway, silently and constantly: who was consulted and who was not, who got thanked from the front, whose name is on it, who was asked to do the thing you were not asked to do, who is regarded as sound. It can be conducted entirely without words, and everybody in the room knows the standings.

And he sat down and called the twelve. Sitting is the posture of a teacher giving formal instruction. What follows is not an aside; it is a lesson, deliberately staged, as if to say: listen, this is for you who will lead my church.

If anyone would be first, he must be last of all and servant of all. Notice what the sentence does not do: it does not condemn the desire. If anyone would be first: the wanting is allowed to stand. Jesus does not tell them ambition is wicked and they should have none. He tells them where the front of the queue actually is. Then the two absolutes make it impossible to soften. Last of all: not last of some, not modest about your position, but bottom. Servant of all: the word is diakonos, the table-waiter, the one who serves the meal while others eat, from which comes our word deacon. Not servant of the deserving, the grateful, the promising, or those who might one day be useful. Of all.

The first who made himself last. The man saying this had the right to the first place in every room he entered. Though he was in the form of God, he did not count equality with God a thing to hold on to, but emptied himself by taking the form of a servant (Philippians 2:6–7). He asks the Twelve to go nowhere he has not gone first. And the road they had argued on was the road he was walking to the bottom: betrayal, a criminal’s death, the lowest place there is. The quarrel about rank was conducted behind the back of the only one who truly outranked them all, while he went down to serve them.

Is it wrong to want to do great things for God? No. Jesus does not rebuke the desire to be first; he redirects it. It is right to long that your life should count, that God should be honoured greatly through you, that you would hear well done at the end. What is wrong is wanting greatness measured by the world’s scale: being seen, consulted, thanked, above others. So ask what your ambition is for. If it is for his glory and others’ good, pursue it by serving. If it is for your name, it will show itself in resentment when someone else is chosen.

What does servant of all look like on an ordinary week? It is measurable, which is what makes it hard. It is easy to feel humble; it is not possible to be a servant in the abstract. It looks like doing the job nobody notices: stacking chairs, washing up, visiting the person who is hard work. It looks like letting someone else have the credit, and being glad. It looks like putting your spouse’s and children’s needs before your evening, and your colleagues’ success before your own advancement. And it looks like serving people who cannot repay you. Service of that kind can be looked up in a diary.

In a sentence. When the disciples were silent with shame about arguing over who was greatest, Jesus taught that whoever wants to be first must be last and servant of all.

On a Tuesday. Who can you serve today without being noticed? Do it, and starve the argument about greatness in your heart: offer to take the task someone else would be thanked for, and say nothing about it.

For worship. The word for servant is the table-waiter’s word, and the Lord of glory took it for himself. He came to wait on sinners, to break the bread and pour out his own blood as the cup. And he has promised that when he returns he will dress himself for service, have his servants recline at table, and come and serve them (Luke 12:37). The first of all will wait at his own feast, and there is no greatness in heaven or on earth like the greatness of that servant.
verseByVerse.note: Teachers sat to teach.

verseByVerse.quote: And he took a child and put him in the midst of them, and taking him in his arms, he said to them, "Whoever receives one such child in my name receives me, and whoever receives me, receives not me but him who sent me."
verseByVerse.commentary:
He took a child, put him in the middle of them, and taking him in his arms said to them: whoever receives one such child in my name receives me; and whoever receives me receives not me but him who sent me.

And he took a child and put him in the midst of them. Having said it, he shows it: an acted parable. Jesus stands a child, perhaps of the household, in the middle of the room, in the space the twelve have made by sitting round. The argument was about who takes the highest place. He puts a child in the centre of it. We have sentimentalised this scene; a first-century adult did not think first of innocence and wonder. Children were loved, but they were not counted important. They had no legal standing, no property, no voice; in the wider Roman world unwanted babies were often exposed at birth. A child could not advance you, defend you, repay you or add anything to your position. So the lesson is not be innocent like this. It is: here is a person who can do absolutely nothing for you.

And taking him in his arms. Mark alone records this tender detail, and he records it twice: here, and when Jesus takes the children in his arms and blesses them (10:16). Peter remembered it, which is why it is here. He is telling the church, thirty years later: while he was explaining greatness to us, he was holding a child. Twelve grown men who have been arguing about rank, sitting in a circle, and the Lord of glory in the middle of them with a small child in his arms. Jesus embraces the one with no status.

Whoever receives one such child in my name receives me. To receive is to welcome a guest: to take someone in, give them your attention and your table, care for them. “In my name”: for my sake, because the child belongs to me. So the standard is exact. Not whoever loves children, but whoever receives, takes trouble over, makes room for, one who has nothing to give in return. Jesus identifies himself with the least important people. The way you treat the least is the way you treat Christ (Matthew 25:40). The disciples argued about who was greatest; greatness lies in welcoming those who can give you nothing back.

And whoever receives me, receives not me but him who sent me. The chain goes all the way up: the child, then Christ, then the Father. Welcome a nobody in Jesus’ name, and you welcome God himself. Which means the greatness of an act is not measured by the significance of the person you did it for. It is measured by who is standing behind them. This is also a claim about Jesus: he is the sent one, who represents the Father fully.

What it does not mean. Not that children are innocent, or that childhood is a model of moral purity. Children are sinners too (Psalm 51:5), and every parent knows it. The point is their status: they are small, dependent and unimportant in the world’s eyes. When Jesus says that we must receive the kingdom like a child (10:15), the point is related: we come with nothing, as dependents.

Does this mean every child belongs to Christ? Not in that sense. In my name means receiving the child for Jesus’ sake, because he cares for such little ones and commands us to. It does not teach that children are born saved or that they enter the covenant by birth or baptism; each child needs to be born again and to come to Christ by faith, which is why we pray for our children and teach them the gospel. But Jesus’ arms around this child show how warmly he welcomes the little ones brought to him, and we believe that those who die in infancy are safe in the hands of a merciful God who saves his elect. Every child is to be welcomed, protected and taught, because the Lord who made them takes them up in his arms.

In a sentence. Embracing a child, Jesus taught that whoever welcomes the least important person in his name welcomes him, and the Father who sent him.

On a Tuesday. Welcome the people who can do nothing for you: children, the lonely, the overlooked, the elderly relative whose conversation goes in circles, the junior colleague, the child in your own house at the end of a day when you have nothing left. In them you welcome Christ. Value those who serve in your church’s children’s ministry, and ask whether you could join them. Everybody is attentive to the people who matter to their position. The kingdom’s ranking is worked out entirely on the others.

For worship. The Son of God, whom the Father sent, put his arms around a child no one counted. That is the God we worship: the high and lofty One who dwells with the lowly, who stoops to take up the small, and who reckons a welcome given to a nobody as given to himself. We were the nobodies, and he took us in his arms.
verseByVerse.note: Children had little status in the ancient world.

verseByVerse.quote: John said to him, "Teacher, we saw someone casting out demons in your name, and we tried to stop him, because he was not following us."
