But Jesus said, "Do not stop him, for no one who does a mighty work in my name will be able soon afterward to speak evil of me. For the one who is not against us is for us.
verseByVerse.commentary:
John said to him: Teacher, we saw someone casting out demons in your name, and we tried to stop him, because he was not following us. But Jesus said: do not stop him, for no one who does a mighty work in my name will be able soon afterwards to speak evil of me. For whoever is not against us is for us.

John said to him. The only time in Mark that John speaks alone. The timing is superb, and John cannot have intended it. Jesus has just said that receiving a nobody in his name is receiving him, and John’s contribution is to report an occasion when they stopped somebody acting in that name. Perhaps the words in my name made his conscience uneasy. Or perhaps he expected approval: he is a Son of Thunder (3:17), and this is the sort of thing thunder does.

We saw someone casting out demons in your name. Someone outside the Twelve, using Jesus’ name, and succeeding, when the disciples had just failed (v. 18). There may be a little jealousy here.

And we tried to stop him, because he was not following us. Look carefully at the reason, because John states it with perfect and damning clarity: not because he was not following you, but us. The man plainly was following Jesus; he was casting out demons in his name. The objection is to his membership, not his master. He was not in the group. The disciples were concerned for their own circle, their own status. Joshua made the same mistake about Eldad and Medad prophesying outside the camp, and Moses answered: Would that all the LORD’s people were prophets (Numbers 11:26–29).

Sectarianism in one clause. That is the whole of it, then and now. There is a way of caring about the kingdom that has quietly become caring about our part of it, where the first question asked about a man’s ministry is not whether Christ is being preached but whose he is. It flourishes among people who are entirely orthodox and entirely sincere, and it produces the strange spectacle of Christians relieved rather than glad when good work is done by somebody outside their circle.

Do not stop him. Flat, immediate, no discussion. Jesus corrects their narrowness.

For no one who does a mighty work in my name will be able soon afterward to speak evil of me. The reasoning is practical rather than sentimental. A man who is really doing good in Jesus’ name is on Jesus’ side. Having just seen that name work, he is not about to start slandering it. Whatever is lacking in his understanding, and whatever his affiliation, he is not on the other side.

For the one who is not against us is for us. A generous principle. In the war between the kingdom of God and Satan (3:23–27), anyone casting out demons in Jesus’ name is fighting on the right side. Elsewhere Jesus says the reverse: Whoever is not with me is against me (Matthew 12:30; Luke 11:23). The two sayings do not contradict; they answer different questions. There the subject is Christ himself, and the men in view are Pharisees who had just called his works the devil’s: toward Jesus there is no neutral ground. Here the subject is a fellow worker plainly on Christ’s side who does not belong to the disciples’ circle: do not treat an ally as an enemy. Read together they are a pair of fences: be generous about the boundaries of the movement, and uncompromising about the claims of the King.

The power in the name. Everything in this exchange turns on whose name was spoken. The man had no commission among the Twelve, and the demons went anyway, because the authority was never in the group. It was in Jesus. His name did what the nine had just failed to do, which is the plainest proof of who he is: the name at which demons flee is the name God has exalted above every name, at which every knee will bow (Philippians 2:9–10). John wanted to guard the name. Jesus shows that the name guards itself, and belongs to no circle but his own.

What it does not mean. Not that anyone who uses Jesus’ name is a true believer. Some who did mighty works in his name he will reject (Matthew 7:22–23), and some who tried to use his name like a spell came to grief (Acts 19:13–16). Nor that doctrine does not matter. The issue here is group loyalty, not truth. Paul could rejoice that Christ was preached even by rivals with bad motives (Philippians 1:15–18), and in the same years curse anyone who preached a different gospel (Galatians 1:8–9). The line is the gospel itself, not our party.

How can I tell whether someone outside my circle is truly on Christ’s side? Look at what he does with Christ and the gospel. Does he confess Jesus as the eternal Son of God come in the flesh, crucified for sinners and risen (1 John 4:2–3)? Does he preach salvation by grace through faith in him, not by works? Does he submit to Scripture as God’s final word? If so, he is a brother even if he differs from you on baptism, church order or the end times, and you should be glad when God uses him. If he denies the heart of the gospel, he is not doing a work in Christ’s name, whatever words he uses, and love for the sheep means warning against him.

In a sentence. When John reported stopping a man who cast out demons in Jesus’ name because he was not one of them, Jesus said not to stop him, for whoever is not against them is for them.

On a Tuesday. Rejoice when Christ is served well by believers in other churches or traditions. They are not your rivals. This week, pray by name for another gospel church in your town, and thank God for something good he is doing through it.

For worship. The kingdom is bigger than our circle, because the King is bigger than we are. He is not threatened by servants he has not introduced to us, and his name does its work wherever it is honestly called upon. We belong to a Lord whose generosity outruns ours, who has sheep not of this fold, and who will gather them all into one flock under one Shepherd.

parallels.desc: whoever is not with me is against me

verseByVerse.quote: For truly, I say to you, whoever gives you a cup of water to drink because you belong to Christ will by no means lose his reward.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For truly, I tell you, whoever gives you a cup of water to drink because you belong to Christ will by no means lose his reward.

The smallest act. Jesus has just told the Twelve not to stop a man outside their circle who worked in his name, and that whoever welcomes a child in his name welcomes him. Now he widens it to the smallest act imaginable: what is done for one of his people, because they are his, counts with God.

Whoever gives you a cup of water to drink. He puts his solemn Truly, I say to you, which he keeps for things he wants underlined, in front of a cup of water. Consider what he could have chosen. He has just spoken of casting out demons. He could have said: whoever preaches, whoever heals, whoever gives up his home. He says a drink of water. In a hot, dry land it is the smallest act of kindness: the well is there and everybody has a cup. It costs almost nothing, needs no skill and no risk, and nobody will ever hear about it. And it will not be forgotten.

Because you belong to Christ. Literally in the name that you are Christ’s. That is the qualifying clause, and it is the whole of it. Not because the giver was impressive, or the act large, or the motive perfectly pure: because of whose the recipient was. The value is not in the water but in the name attached to the person handed the cup, which is exactly what he said two verses earlier about the child. Kindness shown to a disciple because he belongs to Christ is kindness to Christ.

Will by no means lose his reward. “By no means” is the strongest negative in Greek, a double negative: it is not going to be lost. Not overlooked, not mislaid, not too small to register. God notices, remembers and rewards. Nothing done for Christ is lost; God is not unjust so as to overlook your work and the love you have shown for his name in serving the saints (Hebrews 6:10).

What it does not mean. Not that we earn salvation by good works. The reward is God’s gracious recognition of what flows from love for Christ, not wages that put God in our debt. When we have done all we were commanded, we are unworthy servants who have only done our duty (Luke 17:10). And yet he rewards. That is grace upon grace: he gives the faith, works the love, and then crowns his own gifts as if they were ours.

What is the reward? Scripture does not give us a price list, and it is better not to imagine one. The heart of it is the Lord himself: his well done, his joy shared, a deeper capacity to know and enjoy him in the age to come (Matthew 25:21; 1 Corinthians 3:14). Rewards in the New Testament are never a ladder of merit within salvation that makes some saints proud, but the Father’s delight in his children’s love. Every believer’s cup will be full, and every one will cast his crown before the throne.

The list nobody sees. This is worth having if the service you are able to give is very small and entirely unnoticed. Most Christian work is. It is meals cooked, lifts given, chairs put out, a message sent to somebody having a bad week, an hour spent with a person nobody else has time for, prayer for people who never learn they were prayed for. None of it will be described from a platform. All of it is on a list. And he will read the list out one day, and the people named will not recognise their own lives in it: Lord, when did we see you thirsty and give you drink? And he will answer that as you did it to one of the least of these my brothers, you did it to me (Matthew 25:37–40).

The cup he was given. The Lord who promised a reward for a cup of water knew what it was to be thirsty. On the cross he would say, I thirst, and be handed sour wine on a sponge (John 19:28–29; Mark 15:36). And he knew of another cup, the one he would ask the Father to remove: the cup of God’s judgment, which no kindness could ease. He drank that one to the dregs, so that every cup handed to one of his people might be gathered up and honoured. The one who notices the water is the one who drank the wrath.

In a sentence. Even a cup of water given to a disciple because he belongs to Christ will surely be rewarded.

On a Tuesday. No act of kindness to a fellow Christian is too small to count. Give the cup. Think of one believer who would be helped this week by something small and practical, and do it without telling anyone.

For worship. The King of glory keeps a record of cups of water. That is the sort of King he is. He who owns the cattle on a thousand hills stoops to notice a drink handed to a tired disciple, and he will not forget it in eternity. Our God is not a hard master reaping where he did not sow, but a Father who sees in secret and delights to reward.

verseByVerse.quote: "Whoever causes one of these little ones who believe in me to sin, it would be better for him if a great millstone were hung around his neck and he were thrown into the sea.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Whoever causes one of these little ones who believe in me to sin, it would be better for him if a great millstone were hung around his neck and he were thrown into the sea.

The other side. The tone changes completely, and the change is deliberate. He has just promised a reward for the smallest kindness done to one of his people. Now he states what happens at the other end: if small kindnesses to disciples are rewarded, harm to them is judged severely.

One of these little ones who believe in me. Who are the little ones? The child is still in the room, so children are certainly not excluded. But the qualifying phrase is who believe in me, which points wider: any humble, insignificant believer, the small, the new, the fragile, the ones whose faith is genuine and not yet strong. The recent convert. The person hanging on by their fingernails. Anyone whose grip on Christ could be loosened by what you do.

To sin. The verb is skandalizō, to cause to stumble, to trip up. A skandalon was the stick in a trap that sprang it, then any stumbling block. To make a believer stumble is to lead him into sin or cause him to fall away from faith: by false teaching, bad example, abuse, pride or contempt. It covers more than teaching error. It is anything you do that makes it harder for a weak believer to keep walking.

Who believe in me. Notice the claim folded into the phrase. Jesus speaks of faith in himself as the prophets spoke of trust in the LORD, and he binds the little ones to himself so closely that to wound their faith is to strike at him. He is the Servant of whom Isaiah wrote, a bruised reed he will not break, and a faintly burning wick he will not quench (Isaiah 42:3). He handles weak faith with infinite care, and the severity that follows is the measure of it. The millstone is what his tenderness sounds like when it turns to face those who would crush what he is guarding.

A great millstone. Literally a donkey’s millstone. Get the picture right. This is not the small hand-mill a woman turned in her kitchen. It is the huge upper stone of a village mill, the one an animal walked in circles to turn, a slab of rock weighing hundreds of pounds. One man could not lift it.

And he were thrown into the sea. Drowning with a heavy weight was a Roman and Greek form of execution, especially horrifying to Jews because the body would not be buried. There is no coming up. Then hear the comparison, which is the actual sentence: it would be better for him. Jesus is saying that such a death would be the preferable outcome compared with what awaits the one who destroys the faith of a little one. Not that he should be drowned, but that judgment for such a sin will be worse than the worst death imaginable. He does not speak like this about doubters, or the confused, or even his enemies. He speaks like this about people who damage the faith of the small.

Who is this word for? For anybody with influence over somebody weaker, and that is a great many of us. It is a word for parents, whose children’s picture of God is being assembled largely out of what they see at home, and whose faith can be quietly ruined by a father who is one man on Sunday and another on Tuesday. It is a word for anyone who teaches or leads in a church, and for anyone whose conduct is watched by a younger Christian who thinks well of them. And it is a word about ordinary talk. You do not need to preach heresy to trip somebody up. It is done with a cynical remark about a fellow believer in front of a new convert, with running commentary on the church’s failings that a fragile person overhears, with the joke that makes something holy look small. The father in the valley had his faith damaged by disciples who let him down. Somebody put that if you can in his mouth.

What about abuse in the church? This verse is among the most severe Jesus ever spoke, and it bears with full weight on anyone who abuses a child or a vulnerable believer, especially under cover of Christ’s name. Abuse is never to be tolerated, hushed up or managed quietly to protect a reputation, a ministry or a family. Jesus’ concern is for the little one, not for the institution. A church that loves Christ will report abuse to the civil authorities, who are God’s servants to punish wrongdoing (Romans 13:4), will protect and believe and care for victims, and will remove offenders from any position of trust. Forgiveness for a repentant abuser is real, but it never means restoring access or silencing the harmed. If this has happened to you, it was not your fault, and Christ is on your side.

In a sentence. Anyone who causes a humble believer to stumble into sin faces a judgment worse than being drowned with a millstone round the neck.

On a Tuesday. Your example is seen by others: young Christians, your children, new believers. Never be the reason they fall. Ask, without panic and without evasion: who is watching me who is weaker than I am, and is anything I do or say making it harder for them? Then change the thing, today.

For worship. The Lord takes the side of the little ones. The weakest believer, the newest convert, the child who trusts him, is so precious to him that he speaks his most terrible words to protect them. We are held by a Shepherd who will not lose one of his sheep, who carries the lambs in his arms, and who will call every offender to account.
verseByVerse.note: The millstone is the heavy upper stone of a mill turned by a donkey.

verseByVerse.quote: And if your hand causes you to sin, cut it off. It is better for you to enter life crippled than with two hands to go to hell, to the unquenchable fire. And if your foot causes you to sin, cut it off. It is better for you to enter life lame than with two feet to be thrown into hell. And if your eye causes you to sin, tear it out. It is better for you to enter the kingdom of God with one eye than with two eyes to be thrown into hell, 'where their worm does not die and the fire is not quenched.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
If your hand causes you to sin, cut it off. It is better for you to enter life maimed than with two hands to go to hell, to the unquenchable fire. If your foot causes you to sin, cut it off. It is better to enter life lame than with two feet to be thrown into hell. If your eye causes you to sin, tear it out. It is better to enter the kingdom of God with one eye than with two eyes to be thrown into hell, where their worm does not die and the fire is not quenched.

From others to yourself. Having warned them about tripping up other people, he turns to the far more likely danger, which is yourself. And the same verb runs through: skandalizō. What trips others up may be your influence; what trips you up is nearer to hand. Deal with sin in your own life as ruthlessly as God will deal with those who harm his little ones.

Hand, foot, eye. Three examples, in a deliberate order: what you do, where you go, what you look at. Every faculty can become an instrument of sin, and between them they cover most of the ways a person is ruined.

Cut it off … tear it out. Is he asking for literal self-mutilation? No, and the reason is not squeamishness: it would not work. Chapter 7 settled this. Nothing outside a man defiles him; the trouble comes from within, out of the heart (7:21). A man with one hand can still covet, and a blind man can still lust. But do not let that soften it into nothing. This is hyperbole in the service of deadly seriousness: be radical with sin. Whatever leads you into sin, however precious, however much a part of you it seems, get rid of it. A hand is not a luxury, nor is an eye. He deliberately chose things you cannot spare.

Making it concrete. Vagueness here is how the passage gets neutralised. The hand is what you do. The foot is where you go: the house, the road home past a particular door, the company you keep because it is easier than explaining. The eye is what you look at, and in our generation that is very often one object, in your pocket and lit up at midnight. And the surgery Jesus describes is not moderation; it is removal. Not be more careful with it: cut it off. In practice that means the ruthless, concrete, slightly embarrassing measure: the app deleted rather than managed, the phone that does not come upstairs, the account closed, the friendship stepped back from, the route changed, the arrangement told to another Christian so that it can be asked about. Every one of those feels disproportionate. That is the feeling of amputation, and it is exactly the feeling he is describing.

It is better for you to enter life crippled. “Life” here means eternal life, the same as the kingdom of God in verse 47. He calls the kingdom life, and the alternative, three times over, hell. Those are the only two categories in this paragraph. Better to lose something precious now and enter life, than keep everything and lose your soul (8:36).

To go to hell. “Hell” (geenna, Gehenna) is a real place with an address: the Valley of Hinnom, a ravine along the south side of Jerusalem. There, in the darkest days of the kingdom, apostate Israel burned its own children in sacrifice to Molech; Ahaz did it and Manasseh did it (2 Chronicles 28:3; 33:6), and Josiah defiled the place so that it could never be used that way again (2 Kings 23:10). Jeremiah called it the Valley of Slaughter, a place of judgment and corpses (Jeremiah 7:31–32). By Jesus’ day it was the name for the place of final punishment. So Jesus takes a real, smouldering valley that his hearers could have walked to in half an hour and makes it his picture of final judgment: the place fit only for what is utterly rejected.

To the unquenchable fire. Where their worm does not die and the fire is not quenched. The closing line is a quotation of the last verse of Isaiah (66:24), which pictures the corpses of those who rebelled against God. The worm devours and the fire burns, and neither ends. These are images, but images of a reality more terrible, not less, than what they describe.

The tenderest voice speaks of hell. Take one plain observation about the man saying it. Nobody in the Bible speaks about hell as often or as vividly as Jesus does. The tenderest person who ever lived, who held a child while he taught, who groaned over a deaf man, who remembered that a raised girl needed something to eat, is the one who will not let this subject alone. It cannot be dismissed as the harshness of the Old Testament or the invention of a later church. It is on the lips of the Saviour, and he says it three times in six verses because he means his people not to go there.

Where Christians differ: the nature of hell. Some (conditionalists or annihilationists) hold that the wicked are finally destroyed and cease to exist, taking unquenchable fire to mean a fire that does its work completely, and noting that in Isaiah 66:24 the worm and fire consume dead bodies. Others (universalists) hope that all will finally be saved. Verdict: the historic Christian view is that hell is conscious, eternal punishment. The undying worm and unquenched fire speak of punishment that does not end: in Jesus’ use it is the punishment, not its victims, that never finishes. Jesus elsewhere sets eternal punishment alongside eternal life as equally lasting (Matthew 25:46), and Revelation says the smoke of their torment goes up for ever and ever (Revelation 14:11). Jesus’ warnings are given in love, so that none would go there. It is meant to drive us to the one who bore judgment for all who come to him.

Textual note. Some manuscripts add verses 44 and 46, both repeating verse 48. A reader with a King James Bible will find the refrain three times; here the numbers run 43, 45, 47, 48. The two repetitions are missing from the earliest and best manuscripts and were probably added to make the three warnings match. The ESV puts them in footnotes. Nothing has been lost: the sentence stands once, in full force, exactly where Jesus quoted it from Isaiah.

If I keep failing at the same sin, am I going to hell? Not if you belong to Christ. These verses are not a threat hung over the believer who fights and falls; they are a warning to the person who will not fight at all, who keeps the hand because he loves it more than he fears the fire. A Christian still sins, and grieves, and confesses, and gets up (1 John 1:8–9). What marks a true believer is not that the battle is won but that he is in it, on God’s side, using the means God gives. Your hope is not the strength of your surgery but the Saviour who was cut off for you. Cut off what feeds the sin precisely because he has already saved you, and keep running to him.

In a sentence. Jesus calls his followers to deal ruthlessly with anything that leads them into sin, because it is better to lose what is precious than to be thrown into the unending fire of hell.

On a Tuesday. Name the hand, foot or eye in your life: the thing that keeps leading you into sin. Then cut it off, today, in a concrete way you could explain to a friend. Tell one trusted Christian what you have done and ask them to check on you next week.

For worship. The Judge who warns of the unquenchable fire is the Saviour who went into the fire for us. He was cut off from the land of the living, forsaken, so that every one who flees to him might enter life whole. The tenderness that held a child and the solemnity that spoke of Gehenna are one love, and it is that love which has carried us out of the valley of slaughter into the kingdom of God.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that some manuscripts add verses 44 and 46, repeating verse 48. “Hell” renders Gehenna, the Valley of Hinnom by Jerusalem.

parallels.desc: their worm shall not die, their fire shall not be quenched

verseByVerse.quote: For everyone will be salted with fire. Salt is good, but if the salt has lost its saltiness, how will you make it salty again? Have salt in yourselves, and be at peace with one another."
verseByVerse.commentary:
For everyone will be salted with fire. Salt is good, but if the salt has lost its saltiness, how will you make it salty again? Have salt in yourselves, and be at peace with one another.

For everyone will be salted with fire. One of the strangest sentences in Mark, but its two key words are the way in. Fire is the last word of the previous paragraph, where it meant judgment, unquenchable, in Gehenna. Salt comes from somewhere else entirely: you shall season all your grain offerings with salt; you shall not let the salt of the covenant with your God be missing (Leviticus 2:13). Salt was rubbed into every sacrifice laid on the altar, and many were burned with fire. So the saying holds two destinies in one breath, and the same element does opposite things to them. The unrepentant meet the fire that consumes. The disciple, who has just been told to cut off hand and foot rather than perish, meets the fire that purifies: the costly, cleansing fire of a life laid on the altar as a living sacrifice (Romans 12:1).

Which fire? Everyone meets God’s fire; the only question is which kind. Peter tells persecuted Christians not to be surprised at the fiery trial (1 Peter 4:12), for tested faith is more precious than gold refined by fire (1 Peter 1:7). Other readings have been offered: that every believer’s work will be tested by fire (1 Corinthians 3:13), or that the wicked will be preserved, as salt preserves, in the fire of judgment. The reading given here keeps the link with the fire of verse 48 and the salt of the sacrifices, and is the more likely; everyone most likely means every disciple. Some manuscripts add and every sacrifice will be salted with salt, probably taken from Leviticus 2:13 to explain the saying.

Salt is good. Now the tone gentles, and the chapter comes in to land. Salt in that world did two things. It preserved: it was the only thing standing between a household and rotten meat. And it seasoned: it made food taste like something. In the Old Testament it was also a sign of the covenant, a covenant of salt, lasting and unbreakable (Numbers 18:19; 2 Chronicles 13:5). All are pictures of what a disciple is meant to be: the thing that stops the rot, the thing that gives savour, and a life bound to God for good.

The sacrifice salted and burned. Every salted offering laid on Israel’s altar pointed to one. Christ loved us and gave himself up for us, a fragrant offering and sacrifice to God (Ephesians 5:2), and he went into the fire of judgment entire, the fire the unrepentant will meet. Because he was consumed in the place of his people, the fire that reaches them now is never the fire of Gehenna. It is a Father’s refining fire, burning off the dross and leaving gold. The disciple is salted with fire as one who stands inside a covenant of salt that Christ’s blood has made unbreakable.

But if the salt has lost its saltiness, how will you make it salty again? Pure salt cannot lose its saltiness. But the salt of Palestine was scraped from the Dead Sea marshes, mixed with other minerals, and damp could leach out the actual salt, leaving a white powder that looked identical and did nothing. You could not restore it. You threw it out (Matthew 5:13). That is the sober question under the sentence. A disciple who has quietly lost the thing that made him different is not obviously distinguishable from one who has not. He looks the same. He is in the same place on Sunday. He simply no longer preserves anything or gives savour to anything.

Can a true Christian lose his salt and be lost? A true believer cannot finally fall away, because the God who began the work will complete it (Philippians 1:6) and no one can snatch Christ’s sheep from his hand (John 10:28–29). But Jesus’ warnings are one of the means by which he keeps us. Christians can grow cold, compromised and useless for a season, and the warning is meant to wake them. And someone who looked like salt for years may prove never to have been the real thing at all (1 John 2:19). So do not use this verse to torment yourself, and do not use the doctrine of perseverance to ignore it. Go back to Christ, the source of the salt.

Have salt in yourselves. Keep the distinctive quality of discipleship: devotion to Christ, willingness to suffer, purity, the ruthlessness with your own hand and foot and eye. The salt is the self-sacrifice Jesus has been describing since 8:34.

And be at peace with one another. The chapter comes full circle. These men had failed in a valley, been afraid to ask about the cross, argued on the road about which of them was greatest (v. 34), and stopped a man doing good work because he was not of their party. To that group Jesus says: be at peace with one another. And notice the order, because it is a whole Christian ethic in one sentence. Have salt in yourselves comes first: the inward reality. Be at peace with one another follows from it. Peace in a church is not produced by managing personalities. It is what happens when a group of people have each dealt honestly with themselves. People who have been salted with the fire of the cross have nothing left to fight over. In the ancient world, sharing salt at a meal was a sign of friendship.

What if peace with someone seems impossible? Do what lies with you (Romans 12:18). Examine yourself first and own your part without excuses. Go to the person privately and humbly (Matthew 18:15). Forgive as you have been forgiven, which does not mean pretending wrong was not done, but releasing your claim to pay it back. If they will not be reconciled, keep your heart free of bitterness and keep praying for them. Peace does not mean tolerating abuse or ignoring serious sin; sometimes the church’s elders must be involved. But it does mean you will not be the one keeping the quarrel alive.

In a sentence. Every disciple will be refined by fire, like a salted sacrifice; so keep your saltiness, the self-giving of discipleship, and live at peace with one another.

On a Tuesday. Is there a fellow believer you are quarrelling with, or quietly avoiding? Self-denial is the salt that brings peace. Go and make peace, this week, and go first.

For worship. Twelve men wanted to know which of them was the greatest. He held a child, told them to go to the back and serve everybody, warned them what happens to a man who trips up one of the little ones, told them to cut off whatever was taking them down, and then said: be at peace with each other. He was going to Jerusalem to make that peace at his own expense, by the blood of his cross. And on the night he was handed over, he got up from the table, took a towel, and washed the feet of every one of them. He is our peace.
verseByVerse.note: Salt was added to every sacrifice. Salt from the Dead Sea could have its salt leached out and lose its taste.

parallels.desc: with all your offerings you shall offer salt
let your speech be seasoned with salt

9.theology:
What happened on the mountain? The word is metamorphōthē — transformed. And nothing was added; something was, for a moment, no longer withheld. Set it beside Moses, whose face shone coming down Sinai and had to be veiled (Ex. 34:29–35) — but that light was borrowed and fading, which Paul says is why he covered it (2 Cor. 3:13). Here the light comes from inside; the clothes go white because of what is underneath them. Three men were allowed to see, for a few minutes, what was true of him every day they had walked beside him without noticing.

Who will not taste death? (v. 1) Mark's own arrangement answers it: the very next words are and after six days, and Mark almost never gives intervals. Some standing there would see the kingdom come with power — and six days later, three of them did. Peter confirms the reading himself, citing that mountain as evidence of the power and coming of our Lord Jesus Christ (2 Pet. 1:16–18). Serious readers have argued for the resurrection, Pentecost, or AD 70, and the instinct behind those is right — the kingdom comes in power by stages — but after six days is not decoration.

Why could the disciples not cast it out? (v. 29) Not a technique, and not a shortage of authority — he had given it and never withdrawn it. Prayer here is not a step they omitted on the day but the posture of a whole life. They had succeeded before; somewhere between that success and this valley the authority had become a possession rather than a gift held moment by moment. They did not stop believing. They stopped depending — and the two are almost impossible to tell apart from the inside until the day it does not work.

And the verses your Bible skips. A King James Bible has the refrain of v. 48, about the worm that does not die, three times, at vv. 44, 46 and 48. Those two repetitions are a copyist's echo of v. 48 and are absent from the earliest manuscripts, which is why modern Bibles footnote them. Nothing is lost: the sentence stands once, in full force, where Jesus quoted it from Isaiah 66:24.
9.examples:
Then: a father who had watched his son thrown to the ground since childhood, pulled him out of fires and out of water, never heard him speak — and who came looking for Jesus, found the disciples instead, and watched them fail in front of a crowd.

Now: the if you can in his prayer was not there when he set out. The disciples' failure damaged his faith in Christ. That still happens exactly the same way: the church that let someone down, the Christian who wronged them, the leader who fell, the prayer meeting that promised and produced nothing. People come to Christ afterwards with a clause in their mouth that somebody else put there — which is worth remembering by anyone whose conduct is watched by a weaker believer, and it is why v. 42 talks about millstones.

And then watch what the man does with the little he has. I believe; help my unbelief! — a shout, not a formulation, from a man on his knees beside a convulsing child. He will not deny the faith he has, and he will not pretend it is more than it is. He asks Christ to deal with the very thing that disqualifies him.

Most of us are not in one state or the other. We believe and doubt in the same hour about the same thing, and the great temptation is to sort ourselves out before we come — to work up the required confidence and then pray, as though faith were the entry fee. This man brought both halves and dumped them at Christ's feet.

And the boy was healed. That is the answer to the prayer and the vindication of it. Jesus does not say come back when you are sure. He meets the faith that is there, trembling and shot through with doubt, and does the very thing the man's doubt said he could not do. So if your faith this morning is a mess, do not wait for it to improve. Say this man's sentence. It is in the Bible to be prayed.

10.title: The Road, the Ransom, and the Beggar Who Followed
10.text: <sup>1</sup>And he left there and went to the region of Judea and beyond the Jordan, and crowds gathered to him again. And again, as was his custom, he taught them. <sup>2</sup>And Pharisees came up and in order to test him asked, “Is it lawful for a man to divorce his wife?” <sup>3</sup>He answered them, “What did Moses command you?” <sup>4</sup>They said, “Moses allowed a man to write a certificate of divorce and to send her away.” <sup>5</sup>And Jesus said to them, “Because of your hardness of heart he wrote you this commandment. <sup>6</sup>But from the beginning of creation, ‘God made them male and female.’ <sup>7</sup>‘Therefore a man shall leave his father and mother and hold fast to his wife, <sup>8</sup>and the two shall become one flesh.’ So they are no longer two but one flesh. <sup>9</sup>What therefore God has joined together, let not man separate.” <sup>10</sup>And in the house the disciples asked him again about this matter. <sup>11</sup>And he said to them, “Whoever divorces his wife and marries another commits adultery against her, <sup>12</sup>and if she divorces her husband and marries another, she commits adultery.” <sup>13</sup>And they were bringing children to him that he might touch them, and the disciples rebuked them. <sup>14</sup>But when Jesus saw it, he was indignant and said to them, “Let the children come to me; do not hinder them, for to such belongs the kingdom of God. <sup>15</sup>Truly, I say to you, whoever does not receive the kingdom of God like a child shall not enter it.” <sup>16</sup>And he took them in his arms and blessed them, laying his hands on them. <sup>17</sup>And as he was setting out on his journey, a man ran up and knelt before him and asked him, “Good Teacher, what must I do to inherit eternal life?” <sup>18</sup>And Jesus said to him, “Why do you call me good? No one is good except God alone. <sup>19</sup>You know the commandments: ‘Do not murder, Do not commit adultery, Do not steal, Do not bear false witness, Do not defraud, Honor your father and mother.’” <sup>20</sup>And he said to him, “Teacher, all these I have kept from my youth.” <sup>21</sup>And Jesus, looking at him, loved him, and said to him, “You lack one thing: go, sell all that you have and give to the poor, and you will have treasure in heaven; and come, follow me.” <sup>22</sup>Disheartened by the saying, he went away sorrowful, for he had great possessions. <sup>23</sup>And Jesus looked around and said to his disciples, “How difficult it will be for those who have wealth to enter the kingdom of God!” <sup>24</sup>And the disciples were amazed at his words. But Jesus said to them again, “Children, how difficult it is to enter the kingdom of God! <sup>25</sup>It is easier for a camel to go through the eye of a needle than for a rich person to enter the kingdom of God.” <sup>26</sup>And they were exceedingly astonished, and said to him, “Then who can be saved?” <sup>27</sup>Jesus looked at them and said, “With man it is impossible, but not with God. For all things are possible with God.” <sup>28</sup>Peter began to say to him, “See, we have left everything and followed you.” <sup>29</sup>Jesus said, “Truly, I say to you, there is no one who has left house or brothers or sisters or mother or father or children or lands, for my sake and for the gospel, <sup>30</sup>who will not receive a hundredfold now in this time, houses and brothers and sisters and mothers and children and lands, with persecutions, and in the age to come eternal life. <sup>31</sup>But many who are first will be last, and the last first.” <sup>32</sup>And they were on the road, going up to Jerusalem, and Jesus was walking ahead of them. And they were amazed, and those who followed were afraid. And taking the twelve again, he began to tell them what was to happen to him, <sup>33</sup>saying, “See, we are going up to Jerusalem, and the Son of Man will be delivered over to the chief priests and the scribes, and they will condemn him to death and deliver him over to the Gentiles. <sup>34</sup>And they will mock him and spit on him, and flog him and kill him. And after three days he will rise.” <sup>35</sup>And James and John, the sons of Zebedee, came up to him and said to him, “Teacher, we want you to do for us whatever we ask of you.” <sup>36</sup>And he said to them, “What do you want me to do for you?” <sup>37</sup>And they said to him, “Grant us to sit, one at your right hand and one at your left, in your glory.” <sup>38</sup>Jesus said to them, “You do not know what you are asking. Are you able to drink the cup that I drink, or to be baptized with the baptism with which I am baptized?” <sup>39</sup>And they said to him, “We are able.” And Jesus said to them, “The cup that I drink you will drink, and with the baptism with which I am baptized, you will be baptized, <sup>40</sup>but to sit at my right hand or at my left is not mine to grant, but it is for those for whom it has been prepared.” <sup>41</sup>And when the ten heard it, they began to be indignant at James and John. <sup>42</sup>And Jesus called them to him and said to them, “You know that those who are considered rulers of the Gentiles lord it over them, and their great ones exercise authority over them. <sup>43</sup>But it shall not be so among you. But whoever would be great among you must be your servant, <sup>44</sup>and whoever would be first among you must be slave of all. <sup>45</sup>For even the Son of Man came not to be served but to serve, and to give his life as a ransom for many.” <sup>46</sup>And they came to Jericho. And as he was leaving Jericho with his disciples and a great crowd, Bartimaeus, a blind beggar, the son of Timaeus, was sitting by the roadside. <sup>47</sup>And when he heard that it was Jesus of Nazareth, he began to cry out and say, “Jesus, Son of David, have mercy on me!” <sup>48</sup>And many rebuked him, telling him to be silent. But he cried out all the more, “Son of David, have mercy on me!” <sup>49</sup>And Jesus stopped and said, “Call him.” And they called the blind man, saying to him, “Take heart. Get up; he is calling you.” <sup>50</sup>And throwing off his cloak, he sprang up and came to Jesus. <sup>51</sup>And Jesus said to him, “What do you want me to do for you?” And the blind man said to him, “Rabbi, let me recover my sight.” <sup>52</sup>And Jesus said to him, “Go your way; your faith has made you well.” And immediately he recovered his sight and followed him on the way.
10.overview:
Chapter 10 takes the three things people build their lives out of — marriage, children, money — and hands them, one after another, to a man walking to Jerusalem to die.

The Pharisees open with the question that cost John the Baptist his head, and Jesus refuses to argue about grounds for divorce. He goes behind Moses to Genesis: male and female, one flesh, what therefore God has joined together, let not man separate. Then parents bring children and the disciples turn them away, and Jesus is indignant — the only time in Mark that word is used of him, and it is aimed at his own men. Then a rich man runs, kneels, asks the best question in the Gospel, is looked at and loved by the Son of God — and goes home, because there was one thing he would not give.

The second half is a road. Jesus walks ahead with a set face while the twelve follow amazed and the crowd follows afraid, and he tells them for the third time exactly what is waiting: handed over, condemned, given to the Gentiles, mocked, spat on, flogged, killed, raised. James and John's response is to ask for the two best seats — and out of that squabble comes the summit of the Gospel: the Son of Man came not to be served but to serve, and to give his life as a ransom for many.

Then Jericho, and a blind beggar who shouts a messianic title none of the disciples has used, is told to be quiet, shouts louder, throws away the only thing he owns, and follows Jesus up the road. The chapter opened with a rich man who would not follow and closes with a beggar who did.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–31 — Divorce, Children, and the Danger of Riches
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The trap (vv. 1–12). He crosses into Herod's jurisdiction, and the Pharisees immediately ask him about divorce — the question that cost John the Baptist his head. Jesus refuses to argue about grounds and goes behind Moses to Genesis: male and female, one flesh, joined by God.

The children (vv. 13–16). Parents bring their children to be touched, the disciples turn them away as an interruption, and Jesus is indignant — the only time in Mark that word is used of him, and it is aimed at his own men. Then he picks the children up and blesses them.

The rich man (vv. 17–22). A man runs, kneels, and asks the best question in the Gospel. Jesus looks at him and loves him, and asks for the one thing he will not give. He goes away sorrowful, and Mark does not soften the ending.

The impossibility (vv. 23–31). A camel through a needle's eye, disciples asking then who can be saved?, and the only answer there has ever been — with man it is impossible, but not with God.

Three subjects, and one thread running under them: marriage, children, money. The three things people build their lives out of, handled one after another by a man walking to Jerusalem to die.
verseByVerse.theology:
Divorce, and what Mark leaves out. A reader with Matthew open will notice that Mark's version is starker. Matthew twice records an exception — except for sexual immorality (Matt. 5:32; 19:9) — and Mark records none, while adding, for his Roman readers, the case of a wife who divorces her husband.

That is not a contradiction but a difference of purpose. Mark gives the principle in its unguarded, creation-order form, the way a thing is stated when you want its full weight felt. Matthew, writing where the rabbis argued endlessly over grounds, records the one qualification Jesus actually allowed. Paul adds a second — the believer deserted by an unbelieving spouse is not enslaved (1 Cor. 7:15). So the Reformed churches have long recognised two grounds on which the bond may be broken and the innocent party freed: adultery and desertion, and no others.

Mark's silence is not a denial. It is a refusal to lead with the exception — because the moment the exception becomes the headline, hardness of heart starts hunting for a way in. Jesus will not begin where the Pharisees wanted to begin, with the escape clause. He begins with the joining that God himself performs.

And "Why do you call me good?" (v. 18) is not Jesus denying that he is good or that he is God — and note that he never withdraws the word or corrects the man for using it. He holds it up to the light. The young man has tossed off Good Teacher as easy flattery. Jesus stops him: do you know what you are saying? Goodness in the full sense belongs to God alone. So either you should not have called me good — or, if the word is right, you must reckon with who I am. It is not a denial of his deity but a door held open to it.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: a man who ran, knelt, asked the right question, had kept the commandments since boyhood, was looked at and loved by the Son of God — and went home.

Now: he is the most alarming figure in the Gospel precisely because there is nothing wrong with him. He is not a Pharisee, not a hypocrite, not hostile. He is sincere, moral, eager and respectful, and he is the one person in Mark who meets Jesus, is loved by him, and walks away.

And notice what stopped him. Not an argument. Not doubt. One thing he would not hand over.

So the question the passage actually asks is not am I a good person? — he was, by every visible measure. It is: what is the one thing? What would you be unable to say yes to, if Christ named it tonight? For this man it was money, and Jesus went straight to it, because a rival throne is always specific.

The test is not hypothetical either. Most people know the answer within a few seconds and then spend a while explaining why that particular thing is different. He went away sorrowful, which means he knew exactly what he was refusing. Mark records no second visit.

verseByVerse.quote: And he left there and went to the region of Judea and beyond the Jordan, and crowds gathered to him again. And again, as was his custom, he taught them. And Pharisees came up and in order to test him asked, "Is it lawful for a man to divorce his wife?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus left Galilee and went to the region of Judea and beyond the Jordan. Crowds gathered to him again, and, as was his custom, he taught them again. Pharisees came and, to test him, asked: is it lawful for a man to divorce his wife?

Meaning first. Mark 10 is the road to Jerusalem. Leaving Galilee for the last time, Jesus teaches what life in his kingdom looks like: in marriage, which God joined and no one may separate; with children, whom he takes in his arms because the kingdom belongs to those who receive it with empty hands; and with money, which held one eager rich man so tightly that he walked away from eternal life. Salvation, he says, is impossible with man but not with God. Walking ahead toward the city, he foretells his death a third time; James and John ask for the best seats; and he explains his whole life: the Son of Man came to serve and to give his life as a ransom for many. At Jericho a blind beggar cries for mercy, receives his sight and follows him. The rich man had everything and went away; the beggar had nothing and followed.

The setting. Jesus is on his way to Jerusalem and the cross (v. 32), and this chapter gathers what he taught along the road, ending with the Son of Man who came to serve and give his life (v. 45).

The region of Judea and beyond the Jordan. “Beyond the Jordan” is Perea, the land east of the river, which, like Galilee, was ruled by Herod Antipas. That matters for what happens next. Herod had divorced his wife to marry Herodias, who had left his brother, and John the Baptist had been arrested and beheaded for saying it was unlawful (6:17–18). Herod’s fortress of Machaerus, where tradition says John died, was in this very region. Jesus has walked into the jurisdiction of the man who killed John, and the very next thing he is asked about is divorce.

And again, as was his custom, he taught them. Mark says again twice. The pattern of the whole ministry in one sentence: they came, and he taught. Teaching was his first work, ahead of miracles (1:38).

In order to test him. Mark tells us the motive first. The Pharisees did not want instruction. They wanted a trap. If he took a strict line, he might offend the crowds, and Herod, with every chance of John’s fate. If he took a loose line, he could be accused of undermining Moses.

Is it lawful for a man to divorce his wife? All Jews agreed that divorce was permitted. The debate was over the grounds. Deuteronomy 24:1 allowed a man to divorce his wife if he found some indecency in her, and the whole argument turned on that phrase. The school of Rabbi Shammai said it meant sexual immorality only. The school of Rabbi Hillel said it meant anything that displeased him, even spoiling a dish; a later rabbi, Akiba, said finding a prettier woman was enough. Matthew records the question in this form: for any cause? (Matthew 19:3). Mark gives the bare question, the more radical one: is divorce lawful at all?

Nobody has mentioned the wife. And notice the part we feel least: it is a question asked entirely from the man’s side. In that world the initiative was almost always his alone, and a woman put away had no property, no standing and very little future. The Pharisees are debating the limits of a man’s freedom to dispose of a person. Nobody in that conversation has mentioned the wife. Jesus is about to.

Testing the Bridegroom. Mark’s word, to test, is the word for Israel putting God to the test in the wilderness (Psalm 95:9), and the irony runs deep. The prophets had called the LORD Israel’s husband (Isaiah 54:5; Hosea 2:16), the faithful partner of an unfaithful bride, who in Hosea goes after his wife and buys her back (Hosea 3:1–2). Jesus had already called himself the bridegroom (2:19). So the men asking how easily a husband may put away his wife are putting the question to the one Husband whose love has outlasted all his people’s unfaithfulness, and whose errand on this road is to win a bride at the cost of his life.

In a sentence. In Herod’s territory, on the way to Jerusalem, the Pharisees tried to trap Jesus with the disputed question of divorce.

On a Tuesday. Some people ask about marriage only to find the minimum required. Ask instead what God intended. And when you find yourself asking whether something is allowed, stop and ask why you want to know. The question of the outer boundary is usually asked by someone who has already decided what he wants.

For worship. The Lord walked into the territory of the king who had killed his forerunner, and did not soften the truth to save himself. He would not be trapped, flattered or frightened. And in a conversation where powerful men were weighing how easily a wife could be discarded, he was already on her side. Our Saviour is the defender of the defenceless, and he is never afraid of kings.
verseByVerse.note: “Beyond the Jordan” is Perea, the land east of the river, ruled by Herod Antipas — who had imprisoned John for his marriage. Rabbis debated the grounds for divorce.

verseByVerse.quote: He answered them, "What did Moses command you?" They said, "Moses allowed a man to write a certificate of divorce and to send her away." And Jesus said to them, "Because of your hardness of heart he wrote you this commandment.
verseByVerse.commentary:
He answered: what did Moses command you? They said: Moses allowed a man to write a certificate of divorce and send her away. Jesus said to them: because of your hardness of heart he wrote you this commandment.

What did Moses command you? Jesus goes to Scripture, as always. And he answers a question with a question, and his question is a trap of its own, because the verb is precise. He asks what Moses commanded.

Moses allowed a man to write a certificate of divorce and to send her away. They correct him: allowed, not commanded. They are right, and they have just handed him the case. They are referring to Deuteronomy 24:1–4, and read carefully, that passage does not command divorce or even approve it. It regulates something already happening. Its actual command is that a man who has divorced his wife, and she has married another, may not take her back. The certificate of divorce protected the woman: it proved she had been released and could remarry without being accused of adultery, without which she could be suspected and destitute for the rest of her life. It also required a formal process, which might give the husband time to reconsider. Moses was not opening a door; he was limiting the damage on the other side of one already open.

Because of your hardness of heart he wrote you this commandment. “Hardness of heart” (sklērokardia) means stubbornness, an unteachable heart, the phrase Mark used of the Pharisees in the synagogue (3:5) and close to what he has twice said of the disciples (6:52; 8:17): a heart that has thickened until it cannot feel. The law of divorce was a concession to human sin. Because men would divorce their wives anyway, God through Moses set limits to protect the vulnerable. It was never God’s ideal. A law can regulate sin without approving it. And notice the pronoun: he wrote you this commandment. The concession was granted to people like you, for hardness like yours, and you have turned it into an entitlement and come here asking how far it extends.

What God permits and what God intends. This is worth having as a way of reading Scripture, because it is a distinction we constantly lose. The Bible regulates polygamy, slavery, warfare and divorce in a fallen world; it does not commend them, and in every case the regulation is a restraint on a fallen practice, not a blueprint. To read a concession as an endorsement is exactly the mistake being made in this conversation.

Greater than Moses. Watch who is handling the law here. The Pharisees treat Moses as the last word; Jesus explains why Moses wrote what he wrote, and then goes behind him to the beginning. No rabbi spoke like that. He speaks as one who knows the Lawgiver’s mind from the inside, because Moses was faithful in God’s house as a servant and Christ is faithful over it as a Son (Hebrews 3:5–6). And he names the real trouble, the hardness of heart, as the one who came to deal with it. Moses could only limit the damage hard hearts do. The Son came to do something about the hearts.

What it does not mean. Not that Moses was wrong, or that the law was not from God. But laws for a sinful society are not always statements of God’s perfect will. Some laws restrain evil; they do not define good.

In a sentence. Jesus said that Moses’ provision for divorce was a concession to the hardness of human hearts, not a statement of God’s will for marriage.

On a Tuesday. Don’t confuse what God permits because of sin with what he desires. Before you ask whether something is allowed, ask whether it pleases him. And when a verse seems to give you room for what you already wanted, read it again slowly, and ask whether it is a concession to hard hearts or a picture of God’s design.

For worship. Even in his concessions God was kind. In a hard-hearted world he put a paper into the hand of the discarded woman so that she would not be left with nothing. And the Lord who saw the hardness of every heart in that conversation did not answer it with a harsher law. He walked on to Jerusalem to be broken himself, so that God might take out hearts of stone and write his law on hearts of flesh. The Lord who exposed the Pharisees’ hardness is the Lord who came to cure it.
verseByVerse.note: A certificate of divorce freed a woman to remarry.

verseByVerse.quote: But from the beginning of creation, 'God made them male and female.' 'Therefore a man shall leave his father and mother and hold fast to his wife, and the two shall become one flesh.' So they are no longer two but one flesh. What therefore God has joined together, let not man separate."
verseByVerse.commentary:
But from the beginning of creation, God made them male and female. Therefore a man shall leave his father and mother and hold fast to his wife, and the two shall become one flesh. So they are no longer two but one flesh. What therefore God has joined together, let not man separate.

But from the beginning of creation. That is the move, and it is the most important thing in the passage. Asked about Deuteronomy, he goes to Genesis. Asked about the rules for ending a marriage, he goes to what a marriage is. Before sin, before the law of Sinai, God established marriage, and that original design is the standard. Deuteronomy 24 was a concession; Genesis 1 and 2 are the pattern.

God made them male and female. Genesis 1:27. Two sexes, created by God, made for each other. Marriage is not a human invention that societies happen to have adopted and may therefore adapt. It is built into the way people were made, before any law, before any culture, before the fall. This is the foundation of the Christian understanding of marriage as between one man and one woman.

Therefore a man shall leave his father and mother and hold fast to his wife. Genesis 2:24. Jesus treats the narrator’s words in Genesis as God’s own word. There are two verbs worth separating. Leave: a public, decisive break with the strongest tie a person has had up to that point; a new primary loyalty replaces the old one. Marriage begins with a departure, and a marriage in which one party has never actually left home, emotionally or practically, will feel the fault line for decades. Hold fast (proskollēthēsetai): be glued, joined, cleave. The Hebrew behind it is used of clinging to God himself (Deuteronomy 10:20). It is not a mood. It is a decision that is renewed, and does not depend on how the week has gone.

The Maker in the conversation. Matthew records that Jesus attributed these words to the one who created them from the beginning (Matthew 19:4–5), and Mark’s readers know who is speaking. The Word through whom all things were made (John 1:3) is standing in Perea explaining his own design. He was there when the man and the woman were made and joined; he knows what a marriage is because he made the first one. No one has ever had a better right to say what God has joined, and no one has ever honoured a bride as he will honour his.

And the two shall become one flesh. A union of the whole person, physical, emotional and spiritual, of which sexual union is both the expression and the seal. A new unit is created.

So they are no longer two but one flesh. Jesus’ own conclusion; it is his comment on the text. And it is a statement of fact rather than an ideal to be aimed at. Something has actually happened. Two people have been made into a single new reality, and the union is real whatever either of them feels about it on a given morning. Which is why the ending of a marriage is never merely administrative. You cannot separate one flesh without tearing something, and everyone who has been through it knows this in their body long before they can say it.

What therefore God has joined together, let not man separate. The weight of the sentence is in the two agents. God has joined. A wedding is not merely a human contract; the joining is not done by the couple, or the minister, or the registrar. God himself creates the bond, in every genuine marriage, including marriages between people who have never given him a thought. Let not man separate: no human being, not the husband, not the wife, not a court or a rabbi, has the right to tear apart what God did. “Separate” (chōrizetō) is the word used of divorce (1 Corinthians 7:10–11).

What this means on the bad days. This verse is not primarily about ending marriages; it is about how you regard the one you are in. You are not in an arrangement that continues as long as it works. You are in something God did. And that changes what to do in the year that is going wrong, the stretch where you feel nothing, the point at which the thought first arrives that you might have made a mistake. The question in that hour is not, is this still working? It is: what did God join, and what am I doing to keep it? Marriages are rarely separated by one decision. They are separated by a thousand small permissions: the conversation not had, the resentment kept, the friendship at work that becomes the place you are understood. Let not man separate is a command about all of that, and it is addressed to the man in the mirror.

What if my marriage is very unhappy? Unhappiness is not a ground for divorce, but it is a reason to act, not to drift. Pray honestly about it together and alone. Ask for help early: a wise pastor or older couple, and good Christian counselling. Look first at your own part, and confess it. Keep doing the ordinary acts of love when the feeling is absent, because feelings often follow faithfulness. Many couples who came close to the end have found, years later, a deeper marriage than they had at the start. And if the unhappiness is fear because you are being harmed, that is a different matter: you do not have to stay in danger, separation for protection is not sin, and the church must believe and protect you.

What about people who never marry, or who experience same-sex attraction? Jesus’ words define marriage; they do not say that everyone must marry. Jesus himself was single, and Paul calls singleness a gift (1 Corinthians 7:7). A single life given to Christ is full and honourable, not second-class. Those who experience same-sex attraction are not beyond the love or the family of God; the call to them is the same as to every believer, to deny themselves and follow Christ, and the church must be a real family to them (v. 30). But Jesus’ grounding of marriage in God making them male and female means the church cannot bless any other union as marriage.

In a sentence. Going back to creation, Jesus taught that God made marriage as the lifelong union of a man and a woman as one flesh, which no human being may separate.

On a Tuesday. If you are married, God joined you. Treat your marriage as his work, and guard it. Name one small permission you have been allowing that is pulling you apart, and close it this week. And do one thing today that says to your husband or wife: I am still holding fast.

For worship. From the beginning God made man and woman and joined them, and in the joining he was drawing a picture of something greater: Christ and his church (Ephesians 5:31–32). The Bridegroom left his Father’s house to hold fast to a bride who had been unfaithful, and he will never let her go. Every faithful marriage is a small portrait of that love, and every broken one is held under the mercy of the Husband who keeps his vows.

parallels.desc: male and female he created them

verseByVerse.quote: And in the house the disciples asked him again about this matter. And he said to them, "Whoever divorces his wife and marries another commits adultery against her, and if she divorces her husband and marries another, she commits adultery."
verseByVerse.commentary:
In the house the disciples asked him again about this. He said to them: whoever divorces his wife and marries another commits adultery against her; and if she divorces her husband and marries another, she commits adultery.

And in the house the disciples asked him again. The pattern of this Gospel once more: a public statement, then a private question, and the men who get the fuller answer are the ones who ask. They were startled. Matthew records what they said in the house: If such is the case of a man with his wife, it is better not to marry (Matthew 19:10). Jesus’ teaching was stricter than either rabbinic school. These were not men who found this easy.

Whoever divorces his wife and marries another commits adultery against her. Since God’s bond still holds in his eyes, remarriage after a divorce God does not recognise is adultery. Under the rabbinic system a properly executed divorce ended the marriage, and the certificate cleared the man. Jesus says the certificate does not touch what God joined. And “against her” was revolutionary. In Jewish law, adultery was a sin against a husband; a man could only commit adultery against another man, by taking his wife. Jesus says a husband can commit adultery against his own wife. She has rights. Marriage creates obligations on both sides equally.

The wife at the centre. Take the measure of that in a conversation which began with men debating the limits of a man’s freedom to dispose of a person. Nobody in verse 2 mentioned the wife. Jesus puts her at the centre of the sentence and names her as the one who has been wronged. Wherever the gospel has gone, that has followed. The raising of the dignity of women in the societies Christianity touched is not a modern correction applied to an embarrassing text; it starts here, in a house in Perea, with a rabbi telling twelve men that a discarded wife has been sinned against.

And if she divorces her husband and marries another. Jewish law did not normally allow a wife to divorce her husband, but Roman and Greek law did, and it was common among the propertied classes. Mark, writing probably for Roman readers, records that Jesus’ teaching applies to both. Herodias had in fact divorced her husband, which may be in the background. The standard is the same in both directions. There is no double standard here, no allowance for the husband that is denied the wife.

The exceptions. Mark gives the principle without exception. Matthew records an exception: except for sexual immorality (Matthew 19:9; 5:32). Paul adds another: if an unbelieving spouse leaves, the believer is not bound (1 Corinthians 7:15). These exceptions do not contradict Mark. They show that some sins so break the marriage covenant that the innocent party may lawfully end it.

Where Christians differ: divorce and remarriage. Roman Catholic teaching holds that a valid sacramental marriage cannot be dissolved; remarriage while the spouse lives is never permitted, though an annulment may declare that no true marriage existed. Some Protestants hold that remarriage is never right while a spouse lives, even after divorce for adultery. Others allow divorce for many reasons, such as abuse, or simply breakdown. Verdict: the Westminster Confession states the position best grounded in Scripture (Westminster 24.5–6): God’s design is lifelong marriage, and divorce is always a tragedy; but adultery, and wilful desertion that cannot be remedied, are grounds on which the innocent party may divorce and be free to remarry. Abandonment through serious abuse may fall under desertion, and the church should protect the vulnerable. Those who have divorced and remarried wrongly may repent and find full forgiveness in Christ, as with any sin.

Not a list of loopholes. Even where Scripture allows divorce, it never requires it. Adultery and desertion give the innocent party freedom, not an obligation, and where there is genuine repentance, reconciliation is better where it is possible. Hosea took back an unfaithful wife as a picture of God’s love for his people. Some marriages wounded by adultery have been rebuilt, slowly and at great cost, into something stronger. But that is the wronged spouse’s free choice before God, and no one may shame them for using the freedom Christ gives.

What if I am being abused? Abuse is never to be tolerated, excused or covered up, and nothing in Jesus’ words requires you to remain in danger. If you or your children are being hurt, threatened or controlled, your first duty is safety: get to a safe place, call the police where there is violence or threat, and tell someone you trust. Separation for protection is not sin. A husband who abuses his wife is himself breaking the covenant he vowed; headship in Scripture means self-giving love, never domination (Ephesians 5:25). Elders and churches must believe, protect and support victims, involve the civil authorities, and call the abuser to account. Whether divorce is then lawful is a further question, and serious abuse may fall under desertion, but you do not need to settle that question before you get safe.

What if I divorced and remarried before I became a Christian, or on wrong grounds? The sin is real and should be confessed. But a second marriage, once made, is a marriage, and the answer is not to break it, which would add another sin; Moses’ law itself forbade going back to the first spouse after remarriage (Deuteronomy 24:1–4). Christ forgives the repentant fully, and you are to live faithfully where you now are, honouring the vows you made. Paul tells believers to remain in the condition in which they were called (1 Corinthians 7:17–20), and that includes your present marriage. Your past does not disqualify you from grace or from serving God.

A word to the divorced. A word must be said plainly to the reader who is already divorced, perhaps remarried, and reading these hard sentences with a sinking heart, because this is a passage people live inside rather than merely study. The standard has not moved, and it would be no kindness to pretend it has; a church that lowers it to seem gentle has only made grace unnecessary. But hear this clearly. There is no sin named here that the blood of Christ does not cover, and no marriage so broken, by your fault, another’s, or the tangle of both, that grace cannot make something new of what remains. The gospel does not meet you in the marriage you should have had. It meets you in the life you actually have, with a Saviour who came to give his life as a ransom for many (v. 45), the divorced among them.

In a sentence. Jesus taught that divorce and remarriage, whether by husband or wife, is adultery in God’s eyes, because the marriage bond God made still stands.

On a Tuesday. If divorce has touched your life, don’t despair; Christ forgives and restores. If you are married, keep your vows. If you are single, honour marriage in how you speak of it. And if someone in your church is divorced, or is being harmed at home, be the person who believes them, prays for them and stands by them.

For worship. The Lord who would not lower his standard is the Lord who came to bear the sin of those who have broken it. He defended the discarded wife against the men who would put her away, and he defends every wronged and frightened person still. He keeps covenant when we do not, and his faithfulness is the ground on which every repentant sinner stands, whatever lies behind them.
verseByVerse.note: Jewish law did not allow a wife to divorce her husband, but Roman law did; Mark’s wording covers both.

verseByVerse.quote: And they were bringing children to him that he might touch them, and the disciples rebuked them. But when Jesus saw it, he was indignant and said to them, "Let the children come to me; do not hinder them, for to such belongs the kingdom of God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
People were bringing children to him so that he might touch them, and the disciples rebuked them. When Jesus saw it, he was indignant and said to them: let the children come to me; do not hinder them, for to such belongs the kingdom of God.

And they were bringing children to him that he might touch them. After marriage, children: Mark is drawing the household of the kingdom. Parents, probably, wanting his blessing. Luke says some were babies (brephē, Luke 18:15). It was ordinary in that world to bring a child to a respected rabbi or elder for a blessing, and that is all these people are asking: put your hand on him.

And the disciples rebuked them. The verb is strong, the same one used of Jesus rebuking demons and of Peter rebuking Jesus. They did not gently discourage; they told them off. By any ordinary measure their reasoning was sound: the Master is on the road to Jerusalem; he has been teaching all day and has just handled a hostile delegation on divorce; there are weightier matters. Children are not a priority, and somebody has to manage the diary. They had not learned the lesson of 9:36–37. This is the second time in two chapters the disciples have tried to control access to Jesus: they stopped a man casting out demons because he was not one of them (9:38), and now they turn away parents with babies. There is something in religious people that gravitates toward the door.

He was indignant. A strong word (ēganaktēsen), used of Jesus only here, and the same word Mark uses of the ten when they are furious with James and John (v. 41). This is not mild disapproval. Jesus was angry, and he was angry with his own disciples, and the cause was that children were being kept away from him. The Son of God, days from the cross, became visibly angry because somebody turned away a queue of toddlers. What made him angry was not the interruption. It was the gatekeeping.

Let the children come to me; do not hinder them. Two commands, positive and negative. Nothing must stand between children and Jesus. The word hinder is the one used when the Ethiopian asked what prevented him from being baptised (Acts 8:36).

Who hinders children now? It is rarely done deliberately. It is done by treating them as a distraction to be managed until they are old enough to matter: the church that has no room for them, the family in which faith is discussed but never with them, the parent who is too tired at bedtime and always will be. And it is done by the hypocrisy children see at home. Nobody rebukes anybody. The children simply do not get brought.

For to such belongs the kingdom of God. Note the wording: to such, not only to these. He is not saying that children are automatically in and adults are not. The kingdom belongs to people of this kind: those who, like children, have nothing to offer and simply receive. Not because children are innocent, but because they are dependent.

Where Christians differ: children and baptism. Paedobaptists (Presbyterians, Anglicans, Lutherans, Catholics) often appeal to this passage for infant baptism: if the kingdom belongs to children, they should receive the sign of the covenant. Credobaptists (Baptists) answer that Jesus did not baptise these children; he blessed them, and the passage is about how all must receive the kingdom, not about a sacrament. Verdict: the passage shows Christ’s welcome for children and the need to bring them to him, which both sides agree on. It does not mention baptism, and it cannot settle the question. The New Testament pattern links baptism to repentance and faith, so the credobaptist position is best. This is a disagreement among brothers, held charitably.

So how do Baptist parents bring their children to Christ? In every way except the sign that belongs to those who profess faith. Pray for them by name and with them, from the cradle. Teach them the Scriptures and the gospel at home (Deuteronomy 6:6–7; 2 Timothy 3:15). Bring them to worship, where they hear the word and see the people of God. Many churches hold a service of thanksgiving and dedication, in which parents give thanks and promise to raise the child in the Lord. Speak to them of Christ as one who welcomes children, and call them to trust him themselves. Then, when they profess faith and show its fruit, they are baptised. Our brothers who baptise their infants share every one of those aims.

What of children who die young? Scripture gives no age of accountability and no formula, and we should say no more than it says. But it gives firm ground for hope. Elect infants dying in infancy are regenerated and saved by Christ through the Spirit, who works when and where and how he pleases (1689 London Baptist Confession 10.3). David expected to go to the son who died in infancy (2 Samuel 12:23). And the one who took children in his arms and was indignant when they were kept from him is the Judge of all the earth, who will do what is right (Genesis 18:25). Grieving parents may entrust their little ones to that mercy with confidence.

In a sentence. Jesus was indignant when his disciples kept children away, commanding that they be allowed to come, for the kingdom belongs to such as these.

On a Tuesday. Bring your children to Jesus: pray for them, teach them, take them to worship. Never be a hindrance to a child coming to Christ. Tonight, pray with a child, even briefly. And look at your church through a child’s eyes: is there room for them, and does anyone speak to them of Jesus?

For worship. The Lord of glory, setting his face to Jerusalem, had time for babies. He was angry when they were sent away, and he called them to himself. That is the heart of God laid open: not a busy king who tolerates the small, but a Saviour who wants them near. He has never yet turned away anyone who was brought to him with nothing to offer.
verseByVerse.note: Children had little status in the ancient world.

verseByVerse.quote: Truly, I say to you, whoever does not receive the kingdom of God like a child shall not enter it." And he took them in his arms and blessed them, laying his hands on them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Truly, I tell you, whoever does not receive the kingdom of God like a child shall not enter it. And he took them in his arms and blessed them, laying his hands on them.

Truly, I say to you. The amen-formula again, for something he wants underlined. And it is stated negatively, which makes it a condition rather than a compliment: no one enters any other way.

Whoever does not receive the kingdom of God like a child. How does a child receive? What is it about a child? Not innocence: children are not morally blank, and David says he was brought forth in iniquity (Psalm 51:5).
