Not simplicity of mind either, as though faith required us to stop thinking; this is the same Lord who tells us to love God with all our mind (12:30). It is dependence. A small child in that world owned nothing, earned nothing, and could contribute nothing. He did not negotiate for his dinner; he was fed. He did not qualify for his place in the family; he was born into it. Everything he had came to him as a gift from someone bigger, and he took it without embarrassment. The kingdom must be received in exactly that way, as grace, not achievement. This is the gospel in a sentence.

Shall not enter it. A strong negative. This is the only way in. Adults must become like children; they cannot come in as adults, with their merits.

Why this is so hard for competent adults. Every other sphere of life rewards the self-sufficient: the person who earns it, manages it, deserves it, brings something to the table. Here, the qualities that recommend you everywhere else are the disqualifying ones. Receive is the only verb on offer. The rich man who comes running next is the opposite of the child: he asks, what must I do? (v. 17). A child comes with empty hands and is welcomed. A rich man comes with full ones and cannot get in.

What does receiving like a child look like for me? It means coming to God with no bargaining position. You stop presenting your record, your church attendance, your efforts, as reasons God should accept you, and you simply trust what he has promised in Christ. It means believing that he loves you because he is your Father, not because you have performed well this week. And it continues all through the Christian life: you keep receiving forgiveness, strength and guidance as gifts, rather than turning the Christian life into a new way of earning. It does not mean being naive or passive; children who trust their father also obey him. But the obedience grows from being loved, not the other way round.

And he took them in his arms. Only Mark records it, as in 9:36. The verb (enagkalisamenos), to fold in the arms, occurs twice in the whole New Testament, both in Mark. Peter remembered it both times. This is a fisherman, decades later, telling a church that when the Lord of glory dealt with children he did not pat them on the head. He gathered them up. The people brought the children for a touch; he gave them an embrace.

And blessed them, laying his hands on them. “Blessed” (kateulogei) is an intensive form, used only here in the New Testament: he blessed them fervently, again and again, one child at a time, on a road going up to Jerusalem, while grown men stood by wishing he would get on. The laying on of hands was the sign of blessing, as when Jacob blessed Joseph’s sons (Genesis 48:14). And they were the same hands that had taken a dead girl by the hand (5:41) and lifted a convulsing boy from the ground (9:27), and which within weeks would be nailed down and unable to hold anybody at all.

In a sentence. Jesus said that only those who receive the kingdom as a child receives a gift will enter it, and he embraced and blessed the children.

On a Tuesday. Notice this week where you are still trying to earn God’s favour: the guilt after a bad day that keeps you from prayer, the pride after a good one. In both cases do what a child does: come anyway, and receive. And if you have children, let them see you come to God that way.

For worship. On a road where he was carrying the weight of the world, the Lord of glory stopped to gather up children who could bring him nothing, and he blessed them over and over. That is still the way he receives anyone who comes with empty hands: not with a pat on the head but with an embrace. The arms that folded around those children were opened wide on a cross, and they have never closed against anyone brought to him since.

verseByVerse.quote: And as he was setting out on his journey, a man ran up and knelt before him and asked him, "Good Teacher, what must I do to inherit eternal life?" And Jesus said to him, "Why do you call me good? No one is good except God alone.
verseByVerse.commentary:
As he was setting out on his journey, a man ran up, knelt before him and asked: Good Teacher, what must I do to inherit eternal life? Jesus said to him: why do you call me good? No one is good except God alone.

A man ran up and knelt before him. Everything about the approach is right, and Mark makes sure you notice. He ran: a grown man of standing running down a public road, when men of position in that culture did not run, because it was undignified. He does not care. He knelt: in the dirt, in front of an itinerant teacher, in public. Matthew tells us he was young (Matthew 19:20), Luke that he was a ruler (Luke 18:18), and all three that he was rich (v. 22). So he is often called the rich young ruler. He had everything, and still lacked something.

Good Teacher. An unusual title. The rabbis did not use it; Jewish teachers were not normally called good, a word reserved for God. It is warm and sincere, and it is also the kind of compliment a man pays to a respected figure on his way to asking a favour.

What must I do to inherit eternal life? The best question anybody asks in this Gospel, and nobody else asks it. The Pharisees ask about divorce law and signs from heaven; the disciples ask about seats and greatness; this man asks how to be saved. The point is nearly always missed by making him a villain. He is not one. He is eager, humble, urgent, morally serious, and asking the right thing. If he walked into your church you would thank God for him. But note the word do. He thinks eternal life is something to be achieved. And inherit is a strange word to pair with doing: an inheritance is precisely the thing nobody does anything for. You receive it because of who you are in the family. He has used the language of gift and attached it to the language of achievement, and he does not notice. The child two verses ago received. This man wants to know the price.

Why do you call me good? No one is good except God alone. This has been seized on for centuries as though Jesus were denying that he is good, or denying that he is God. He is doing neither, and notice that he never withdraws the word or corrects the man for using it. He holds it up to the light. Do you know what you have just said? Goodness in the full and final sense belongs to God and to nobody else. Which leaves two possibilities, and the man never works out which one he is in. Either you should not have called me good, in which case you have come running and kneeling to the wrong person; or the word is right, and you must reckon with who is standing in front of you. It is not a denial of his deity. It is a door held open to it. He came asking what he must do, and the deeper question, the one he never reaches, is who is this?

Preparing for what follows. The question does a second thing. If only God is good, then the man is not good either, whatever he thinks about his keeping of the commandments. Jesus has quietly set the standard at the height of God himself, and every human record falls short of it.

What it does not mean. Not a confession by Jesus that he is a sinner, as some have argued. The New Testament is clear that he was without sin (2 Corinthians 5:21; Hebrews 4:15; 1 Peter 2:22).

Compliment or confession? There is a hard little test here for the way we talk about Jesus. It is possible to say very warm things about him and mean very little: to call him wonderful, loving, good, the greatest teacher who ever lived, and to be paying a compliment rather than making a confession. Many people today will happily call Jesus good who will not call him Lord. He is quite capable of stopping a man mid-sentence and asking whether he knows what he is saying. If he is good as only God is good, then he must be worshipped and obeyed, not merely admired.

In a sentence. A rich man ran to Jesus asking what he must do to inherit eternal life, and Jesus challenged his casual use of “good”, since only God is good.

On a Tuesday. If you think of God’s standard as good the way you are good, think again. Only God is good, which is why we need grace. And when you speak of Jesus to a friend this week, do not stop at saying he was a good man. Say who he is.

For worship. Only God is good, and the one who said so was standing in the road, loving the man who had called him good without knowing why. Every perfection of God was there in a human face: holiness without hardness, truth without coldness, goodness that could not be flattered. He is not a good teacher. He is the Good, come down to seek those who are not.
verseByVerse.note: Matthew says he was young, Luke that he was a ruler. Jesus does not deny his goodness; he asks the man to think about what he is saying.

verseByVerse.quote: You know the commandments: 'Do not murder, Do not commit adultery, Do not steal, Do not bear false witness, Do not defraud, Honor your father and mother.'" And he said to him, "Teacher, all these I have kept from my youth."
verseByVerse.commentary:
You know the commandments: do not murder, do not commit adultery, do not steal, do not bear false witness, do not defraud, honour your father and mother. The man said: Teacher, all these I have kept from my youth.

You know the commandments. Jesus begins where the man began. The question was what must I do, so Jesus goes to God’s law: not because keeping it is how anyone is saved, but because it is the mirror the man needs to look into. If the question is about doing, the law sets out what to do.

The list. Jesus lists the second table of the Ten Commandments, the commandments about our neighbour: the sixth, seventh, eighth and ninth, then the fifth. Not one of the first four is mentioned: no other gods, no idols, the name, the Sabbath. That is deliberate, and it is a trap set with great gentleness. The man’s problem is going to turn out to be a first-table problem, a rival god, and Jesus recites only the commandments the man can pass, and waits. He also leaves out the tenth, about desire. Those are where the man will be exposed.

Do not defraud. This is not one of the ten. It appears in the law elsewhere: you shall not oppress your neighbour or rob him, and the wages of a hired worker shall not remain with you all night (Leviticus 19:13; also Deuteronomy 24:14; Malachi 3:5). It may stand for the tenth commandment, since defrauding is covetousness in action. And it is the one commandment on the list that a wealthy landowner in first-century Palestine would have been most likely to break, and least likely to notice himself breaking: withholding what is owed, especially to a labourer. It is the sin of the account book, not the bedroom. He is being probed, kindly, at the exact point of his danger, and he does not feel a thing.

Teacher, all these I have kept from my youth. He drops the good; something in the first exchange registered. His claim is sincere, and by outward standards perhaps true. Jesus does not contest it, and Mark’s next sentence is that Jesus loved him. Paul could say the same of his life before Christ: as to righteousness under the law, blameless (Philippians 3:6). But it is the most self-condemning sentence in the chapter. A man who has genuinely understood any commandment does not talk like this. He has not understood how deep God’s law goes, reaching the anger and lust of the heart (Matthew 5:21–28). All these I have kept is the language of a man who has treated the law as a checklist and is waiting to be told the remaining item. And if he has kept everything, why does he still feel the lack? Matthew records him asking: What do I still lack? (Matthew 19:20).

What he still assumes. He thinks something is missing that can be added. He has the impression that the account is nearly complete and one more entry will balance it. What he is about to be shown is not an additional item. It is that the whole account belongs to somebody else.

Why does Jesus point him to the law if we are not saved by keeping it? Because the law shows us our sin and drives us to Christ (Romans 3:20; Galatians 3:24). A man who thinks he has kept it needs to see that he has not, and Jesus is leading him there with great care. The law is also good as a guide for those already saved, showing how to love God and neighbour. What it can never do is make us right with God, because no one keeps it from the heart. Christ kept it perfectly for us, and his obedience is counted to all who trust him.

In a sentence. Jesus pointed the man to the commandments about his neighbour, and the man sincerely claimed to have kept them all since his youth.

On a Tuesday. Outward obedience can hide an unexamined heart. Ask God to search you (Psalm 139:23–24). Take the commandment you are surest you keep, and read Jesus’ deeper meaning of it in Matthew 5. Then go to Christ, not to a new resolution.

For worship. The Lord knew exactly where this man’s heart was bound, and he did not expose it with a blow. He drew it out with questions, gently, the way a physician probes for the place that hurts. The law that condemns us is in his hands a tool of mercy, and its whole demand was met by him, who alone could say with truth, all these I have kept, and kept them in our place.
verseByVerse.note: Jesus lists the commandments about one’s neighbour; “do not defraud” is not one of the Ten in so many words; it may stand for the tenth, against coveting (cf. Lev 19:13).

parallels.desc: the second table of the Ten Commandments

verseByVerse.quote: And Jesus, looking at him, loved him, and said to him, "You lack one thing: go, sell all that you have and give to the poor, and you will have treasure in heaven; and come, follow me." Disheartened by the saying, he went away sorrowful, for he had great possessions.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus, looking at him, loved him, and said to him: you lack one thing. Go, sell all that you have and give to the poor, and you will have treasure in heaven; and come, follow me. Disheartened by the saying, he went away sorrowful, for he had great possessions.

And Jesus, looking at him, loved him. Only Mark records this, and it is one of the tenderest half-sentences in the Bible, and the key to the passage. The verb for looking means to fix the eyes on somebody: a deliberate, held gaze, not a glance. And then: he loved him. It is the only place in this Gospel where we are told that Jesus loved a particular individual. Everything hard that follows must be read inside that. What follows is not harsh. It is love. Jesus saw his sincerity and his need, and the demand he makes is the loving cure for what was killing him.

You lack one thing. Which must have been a relief for about two seconds. He came asking what was still outstanding, and here it is, a single item. For all his keeping of the law, there is a gap. His wealth had his heart. It was his god. He had broken the first commandment, you shall have no other gods before me (Exodus 20:3), and the tenth.

Go, sell all that you have and give to the poor. The surgery: cut out the idol. Notice what the demand does. It exposes a first-table problem with a second-table instruction. The man had passed the whole list about neighbours; Jesus now finds out, in one sentence, whether he has any other gods, and the answer comes back at once.

Is this required of every Christian? No, and the Gospels themselves settle it. Jesus does not ask everyone to sell everything. Peter kept his house in Capernaum (1:29). Zacchaeus gave away half, and was told that salvation had come to his house (Luke 19:8–9). Joseph of Arimathea was rich and remained so, and his money bought the tomb. Jesus does not issue this command to anyone else in the New Testament. It is not a universal rule. It is a scalpel, and it goes to one man’s one thing. He asks this man to give up the thing that stood between him and God. For him, it was money. But the principle is universal: Christ has the right to ask for anything you love more than him.

And you will have treasure in heaven. Not a payment for salvation, but a promise. See the shape of the offer, because it is not asceticism. Jesus does not tell him to be poorer. He tells him to trade: give away treasure on earth and receive treasure in heaven (Matthew 6:19–21), which is the better end of any bargain ever offered to a human being. He would not be poorer at all.

And come, follow me. The real point. Selling everything was the means; following Jesus was the end. Eternal life is not earned by giving away money, but found in following Christ. The man had asked what to do; Jesus answers with the call to discipleship. Love of God, the first table, is shown in following the one in whom God has come. He is being invited to join the Twelve, and that is the real prize, not the treasure.

Disheartened by the saying. “Disheartened” (stygnasas) means his face fell, darkened like a gloomy sky; the word is used of a lowering, overcast sky in Matthew 16:3. You can see it happen.

He went away sorrowful, for he had great possessions. The only person in the Gospels personally called by Jesus to follow him who refused. He went away. He wanted eternal life, but not more than he wanted his money. And the sorrow is real. He is not angry, not scoffing, not arguing. He knows exactly what he is refusing and refuses it anyway, and he is miserable about it. There is such a thing as sorrow that is not repentance, grief over the cost of obedience that never actually obeys, and this man is its portrait. Mark gives the reason last, flat, without comment, and the phrasing is the wrong way round. He did not have great possessions. They had him.

Jesus let him go. Notice what Jesus does not do. He does not call after him. He does not soften the terms, offer a smaller figure, or suggest they talk it over at dinner. The Son of God, who loved this man, watched him walk away and let him go. That is what love looks like when it will not lie to you. A love that lowered the price would have been the crueller thing: it would have sent him home comfortable, with his idol intact, thinking himself safe. Mark records no second visit. The saddest verse in the Gospel is a man walking down a road with everything he came for still in his hands.

What it does not mean. Not that salvation is by giving away your wealth, or that riches are themselves evil. But anything you love more than Christ will keep you from him, and Christ has the right to ask for it.

How do I know what my one thing is? Ask what you could not bear to lose, what you turn to for security when you are afraid, what you think about when your mind is free, and what you would be most angry to have taken away. Ask what you are most reluctant to bring under Christ’s word: your money, a relationship, your reputation, your comfort, your career, your plans for your children. The one thing is usually not a wicked thing but a good thing loved too much. And the test is often money, because money is the most portable god there is. Look at your bank statement and your diary; they tell the truth about the heart.

In a sentence. Out of love, Jesus told the man to give up the wealth that ruled him and follow him, but he went away sad, because he could not let go.

On a Tuesday. What is your one thing, the thing you could not give up for Christ? Look at it honestly, and give it to him. Then do something concrete that loosens its grip this week: a generous gift that costs you, an hour given that you wanted for yourself, a plan surrendered in prayer.

For worship. Jesus looked at him and loved him, and that same look rests on everyone who comes to him. His love will not flatter us to keep us comfortable; it tells us the truth so that it can set us free. And where this man would not let go of his riches to follow Christ, Christ let go of all his riches to come after us: though he was rich, yet for our sake he became poor, so that we by his poverty might become rich (2 Corinthians 8:9).
verseByVerse.note: Only Mark notes that Jesus looked at him and loved him.

verseByVerse.quote: And Jesus looked around and said to his disciples, "How difficult it will be for those who have wealth to enter the kingdom of God!" And the disciples were amazed at his words. But Jesus said to them again, "Children, how difficult it is to enter the kingdom of God! It is easier for a camel to go through the eye of a needle than for a rich person to enter the kingdom of God."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus looked around and said to his disciples: how difficult it will be for those who have wealth to enter the kingdom of God! The disciples were amazed at his words. But Jesus said to them again: children, how difficult it is to enter the kingdom of God! It is easier for a camel to go through the eye of a needle than for a rich person to enter the kingdom of God.

And Jesus looked around. At his disciples, as the rich man walked away. What follows is not aimed at the departing figure; it is for the men staying.

How difficult it will be for those who have wealth to enter the kingdom of God! Riches are dangerous. They give a sense of security and self-sufficiency, of not needing God (Deuteronomy 8:11–14). They tie the heart to this world. They make it hard to receive the kingdom like a child, with empty hands, because full hands cannot receive.

And the disciples were amazed at his words. To understand why they were staggered, you have to know what they had been taught. In the Old Testament prosperity is repeatedly a sign of God’s favour: Abraham, Job, Solomon (Deuteronomy 28:1–14; Job 42:10). The popular theology of the day drew the obvious conclusion: a rich man is a blessed man. And the rich could afford to give alms, offer sacrifices, keep the law scrupulously and study it at leisure. If anyone was going to make it, surely he was. If the rich can hardly enter, what hope for anyone?

Children, how difficult it is to enter the kingdom of God! He says it a second time, and the second time he takes the qualification off. Verse 23 was about the wealthy. Verse 24 is about everybody. The rich man’s case is not a special category; it is the general human case with the difficulty made visible. And notice the word he begins with: Children. It is tender, it links back to the children of verse 15, and it is the only time he addresses the disciples this way in Mark. He is about to say the hardest thing in the chapter, and he opens it the way a father does.

The man who refused the kingdoms of the world. Only one man has faced the pull of wealth at its largest and not given an inch. In the wilderness the devil showed Jesus all the kingdoms of the world and their glory, and offered him the lot for one act of worship, and he answered that God alone is to be worshipped and served (Matthew 4:8–10). The rich man could not let go of his estates. The Son turned down the world, and chose instead the road to a cross, so that people whose hands are full of lesser things could be given the kingdom.

It is easier for a camel to go through the eye of a needle. The camel was the largest animal anyone in Palestine handled; a needle’s eye, the smallest opening anyone used. It is deliberate, comic exaggeration, meant to say: impossible. A similar Jewish saying spoke of an elephant passing through a needle’s eye.

Two ways of softening it. Two old softenings of the saying should both be laid aside. The first says the eye of a needle was a small gate in the wall of Jerusalem, which a camel could squeeze through on its knees once unloaded. There is no evidence for such a gate; the story appears only in the Middle Ages, and it turns the saying into encouraging advice, that with a little humility and less baggage you can just about manage, which is the opposite of the point. The second suggests a scribal confusion between kamēlos (camel) and kamilos (rope); the manuscripts do not support it, and it would not help, since a ship’s rope will not go through a needle either. Jesus means exactly what the disciples heard: humanly impossible (v. 27). Their reaction proves they heard it that way, and he does not correct them.

Am I rich? Almost certainly, by the measure that matters here. Anyone with a home, a change of clothes, food that is not in question this week and medical care within reach is, by every standard the world has known and most it knows now, rich. This is not a passage about bankers. And wealth is dangerous not only for what it buys but for what it makes us feel: safe, competent, in control, without need. The question is not how much you have but whether it has you. Signs that it does: anxiety about money that crowds out trust, reluctance to give, envy of those with more, and a life arranged around keeping what you have.

In a sentence. Jesus told his amazed disciples that it is so hard for the rich to enter the kingdom that a camel would more easily pass through the eye of a needle.

On a Tuesday. By the world’s standards, most readers of this are rich. Hold your wealth with an open hand. Decide this week on one regular act of generosity that you will feel, and give it quietly. Pray for the rich people you know, beginning with yourself.

For worship. The Lord did not soften the impossible to make it bearable, because he intended to do the impossible himself. He looked at a camel and a needle and was not troubled, for he is the God who makes a way where there is none. The door that no one can force has been opened from the inside, by the one who owned everything and laid it all down.
verseByVerse.note: The camel was the largest animal in the land; the picture is deliberate exaggeration. The idea of a gate called “the Eye of the Needle” is a much later invention.

verseByVerse.quote: And they were exceedingly astonished, and said to him, "Then who can be saved?" Jesus looked at them and said, "With man it is impossible, but not with God. For all things are possible with God."
verseByVerse.commentary:
They were exceedingly astonished and said to him: then who can be saved? Jesus looked at them and said: with man it is impossible, but not with God. For all things are possible with God.

Then who can be saved? Exceedingly astonished, stronger than the amazement of verse 24: the second saying has hit harder than the first. And their question is exactly the right one, which is worth saying because the disciples so often get things wrong. Here they reason perfectly. If the man with every visible advantage, money, morality, eagerness, a clean record from boyhood, cannot get in, then no one can. They have understood that the difficulty is not a matter of degree. It is not that the rich have further to walk; it is that the door will not admit anyone under their own power. And it is not academic for them. They have left everything, and if wealth cannot buy entry, neither can renunciation.

Jesus looked at them. A deliberate, steady look, Mark’s third look in this passage. He looked at the rich man and loved him (v. 21); he looked around at the disciples (v. 23); now he fixes his gaze on them again before he answers, because what is coming is the most important sentence in the passage and he wants them looking back.

With man it is impossible. Yes, they had understood. Take it seriously, because we habitually take it as an exaggeration. Not difficult. Not unlikely without help. Not achievable by the exceptionally devout. Impossible, with the same total force as the camel and the needle. No one, rich or poor, can save himself: not by keeping commandments, giving money, or any effort. No one has ever saved himself, contributed to it, met God halfway, or made himself a better prospect. Not the rich man with his clean record, not Peter with his abandoned boat, not you. This is the heart of the gospel’s bad news: we are unable.

But not with God. For all things are possible with God. And this is the good news, and it is the whole of Christianity. The impossibility is real and total, and it is God’s to solve, and he has solved it. What man cannot do, God does. It echoes the angel’s word to Sarah, laughing at the promise of a son: Is anything too hard for the LORD? (Genesis 18:14). Salvation is God’s work from beginning to end: he gives the new heart, he grants repentance and faith, he draws us (John 6:44; Ephesians 2:8–9). If God can save a rich man, and he can, as Zacchaeus and Joseph of Arimathea prove, he can save anyone. A camel through a needle is no harder for him than a world out of nothing.

God helps those who help themselves? This verse quietly demolishes the most popular religious sentence in the English language. It is not in the Bible, and it is the exact reverse of what Jesus says here. God saves those who cannot help themselves, which is everybody. And notice how it will be done, because it is not left in the air. The man saying it is on the road to Jerusalem, and in eighteen verses he will say why: to give his life as a ransom for many (v. 45). The impossibility is not overcome by a change in the requirements. It is overcome by a death.

What it does not mean. Not that people have no responsibility to repent and believe. But even our repentance and faith are God’s gifts, the fruit of his grace, not our contribution to it.

If salvation is God’s work, what do I do? Call on him. The God for whom all things are possible commands everyone to repent and believe the gospel (1:15), and promises that everyone who calls on the name of the Lord will be saved (Romans 10:13). His sovereignty is not a reason to wait passively; it is the reason to hope, because your salvation does not depend on a strength you do not have. If you want Christ, that wanting is already his work in you. Come to him and you will find that he has been drawing you all along. And keep praying for others, because nothing in them is beyond his reach.

In a sentence. Jesus told his astonished disciples that salvation is impossible for human beings but not for God, for whom all things are possible.

On a Tuesday. If you have ever looked honestly at yourself and concluded that you have no business being in the kingdom of God, you have understood verse 27 better than most. That is the correct assessment, and Jesus made it first, and then said the words that answer it: but not with God. Write down the name of the person you think least likely to be saved, and pray for them this week with confidence.

For worship. The impossible was always God’s to do, and he has done it. He brought a persecutor to his knees on the Damascus road and a tax collector down from a tree, and he has raised dead hearts like ours to life. The Son who said with man it is impossible walked on to Jerusalem and made a way with his own blood. Nothing is too hard for the Lord, and the impossible thing he did for us at the cross is the guarantee of every lesser mercy.

parallels.desc: is anything too hard for the LORD?

verseByVerse.quote: Peter began to say to him, "See, we have left everything and followed you." Jesus said, "Truly, I say to you, there is no one who has left house or brothers or sisters or mother or father or children or lands, for my sake and for the gospel, who will not receive a hundredfold now in this time, houses and brothers and sisters and mothers and children and lands, with persecutions, and in the age to come eternal life. But many who are first will be last, and the last first."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Peter began to say to him: see, we have left everything and followed you. Jesus said: truly, I tell you, there is no one who has left house or brothers or sisters or mother or father or children or lands for my sake and for the gospel who will not receive a hundredfold now in this time, houses and brothers and sisters and mothers and children and lands, with persecutions, and in the age to come eternal life. But many who are first will be last, and the last first.

See, we have left everything and followed you. Mark’s began to say is delicate, as though Peter started the sentence and thought better of finishing it. And it is Peter all over: honest, blurted, and not quite what it should be. The rich man has just failed to leave everything. Peter has watched him go, heard about the camel, heard that it is impossible, and what comes out is: we did, though. It is true (1:18, 20). Matthew adds his question: What then will we have? (Matthew 19:27). There is a hint of self-congratulation, and a real question underneath that is not entirely unworthy. These men had left boats, nets, a business, a home. It cost them something real. But it is the wrong question two verses after with man it is impossible. He is doing arithmetic again.

There is no one who has left. Jesus does not rebuke Peter. He answers generously, with an amen-formula on the front, and promises reward. The list is specific: house, brothers, sisters, mother, father, children, lands, everything a man in that world had. Following him costs. In the early church many converts were disowned by their families or lost their property (Hebrews 10:34), and in many countries they still are.

For my sake and for the gospel. As in 8:35, only Mark adds and for the gospel. The cost is borne for Jesus and his message. Loss as such is not commended. Christians are not called to abandon families as a spiritual achievement; what is in view is what following him costs when it costs something.

Who will not receive a hundredfold now in this time. Not only in heaven: now. And he repeats the list. A hundredfold is the extravagant number from the parable of the sower (4:8, 20), the yield that made no agricultural sense. How? In the family of God. He is not promising that a man who gives up a house will be given a hundred houses. He is promising the church. The one who loses his earthly family gains brothers, sisters and mothers in the church (3:34–35), homes opened to him, and a share in all that belongs to the people of God (Acts 2:44–46). That is not poetry; it is what happened. Paul greets a woman in Rome as one who had been a mother to him as well (Romans 16:13). And notice that fathers is missing from the list of what is received: in God’s family there is one Father (Matthew 23:9).

Can this be tested? It is one of the few promises of Christ that can be tested this month. The believer with no family who is never alone at Christmas. The convert cut off by his relatives who has more people praying for him than he can count. The student far from home given a key to a church family’s house. If your church is not that for somebody, this verse is an indictment before it is a comfort.

With persecutions. Only Mark adds this, and it is honest. He puts it in the middle of the blessings, unemphasised, as one of the things received. Nobody left persecutions behind; everybody is given them. It is the most honest recruitment sentence ever spoken, and it is the reason this promise cannot be mistaken for a prosperity scheme. The hundredfold arrives with trouble attached, in the same parcel. The reward is not a comfortable life. Mark’s readers in Rome knew this well.

Is this a promise that God will make me wealthy if I give? No. The prosperity teaching that uses this verse to promise money in return for gifts has turned it upside down. The hundredfold is relational and spiritual, found in the family of God, and it comes with persecutions. Jesus had nowhere to lay his head, and Paul knew hunger and need while content in Christ (Philippians 4:11–13). God does provide for his children, and generosity is never a loss in the end. But the promise is that you will never lose by following Christ, not that following Christ is a financial investment.

And in the age to come eternal life. The answer to the rich man’s question (v. 17). What he would not give up everything for, they will receive.

But many who are first will be last, and the last first. A warning, aimed straight at the man who said we have left everything. The rich and powerful, first in this world, may be last in the kingdom; the disciples, last in the world’s eyes, will be first. But also: those who think of themselves as first because of their sacrifices may find themselves last. The kingdom’s order is not a league table with the earliest and most sacrificial at the top. Reward is grace, not wages earned (Matthew 20:1–16).

In a sentence. Jesus promised that everyone who leaves family and property for him and the gospel will receive a hundred times more now, in God’s family, with persecutions, and eternal life to come.

On a Tuesday. If following Christ has cost you family or property, look around at the church. These are your brothers, sisters and mothers. And if you have a home, open it to those who have lost theirs. Invite someone this week who has no family nearby, and be their hundredfold.

For worship. No one has ever out-given Christ. He takes nothing from his people that he does not repay a hundred times, now, in a family that spans the earth, and then in an inheritance that cannot fade. He left his Father’s house and his heavenly glory for us, with persecutions, and the reward of his sacrifice is a family beyond number, gathered in his name, with one Father over all.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 32–52 — The Road to Jerusalem, the Ransom, and Bartimaeus
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Walking ahead (vv. 32–34). Mark gives us a picture worth stopping over: a road going up to Jerusalem, Jesus striding out in front, and behind him a group that is amazed and a crowd that is frightened. Then he tells them, for the third and most detailed time, exactly what is waiting — handed over, condemned, given to the Gentiles, mocked, spat on, flogged, killed, raised.

The request (vv. 35–45). And immediately James and John ask for the two best seats. The other ten are furious, which is not righteous indignation but competition. So Jesus lays down the law of his kingdom — the great one is the servant, the first is the slave — and grounds it in himself: he came to give his life as a ransom for many.

Jericho (vv. 46–52). The last miracle before Jerusalem. A blind beggar shouts a messianic title that none of the disciples has yet used, is told to be quiet by the crowd, shouts louder, throws away the only thing he owns, and follows Jesus up the road to the cross.

The chapter opened with a rich man who would not follow and closes with a beggar who did.
verseByVerse.theology:
Mark 10:45 is the theological centre of this Gospel, and every word repays weighing.

A ransom — lytron — was the price paid to set a captive free: the sum laid down to buy a slave out of bondage or a prisoner off the block. Jesus says his own life is that price.

And a ransom is a substitute — one thing given instead of another. He does not merely die for our benefit; he dies in our stead, the many going free because the One is handed over.

Behind it stands Isaiah 53, where the Servant poured out his soul to death and bore the sin of many, and by his knowledge shall the righteous one, my servant, make many to be accounted righteous (Isa. 53:11–12). That word many rings through the prophecy, and Jesus claims it as his own errand.

And to whom is the price paid? Not, as some early teachers imagined, to the devil, as though Satan held a rightful claim. The debt is owed to the justice of God — and God, in the person of his Son, pays it himself.

Here, then, is why he came. Not first to teach, or to heal, or even to model servanthood, though he did all three. To die in the room of sinners who could never buy themselves back. Nineteen verses earlier the disciples asked then who can be saved? and were told with man it is impossible, but not with God. This is how.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: the same question — What do you want me to do for you? — asked twice in fifteen verses.

It is put to James and John in verse 36 and to a blind beggar in verse 51. Mark has done that deliberately, and the two answers are the whole chapter.

James and John ask for glory. They open with a blank cheque — we want you to do for us whatever we ask — and then name the two best seats in the kingdom. They get a redirection and a warning.

Bartimaeus asks for mercy, and then for sight. He gets exactly what he asks for, immediately.

Now: the question is still being asked, and most of us answer it more like the brothers than the beggar. The blank-cheque prayer — do what I have decided — dressed up religiously. The request framed around position, comfort, and being noticed.

And notice what makes Bartimaeus's answer better. It is not humility as a technique. He asked for the thing he actually needed, from someone he had correctly identified, having first asked for mercy rather than a favour. He had no credentials, no standing, and no way of repaying anybody — which is precisely the child of verse 15, arriving at the other end of the chapter with nothing in his hands.

verseByVerse.quote: And they were on the road, going up to Jerusalem, and Jesus was walking ahead of them. And they were amazed, and those who followed were afraid. And taking the twelve again, he began to tell them what was to happen to him,
verseByVerse.commentary:
They were on the road, going up to Jerusalem, and Jesus was walking ahead of them. They were amazed, and those who followed were afraid. Taking the Twelve aside again, he began to tell them what was going to happen to him.

And they were on the road, going up to Jerusalem. The first time Mark names the destination. Going up is literal as well as idiomatic. Jerusalem stands about 2,500 feet (750 m) up in the Judean hills, and the road from Jericho, in the Jordan valley below sea level, climbs about 3,500 feet (1,000 m) in 15 miles (25 km) through the wilderness. But every Jew said up to Jerusalem whatever the compass said, because the city of God was always up.

And Jesus was walking ahead of them. Stop on that, because it is one of the great pictures in the Gospel and Mark paints it in a handful of words, probably from Peter’s memory. He is out in front. Not being led, not carried along by events, not swept toward Jerusalem by a movement that has got out of hand. He is setting the pace, resolute, going to his death on purpose. Luke says: he set his face to go to Jerusalem (Luke 9:51). Isaiah had said it centuries earlier in the Servant’s voice: I have set my face like a flint, and I know that I shall not be put to shame (Isaiah 50:7). He is not dragged to the cross; he walks ahead to it, faster than the men following. A shepherd goes before his sheep (John 10:4).

And they were amazed, and those who followed were afraid. Something in his manner awed them. Two groups may be meant: the Twelve, who were amazed, and the wider group of pilgrims behind, who were afraid, picking up the atmosphere without understanding it. So this is the procession: one man striding ahead with a set face, a cluster of disciples staring after him in alarm, and a straggle of frightened people behind. They sensed that something terrible lay ahead.

Amazed and afraid on the road. The Christian life is often exactly like this. There are stretches where following Christ means going in a direction that plainly costs something, where you do not understand what is happening, and where the honest description of your state is amazed and afraid. And the one thing the picture gives you is the one thing that helps: he is in front. Not waiting at the destination, not sending instructions from a distance. On the road, ahead, going first, and there is nothing coming that he has not already walked into.

Is it wrong to be afraid as a Christian? No. The disciples were afraid on this road, and Jesus himself was greatly distressed in Gethsemane (14:33). Fear is a human response to real danger and loss. What Scripture forbids is fear that rules us and turns us back from obedience. The answer to fear is not pretending, but looking at the one who walks ahead: when I am afraid, I put my trust in you (Psalm 56:3). Follow him while you are still afraid. Courage is not the absence of fear but walking on with him through it.

And taking the twelve again. Aside, privately, the third time he has done this. They have not understood the first two attempts, and he tries a third, in more detail than ever. He knows what is coming, and he will not let them arrive in Jerusalem without having been told.

In a sentence. On the road up to Jerusalem, Jesus walked ahead of his awed and frightened followers and began to tell the Twelve what would happen to him.

On a Tuesday. Jesus walks ahead of you into every hard road. Follow him there. Name the road you are dreading this week, the appointment, the conversation, the loss, and say to him in prayer: you have gone ahead of me; I will follow.

For worship. Behold the Lamb walking to the altar of his own accord. No one took his life from him; he laid it down, and he went up to Jerusalem at the head of the line, with his face like flint. Every step was love choosing the cross, and he has walked every dark road ahead of his people, so that none of us will ever go anywhere he has not already been.
verseByVerse.note: Jerusalem stands high in the hills; one always went “up” to it.

verseByVerse.quote: saying, "See, we are going up to Jerusalem, and the Son of Man will be delivered over to the chief priests and the scribes, and they will condemn him to death and deliver him over to the Gentiles. And they will mock him and spit on him, and flog him and kill him. And after three days he will rise."
verseByVerse.commentary:
See, we are going up to Jerusalem, and the Son of Man will be handed over to the chief priests and the scribes. They will condemn him to death and hand him over to the Gentiles. They will mock him, spit on him, flog him and kill him. And after three days he will rise.

See, we are going up to Jerusalem. “See” (idou): look, pay attention. This is the fullest of the three predictions (8:31; 9:31): the first named the rejecting parties, the second added the handing over, and this one gives the sequence step by step, eight items in all, almost a summary of chapters 14 to 16.

Delivered over to the chief priests and the scribes, and they will condemn him to death. Handed over, that word again (9:31): betrayed into the hands of the Jewish leaders (14:10, 43), who will pass sentence in the Sanhedrin (14:64).

And deliver him over to the Gentiles. Handed over a second time, and this is new. It is a shocking thing to say to Jewish men: the leaders of Israel will pass their own Messiah to the pagans. The Jewish leaders did not have the right to carry out executions under Roman rule (John 18:31), and so they would hand him to Pilate (15:1). It also explains what kind of death is coming. The Sanhedrin’s own penalty was stoning; only Rome crucified. When he says Gentiles, he is saying cross without using the word. God’s Messiah would be rejected by both Jews and Gentiles; the whole world is guilty (Acts 4:27).

And they will mock him and spit on him, and flog him and kill him. Four verbs, and every one was fulfilled: mocking (14:65; 15:17–20, 29–32), spitting (14:65; 15:19), flogging (15:15), killing (15:24, 37). The mocking and the spitting are worth noticing, because they are not necessary to an execution. Rome could have killed him efficiently. The contempt is gratuitous, and he names it in advance, which means he walked toward it knowing not only that he would die but that he would be humiliated first. Isaiah had foretold it: I gave my back to those who strike, and my cheeks to those who pull out the beard; I hid not my face from disgrace and spitting (Isaiah 50:6). Roman flogging, with a whip of leather straps weighted with bone or metal, was so savage that men sometimes died under it.

And after three days he will rise. The eighth item, and it is on the end of every one of the three predictions. He has never once mentioned the death without the resurrection, and the disciples have never once mentioned the resurrection.

Hearing only what we want. Now put the whole speech beside what happens next, because Mark has arranged it and it is devastating. He has just described, in eight stages, being condemned, handed to pagans, mocked, spat on, whipped and executed. And the response of two of his closest friends, in the next verse, is to ask for the best seats. They heard the word glory and nothing else. We do the same with Scripture constantly: the promise received, the cost skipped over; the comfort taken, the command left; a sermon about the cross followed by a conversation about lunch. The disciples are not a different species. They are us, with better excuses, because at least they had never seen a resurrection.

Why did Jesus have to suffer so much, and not simply die? Because he was bearing the full weight of human sin, and sin is not only guilt but shame. We have despised God and treated his glory with contempt, and Christ received contempt in our place: the spitting, the mockery, the stripping, the curse of hanging on a tree (Galatians 3:13). He who for the joy set before him endured the cross, despising the shame (Hebrews 12:2), took our shame so that we might be clothed with his honour. And his suffering shows us what our sin deserves and how great his love is. Nothing was wasted, and nothing was accidental.

In a sentence. Jesus told the Twelve in detail that in Jerusalem he would be betrayed, condemned, handed to the Gentiles, mocked, spat upon, flogged and killed, and would rise after three days.

On a Tuesday. When you read about the cross, slow down. Do not skip from the prediction to the glory as James and John did. This week, read Mark 15 slowly once, and stay with each verb: mocked, spat upon, flogged, killed. Then read 16:6 and give thanks.

For worship. He knew every detail of what he would suffer, and still walked ahead. That is the measure of his love. The face that shone on the mountain he gave to those who spat; the back that bore the cross he gave to those who struck. He hid not his face from shame, so that we would never have to hide ours from God. And on the third day he rose, exactly as he said.
verseByVerse.note: This third prediction is the fullest, naming the Gentiles, mocking, spitting and flogging.

parallels.desc: I gave my back to those who strike

verseByVerse.quote: And James and John, the sons of Zebedee, came up to him and said to him, "Teacher, we want you to do for us whatever we ask of you." And he said to them, "What do you want me to do for you?" And they said to him, "Grant us to sit, one at your right hand and one at your left, in your glory."
verseByVerse.commentary:
James and John, the sons of Zebedee, came to him and said: Teacher, we want you to do for us whatever we ask. He said to them: what do you want me to do for you? They said: grant us to sit, one at your right hand and one at your left, in your glory.

The contrast. Each time Jesus predicts his suffering, the disciples respond with something that shows they have not understood: Peter’s rebuke (8:32), the argument about greatness (9:34), and now this. Immediately after hearing that he will be spat on and killed, two of his closest friends ask for the best seats.

James and John, the sons of Zebedee. Two of the inner three: the men who were on the mountain of transfiguration, who were in the room when the little girl was raised, and who will be taken further into Gethsemane than anybody else. They are also the Sons of Thunder (3:17), and it shows. Matthew says their mother asked on their behalf (Matthew 20:20). She was probably Salome, possibly the sister of Mary, which would make them Jesus’ cousins (compare 15:40 with Matthew 27:56 and John 19:25). Family closeness may have encouraged the request. Both accounts are true: she asked, they stood by, and Mark puts the responsibility where the ten put it (v. 41).

Teacher, we want you to do for us whatever we ask of you. Look at the shape of that before the content, because the form of the request is as revealing as the substance. They do not ask a question. They ask him to agree to a question before they put it. It is a blank cheque, signed in advance, and it is how a child approaches a parent when he already suspects the answer will be no. Herod had made such a promise (6:22–23), with disastrous results.

Praying with a blank cheque. Hold this against our praying, because the same move is available in more respectable clothing. There is a way of praying that is not asking but informing: a decision already taken, brought to God for endorsement rather than judgment. Lord, bless what I have determined to do. The words are reverent; the transaction is a blank cheque.

What do you want me to do for you? He does not agree to the blank cheque. He asks them to say it out loud. And mark this question, because Jesus will ask the very same question of blind Bartimaeus fifteen verses later (v. 51). The same words to two very different people, and the two answers are the point of the chapter: they ask for glory, he asks for sight.

Grant us to sit, one at your right hand and one at your left, in your glory. To sit at a king’s right and left was the place of highest honour and power: the chief ministers who share the throne room. They are not asking to be useful. They are asking for the top two positions in the government of the universe, and they are asking for both, which means they have already decided that the other ten are not getting them. They want the glory without the cross, and they want it for themselves, above the others.

Something right in it. There is something almost admirable buried in it, and it should be said. They believe him. He has just told them he is going to be spat on and killed, and they are still asking about his glory, which means that somewhere in them is a genuine conviction that this man is going to reign. They have seen that glory on the mountain. That is more than the crowd had. But it sits on top of a deafness so complete it is hard to credit.

Who was at his right and left? Notice where he is standing while they ask: on a road, going up, walking ahead of them toward the day when there will in fact be a man on his right and a man on his left. They will be two criminals on crosses, and his glory will be the cross (15:27).

Is it wrong to ask God for things for myself? No. Jesus invites us to ask (Matthew 7:7), and he does not scold James and John for asking but for not knowing what they asked. Pray freely for your needs, your family, your work, your health. What is wrong is praying for position over others, and praying as though God existed to serve our plans. The best prayers have the shape of the Lord’s Prayer: his name, his kingdom, his will first, and then our daily bread, forgiveness and protection. Ask boldly, and let him correct the request.

In a sentence. Straight after Jesus predicted his suffering, James and John asked him for the highest places of honour in his glory.

On a Tuesday. Look at your last few prayers and ask whether any were blank cheques, decisions already made and brought to God to sign. Bring one of them back to him today and ask for his will instead.

For worship. The King who was asked for thrones answered with patience. He did not dismiss his foolish friends; he went on to the cross for them, where his only courtiers were two dying thieves. His glory was not a seat above others but a death beneath them, and the thrones he gives at last are given freely to sinners who once asked for them for all the wrong reasons.
verseByVerse.note: To sit at a king’s right and left was the place of highest honour.

verseByVerse.quote: Jesus said to them, "You do not know what you are asking. Are you able to drink the cup that I drink, or to be baptized with the baptism with which I am baptized?" And they said to him, "We are able." And Jesus said to them, "The cup that I drink you will drink, and with the baptism with which I am baptized, you will be baptized, but to sit at my right hand or at my left is not mine to grant, but it is for those for whom it has been prepared."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus said to them: you do not know what you are asking. Are you able to drink the cup that I drink, or to be baptised with the baptism with which I am baptised? They said: we are able. Jesus said: the cup that I drink you will drink, and with the baptism with which I am baptised you will be baptised; but to sit at my right hand or at my left is not mine to grant; it is for those for whom it has been prepared.

You do not know what you are asking. Not you should not have asked; not how dare you. He tells them, gently, that they have no idea what they have requested. They do not know what his glory involves, or the path to it. Which is the first mercy in the passage. God does not grant our prayers according to our understanding of them. If he did, most of us would have been undone years ago by things we asked for confidently. There is a great deal to be thankful for in the prayers he has declined.

The cup that I drink. In the Old Testament the cup is often a picture of God’s judgment and wrath, which the wicked must drink: in the hand of the LORD there is a cup with foaming wine, and all the wicked of the earth shall drain it down to the dregs (Psalm 75:8; Isaiah 51:17, 22; Jeremiah 25:15–28). Jesus will pray in Gethsemane, on his face in the dirt: Remove this cup from me (14:36). The cup he drinks is the wrath of God against sin, which he takes in our place. This is penal substitution: Christ bears the penalty that sinners deserved.

Or to be baptized with the baptism with which I am baptized. Baptism here is not water. It means being overwhelmed, submerged, as by a flood: all your breakers and your waves have gone over me (Psalm 42:7; 69:1–2). Jesus speaks of his coming suffering and death as a baptism (Luke 12:50). So he is asking them: can you be drowned in what is about to drown me? Can you drink what I am going to drink?

We are able. Brave and ignorant, instantly, with no idea what they have agreed to. It is easy to laugh at, and Peter will say much the same at the last supper (14:31). But do not miss what is right in it: they mean it. These men are not cynics. Their loyalty at that moment is genuine; it is just standing on nothing.

The cup that I drink you will drink. And the reply is not sarcasm. It is a prophecy, and it came true. James was the first of the apostles to be martyred, put to the sword by Herod Agrippa in Jerusalem about AD 44 (Acts 12:2). John was exiled to Patmos for the word of God and the testimony of Jesus (Revelation 1:9) and, by tradition, lived to old age. They asked for thrones and were promised suffering, and they got the suffering, and they did not fall away when it came. But their cup will not be the same as his. Only he drinks the cup of God’s wrath for sin. Theirs is the cup of suffering for his sake (Colossians 1:24 speaks of this in a different sense).

Will I have to drink the cup of God’s wrath? Never, if you belong to Christ. That is the whole point of his drinking it. For those in Christ Jesus, condemnation is gone for good (Romans 8:1). He drained it to the dregs, and there is nothing left in it for his people. What you may be given is a different cup: suffering for his name, trials, losses, the ordinary weight of following him in a fallen world. That cup is real and sometimes bitter, but it is mixed by a Father’s hand for your good, and he drinks it with you. Never confuse the two.

But to sit at my right hand or at my left is not mine to grant. Not that Jesus lacks authority, or that he is not God. This is the Son speaking of the ordered work of the Trinity, in which allotting places in the kingdom belongs to the Father, the same submission he shows in Gethsemane and on the cross (13:32). He does not say the seats do not exist, or that no one assigns them. He says they are not his to hand out on request.

But it is for those for whom it has been prepared. Prepared by God, in his eternal purpose. Matthew adds: by my Father (Matthew 20:23). The places of honour in the kingdom are not won by ambition or asking, but by God’s sovereign appointment. There is a divine allocation, already made, and it is not open to lobbying. You cannot secure a place in the kingdom of God by asking for it, deserving it, arriving early, or knowing the right person, and there is enormous relief in that for anyone who has ever felt they were losing a race they did not want to be running.

In a sentence. Jesus told James and John they did not understand that his glory comes through the cup of suffering and wrath; they would suffer too, but places of honour are the Father’s to give.

On a Tuesday. Following Christ will involve a cup of suffering. But he has drunk the cup of wrath, so you never will. When suffering comes this week, say it to yourself: this is not wrath; that cup is empty. And thank God for one prayer of yours he wisely refused.

For worship. He took the cup that was ours, foaming with the wrath we had stored up, and he drank it to the bottom. He went under the waves so that we would not drown. And the Father who prepared places in his kingdom prepared them for people who had asked for the wrong things, because the Son had drunk the right cup. Blessed be the Lamb who drank it dry.
verseByVerse.note: The “cup” is the Old Testament picture of God’s judgment poured out; “baptism” pictures being overwhelmed by suffering. James was later killed by Herod Agrippa.

parallels.desc: the waters have come up to my neck
I have a baptism to be baptized with

verseByVerse.quote: And when the ten heard it, they began to be indignant at James and John. And Jesus called them to him and said to them, "You know that those who are considered rulers of the Gentiles lord it over them, and their great ones exercise authority over them. But it shall not be so among you. But whoever would be great among you must be your servant, and whoever would be first among you must be slave of all.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When the ten heard this, they began to be indignant at James and John. Jesus called them to him and said: you know that those who are considered rulers of the Gentiles lord it over them, and their great ones exercise authority over them. But it shall not be so among you. Whoever would be great among you must be your servant, and whoever would be first among you must be slave of all.

They began to be indignant at James and John. The word is the one used of Jesus when the children were turned away (v. 14), and here it means they were furious. Mark does not need to say why: not because the request was wrong, but because the two had got in first. Nobody says, how could you speak like that when he has just told us he will be killed? The ten had the same ambitions. They had already argued about this on the road in chapter 9 and been given a child and a lesson. Nothing has taken. The ambition went underground and has now surfaced as outrage at somebody else’s ambition, which is the usual way it appears in religious company. Almost nobody says I want to be the greatest. A great many people are quietly annoyed when somebody else is treated as though they were.

And Jesus called them to him. All twelve. He does not deal with James and John separately or take the ten’s side. The disease is general, and the treatment is given to the whole group.

Those who are considered rulers of the Gentiles. He points at the world they can see. Rome is the model: a system in which authority runs downward as pressure, and greatness is measured by how many people have to do what you say. And there is a barb in considered, those who seem to rule. Their eminence is a matter of general opinion. Their power is not what it looks like; the real ruler is God.

Lord it over them … exercise authority over them. Both verbs have a prefix (kata-) that means power pressed downward, against people, to dominate. The world’s pattern of leadership is power over others for the leader’s benefit. Rome knew it well.

But it shall not be so among you. A flat contradiction. Not it should not, but it is not: this is not how my community works. It is not advice. It is a prohibition on importing the world’s model of authority into the church, and church history is very largely the story of ignoring it, in cathedrals and small congregations alike, wherever a man has discovered that a position in the things of God can be used to make other people smaller.

The one ruler who never lorded it. Jesus is not describing an authority he lacks. He is the ruler of kings on earth (Revelation 1:5), the one to whom the Father has promised the nations as his heritage (Psalm 2:8), and all authority in heaven and on earth would soon be given to him (Matthew 28:18). Of all who have ever held power, he alone had the right to press it down on everyone, and he never once did. He would not cry aloud or make his voice heard in the street (Isaiah 42:2); he used his power to heal, feed, forgive, and finally to die. The kingdom’s rule for leaders is a portrait of its King.

Whoever would be great among you must be your servant. “Servant” (diakonos): one who waits at table. A servant has a role, and can, at the end of the day, go home.

And whoever would be first among you must be slave of all. “Slave” (doulos) goes further still: one who belongs to another and has no rights, no time of his own, and no choice about whom he serves. Two rungs down: servant, slave. The way up is down. And once again the ambition is not forbidden: whoever would be great, whoever would be first. He does not say stop wanting to matter. He redirects the wanting and gives it a road, and the road runs downward. And slave of all removes the last escape, which is choosing whom to serve. All: including the ten who are furious with you, and the two who went behind your back.

What it does not mean. Not that there is no authority in the church. Elders are to lead and be obeyed (Hebrews 13:17; 1 Thessalonians 5:12). But Christian authority is exercised as service, for the good of others, never for the leader’s benefit: shepherd the flock, not domineering over those in your charge, but being examples (1 Peter 5:1–3).

What about authority at home? The same rule holds. Scripture gives husbands headship and parents authority, and both are real. But Jesus defines all authority among his people by this verse: it is used for the good of those under it, and never to dominate, control or frighten. A husband is to love his wife as Christ loved the church and gave himself up for her (Ephesians 5:25); fathers are not to provoke their children (Ephesians 6:4). A man who uses headship to demand, belittle or harm has not understood headship at all, and abuse is never to be tolerated in the name of authority. The test of all Christian leadership is the towel and the cross.

In a sentence. When the others resented James and John, Jesus taught that in his kingdom, unlike the world, greatness is shown by being a servant and the first must be the slave of all.

On a Tuesday. If you lead at work, home or church, ask: am I using my power for others or for myself? Name one person under your authority and do something this week that serves their good at a cost to your convenience. And notice where you are quietly annoyed that someone else has been honoured.

For worship. The Lord of all made himself the slave of all. He who has every right to rule did not lord it over us; he knelt and washed our feet, and then he bore our sin. There is no authority in heaven or earth like his, and none so gentle. Every true leader in his church holds a borrowed towel.

verseByVerse.quote: For even the Son of Man came not to be served but to serve, and to give his life as a ransom for many."
verseByVerse.commentary:
For even the Son of Man came not to be served but to serve, and to give his life as a ransom for many.

The key verse of Mark. This one sentence sums up the whole purpose of Jesus’ coming. It explains the three passion predictions and everything that follows in chapters 11 to 16. And it arrives as a because. He has just told them to go to the bottom, and this is the reason: not a principle, but a Person, and what that Person is walking toward.

For even the Son of Man. That title is not a modest one. It comes from Daniel 7, where one like a son of man comes with the clouds of heaven and is given dominion and glory and a kingdom, that all peoples, nations and languages should serve him (Daniel 7:13–14). Read that last phrase again. In Daniel the whole world serves him. If anyone had the right to be served, it was he.

Came not to be served but to serve. “Came” implies that he came from somewhere, from heaven, with a purpose. And the purpose reversed every expectation. The one figure in Scripture entitled to universal service arrived and declined it. The King came as a servant. He washed his disciples’ feet (John 13:1–17). He took the form of a servant (Philippians 2:7).

And to give his life. The supreme service: his life itself. Not taken from him but given (John 10:18).

As a ransom. A “ransom” (lytron) belongs to the marketplace: the price paid to free a slave, a prisoner of war, or someone condemned to death. In the Old Testament the firstborn were redeemed with a payment (Numbers 3:46–48), and a man whose ox had killed someone could pay a ransom for his own life (Exodus 21:30). We are slaves of sin and under the sentence of death (Romans 6:23). Jesus pays the price of our freedom, and the currency is his own life.

To whom was the ransom paid? Not to Satan, as some of the early fathers imagined, as though the devil held a rightful claim over us that God had to buy out. He holds no such claim; he is a thief with stolen goods (3:27), and God owes him nothing. The debt is owed to the justice of God, whose law we have broken. And God, in the person of his Son, pays it himself. So there is no drama here of an angry Father and a reluctant Son. It is one God, Father, Son and Spirit, in perfect love, resolving in himself what could not be resolved any other way.

For many. “For” (anti) means in place of, instead of: one thing given instead of another, the way a substitute steps into a queue. This is substitution. He does not merely die for our benefit; he dies in our stead. The many go free because the One is handed over. The word many tolls through Isaiah 53, where the servant pours out his soul to death and bears the sin of many (Isaiah 53:12), and Jesus claims it as his own errand.

Who are the many? “Many” contrasts the one who dies with the great number of those for whom he dies. The phrase comes from Isaiah 53, where the servant bears the sin of many and makes many to be accounted righteous. Reformed theology reads this as definite: Christ gave his life as a ransom for his people, those the Father had given him (John 10:11, 15; 17:9), and his death actually secures their freedom. A ransom that is paid frees the captive. Other traditions read many as all, a universal offer. Verdict: the ransom is real and effective; it does not merely make freedom possible but actually purchases it for the many. This is definite atonement. And the gospel offer still goes freely to all, since no one who comes to Christ will be turned away (John 6:37). His death is sufficient for all and is offered to all.

How do I know I am one of the many? Not by trying to read God’s secret decree, but by coming to Christ. The invitation is to everyone: whoever comes to me I will never cast out (John 6:37). If you trust Jesus as your Saviour and Lord, you are one of the many he ransomed, because the faith that comes to him is itself the fruit of his ransom. Assurance grows as you look to his promises, as the Spirit testifies with your spirit that you are God’s child (Romans 8:16), and as you see the fruit of a changed life. The doctrine of definite atonement is not a wall to keep you out. It is a guarantee that, if you are his, nothing can undo what he paid for you.

The answer to the disciples’ question. Nineteen verses ago the disciples asked, then who can be saved? and he told them it was impossible with man and possible with God. This is how. Not by a lowering of the requirement, but by a payment. And notice where this sentence is placed. It is not in a sermon on the atonement. It is the closing argument in a squabble about who gets the best seats. Twelve men are jostling for position, and he settles it by telling them that he is going to be sold for their freedom. Everything in the Christian life that is asked of you is asked on the basis of that. You are not told to serve because service is noble. You are told to serve because the one who owned everything went to the bottom and stayed there, until it killed him, and bought you on the way down.

In a sentence. The Son of Man came not to be served but to serve, and to give his life as the price that frees many, in their place.

On a Tuesday. You were bought at a price (1 Corinthians 6:20). Your time, body and money belong to the one who paid for them. Today, when you are asked to serve someone and feel the reluctance rise, remember who served you, and at what cost.

For worship. The Son of Man, whom every nation will one day serve, came down to serve us. The one who owed nothing paid everything, and the price of our freedom was not silver or gold but his precious blood, like that of a lamb without blemish or spot (1 Peter 1:18–19). He came from heaven for this one errand and did not turn aside from it, even to save himself. And the many he ransomed will stand before him at last and sing that he was slain, and by his blood ransomed people for God from every tribe and language and people and nation (Revelation 5:9).
verseByVerse.note: A ransom was the price paid to free a slave or captive.

parallels.desc: he bore the sin of many

verseByVerse.quote: And they came to Jericho. And as he was leaving Jericho with his disciples and a great crowd, Bartimaeus, a blind beggar, the son of Timaeus, was sitting by the roadside. And when he heard that it was Jesus of Nazareth, he began to cry out and say, "Jesus, Son of David, have mercy on me!" And many rebuked him, telling him to be silent. But he cried out all the more, "Son of David, have mercy on me!"
verseByVerse.commentary:
They came to Jericho. As he was leaving Jericho with his disciples and a great crowd, Bartimaeus, a blind beggar, the son of Timaeus, was sitting by the roadside. When he heard that it was Jesus of Nazareth, he began to cry out: Jesus, Son of David, have mercy on me! Many rebuked him, telling him to be silent, but he cried out all the more: Son of David, have mercy on me!

And they came to Jericho. About 15 miles (25 km) north-east of Jerusalem, near the Jordan: the last stop before the climb to the city. Passover is days away, and the road is thick with pilgrims. This is the second healing of a blind man, matching the one at Bethsaida (8:22–26); between them Jesus has taught about the cross while his disciples were blind to it, and now a blind man sees and follows him, a model disciple set against James and John.

As he was leaving Jericho. Luke says as he drew near to Jericho (Luke 18:35), and Matthew mentions two blind men (Matthew 20:30). These are not contradictions. There were two Jerichos in Jesus’ day, the ancient ruined site and the new Herodian town a short distance away; Jesus may have been leaving one and approaching the other. And Mark names the one blind man who was known to the early church; he does not say there was only one.

Bartimaeus, a blind beggar, the son of Timaeus. The only person healed in Mark who is named. Not the leper, not the paralytic, not the man among the tombs, not the woman with the bleeding: this man is named twice over, Bartimaeus and son of Timaeus, since “Bar” is Aramaic for son of, and Mark translates. The likeliest reason is the best one: the church knew him. He was still around when Mark wrote, or well enough remembered that people could say, yes, we know him. This is a signed piece of testimony.

Sitting by the roadside. His position is the whole of his life in one phrase. Not going anywhere. Beside the road while everybody else walks up it.

Jesus of Nazareth. The crowd’s name for him: a man from a small town. Bartimaeus cannot see anything. All he has is the noise of a crowd and a name passed down the line, and he acts on it instantly.

Jesus, Son of David. Bartimaeus’ name for him, and a far greater one. Son of David is a messianic title: the promised king from David’s line, whose throne God would establish for ever (2 Samuel 7:12–16), the shoot from the stump of Jesse (Isaiah 11:1). And it is the first time in Mark anyone uses it: not the crowds, who thought he was Elijah or a prophet; not the Pharisees; not the Twelve. A blind beggar shouts it in public, days before Passover. Everyone in this chapter who can see has misunderstood him. The rich man called him Good Teacher and went home. James and John asked for thrones. The man who cannot see anything names him correctly at the first attempt. The Messiah was expected to give sight to the blind (Isaiah 35:5; 61:1). And Jesus does not silence him: the hour for the secret is ending. He is about to enter Jerusalem as the Son of David (11:10).

Have mercy on me! The cry of one with no claim, only need. Not heal me, not yet: mercy, which is what you ask for when the only ground of the request is the character of the one you are asking. It is the prayer of the tax collector (Luke 18:13), and the church has prayed it for centuries: Kyrie eleison, Lord, have mercy. The rich man asked what he must do; James and John asked for what they thought they deserved. The beggar asks for mercy, and he is the only one in the chapter who gets exactly what he came for.

And many rebuked him, telling him to be silent. That word rebuked again: the disciples used it on the parents with children (v. 13). A beggar was a nuisance. There is a distinguished rabbi passing with a following, on a solemn pilgrimage road, and a beggar is bawling at him. Somebody should keep him quiet.

But he cried out all the more. Persistent, unembarrassed, desperate faith. He gets louder, and he says the same thing again. He knows this is his one chance; Jesus is passing by and will not come this way again. He is blind, destitute, sitting in the dust, and being disapproved of by respectable people is not a price he is troubled by.

What if others discourage me from coming to Christ? Then do what Bartimaeus did: cry out all the more. Some are discouraged by a family that finds faith excessive, some by a church that made them feel they did not fit, some by an inner voice that says they are too much, too messy, too late. The crowd told this man to be quiet, and the crowd was wrong. Jesus stopped for the shouting. No one is turned away by him for being an embarrassment to others. And if you are part of the crowd, be careful whom you silence.

In a sentence. As Jesus left Jericho, blind Bartimaeus cried out to him as the Son of David for mercy, and would not be silenced.

On a Tuesday. Pray the beggar’s prayer: Son of David, have mercy on me. Pray it on the way to work, before a hard conversation, when you have failed again. And don’t let anyone shame you out of crying to Jesus.

For worship. The beggar saw what the seeing could not: that the man from Nazareth was David’s greater Son, the King who had come. And the King was not too grand to hear a blind man in the dust. Mercy is his delight. Every cry of Lord, have mercy, from Jericho to this morning, has reached the ears of a King who loves to answer it.
verseByVerse.note: Jericho lay about 15 miles north-east of Jerusalem, near the Jordan. Bartimaeus means “son of Timaeus.” “Son of David” is a title for the Messiah.
