verseByVerse.quote: And Jesus stopped and said, "Call him." And they called the blind man, saying to him, "Take heart. Get up; he is calling you." And throwing off his cloak, he sprang up and came to Jesus.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus stopped and said: call him. They called the blind man, saying to him: take heart; get up; he is calling you. Throwing off his cloak, he sprang up and came to Jesus.

And Jesus stopped. Three words, and they may be the loveliest in the chapter. Consider the scene they interrupt. This is the road to Jerusalem. He has been walking ahead of everybody with a set face (v. 32). He has three times told his disciples what is waiting at the top of that hill. There is a crowd around him, a Passover ahead of him, and a cross at the end of the week, with the weight of the world on him. And he stops, in the road, because a blind man is shouting. The Son of God on his way to die halts the whole procession for one beggar whom everybody else was trying to silence. Nothing in his life was ever too urgent for a person.

Call him. He does not go to Bartimaeus. He tells the people who have been telling the man to be quiet to go and fetch him, and Bartimaeus must respond. That is deliberate. The crowd that hindered is made to be the crowd that brings.

Take heart. Get up; he is calling you. Three short commands, and listen to the change in their voices. Thirty seconds ago they were telling him to be quiet. Now they are encouraging him. It is the same people. Nothing has changed except that Jesus stopped, and the moment he took an interest, so did they. There is a warning in that for anybody in a church: the person you find embarrassing, inconvenient, too loud or too needy may be the one Christ is calling. And these could be the words of every evangelist: take heart, get up, Jesus is calling you.

And throwing off his cloak. Mark’s details are so specific that they strongly suggest an eyewitness, and the cloak is the one to stop on. A beggar’s outer cloak was not merely a garment. It was his equipment: spread on the ground to catch the coins people threw, his bed at night and his shelter from the cold, the one possession the law protected, since a cloak taken in pledge had to be returned by sundown (Exodus 22:26–27). It was, quite literally, all he had. And he throws it aside, in the road, blind, with no idea where it will land or whether he will find it again.

Two men at either end of a chapter. Set that against the man at the start. A rich man was asked to give up his possessions for Christ and went away sorrowful, because he had a great many (v. 22). A blind beggar, asked for nothing at all, threw away the only thing he had because it might slow him down. One had much and would not let go of any of it. One had one thing and did not think about it twice.

He sprang up and came to Jesus. The verb means to leap. Eager, joyful, at once: a blind man jumping to his feet and moving toward a voice. He does not know how far it is. He does not know what is in the way. He heard, he is calling you, and that was enough.

How does Jesus call people today? Through the gospel, spoken by ordinary people. Just as he used the crowd to call Bartimaeus, he uses preachers, parents, friends and colleagues to say: take heart, get up, he is calling you. When the Spirit takes that word and opens a heart, the call is effectual, and the sinner comes freely and gladly, as this man sprang up (Romans 8:30; 10:14–17). So if you have heard the gospel and feel its pull, do not wait for a voice from heaven; this is his call. And if you know him, you are part of the crowd he sends. Tell someone.

In a sentence. Jesus stopped and called Bartimaeus, who threw off his cloak, sprang up and came to him.

On a Tuesday. Jesus is calling you. What cloak do you need to throw aside to come to him: a security, a habit, a reputation, a grievance? And whom might he be sending you to call this week with the words, take heart, he is calling you?

For worship. The Lord stopped. On the road to the cross, with the whole weight of the world’s salvation before him, he stopped for one blind man. He has never been too busy for a sinner who calls on him, and he never will be. The same voice that called Bartimaeus out of the dust calls the dead to life, and those he calls come running, leaving everything behind.
verseByVerse.note: A beggar’s cloak was spread to collect coins and was also his covering at night.

verseByVerse.quote: And Jesus said to him, "What do you want me to do for you?" And the blind man said to him, "Rabbi, let me recover my sight." And Jesus said to him, "Go your way; your faith has made you well." And immediately he recovered his sight and followed him on the way.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus said to him: what do you want me to do for you? The blind man said: Rabbi, let me recover my sight. Jesus said: go your way; your faith has made you well. Immediately he recovered his sight and followed him on the way.

What do you want me to do for you? The same question, word for word, that he asked James and John (v. 36). Mark has done this deliberately, and everything he wants to say about this chapter is in the two answers. They opened with a blank cheque and asked for the two best seats. This man is asked the identical question, and the difference is total. And notice that Jesus asks at all. It could hardly be more obvious what a blind beggar wants. But Jesus asks him to say it: to express his need and his faith. He will not do things to people over their heads, and he gives the man a dignity nobody had shown him in years.

Rabbi. Literally Rabbouni, my master, a more personal and reverent form than the ordinary Rabbi. It appears elsewhere in the New Testament only on the lips of Mary Magdalene in the garden when she recognises the risen Christ (John 20:16).

Let me recover my sight. He asks for the one thing he actually needs, in one clause, with no preamble. “Recover” suggests he once could see. And note what he does not ask for. Not money, which is what he had asked passers-by for all his life and which would have solved his immediate problem. Sight, which once given would end his livelihood and require him to start again. He asks for the thing that will cost him his old life.

Go your way; your faith has made you well. “Made you well” (sesōken) is literally has saved you, the same word Jesus spoke to the woman with the bleeding (5:34). Physical healing and spiritual salvation are both in it. Something more than eyesight has happened here. And note where the faith was located: not in the quality of his theology, though he got the title right, and not in his persistence, though he had plenty. His faith was the empty hand that received what Jesus gave; the power was Jesus’. Faith saves because of whom it takes hold of, and this man took hold of the Son of David and would not be shouted down.

And immediately he recovered his sight. No touch, no saliva, no clay, and no second stage, unlike the man at Bethsaida (8:22–25). Just the word.

And followed him on the way. The last words of the section, and the most important. Jesus told him to go his way, free to go home, find his cloak, start a life. And he does not go his way. He goes Christ’s. Given his freedom and his eyes in the same breath, the first thing he does with both is get on the road to Jerusalem behind the man who healed him. And on the way in this Gospel is never merely geography: it is the road to Jerusalem and the cross (v. 32), the road the disciples have been walking amazed and afraid. He is the last person healed in Mark before the passion, and the picture of the true disciple, which the Twelve should be: his eyes opened, he follows Jesus to the cross. This is what Mark wants for his readers.

How the chapter ends. It closes where no one could have predicted. It began with a wealthy, moral, eager man who asked the right question, was looked at and loved, and went home with everything he came with. It ends with a blind beggar in the dust, with one cloak to his name, who shouted until he was heard, threw the cloak away, asked for mercy, and followed Jesus to Jerusalem. That is what the kingdom of God looks like from the inside, and it is exactly what Jesus said in verse 15, when he took a child in his arms: the ones who get in are the ones who come with nothing and simply receive.

Does Jesus still heal the blind? He can, and he sometimes heals in answer to prayer, and we should pray for the sick with confidence in his power and submission to his will (James 5:14–15). But Mark tells this story above all as a picture of salvation: we are all born blind to God, and only Christ’s word can open our eyes (2 Corinthians 4:4–6). The greater miracle, which he performs every day, is the opening of hearts to see his glory in the face of Jesus. And for those who are not healed in this life, the promise is sure: in the resurrection the eyes of the blind will be opened for ever (Isaiah 35:5).

In a sentence. Asked what he wanted, Bartimaeus asked for his sight, received it at once through faith, and followed Jesus on the way to Jerusalem.

On a Tuesday. Has Jesus opened your eyes? Then follow him on the way, wherever it leads. Ask yourself where you are going with the freedom he has given you: your own way, or his. And bring him your real need today in one plain sentence, as Bartimaeus did.

For worship. He opened the eyes of the blind with a word, and the first thing the healed man saw was the face of Jesus. That is the gift he gives every one of his people: to behold the glory of God in the face of Christ, and then to follow him on the way. The Son of David who stopped for a beggar is still on the road, still asking what we want, still giving sight, and still leading his people up to Jerusalem, through the cross, to glory.

parallels.desc: the eyes of the blind opened

10.theology:
Divorce, and what Mark leaves out. Matthew twice records an exception — except for sexual immorality (Matt. 5:32; 19:9) — and Mark records none, while adding, for his Roman readers, the case of a wife who divorces her husband. Not a contradiction but a difference of purpose: Mark gives the principle in its unguarded, creation-order form, the way a thing is stated when you want its full weight felt; Matthew, writing where the rabbis argued endlessly over grounds, records the one qualification Jesus allowed. Paul adds a second — the believer deserted by an unbelieving spouse is not enslaved (1 Cor. 7:15). So the Reformed churches have long recognised two grounds on which the bond may be broken and the innocent party freed: adultery and desertion, and no others. Mark's silence is not denial but a refusal to lead with the exception — because the moment the exception becomes the headline, hardness of heart starts hunting for a way in.

"Why do you call me good?" is not a denial that Jesus is good or that he is God, and he never withdraws the word or corrects the man for using it. He holds it up to the light. Good Teacher was easy flattery; Jesus stops him and asks whether he knows what he is saying. Either the word should not have been used — or it is right, and the man must reckon with who is standing in front of him. A door held open, not a door shut.

And v. 45 is the theological centre of Mark. A ransom (lytron) is the price paid to buy a captive out of bondage. The word rendered for is anti — in the place of, one thing given instead of another — so he does not merely die for our benefit but in our stead. Behind it stands Isaiah 53, where the Servant poured out his soul to death and bore the sin of many (Isa. 53:12), that word many tolling through the prophecy and claimed here by Jesus as his own errand. And the price is not paid to the devil, as some early teachers imagined — he is a thief with stolen goods (3:27) and God owes him nothing. The debt is owed to the justice of God, and God in the person of his Son pays it himself.
10.examples:
Then: the same question asked twice, fifteen verses apart. What do you want me to do for you? — to James and John (v. 36), and to a blind beggar (v. 51).

The brothers open with a blank cheque — we want you to do for us whatever we ask — and name the two best seats in the kingdom. Bartimaeus asks for mercy, and then for sight.

Now: most of us pray more like the brothers than the beggar. The blank cheque dressed up religiously — a decision already taken, brought to God for endorsement rather than judgement. The request framed around position, comfort, and being noticed.

And note what actually makes Bartimaeus's answer better. Not humility as a technique. He had correctly identified who was passing — Son of David, a messianic title not one of the disciples had yet used out loud — and he asked for mercy, which is what you ask for when you have no claim of any kind and the only ground of the request is the character of the one you are asking.

And then there is the cloak (v. 50). A beggar's outer cloak was his equipment: spread on the ground to catch coins, his bed at night, his shelter, and the one possession the Law protected (Ex. 22:26–27). It was everything he owned. He flung it aside, blind, with no idea where it landed, because it might slow him down by four seconds.

Set that against the man at the start of the chapter, asked to give up his possessions and going away sorrowful because he had a great many. One had much and would not let go of any of it; one had a single thing and did not think about it twice. Mark put them at opposite ends of the same chapter on purpose.

11.title: Leaves Without Fruit
11.text: <sup>1</sup>Now when they drew near to Jerusalem, to Bethphage and Bethany, at the Mount of Olives, Jesus sent two of his disciples <sup>2</sup>and said to them, “Go into the village in front of you, and immediately as you enter it you will find a colt tied, on which no one has ever sat. Untie it and bring it. <sup>3</sup>If anyone says to you, ‘Why are you doing this?’ say, ‘The Lord has need of it and will send it back here immediately.’” <sup>4</sup>And they went away and found a colt tied at a door outside in the street, and they untied it. <sup>5</sup>And some of those standing there said to them, “What are you doing, untying the colt?” <sup>6</sup>And they told them what Jesus had said, and they let them go. <sup>7</sup>And they brought the colt to Jesus and threw their cloaks on it, and he sat on it. <sup>8</sup>And many spread their cloaks on the road, and others spread leafy branches that they had cut from the fields. <sup>9</sup>And those who went before and those who followed were shouting, “Hosanna! Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord! <sup>10</sup>Blessed is the coming kingdom of our father David! Hosanna in the highest!” <sup>11</sup>And he entered Jerusalem and went into the temple. And when he had looked around at everything, as it was already late, he went out to Bethany with the twelve. <sup>12</sup>On the following day, when they came from Bethany, he was hungry. <sup>13</sup>And seeing in the distance a fig tree in leaf, he went to see if he could find anything on it. When he came to it, he found nothing but leaves, for it was not the season for figs. <sup>14</sup>And he said to it, “May no one ever eat fruit from you again.” And his disciples heard it. <sup>15</sup>And they came to Jerusalem. And he entered the temple and began to drive out those who sold and those who bought in the temple, and he overturned the tables of the money-changers and the seats of those who sold pigeons. <sup>16</sup>And he would not allow anyone to carry anything through the temple. <sup>17</sup>And he was teaching them and saying to them, “Is it not written, ‘My house shall be called a house of prayer for all the nations’? But you have made it a den of robbers.” <sup>18</sup>And the chief priests and the scribes heard it and were seeking a way to destroy him, for they feared him, because all the crowd was astonished at his teaching. <sup>19</sup>And when evening came they went out of the city. <sup>20</sup>As they passed by in the morning, they saw the fig tree withered away to its roots. <sup>21</sup>And Peter remembered and said to him, “Rabbi, look! The fig tree that you cursed has withered.” <sup>22</sup>And Jesus answered them, “Have faith in God. <sup>23</sup>Truly, I say to you, whoever says to this mountain, ‘Be taken up and thrown into the sea,’ and does not doubt in his heart, but believes that what he says will come to pass, it will be done for him. <sup>24</sup>Therefore I tell you, whatever you ask in prayer, believe that you have received it, and it will be yours. <sup>25</sup>And whenever you stand praying, forgive, if you have anything against anyone, so that your Father also who is in heaven may forgive you your trespasses.” <sup>27</sup>And they came again to Jerusalem. And as he was walking in the temple, the chief priests and the scribes and the elders came to him, <sup>28</sup>and they said to him, “By what authority are you doing these things, or who gave you this authority to do them?” <sup>29</sup>Jesus said to them, “I will ask you one question; answer me, and I will tell you by what authority I do these things. <sup>30</sup>Was the baptism of John from heaven or from man? Answer me.” <sup>31</sup>And they discussed it with one another, saying, “If we say, ‘From heaven,’ he will say, ‘Why then did you not believe him?’ <sup>32</sup>But shall we say, ‘From man’?”—they were afraid of the people, for they all held that John really was a prophet. <sup>33</sup>So they answered Jesus, “We do not know.” And Jesus said to them, “Neither will I tell you by what authority I do these things.”
11.overview:
After ten chapters of hushing everyone who worked out who he was, Jesus stages a public claim to the throne — and does it on a borrowed donkey's foal, exactly as Zechariah said the king would come. The crowd throws down cloaks as they did for Jehu, spreads leafy branches cut from the fields, and shouts the Passover psalm at him: Hosanna — save now. They are right about who he is and wrong about what he came to do, and by Friday the road is empty.

Then he goes into the temple, looks around at everything, and leaves, because it is late.

What he does the next morning is therefore not a loss of temper. He had seen all of it the night before, slept on it, and walked two miles back. And Mark wraps the temple inside a fig tree to tell you what it means: a tree in full leaf and no fruit, cursed on the way in; the tables overturned; and on the third morning the tree dead to its roots. Israel's worship that week was magnificent from a distance. He came near, and found leaves.

Out of the dead tree comes the great teaching on faith, prayer and forgiveness. And the chapter ends with the Sanhedrin asking the right question — by what authority? — and being handed one question in return that would have led them home, and spending it instead on a calculation about the crowd.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–26 — The Entry, the Fig Tree, and the Temple
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The entry (vv. 1–11). After nine chapters of silencing everyone who worked out who he was, Jesus stages a public claim to be king — and does it on a borrowed donkey's foal, exactly as Zechariah said. The crowd sings the Passover psalm at him. Then he walks into the temple, looks around at everything, and goes out to Bethany because it is late.

The tree (vv. 12–14). The next morning, hungry, he goes to a fig tree in full leaf and finds nothing on it — and Mark adds the detail that makes the whole thing intelligible: it was not the season for figs. He curses it, and the disciples hear him.

The temple (vv. 15–19). And then he does to the temple what he has just done to the tree. Tables over, seats over, the traffic stopped — and two verses of Scripture that between them tell the leadership exactly what their house has become.

The lesson (vv. 20–26). Next morning the tree is dead to the roots, and out of that comes the great passage on faith, prayer and forgiveness.

Mark has wrapped the temple inside the fig tree deliberately. The tree is the temple: leaves and no fruit, an advertisement with nothing behind it, and it is finished.
verseByVerse.theology:
Was it fair to curse a tree for having no figs out of season? The objection is old and it deserves a proper answer, and the answer turns on the leaves.

A Palestinian fig produces its fruit before or alongside its leaves, not after. In early spring the branches put out small green knobs — the paggim — which are edible, and a hungry traveller ate them. The leaves follow. So a tree standing in full leaf is making a claim: there is fruit here.

The main harvest was months away, which is exactly why Mark tells us it was not the season for figs. He is not embarrassed by the detail; he supplies it, so that no reader can mistake this for agricultural pique. Nobody was owed a crop. What the tree owed was consistency with its own appearance, and it had none.

And then look where Mark has put it. He splits the story in two and wedges the temple between the halves — curse (vv. 12–14), temple (vv. 15–19), withered (vv. 20–21). It is his habitual sandwich, and it is never accidental. The tree interprets the temple.

Israel's worship at that moment was in full leaf: the courts crowded, the sacrifices running, the festival packed, the money changing hands. From a distance it looked like the healthiest religion in the world. He came near, looked around at everything (v. 11), found nothing, and the next morning both the tree and the temple were under sentence.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: a den of robbers — the phrase everybody quotes and almost nobody reads properly.

A robbers' den is not where the robbery happens. It is the cave they retreat to afterwards, where they divide the takings and feel perfectly safe. That is the charge, and Jeremiah, whom Jesus is quoting, spells it out: Will you steal, murder, commit adultery, swear falsely... and then come and stand before me in this house, which is called by my name, and say, 'We are delivered!' (Jer. 7:9–11).

Now: the accusation is not primarily about commerce in church buildings. It is about using religion as a safe house — going out into the week, doing what you do, and coming back on Sunday to feel delivered.

That is a test anyone can run. Does your churchgoing make you more uncomfortable about the way you conduct your business, or less? If a man can hold a grudge for eleven years, cut corners at work, be cold at home — and find that an hour on Sunday settles his conscience without changing any of it, then he has not been worshipping. He has been using the den.

And note where the tables were standing. The trading filled the Court of the Gentiles, the one place a non-Jew was permitted to pray — which is why Mark alone keeps Isaiah's full phrase, for all the nations. The arrangement that made the insiders comfortable had physically evicted the outsiders, and nobody had noticed.

verseByVerse.quote: Now when they drew near to Jerusalem, to Bethphage and Bethany, at the Mount of Olives, Jesus sent two of his disciples and said to them, "Go into the village in front of you, and immediately as you enter it you will find a colt tied, on which no one has ever sat. Untie it and bring it. If anyone says to you, 'Why are you doing this?' say, 'The Lord has need of it and will send it back here immediately.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
As they drew near to Jerusalem, to Bethphage and Bethany at the Mount of Olives, Jesus sent two of his disciples. He told them: go into the village ahead of you, and as soon as you enter it you will find a colt tied up that no one has ever sat on. Untie it and bring it. If anyone asks why you are doing this, say: the Lord needs it and will send it back here at once.

Meaning first. Mark 11 begins the last week of Jesus’ life. After ten chapters of hushing demons and the healed, Jesus now makes a public claim: he rides a colt down the Mount of Olives as Zechariah’s humble King, greeted with cloaks, branches and the Passover cry, Hosanna, save us. Next morning he curses a fig tree full of leaves and empty of fruit, then overturns the traders’ tables in the Gentiles’ court of prayer. The withered tree interprets the scene: the temple, splendid in leaf and barren, stands under judgment. Jesus teaches faith, bold prayer and forgiveness, and when the rulers question his authority, his question about John exposes them. The King has come to his house, and the house has not known him.

The setting. Mark gives six of his sixteen chapters (11 to 16) to this one week, which shows where the weight of the gospel lies: in the death and resurrection of Jesus. It is Passover, when pilgrims swelled Jerusalem several times over and the Roman governor came up from Caesarea with extra troops, because this was the week riots started.

Bethphage and Bethany, at the Mount of Olives. Two villages on the ridge just east of Jerusalem across the Kidron valley. Bethany, about two miles (3 km) out, was the home of Mary, Martha and Lazarus, where Jesus stayed this week (v. 11). And the geography is loaded. From the Mount of Olives you look straight down onto the temple platform, and it is where Zechariah says the LORD will stand when he comes for his people: on that day his feet shall stand on the Mount of Olives (Zechariah 14:4). He approaches from the one direction the prophets had marked.

Go into the village in front of you. For ten chapters this man has walked everywhere, and on this one occasion he sends ahead for something to ride. The entry is staged, and that is the point. After so long hushing the healed, he now makes a public, prophetic claim before a Passover crowd. The secret is over. He has decided the hour.

You will find a colt tied. A young donkey; Matthew mentions its mother as well (Matthew 21:2), because Zechariah’s prophecy names both, while Mark and Luke mention only the colt Jesus rode. To mention more is not to contradict. Jesus knew it would be there, either by divine foreknowledge, for Mark has shown us Jesus knowing men’s thoughts (2:8), or by a prior arrangement with the owner. Either way, he is in control. Every step of this week is deliberate.

On which no one has ever sat. An animal used for a sacred purpose had to be one that had never been put to ordinary work: the red heifer on which a yoke has never come (Numbers 19:2; Deuteronomy 21:3), the cows that drew the ark and had never been yoked (1 Samuel 6:7). This colt is set apart for holy use, for the King, and Mark expects you to know it.

The Lord has need of it. “The Lord” (ho kyrios) could mean simply its master, Jesus as the one with the right to it, but Mark’s readers would hear the fuller meaning. The Lord of all creation borrows a donkey. And there is something in the phrase for anyone who owns anything. The Lord of glory, who made the animal, asks for the use of it.

And will send it back here immediately. A promise to return it. The King borrows; he does not seize, as the kings of Israel did (1 Samuel 8:16–17). That is how he deals with what is yours: the money, the house, the car, the spare room, the evenings. He has every right to take, and he asks. And nothing lent to him has ever failed to come back larger than it went.

Does God really need anything from me? Not in the sense of lacking it. He is not served by human hands as though he needed anything, since he himself gives to all life and breath and everything (Acts 17:25). But he chooses to use what his people give, and he honours it by calling it a need. That is grace: the Lord who could ride on the clouds asks to borrow a donkey, so that an ordinary villager’s property becomes part of the coronation of the King. Your gifts, time and skills are not necessary to him, and they are wanted by him.

In a sentence. Approaching Jerusalem for the last week of his life, Jesus deliberately sent two disciples to bring an unridden colt for him to ride.

On a Tuesday. The Lord has need of it. What do you have that he might want to borrow for his purposes? Hold it ready. Name one possession, skill or hour this week and offer it to him in prayer, and then to someone in his church who could use it.

For worship. The King of glory rode into his city on a borrowed colt, as he had been laid in a borrowed manger and would be laid in a borrowed tomb. He who owns the cattle on a thousand hills chose to need, so that a villager’s donkey could carry the Son of God to his coronation and his cross. Every detail of the week of his death lay in his hand, and he used that sovereignty to make room for ordinary people to give. Blessed is the Lord who has every right to command, and comes to us asking.
verseByVerse.note: Bethphage and Bethany were villages on the Mount of Olives, just east of Jerusalem. An animal never ridden was fit for a sacred purpose.

parallels.desc: a heifer on which a yoke has never come

verseByVerse.quote: And they went away and found a colt tied at a door outside in the street, and they untied it. And some of those standing there said to them, "What are you doing, untying the colt?" And they told them what Jesus had said, and they let them go.
verseByVerse.commentary:
They went and found a colt tied at a door, outside in the street, and they untied it. Some of the people standing there said: what are you doing, untying the colt? They told them what Jesus had said, and the people let them go.

And found a colt tied at a door outside in the street. Exactly as he said. Mark gives the confirmation in the flattest possible language, which is his way of underlining it: they went, they found, they untied. And the details are precise, as if from an eyewitness: the door, the street, the bystanders. Somebody remembered exactly where the animal was standing.

What are you doing, untying the colt? A natural question: two strangers taking someone’s donkey. Mark tells it with an eyewitness’s restraint, and it is entirely believable. Nobody in a village stands by while their livestock walks off.

And they told them what Jesus had said, and they let them go. They repeated the sentence they had been given, and the objection evaporated. Perhaps the owners knew him, or had been asked in advance. Either way, the word of Jesus was enough, and it came true in every detail.

Two errands, one Lord. Mark tells two errands of this week in almost the same words. Here two disciples are sent ahead and find a colt just as he said; later two are sent and find a man carrying a water jar and a furnished upper room, just as he said (14:13–16). The Lord who knew where the colt stood knew who would betray him, that Peter would deny him three times before the rooster crowed twice, and that he would rise on the third day (10:33–34; 14:30). He did not stumble into Jerusalem and get caught. He went up knowing every door and every street of the road to the cross, and walked it anyway, for us.

Going with nothing but the word. The disciples had no documents and no explanation that would satisfy anybody, only a sentence they had been told to say, and it held. That is a fair picture of much Christian obedience: you go with the word you were given, into a situation you cannot control, and you find that it holds.

The people who lent. Somebody let their animal go. Mark does not name them. On the most significant morning of that year they handed over their property to two strangers on the strength of a sentence, and the King rode into his city on it. The Gospels are full of such anonymous lenders: the man who lent the upper room, the owner of the boat, the boy with five loaves and two fish. Each is in the story because something they owned was asked for and they did not say no.

What if God asks for something and I do not know why? Then you are where these disciples were, and where the owners were. Obedience often comes before understanding. God does not always explain; he commands, and he shows himself faithful afterwards. Test any sense of calling by Scripture, and seek wise counsel, because not every impulse is his voice. But where his word is plain, to give, to forgive, to speak, to serve, do not wait until you see the whole picture. You will see it later, and you will be glad you said yes.

In a sentence. The disciples found the colt exactly as Jesus had said, and when questioned, repeated his words and were allowed to take it.

On a Tuesday. Jesus’ word comes true in small things and great. Obey it in the small ones, and trust it for the great. And be one of the anonymous lenders: someone this week will ask for something you could give. Say yes.

For worship. Blessed be the Lord whose word does what it says. Two men went out with nothing but his sentence, and a stranger’s door opened and a tied colt was loosed for the King. That same word has since gone out to the ends of the earth, and wherever it is spoken, what was bound is set free and handed over to him. Not one thing he has said has ever fallen to the ground, and his people may lean their whole weight on every promise.

verseByVerse.quote: And they brought the colt to Jesus and threw their cloaks on it, and he sat on it. And many spread their cloaks on the road, and others spread leafy branches that they had cut from the fields.
verseByVerse.commentary:
They brought the colt to Jesus and threw their cloaks on it, and he sat on it. Many spread their cloaks on the road, and others spread leafy branches they had cut from the fields.

And he sat on it. There is no saddle, so the disciples improvise with their outer cloaks, the second time in two chapters that a cloak has been thrown down before him (10:50). And it is a deliberate act of prophetic symbolism. Jesus had walked everywhere. Now, for the last two miles, he rides. Zechariah had foretold it: Rejoice greatly, O daughter of Zion! Behold, your king is coming to you; righteous and having salvation is he, humble and mounted on a donkey, on a colt, the foal of a donkey (Zechariah 9:9). Mark does not quote it (Matthew 21:5 and John 12:15 do), but the action speaks for itself. Jesus is publicly claiming to be the King. The time for secrecy is over.

An unbroken colt. There is an unremarked wonder in the sentence. This is an animal that has never been ridden, in a noisy crowd, on a festival road, with a man on its back for the first time in its life. Anyone who has been near an unbroken young donkey knows what usually happens. Nothing happens. It carries him. The one creature in Jerusalem that week that did exactly what he wanted was a donkey.

A donkey, not a horse. Kings went to war on horses. A donkey was the mount of peace. Solomon rode David’s mule to his coronation (1 Kings 1:33–40). Zechariah goes on: God will cut off the chariot and the war horse, and the King shall speak peace to the nations (Zechariah 9:10). So the choice of animal is a sermon. He is claiming the throne and telling the crowd what kind of king he is, in the same gesture. He comes as a king, but a humble king of peace, not a warrior to overthrow Rome. They will get the first half and miss the second.

And many spread their cloaks on the road. This is not mere enthusiasm; it is protocol, and everyone present knew what it meant. When Jehu was proclaimed king, the people took their garments and put them under him on the bare steps and proclaimed him king (2 Kings 9:13). Putting your cloak in the dirt for a man to ride over is a coronation gesture. It says: this is my king, and I will spend something to say so. And a cloak was not cheap. It was the garment the law protected, a man’s covering and often his bedding. They are laying down what they own for him to walk on.

And others spread leafy branches. Mark’s word means leafy branches cut from the fields; John specifies palms (John 12:13), which gives us Palm Sunday. Palms had been waved when Simon Maccabeus liberated Jerusalem (1 Maccabees 13:51) and later appeared on the coins of the revolts against Rome. So the crowd is doing something precise, and political: cloaks for a king, branches for a liberator.

Right about who, wrong about what. Here is the ache under the whole scene. They are right about who he is and wrong about what he came to do. The man they are welcoming as the liberator of Israel is riding toward an execution, and within five days a crowd in this city will be shouting for it. And it is not only first-century enthusiasm. It is possible to be genuinely thrilled about Jesus, to sing loudly, to spend something on him, and to be expecting an entirely different Christ from the one who is actually coming: a Christ who will sort out your circumstances, vindicate your side, and deliver you from the things you want delivering from. The cloaks were sincere. Nobody was pretending. And by Friday the road was empty.

How do I avoid following a Jesus of my own making? Keep reading the whole of the Gospels, especially the parts that unsettle you, and let him define himself. The real Jesus came to save from sin before he saves from circumstances, calls us to a cross before he gives a crown, and is Lord over our politics, not a mascot for them. Ask what you expect him to do for you, and whether that expectation comes from his word or your wishes. When he disappoints your plans, do not leave the road; he is doing something greater than you asked.

In a sentence. Jesus rode the colt toward Jerusalem, fulfilling Zechariah’s prophecy of the humble king, and the crowds honoured him with cloaks and branches.

On a Tuesday. Lay down your cloak before the King: give him the honour and the things that are yours. And ask yourself where you have cast him as the King you wanted rather than the King he is.

For worship. Blessed be the King who chose a donkey. He could have come on the clouds with ten thousand angels, and he came at walking pace on a colt that had never been ridden, gentle with a creature and gentle with a crowd that would soon desert him. They laid down their cloaks for him; he laid down his life for them, and made peace by the blood of his cross. And the same King will come again, and the road will be lined with every nation, and no one will mistake what kind of King he is.
verseByVerse.note: Spreading cloaks on the road was a gesture of homage to a king.

parallels.desc: your king, mounted on a donkey

verseByVerse.quote: And those who went before and those who followed were shouting, "Hosanna! Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord! Blessed is the coming kingdom of our father David! Hosanna in the highest!"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Those who went ahead and those who followed were shouting: Hosanna! Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord! Blessed is the coming kingdom of our father David! Hosanna in the highest!

Hosanna! A Hebrew expression (hôšî‘â nā’) meaning save, we pray, or save now, from Psalm 118:25. It is a cry for help, a plea addressed to God. Over time it had become a shout of praise and acclamation, like God save the king. Both meanings fit: the crowd praises Jesus, and unknowingly prays for exactly what he has come to do. And it comes from a specific place: Psalm 118, the last of the Hallel psalms (113 to 118) sung at Passover. Every pilgrim on that road had been singing it all week.

Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord! Psalm 118:26, the very next line of the psalm. In its original setting it was the greeting called out to pilgrims arriving at the temple gates. But he who comes had also become a title for the Messiah: it is what John the Baptist’s messengers asked, are you the one who is to come? (Matthew 11:3). The crowd sings it to Jesus. And the same psalm speaks of the stone the builders rejected (Psalm 118:22), which Jesus will quote against the leaders within a day or two (12:10). He is listening to what they are singing.

Blessed is the coming kingdom of our father David! Only Mark records this line. Here the crowd goes beyond the psalm and says what it means: the restoration of David’s monarchy, a real throne in this city, under Roman occupation, at Passover. It is an enormously dangerous thing to shout. The kingdom is indeed coming, but not as they imagine, and within days a crowd will be shouting for his crucifixion (15:13–14). The final cry, Hosanna in the highest, calls on the highest heavens to hear and join the praise.

What it does not mean. Not that the crowd understood Jesus. They acclaimed him as a political Messiah. But their words were truer than they knew. He is the Son of David, and he has come to save.

The right prayer, not recognised. That is the terrible irony of the scene. They were shouting the right word. Save now was exactly the right request, made to exactly the right person, at exactly the right hour. They simply had no idea what they were asking for. They wanted saving from Rome, and he had come to save them from something worse, and the salvation they were shouting for would be accomplished by Friday afternoon in a manner that would empty this road. He heard the prayer. He answered it. And almost nobody who prayed it recognised the answer when it came.

Are the crowds of Palm Sunday the same people who shouted crucify him? Probably not all of them, and we should not be too neat. Many of the Palm Sunday crowd were Galilean pilgrims who had followed Jesus; the crowd before Pilate was gathered in the city early in the morning and stirred up by the chief priests (15:11). But the point holds either way. Popular enthusiasm is fickle, and no one should build his faith on the mood of a crowd, including the crowd at church. And all of us, Jew and Gentile, have the same heart that can praise him one day and reject him the next. That is why we need a Saviour, not just a hero.

In a sentence. The crowds hailed Jesus with the pilgrim psalm, crying “Hosanna” and blessing the coming kingdom of David, not knowing how truly they spoke.

On a Tuesday. Christians still sing these words at the Lord’s Supper and in worship. When you say Hosanna, mean both: praise him, and ask him to save. Pray it this week for someone who needs saving and does not know it.

For worship. Hosanna: save now. The Son of David rode beneath that prayer knowing that the only way to answer it ran past the city gate to a hill outside the wall. He did not save the pilgrims from Rome; he saved his people from their sins, from death and from the wrath to come, and he did it before the week was out. Every hosanna since, in every tongue, rises to a King who has already done what it asks, and who will come again to hear it sung with understanding.
verseByVerse.note: “Hosanna” means “save, we pray,” and had become a shout of praise.

parallels.desc: blessed is he who comes in the name of the LORD

verseByVerse.quote: And he entered Jerusalem and went into the temple. And when he had looked around at everything, as it was already late, he went out to Bethany with the twelve.
verseByVerse.commentary:
He entered Jerusalem and went into the temple. When he had looked around at everything, as it was already late, he went out to Bethany with the Twelve.

And he entered Jerusalem and went into the temple. This is where the procession has been heading all along. Not the palace, not the Roman fortress, not the governor’s residence: the temple. The Messiah goes straight to the house of God. Malachi had promised exactly this: the Lord whom you seek will suddenly come to his temple. But who can endure the day of his coming, and who can stand when he appears? For he is like a refiner’s fire (Malachi 3:1–2).

The temple. Herod’s temple, under construction for more than forty years (John 2:20), was one of the wonders of the ancient world: white marble and gold, on an enormous platform covering about 35 acres (14 hectares). The Greek word here (hieron) means the whole temple complex, with its courts, not just the sanctuary building.

And when he had looked around at everything. An inspection, and one of the most quietly ominous sentences in the Gospel. Only Mark records it. He walked about the courts and looked at everything: the traders, the tables, the coins, the birds in cages, the traffic across the Court of the Gentiles, the whole arrangement, seen by the one person present who knew what the building was for. Jesus looks at everything, as a master inspects his house, or as God looks for fruit from his vineyard (Isaiah 5:1–7). And he did not say a word. Tomorrow he will act on what he saw.

As it was already late, he went out to Bethany with the twelve. He lodged outside the city each night of this week (v. 19; 14:3; Luke 21:37). Jerusalem was overcrowded at Passover, and dangerous for him.

What it does not mean. Not an anticlimax. The crowd has just called him king. The palms are on the road. Every expectation says something is about to happen, and he looks round, notices the time, and leaves for supper in a village two miles away. Mark tells it deliberately: the King has come, looked, and will judge. The quiet inspection prepares for the cursing of the fig tree and the cleansing of the temple.

Judgment, not temper. Two things follow from the timing. First, what he does next day is not a loss of temper. He saw all of it the night before, slept on it, walked two miles back, and then overturned the tables: a considered act, which is what makes it judgment. Second, the inspection is itself the warning. Before God acts, God looks: he came down to see Babel (Genesis 11:5) and Sodom (Genesis 18:21), and the risen Christ walks among the lampstands saying to church after church, I know your works (Revelation 2–3).

Should I be afraid of Christ looking at my life? If you are not his, his gaze is a warning to flee to him while there is time. If you are his, it is the look of a Saviour who already knows the worst and has paid for it. Nothing he finds will surprise him, and nothing will make him cast you out (John 6:37). But his look is still searching, because he loves his house too much to leave it cluttered. Let it lead you to honest confession, not to hiding. The safest place for a sinner is under the eyes of the Lord who died for him.

In a sentence. Jesus entered Jerusalem and went to the temple, where he looked around at everything, before returning to Bethany for the night.

On a Tuesday. The Lord looks at everything in his house: in his church, and in your life. What does he see? Pray Psalm 139:23–24 today, and ask him to show you one thing he wants changed.

For worship. He looked around at everything, said nothing, and went out to Bethany for the night. The eyes that searched the temple courts see every heart, and they are never hasty and never unjust. Yet the Lord who inspected the house had come to replace it: within the week his own body would be the temple destroyed and raised in three days, where sinners meet a holy God and live. The one whose gaze no one escapes is the one who became our hiding place.
verseByVerse.note: Bethany was about two miles east of Jerusalem.

verseByVerse.quote: On the following day, when they came from Bethany, he was hungry. And seeing in the distance a fig tree in leaf, he went to see if he could find anything on it. When he came to it, he found nothing but leaves, for it was not the season for figs. And he said to it, "May no one ever eat fruit from you again." And his disciples heard it.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The next day, as they came from Bethany, he was hungry. Seeing in the distance a fig tree in leaf, he went to see if he could find anything on it. When he came to it, he found nothing but leaves, for it was not the season for figs. And he said to it: may no one ever eat fruit from you again. And his disciples heard it.

The structure. Mark sandwiches the cleansing of the temple between two halves of the fig tree story: the curse (vv. 12–14), the temple (vv. 15–19), the withered tree (vv. 20–21). He often does this (3:20–35; 5:21–43; 6:7–30), never by accident, and each story interprets the other.

He was hungry. Three words that are easy to skim. The Son of God, walking two miles into the city before breakfast, wanting something to eat. Truly human. Mark keeps giving us this: asleep on a cushion in a storm, hungry on a road.

A fig tree in leaf. He sees it from a distance, and what he sees is leaves, and the objection people raise dissolves once you know how a fig tree works. Fig trees in Palestine produced leaves in March or April, and with them, or even before, small early knobs (paggim) that were edible, though not very tasty, and that local people ate. The main crop came in June and later. A tree in full leaf, visible from a distance, ought to have had these early fruits; it was making a claim: there is something here. If it had leaves but no early fruit, it would not bear at all that year. Its leaves were a false advertisement.

For it was not the season for figs. Mark’s note explains why there were no ripe figs: it was Passover, early spring. But it is the key to the passage, not an embarrassment in it. Mark puts it there so that no reader can mistake this for pique over a missed breakfast. Nobody was owed a crop. What the tree owed was consistency with its own advertisement, and it had none. It was the only tree on that road claiming to have something, and it was the only tree with nothing. The cursing is not a fit of temper at an innocent tree. It is an acted parable, like the prophets’ symbolic actions (Jeremiah 13:1–11; 19:1–13).

Did Jesus not know there would be no fruit? He went to the tree as a man looking for fruit, and that was the point of the acted parable: he came to Israel looking for fruit and found only leaves. It was a deliberate sign, not a mistake. In his human nature he did not display all he knew at every moment, but nothing here took him by surprise.

The fig tree in the prophets. The fig tree was a recognised picture of Israel. Like grapes in the wilderness I found Israel; like the first fruit on the fig tree in its first season, I saw your fathers (Hosea 9:10). When I would gather them, declares the LORD, there are no grapes on the vine, nor figs on the fig tree; even the leaves are withered (Jeremiah 8:13). Micah uses the same image (Micah 7:1). God came looking for fruit in his people and found none.

May no one ever eat fruit from you again. The only miracle of judgment in the Gospels, and it is performed on a tree, which should tell us it is a sign. The man who healed on a hundred roads curses a plant, once, for a reason: it is a sentence pronounced on fruitless religion. And his disciples heard it. It was said aloud, deliberately, to be remembered, and in seven verses Peter will remember it (v. 21).

The tree is the temple. Israel’s worship that week was in magnificent leaf, which is religious activity, and bare of fruit, which is true worship and righteousness. The courts were packed for Passover; the sacrifices ran from dawn; the money moved. From the road it looked like the healthiest religion on earth. He came near, looked around at everything (v. 11), and found nothing but leaves. The sentence the tree received would be carried out on the building forty years later, when not one stone was left on another (13:2).

The owner comes for his fruit. Within a day Jesus tells the rulers the same story in words: a man planted a vineyard, sent servant after servant for his share of the fruit, and last of all sent his beloved son, whom they killed (12:1–8). The hungry man at the fig tree is that Son, the Lord of the harvest come in person. He is also what Israel was meant to be: the one Israelite whose life was all fruit and no mere leaves, loving God with all his heart and his neighbour as himself. The barren tree would wither, and the fruitful Son would be cut down for the barren, so that branches grafted into him might live and bear fruit for God.

What it does not mean. Not that Jesus was unreasonable or petulant. And not that God has rejected the Jewish people for ever (Romans 11:1–2, 25–29). The judgment fell on the temple and the leadership that rejected their Messiah, and the temple was destroyed in AD 70.

Leaves and fruit in my life. The tree was not condemned for being fruitless in season. It was condemned for advertising. Leaves are what other people can see: the attendance, the vocabulary, the reputation for soundness, the Bible on the table. Fruit is what is actually there: love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faithfulness, gentleness and self-control (Galatians 5:22–23), and lives changed by the gospel. He is not in the distance any more. He comes near, and looks.

What if I feel fruitless? A tender conscience that grieves over little fruit is itself a sign of life; the fig tree felt nothing. Fruit is not something you manufacture by effort but something the Spirit grows as you abide in Christ (John 15:4–5), through his word, prayer, the Lord’s Supper and the fellowship of his people. It often grows slowly and is more visible to others than to yourself. Ask a mature Christian who knows you what they see. And bring your barrenness to the Lord who promised that the one who abides in him bears much fruit.

In a sentence. Finding a fig tree full of leaves but with no fruit, Jesus cursed it, an acted parable of God’s judgment on the fruitless temple.

On a Tuesday. Leaves without fruit: religious activity without faith, love and obedience. God is looking for fruit (John 15:8; Galatians 5:22–23). Pick one fruit of the Spirit you lack most and ask God for it daily this week, and look for one place to show it.

For worship. The Lord of the harvest stood hungry on a road, and the tree had nothing to give him. He has never stopped coming to his people for fruit, and he never comes empty-handed: he brings the Spirit who makes dry wood green. What he looked for in Israel and did not find, he became in his own life, and whatever fruit he finds in us at the last will be his own work, every fig of it, to the praise of his Father.
verseByVerse.note: Leaves on a fig tree normally promise early fruit. The fig tree was a prophetic picture of Israel.

parallels.desc: no figs on the fig tree

verseByVerse.quote: And they came to Jerusalem. And he entered the temple and began to drive out those who sold and those who bought in the temple, and he overturned the tables of the money-changers and the seats of those who sold pigeons. And he would not allow anyone to carry anything through the temple.
verseByVerse.commentary:
They came to Jerusalem. He entered the temple and began to drive out those who sold and those who bought in the temple. He overturned the tables of the money-changers and the seats of those who sold pigeons, and he would not allow anyone to carry anything through the temple.

What was happening in the temple. The trading took place in the Court of the Gentiles, the vast outer courtyard and the only part of the temple where non-Jews could pray; beyond it a low barrier carried notices in Greek and Latin threatening death to any Gentile who went further. Pilgrims needed certified unblemished animals, easier bought on the spot than driven from Egypt or Babylon, and they paid the temple tax in Tyrian shekels, because Roman coins bore the emperor’s image and a divine title. The money-changers exchanged currency at a profit. The trade was controlled by the high priestly family and was a source of their great wealth.

What he attacks and what he does not. He does not attack the sacrificial system; God had commanded the sacrifices, and the animals were needed. He does not attack the changing of money as such. The offence is where all of it was happening, and what it had become. The one part of the house of God available to the nations of the world had been turned into a livestock market and a bureau de change. If a God-fearing Greek or an Ethiopian came to Jerusalem to pray, this is where he had to stand: among the cattle pens, the coin tables and the pigeon cages, in the noise.

He overturned the tables of the money-changers and the seats of those who sold pigeons. He did not just preach against it; he drove out sellers and buyers and emptied the market. And note which stall Mark singles out. Pigeons were the sacrifice the poor could afford (Leviticus 5:7; 12:8), as Jesus’ own parents had offered when they presented him in this very building (Luke 2:24). The prices were reportedly outrageous. Profiting from the poor in the house of God was especially offensive, and it is those seats that go over.

And he would not allow anyone to carry anything through the temple. Only Mark records this. The courts were used as a short cut between the city and the Mount of Olives; the rabbis themselves later forbade it. Jesus stopped the traffic. For some part of that day nothing moved: no trading, no changing, no carrying. And for the first time in years a Gentile could have stood in that court and prayed. He has cleared the room for the people nobody thought about.

Cleansing or judgment? Both. It was a cleansing: the temple was restored, for a moment, to its purpose. But it was also an acted prophecy of judgment, like the fig tree. Jesus was not reforming the temple but announcing its end. He himself would be the new temple (John 2:19–21; 14:58), the place where God meets his people, and the court he cleared for the nations for one afternoon he would open for ever when the curtain of the temple was torn in two at his death (15:38).

One cleansing or two? John records a cleansing at the start of Jesus’ ministry (John 2:13–22). Some think there was only one, placed differently for theological reasons. But there is no difficulty in Jesus doing it twice, at the beginning and end of his ministry; the details and the words differ, and the abuse was the kind that would have returned.

Was Jesus’ anger sinful, and may I copy it? His anger was holy: zeal for his Father’s house (John 2:17), aimed at the abuse of God’s worship and of the poor, controlled, considered overnight, and without any personal grudge. Ours is rarely so pure. Scripture allows righteous anger, be angry and do not sin (Ephesians 4:26), but most of our anger is about our own rights and comfort, and the anger of man does not produce the righteousness of God (James 1:20). This passage gives no licence for violence or for taking the law into our own hands. It does call us to care about what God cares about: his worship, his glory, and the outsider and the poor.

In a sentence. Jesus drove out the traders and money-changers from the Court of the Gentiles, overturned their tables, and stopped the temple from being used as a short cut.

On a Tuesday. What commercial or worldly business has crept into the place where you meet with God? Let him overturn the tables. That might be a distraction in your time of prayer, a grudge carried into worship, or a church programme that leaves no room for the outsider.

For worship. The Son put the pigeon-sellers’ seats on the floor because the poor were being fleeced in his Father’s house, and within days he was himself the sacrifice no money could buy. No dove, no shekel, no table stands between the sinner and God now: rich and poor, Jew and Gentile, come through his blood alone. He has cleared the way for the nations, and the door he opened is still open.
verseByVerse.note: The trading happened in the outer court, the only place Gentiles could pray. Pigeons were the sacrifice the poor could afford. Money-changers exchanged coins into the currency accepted for the temple tax.

parallels.desc: pigeons for those who cannot afford a lamb

verseByVerse.quote: And he was teaching them and saying to them, "Is it not written, 'My house shall be called a house of prayer for all the nations'? But you have made it a den of robbers." And the chief priests and the scribes heard it and were seeking a way to destroy him, for they feared him, because all the crowd was astonished at his teaching. And when evening came they went out of the city.
verseByVerse.commentary:
He was teaching them and saying: is it not written, My house shall be called a house of prayer for all the nations? But you have made it a den of robbers. The chief priests and the scribes heard it and were looking for a way to destroy him, for they feared him, because all the crowd was astonished at his teaching. And when evening came they went out of the city.

Is it not written. Mark’s word is teaching. The tables are on the floor and the birds are loose, and what he is doing is a lesson, and he grounds it, as always, in Scripture. He combines two prophets.

My house shall be called a house of prayer for all the nations. Isaiah 56:7, and the context decides everything. Isaiah 56 is God’s promise to the outsider: the foreigner who has joined himself to the LORD and the eunuch, the two excluded from the assembly under the old arrangements (Deuteronomy 23:1–8). God will bring them to his holy mountain and make them joyful in his house of prayer. Only Mark keeps the phrase for all the nations, and the Gospel written for Gentiles in Rome keeps it for a reason: the market stood in the one court where the nations could pray. It had evicted precisely the people the verse was about. And “my house”: Jesus speaks of the temple as his Father’s, and his own.

But you have made it a den of robbers. Jeremiah 7:11, from Jeremiah’s sermon at the temple gate before its first destruction by Babylon in 586 BC. A robbers’ den is not where the robbery happens. It is where the thieves retreat afterwards, to count it out and feel safe. The people would steal, murder, commit adultery and swear falsely, and then come and stand in God’s house and say, We are delivered, only to go on doing the same (Jeremiah 7:9–10). Jeremiah warned that God would destroy the house, as he had destroyed Shiloh (Jeremiah 7:12–14). The leaders were using the temple as a refuge from the consequences of their sins, and the quotation carries its threat with it: as before, the temple will fall.

Using the den. The test still works. Does your churchgoing make you more uncomfortable about how you conduct the rest of your week, or less? A man who can hold a grudge for eleven years, sharpen his invoices, be cold to his wife, and find that an hour on Sunday settles his conscience without altering any of it, has not been worshipping. He has been using the den.

The eunuch and the foreigner come home. Isaiah named two outsiders, and within a few years both were brought in, not through this court but through Christ. An Ethiopian eunuch, going home from worshipping in Jerusalem, was reading Isaiah 53 in his chariot when Philip told him the good news about Jesus, and he was baptised on the road (Acts 8:26–39). Jesus did not merely clear a court; he became the house. In him, crucified for all nations, God’s house of prayer stands open to every people, and the outsider Isaiah promised to make joyful is made joyful at last.

And the chief priests and the scribes heard it and were seeking a way to destroy him. The first time the chief priests appear as Jesus’ enemies in Mark. Until now the opposition was mainly from Pharisees and scribes (3:6). Now the temple authorities, whose institution, authority and income he had challenged, join in. The plot to kill him begins in earnest (14:1).

For they feared him, because all the crowd was astonished at his teaching. They could not arrest him openly, because the crowds hung on his words. They will have to do it at night, and they will need somebody on the inside. When evening came he went back out of the city, as the night before; he will not sleep in Jerusalem this week until the night they come for him.

Is my church a house of prayer for all nations? Ask what an outsider meets when he comes in. Can a stranger, an immigrant, a person of another class or background, find a welcome and room to pray, or does he meet a closed circle, insider language and a busy programme with no space for him? Do we pray for the nations, support mission, and welcome those from other cultures as family? The temple courts were cluttered with good things put in the wrong place. Our clutter is usually good things too. Clear room for the people Jesus cleared room for.

In a sentence. Quoting Isaiah and Jeremiah, Jesus accused the leaders of turning God’s house of prayer for all nations into a robbers’ hideout, and they began plotting to kill him.

On a Tuesday. Before your next Sunday, examine your week honestly: is there a sin you have been carrying into worship and out again unchanged? Confess it and turn from it. And speak this week to someone at church who looks like an outsider.

For worship. Blessed be the Lord who keeps a house of prayer and fills it with outsiders. He looked at a court full of coins and cages and saw the nations who could not get in, and he gave his life to make room for them. Now the church gathered from every tribe and tongue is his house, its prayers rising through his blood, its door held open by his own pierced hand. The robbers’ den fell, and the house of prayer he built will stand for ever.
verseByVerse.note: Only Mark keeps “for all the nations” from Isaiah’s words.

parallels.desc: a house of prayer for all peoples

verseByVerse.quote: As they passed by in the morning, they saw the fig tree withered away to its roots. And Peter remembered and said to him, "Rabbi, look! The fig tree that you cursed has withered." And Jesus answered them, "Have faith in God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
As they passed by in the morning, they saw the fig tree withered away to its roots. Peter remembered and said to him: Rabbi, look! The fig tree that you cursed has withered. Jesus answered them: have faith in God.

They saw the fig tree withered away to its roots. The third morning of this chapter, on the same road, and the tree is dead. Not wilted, not dropping leaves: completely dead, killed from the roots up, from the part nobody can see, within a day. Complete judgment: their root is dried up, they shall bear no fruit (Hosea 9:16; Job 18:16). Matthew, compressing, says it withered at once (Matthew 21:19). Mark, following the days as they came, gives us the two mornings, which means the disciples walked past this tree twice, and the second time it was a dead stick.

Rabbi, look! The fig tree that you cursed has withered. Peter remembered: they had heard him say it, and now they stand before the result, and very likely this is Peter’s own memory behind Mark’s account. You can hear the astonishment. There is no reflection in it, just pointing, and Peter tells it against himself, as usual: I saw a dead tree and got excited about the tree. The withering is not the point. The temple is the point, and he has walked past that twice as well.

The curse he would carry. The disciples stand in front of a tree under a curse. Within three days the Lord who spoke that curse would himself be hanged on a tree, and Paul draws the line plainly: Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law by becoming a curse for us, for it is written, Cursed is everyone who is hanged on a tree (Galatians 3:13). The sentence on fruitless religion is real, and it falls; but the only fruitful Israelite who ever lived went under it in the place of the fruitless. That is why Have faith in God is good news and not a threat.

And Jesus answered them, Have faith in God. A surprising response. Jesus does not explain the fig tree, though he will spell out the temple’s end soon enough (13:2). He turns to faith, because the temple, the centre of Israel’s worship, is under judgment. Where will God’s people meet with him now? Not in a building, but through faith in God, and prayer. They have watched a word spoken to a tree, and the tree obeyed, and they are about to be sent into a world of things far more immovable than a fig.

Faith in God, not faith in faith. The Greek is literally have faith of God, and the sense is faith whose object is God: not faith in the power of your own believing, which is a modern superstition and a cruel one, but faith in a Person, who hears, and decides, and is good. That distinction governs the promises that follow, which are among the most abused sentences in the Bible.

Where do I meet God now that there is no temple? In Christ. He is the true temple, the place where God dwells with men (John 2:19–21). Through him every believer may draw near to God at any time and in any place, by the Spirit (Hebrews 10:19–22; John 4:21–24). The church, the gathered people of God, is now his temple too (1 Corinthians 3:16; Ephesians 2:19–22), which is why meeting with God’s people on the Lord’s Day matters. You do not need a holy building, a priest or a pilgrimage. You need Christ, and faith in God through him.

In a sentence. The next morning, Peter pointed out that the cursed fig tree had withered to its roots, and Jesus told them: have faith in God.

On a Tuesday. Faith is not faith in faith, or in a building, or in your own prayers. Have faith in God. When you pray this week, begin by remembering who he is before you say what you want: his power, his wisdom, his goodness, his promises in Christ.

For worship. The word that dried a fig tree to its roots is the word that calls the dead out of their graves. He has spoken judgment on every religion of leaves, and then carried its curse in his own body, so that faith in God now rests on a Son who was cursed and is risen. The stones of the temple are gone; the living Lord remains, and through him the weakest believer speaks to the Most High and is heard.

verseByVerse.quote: Truly, I say to you, whoever says to this mountain, 'Be taken up and thrown into the sea,' and does not doubt in his heart, but believes that what he says will come to pass, it will be done for him. Therefore I tell you, whatever you ask in prayer, believe that you have received it, and it will be yours.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Truly, I tell you, whoever says to this mountain, be taken up and thrown into the sea, and does not doubt in his heart, but believes that what he says will come to pass, it will be done for him. Therefore I tell you, whatever you ask in prayer, believe that you have received it, and it will be yours.

Whoever says to this mountain. “This mountain”: they were on the Mount of Olives, within sight of the temple mount, Mount Zion. Moving a mountain was a proverbial expression for doing something impossible (1 Corinthians 13:2); rabbis who were great scholars were called uprooters of mountains. But this mountain may also be pointed. The temple mount, the great obstacle of unbelief and opposition, which he had just pronounced fruitless, can be removed by God in answer to prayer. Zechariah prophesied that the Mount of Olives would be split in the day of the Lord (Zechariah 14:4), and that before Zerubbabel a great mountain would become a plain (Zechariah 4:7).

Be taken up and thrown into the sea. From the Mount of Olives, on a clear day, you can see down toward the Dead Sea. And does not doubt in his heart: the word (diakrithē) means to be divided, wavering like a wave of the sea driven and tossed by the wind (James 1:6–8), as opposed to faith that rests entirely on God and believes that what he says will come to pass.

Whatever you ask in prayer, believe that you have received it, and it will be yours. “Have received” (elabete) is a past tense: believe it as already given. Faith counts God’s answer as certain before it is seen (Hebrews 11:1).

What it plainly does say. Do not soften it first. Jesus means his people to pray with enormous boldness, to ask for things far beyond their resources, and to expect God to act. Most of us are not in danger of presumption; we are in danger of praying for nothing much, in case nothing happens. The whole point of the mountain is that it is too big, and he tells them to say so out loud.

What it does not mean. Not a blank cheque for anything we want, or a technique for making God do our will by believing hard enough. That reading turns prayer into a technique and God into a force. Prayer in faith is prayer according to God’s will (1 John 5:14–15), in Jesus’ name (John 14:13–14), from a heart that seeks his kingdom (Matthew 6:10, 33). Paul asked three times about his thorn and was told no, and given something better instead (2 Corinthians 12:8–9). The promise is about the power of God, not the power of positive thinking.

The prayer that was not granted. The boldness of this promise rests on a garden a few hundred yards from where it was spoken. There, within days, the one man who never doubted in his heart asked his Father to remove the cup, and the cup did not pass: not what I will, but what you will (14:36). The Father did not take the cup from his Son, so that he could say yes to us. The mountain of our guilt, which no faith of ours could shift, was cast into the depths of the sea when Christ drank that cup (Micah 7:19). Every bold request a believer makes is made in his name and heard for his sake. We ask for mountains to move because the greatest one has already been moved.

I prayed in faith and did not receive. Was it my fault? Very likely not, and this is written for you, because you are the person this passage most often wounds. Heaping blame on your faith only adds a second grief to the first. Prayer that moves mountains is real, and you should ask for mountains to move. But it is prayer offered to a Father, not an incantation aimed at a force. A good Father sometimes gives what we did not ask because it is better than what we did, and sometimes withholds what we begged for, because his love can see the whole of a story we can see only the middle of. His no, when it comes, is as wise and as kind as the yes you were hoping for. Keep praying, keep trusting, and bring him the grief as well.

What mountains should I pray about? The ones that are truly beyond you and plainly on God’s heart. The conversion of a hardened friend or child. Your own besetting sin. The spread of the gospel among an unreached people. The unity of a divided church. Courage in persecution. Provision in real need. These are mountains he has promised to move in his time, because they concern his kingdom. Pray about them specifically, persistently and expectantly, and watch for his answers, which often come in ways you did not foresee.

In a sentence. Jesus promised that prayer in undivided faith in God can remove mountains, and that whatever is asked in such faith, believing it already given, will be received.

On a Tuesday. What mountain stands in your way: a sin, a person who resists the gospel, a situation? Pray to God about it with faith that he is able. Write it down, pray about it every day this week, and add to your prayer the words Jesus prayed: yet not what I will, but what you will.

For worship. Nothing is too hard for the God we pray to. He divided the sea, he made the sun stand still, he rolled the stone from a sealed tomb, and he turns hearts of stone to flesh. He bids the weakest of his children stand before the mountain in front of them and ask him for great things. And when he says no, he is the same God still, wise, good and faithful, a Father whose every answer to his children has been shaped by the cross of his Son.

parallels.desc: faith like a grain of mustard seed
ask in faith, with no doubting

verseByVerse.quote: And whenever you stand praying, forgive, if you have anything against anyone, so that your Father also who is in heaven may forgive you your trespasses."
verseByVerse.commentary:
And whenever you stand praying, forgive, if you have anything against anyone, so that your Father in heaven may also forgive you your trespasses.

And whenever you stand praying. Jews commonly prayed standing (1 Samuel 1:26; Luke 18:11, 13), with hands lifted. So this is not a special occasion but the daily one: every time you pray.

Forgive, if you have anything against anyone. Having said that a believing man can move a mountain, he names the thing that will stop him. The join is the most practical thing in the chapter, and it is easily missed. Jesus goes straight from whatever you ask in prayer to forgive, without a pause. Faith is the first condition of answered prayer (v. 24); forgiveness is the second. Unforgiveness blocks prayer. You cannot come to God holding a grudge. Take the scope seriously, because every word widens it. Anything: not only the large injuries, but the slight, the exclusion, the remark, the thing said about you at work. Against anyone: no exceptions for family, for the person who has never apologised, for the one who does not know they did it, for the dead. And notice that the initiative is yours. You stand up to pray; you find something in your hand; you put it down.

So that your Father also who is in heaven may forgive you your trespasses. The only time Mark has your Father in heaven, so common in Matthew, and close to the Lord’s Prayer (Matthew 6:12, 14–15). “Trespasses” (paraptōmata): false steps, stumbling off the path.

The one who forgave first. The man who said this would within the week stand in the place of the greatest injury anyone has suffered: betrayed by a friend, deserted by the rest, mocked, stripped and nailed up. And his prayer there was for his executioners: Father, forgive them, for they know not what they do (Luke 23:34). He never asks of us what he has not done first. More than that, his death is why the Father can forgive at all: he forgives our trespasses because the Son bore them. When a Christian puts down a grudge, he is not achieving a moral feat. He is letting the cross of Christ have its way in one more relationship.

What it does not mean. Not that we earn God’s forgiveness by forgiving others. God forgives freely, because a ransom was paid (10:45). But a person who has truly received God’s forgiveness will forgive others (Matthew 18:21–35; Ephesians 4:32). A man who has grasped what he has been let off does not seize a fellow servant by the throat over a few coins, and if he does, the question is not whether he has forfeited his forgiveness but whether he ever understood it. Nor does forgiveness mean pretending that wrong was not wrong, or always restoring trust at once. It means letting go of the debt and the desire for revenge, and leaving judgment to God (Romans 12:19).

Must I forgive someone who has not repented? Forgiveness has two parts. Jesus also says, if he repents, forgive him (Luke 17:3), and both are true. The first part is in your heart before God: letting go of the grudge and the wish for revenge, and handing the case to him. That is commanded here, whether or not the other person repents. The second is the restored relationship, and that waits for repentance, as God’s own reconciliation with us does. So a believer wronged by someone unrepentant, even an abuser, must not nurse bitterness, but is not required to pretend nothing happened, to trust where trust has not been earned, or to return to danger. Reporting a crime and seeking justice is not unforgiveness.

What if I cannot feel forgiving? Jesus’ instruction is not that you should feel differently about them. It is that you should let it go, in prayer, deliberately, now, and go on doing it whenever it comes back, because it will. Forgiveness is first a decision before it is a feeling. Tell God honestly how much it hurts, hand the person and the wrong to him as the righteous Judge, ask him to bless them, and refuse to rehearse the injury. Feelings often follow slowly. Remember how much you have been forgiven; that is the fuel. And if the wound is deep, seek a wise pastor’s help. There is a name you thought of while reading this. Start there.

Textual note. Some manuscripts add verse 26: But if you do not forgive, neither will your Father who is in heaven forgive your trespasses. The numbers here run 25, then 27.
