It is missing from the earliest and best manuscripts, and was probably added from Matthew 6:15, perhaps written in a margin and later taken into the text. The ESV puts it in a footnote. Nothing has been lost: the truth stands plainly in verse 25, and Jesus does teach it in Matthew, where it belongs.

In a sentence. When you pray, forgive anyone you hold anything against, so that your Father may forgive you.

On a Tuesday. Before you pray today, ask: is there anyone I have not forgiven? Let it go before God, then pray. If it is someone you can safely speak to, consider whether you need to go and be reconciled this week.

For worship. Our Father in heaven keeps no ledger against his children. Every false step off the path has been met by the blood of his Son, and so we stand to pray before a throne where nothing is held against us. The God who had every right to hold everything against us has let it all go, and his mercy toward us is the spring from which our mercy flows, and it never runs dry.
verseByVerse.note: Jews commonly prayed standing. The ESV notes that some manuscripts add verse 26: “But if you do not forgive, neither will your Father who is in heaven forgive your trespasses.”

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The challenge. They come back into the city and the full weight of the establishment is waiting: chief priests, scribes and elders — the three constituencies of the Sanhedrin, which is to say the supreme court of Judaism has sent a delegation to meet him in the temple courts.

Their question is the right one and the only one: by what authority are you doing these things? A man has stopped the temple trade, halted the traffic across the courts, and is now teaching daily on the premises. Somebody has to ask who authorised it.

The counter-question. Jesus offers to answer if they will answer one of his: was John's baptism from heaven or from man?

It is not evasion, and it is not a debating trick. John's commission was the same kind as his own — direct from God, without institutional sanction — so anyone who can assess the one can assess the other.

The calculation. And Mark lets us listen in while they work out what to say, which is the most damning thing in the chapter: they weigh both answers by what each will cost them, and the question of what is actually true never comes up.
verseByVerse.theology:
Why does Jesus refuse to answer? It looks at first like a rabbinic sparring move, and it is much more than that.

He is not withholding truth from honest enquiry — he has never once done that in this Gospel. He explained the parables privately to anyone who stayed and asked (4:10, 34); he answered a scribe who asked about the greatest commandment and told him he was not far from the kingdom (12:34); he answered the rich man who ran and knelt (10:17-22).

What he refuses is to give an answer to men who have already demonstrated they will not deal honestly with an answer. They have John's case in front of them — a prophet the entire nation recognised — and they cannot bring themselves to say publicly what they think about him, because both possible verdicts are expensive.

And that is a settled principle, not a mood: do not give dogs what is holy, and do not throw your pearls before pigs (Matt. 7:6). He will stand silent in front of Herod, who wanted a miracle for entertainment (Luke 23:9), and largely silent before Pilate.

So the withdrawal of light is itself a judgement — and a merciful one, because more truth given to a man determined to reject it only deepens the guilt of the rejecting.

And note what their answer costs them. We do not know is a lie, spoken publicly by the highest religious authority in Israel, about the most famous prophet of their own generation. To protect their position they declared themselves incompetent — and having done so, they had no ground left from which to judge anybody's authority, including his.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: If we say, "From heaven," he will say, "Why then did you not believe him?" But shall we say, "From man"? — and they were afraid of the people.

Read the deliberation again and notice what is missing from it. Two options are weighed. Each is assessed for consequences. And at no point does anybody in that huddle ask: which of these is true?

That question is simply absent. These are the most religiously educated men in the nation, standing in the temple, discussing a prophet's commission — and truth is not one of the factors.

Now: the mechanism is not first-century and it is not confined to unbelievers. It is the standing temptation of any institution, church or person with more to lose from the truth than from avoiding it.

It is the doctrine quietly not preached because of who would leave. The sin not named because of who is in the family. The question about your own life you have never taken to God because you already know roughly what the answer costs.

And it ends the way it ended here: not in a lie you tell somebody else, but in we do not know — a shrug that feels like humility and is in fact a decision. They walked away with their positions intact and no answer at all, and it is the last conversation they have with him before they arrest him.

verseByVerse.quote: And they came again to Jerusalem. And as he was walking in the temple, the chief priests and the scribes and the elders came to him, and they said to him, "By what authority are you doing these things, or who gave you this authority to do them?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
They came again to Jerusalem. As he was walking in the temple, the chief priests, the scribes and the elders came to him and said: by what authority are you doing these things, or who gave you this authority to do them?

And as he was walking in the temple. The third entry into the city in three days, back to the building he has just judged. He is in the colonnades around the courts, where teachers gathered with their students (John 10:23). Not outside making speeches about the temple, but inside it, walking about, teaching daily, entirely at home. He overturned the tables yesterday and he is back this morning, behaving as though the place belonged to him. Which, as he has already said, it does: my house (v. 17).

The chief priests and the scribes and the elders. The three groups that made up the Sanhedrin, the supreme Jewish council of seventy-one members, presided over by the high priest: the chief priests, the temple aristocracy; the scribes, the legal experts; and the elders, the lay heads of leading families. The same three groups Jesus had named in his first prediction of his death (8:31). This is not a heckler. It is an official delegation.

By what authority are you doing these things? “These things”: above all the clearing of the temple, but also the entry, the teaching, everything. The temple was under the authority of the high priest; who gave this Galilean the right to interfere? It is a legitimate question for the guardians of the temple. If a stranger did the same in any church today, the elders would be right to ask. But it is also a trap. If Jesus claimed his authority came from God directly, they could charge him with blasphemy. If he claimed human authority, they could dismiss him; he had no rabbinic ordination and no official position.

Or who gave you this authority to do them? That is the real question, and it reveals how they think. In their world, authority came through channels. A man was trained, appointed, licensed. The question assumes there must be a name: a school, a rabbi, a body that stands behind him. And the answer is that nobody gave it to him, or rather, the Father did (1:11; 9:7). That has been the issue since the first chapter, when the crowd at Capernaum said he taught as one who had authority, and not as the scribes (1:22). Their authority was derived, cited, borrowed. His is not derived from anyone. There is no name to give them but one, and if he says it plainly here, three days before Passover, the week ends at once.

Do church leaders have authority? Yes, a real but derived authority, given by Christ to serve his people through his word (Hebrews 13:17; 1 Peter 5:1–4). Elders rightly ask who sent a teacher, and churches rightly test those who claim to speak for God (1 John 4:1). But all church authority is under Christ and under Scripture. It must never be used, as the Sanhedrin used theirs, to shield an institution from the truth or to silence a just rebuke. When leaders and Christ conflict, Christ wins.

In a sentence. An official delegation of the Sanhedrin demanded to know by what authority Jesus had acted in the temple, and who had given it to him.

On a Tuesday. The question of Jesus’ authority is the question for every person: does he have the right to command your life? Name one area where you have been treating his word as advice rather than command, and submit it to him today.

For worship. He needs no one’s licence. The Father who tore the heavens at the Jordan and spoke from the cloud on the mountain gave him his authority, and after the cross he would say, All authority in heaven and on earth has been given to me (Matthew 28:18). The council that questioned him sat in his house by his leave. Every throne and every pulpit still answers to him, and his word is the last word.
verseByVerse.note: The chief priests, scribes and elders together made up the Sanhedrin, the ruling council.

verseByVerse.quote: Jesus said to them, "I will ask you one question; answer me, and I will tell you by what authority I do these things. Was the baptism of John from heaven or from man? Answer me."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus said to them: I will ask you one question; answer me, and I will tell you by what authority I do these things. Was the baptism of John from heaven or from man? Answer me.

I will ask you one question. Answering a question with a question was a recognised rabbinic method of debate. It is not an evasion. He offers a fair bargain: one question, and he will tell them what they came for. If they answer honestly, they will have answered their own question, which is exactly why they will not. And only Mark records his repeated demand, Answer me: he will not let it pass as a flourish. Jesus is now examining them.

Was the baptism of John from heaven or from man? “The baptism of John” stands for his whole ministry: his preaching of repentance and his baptism. “From heaven” is a reverent Jewish way of saying from God, avoiding the divine name. Did John’s ministry come from God, or was it a merely human movement? There is no third option.

A genuine parallel. The question is not a trick. John had no institutional standing whatever. He held no office, belonged to no school, had no ordination and was not attached to the temple, though as a priest’s son he could have been (Luke 1:5). He appeared in the wilderness, preached, baptised, and was recognised by the nation as a prophet. His authority came directly from God, without a single human channel, which is precisely the kind of authority Jesus has. So the question is: you have already had one case exactly like mine; what did you conclude about it? If they cannot assess John, a man dead a year or two whose ministry the whole country witnessed, they have disqualified themselves as judges of anybody’s commission.

Why this question? Because John had pointed to Jesus. He had announced the coming of one mightier than himself (1:7), and at Jesus’ baptism by John the Spirit descended and the Father spoke (1:10–11). If John was from God, then his testimony about Jesus was true, and Jesus’ authority came from God. The two are bound together. To accept John is to accept Jesus. And there is mercy in it. Anyone who honestly settled the question of John would have been carried straight to the answer about Christ. Jesus has handed them the one question in the world that would have led them home.

In a sentence. Jesus replied by asking whether John’s baptism came from God or from men, since the answer to that settled the source of his own authority.

On a Tuesday. Sometimes the question we ask God is already answered by what he has shown us. Have you responded to what you already know? Before you ask him for more light, obey the light you have.

For worship. Blessed be the Lord whose questions are mercies. He stood before men who had already decided against him and still held out the one road that led home, through the wilderness prophet to the Lamb of God whom the prophet had named. He never refuses truth to an honest heart. The Law, the Prophets and the Baptist’s cry all point one way, and at the end of the pointing stands the Son, holding the door open even to his judges.
verseByVerse.note: “From heaven” means from God.

verseByVerse.quote: And they discussed it with one another, saying, "If we say, 'From heaven,' he will say, 'Why then did you not believe him?' But shall we say, 'From man'?"—they were afraid of the people, for they all held that John really was a prophet. So they answered Jesus, "We do not know." And Jesus said to them, "Neither will I tell you by what authority I do these things."
verseByVerse.commentary:
They discussed it with one another: if we say, from heaven, he will say, why then did you not believe him? But shall we say, from man? They were afraid of the people, for they all held that John really was a prophet. So they answered Jesus: we do not know. And Jesus said to them: neither will I tell you by what authority I do these things.

And they discussed it with one another. Now Mark lets us stand inside the huddle and listen. This is the supreme court of Israel, in the temple, working out what to say, and it is the most damning paragraph in the chapter. Notice what they do not ask: is it true? They ask only: what are the consequences of each answer for us? They are not seeking truth but calculating.

If we say, From heaven, he will say, Why then did you not believe him? They see it instantly. They had not believed John. Luke records that the Pharisees and lawyers rejected the purpose of God for themselves, not having been baptised by him (Luke 7:30). They know perfectly well that if they concede he was sent by God, they are condemned out of their own mouths. They had already made a decision about John and knew it was indefensible. They are not weighing evidence; they are managing an exposure.

They were afraid of the people, for they all held that John really was a prophet. But shall we say, From man? The sentence breaks off, and Mark finishes it for them, as though the calculation were too naked to write out. John had been executed by Herod and was revered as a martyr prophet; the historian Josephus confirms how deeply he was honoured. To deny him publicly in the temple at Passover could provoke a riot, and Luke adds that they feared being stoned (Luke 20:6). One road costs them their credibility; the other costs them their safety.

The question never asked. Two options are considered, each assessed for consequences, and no one in that circle asks which is true. The most religiously trained men in the nation, in the house of God, discuss whether a prophet was sent by God, and truth is not a factor. That is what institutional self-preservation does to a mind, and it is the standing temptation of any church, board or person with more to lose from the truth than from avoiding it: the doctrine not preached because of who would leave, the sin not named because of whose family it is in, the question about your own life never put to God because you already know roughly what the answer would cost.

So they answered Jesus, We do not know. Four words, and they are a lie, told publicly by the highest religious authority in Israel about the most famous prophet of their own generation. And it is the perfect lie, because it sounds like humility. It is also a confession of failure. The religious authorities, whose job was to judge true and false prophets (Deuteronomy 18:20–22), declared themselves unable to judge the greatest prophet of their generation. They disqualified themselves from judging Jesus.

Is it wrong to say I do not know? Not when it is true. Honest uncertainty is not a sin, and God is patient with those who are genuinely seeking. Many questions in Scripture are hard, and humility often says, I do not yet know. But we do not know can also be a position taken because it is the cheapest one available: a way of never having to say yes and never having to say no, and of keeping every door open by walking through none of them. The test is whether you want the answer. If you are really seeking, keep reading, asking and praying, and God will meet you (Jeremiah 29:13). If you are avoiding, admit it.

Neither will I tell you by what authority I do these things. He keeps his word exactly. The bargain was one question for one question; they refused, and so does he. Not a refusal to tell the truth, but a refusal to give it to those who would not receive it (Matthew 7:6). They had already decided. And it is judgment, the most sobering thing in the chapter, because the withdrawal of light from a man who has decided against it is itself a mercy of a terrible kind. More truth given to someone determined to reject it would only deepen the guilt of the rejecting.

He would tell them soon enough. And yet, in the parable that follows, he does tell them, in a form they cannot miss (12:1–12): he is the beloved Son. And the next time they ask him a direct question about who he is, at night, in the high priest’s house, he will answer it in full, and they will tear their clothes and condemn him for it (14:61–64). He was never unwilling to tell them. He was waiting for the hour when the answer could not be turned into anything else, and that hour was a cross.

In a sentence. Afraid of either answer, the leaders said they did not know whether John was from God, so Jesus refused to tell them the source of his authority.

On a Tuesday. We do not know is sometimes not honesty but evasion. Don’t let fear of the consequences keep you from saying what you know is true about Jesus. Think of one place, at work, in your family, among friends, where you have kept quiet about him to keep the peace, and ask God for courage to speak.

For worship. The Truth stood in the temple, and the supreme court of Israel would not ask what was true. He did not argue his way out of their trap. He walked on into the one they were setting, and on the cross he gave his answer in blood, and at the empty tomb the Father gave his. The authority they would not name has been declared to the whole world: Jesus Christ is Lord, the Son sent from heaven, and every calculation made against him has come to nothing.

11.theology:
Was it fair to curse a tree out of season? The answer turns on the leaves. A Palestinian fig produces its fruit before or alongside its leaves, not after — in spring the branches put out small edible knobs, the paggim, and a hungry traveller ate them. So a tree in full leaf is making a claim. Mark's clause it was not the season for figs is not an embarrassment but the key: he supplies it so no reader mistakes this for pique over a missed breakfast. Nobody was owed a crop. What the tree owed was consistency with its own advertisement, and it had none.

And the placement is the interpretation. Mark splits the story and wedges the temple into the gap — curse, temple, withered — his habitual sandwich, never accidental. The fig tree was Israel's own image for itself (Hos. 9:10; Jer. 8:13), and the sentence pronounced here is carried out on the building in 13:2.

A den of robbers (Jer. 7:11) is the most misquoted phrase in the chapter. A robbers' den is not where the robbery happens; it is the cave they retreat to afterwards, where they feel safe. Jeremiah spells it out at the temple gate: Will you steal, murder, commit adultery... and then come and stand before me in this house, which is called by my name, and say, 'We are delivered!' The charge is not commerce in church. It is using religion as a safe house.

And v. 17 keeps a clause the other Gospels drop. Matthew and Luke both quote Isaiah 56:7 and stop before the final phrase; Mark keeps for all the nations — the Gospel written for Gentiles preserving the clause about Gentiles. Isaiah 56 is God's promise about the foreigner and the eunuch, the two categories explicitly excluded under the old arrangements; and the trading filled the Court of the Gentiles, the one place a non-Jew could stand. The arrangement had physically evicted the very people the verse was about.
11.examples:
Then: whatever you ask in prayer, believe that you have received it, and it will be yours — a promise that has been made to carry a weight it was never meant to bear.

What it does say: pray with enormous boldness, ask for what is far beyond your resources, expect God to act. Most of us are not in danger of presumption. We are in danger of praying for nothing much in case nothing happens, and the whole point of the mountain is that it is too big.

What it does not say: that sufficient certainty compels God. That reading makes prayer a technique and God a force, and it is refuted most decisively by the man saying it — within days, in a garden a few hundred yards away, he asks his Father to remove the cup and adds yet not what I will, but what you will (14:36), and the cup does not pass. If unqualified confidence always secured the request, that prayer is unintelligible. Paul asked three times about the thorn and was told no (2 Cor. 12:8–9); John, who heard this saying, wrote in the qualifier himself — if we ask anything according to his will he hears us (1 Jn. 5:14).

Now: to the reader who asked and did not receive — your faith was very likely not the problem, and blaming it only adds a second grief to the first. Believe boldly, ask for great things, and trust him enough to want his will more than your own, knowing that his no, when it comes, is as wise and as kind as the yes you hoped for.

And note what he says next (v. 25), with no pause: whenever you stand praying, forgive. Having promised that a believing man can move a mountain, he immediately names the thing that blocks the pipe. There is a name — you thought of it while reading this — and the instruction is not to feel differently, but to put it down, deliberately, now, and again whenever it comes back.

12.title: The Beloved Son and the Widow’s Two Coins
12.text: <sup>1</sup>And he began to speak to them in parables. “A man planted a vineyard and put a fence around it and dug a pit for the winepress and built a tower, and leased it to tenants and went into another country. <sup>2</sup>When the season came, he sent a servant to the tenants to get from them some of the fruit of the vineyard. <sup>3</sup>And they took him and beat him and sent him away empty-handed. <sup>4</sup>Again he sent to them another servant, and they struck him on the head and treated him shamefully. <sup>5</sup>And he sent another, and him they killed. And so with many others: some they beat, and some they killed. <sup>6</sup>He had still one other, a beloved son. Finally he sent him to them, saying, ‘They will respect my son.’ <sup>7</sup>But those tenants said to one another, ‘This is the heir. Come, let us kill him, and the inheritance will be ours.’ <sup>8</sup>And they took him and killed him and threw him out of the vineyard. <sup>9</sup>What will the owner of the vineyard do? He will come and destroy the tenants and give the vineyard to others. <sup>10</sup>Have you not read this Scripture: ‘The stone that the builders rejected has become the cornerstone; <sup>11</sup>this was the Lord’s doing, and it is marvelous in our eyes’?” <sup>12</sup>And they were seeking to arrest him but feared the people, for they perceived that he had told the parable against them. So they left him and went away. <sup>13</sup>And they sent to him some of the Pharisees and some of the Herodians, to trap him in his talk. <sup>14</sup>And they came and said to him, “Teacher, we know that you are true and do not care about anyone’s opinion. For you are not swayed by appearances, but truly teach the way of God. Is it lawful to pay taxes to Caesar, or not? Should we pay them, or should we not?” <sup>15</sup>But, knowing their hypocrisy, he said to them, “Why put me to the test? Bring me a denarius and let me look at it.” <sup>16</sup>And they brought one. And he said to them, “Whose likeness and inscription is this?” They said to him, “Caesar’s.” <sup>17</sup>Jesus said to them, “Render to Caesar the things that are Caesar’s, and to God the things that are God’s.” And they marveled at him. <sup>18</sup>And Sadducees came to him, who say that there is no resurrection. And they asked him a question, saying, <sup>19</sup>“Teacher, Moses wrote for us that if a man’s brother dies and leaves a wife, but leaves no child, the man must take the widow and raise up offspring for his brother. <sup>20</sup>There were seven brothers; the first took a wife, and when he died left no offspring. <sup>21</sup>And the second took her, and died, leaving no offspring. And the third likewise. <sup>22</sup>And the seven left no offspring. Last of all the woman also died. <sup>23</sup>In the resurrection, when they rise again, whose wife will she be? For the seven had her as wife.” <sup>24</sup>Jesus said to them, “Is this not the reason you are wrong, because you know neither the Scriptures nor the power of God? <sup>25</sup>For when they rise from the dead, they neither marry nor are given in marriage, but are like angels in heaven. <sup>26</sup>And as for the dead being raised, have you not read in the book of Moses, in the passage about the bush, how God spoke to him, saying, ‘I am the God of Abraham, and the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob’? <sup>27</sup>He is not God of the dead, but of the living. You are quite wrong.” <sup>28</sup>And one of the scribes came up and heard them disputing with one another, and seeing that he answered them well, asked him, “Which commandment is the most important of all?” <sup>29</sup>Jesus answered, “The most important is, ‘Hear, O Israel: The Lord our God, the Lord is one. <sup>30</sup>And you shall love the Lord your God with all your heart and with all your soul and with all your mind and with all your strength.’ <sup>31</sup>The second is this: ‘You shall love your neighbor as yourself.’ There is no other commandment greater than these.” <sup>32</sup>And the scribe said to him, “You are right, Teacher. You have truly said that he is one, and there is no other besides him. <sup>33</sup>And to love him with all the heart and with all the understanding and with all the strength, and to love one’s neighbor as oneself, is much more than all whole burnt offerings and sacrifices.” <sup>34</sup>And when Jesus saw that he answered wisely, he said to him, “You are not far from the kingdom of God.” And after that no one dared to ask him any more questions. <sup>35</sup>And as Jesus taught in the temple, he said, “How can the scribes say that the Christ is the son of David? <sup>36</sup>David himself, in the Holy Spirit, declared, ‘The Lord said to my Lord, “Sit at my right hand, until I put your enemies under your feet.”’ <sup>37</sup>David himself calls him Lord. So how is he his son?” And the great throng heard him gladly. <sup>38</sup>And in his teaching he said, “Beware of the scribes, who like to walk around in long robes and like greetings in the marketplaces <sup>39</sup>and have the best seats in the synagogues and the places of honor at feasts, <sup>40</sup>who devour widows’ houses and for a pretense make long prayers. They will receive the greater condemnation.” <sup>41</sup>And he sat down opposite the treasury and watched the people putting money into the offering box. Many rich people put in large sums. <sup>42</sup>And a poor widow came and put in two small copper coins, which make a penny. <sup>43</sup>And he called his disciples to him and said to them, “Truly, I say to you, this poor widow has put in more than all those who are contributing to the offering box. <sup>44</sup>For they all contributed out of their abundance, but she out of her poverty has put in everything she had, all she had to live on.”
12.overview:
This is the last day Jesus ever taught in the temple, and it is one long interrogation. Three delegations come at him in turn, each with a question designed to finish him, and by verse 34 nobody dares ask him anything at all.

He opens by answering the challenge they refused to answer, with a story. A vineyard is planted at great expense, leased out, and the owner sends for his share — and the tenants beat one servant, humiliate another, kill a third, and go on doing it. Then, having nobody else, the owner sends a beloved son, which in this Gospel is a phrase that has twice come out of heaven. They recognise him, kill him, and throw him out of the vineyard. Mark says the leaders understood the parable perfectly — and went away to arrange the arrest.

Then the traps: a coin with Caesar's face on it, and a riddle about a woman with seven husbands. He answers the first in sixteen words that have shaped Christian political thought ever since, and the second from a single present-tense verb in the burning bush.

Then one honest scribe asks a real question and is told he is not far from the kingdom of God. And the chapter ends with Jesus sitting down opposite the treasury, watching people give, and calling his disciples over to look at a widow putting in two of the smallest coins in the empire — everything she had to live on, three days before he did the same.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–27 — The Tenants, Caesar’s Coin, and the Resurrection
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The parable (vv. 1–12). They asked by what authority he acts, and refused to answer his question. So he tells them a story about a vineyard, and it is the least veiled parable he ever told: an owner, a run of beaten and murdered servants, and finally a beloved son. They understood it perfectly — Mark says so — and went away to arrange the arrest.

The coin (vv. 13–17). Pharisees and Herodians together again, opening with flattery and closing a trap with two jaws: endorse the tax and lose the crowd, oppose it and be reported for sedition. He asks for a coin, asks whose face is on it, and gives an answer nobody has improved on.

The riddle (vv. 18–27). Then the Sadducees, with a seven-husbands puzzle designed to make resurrection look absurd — and he answers them from the one part of the Bible they accepted, out of a single present-tense verb.

Three challenges from three different quarters, all in one day, all of them designed to end him — and by verse 34 nobody dares ask him anything else.
verseByVerse.theology:
Render to Caesar (v. 17) cuts in two directions at once, and both must be held.

On one side, a real obligation. Jesus does not say the tax is illegitimate or that a man of God may treat the government as an enemy to be defied. The coin is Caesar's; give it to him. Paul draws the same line plainly: the governing authority is God's servant for the ordering of society, so pay your taxes, keep the law, honour the office (Rom. 13:1–7; 1 Pet. 2:13–17). Christianity is not anarchy, and a faith that despises all earthly authority has not understood this verse.

On the other side, the obligation is bounded. Caesar may claim the coin; he may not claim the soul. The image on the denarius marks what is his; the image of God stamped on the man marks what is God's — and what is God's, Caesar must never be given.

So the same verse that tells you to pay the tax tells you where obedience stops. The moment the state demands what belongs to God alone — worship, or the violation of God's clear command — the Christian renders to God and not to Caesar. We must obey God rather than men, the apostles answered the very Sanhedrin that plotted this trap (Acts 5:29). It is the fault line the martyrs died on: they would pay any tax Rome levied and pray for its emperor, but they would not drop the pinch of incense that called Caesar Lord, because that title was God's.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: the Sadducees, and the ground Jesus chooses to fight them on.

They were the aristocratic priestly party who ran the temple — wealthy, powerful, politically pragmatic — and they held that only the five books of Moses carried full authority. They also say that there is no resurrection, nor angel, nor spirit (Acts 23:8).

Which is why Jesus does not answer from the obvious places. He could have quoted Daniel — many of those who sleep in the dust of the earth shall awake (Dan. 12:2) — or Isaiah 26:19, and they would simply have waved those books away. Instead he beats them on their own chosen ground, reaching into the Torah, into the burning bush that every priest knew by heart, and finding the resurrection in a present-tense claim: I am the God of Abraham. Not was. Abraham has been dead four hundred years and God speaks of him in the present tense.

Now: he does not merely win the argument. He wins it inside the fence they built themselves, proving that the hope they denied was lying all along in the only Scriptures they would accept.

And note the diagnosis he gives first: you know neither the Scriptures nor the power of God. Those are the two ways to go wrong, and they are still the two. Some err because they do not know the text; some because they know the text and have quietly decided what God is not able to do.

verseByVerse.quote: And he began to speak to them in parables. "A man planted a vineyard and put a fence around it and dug a pit for the winepress and built a tower, and leased it to tenants and went into another country. When the season came, he sent a servant to the tenants to get from them some of the fruit of the vineyard.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus began to speak to them in parables. A man planted a vineyard, put a fence around it, dug a pit for the winepress and built a watchtower. Then he leased it to tenants and went into another country. When the season came, he sent a servant to the tenants to collect from them his share of the fruit of the vineyard.

Meaning first. Mark 12 is Jesus’ last day of public teaching in the temple, and every scene asks who he is and what is owed to God. A parable tells of tenants who beat the owner’s servants and kill his beloved son; but the rejected stone becomes the cornerstone. Then come the traps: Caesar’s tax, answered with the coin that bears Caesar’s image and the people who bear God’s; the Sadducees’ seven brothers, answered from the burning bush; and an honest scribe’s question about the greatest commandment. Jesus then asks the question no one can answer: how can the Messiah be David’s son and David’s Lord? He warns against scribes who devour widows’ houses, and ends with a poor widow who gives everything she has, three days before he gives his life.

The setting. The same scene as 11:27–33: in the temple, to the chief priests, scribes and elders, who had just asked by what authority he acted. Jesus refused to answer directly. Now he answers in a parable, the least veiled he ever told, and they understand it perfectly (v. 12).

A man planted a vineyard and put a fence around it and dug a pit for the winepress and built a tower. Stop there, because the first sentence is a quotation and every man listening knew it. Isaiah’s Song of the Vineyard uses almost the same words: my beloved had a vineyard on a very fertile hill; he dug it and cleared it of stones, planted choice vines, built a watchtower and hewed out a wine vat (Isaiah 5:1–2). And Isaiah says what it means: the vineyard of the LORD of hosts is the house of Israel (Isaiah 5:7). God looked for good grapes and found only wild ones; he looked for justice, but behold, bloodshed. So before a single character has acted, the delegation knows exactly what this story is about. It is about them.

Everything the owner did. Every detail is an investment. The fence kept out animals; the winepress was a pit cut in rock where grapes were trodden; the tower was for a watchman to sleep in, and for storage. This is not a man who threw seed at some ground. He has spent years and money on the land and prepared it thoroughly before anyone else touches it. The owner did everything to make it fruitful.

And leased it to tenants. This is the change from Isaiah. In Isaiah, the vineyard is at fault. Here, the tenants are: the leaders to whom God had entrusted his people. Absentee landlords leasing to tenant farmers were common in Galilee, and so was resentment of them. The tenants worked the land and paid rent with a share of the harvest. They owned nothing. And that is the position of everyone who has ever been given anything by God: a church, a family, a gift, a life. None of it is freehold. The parable turns on the difference between a tenant and an owner, and on what happens to a man who forgets which he is.

When the season came, he sent a servant. The owner went into another country: God had entrusted Israel to its leaders and given them time. A new vine takes about four years to produce a crop (Leviticus 19:23–25). Then the owner sent for his share, and note the modesty of the request: some of the fruit, the agreed share, in the season it was due. He has every right, and he asks. The servants are the prophets, often called God’s servants (Jeremiah 7:25; Amos 3:7).

The teller is the Son. Isaiah sang his song for my beloved, the owner of the vineyard (Isaiah 5:1). When Jesus retells it, the word beloved returns at the climax, attached to the owner’s son (v. 6). The man telling the story in the temple courts is the one it is moving toward. He stands among the tenants as the Son who has come for the fruit, and, uniquely, as the one Israelite who has rendered it: every season of his life has been given back to his Father whole. What the vineyard owed and never paid, he is about to pay with his life.

What fruit does God want from me? The same fruit he wanted from Israel: justice, mercy and faithfulness (Micah 6:8), love for him and for neighbour (vv. 30–31), and the fruit of the Spirit (Galatians 5:22–23). It is not a percentage of your achievements but a life given back to the one who gave it. He has planted you in a family, a church, a workplace, and supplied everything you need. He asks for the fruit of trust, obedience, worship and love, in the season he has given you, which is now.

In a sentence. In a parable drawing on Isaiah’s vineyard, Jesus told of an owner who prepared a vineyard, leased it to tenants, and sent a servant for his share of the fruit.

On a Tuesday. God has given you everything you need to bear fruit for him. What fruit is he looking for in your life this season? List three things he has entrusted to you, and ask what he is owed from each.

For worship. The Lord of the vineyard spared nothing. He chose a people, planted them on a fertile hill, fenced them with his law and kept watch over them, and in the fullness of time he planted his own Son among them, the true Vine, whose branches bear fruit. All we have is his, lent with generous hands, and the One who has every right to demand the whole gave everything first.
verseByVerse.note: The setting echoes Isaiah’s song of the vineyard, where the vineyard is Israel. Absentee landlords commonly leased land to tenant farmers.

verseByVerse.quote: And they took him and beat him and sent him away empty-handed. Again he sent to them another servant, and they struck him on the head and treated him shamefully. And he sent another, and him they killed. And so with many others: some they beat, and some they killed.
verseByVerse.commentary:
They took the servant, beat him and sent him away empty-handed. Again the owner sent another servant, and they struck him on the head and treated him shamefully. He sent another, and they killed him. And so with many others: some they beat, and some they killed.

The history of Israel’s prophets. Now the parable turns, and Mark makes us watch it happen again and again, with the violence escalating each time. The parable summarises centuries. God sent prophet after prophet to call his people to repentance and fruitfulness, and they were rejected, persecuted and killed (2 Chronicles 24:19–22; 36:15–16; Nehemiah 9:26; Jeremiah 26:20–23; Matthew 23:29–37; Acts 7:52; Hebrews 11:36–38).

And sent him away empty-handed. The first servant is assaulted and returned with nothing, a message as much as an assault. There will be no rent. The fruit was withheld. God received nothing from them.

They struck him on the head and treated him shamefully. Worse. The word can mean wounded in the head, and some think Mark’s readers would hear an echo of John the Baptist (6:27), the latest of the servants. Treated him shamefully means he was publicly humiliated as well as hurt.

And him they killed. Now the line is crossed. And so with many others: Jesus stops counting, because the pattern never changed. The record is exact. Jeremiah was beaten and put in the stocks by the temple’s chief officer (Jeremiah 20:2) and left in the mud of a cistern (Jeremiah 38:6). Zechariah son of Jehoiada was stoned in the court of the house of the LORD (2 Chronicles 24:20–21). Micaiah was struck and imprisoned (1 Kings 22:24–27). Tradition says Isaiah was sawn in two. And Stephen will put the same charge to the same council within a few years, and it will cost him his life: which of the prophets did your fathers not persecute? (Acts 7:52).

An owner who keeps sending. The story is not primarily about the tenants. After the first beating, any landlord in that room would have gone to law or come with force. This one sends another man, and another, and after a murder, more still. The tenants must have thought him a fool. That is the point: God’s patience with his rebellious people was astonishing. The astonishing thing is not human wickedness, which anyone could predict. It is that after the beating, the humiliation and the killing, there is still somebody else at the gate.

Every bruised servant points ahead. The beaten servants are not only a record of Israel’s sin; they are a road sign. Every prophet who was struck, mocked or killed suffered a small share of what the last messenger would suffer in full. Jeremiah in the stocks, Zechariah stoned in the courts, John beheaded in a dungeon: their sufferings run like a dotted line toward a hill outside the city. And the one telling the story is not watching from outside. He would weep over Jerusalem as the one who had longed to gather her children (Matthew 23:37). The patience of the owner has a face, and it is his.

Why does God put up with so much? Because he is slow to anger and abounding in steadfast love, and because he is not wishing that any should perish, but that all should reach repentance (2 Peter 3:9). His patience is not weakness or indifference; it is mercy giving time to turn. But patience has an end, as the parable goes on to show: the owner will come and destroy the tenants (v. 9), and the time to respond is while he is still sending. If you have been resisting God’s word for years, his patience is not a sign that the matter is closed. It is the reason you are still being called.

In a sentence. The tenants beat, insulted and killed servant after servant, as Israel’s leaders had rejected God’s prophets through the centuries.

On a Tuesday. How have you treated God’s messengers when they called you to repent: the preacher, the friend, the verse that would not leave you alone? Thank God for his patience, and don’t presume on it. Do the thing you have been putting off today.

For worship. The patience of God outran every insult. Servant after servant came back bruised or did not come back at all, and still he sent, until he sent the One who came back not bruised but crucified, and then rose and sent again, this time to the ends of the earth. There is no human love like it. He has borne with us as he bore with them, and he is bearing with us still.

parallels.desc: they mocked the messengers of God

verseByVerse.quote: He had still one other, a beloved son. Finally he sent him to them, saying, 'They will respect my son.' But those tenants said to one another, 'This is the heir. Come, let us kill him, and the inheritance will be ours.' And they took him and killed him and threw him out of the vineyard.
verseByVerse.commentary:
He had still one other, a beloved son. Finally he sent him to them, saying: they will respect my son. But those tenants said to one another: this is the heir. Come, let us kill him, and the inheritance will be ours. And they took him, killed him, and threw him out of the vineyard.

He had still one other, a beloved son. Read it slowly, because both halves are heavy. He had still one other: the servants are exhausted; there is nobody else to send; what remains is not another employee. A beloved son: and here the parable stops being a story about someone else, because that phrase has occurred twice already in this Gospel and both times it came out of heaven. At the Jordan: You are my beloved Son (1:11). On the mountain: This is my beloved Son; listen to him (9:7). Here Jesus answers the leaders’ question about his authority (11:28): he is not one more servant, one more prophet. He is the Son. And beloved may again carry the sense of only, as with Isaac, the only son whom Abraham loved (Genesis 22:2). He is telling them who he is and what they are about to do, in a story, days before they do it.

Finally he sent him to them. “Finally” (eschaton): last of all. There is no one after the Son. He is God’s final word: in these last days God has spoken to us by his Son (Hebrews 1:1–2).

They will respect my son. The last card, and the owner’s expectation is what any reasonable man would think. A servant can be brushed aside; the heir is the owner in person. Surely this settles it. The patience of the owner goes beyond reason. And there is a cost in the sending that a first-century listener would feel at once. This man has already lost servants to these tenants. He knows what they do to the people he sends. And he sends his son. The Father’s love for his rebellious people led him to send his Son: he who did not spare his own Son but gave him up for us all (Romans 8:32).

Did God not know what would happen to his Son? He knew perfectly. The parable speaks as a human landlord would, to show the depth of the tenants’ guilt and the patience of the owner. But Jesus himself is telling the story, and he knows its ending. The Father sent the Son knowing he would be killed, and the Son came knowing it, because it was the plan of God from before the foundation of the world that the Son should die for sinners (Acts 2:23; 1 Peter 1:20). That is not less love but more. They did not surprise God. He sent his Son into their hands on purpose.

This is the heir. Come, let us kill him, and the inheritance will be ours. Notice that they recognise him. That is the horror of the parable and the horror of Good Friday. They do not kill the son by mistake. They kill him because they know exactly who he is. Under the law of the day, land without an heir might pass to those who had occupied and worked it. This exposes the leaders: their rejection of Jesus is not ignorance but rebellion. They want the vineyard, God’s people, for themselves, without God. And “Come, let us kill him” is what Joseph’s brothers said about the favoured son (Genesis 37:20).

The logic of all sin. Their reasoning is the reasoning of every human rebellion against God, stated with unusual honesty: the inheritance will be ours. Get rid of the heir, and the estate is ours to keep. It is the serpent’s offer in a garden, you will be like God, and it is the whole logic of sin, which is never finally about pleasure but about ownership. We want our lives without their Lord.

And they took him and killed him and threw him out of the vineyard. The bare violence of it, in one sentence, with no adjectives. Leaving the body unburied was the final insult. Jesus is predicting his own death, and his enemies’ part in it, to their faces. Matthew and Luke say they threw him out and then killed him (Matthew 21:39; Luke 20:15), which matches Jesus’ crucifixion outside the city wall: Jesus also suffered outside the gate in order to sanctify the people through his own blood (Hebrews 13:12). He is standing in the temple describing his own murder, in the third person, to the men who will commit it, and they are listening.

In a sentence. Last of all, the owner sent his beloved son, and the tenants, recognising him as the heir, killed him to seize the vineyard for themselves.

On a Tuesday. Ask where you are still saying, in small ways, the inheritance will be mine: your time, your body, your money, your future, kept back from the Son who has the right to them. Hand one of them back to him today.

For worship. God sent his only, beloved Son to rebels like us. He knew what we would do, and sent him anyway. This is love: not that we loved God, but that he loved us and sent his Son to be the propitiation for our sins (1 John 4:9–10). The Heir was thrown out of the vineyard so that the tenants who killed him could be brought in as sons and share his inheritance.
verseByVerse.note: “Beloved son” echoes the Father’s voice at the baptism and transfiguration.

verseByVerse.quote: What will the owner of the vineyard do? He will come and destroy the tenants and give the vineyard to others. Have you not read this Scripture: 'The stone that the builders rejected has become the cornerstone; this was the Lord's doing, and it is marvelous in our eyes'?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
What will the owner of the vineyard do? He will come and destroy the tenants and give the vineyard to others. Have you not read this Scripture: The stone that the builders rejected has become the cornerstone; this was the Lord’s doing, and it is marvellous in our eyes?

What will the owner of the vineyard do? He asks the question and answers it himself. Matthew records that the listeners themselves answered (Matthew 21:41), and so condemned themselves, as David did when Nathan told him the parable of the lamb (2 Samuel 12:1–7). There is no ambiguity left, and none intended.

He will come and destroy the tenants. Judgment on the leaders who rejected the Son. Fulfilled within forty years, in AD 70, when Rome destroyed Jerusalem and the temple, and the priestly aristocracy and the Sanhedrin came to an end. Jesus will soon foretell it stone by stone (13:2).

And give the vineyard to others. To whom? To new tenants: the apostles and the leaders of the church, Jewish and Gentile, who would care for God’s people under Christ; Matthew says to a people producing its fruits (Matthew 21:43). Notice that the vineyard is not destroyed. God’s people continue; the wicked tenants are replaced. And the others turn out to include Gentiles from every nation, which is what Peter tells this very council: the stone rejected by you, the builders, has become the cornerstone (Acts 4:11).

Has God finished with the Jewish people? No. The parable is aimed at the tenants, the leaders standing in front of him, not at a nation. Paul spends three chapters denying that inference: God has not rejected his people whom he foreknew (Romans 11:2), and a remnant chosen by grace believes even now. Christians differ on what Romans 11 promises for Israel’s future: many expect a great turning of the Jewish people to Christ before the end, while others read all Israel as the whole people of God, Jew and Gentile, gathered in through history. Both agree that Jews are saved in the same way as Gentiles, through faith in Jesus the Messiah, and that Christians must never despise the people from whom Christ came.

A warning to every church. It is also a warning to every congregation that has assumed its position is permanent. A lampstand can be removed (Revelation 2:5). Tenancy is not freehold. Churches and denominations that once preached the gospel and now deny it have learned this. The vineyard is the Lord’s, and he gives its care to those who will render him the fruit.

The stone that the builders rejected has become the cornerstone. Have you not read: a sting, put to professional scribes. Psalm 118:22–23 comes from the psalm the crowds had sung at his entry two days earlier (11:9); they sang verse 26 at him, and now he reads them verse 22. The picture changes from vineyard to building, perhaps with a Hebrew play on son (ben) and stone (eben). The builders are the leaders, the professionals whose job is to know which stones are usable. They examined this one and threw it away. But God picked it up and made it the cornerstone, which sets the line of every wall. The parable does not end with the son’s death. It ends with resurrection, told in the language of masonry: the rejected stone is not on the spoil heap where they threw it. It is holding up the house. The apostles preached exactly this (Acts 4:10–11; 1 Peter 2:4–8; Ephesians 2:20).

This was the Lord’s doing, and it is marvelous in our eyes. The rejection and the vindication are both God’s work. The builders were not thwarted by an accident. What they meant as rejection was the very thing God was doing. Human evil and divine purpose meet at the cross (Acts 2:23). The result is wonderful.

In a sentence. The owner will destroy the wicked tenants and give the vineyard to others, and the rejected stone will become the cornerstone by God’s marvellous doing.

On a Tuesday. The one rejected by the world is the cornerstone of God’s new temple, the church. Build your life on him. When you are mocked or set aside for his sake, remember that you are being built on a stone the world also rejected, and that God has the last word.

For worship. The stone the experts threw on the spoil heap is the stone that holds up the house of God. They examined him, rejected him and buried him, and on the third morning the Father lifted him and set him at the head of the corner, and every living stone since, from every nation, has been laid in line with him. Nothing in heaven or earth will ever move him, and those built on him will stand as long as he does.

verseByVerse.quote: And they were seeking to arrest him but feared the people, for they perceived that he had told the parable against them. So they left him and went away.
verseByVerse.commentary:
They were looking for a way to arrest him, but they feared the people, for they perceived that he had told the parable against them. So they left him and went away.

For they perceived that he had told the parable against them. They understood perfectly. Unlike the parables of chapter 4, which outsiders did not understand (4:11–12), this one was plain. They knew they were the tenants, they knew who the beloved son was, and they knew what was being said about their future. Which removes the most convenient excuse anyone has ever offered for rejecting Christ. These men were not confused. Their problem was never information.

And they were seeking to arrest him. Told they are the men who murder the heir, they go away to arrange the murder of the heir. The warning becomes the occasion of the crime it warns about. That is what a hardened heart does with the truth: it does not soften; it uses the light to see by while it does the thing the light exposed.

But feared the people. Again (11:18, 32). Not conscience: crowd management. The city is full for Passover, the throng hears him gladly (v. 37), and a public arrest would start a riot with the governor in town. They will need to take him secretly, at night, through a traitor (14:1–2, 10–11).

Held back until his hour. They wanted him that afternoon and could not lay a hand on him. Mark gives the human reason, the crowd; the deeper reason is that the Son was keeping his own appointment. He had just told them the story they would act out, and he would let them act it out only when he chose: at Passover, on the night he took bread and said, This is my body. The tenants thought they were deciding when the heir would die. The heir had decided, and he had decided for the sake of men like these.

So they left him and went away. The saddest clause in the chapter. They were standing in front of the Son of God, who had just told them who he was, what they were about to do, and what it would cost them. Nobody dragged them off. They simply turned round and walked. It is possible to understand the gospel completely and to walk away, not in rage or confusion, but because it costs too much. That is the most ordinary way in the world of being lost.

What should I do when a sermon or a passage exposes me? Do not leave and go away. Stay under it. Admit to God what it has shown you, plainly, without excuses. Ask him what repentance looks like here, and take the first step today, while the word is still sharp. If it involves someone you have wronged, go to them. And do not resent the preacher or the friend God used. The leaders hated Jesus for telling them the truth. A softened heart thanks God for the wound that leads to healing.

In a sentence. Understanding that the parable was aimed at them, the leaders wanted to arrest Jesus at once but held back for fear of the crowd.

On a Tuesday. To recognise yourself in God’s word is not enough. It must lead to repentance, not resentment. The next time Scripture finds you out, stop reading and pray before you move on.

For worship. The Son told his murderers the truth to their faces, and the truth was still an offer. Even this parable held out the stone they could have built on. He did not chase them; he let them go, and then he let them take him, so that the rejected stone could become the cornerstone for a multitude of sinners who, unlike them, turned back.

verseByVerse.quote: And they sent to him some of the Pharisees and some of the Herodians, to trap him in his talk. And they came and said to him, "Teacher, we know that you are true and do not care about anyone's opinion. For you are not swayed by appearances, but truly teach the way of God. Is it lawful to pay taxes to Caesar, or not? Should we pay them, or should we not?" But, knowing their hypocrisy, he said to them, "Why put me to the test? Bring me a denarius and let me look at it."
verseByVerse.commentary:
They sent to him some of the Pharisees and some of the Herodians, to trap him in his words. They came and said: Teacher, we know that you are true and do not care about anyone’s opinion. You are not swayed by appearances, but truly teach the way of God. Is it lawful to pay taxes to Caesar, or not? Should we pay them, or should we not? But knowing their hypocrisy, he said to them: why put me to the test? Bring me a denarius and let me look at it.

A series of tests. Mark now records three questions put to Jesus by different groups (vv. 13–34), and then one he puts to them (vv. 35–37). Each is meant to trap him. Each fails. This is the Messiah examined in the temple, like a Passover lamb examined for blemishes before being sacrificed. He is found without fault.

Some of the Pharisees and some of the Herodians. An unlikely alliance, as in Galilee (3:6). The Herodians supported Herod’s family, and so the Roman rule that kept them in power; the Pharisees resented Roman rule as an insult to God’s people. Nothing unites opposites like a shared hatred of the light. They were sent by the Sanhedrin, now working through proxies, to trap him in his talk, a hunting word (agreusōsin) for snaring wild animals.

Teacher, we know that you are true. Flattery, to set him up. And notice what they praise him for: independence, fearlessness, indifference to what people think. That is precisely the quality they need him to display in the next thirty seconds. They are not complimenting him; they are winding him up and pointing him at a cliff. And every word was true. He was true, impartial, and taught the way of God. They said it without believing it, and described him accurately for the purpose of destroying him.

How flattery works. It is rarely a lie. It is a true thing said by somebody who wants something, and the tell is not the content but the timing: it arrives immediately before the request. Anyone with responsibility should learn to feel a cold draught when a conversation opens like this one. And it is worth asking the other way round: do you ever praise people in order to get something from them?

Is it lawful to pay taxes to Caesar, or not? They ask it twice, to shut off any escape into generality: yes or no. The tax was a poll tax, a head tax paid by every adult directly to the Roman treasury. It had been imposed when Judea came under direct Roman rule in AD 6, and provoked a revolt led by Judas the Galilean (Acts 5:37), who taught that paying it was treason to God, the only king. It was a symbol of subjection. The trap had two jaws. If Jesus said yes, he would lose the crowd, who hated the tax and hoped he would liberate them. If he said no, the Herodians could report him to the Romans as a rebel. Either answer would destroy him. And at his trial they will accuse him of exactly that: forbidding us to give tribute to Caesar (Luke 23:2).

But, knowing their hypocrisy. He saw through the flattery to the trap, and he names it before he answers: why put me to the test? He does not pretend the flattery was sincere.

Bring me a denarius and let me look at it. A silver coin, a day’s wage for a labourer, and the coin in which the tax was paid. With that sentence he takes control of the exchange. Jesus apparently did not carry one. They did, even in the temple. Somebody in that group of scrupulous men has a denarius in his pocket and hands it over. The trap is already sprung, and they have not noticed.

In a sentence. Pharisees and Herodians flattered Jesus and then tried to trap him with the question of paying the Roman tax, and he asked them for a coin.

On a Tuesday. Flattery is a trap. Be wary of praise that comes with a question attached. And when you are cornered by a question designed to make you look foolish, take your time, as he did, and look for the truth beneath it.

For worship. No trap held him, no flattery moved him, no fear bent him. Pharisee and Herodian, priest and scribe brought their questions like inspectors to the Passover lamb, and every one went away having found nothing. He is everything they said of him without meaning it: true, swayed by no one, teaching the way of God in truth. More than that, he is the way of God, and he walked it all the way to the altar.
verseByVerse.note: The Herodians supported Herod’s family and so Roman rule; the Pharisees resented Rome. The poll tax was paid directly to Rome and bitterly resented. The ESV notes that a denarius was a day’s wage.

verseByVerse.quote: And they brought one. And he said to them, "Whose likeness and inscription is this?" They said to him, "Caesar's." Jesus said to them, "Render to Caesar the things that are Caesar's, and to God the things that are God's." And they marveled at him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
They brought one. He said to them: whose likeness and inscription is this? They said: Caesar’s. Jesus said to them: render to Caesar the things that are Caesar’s, and to God the things that are God’s. And they marvelled at him.

Whose likeness and inscription is this? Take the coin in your hand for a moment, because the whole answer is stamped on it. The denarius of Tiberius, emperor at the time, carried his head in profile and, round the edge, Tiberius Caesar, son of the divine Augustus. On the other side, high priest. So it is not merely a coin with a portrait. It is a small metal blasphemy: a claim that a living man is the son of a god and the chief priest of the world. To devout Jews it was doubly offensive: a graven image (Exodus 20:4), and a claim to divinity. Mark’s word for likeness is eikōn, image.

Render to Caesar the things that are Caesar’s. Caesar’s, they answer, because there is only one answer, and by producing the coin they have shown that they use Caesar’s money and enjoy his roads and protection. “Render” (apodote) means give back, repay a debt. The coin bears Caesar’s image; it is his; give it back. Paul and Peter teach the same (Romans 13:1–7; 1 Peter 2:13–17). The state has a legitimate, God-given authority in its own sphere. A faith that despises all earthly authority has not read this verse.

And to God the things that are God’s. The deeper point, and where the sentence detonates. What bears God’s image? Human beings: God created man in his own image (Genesis 1:26–27). The coin belongs to Caesar because it bears his image; you belong to God because you bear his. Give Caesar his coin; give God yourself, all of you, because there is no part of a human being that is not stamped. He has answered the tax question and then, in a few more words, put the questioners themselves on the scales. And Caesar’s claims are limited by God’s. Caesar’s inscription claimed divinity; Jesus denies it. Caesar is owed taxes, not worship. When Caesar demands what belongs to God, we must obey God rather than men (Acts 5:29).

The fault line of the martyrs. He does not say how much belongs to Caesar; that will vary with the government you live under. He fixes only the limit, and the limit is everything that is God’s. That is the line the early martyrs died on. They paid every tax Rome levied and prayed for the emperor, and would not drop the pinch of incense that called Caesar Lord.

Son of the divine, high priest. Look again at the coin in his hand. It called Tiberius son of a god and high priest. The man holding it, in the temple, is the true Son of God, days from offering himself as the great high priest who brings his own blood. And Mark’s word for likeness, eikōn, is the word Paul uses for Christ: he is the image of the invisible God (Colossians 1:15). We were made in God’s image and defaced it; the Son, who is that image perfectly, came to renew it in us (Colossians 3:10). Render to God the things that are God’s: the Son did it first, giving back to his Father a whole human life with nothing withheld.

And they marveled at him. The trap had failed. He had neither endorsed Roman rule unconditionally nor called for revolt. He had put both in their place. They came to trap him and went away astonished.

Where Christians differ: church and state. Christians have understood this saying in many ways: as dividing life into two separate spheres, secular and sacred; as subordinating the church to the state; or as subordinating the state to the church. Verdict: Jesus does not make Caesar and God equal partners. Everything belongs to God, including Caesar (Romans 13:1). The state has real but limited authority under God, and Christians should be good citizens, paying taxes and honouring rulers. But their final loyalty is to God, and they may not give the state what belongs to God alone.

Must I pay taxes to a government I think is unjust? Yes, in ordinary circumstances. Tiberius was a pagan emperor whose government occupied Israel, and Jesus still said render. Paul wrote Romans 13 under Nero. Paying taxes, obeying laws, praying for rulers (1 Timothy 2:1–2) and honouring them is part of rendering to Caesar, even when we disagree with how the money is spent. Christians may work by lawful means to change unjust laws and should speak for justice. But disobedience is right only when the state commands what God forbids, or forbids what God commands, such as worship, the gospel or the protection of life. Then we obey God, openly and peaceably, and accept the cost.

In a sentence. Jesus answered that what bears Caesar’s image should be given back to Caesar, and what bears God’s image, ourselves, to God.

On a Tuesday. Pay your taxes honestly. And remember whose image you bear: give yourself wholly to God. Pray this week by name for those who govern you, and ask where any authority, a boss, a party, a cause, has been claiming the loyalty that belongs to God alone.

For worship. The emperor’s coin has long been melted down, and the face on it is dust. But every human face still carries the stamp of its Maker, and in the Son the defaced image is being made new, one believer at a time, until we see him and are like him. Caesar was given back his coin. God, who has every claim on us, first gave himself for us, and so we are his twice over, by making and by buying.
verseByVerse.note: The coin bore the emperor’s head — probably Tiberius — and an inscription calling him son of the divine Augustus.

verseByVerse.quote: And Sadducees came to him, who say that there is no resurrection. And they asked him a question, saying, "Teacher, Moses wrote for us that if a man's brother dies and leaves a wife, but leaves no child, the man must take the widow and raise up offspring for his brother. There were seven brothers; the first took a wife, and when he died left no offspring. And the second took her, and died, leaving no offspring. And the third likewise. And the seven left no offspring. Last of all the woman also died. In the resurrection, when they rise again, whose wife will she be? For the seven had her as wife."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Sadducees came to him, who say that there is no resurrection, and asked him: Teacher, Moses wrote for us that if a man’s brother dies and leaves a wife but no child, the man must marry the widow and raise up children for his brother. There were seven brothers. The first married, and died leaving no children. The second married her, and died leaving no children, and the third likewise. None of the seven left children. Last of all the woman also died. In the resurrection, when they rise again, whose wife will she be? For all seven had her as wife.

And Sadducees came to him, who say that there is no resurrection. The only time they appear in Mark. The Sadducees were the aristocratic priestly party, including the high priestly families who controlled the temple Jesus had just disrupted: wealthy, politically conservative, cooperating with Rome. They accepted only the five books of Moses as fully authoritative, rejected the Pharisees’ oral tradition, and denied the resurrection, angels and spirits (Acts 23:8), arguing that Moses never taught life after death.

Moses wrote for us. They begin with Moses, the only authority they accept: Deuteronomy 25:5–10, the law of levirate marriage (from Latin levir, brother-in-law). If a man died childless, his brother married the widow, and the first son carried on the dead man’s name and inheritance. In a world with no pensions and no property rights for women, a childless widow was destitute, and the law provided for her. It is a mercy, the background to the book of Ruth, and the Sadducees are about to turn it into a weapon.

There were seven brothers. Not a real case but probably a stock argument against the Pharisees, with seven chosen for maximum absurdity: if Moses commanded levirate marriage, and the resurrection would make it absurd, then Moses could not have believed in the resurrection.

The woman nobody noticed. Watch the telling, because it is as revealing as the argument. Seven men are named as taking her. She is the object of every sentence and the subject of none, until she is disposed of at the end: last of all the woman also died. There is no suggestion anywhere in their story that she is a person. Seven bereavements; seven times widowed, childless and passed along. Nobody in that conversation gives it a thought. Jesus, who noticed the wife in chapter 10 and will notice the widow at the end of this chapter, is about to answer men who use a suffering woman as a debating prop.

In the resurrection, when they rise again, whose wife will she be? Not really a question but a joke. And notice the assumption beneath it, which Jesus goes straight for: they picture the resurrection as this life continued, with the same arrangements and property law running on for ever. That is the mistake of a great many people who have never heard of a Sadducee.

Asking the Resurrection about the resurrection. The joke is told to the one person in the world it could not touch. Within the week the man they were mocking would be laid in a tomb and walk out of it, the firstfruits of those who have fallen asleep (1 Corinthians 15:20). He had already said so three times on the road (8:31; 9:31; 10:34). The Sadducees were not debating a theory with a rabbi; they were asking the Resurrection whether there would be one. And the widow they passed from brother to brother has a better hope than any levirate law could give: not a name kept alive by a son, but life itself, kept by the Son.

In a sentence. The Sadducees, who denied the resurrection, tried to make it look absurd with the story of a woman who married seven brothers in turn.

On a Tuesday. Mocking questions about the faith are nothing new. Don’t be thrown by them; Jesus has answers. When a friend raises one, take it seriously, look beneath it for the assumption it rests on, and answer with gentleness and respect (1 Peter 3:15).

For worship. The clever men brought their riddle to the Lord of life, and he was neither embarrassed nor amused. He saw the woman they had made a prop, seven times bereaved, and he answered for her as well as for them. Our hope does not rest on our skill at untying every knot in an argument, but on the God who raises the dead, and on the Son who holds every widow, and every name, in his hand.
verseByVerse.note: The Sadducees, the priestly party, denied the resurrection. Levirate marriage kept a dead man’s name alive.

verseByVerse.quote: Jesus said to them, "Is this not the reason you are wrong, because you know neither the Scriptures nor the power of God? For when they rise from the dead, they neither marry nor are given in marriage, but are like angels in heaven.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus said to them: is this not why you are wrong, because you know neither the Scriptures nor the power of God? For when they rise from the dead, they neither marry nor are given in marriage, but are like angels in heaven.

Is this not the reason you are wrong. “Wrong” (planasthe) means to wander, to go astray, to be deceived. He answers the joke with a diagnosis, and a blunt one, delivered to men who were the professional custodians of both Scripture and temple. The educated elite are lost.

Because you know neither the Scriptures nor the power of God. Two causes of error, still the two causes of most theological error. They had the Scriptures largely by memory, but did not see what they teach, as the burning bush will show humiliatingly. And they could not imagine that God can raise the dead and make a new kind of life. They had shrunk God to the size of their own imagination.

The quiet unbelief of realism. That second failure is common among religious people, and it does not announce itself as unbelief. It sounds like realism. It is the settled assumption that God will not act, that this marriage will not change, that this person will not be converted, that nothing much is going to happen: an assumption formed not from Scripture but from experience, and then read back into Scripture.

For when they rise from the dead, they neither marry nor are given in marriage. He denies their premise. The age to come is not this age with the same furniture. Resurrection life is not simply this life continued. Marriage belongs to this age. Its purposes, companionship, the bringing of children into the world, and the picture of Christ and the church, will be fulfilled. In the new creation there will be no death, so no need for children to carry on the family line, and no levirate marriage. The whole basis of their story falls apart.

But are like angels in heaven. Not that we become angels, or lose our bodies or our identities. But like angels, we will not die (Luke 20:36), and will not marry. The comparison is specific to the matter in hand. And the Sadducees did not believe in angels either; Jesus corrects them on that too.

What it does not mean. Not that married love is lost, or that spouses will not know each other in heaven. Every relationship will be taken up into something greater: perfect love for God and for one another, in the marriage of Christ and his bride, the church (Revelation 19:7–9), to which every earthly marriage points.

I have buried my husband or wife. What does this mean for us? Take it slowly, and take the whole of it. Jesus does not say love ends, or that you will not know one another. Every fear that the resurrection means less, fewer people, thinner relationships, a vague eternity, is the Sadducees’ mistake in reverse, and the Bible never suggests it. Paul expected to know the Thessalonians at Christ’s coming (1 Thessalonians 2:19). Marriage as an institution ends not because it was too small but because it was a signpost to Christ and the church (Ephesians 5:32), and you take the signpost down when you arrive. Nothing good will be lost: not the years, not your knowledge of each other, not the love. It will be taken up into something so much larger that what you fear losing will look, when you are standing in it, like the smaller version of what you have.

In a sentence. Jesus told the Sadducees they were wrong because they knew neither the Scriptures nor God’s power: in the resurrection there is no marriage, for the risen are like the angels.

On a Tuesday. When you are puzzled by a question about heaven, remember the two keys: what Scripture says, and how great God’s power is. And name one situation you have quietly decided God will not change. Pray about it this week as one who knows the power of God.

For worship. The power of God is greater than our imagination and his word deeper than our reading. The God who formed the first body from dust will raise his people incorruptible, and bring them not into a continuation of this age but to the wedding of his Son, where every faithful earthly love finds what it was pointing to. Marriage was the sign; the Bridegroom is the substance, and he is coming for his bride.

verseByVerse.quote: And as for the dead being raised, have you not read in the book of Moses, in the passage about the bush, how God spoke to him, saying, 'I am the God of Abraham, and the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob'? He is not God of the dead, but of the living. You are quite wrong."
verseByVerse.commentary:
And as for the dead being raised, have you not read in the book of Moses, in the passage about the bush, how God spoke to him, saying: I am the God of Abraham, and the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob? He is not God of the dead, but of the living. You are quite wrong.

Have you not read in the book of Moses. Now he goes on the attack, and the choice of ground is masterly. He could have quoted Daniel, many of those who sleep in the dust of the earth shall awake (Daniel 12:2), or Isaiah, your dead shall live (Isaiah 26:19). Those texts are decisive, and the Sadducees would have waved them away, because they did not grant full authority to the Prophets. So Jesus answers from the books they did accept. Have you not read is a devastating question to put to men whose profession is reading, and he asks it twice in this chapter (v. 10).

In the passage about the bush. This is how passages were located before chapter and verse numbers were added. The burning bush is Exodus 3, one of the best-known passages in the Bible, which every priest in that delegation knew by heart.

I am the God of Abraham, and the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob. Exodus 3:6. God said this to Moses centuries after the three patriarchs had died. Their bones were in the cave of Machpelah, and everyone knew it. And note the tense: I am, not I was.

He is not God of the dead, but of the living. Jesus’ argument is not a play on grammar. It rests on what a covenant is.
