God had bound himself to Abraham personally, to be God to you and to your offspring after you (Genesis 17:7). If Abraham had simply ceased to exist, God would be describing himself by a relationship with nobody, the God of a memory. If God is still their God, they are still alive to him; Luke adds, for all live to him (Luke 20:38). And his promises to them concerned not only their souls but their bodies, the land, an inheritance. The living God will not leave his friends in the grave.

A deep argument. Jesus grounds the resurrection not in a single proof text but in the character of God and his covenant faithfulness. God is not ashamed to be called their God, for he has prepared for them a city (Hebrews 11:16). He put their names into his own title, permanently, and he is not the God of dust. No wonder Mark alone records the final sentence: You are quite wrong, greatly and utterly mistaken.

The voice from the bush. There is a further wonder. The God who said I am to Moses from the bush is the God whom Jesus calls his Father, and Jesus speaks here not as one more rabbi interpreting the text but as the one who would say, before Abraham was, I am (John 8:58). The promise to Abraham, to be God to you and to your offspring, comes to rest on Abraham’s one true offspring, who is Christ (Galatians 3:16). The patriarchs live to God because God keeps covenant, and he keeps it in his Son, who within the week would go down into death and come up again as the pledge that the God of the living keeps every one of his own.

Do believers who die now go to sleep until the resurrection? No. This passage is one of the clearest answers. Abraham, Isaac and Jacob were alive to God centuries before the resurrection of the body. Believers who die go at once to be with Christ, which is far better (Philippians 1:23; 2 Corinthians 5:8), conscious and at rest in his presence, as the thief on the cross was promised: today you will be with me in paradise (Luke 23:43). Scripture calls death sleep because the body rests and will be woken, not because the soul is unconscious. And there is no purgatory between: the believer’s soul, made perfect in holiness, is received at once into glory, waiting for the redemption of the body at Christ’s return.

More in your Bible than you have found. Take away the thing bigger than the argument. The resurrection is not a late addition, invented between the Testaments or imported by the church. It was lying in the most familiar passage of the books of Moses, in a present-tense verb, and the men who read that passage every year had never seen it. Remember that next time you read a chapter you think you know. He found the resurrection of the dead in I am.

In a sentence. Jesus showed from the burning bush that God is still the God of the long-dead patriarchs, and so they live to him and will be raised, for he is the God of the living.

On a Tuesday. If God is your God, death cannot end your relationship with him. Say it at the graveside of a believer, and say it to yourself on the hardest day: he is my God, and he is the God of the living. Then read a familiar passage slowly this week, looking for what you have missed.

For worship. The Lord spoke from a bush that burned and was not consumed, over patriarchs who had been dust for centuries, and he said, I am their God. He has bound himself to his people with a covenant death cannot break, and put their names into his own. No believer will ever be to him a memory or a name on a stone. He is the God of the living, who brought again from the dead our Lord Jesus, the great shepherd of the sheep, and he will not leave one of his flock in the ground.
verseByVerse.note: “The passage about the bush” is how a passage was located before chapter and verse numbers existed. Jesus answers from the books of Moses, which the Sadducees accepted.

parallels.desc: the God of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 28–44 — The Great Commandment, David’s Lord, and the Widow
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The one honest question (vv. 28–34). After a day of traps, a scribe asks something he actually wants to know — which commandment is the most important. He gets the Shema and Leviticus 19, agrees warmly, and is told he is not far from the kingdom of God. And after that, nobody dares ask anything at all.

The question he asks them (vv. 35–37). So Jesus asks one instead, and it is the deepest thing he says in public. If the Christ is David's son, why does David call him Lord?

The warning (vv. 38–40). Then a warning about the men in the long robes who love the greetings and the best seats, say long prayers for show, and devour widows' houses.

The widow (vv. 41–44). And he goes and sits down opposite the treasury and watches people give — and the last thing he does in this temple before he leaves it forever is point out a woman putting in two of the smallest coins in circulation.

Mark has put her immediately after devour widows' houses, and that is not an accident.
verseByVerse.theology:
Psalm 110 and the deepest disclosure in the Gospel. Jesus takes the most quoted psalm in the New Testament and asks a question nobody could answer.

Everyone agreed the Christ would be David's son — the promise ran through the whole Old Testament (2 Sam. 7:12–16; Isa. 11:1). And in Psalm 110, David writes: The LORD says to my Lord: "Sit at my right hand. The first LORD is God; the second is somebody David calls my Lord.

In that culture the point is unanswerable. Honour ran upward from son to father, never downward. A man does not call his own descendant his lord.

So: how can the Christ be David's son and David's Lord at once? Mark records no answer, and the crowd hears him gladly, and nobody says a word.

The answer is that both are true, and it takes the whole New Testament to say it. Concerning his Son, who was descended from David according to the flesh and was declared to be the Son of God in power according to the Spirit of holiness by his resurrection (Rom. 1:3–4). David's son by birth; David's Lord from eternity.

And notice which verse of the psalm he quotes: sit at my right hand, until I put your enemies under your feet. He asks this in the temple, on the Tuesday, surrounded by the men who will have him killed on the Friday. They are the enemies in the sentence, and he quotes it to their faces.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: You are not far from the kingdom of God.

The scribe has answered magnificently. He has the doctrine of God right, the summary of the law right, and the priorities right — he even says out loud, as a temple professional, that love of God and neighbour outweighs the whole sacrificial system, which is a remarkable thing for such a man to concede.

And Jesus does not say you are in. He says not far.

Now: that is the most uncomfortable commendation in the Gospel, because not far is still outside, and it is the address of a great many people who have been in church all their lives.

The gap between near and in is not a gap in knowledge. This man's theology was better than the Twelve's. The gap is a Person. He was standing three feet away, and the question was never whether the scribe could give the right answer about the law but whether he would follow the man who was about to keep it for him.

So it is worth asking plainly: could you give the right answers, and never have come? Right doctrine is the beginning and it is not the destination. Being able to describe a door is not the same as walking through it — and Mark never tells us whether this man did.

verseByVerse.quote: And one of the scribes came up and heard them disputing with one another, and seeing that he answered them well, asked him, "Which commandment is the most important of all?" Jesus answered, "The most important is, 'Hear, O Israel: The Lord our God, the Lord is one. And you shall love the Lord your God with all your heart and with all your soul and with all your mind and with all your strength.' The second is this: 'You shall love your neighbor as yourself.' There is no other commandment greater than these."
verseByVerse.commentary:
One of the scribes came up and heard them disputing. Seeing that Jesus answered them well, he asked him: which commandment is the most important of all? Jesus answered: the most important is, Hear, O Israel: the Lord our God, the Lord is one. And you shall love the Lord your God with all your heart and with all your soul and with all your mind and with all your strength. The second is this: you shall love your neighbour as yourself. There is no other commandment greater than these.

And one of the scribes came up. At last, somebody honest. A different kind of questioner: he has been listening, he is impressed, not hostile, and he asks because he wants to know. Matthew’s version has a harder edge and suggests it was still a test (Matthew 22:35), but Mark shows his sincerity (v. 34). Perhaps he was a man whose motives improved as the conversation went on. That happens.

Which commandment is the most important of all? A live question, not an idle one. The rabbis counted 613 commandments in the law: 248 positive and 365 negative. They debated which were heavy and which light, and whether one could summarise the whole. Rabbi Hillel, a generation earlier, had said: What is hateful to you, do not do to your neighbour; that is the whole law, the rest is commentary.

Hear, O Israel: The Lord our God, the Lord is one. Deuteronomy 6:4, the Shema (Hebrew for hear), recited twice daily by devout Jews and written on the doorposts of the house. Only Mark includes it, and Jesus begins one line earlier than he needed to: asked for a commandment, he starts with a statement of fact. He does not begin with what you must do, but with who God is. There is one God, and only one, not a department of life alongside others; and so he alone is to be loved with everything. A rival would deserve a share. He has none. Christians confess the same one God, as Father, Son and Holy Spirit (1 Corinthians 8:6).

And you shall love the Lord your God. Deuteronomy 6:5. Love here (agapēseis) is not mainly a feeling but a commitment of the whole person, shown in loyalty and obedience: if you love me, you will keep my commandments (John 14:15).

With all your heart and with all your soul and with all your mind and with all your strength. Deuteronomy has heart, soul and might; Jesus adds mind. The four are not separate parts but the whole person, from every angle, and the point of listing them is to leave nothing out. Heart: in Hebrew thought, the control room, what you decide, want and are committed to. Soul: the life itself. Mind: God is to be loved with the intellect, and lazy thinking about him is not humility. Strength: the body, the energy, the money, the hours. Which makes it concrete rather than mystical. Loving God with your strength is a question about your diary and your bank statement. Loving him with your mind is a question about whether you have ever taken the trouble to understand what you believe. Nothing held back.

The second is this: You shall love your neighbor as yourself. Leviticus 19:18. Jesus was asked for one commandment and gave two, and the second flows from the first: whoever says I love God and hates his brother is a liar (1 John 4:20–21). He lifts it from a chapter full of instructions about wages, harvests, the deaf, the blind and honest scales. As yourself is not a command to love yourself first but an assumption that you already do. You know how attentively you consider your own comfort, reputation and future. That much, to him. There is no other commandment greater than these: all the others hang on them (Matthew 22:40), and love is the fulfilling of the law (Romans 13:8–10).

Heart, soul, mind and strength, on a cross. Within three days the man who recited this would fulfil it in a single act. With all his heart he said in the garden, not what I will, but what you will. With all his soul he poured it out to death. With all his mind he held to Scripture to the last, praying a psalm on the cross. With all his strength he carried the beam until another had to carry it for him. And in the same act he loved his neighbour, not merely as himself but above himself, bearing the sins of the people who put him there. The greatest commandment has the shape of the cross.

Who is my neighbour? Jesus answered that question with the parable of the Good Samaritan (Luke 10:29–37): your neighbour is anyone in need whom God puts in your path, including the stranger and the enemy. Begin with those nearest: your family, your church, the people next door and at work. Then widen it to the person who is different from you, the one who cannot repay you, and the one who has wronged you. Loving your neighbour is not first a feeling but a practice: patience, honesty, help, hospitality, forgiveness and the gospel itself.

What it does not mean. Not that we can be saved by loving God and neighbour. No one has ever kept these two commandments fully, except Jesus; nobody has kept the first for a single hour. They expose our need (Romans 3:20). In Christ, forgiven, we begin to keep them by the Spirit (Romans 8:4).

In a sentence. Asked for the greatest commandment, Jesus gave the Shema’s command to love the one God with your whole being, and joined to it the command to love your neighbour as yourself.

On a Tuesday. Pray through the four: Lord, I love you with my heart, my soul, my mind, my strength. Where is my love for you incomplete? Then choose one neighbour and one concrete act of love for them before the week is out.

For worship. The Lord our God, the Lord is one, and there is no rival to share our love with him, because there is no one like him. He is worthy of every beat of the heart and every hour of strength, and he has given himself to us more wholly than we were ever asked to give ourselves to him. The love he commands he first poured out in his Son, and by his Spirit he is writing it now on hearts that were once stone.
verseByVerse.note: “Hear, O Israel” (the Shema) was recited daily by devout Jews.

verseByVerse.quote: And the scribe said to him, "You are right, Teacher. You have truly said that he is one, and there is no other besides him. And to love him with all the heart and with all the understanding and with all the strength, and to love one's neighbor as oneself, is much more than all whole burnt offerings and sacrifices." And when Jesus saw that he answered wisely, he said to him, "You are not far from the kingdom of God." And after that no one dared to ask him any more questions.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The scribe said to him: you are right, Teacher. You have truly said that he is one, and there is no other besides him; and to love him with all the heart, with all the understanding and with all the strength, and to love one’s neighbour as oneself, is much more than all whole burnt offerings and sacrifices. When Jesus saw that he answered wisely, he said to him: you are not far from the kingdom of God. And after that no one dared to ask him any more questions.

You are right, Teacher. Only Mark records the scribe’s response. A scribe agrees with Jesus, warmly, and repeats the answer back in his own words, which is what a man does when something has gone in. And there is no other besides him is his own phrase, from Deuteronomy 4:35 and Isaiah 45:21. He is not parroting. He is thinking.

Is much more than all whole burnt offerings and sacrifices. Now stop, because of who is speaking and where he is standing. This is a scribe, in the temple courts, during Passover week, with the smoke of the altar going up near by and the whole machinery of sacrifice running around him, and he says that loving God and neighbour matters more than all of it. He echoes the prophets: to obey is better than sacrifice (1 Samuel 15:22); I desire steadfast love and not sacrifice (Hosea 6:6; Micah 6:6–8). He has understood what the chief priests had not. The temple’s sacrifices, without love, were empty, like the leaves of the fig tree (11:13). He has read his Bible and believed it, and he is honest enough to say so in the one place where saying it costs something.

Does this mean sacrifice did not matter? No. God commanded the sacrifices, and they pointed to the one sacrifice of Christ, which does what love alone could not: it takes away sin (Hebrews 10:1–14). What the prophets and this scribe condemned was sacrifice without love, ritual offered by people who did not love God or their neighbour. The same is true of our worship. Attendance, singing, giving and the Lord’s Supper are good gifts, but God is not pleased by them from a heart that is cold toward him and hard toward others.

You are not far from the kingdom of God. Jesus saw that he answered wisely (nounechōs, thoughtfully), and said one of the most searching sentences in the Gospel. It is genuine praise. The man has the doctrine of God, the summary of the law and the priorities right, and he is told so. And not far is still outside. Near the kingdom is not in the kingdom, and there is no other category. He is closer than anyone else in this chapter, and he is on the wrong side of a line.

What did he lack? Not information; he knew more than most of the Twelve. He needed to see that he could not keep these commandments, and to recognise and follow the one who was speaking to him, the King. The gap is a Person, and he is three feet away. The whole chapter has been asking who Jesus is: the beloved son in the vineyard, the rejected stone, David’s Lord. Understanding the law is not the same as entering the kingdom. A person can be very close and still outside. Mark never tells us what he did. The account simply stops, and the man walks out of the Gospel one step from home.

Could I be not far but not in? Yes, and the question should be asked plainly. A person can hold sound doctrine, love a good sermon, defend the faith competently, grow up in a Christian home, and be near. Being able to describe a door is not the same as walking through it. The test is not what you know but whether you have come to Christ: turned from your sin, trusted him alone for forgiveness, and given yourself to follow him. If you are not sure, do not stay in the doorway. Come to him today; he has promised not to cast out anyone who comes.

And after that no one dared to ask him any more questions. Jesus has answered every challenge. Three parties have tried and all three have been dismantled. His opponents are silenced, and the silence is the verdict.

In a sentence. The scribe agreed that love for God and neighbour is greater than all sacrifices, and Jesus told him he was not far from the kingdom of God.

On a Tuesday. Being close is not enough. If you understand the gospel but have not come to Christ, don’t stay not far. Come in. And if you have come, pray this week for someone you know who is near but not yet in.

For worship. The Lord saw a man answer wisely and was glad, and spoke to him kindly. He loves to draw the near ones in. The kingdom is not far from any of us, because the King has come close, close enough to be spoken to in the temple, close enough to be nailed to a cross. The door is open, and he is the door.

parallels.desc: to obey is better than sacrifice

verseByVerse.quote: And as Jesus taught in the temple, he said, "How can the scribes say that the Christ is the son of David? David himself, in the Holy Spirit, declared, 'The Lord said to my Lord, "Sit at my right hand, until I put your enemies under your feet."' David himself calls him Lord. So how is he his son?" And the great throng heard him gladly.
verseByVerse.commentary:
As Jesus taught in the temple, he said: how can the scribes say that the Christ is the son of David? David himself, in the Holy Spirit, declared: The Lord said to my Lord, sit at my right hand, until I put your enemies under your feet. David himself calls him Lord. So how is he his son? And the great crowd heard him gladly.

How can the scribes say that the Christ is the son of David? Nobody dares ask him anything more, so now he asks the decisive question. The scribes were right to say it (2 Samuel 7:12–16; Isaiah 11:1; Jeremiah 23:5), and it is not an attack on the doctrine. Bartimaeus had called Jesus Son of David and been commended (10:47–48), and the crowds had hailed the kingdom of David (11:10). But is that all the Messiah is, a new king like David? Jesus is asking whether it is the whole of it.

David himself, in the Holy Spirit, declared. Before the quotation, notice the doctrine of Scripture packed into the phrase. David himself: so the psalm is his. In the Holy Spirit: so it is also God’s. Two authors, one text, and no tension between them. Jesus affirms that David wrote Psalm 110, and that he wrote it inspired by the Spirit. Scripture is God’s word through human authors (2 Peter 1:21). That is how Jesus read his Bible.

The Lord said to my Lord, Sit at my right hand. Psalm 110:1, the Old Testament verse most often quoted or alluded to in the New. In Hebrew the first Lord is the divine name, printed LORD in small capitals; the second is adoni, my master, a title of superior rank. God speaks to someone David calls his master, and seats him at his right hand, the place of supreme honour, sharing God’s throne.

Until I put your enemies under your feet. Victory over every enemy. Conquered kings had the victor’s foot placed on their necks (Joshua 10:24). And notice which line he chose. He is standing in the temple, surrounded by men who have already resolved to kill him, and he quotes to their faces a promise about what God will do with the enemies of his Christ.

David himself calls him Lord. So how is he his son? The puzzle, and in that culture the difficulty is total. Honour flowed upward: a son honoured his father, a descendant his ancestor, never the reverse. Abraham does not call Isaac my lord. Yet the greatest king Israel ever had looks down the centuries at his own descendant and calls him Master. If David calls the Messiah my Lord, the Messiah must be greater than David. How can he be both David’s descendant and David’s Lord? Mark records no answer. Nobody had one.

The answer Jesus leaves them to find. He is the Son of David by human birth, and the Son of God, David’s Lord, by nature: concerning his Son, who was descended from David according to the flesh and was declared to be the Son of God in power by his resurrection from the dead (Romans 1:3–4). Both human and divine. The one who came from David’s line existed before David did, which is why he can say, before Abraham was, I am (John 8:58). This is the deepest thing Jesus discloses about himself in public in this Gospel, and he does it as a riddle, days before the cross, because a claim like that stated flatly in the temple would end the week early. At his trial he will apply Psalm 110 to himself directly (14:62).

Why must the Saviour be both David’s son and David’s Lord? Because only such a Saviour could save us. As David’s son, a real man, he could stand in our place, obey the law we broke, and die the death we deserved. As David’s Lord, God the Son, his obedience and death have infinite worth, enough to pay for a multitude, and death could not hold him. A merely human Messiah could be admired but not trusted with our souls; a God who never became man could not die for us. The Lord who is David’s son is the one Mediator between God and men (1 Timothy 2:5), and he reigns now at the Father’s right hand.

And the great throng heard him gladly. The professionals have gone silent; the ordinary people are delighted to see the experts outmatched. It is the last note of his public teaching in this Gospel, and within days the same city will be shouting for his execution.

In a sentence. Quoting Psalm 110, Jesus showed that the Messiah is more than David’s son, since David calls him Lord, pointing to his own divine identity.

On a Tuesday. When you pray to Jesus today, remember who he is: not only the man of Galilee but David’s Lord, seated at the right hand of God. Bring him the enemies you face, sin, fear, death, knowing that every one of them will be put under his feet.

For worship. The child laid in a manger in David’s town is the Lord to whom David bowed a thousand years before he was born. The hands that were nailed to a cross hold the sceptre at the Father’s right hand, and every enemy that rose against him in that temple will lie beneath his feet. The last enemy to be destroyed is death, and the Lord of David has already walked out of its house.
verseByVerse.note: Psalm 110:1 is among the Old Testament verses most often quoted in the New.

verseByVerse.quote: And in his teaching he said, "Beware of the scribes, who like to walk around in long robes and like greetings in the marketplaces and have the best seats in the synagogues and the places of honor at feasts, who devour widows' houses and for a pretense make long prayers. They will receive the greater condemnation."
verseByVerse.commentary:
In his teaching he said: beware of the scribes, who like to walk around in long robes and like greetings in the marketplaces and have the best seats in the synagogues and the places of honour at feasts, who devour widows’ houses and for a pretence make long prayers. They will receive the greater condemnation.

Beware of the scribes. Not every scribe; one had just been commended (v. 34). This is not a blanket condemnation of a profession. It is a warning about what religious office does to a man who lets it, and the pattern was common enough to be a danger. And it is spoken publicly, to the crowd, about the most respected class in the community. Beware means watch out, keep your eyes open. He is telling ordinary people to be alert to their own religious leaders.

Who like to walk around in long robes. Long, white linen robes, sometimes reaching to the ground, marked out men of learning and rank. Note the verb: they like to walk around in them. It is not the robe that is condemned but the strolling, the enjoyment of being seen in a garment that says what you are. The problem is the love of display.

And like greetings in the marketplaces and have the best seats in the synagogues and the places of honor at feasts. Respectful public greetings with titles, Rabbi, master; people stood when a scribe passed. In the synagogue, the bench at the front facing the congregation, where everyone could see them; at feasts, the seats nearest the host. Their religion has become a means to status.

The appetite for honour. Read the four together and a portrait emerges, and it is not at first of a wicked man. It is of a man who has come to need the deference. None of these things is a sin in itself; a robe is a robe and a seat is a seat. What is described is an appetite, the quiet, constant, unadmitted pleasure of being thought well of, which grows so slowly that nobody notices it arriving. And it is entirely available now, without a robe: in whose name gets mentioned, who is asked to pray, who is consulted, who is thanked from the front.

Who devour widows’ houses. Now the charge turns from vanity to something far worse. Widows were the most vulnerable people in Israel, without a husband’s protection, and God commanded special care for them (Exodus 22:22–24; Deuteronomy 10:18; Isaiah 1:17). Scribes were not supposed to be paid for teaching, and relied on gifts. Some apparently exploited widows’ generosity, or charged them for legal advice, or managed their estates as trustees and took advantage, eating up their property. A religious profession was being used to strip the assets of the most defenceless people in the land.

And for a pretense make long prayers. Long, public prayers that make them look holy while they cheat the vulnerable: the hypocrisy of Isaiah 29:13 again (7:6). And the two halves belong together, which is the horror of it. The long prayer is not incidental to the exploitation; it is the instrument of it. It is what persuades the widow that her money is safe with such a man.

They will receive the greater condemnation. Greater because they knew the law better than anyone (James 3:1; Luke 12:47–48), and because they used religion to cover their sins. To use the name of God as the tool of a fraud is worse than the fraud. There are degrees of punishment in hell, according to knowledge and privilege.

Robes, greetings and seats, reversed. Every mark of honour the scribes loved, Jesus would receive in mockery within the week. They loved long robes; soldiers would dress him in purple, then strip him and gamble for his clothes (15:17, 20, 24). They loved greetings in the marketplace; he would be greeted with Hail, King of the Jews, and spat on (15:18–19). They loved the places of honour; his place would be between two robbers (15:27). They prayed long for show; he prayed in the dust of a garden, unseen. And where they devoured widows’ houses, he, dying, provided for his own widowed mother (John 19:26–27). The true Teacher took the lowest seat.

How should a church protect the vulnerable from its own leaders? By taking this warning seriously rather than assuming it applies only to others. Leaders should be accountable to other elders, with no one beyond question. Money should be handled openly, by more than one person, with proper records. No one should be pressed to give, sign over property or trust a leader with their affairs under spiritual pressure. Widows, the elderly, the disabled and the lonely should be cared for by the whole church, not left to one person’s influence. And when a leader is found exploiting or abusing anyone, it must be dealt with openly and firmly, reported where the law requires, and never covered to protect a ministry.

In a sentence. Jesus warned against scribes who love religious status, exploit widows and pray long prayers for show, for they will receive greater judgment.

On a Tuesday. Watch your own heart for the love of being seen and honoured, especially if you lead in church. God judges teachers more strictly. Ask yourself honestly what you enjoy most about any role you hold, and whether you would serve as gladly if no one noticed.

For worship. The Lord who exposed the scribes is the defender of widows, a father to the fatherless and protector of the helpless in his holy habitation. He sees through every long prayer to the heart that prays it, and not one coin taken from the poor is forgotten by him. The great High Priest wears no robe for display; he laid his glory aside, and he still bends down to the people the powerful step over.
verseByVerse.note: Long robes marked out men of learning and rank.

verseByVerse.quote: And he sat down opposite the treasury and watched the people putting money into the offering box. Many rich people put in large sums. And a poor widow came and put in two small copper coins, which make a penny.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus sat down opposite the treasury and watched the people putting money into the offering box. Many rich people put in large sums. A poor widow came and put in two small copper coins, which make a penny.

The contrast. Straight after the scribes who devour widows’ houses comes a widow, perhaps one of their victims. Mark has laid the two side by side deliberately. And this is Jesus’ last scene in the temple, his last public teaching in Mark. He is finished with the arguments.

And he sat down opposite the treasury. He crosses the court, sits down, and watches, directly opposite. The treasury was probably in the Court of the Women, so called because women could go that far and no further. There were thirteen trumpet-shaped collection chests there, each marked for a different purpose. Silver rattling down a bronze trumpet made a noise, and a great many coins made a great deal of noise. Giving in that court was audible.

And watched. Jesus watches how people give. He sat and watched, deliberately, for some time, on the last day he ever taught in that building. Not the accounts, not the total: he watched the people, their faces and hands. It is the plainest statement in the Bible that Christ watches giving. He still does. There is no anonymous giving; there is only giving that other people cannot see.

Many rich people put in large sums. Perhaps noisily: coins thrown into the trumpet-shaped chests would rattle. Jesus does not condemn them, and neither should we. These were large gifts, genuinely given, to the house of God, and the temple was maintained by them. Nothing here says they were hypocrites. But they were audible.

Two small copper coins, which make a penny. She is a poor widow (ptōchē, a beggar’s poverty), two verses after who devour widows’ houses, which is no coincidence. The lepton (literally thin one) was the smallest coin in circulation, about 1/128 of a denarius, a day’s wage. Mark translates it for his readers in Rome: two lepta made a quadrans, the smallest Roman coin. He wants them to feel how little it was. Into a bronze trumpet, it would have made almost no sound at all.

She gave both. Note that there were two. That detail is the quiet devastation of the story. She could have kept one. Nobody would have known, nobody would have blamed her, and half of nearly nothing is still something to a woman with no income. She had the one choice available to a person with two coins, and she gave both.

Does Jesus really see what I give? Yes. He sees the amount, and he sees what it costs, and he sees the heart. That should humble anyone who gives for show, and it should comfort anyone who gives quietly and little. Many Christians keep their giving secret, rightly (Matthew 6:3–4). It is not secret from him. He knows the gift you made when you could barely afford it, and the one you held back when you could easily have given. Give to him, not to the people who might notice.

In a sentence. Sitting opposite the temple treasury, Jesus watched the rich put in large sums and a poor widow put in two tiny coins.

On a Tuesday. Jesus sees what you give, and how. Give as one who knows he is watching. Before you next give to your church or to the poor, pause and give it consciously to him.

For worship. The Lord of heaven sat in the temple court and watched an old woman drop two coins into a box, and he cared. Nothing done for him escapes his eyes, and nothing small is small to him. The God who numbers the stars counts the widow’s mites.
verseByVerse.note: The treasury was probably in the Court of the Women, with collection chests for offerings. Her two coins were the smallest in circulation, a tiny fraction of a day’s wage.

verseByVerse.quote: And he called his disciples to him and said to them, "Truly, I say to you, this poor widow has put in more than all those who are contributing to the offering box. For they all contributed out of their abundance, but she out of her poverty has put in everything she had, all she had to live on."
verseByVerse.commentary:
He called his disciples and said to them: truly, I tell you, this poor widow has put in more than all those who are contributing to the offering box. For they all contributed out of their abundance, but she out of her poverty has put in everything she had, all she had to live on.

And he called his disciples to him. He gathers them round, which he does when something matters. They have been looking elsewhere, at the rich, or at the buildings; within minutes one of them will say, look, Teacher, what wonderful stones (13:1). He calls them over to look at a woman with two of the smallest coins in the empire. This is a lesson for them, and for every disciple.

This poor widow has put in more than all those who are contributing. The amen-formula, for something that must not be missed, and then a statement that is false by every measure the treasury could apply. She put in a fraction of a penny; they put in large sums. He is using a different set of scales. God measures gifts not by the amount but by the cost, and by the heart. They all contributed out of their abundance: real gifts, honestly given, and nothing in their lives changed on the way home.

But she out of her poverty has put in everything she had, all she had to live on. Literally her whole life (holon ton bion autēs). She put her life in the box. She gave everything and kept nothing, trusting God to provide her next meal. This is the giving of total trust. And the kingdom’s arithmetic cuts both ways. No one can buy standing with God by the size of a gift; the largest cheque in the country is small change if it costs the giver nothing. And the gift you are embarrassed by, the small amount from a pension, the hour given by someone with almost no hours, is registered by Christ as larger than the endowment.

The wider meaning. She stands in contrast to the rich man who would not give up his possessions (10:22), and to the scribes who devour widows’ houses (v. 40). She has done, in a small way, what the first commandment requires: loved God with all her strength, with all she had (v. 30). And she is a picture of what Jesus is about to do. The Son of Man came to give his life as a ransom for many (10:45), and he is sitting in that court days from the cross, watching a poor woman put in everything she had. The next time Mark mentions an offering of everything, it is the cross.

Where Christians differ: praise or lament? Some argue that Jesus is not praising her but lamenting a temple system that took the last coins of the poor, continuing his condemnation of the scribes. Verdict: there is truth in that context, as the scribes who devour widows’ houses stand just before her, and Jesus will predict the temple’s destruction next (13:2). But his words are clearly commendation: she put in more than all. He honours her faith and devotion, whatever the corruption of those who received it. She did not give to a system; she gave to God, in the only way available to her, and he saw it and said so out loud. Because he did, a woman whose name nobody recorded is known to every Christian on earth.

What it does not mean. Not that every Christian must give away everything they have, or that the amount of giving does not matter. But it shows that God values sacrificial, trusting giving, and that no gift is too small if it is given wholeheartedly.

Should the poor give everything they have? Jesus commends her heart; he does not command the poor to give away their living. Paul says a gift is acceptable according to what a person has, not according to what he does not have (2 Corinthians 8:12), and that a believer must provide for his own household (1 Timothy 5:8). And this passage stands immediately after Jesus’ warning against those who devour widows’ houses (v. 40): no church or ministry may press the poor to give beyond their means. A church should be giving to its widows, not taking their last coins.

How much should I give? The New Testament sets no fixed percentage, but it sets a pattern: give regularly, in proportion to what God has given you (1 Corinthians 16:2), generously, cheerfully and not under compulsion (2 Corinthians 9:6–7), and sacrificially, so that it costs you something. Many Christians take the Old Testament tithe as a sensible starting place and go beyond it as God prospers them. Give first to your local church, which feeds you with the word, and then to the poor and the spread of the gospel. Ask not how little you can give, but what it would look like to trust God with more.

In a sentence. Jesus told his disciples that the widow had given more than all the rich, because they gave from their surplus, and she gave everything she had to live on.

On a Tuesday. Does your giving cost you anything? Give as an act of worship and trust, not leftovers. Look at your giving this month, and decide on one step that would need faith.

For worship. She put in her whole life, and three days later he put in his. The widow gave all she had to live on into the hands of God, and the Son gave all he was into the hands of sinners, to ransom them. He was rich and became poor for us. Then he got up, walked out of the temple, and never went back, because the true offering was about to be made, once for all, outside the city wall.

12.theology:
Render to Caesar cuts in two directions and both must be held. It establishes a real obligation — the coin bears his image, so give it to him, and Paul says the same (Rom. 13:1–7; 1 Pet. 2:13–17). Christianity is not anarchy. And it bounds that obligation absolutely: Caesar may claim the coin, but what bears God's image belongs to God, and man bears it (Gen. 1:27). So the same verse that tells you to pay the tax tells you where obedience stops. We must obey God rather than men (Acts 5:29) was said to this same council. The martyrs paid every tax Rome levied and would not drop the pinch of incense that called Caesar Lord.

The Sadducees and the ground he chose. They were the priestly aristocracy who accepted only the five books of Moses and denied resurrection, angels and spirits alike (Acts 23:8). So Jesus does not quote Daniel 12:2 or Isaiah 26:19; they would have waved those away. He goes into the Torah, into the burning bush every priest knew by heart, and finds the resurrection in two words: I am the God of Abraham — spoken centuries after Abraham died. A covenant of that kind cannot be ended by the death of one party without God's own word failing. He wins the argument inside the fence they built themselves.

David's son and David's Lord. In Psalm 110:1 the first LORD is the divine name and the second is my lord, a title of superior rank. In that culture honour ran upward only; no man called his own descendant his master. So how is the Christ both? Mark records no answer, and the whole New Testament is the answer: descended from David according to the flesh and was declared to be the Son of God in power... by his resurrection from the dead (Rom. 1:3–4). David's son by birth; David's Lord from eternity. And note the line he quotes — until I put your enemies under your feet — spoken in the temple to the men who would kill him on Friday.
12.examples:
Then: two lepta, the thinnest coins in circulation, dropped into a bronze trumpet-mouthed chest that made almost no sound.

And the detail that undoes you is that there were two. She could have kept one. Nobody would have known and nobody would have blamed her, and half of nearly nothing is still something to a woman with no income. She had the one choice available to a person with two coins, and she gave both.

Now: the measure is not the amount but what is left afterwards. The rich gave real gifts, honestly, and nothing in their lives changed on the way home. She gave and had nothing — all she had to live on.

That cuts both ways. No one buys standing with God by the size of a gift; the largest cheque in the country is small change if it costs the giver nothing. And the gift you are embarrassed by — the small amount from a pension, an hour from someone who has almost no hours — is registered by Christ as larger than the endowment.

Is he commending her or lamenting her? Both, and the passage is stronger for holding them together. He has just denounced the men who devour widows' houses, two verses earlier, and the building her money maintains has forty years left. He does not commend the machinery for taking it. And he commends her without a single qualification — she gave to God in the only way available to her, and because he said so out loud, a woman whose name nobody recorded is known to every Christian on earth.

And note where he was sitting. The Son of Man came to give his life as a ransom for many (10:45), and he spent one of his last hours in that temple watching a woman put in everything she had to live on. She is the only other person in the story who does what he is about to do on Friday.

13.title: Stay Awake
13.text: <sup>1</sup>And as he came out of the temple, one of his disciples said to him, “Look, Teacher, what wonderful stones and what wonderful buildings!” <sup>2</sup>And Jesus said to him, “Do you see these great buildings? There will not be left here one stone upon another that will not be thrown down.” <sup>3</sup>And as he sat on the Mount of Olives opposite the temple, Peter and James and John and Andrew asked him privately, <sup>4</sup>“Tell us, when will these things be, and what will be the sign when all these things are about to be accomplished?” <sup>5</sup>And Jesus began to say to them, “See that no one leads you astray. <sup>6</sup>Many will come in my name, saying, ‘I am he!’ and they will lead many astray. <sup>7</sup>And when you hear of wars and rumors of wars, do not be alarmed. This must take place, but the end is not yet. <sup>8</sup>For nation will rise against nation, and kingdom against kingdom. There will be earthquakes in various places; there will be famines. These are but the beginning of the birth pains. <sup>9</sup>But be on your guard. For they will deliver you over to councils, and you will be beaten in synagogues, and you will stand before governors and kings for my sake, to bear witness before them. <sup>10</sup>And the gospel must first be proclaimed to all nations. <sup>11</sup>And when they bring you to trial and deliver you over, do not be anxious beforehand what you are to say, but say whatever is given you in that hour, for it is not you who speak, but the Holy Spirit. <sup>12</sup>And brother will deliver brother over to death, and the father his child, and children will rise against parents and have them put to death. <sup>13</sup>And you will be hated by all for my name’s sake. But the one who endures to the end will be saved. <sup>14</sup>But when you see the abomination of desolation standing where he ought not to be (let the reader understand), then let those who are in Judea flee to the mountains. <sup>15</sup>Let the one who is on the housetop not go down, nor enter his house, to take anything out, <sup>16</sup>and let the one who is in the field not turn back to take his cloak. <sup>17</sup>And alas for women who are pregnant and for those who are nursing infants in those days! <sup>18</sup>Pray that it may not happen in winter. <sup>19</sup>For in those days there will be such tribulation as has not been from the beginning of the creation that God created until now, and never will be. <sup>20</sup>And if the Lord had not cut short the days, no human being would be saved. But for the sake of the elect, whom he chose, he shortened the days. <sup>21</sup>And then if anyone says to you, ‘Look, here is the Christ!’ or ‘Look, there he is!’ do not believe it. <sup>22</sup>For false christs and false prophets will arise and perform signs and wonders, to lead astray, if possible, the elect. <sup>23</sup>But be on guard; I have told you all things beforehand. <sup>24</sup>But in those days, after that tribulation, the sun will be darkened, and the moon will not give its light, <sup>25</sup>and the stars will be falling from heaven, and the powers in the heavens will be shaken. <sup>26</sup>And then they will see the Son of Man coming in clouds with great power and glory. <sup>27</sup>And then he will send out the angels and gather his elect from the four winds, from the ends of the earth to the ends of heaven. <sup>28</sup>“From the fig tree learn its lesson: as soon as its branch becomes tender and puts out its leaves, you know that summer is near. <sup>29</sup>So also, when you see these things taking place, you know that he is near, at the very gates. <sup>30</sup>Truly, I say to you, this generation will not pass away until all these things take place. <sup>31</sup>Heaven and earth will pass away, but my words will not pass away. <sup>32</sup>“But concerning that day or that hour, no one knows, not even the angels in heaven, nor the Son, but only the Father. <sup>33</sup>Be on guard, keep awake. For you do not know when the time will come. <sup>34</sup>It is like a man going on a journey, when he leaves home and puts his servants in charge, each with his work, and commands the doorkeeper to stay awake. <sup>35</sup>Therefore stay awake—for you do not know when the master of the house will come, in the evening, or at midnight, or when the rooster crows, or in the morning— <sup>36</sup>lest he come suddenly and find you asleep. <sup>37</sup>And what I say to you I say to all: Stay awake.”
13.overview:
They come out of the temple and a disciple points at the stonework — and he was right to. Herod's platform covers thirty-five acres; the largest block still visible weighs several hundred tons; Josephus says the gold front was too bright to look at in the morning sun. Building had been going on for some forty-six years when Jesus first spoke of it (John 2:20), and it was not finished until AD 63.

Jesus says not one stone will be left on another, and seven years after the last workman went home it was gone.

Four disciples take him aside on the Mount of Olives, looking straight across at the building, and ask when and how they will know. What follows is the longest teaching in Mark before the passion, and its most striking feature is what it refuses to give. He describes signs and then says they do not mean what people will say they mean — the end is not yet. He describes the fall of Jerusalem in detail, and the flight, and the unequalled distress, and sets it inside a generation. And then, at v. 32, the discourse turns a corner: of his own coming there is no sign, no timetable, and no one knows the day — not the angels, not even the Son.

What is left, four times over, is a command. Stay awake — which the parable at the end defines not as scanning the horizon but as being found at your post, doing the work you were left. And in the next two chapters Mark walks his reader through all four watches of the night, and the disciples fail at every one.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–23 — Signs, Perseverance, and the Abomination
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The stones (vv. 1–4). They come out of the temple and a disciple points at the masonry, and Jesus says that not one of those stones will be left standing on another. Four of them come to him privately on the Mount of Olives, looking straight across at the building, and ask when.

The age (vv. 5–13). His answer begins by taking away the thing they wanted. Deceivers will come; wars will come; earthquakes and famines will come — and none of it means what people will say it means. The end is not yet. The church will be beaten in synagogues and hauled before governors, betrayed by brothers and fathers and children, hated by everyone. And in the middle of the list, one line that is not a disaster at all: the gospel must first be proclaimed to all nations.

The crisis (vv. 14–23). Then something specific: an abomination standing where it ought not to be, and instructions so urgent that a man on his roof is not to go downstairs for his belongings. Forty years later, Roman legions came up the valley.

Notice what the discourse never gives them: a date. It gives signs that will be misread, warnings that will be needed, and one command repeated four times — stay awake.
verseByVerse.theology:
Two questions, two answers, one discourse. The key to Mark 13 is that the disciples asked about the temple (v. 4), and Jesus answers about the temple and about his own coming, and the seam between them is visible if you look for it.

Everything down to v. 30 is hedged with signs and set inside a timeframe: false messiahs, wars, the abomination in the holy place, the flight from Judea, unequalled distress — and this generation will not pass away until all these things take place. Every one of those things did happen, in the horror of AD 70, some forty years on. That is why the fig tree can say the season is near, at the very gates.

Then look at the hinge in v. 32: But concerning that day or that hour, no one knows. The but turns a corner. From here Jesus says the opposite of everything before — no sign, no timetable, nobody knows, it arrives like a householder in the night.

So the discourse deliberately holds two comings apart: the near judgement on Jerusalem, marked with signs and dated inside a generation, and the far return of the Son of Man, without sign or date. Read this way — and it is the reading the seams of the text ask for — Jesus was not mistaken by a single day. He said the temple would fall in their lifetime, and it did. He said his own coming would be unmarked and unknown, and it remains so.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: the gospel must first be proclaimed to all nations (v. 10) — one bright, forward-driving line dropped into the middle of a catalogue of disasters.

It is the only item in the list that is not something to be endured but something to be done, and the little word first makes it a milestone: history will not close until the good news has reached every people.

Now: that turns the whole grim catalogue inside out. The wars and betrayals and floggings are not the church waiting helplessly for the end. They are the conditions under which the gospel travels — and often it travels furthest precisely by way of those dragged before governors and kings (v. 9). Paul reached Caesar's household because he was arrested. The persecution is not an interruption of the mission; it is one of its engines.

So the age between the resurrection and the coming has a task, and not merely a fear. Every tribe that hears is the clock of the world moving one turn closer to the dawn — which is why a Christian reading the news is not simply watching the world fall apart. He is watching the field in which the seed is being sown.

verseByVerse.quote: And as he came out of the temple, one of his disciples said to him, "Look, Teacher, what wonderful stones and what wonderful buildings!" And Jesus said to him, "Do you see these great buildings? There will not be left here one stone upon another that will not be thrown down."
verseByVerse.commentary:
As Jesus came out of the temple, one of his disciples said to him: look, Teacher, what wonderful stones and what wonderful buildings! Jesus said to him: do you see these great buildings? There will not be left here one stone upon another that will not be thrown down.

Meaning first. Mark 13 is Jesus’ longest speech in this Gospel, given on a hillside facing the temple he has just declared doomed. The disciples admire the stones; Jesus says not one will be left on another. They ask when, and he answers with warnings rather than a timetable: deceivers, wars and famines that are only the beginning of birth pains, persecution while the gospel goes to all nations, and, when the abomination of desolation stands in the holy place, flight from Judea. All this came upon Jerusalem within that generation, in AD 70. Then he lifts their eyes to the far horizon: the Son of Man coming in clouds with great power and glory to gather his elect. Of that day no one knows but the Father, so the chapter ends with one command for all: stay awake. At its centre stands its comfort: his words will not pass away.

The setting. Chapter 13 is called the Olivet Discourse because it was given on the Mount of Olives (v. 3). The disciples’ question has two parts, the fall of this building and the end of the age, and the discourse gives each its due. It stands between Jesus’ last day of public teaching and the account of his death. He has just watched a widow put her last two coins into the treasury (12:41–44), and now he walks out of the temple for the last time.

And as he came out of the temple. A solemn departure, and Mark’s geography is doing work. In Ezekiel’s vision the glory of God left a defiled temple, paused at the threshold, and went out to the mountain east of the city before Babylon destroyed it (Ezekiel 10:18–19; 11:23). Now the Lord of the temple walks out of it and climbs that same mountain (v. 3). The prophets had said the LORD would suddenly come to his temple (Malachi 3:1). He came, he taught in its courts, he cleansed it, he was rejected in it, and now he leaves it to its fate.

Look, Teacher, what wonderful stones and what wonderful buildings! You cannot blame the man. The disciples were Galileans from the country, and Herod’s temple was one of the wonders of the ancient world. Herod began rebuilding it in 20/19 BC, and the work went on until AD 63, seven years before it was destroyed. The platform covers about thirty-five acres; you can still walk on it. The retaining walls were dressed limestone cut so precisely that they needed no mortar, and the largest block still visible in the Western Wall tunnels weighs several hundred tons. Josephus says that at sunrise the gold-faced sanctuary was too bright to look at, and from a distance the mountain looked like a peak covered with snow. The rabbis said that whoever had not seen Herod’s temple had never seen a beautiful building.

Do you see these great buildings? Not a dismissal. He grants the premise: yes, look at them. Jesus never pretends that human achievement is small. He measures it against eternity.

There will not be left here one stone upon another that will not be thrown down. The Greek doubles its negative (ou mē): this will surely happen. Seven years after the last workman went home, it was gone. In AD 70 the Roman general Titus took Jerusalem after a terrible siege. Josephus, who was there, describes the sanctuary burning; a later tradition adds the gold melting into the joints between the stones and soldiers prising them apart to get at it. Josephus says the city was so levelled that visitors could hardly believe it had ever been inhabited. The fig tree had withered (11:20), and now the temple it pictured follows it.

Why does the Western Wall still stand? Because it is part of the retaining wall Herod built around the temple platform, not part of the temple itself. Jesus spoke of these great buildings, the sanctuary and its courts, and of them not one stone was left on another. The platform survived as a ruin; the house of God on it did not.

Heard as blasphemy. We hear this sentence as history; they heard it as something close to blasphemy. This was not merely a large building. It was the house of God, the place where atonement was made, the centre of the religious life of every Jew on earth, the guarantee of the covenant. To say it would be levelled was to say something no one could hear calmly. Jeremiah nearly died for saying less (Jeremiah 26:8–9), and a twisted version of this very saying will be produced at Jesus’ trial in two days’ time (14:58).

Why did the temple have to fall? Because its work was finished. The temple was the place where a holy God dwelt among a sinful people, and where sacrifice was offered day after day so that they could draw near. All of that pointed to Jesus. He is the true temple, God dwelling with us in the flesh (John 1:14; 2:19–21), and within days his body will be torn down and raised again in three days. When he died, the curtain of the temple was torn from top to bottom (15:38). Once the one sacrifice for sins had been offered for all time (Hebrews 10:12), a building where lambs were slain could only be a denial that he had come. Its destruction was judgment on a city that rejected him, and it was also God clearing the stage of a shadow once the substance had arrived.

Does this mean church buildings do not matter? No. A place set aside for worship is a good gift, and it is right to build it well and care for it. But it is never the house of God in the sense the temple was. The church is the people, the living stones built on Christ (1 Peter 2:4–5), and the Spirit dwells in them (1 Corinthians 3:16). A congregation that loses its building has lost a roof, not God. And a congregation that would rather keep its building than keep the gospel has already lost the thing that mattered.

In a sentence. As his disciples admired the magnificent temple, Jesus predicted its complete destruction, fulfilled when Rome levelled it in AD 70.

On a Tuesday. That disciple was admiring the most permanent-looking thing in his world, the biggest, the most expensive, the most obviously here to stay, and it had forty years left. What survived that generation was not the masonry. It was twelve men, most of them poor, and a message. Everything you can point at and call impressive is on a clock: the company, the reputation, the house, the body. Ask what you are actually building with, because the stones are always the wrong answer, and they always look like the right one. Build your life on what cannot be shaken (Hebrews 12:27–28): the word of Christ, the people of Christ, and treasure laid up where nothing is thrown down.

For worship. The Lord of the temple walked out of it, and did not leave his people homeless. He went from that hillside to a cross, and there his own body was thrown down like the stones, so that God could dwell with sinners for ever without a curtain between. The glory that left Herod’s house came to rest in a crucified and risen man, and in him we have a temple no army can take: one whose foundation is laid in heaven, whose stones are living, and whose light is the Lamb.
verseByVerse.note: Herod the Great had rebuilt the temple on a vast scale, with some stones many yards long. The Romans destroyed it in AD 70.

verseByVerse.quote: And as he sat on the Mount of Olives opposite the temple, Peter and James and John and Andrew asked him privately, "Tell us, when will these things be, and what will be the sign when all these things are about to be accomplished?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
As he sat on the Mount of Olives opposite the temple, Peter, James, John and Andrew asked him privately: tell us, when will these things be, and what will be the sign when all these things are about to be accomplished?

And as he sat on the Mount of Olives opposite the temple. From this ridge across the Kidron valley you look straight down onto the temple platform, the gold catching the light. So the whole discourse is delivered with the building in view: he is telling four men what will happen to what they can see. He sits, the posture of a teacher and of a judge, facing the house he has just condemned. And the place carries prophecy of its own. The glory of the LORD left the temple and stood on this ridge (Ezekiel 11:23), and Zechariah says that on the day of the LORD his feet shall stand on the Mount of Olives (Zechariah 14:4). The glory left the temple and stopped on this hill. And here he sits.

Peter and James and John and Andrew asked him privately. The first four disciples called from their nets (1:16–20), named together again as at the house in Capernaum (1:29). Privately: the great crowd that heard him gladly in the temple (12:37) is gone. This is the last extended teaching in Mark before the passion, given to four men on a hillside who will lead the church through everything it describes.

Tell us, when will these things be? Two questions, and everything about how you read this chapter depends on noticing them. The first asks for a date. And notice what it asks about. Not the end of the world; Mark’s version has no such phrase. These things are the stones. He said the temple would be flattened, and they want to know when.

And what will be the sign when all these things are about to be accomplished? The second asks for a warning, a marker visible in advance. The verb (synteleisthai) means brought to completion, and it suggests that in their minds the fall of the temple and the end of all things belonged together. Matthew makes that explicit: what will be the sign of your coming and of the close of the age? (Matthew 24:3). Jesus’ answer will gently separate the two. The temple will fall within their generation, with signs (v. 30). The end of the age will come at a time no one knows, without them (v. 32).

A question refused in the form it was put. It is exactly what any of us would ask, and the discourse declines to answer it as asked. He will give them signs, and then tell them the signs do not mean what they will be tempted to think. He will give a timeframe for the temple, and then say that of his own coming nobody knows the day or the hour, not even the Son. And he will end with the one thing they actually need: stay awake. The chapter was built to withhold a date, not out of secrecy but out of love. A man who knows the date will prepare on the last afternoon. A man who does not must live ready every day. The refusal is the pastoral care.

Where Christians differ: how to read this chapter. Some (preterists) take the whole discourse as fulfilled in AD 70. Some (futurists, especially dispensationalists) take most of it as describing a future tribulation before a millennium. Others see it as speaking of both, with the near event foreshadowing the far. Verdict: the best reading, held widely in Reformed and amillennial interpretation, is that verses 5–23 speak mainly of the period leading to the fall of Jerusalem in AD 70, which also serves as a pattern of the troubles of the whole church age; verses 24–27 speak of the second coming of Christ at the end of the age; verses 28–31 return to the destruction of the temple within that generation; and verses 32–37 speak of the unknown day of the end. There is no secret rapture here; the gathering of the elect is at Christ’s visible return (v. 27).

What does amillennial mean? It is the name for the view that the thousand years of Revelation 20 is not a future golden age on earth after Christ returns, but a picture of the present age, in which Christ reigns from heaven, Satan is bound so that the gospel goes to the nations, and the souls of believers who die reign with him. On this view there is one future return of Christ, followed at once by the resurrection of all the dead, the last judgment, and the new heavens and new earth. That is how this chapter reads too: one public coming, one gathering of the elect, and no second stage. Many godly Christians hold other views, and this is not a test of fellowship. But it keeps the eyes where Jesus puts them, on his coming rather than on a calendar.

Is it wrong to be curious about the future? No. The disciples asked, and Jesus answered them at length; he did not rebuke the question. God has told us a great deal about the end, and it is meant to be read and treasured. What goes wrong is curiosity that wants control, that treats prophecy as a puzzle for the clever and the end as a date to be extracted. Notice that almost everything Jesus says here is an instruction: do not be led astray, do not be alarmed, be on your guard, flee, do not believe it, learn, stay awake. Ask about the future, and expect to be told how to live today.

In a sentence. Sitting opposite the temple on the Mount of Olives, Jesus was asked privately by four disciples when it would be destroyed and what sign would precede it.

On a Tuesday. Notice what you most want from the Bible about the future. If it is a date, a chart, or the satisfaction of knowing more than others, take the hint of this chapter and put the question down. If it is to be ready, ask him, and listen to his answer, which is mainly about how to live until he comes. Read the rest of the chapter this week and underline every command. There are about twenty of them, and not one of them is to calculate.

For worship. He sat on the mountain of the prophets, the place where the departing glory paused and where his feet will one day stand, and he spent his last free hours not defending himself but preparing four frightened men for a future he would face first. He saw it all: the fire, the siege, the scattering, the long centuries, the last day. None of it surprised him and none of it was out of his hands. The Judge of the temple was also the shepherd of the four, and he still is: the Lord of history, who tells his people what they need and keeps back what they could not bear.
verseByVerse.note: The Mount of Olives faces the temple across the Kidron Valley.

parallels.desc: his feet shall stand on the Mount of Olives

verseByVerse.quote: And Jesus began to say to them, "See that no one leads you astray. Many will come in my name, saying, 'I am he!' and they will lead many astray. And when you hear of wars and rumors of wars, do not be alarmed. This must take place, but the end is not yet. For nation will rise against nation, and kingdom against kingdom. There will be earthquakes in various places; there will be famines. These are but the beginning of the birth pains.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus began to say to them: see that no one leads you astray. Many will come in my name, saying, I am he! and they will lead many astray. When you hear of wars and rumours of wars, do not be alarmed. This must take place, but the end is not yet. For nation will rise against nation, and kingdom against kingdom. There will be earthquakes in various places; there will be famines. These are but the beginning of the birth pains.

See that no one leads you astray. They asked when; his first word is watch out. Before a single sign is described, the danger is named, and it is not the wars or the earthquakes. It is being deceived. The verb (blepete, see, watch) runs through the chapter like a bell (vv. 5, 9, 23, 33), and the theme of deception returns three more times (vv. 6, 22, 23). Jesus’ first concern is not information but protection.

Many will come in my name, saying, I am he! Not claiming to be Jesus of Nazareth, but claiming the role he holds: I am the Messiah (Matthew 24:5), perhaps even taking on the divine name, I am (egō eimi, see 6:50). And it happened almost at once. Gamaliel names Theudas, who promised to part the Jordan, and Judas the Galilean (Acts 5:36–37). There was the Egyptian who led thousands into the wilderness and out to this very Mount of Olives, promising that the walls of Jerusalem would fall at his command (Acts 21:38). Josephus describes many more, and in the final revolt men such as Simon bar Giora took royal and messianic airs. The pattern has never stopped. And note its exact shape: they come in my name. Not opposing Christ but claiming him, which is why the danger is to the church and not to the world.

And when you hear of wars and rumors of wars, do not be alarmed. This must take place, but the end is not yet. The word for alarmed (throeisthe) means shaken, thrown into alarm. He does not say the wars will be small; he tells his people how to receive the reports. Then two clauses that between them dismantle a whole industry. This must take place: the little word dei, divine necessity, the word used of his own suffering (8:31). History is not out of hand. But the end is not yet: these things are not the countdown. He is deliberately disconnecting the calamities from the calendar.

For nation will rise against nation, and kingdom against kingdom. There will be earthquakes in various places; there will be famines. He lists them, and every generation since has had all three. In the decades before AD 70 there were wars on the Roman frontiers and revolts in Britain and the East, a severe famine under Claudius (Acts 11:28), and great earthquakes, one destroying Laodicea around AD 60 and another striking Pompeii in 62. And every generation since has produced people certain that theirs was the last.

These are but the beginning of the birth pains. The prophets used labour as a picture of the sufferings before God’s new age (Isaiah 26:17–19; 66:7–9; Micah 4:9–10). Labour pains are real agony, they mean that something is coming, and the early ones tell you almost nothing about how long it will be. Paul uses the same picture: the whole creation has been groaning together in the pains of childbirth until now (Romans 8:22). The world is not simply decaying. It is in labour.

The one who really is he. The deceivers will say I am he, because the title is the most precious thing in the world, and it already has an owner. Jesus alone can say it truly: he said it on the water to frightened men (6:50), and he will say it before the high priest, I am, and you will see the Son of Man (14:62). Every false messiah is a forgery of him, which is why his people are not finally fooled: the sheep know the voice. And the birth pains are bound up with him too. The new age they labour toward was born on the morning he rose, the firstborn from the dead (Colossians 1:18), and every groan since is creation straining toward the day his risen life fills the world.

Are the wars and disasters in the news signs that the end is near? Not in the sense people usually mean. Jesus lists exactly these things and then says the end is not yet. They are the normal weather of the whole age between his first and second coming, not a countdown that lets you work out a date. In another sense they are signs of something: that this world is broken, that it is groaning for redemption, and that Christ’s words are true. So every disaster should send you to prayer, to compassion and to the gospel, and none of them should send you to a chart.

How should I read the news? As someone told in advance what the age would look like. When the next catastrophe arrives, two responses are available and both are wrong: panic, the anxious scanning of events for the pattern, and the calculating excitement that treats disaster as a timetable, which has produced a long line of confident predictions and an equally long line of quiet retractions. Jesus forbids both in one sentence: do not be alarmed, the end is not yet. Then get on with the work he gave you: pray for those suffering, give where you can, and tell people about the only kingdom that will not be shaken.

In a sentence. Jesus warned his disciples not to be deceived by false messiahs or alarmed by wars, earthquakes and famines, which are the beginning of the birth pains, not the end.

On a Tuesday. Notice what the news does to you. If you finish reading it more anxious, or more excited about the end, than you were before, you have heard the headlines and not the Lord. Before you open the news tomorrow, say his words to yourself: this must take place, but the end is not yet. And when someone tells you with great confidence what the latest crisis means for the timetable of prophecy, you are free to be kind and to decline. Jesus has already told you what it means.

For worship. He is not alarmed, and that is why we need not be. The wars that fill the headlines are not news to the one who said this must take place, and the earth that shakes beneath us is the footstool of the one who stilled the sea with a word. The groans of creation are not the death rattle of a world God has abandoned. They are labour pains, and the child that is coming is a new creation where righteousness dwells. Behind every rumour of war stands the Lamb who holds the scroll of history, and he has never once lost his place in it.
verseByVerse.note: Birth pains are a prophetic image for the troubles before God’s new age.

verseByVerse.quote: But be on your guard. For they will deliver you over to councils, and you will be beaten in synagogues, and you will stand before governors and kings for my sake, to bear witness before them. And the gospel must first be proclaimed to all nations. And when they bring you to trial and deliver you over, do not be anxious beforehand what you are to say, but say whatever is given you in that hour, for it is not you who speak, but the Holy Spirit.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But be on your guard. For they will hand you over to councils, and you will be beaten in synagogues, and you will stand before governors and kings for my sake, to bear witness before them. And the gospel must first be proclaimed to all nations. When they bring you to trial and hand you over, do not be anxious beforehand about what you are to say, but say whatever is given you in that hour, for it is not you who speak, but the Holy Spirit.

But be on your guard. For they will deliver you over to councils. Literally, see to yourselves: what is coming is coming to you. Deliver over (paradōsousin) is the very word used of Jesus being handed over (9:31; 10:33). The disciples will walk their master’s road. Councils (synedria) were the local Jewish courts as well as the Sanhedrin in Jerusalem.

And you will be beaten in synagogues, and you will stand before governors and kings for my sake. Read Acts with this verse open and it is a table of contents. Councils: Peter and John before the Sanhedrin (Acts 4–5). Beaten in synagogues: Paul received forty lashes less one five times (2 Corinthians 11:24). Governors: Felix and Festus (Acts 24–25). Kings: Agrippa (Acts 26), and finally Caesar himself. Note also where the first blows land: in synagogues. The persecution begins at home, among their own people, in the buildings they grew up in. It usually does.

To bear witness before them. And there is the turn. The purpose clause is not to suffer but to bear witness. The dock is a pulpit. Every one of those trials put the gospel in front of an audience it would never otherwise have reached, which is exactly what Paul says from prison: what has happened to me has really served to advance the gospel (Philippians 1:12). Kings who would never have entered a church heard the resurrection preached because a prisoner was brought before them in chains.

And the gospel must first be proclaimed to all nations. One bright line dropped into the middle of a catalogue of disasters, and it must not be missed. It is the only item in the list that is not something to be endured but something to be done. The same dei, must, as verse 7: the wars are a divine necessity, and so is this. And the little word first makes it a milestone. History will not close until the good news has reached every people. This is the real sign of the age between the comings: not wars, but mission. It turns the whole grim catalogue inside out. Persecution is not an interruption of the mission; it is one of its engines. The gospel travelled furthest along the roads that arrested men were dragged down. A Christian reading the news is not watching the world fall apart. He is watching the field in which the seed is being sown.

Has this already happened? In one sense, yes: Paul could say before AD 70 that the gospel had been proclaimed in all creation under heaven (Colossians 1:23; see Romans 1:8; Colossians 1:6). In its fullest sense it goes on until the end (Matthew 24:14; 28:19–20). But Christ’s return is not triggered by our success, as though the church could finish a list and bring him back. The day is fixed by the Father (v. 32). Our part is to be faithful in the task, and to know that it cannot fail, because the Lord of the harvest has said it must be done.

And when they bring you to trial and deliver you over, do not be anxious beforehand what you are to say. A promise for the dock. When a believer is dragged before a hostile court with no lawyer and no idea of the charge, God undertakes to supply the words in the moment. Stephen’s face and speech are its fulfilment (Acts 6:10, 15; 7), and so is the boldness of two uneducated fishermen that astonished the council (Acts 4:8, 13). It is not a licence for the preacher who has not opened his Bible all week. Paul told Timothy to do his best to present himself as a worker rightly handling the word of truth (2 Timothy 2:15), and asked for his books and parchments from prison (2 Timothy 4:13). The unprepared sermon is presumption wearing faith’s coat. For it is not you who speak, but the Holy Spirit: the believer in that courtroom is not alone, and not finally the one on trial. The Spirit sent by the risen Christ stands beside the accused as his advocate.

Should I prepare to speak about my faith, then? Yes, in ordinary life. Peter tells every believer to be always prepared to make a defence to anyone who asks for a reason for the hope that is in you, with gentleness and respect (1 Peter 3:15). Know the gospel well enough to say it simply; think about the questions your friends actually ask.
