What this verse removes is not preparation but fear: the sleepless rehearsal of what you will say if you are ever questioned, arrested or mocked for Christ. When that hour comes, you will not be left to your own resources.

What if I am never persecuted? Does that mean my faith is weak? No. The fact that you live in a place of relative freedom is a mercy to be thanked for, not a failure to be ashamed of (1 Timothy 2:1–2). Jesus does not promise every believer the same measure of suffering. But all who desire to live a godly life in Christ Jesus will meet opposition in some form (2 Timothy 3:12), even if only quiet contempt. And you belong to a body that is suffering right now in many countries. If one member suffers, all suffer together (1 Corinthians 12:26). Your part may be to pray, to give, and to speak up for them.

In a sentence. Jesus warned that his disciples would be persecuted and tried before Jewish and Gentile authorities, giving them opportunity to witness, while the gospel goes to all nations, and the Spirit gives them words.

On a Tuesday. Pray today, by name if you can, for Christians on trial for their faith around the world, and for the gospel to reach a people that has not yet heard it. Then think of the place where you are most likely to be asked about Christ this week, at work, at the school gate, in the family, and ask the Spirit for courage there. The courtroom in your life may only be a lunch table. It is still a pulpit.

For worship. The Son of God was handed over first. He stood before the council and the governor, was beaten, and bore the good confession that has broken the power of every court that has tried his people since. Now he sends his Spirit to stand beside the accused, so that fishermen confound scholars and prisoners preach to kings. Not one people for whom he died will be left unreached. The King is gathering his harvest, and even his enemies are carrying it to the barns.
verseByVerse.note: The councils were local Jewish courts; synagogues had the authority to flog.

parallels.desc: Peter and John before the council

verseByVerse.quote: And brother will deliver brother over to death, and the father his child, and children will rise against parents and have them put to death. And you will be hated by all for my name's sake. But the one who endures to the end will be saved.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Brother will hand brother over to death, and the father his child, and children will rise against parents and have them put to death. And you will be hated by all for my name’s sake. But the one who endures to the end will be saved.

And brother will deliver brother over to death, and the father his child. Deliver over is what he has said will be done to him (10:33). Now it is done to his people, by their own. Take the sentence slowly, because we read it as a general statement about hard times and it is not general at all. It names the closest bonds human beings have, in order. Brother: the person you grew up beside. Father: and note the direction, a father hands over his child.

And children will rise against parents and have them put to death. It is Micah’s picture of a society in total moral collapse, where a man’s enemies are the men of his own house (Micah 7:6), and Jesus echoes it because it is precisely what following him will cost some of his people. He had already said he came not to bring peace but a sword, dividing families over him (Matthew 10:34–36). In the persecution under Nero, Tacitus records, Christians were convicted on the information of others. It has cost exactly this in every century, and it does now, especially for converts from other religions. There are believers today whose own families reported them.

And you will be hated by all for my name’s sake. All: by every kind of person, Jew and Gentile. Tacitus says Christians were hated for their abominations and condemned for hatred of the human race. The reason Jesus gives is my name. They are hated because they belong to him. Not for being difficult, or rude, or politically inconvenient, and it is worth being honest that Christians sometimes attract dislike for other reasons entirely and then claim this verse. The promise is for hatred earned by belonging to him.

Hated for his name. If your own family regards your faith as a betrayal, if you have lost a brother’s respect or a father’s welcome over it, hear that your Lord said this would happen, said it in advance, and knew it from the inside. His own family came to take him away by force, believing he was out of his mind (3:21). His brothers did not believe in him (John 7:5). You are not on a road he has not walked.

But the one who endures to the end will be saved. The sentence that has kept anxious believers awake, so let it be answered straight. Endures (hypomeinas) means remains under the weight, does not give up. Will be saved means saved eternally, not rescued from death. It is not salvation by stamina; we are saved by grace through faith, not by the strength of our grip. Endurance is not the price of salvation; it is the evidence of it. The rocky ground also received the word with joy, had no root, and fell away when the heat came (4:16–17). The falling away did not cancel a genuine faith; it revealed a shallow one.

Where Christians differ: endurance and perseverance. Some take this to mean that a true believer can lose salvation if he does not endure. Verdict: endurance is required, and it is real; those who fall away permanently show that they never truly belonged (1 John 2:19). But God himself keeps his elect so that they will endure (v. 20; John 10:28–29; Philippians 1:6; 1 Peter 1:5). The perseverance of the saints means that the saints do persevere, because God preserves them. The warning is one of the means God uses to keep them.

The guarantee in the same chapter. If you are reading that verse and asking, will I hold on?, which is the right question and a healthy one, read on seven verses. For the sake of the elect, whom he chose, he shortened the days (v. 20). Read on to verse 27, where the Son of Man sends out his angels and gathers his elect from the four winds. He does not lose them. The shepherd who counts them at the beginning counts them at the end, and the number is the same: no one will snatch them out of my hand (John 10:28). So the command is real and so is the promise, and they are not in competition. Endure is what you are told to do. He shortened the days for the elect is why you will.

Should I cut off family members who oppose my faith? No, not on your side. Jesus warns that they may turn against you; he never tells you to turn against them. Keep honouring your parents, keep loving your brothers and sisters, keep the door open, and pray for them by name. Christ must come first, so when they demand that you deny him, stop worshipping, or give up your church, you must obey God rather than men (Acts 5:29). But that is a refusal, not a rejection. Wise distance may be necessary if there is real danger or abuse, and you should seek help from your church if there is. Even then, the aim is that they would one day see Christ in the way you bore it.

I have doubted and stumbled. Have I failed to endure? Enduring is not the same as never wavering. Peter denied Christ three times in one night and was restored (14:72; John 21:15–19). The one who endures is the one who keeps coming back to Christ, however weakly, and does not finally walk away from him. If you are troubled by your stumbling and still clinging to him, that is what endurance looks like from the inside. Falling away is a settled turning from Christ, not the struggle of a weak believer who hates his sin and keeps running back to the cross.

In a sentence. Jesus warned that even family members would betray believers to death, and they would be hated for his name, but those who endure to the end will be saved.

On a Tuesday. If following Christ has cost you a family relationship, you are not alone, and he knows. Write one line of prayer for that person today, and do one kind thing for them this month that does not require them to agree with you. And if you have never paid any price for his name, thank God for that freedom, and ask whether you would be willing to. Keep enduring, and trust him to keep you; the keeping is his work before it is yours.

For worship. He was the brother handed over by his own, the Son delivered up by the Father for us all, the one hated without a cause. He walked every inch of this road before he asked anyone to follow, and at the end of it he did not lose one of those the Father gave him. Our endurance rests on his: on the hands that hold us, on the intercession that never stops, on the love that will bring every elect child home. He who calls you to endure is the one who will keep you from stumbling and present you blameless before the presence of his glory with great joy (Jude 24).

parallels.desc: a man’s enemies are the men of his own house

verseByVerse.quote: But when you see the abomination of desolation standing where he ought not to be (let the reader understand), then let those who are in Judea flee to the mountains. Let the one who is on the housetop not go down, nor enter his house, to take anything out, and let the one who is in the field not turn back to take his cloak.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But when you see the abomination of desolation standing where he ought not to be (let the reader understand), then let those who are in Judea flee to the mountains. Let the one who is on the housetop not go down or enter his house to take anything out, and let the one in the field not turn back to take his cloak.

But when you see the abomination of desolation standing where he ought not to be. Now the discourse turns from the general to the specific, and this is the sign they asked for in verse 4. The phrase comes from Daniel (9:27; 11:31; 12:11). An abomination is something detestable to God, and the word is the standard Old Testament term for an idol. Of desolation means that causes desolation, a desecration so vile that it drives God’s worship out and leaves his sanctuary empty. Daniel’s words had already seen one fulfilment. In 167 BC the Syrian king Antiochus IV Epiphanes set up an altar to Zeus on the altar of burnt offering and sacrificed pigs there; the book of 1 Maccabees calls it a desolating sacrilege (1 Maccabees 1:54). That is what the phrase meant to every Jew who heard it: the worst thing that has ever happened, happening again.

Standing where he ought not to be. Let the reader understand. Mark’s Greek is deliberately odd: the participle is masculine, though abomination is neuter. This is not merely a thing set up in the holy place; it is somebody. And Mark’s aside, to whoever is reading this aloud in a congregation, is a nudge, not a puzzle: this is coded, be alert, and when it happens do not stand about discussing it.

What was the abomination? Luke gives Jesus’ words in a form his Gentile readers could not miss: when you see Jerusalem surrounded by armies, then know that its desolation has come near (Luke 21:20). A generation later Roman legions came up the valleys carrying their standards, which bore the emperor’s image and were treated as objects of worship. When the temple fell, Josephus records, the soldiers brought those standards into the temple court and offered sacrifice to them there. Earlier, in AD 67–68, Zealot factions had occupied the temple, committed murders in its courts and installed a false high priest, and some see that defilement as part of the fulfilment. The masculine he most likely points to the Roman commander and his army.

Is this fulfilled in AD 70, or by a future Antichrist? Many Christians, especially dispensationalists, expect a future ruler to set himself up in a rebuilt temple (2 Thessalonians 2:3–4; Revelation 13). But Luke’s version and the instruction itself point to AD 70: the remedy is to flee from Judea to the mountains, which only makes sense of a crisis in that land in that century. The more likely reading is that this is the Roman desecration and destruction. Paul’s man of lawlessness shows that a final rebellion against God is still to come before Christ returns, and Antiochus and Titus are both foreshadowings of it. But that is not what Jesus warns of here.

Run, do not fight. Those in Judea are to flee to the mountains, not defend the holy city. Every nationalist instinct in that country said the opposite, and the Zealots acted on it, and it destroyed them. And the church historian Eusebius records that it worked: the Christians of Jerusalem, warned by a prophecy, left the city before the siege closed, crossed the Jordan to Pella, and survived. A church took its Lord’s word literally and lived.

The desolation he went into. The disciples are told to run from a desolated holy place. Their Lord was about to walk into a desolation of his own. Within days, on a hill outside these walls, he would cry, My God, my God, why have you forsaken me? (15:34), abandoned in the place of sinners so that sinners would never be abandoned. The temple Rome would profane was already finished as the place of meeting with God, because the true holy place was the crucified and risen Christ. That is why his people could leave the building behind without leaving God: they ran with him, not from him.

Let the one who is on the housetop not go down, nor enter his house, to take anything out. Houses had flat roofs with an outside stair, used for sleeping, drying figs and praying. The instruction is: when you see it, go down the outside steps and keep going. Do not step inside for anything.

And let the one who is in the field not turn back to take his cloak. A man working in a field took off his outer cloak and left it at the edge. It was expensive; it was his blanket at night; and the Law protected it from creditors precisely because a poor man could not do without it (Exodus 22:26–27). Leave it. And the picture behind this is unmistakable to anyone who knows Genesis. Another family was told to get out of a doomed city and not look back, and one of them turned round (Genesis 19:17, 26). Jesus makes the connection himself in Luke: remember Lot’s wife (Luke 17:32).

Is it right for a Christian to flee persecution? Yes, when fleeing is possible without denying Christ. Jesus commands it here, and elsewhere tells his disciples that when they are persecuted in one town they should flee to the next (Matthew 10:23). Paul was let down the wall of Damascus in a basket (Acts 9:25). Fleeing is not cowardice, and staying is not always faith. What is never allowed is to save your life by disowning him. Sometimes a believer is called to stay, as shepherds stay with their flocks, and many have died faithfully doing so. Seek wisdom, take counsel, and trust that the Lord who told the Jerusalem church to run is the Lord of both choices.

In a sentence. When they saw Daniel’s abomination of desolation, the desecration of the temple by Rome, the disciples were to flee from Judea at once, without stopping for anything.

On a Tuesday. This is tactical advice for a crisis in AD 70, and it is also a permanent picture of what judgment does to the value of possessions. There comes a moment when the cloak is not worth the four seconds, and everything you own is exactly that cloak. Ask what in your life you would turn back for, and hold it more loosely today. And when Scripture tells you to flee, from sexual immorality (1 Corinthians 6:18), from idolatry (1 Corinthians 10:14), from the love of money (1 Timothy 6:10–11), take it as literally as the Jerusalem church did. Do not go back inside for one last thing.

For worship. The Lord who saw the armies coming forty years ahead also saw the believers on the rooftops, and gave them the word that saved their lives. He does not only predict judgment; he opens the way out of it. Lot’s wife looked back at a city she loved more than her deliverer. Christ’s people looked forward to a Lord they loved more than their city, and he brought them over the Jordan and through. He is the shelter in the mountains still, and no one who runs to him is turned away.
verseByVerse.note: Daniel foresaw an idolatrous desecration of the temple; it was foreshadowed in 167 BC, when Antiochus IV set up a pagan altar there. Luke speaks of Jerusalem surrounded by armies. Roofs were flat and reached by an outside stair.

verseByVerse.quote: And alas for women who are pregnant and for those who are nursing infants in those days! Pray that it may not happen in winter. For in those days there will be such tribulation as has not been from the beginning of the creation that God created until now, and never will be. And if the Lord had not cut short the days, no human being would be saved. But for the sake of the elect, whom he chose, he shortened the days.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And alas for women who are pregnant and for those who are nursing infants in those days! Pray that it may not happen in winter. For in those days there will be such tribulation as has not been from the beginning of the creation that God created until now, and never will be. And if the Lord had not cut short the days, no human being would be saved. But for the sake of the elect, whom he chose, he shortened the days.

And alas for women who are pregnant and for those who are nursing infants in those days! He has just told them to run without stopping for a coat, and now he thinks about who cannot run. That is the tenderness in the middle of the terror, and it is easy to read past. The Son of God, describing the fall of a city forty years away, pauses over the women who will be nine months pregnant that week and the mothers with a baby at the breast. He is not delivering a strategic assessment. He is imagining particular people, and it costs him something. The word is not a curse but a cry of grief.

Pray that it may not happen in winter. And then something more remarkable still: he tells them to pray about the timing. Winter in Judea means rains, swollen wadis, impassable tracks, the Jordan in flood and cold nights in the open. So: ask God to arrange the date of a judgment he has already determined, so that the flight will be survivable. That settles something about prayer. A thing can be fixed in the purpose of God and still be a proper subject of prayer, and God’s sovereignty over an event is not a reason to stop asking about its details. God ordains the means as well as the end, and our prayers are among the means. Jesus tells them to pray about the weather during the fall of Jerusalem. Nothing is too settled to pray about, and nothing is too small.

For in those days there will be such tribulation as has not been from the beginning of the creation that God created until now, and never will be. The prophets’ language for a catastrophe beyond comparison (Daniel 12:1; Joel 2:2). Josephus, an eyewitness, describes famine so complete that people ate leather, a mother who ate her own child, crucifixions outside the walls at up to five hundred a day until there was no more wood, and at the end the city burned and its people killed or enslaved. He puts the dead at over a million; even a heavily discounted figure is a horror. And never will be matters for interpretation: Jesus is speaking of an event inside history, not the very end, for there will be time after it.

And if the Lord had not cut short the days, no human being would be saved. Saved here means survived. Read it as it stands. Left to run its course, the thing would have consumed everybody. Nothing in human resistance was going to stop it. The siege lasted about five months; had it gone on, no one would have come out.

But for the sake of the elect, whom he chose, he shortened the days. The pastoral heart of the whole discourse. The tribulation is bounded, not by the exhaustion of evil or the strength of the church: God shortens it. And the reason is not general benevolence. It is for the sake of the elect (eklektous), whom he chose: Mark says it twice in one breath. God’s sovereign choice of his people governs even the length of a war. It does not promise that they are exempt; they were in Judea, and Christians have been in every horror since. It promises something better: they are the reason it stops. Behind the worst of history there is a hand on the clock, set by love for particular, named people (Romans 8:28).

Was the fall of Jerusalem God’s judgment on the Jewish people as a race? It was a judgment on that generation’s rejection of the Messiah, as Jesus wept over the city and said (Luke 19:41–44), and as the parable of the tenants had warned (12:9). But it was never a licence for hatred of Jewish people. Jesus himself, his mother, every apostle and the whole first church were Jews, and those who fled to Pella were Jewish believers. The guilt for the death of Christ is shared by Jew and Gentile alike (Acts 4:27), and his blood was shed for both. The church’s long history of contempt for the Jews is a sin, not an application of this passage. Paul speaks of them with tears, and still prays for their salvation (Romans 10:1).

If God has decreed what will happen, why should I pray? Because he has decreed our prayers too, and works through them. Jesus held both truths in one sentence: the days are fixed by God, and his people should pray about them. Prayer is not an attempt to change God’s mind from outside his plan; it is one of the ways his plan unfolds. We do not know the decree, but we do know the command, and we are told to ask (James 4:2). So pray about the timing of the operation, the weather on the journey, the length of the trial. The God who shortened the days for the elect still listens.

In a sentence. The siege of Jerusalem would bring unparalleled suffering, but God shortened those days for the sake of the people he had chosen.

On a Tuesday. When you cannot see how a thing can go on and anyone survive it, the persecution in that country, the sickness in this house, the years that have been taken, the promise is not that you will be lifted out. It is that there is a limit, that the limit was fixed before it started, and that it was fixed for your sake (1 Corinthians 10:13). Say that to yourself this week about the hardest thing you are carrying. And then pray about its details, small and large, as Jesus told his disciples to pray about winter.

For worship. The Lord who saw the siege coming did not look at it like a general. He grieved over pregnant women and nursing mothers, and taught his people to pray about the weather. That same heart holds the clock of history: no suffering of his people runs a minute longer than he has decided, and he has decided in love. And the one who shortened their days did not shorten his own. He did not cut short the cup but drank it to the dregs, so that our tribulations would be bounded and his love would not.
verseByVerse.note: Winter rains made roads and river crossings hard.

parallels.desc: a time of trouble such as never has been

verseByVerse.quote: And then if anyone says to you, 'Look, here is the Christ!' or 'Look, there he is!' do not believe it. For false christs and false prophets will arise and perform signs and wonders, to lead astray, if possible, the elect. But be on guard; I have told you all things beforehand.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then if anyone says to you, look, here is the Christ! or, look, there he is! do not believe it. For false christs and false prophets will arise and perform signs and wonders, to lead astray, if possible, the elect. But be on guard; I have told you all things beforehand.

Do not believe it. If anyone says to you, Look, here is the Christ! or Look, there he is!, do not believe it. He returns to the danger he opened with (v. 5), and it is significant that he ends the section here rather than with the tribulation. The worst thing in this passage is not the siege. It is deception. In times of crisis people look for a deliverer and will follow anyone who claims to be one. Josephus records that during the siege false prophets told the people to wait in the temple for signs of deliverance, until it burned with them inside.

Here and there. Note the specific form it takes: here and there, a location. Somebody has him, somewhere, and you must go and see. That is the mark of the counterfeit, and Matthew spells out why it cannot be true: the real coming will be like lightning from east to west (Matthew 24:27). Christ’s return will not be a local event that needs announcing. Nobody will need to be told where to look (v. 26).

For false christs and false prophets will arise and perform signs and wonders. Here is the thing that must be said plainly, because it cuts against an instinct many Christians have. The signs will work. Jesus does not say they will be tricks or that the wonders will be faked. The Bible is consistent about this. Pharaoh’s magicians duplicated the first plagues (Exodus 7:22). Deuteronomy legislates for exactly this case: if a prophet gives a sign and it comes to pass, and then says let us go after other gods, you shall not listen, for the LORD is testing you (Deuteronomy 13:1–3). Paul warns of a coming lawlessness with false signs and wonders (2 Thessalonians 2:9; see Revelation 13:13–14). So the supernatural is not self-authenticating. A thing can be genuinely inexplicable and not be from God, which means that it works is never, by itself, a reason to follow anybody.

The test is truth, not power. The test is the doctrine underneath it: does this lead people to the Christ who came in the flesh, died on a cross and rose, or away from him? Deuteronomy’s test is John’s (1 John 4:2–3). Miracles, crowds, fame, emotional intensity and visible success prove nothing either way.

To lead astray, if possible, the elect. Two things in that clause, and they hold together. The elect are the target. Not the world, which needs no deceiving; the deception is aimed at the church, by people using Christ’s name. If possible: the phrase implies that it is not possible, and it is a quiet reassurance without being a licence for carelessness. The attempt will be made and it will be formidable, and God’s people will not finally be lost, because he keeps them (John 10:27–29). But the way they are kept is not by magic. It is by remembering what they were told: I have told you all things beforehand (v. 23).

But be on guard; I have told you all things beforehand. The fourth warning in the chapter, and the reason given is a mercy. God protects his people from deception not by making them incapable of being fooled, but by telling them in advance and expecting them to remember. Forewarned is forearmed, but only for somebody who has read the warning: know your Bible well enough that a false thing sounds wrong when you hear it.

How do I recognise a false teacher today? Ask three questions. First, what does he say about Jesus: is Christ fully God and fully man, crucified for sinners and risen, the only way to the Father? Second, what does he say about the gospel: is salvation by grace through faith, or is it something you earn, buy or unlock with a technique? Third, where does he point you: to Scripture and to Christ, or to himself, his new revelation, his special experiences, his secret knowledge of the date? Watch the fruit of his life as well (Matthew 7:15–20), but begin with his doctrine. A teacher who is warm, gifted and successful can still be wrong, and one who is plain and unknown can be right.

Can a true Christian be deceived at all? Yes, for a time and in part. Believers can be misled on many things, and the Galatians were led a long way before Paul wrote to them (Galatians 3:1). What this verse promises is that the elect will not be finally carried away from Christ. God uses his word, his church and his Spirit to bring his people back. So do not be proud, as if you could never be fooled, and do not despair, as if one error has ruined you. Stay close to the Scriptures and to a faithful church, and test what you hear (1 John 4:1).

In a sentence. Jesus warned against false messiahs and prophets whose signs could deceive even the elect, if that were possible, and said he had told them everything beforehand.

On a Tuesday. Test every teacher by Scripture, not by impressive signs or the size of the crowd. Next time something you see online or hear in church moves you deeply, ask before you share it: is it true, and where is that in the Bible? And read the Gospels regularly enough that you know the real Christ by sight. You have been told beforehand; make sure you have actually read what you were told.

For worship. There is only one Christ, and he does not need to be found in a desert or behind a door. He is not here or there; he is risen and reigning, and when he comes every eye will see him. False christs need crowds and wonders to hold their followers. The true Christ holds his by name. He told us everything beforehand because he loves us, and he guards his elect because he bought them. The deceiver can perform signs, but he cannot snatch one sheep from the Shepherd’s hand, and in the end every counterfeit will be exposed by the brightness of the real one.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 24–37 — The Coming of the Son of Man and the Call to Watchfulness
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The coming (vv. 24–27). Sun darkened, moon gone out, stars falling, the powers shaken — and then the Son of Man, coming in clouds with great power and glory, sending out angels to gather his people from the four winds. It is Daniel 7 arriving, spoken by a man three days from a public execution.

The fig tree (vv. 28–31). A lesson in reading signs, and the most argued-over verse in the chapter: this generation will not pass away until all these things take place. And then a claim no creature could make — heaven and earth will go, and his words will not.

The hinge (v. 32). But concerning that day or that hour, no one knows — not the angels, not the Son. Everything before this verse had signs. Nothing after it does.

The command (vv. 33–37). A householder goes away, leaves each servant a job, tells the doorkeeper to stay awake — and might come back at any of the four watches of the night. Stay awake, four times over, and the last words are addressed past the four men on the hillside to everybody.

And Mark's reader is about to walk through all four watches in the next two chapters, with the disciples failing at every one.
verseByVerse.theology:
Not even the Son (v. 32) is the verse most often used against the deity of Christ. Arius built on it in the fourth century; it is still reached for today. If Jesus did not know the day, the argument runs, he cannot be God.

The answer the church has always given is not a dodge but the heart of who Christ is: the one person, the eternal Son, took to himself a complete human nature without ceasing to be fully God, so that from the incarnation there are two natures in the one Lord. According to his divine nature he is omniscient, upholding the universe; according to his human nature he learned to speak, grew tired, and — as Luke says plainly — increased in wisdom (Luke 2:52), which a mind that already knew everything could not do. So the single person can truly say I do not know as a man, while as God he knows the hour perfectly.

It is no more a contradiction than that the same Jesus could sleep in the stern of a boat and then stand up and silence the storm with a word (4:38–39). The one he did as a weary man; the other as the Lord of creation.

And Mark has set the proof of it one verse earlier, for anyone with eyes. In v. 31 this same speaker says heaven and earth will pass away, but my words will not pass away — a claim no creature could dare make, setting his own words above the entire created order. In v. 32 the same mouth says he does not know the day.

The starkest claim to deity and the starkest confession of human limitation, one breath apart, both true. That is not a prophet who overreached in v. 31, nor a mere man who was honest in v. 32. It is God become man — and this verse, far from disproving his deity, is one of the clearest windows in the Gospel onto the two natures in the one Christ.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: a householder goes away and leaves his servants each with his work, and tells the doorkeeper to stay awake.

Notice how the parable defines watchfulness, because it is not what the word suggests. The servants are not told to sit at the window scanning the road. They are given jobs. Watching, in this parable, is doing what you were left to do — and the doorkeeper's post is itself a task.

Now: which corrects both of the standard mistakes about the Lord's return.

One is the anxious calculation that treats every crisis as a countdown and produces confident predictions and quiet retractions. The other is the practical forgetting that lives as though he is not coming at all.

Jesus rules out both with one image. The man who is ready is not the man who worked out the date; it is the man found at his post, doing his work, whenever the door opens. Blessed is that servant whom his master will find so doing when he comes (Matt. 24:46).

So the honest question is not when? — he has refused that four times. It is: what did he leave me to do, and am I doing it? If he came back this evening, would he find you at the post or asleep in it? That is a question about this week's ordinary duties, and it is the only question this chapter finally asks.

verseByVerse.quote: But in those days, after that tribulation, the sun will be darkened, and the moon will not give its light, and the stars will be falling from heaven, and the powers in the heavens will be shaken.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But in those days, after that tribulation, the sun will be darkened, and the moon will not give its light, and the stars will be falling from heaven, and the powers in the heavens will be shaken.

But in those days, after that tribulation. A marker in the text: something else is now in view. But sets it against what came before. After that tribulation means after the distress of the siege (v. 19) and the whole period of the church age that it represents. Jesus does not say how long after. The horizon has moved, and the prophet’s telescope is now on the far mountain range.

The sun will be darkened, and the moon will not give its light. Every phrase echoes the prophets. The sun will be dark at its rising, and the moon will not shed its light: Isaiah 13:10, against Babylon. The sun and the moon are darkened, and the stars withdraw their shining: Joel 2:10 (also 2:31; 3:15). Ezekiel uses the same words against Egypt (Ezekiel 32:7–8). It is the settled prophetic vocabulary for the day God acts in judgment, used for events inside history, the fall of Babylon and the ruin of Edom, as well as for the last day: the world turned upside down, the powers falling, God acting.

And the stars will be falling from heaven, and the powers in the heavens will be shaken. All the host of heaven shall rot away, and the skies roll up like a scroll (Isaiah 34:4). The powers (dynameis) may be the heavenly bodies, or the spiritual powers people worshipped through them (Ephesians 6:12). Either way, the whole created order is shaken by the coming of its maker (Haggai 2:6; Hebrews 12:26–27).

What the imagery says. Do not let the argument about timing obscure what the imagery says, because that is not in dispute. The sun, moon and stars were the fixed points, what you steer by, plant by and set your calendar by; they had not failed once since the fourth day of creation. To say the lights go out is to say that the last reliable things are not reliable, and the shaking of the powers says that whatever holds the machinery in place is not exempt either. The building was going to fall (v. 2); now the sky. He has spent twenty verses removing everything a person might lean on, the temple, the nation, the family, the possessions, and now the stars, and he is about to name the one thing that is not going anywhere: his words.

Darkness at noon. Mark’s readers would not have to wait long to see this language begin to come true. Three days later, as Jesus hung on the cross, darkness came over the whole land from the sixth hour until the ninth (15:33). The sign of the day of the LORD fell first on one man outside the city, as he bore the judgment the prophets had described. That is why the shaking of the heavens is not a terror for his people. The darkness that will cover the old creation at his coming has already covered him, and those who are in him have nothing left to fear from the day the lights go out.

Where Christians differ: AD 70 or the end? Some (preterists, and some others such as R. T. France and N. T. Wright) take verses 24–27 as prophetic imagery for the fall of Jerusalem and Christ’s vindication in AD 70, since the prophets used such language for historical judgments. Others take it as the end of the world and the second coming. Verdict: after that tribulation marks a new stage, and the gathering of the elect from the whole earth (v. 27) and the coming of the Son of Man in glory (8:38; 14:62) describe the visible return of Christ at the end of the age, as the New Testament elsewhere teaches (1 Thessalonians 4:16–17; 2 Thessalonians 1:7–10). The cosmic imagery may be partly symbolic, but it points to a real event that ends history.

Will the universe literally be destroyed? Scripture speaks of the present heavens and earth passing away and being dissolved by fire (2 Peter 3:10–12), and also of creation being set free from its bondage to decay (Romans 8:19–21). The best way to hold these together is that God will not throw his creation away but purge and renew it, as a refiner purifies gold. What passes away is the old order, marred by sin and curse. What comes is a new heavens and a new earth in which righteousness dwells (2 Peter 3:13; Revelation 21:1–5). So the shaking of the heavens is not the end of God’s world. It is the end of the world as we have known it, and the beginning of the world as he always meant it to be.

In a sentence. After the tribulation, the heavens themselves will be shaken, the prophets’ picture of God coming in judgment, here pointing to the end of the age.

On a Tuesday. Make a short list of the things you treat as fixed points: your health, your savings, your country, your family’s good name, the ordinary rhythm of your week. They are good gifts, and every one of them belongs to a creation that will be shaken. Thank God for each, and then say aloud which of them you would still have if the lights went out. Fix your hope on the kingdom that cannot be shaken, and you will find you can enjoy the rest without clutching it.

For worship. He made the sun on the fourth day and set the stars in their courses, and they have obeyed him without a single failure for all the ages of the world. When he comes, they will bow. The lights men worshipped will go dark before the Light of the world, and the powers they feared will be shaken by the one who disarmed them at the cross. The Lord who let the sun be darkened over his own head at noon will come through the heavens in a brightness that needs no sun at all.
verseByVerse.note: Prophets used cosmic images like these for great acts of God’s judgment.

parallels.desc: the stars will not give their light

verseByVerse.quote: And then they will see the Son of Man coming in clouds with great power and glory. And then he will send out the angels and gather his elect from the four winds, from the ends of the earth to the ends of heaven.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And then they will see the Son of Man coming in clouds with great power and glory. And then he will send out the angels and gather his elect from the four winds, from the ends of the earth to the ends of heaven.

And then they will see the Son of Man coming in clouds with great power and glory. This is Daniel 7:13–14, and Jesus draws on it directly: with the clouds of heaven there came one like a son of man, and to him was given dominion and glory and a kingdom, that all peoples, nations and languages should serve him. In Daniel he comes to the Ancient of Days to receive the kingdom. Here, having received it, he comes in glory to the earth. Three things are packed into the sentence.

The clouds. In the Old Testament, cloud is where God is: the pillar in the wilderness, the cloud that filled the tabernacle, the cloud on Sinai, the cloud on the mountain of transfiguration (9:7). To come with the clouds is not a description of weather. It is a claim to deity, and the high priest will understand it perfectly when Jesus says it under oath at his trial, and will tear his robes (14:62).

They will see. The whole of this Gospel has been about people not seeing: the blind man who saw men like trees walking, the disciples with eyes who did not see (8:18, 24). That ends here. They will see means all people. His return will be visible and public, not secret: every eye will see him, even those who pierced him (Revelation 1:7). Nobody will need to be told where to look.

With great power and glory. Now hold this against the calendar. He says it on the Tuesday of the last week. On Friday he will be nailed up naked outside the city with a mocking placard over his head, and the men who arranged it will stand underneath telling him to come down. The one who says great power and glory is three days from the most public humiliation the ancient world could devise. Both are true. His first coming was in weakness; his second will be in power. And the second is how the first is vindicated. The one about to be crucified will return as Lord of all.

Is this the second coming or the judgment on Jerusalem in AD 70? Some, reading Daniel 7 carefully, note that there the Son of Man comes to the Ancient of Days to receive the kingdom, and take these verses as Christ’s vindication shown in the temple’s fall. The more likely reading is that here the far horizon breaks through. People will see him; the elect are gathered from the ends of the earth to the ends of heaven; and Jesus speaks of his final coming in the same terms elsewhere (8:38; 14:62). As in the prophets, the near judgment and the final one appear in one view, and these verses are where the final one shows.

And then he will send out the angels and gather his elect from the four winds. After twenty verses of warnings, the end of the story, and it is not a courtroom scene. Mark says nothing here about thrones or separation, though the rest of Scripture makes clear that judgment will follow. The one thing the Son of Man is shown doing when he comes is collecting his people. The angels are his angels (8:38); the elect are his elect, the Father’s chosen and Christ’s own. The language is the old promise of regathering: if your outcasts are in the uttermost parts of heaven, from there the LORD will gather you (Deuteronomy 30:4; Isaiah 43:5–6; Zechariah 2:6). And now it includes believers from every nation, since the gospel will have been preached to all nations (v. 10).

From the ends of the earth to the ends of heaven. The reach of it is total: from the four winds, from one horizon to the other. Mark piles the phrases up so that there is nowhere a believer can have been put that is outside its sweep. Christians have been scattered by exile, slavery, war, famine, prison and the sea. They have died in places nobody recorded and been buried where nobody knows. He sends his angels and gathers his elect, his own, chosen, named, and does not leave one of them behind. He is coming to collect what is his.

No secret rapture. Some (dispensationalists) teach that believers will be secretly taken from the earth before a seven-year tribulation, and that this passage describes a later stage. Verdict: the gathering of the elect happens at Christ’s visible coming in glory, after the tribulation (v. 24), just as Paul describes the gathering of believers to meet the Lord at his public return with a shout and a trumpet (1 Thessalonians 4:16–17; 2 Thessalonians 2:1). There is one return of Christ, public and glorious, at which his people are gathered to him. The church is not promised escape from trouble, but keeping through it (v. 13).

What happens to believers who have already died? They are with Christ now, consciously, which is far better (Philippians 1:23; 2 Corinthians 5:8). They are not asleep in the sense of being unaware, and they are not in a place of purging; their souls are made perfect in holiness and wait for the redemption of their bodies. When Christ comes, God will bring them with him, their bodies will be raised imperishable, and the living will be changed and caught up together with them (1 Thessalonians 4:14–17; 1 Corinthians 15:51–52). The gathering from the four winds includes every grave. No believer who has died is behind, and none will miss that day.

What will happen to those who are not gathered? Mark’s verse speaks only of the elect, but Jesus says plainly elsewhere that when the Son of Man comes in his glory he will sit on his throne and separate the nations, and those who do not know him will go away into eternal punishment (Matthew 25:31–46; 2 Thessalonians 1:7–9). That is why the gospel must first be preached to all nations (v. 10). The same coming that is the hope of the church is the terror of the unbelieving world, and the time to be reconciled to the King is before he appears, while he is still calling.

In a sentence. All will see the Son of Man coming in the clouds with great power and glory, and he will send his angels to gather his chosen people from every corner of the earth.

On a Tuesday. Think of a believer you have lost, buried perhaps far away, or one who died alone. He has not lost track of them, and on that day the angels will be sent for them by name. Let that change how you grieve: with tears, but not as those who have no hope (1 Thessalonians 4:13). And think of one person who does not yet know Christ, and pray for them today, because the same day that gathers his people will also reveal those who refused him.

For worship. The one who was lifted up in shame will be seen in glory. He was gathered by no one: he died alone, deserted by his friends, and was laid in another man’s tomb. Because he was abandoned, his people never will be. He will send his angels to the four winds, to the deserts and the seabed and the graves no one tends, and gather every one the Father gave him. The Shepherd will count his flock on that day, and find it whole.

parallels.desc: one like a son of man with the clouds

verseByVerse.quote: "From the fig tree learn its lesson: as soon as its branch becomes tender and puts out its leaves, you know that summer is near. So also, when you see these things taking place, you know that he is near, at the very gates.
verseByVerse.commentary:
From the fig tree learn its lesson: as soon as its branch becomes tender and puts out its leaves, you know that summer is near. So also, when you see these things taking place, you know that he is near, at the very gates.

From the fig tree learn its lesson. Lesson is literally parable (parabolē). The last time a fig tree appeared in this Gospel it was in full leaf with nothing on it, and he cursed it, and it was an acted parable of the temple (11:13–21). They are standing on the same mountain, and now the same tree teaches something positive.

As soon as its branch becomes tender and puts out its leaves, you know that summer is near. It is worth knowing why the fig in particular. Most trees in that country are evergreen, the olive, the carob, the pine, so they tell you nothing about the season. The fig is bare all winter and one of the last to bud. When the sap rises and the fig breaks into leaf in late spring, the hot season is coming. Nobody needs training to read it. A child could. That is the point of the image: the sign is unmistakable and requires no expertise, and it does not give you a date. It gives you a season.

So also, when you see these things taking place. The application, and everything turns on how much these things covers. The phrase points back to what he has described leading up to the destruction of the temple (vv. 5–23): the false messiahs, the wars, the abomination in the holy place, the flight from Judea, the unequalled distress. Those are the buds on the branch. The disciples had asked for a sign (v. 4); this is it.

You know that he is near, at the very gates. He or it: the Greek can mean either, the destruction of the temple they asked about, or the Son of Man. Either way, when the signs appear the event is close, as near as someone standing at the city gate. And the image prepares for the closing parable of a householder returning to a house where a doorkeeper is meant to be awake.

The one at the gates. The last time Jesus passes through the gates of Jerusalem in this Gospel, he goes out under a cross, to suffer outside the gate (15:20–22; Hebrews 13:12). The one who is near, at the very gates, whether in judgment on the city or at his final coming, is the same Lord who was thrown out of them. The city that expelled him would find him at its gates as Judge within a generation. And his people read every budding branch as the nearness of a Friend, because the one standing at the door has already gone through death for them.

The right response to a budding tree. The right response to a budding fig tree is not to calculate the exact date of midsummer. It is to get ready for hot weather. The signs in this chapter were never given so that anyone could work out a timetable; he has said the end is not yet (v. 7) and will say no one knows (v. 32). They were given so that when the world goes dark his people would not panic, would recognise the season, and would keep working. That is a rebuke to a whole industry of date-setting, and equally to the opposite error. A man who ignores the tree entirely is caught out by the summer just as surely as the man who publishes a date for it and is wrong.

Should I be looking for signs today, then? Not to fix a date, but to stay awake. The particular signs Jesus gave here belonged to the fall of Jerusalem, and that generation saw them. For us the lesson of the fig tree still holds in its broader sense: the whole age since the resurrection is the last days (Hebrews 1:2; 1 John 2:18), and everything that happens in it should remind us that summer is coming. So when you see false teachers, persecution, wars and the gospel spreading, do not reach for a calculator. Reach for your work, your Bible and your prayers, because the season you are living in is the season before his coming.

In a sentence. As fig leaves signal that summer is near, so the events Jesus described would show that the end of the temple was at the gates.

On a Tuesday. Learn to read the times in the light of Scripture, not to calculate dates but to stay alert and faithful. Look out of a window today at something growing and let it preach to you: God keeps his seasons, and what he has promised is on its way. Then ask what you would want to have finished, put right or said if summer came this week, and do one of those things before Sunday.

For worship. The Lord of the fig tree is the Lord of the seasons and of history. He curses barren religion and makes dead wood bud. Every spring he keeps the promise he made to Noah, that seedtime and harvest, summer and winter shall not cease, and every spring preaches that his word does not fail. The tree that once stood for a fruitless temple now teaches his people hope, and the Lord who stands at the door is the one who knocks and comes in to eat with those who open to him.
verseByVerse.note: Unlike many trees in Israel, the fig loses its leaves in winter; its new leaves mark the coming of summer.

verseByVerse.quote: Truly, I say to you, this generation will not pass away until all these things take place. Heaven and earth will pass away, but my words will not pass away.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Truly, I tell you, this generation will not pass away until all these things take place. Heaven and earth will pass away, but my words will not pass away.

Truly, I say to you, this generation will not pass away until all these things take place. The verse sceptics reach for first: here, they say, Jesus promised his return within his hearers’ lifetime, and he did not come. If that were the meaning, it would be a plain failed prophecy. It is not, and the discourse shows why. This generation (hē genea hautē) everywhere else in Mark means the people then living (8:12, 38; 9:19). All these things refers to the events of verses 5–23, leading to the destruction of the temple, the thing the disciples asked about (v. 4).

Two comings held apart. The false messiahs, the wars, the abomination in the holy place, the flight from Judea, the unequalled distress: every one took place within that generation, in AD 70, some forty years on, within the lifetime of many who heard him. The temple fell exactly as he said, down to the last stone. Then comes the hinge: but concerning that day or that hour, no one knows (v. 32). From there Jesus speaks of his final coming, and says the opposite of everything before: no sign, no timetable, nobody knows the day, it arrives while the house is asleep. So the discourse deliberately holds two comings apart: the near judgment on Jerusalem, hedged with signs and set inside this generation, and the far return of the Son of Man, without sign or date.

Where Christians differ: this generation. Some take this generation to mean the Jewish race, or the human race, or the generation alive at the end, which sees the signs. Some critics conclude that Jesus expected the end of the world within a generation and was mistaken. Verdict: the plain meaning is Jesus’ contemporaries. All these things refers to the events leading to the destruction of the temple, which did take place within that generation. Jesus then carefully distinguishes that day (v. 32), the day of his coming, whose timing no one knows. He was not mistaken.

But what of verses 24–27? Do they not come before this verse? They do, but these things in verse 29 are what you see before he is near, the signs and not the event they point to. These things are the false messiahs, wars, persecution, the desolation and the flight (vv. 5–23). The coming of verses 26–27 is the event those signs foreshadow, and of its day no one knows (v. 32). Read this way, and it is the reading the seams of the text ask for, Jesus was not mistaken by a single day. He told them the temple would fall in their lifetime, and it did. He told them his own coming would be unmarked and unknown, and it remains so.

Words that outlast the universe. Heaven and earth will pass away, but my words will not pass away: over both comings stands one of the most extraordinary sentences in the Bible, easy to skate over because it sounds like familiar piety. He has spent the chapter dismantling every permanence. The temple: gone. The nation: scattered. The family: divided. The possessions: not worth turning back for. The sun and moon and stars: put out. Now he adds heaven and earth, the whole created order, and sets his own words above it.

Who is speaking. A Galilean carpenter on a hillside with four fishermen, two days from arrest, with no writings, no institution and no army, says that when the universe has gone, the sentences he has spoken this afternoon will still be standing. No prophet ever said such a thing. They said, thus says the LORD, and put the permanence where it belonged: the word of our God will stand forever (Isaiah 40:8; Psalm 119:89). Jesus says my words. That is a claim to deity as clear as any in the Gospel, and it stands one verse before the sentence people use to deny his deity. And it guarantees everything he has said: the temple will fall, he will return, the elect will be gathered.

Why has he not come after two thousand years? Peter answers this directly. With the Lord one day is as a thousand years, and a thousand years as one day; the Lord is not slow to fulfil his promise as some count slowness, but is patient, not wishing that any should perish, but that all should reach repentance (2 Peter 3:8–9). The delay is not forgetfulness or failure. It is mercy, the time in which the gospel goes to all nations and the last of his elect are gathered in. Every year he waits, more people are saved. And Jesus never said he would come soon in the sense of a date. He said no one knows, and stay awake.

In a sentence. Jesus solemnly promised that the events leading to the temple’s destruction would happen within that generation, and declared his words more lasting than heaven and earth.

On a Tuesday. Everything else in your life will pass away. Jesus’ words will not. Build on them, literally: choose one sentence of his this week, perhaps this one, and learn it by heart, so that it is in you when other things are taken. And when someone tells you that Jesus got the end wrong, you need not be shaken. Show them this chapter, the two questions and the hinge, and tell them that he got the temple right to the last stone.

For worship. When the stars have fallen and the mountains are gone, his words will still be standing. No promise of his has ever lapsed, and no sentence he spoke has ever been retracted. The temple fell on his word; the elect will be gathered on his word; and the sinner who trusts him is forgiven on his word, with a security more lasting than the universe. The Word made flesh spoke on that hillside, and what he said there will still be true when there is no hillside left.

parallels.desc: the word of our God will stand forever

verseByVerse.quote: "But concerning that day or that hour, no one knows, not even the angels in heaven, nor the Son, but only the Father.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But concerning that day or that hour, no one knows, not even the angels in heaven, nor the Son, but only the Father.

But concerning that day or that hour. But: a contrast, and the hinge of the whole discourse. Jesus turns from these things (v. 30), which would happen within a generation, to that day. Everything before this had signs and a timeframe. Everything after it has neither. That day is the Old Testament’s own phrase for the day of the LORD, the day of final judgment and salvation (Amos 8:9; Zechariah 14:4–9), and here it is the day of the Son of Man’s coming (v. 26).

No one knows. Not even the angels in heaven, nor the Son, but only the Father. No human being can know when Christ will return: no sign, no marker, no calculation, a fact that ought to have retired the date-setting business permanently and never has. The very claim to know is a mark of a false teacher. And notice the ascending scale: not men, not angels who stand in God’s presence, not the Son. He goes as high as it is possible to go before stopping at the Father, and the effect is to slam the door. The Father has fixed the time by his own authority (Acts 1:7).

Nor the Son. No verse in Mark is wielded more often against the deity of Christ, and it is a statement the church would never have invented. Arius built on it in the fourth century: if Jesus did not know the day, he cannot be God. The answer the church has always given, from the early fathers through the Reformers, is the heart of who Christ is. The eternal Son took to himself a complete human nature without ceasing to be fully God, so that there are two natures in the one Lord. According to his divine nature he knows all things. According to his human nature he learned to speak, grew tired, and increased in wisdom (Luke 2:52), which a mind that already knew everything could not do. In becoming man, the Son willingly accepted the limits of a human mind, and did not draw on his divine knowledge in his human consciousness except as the Father willed. This is part of his humbling (Philippians 2:6–8), and of his perfect obedience.

The same structure as the storm. That is no more a contradiction than that the same Jesus could sleep in the stern of a boat because he was exhausted, and then stand up and silence a hurricane with a word (4:38–39). The one he did as a weary man; the other as the Lord of creation. Nobody finds that passage a problem, and it is the identical structure.

What it does not mean. Not that Jesus is less than fully God, as Arians argued from this verse. Notice the order: men, angels, the Son, the Father. Jesus places himself above the angels, alongside the Father, as the Son. And Mark has set the proof one verse back: the same speaker who says he does not know the day has just said that heaven and earth will pass away but his words will not, a claim no creature could dare to make. The starkest claim to deity in the Gospel and the starkest confession of human limitation, one breath apart, both true: that is the profile of God become man.

Does the risen Christ know the day now? Scripture does not say directly, and we should be modest. But many theologians have thought that the limitation belonged to the days of his humiliation. The risen and exalted Christ has received all authority in heaven and on earth (Matthew 28:18), and in Revelation it is he who is given the revelation of what must soon take place to show to his servants (Revelation 1:1). What is certain is that he is no longer in the state of humbling, and that the day is safe in the hands of the Father who has given all judgment to the Son (John 5:22). Either way, it is not ours to know.

So what am I to do with not knowing? Treat it as a gift rather than a gap. If you knew the day, you would be tempted to put off repentance, obedience and kindness until the last moment, and to live the rest of the time for yourself. Not knowing means every day is a day to be ready. It also frees you: you are not responsible for working out God’s calendar, only for being faithful in yours. Plan for the future, as wise servants do, and hold your plans in open hands: if the Lord wills, we will live and do this or that (James 4:15).

In a sentence. No one knows the day or hour of Christ’s return, not the angels, not the Son in his human nature, but only the Father.

On a Tuesday. If Jesus did not know the day, ignore anyone who claims to, and do not forward the video that does. Your task is not to calculate but to be ready. Ask yourself one honest question today: is there anything I am putting off until later that I would not want to be putting off if I knew he was coming this week? Then do it now, because you do not know that he is not.

For worship. The Son who knows the end from the beginning stood on a hillside with a human mind and said that the day was his Father’s secret. He emptied himself so far that he would not reach for what his Father had not given him, and he said so honestly to four men who would have given anything for a date. Such humility belongs to God alone. The Lord of time submitted to time for us, and the one who will come on that day once entered our days, so that we could stand unafraid when it comes.

parallels.desc: not for you to know times or seasons

verseByVerse.quote: Be on guard, keep awake. For you do not know when the time will come. It is like a man going on a journey, when he leaves home and puts his servants in charge, each with his work, and commands the doorkeeper to stay awake.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Be on guard, keep awake. For you do not know when the time will come. It is like a man going on a journey, when he leaves home and puts his servants in charge, each with his work, and commands the doorkeeper to stay awake.

Be on guard, keep awake. For you do not know when the time will come. The practical point of the whole discourse. Two commands, and the reason given is the ignorance he has just confessed. Because nobody knows, therefore watch. The uncertainty is not a problem to be solved but the very ground of the instruction. Keep awake (agrypneite) means stay sleepless, alert. The time (kairos) is the appointed moment.

It is like a man going on a journey, when he leaves home and puts his servants in charge. Every clause is load-bearing. The man is Jesus, about to leave by his death, resurrection and ascension, and to return. The master is genuinely absent, not watching from around the corner, and the house runs without him for an indefinite period, which is exactly the situation of the church between the ascension and the return. And he does not lock the doors or leave a caretaker. He hands the running of the house to the people who work in it: real authority, real responsibility, real trust.

Each with his work. Stop there, because this phrase defines what watchfulness means in this chapter, and it is not what the word suggests to us. Every servant has a job, and it is his job, specific, assigned, different from the next man’s. The servants in this parable are not standing at the window scanning the road. They are working. Watching, here, is doing the thing you were left to do. Waiting for Christ is not passive; every believer has work prepared for him (Ephesians 2:10), and it is never in vain (1 Corinthians 15:58).

And commands the doorkeeper to stay awake. One man has a post at the door, ready to open the moment the master knocks, at any hour. His job happens to be the watching, which is the one occupation in the household that produces nothing visible and looks, to anyone passing, like doing nothing at all. It is still work, and he was told to do it. The doorkeeper may picture church leaders, who keep watch over souls (Hebrews 13:17), or every believer. Either way, someone is meant to be listening for the knock.

Two mistakes ruled out. The parable cuts against both standard mistakes: anxious calculation, which reads every crisis as a countdown, and practical forgetting, which lives as though he is not coming back because he has not come back yet. The man who is ready is not the man who worked out the date. He is the man found at his post when the door opens.

How do I know what my work is? Start with what is already in front of you, because the master assigned it. Your calling in the home: a husband loving his wife, parents raising children in the Lord, children honouring parents. Your calling in the world: the job you are paid for, done honestly and well as for the Lord (Colossians 3:23). Your calling in the church: the gifts the Spirit has given you, used for others (1 Peter 4:10). And the calling of every believer: to pray, to love your neighbour, and to make Christ known. You do not need a dramatic sense of destiny. You need to be faithful in what he has put in your hands.

Does watching mean I should not plan for the future? No. Servants left in charge of a house for an indefinite period must plan: repair the roof, sow the field, save for the winter. Paul rebuked those who stopped working because they thought the end was near (2 Thessalonians 3:10–12). Plan your career, save for your children, build things that will take years. Watchfulness is not idleness and it is not panic. It is doing everything as someone who will give an account to the master, and holding it all ready to be handed back.

In a sentence. Because no one knows the time, Jesus’ followers must stay alert, like servants each doing their work and a doorkeeper keeping watch while their master is away.

On a Tuesday. This turns the whole chapter into a question you can actually answer this week. Not when? He has refused that four times. But: what did he leave me to do, and am I doing it? The children in your house. The work you are paid for. The person you were asked to visit. The gift you have not used in three years. Each with his work. Pick one of them and do it today as if the door might open tonight.

For worship. The master who went away is the one who came first as a servant, and did the work the Father gave him to the last word: it is finished. He did not leave his house empty. He gave his servants his authority, his Spirit and his trust, and he gives every one of them work that matters to him. Nothing done for him is lost; every cup of cold water is remembered. And the absence is not for ever. He is coming back to the house he bought with his blood, and the one who knocks will be the one who once stood outside and was rejected, and who now comes home in glory to share his joy with his servants.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore stay awake—for you do not know when the master of the house will come, in the evening, or at midnight, or when the rooster crows, or in the morning— lest he come suddenly and find you asleep. And what I say to you I say to all: Stay awake."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Therefore stay awake, for you do not know when the master of the house will come, in the evening, or at midnight, or when the rooster crows, or in the morning, lest he come suddenly and find you asleep. And what I say to you I say to all: stay awake.

Therefore stay awake, for you do not know when the master of the house will come. He lists the four watches of the Roman night: evening, midnight, cockcrow, morning; roughly six to nine, nine to twelve, twelve to three, three to six. The whole of the dark, divided up, and he could come in any of them.

In the evening, or at midnight, or when the rooster crows, or in the morning. Now look at what Mark does with those four watches in the next two chapters, because it is one of the most remarkable things in this Gospel and easy to miss. In the evening: when it was evening, he came with the twelve (14:17), and they sat down to the supper. At midnight: Gethsemane, where he asks them to watch with him, and comes back and finds them sleeping, three times, and says to Peter, could you not watch one hour? (14:37). When the rooster crows: the courtyard, and Peter’s third denial, and immediately the rooster crowed a second time (14:72). In the morning: as soon as it was morning, the chief priests held a consultation and delivered him to Pilate (15:1). All four watches, in order, in the space of a single night. Mark has written the parable into the passion narrative.

Lest he come suddenly and find you asleep. That is exactly what happens. He came to them in the garden, at his hour of greatest need, and found them asleep, and the words Mark uses are the words of this parable. Stay awake is the same verb, three times in Gethsemane (14:34, 37, 38). So the disciples were told this on Tuesday and failed it on Thursday, and Mark makes sure his reader sees it. Sleep is a picture of spiritual unreadiness: complacency, carelessness, being absorbed in this world (Romans 13:11–14; 1 Thessalonians 5:4–8).

A mercy, not merely an indictment. The men who failed the test in the garden are the men Christ went to the cross for, and restored on a beach, and sent to the ends of the earth. Failing to watch is not the end of a disciple. But do not imagine, reading this comfortably, that you would have stayed awake. They loved him and they were exhausted and they meant it, and they could not manage an hour.

And what I say to you I say to all: Stay awake. The last words of the discourse, and of Jesus’ teaching before the passion, and they are addressed past the four men on the hillside to everyone who would ever read this, including the person holding this book. So the chapter that began with a question about dates ends with a command instead. Not calculate. Not be afraid. Stay awake: at your post, doing your work, in a house whose master is coming back.

What does spiritual sleep look like? It rarely looks like open rebellion. It looks like prayer slowly crowded out by busyness, Scripture read without expecting to meet God, sin tolerated because it has become familiar, and a heart more excited about the next holiday than about the return of Christ. It is the condition of the five foolish virgins, who were not wicked, only unprepared (Matthew 25:1–13). Its great symptom is that you do not notice it, because sleepers rarely know they are asleep. That is why the command is repeated so often, and why we need one another to say it: wake up.

I know I am spiritually drowsy. What do I actually do? First, admit it to God plainly, and do not wait to feel awake before you come to him. Then return to the simple means he has given: his word read daily and slowly, prayer at a set time, the Lord’s Day with his people, and the Supper. Cut out what dulls you, whether it is a habit of the screen, a hidden sin or a constant noise. Find a believer who will ask you honestly how you are doing. And remember Gethsemane: the remedy for sleepy disciples was not their resolve but his intercession. He prayed for Peter that his faith would not fail (Luke 22:32), and he prays for you.

In a sentence. Since the master may come at any hour, Jesus commanded all his followers to stay awake, so that he will not come suddenly and find them asleep.

On a Tuesday. If Jesus came today, would he find you awake: living for him, doing his work, ready to meet him? Do not answer with a feeling; answer with a list of what you did yesterday. Then live this day as if it might be the day: say the word you have been putting off, confess the sin you have been excusing, do the work you were given, and go to bed tonight in peace, because the master you are waiting for is the one who loves you.

For worship. And then he gets up off that hillside and walks down into the four watches of his own night, the evening, the midnight, the cockcrow and the morning, awake through every one of them, while everybody who loved him slept. He watched when they could not. He prayed while they slept. He stayed awake through the darkest night in history, so that his sleeping, failing, forgiven disciples would be found ready when he comes. Our watchfulness is only ever a small reflection of his. The master of the house never slumbers nor sleeps, and when he comes suddenly, he will come for those he has kept awake by his grace.
verseByVerse.note: These are the four Roman watches of the night, roughly from 6 p.m. to 6 a.m.

13.theology:
Two questions, two answers, one discourse. The key to Mark 13 is that the disciples asked about the temple (v. 4), and the seam between the two answers is visible if you look for it. Everything down to v. 30 carries signs and a timeframe — false messiahs, wars, the abomination in the holy place, the flight from Judea — and this generation will not pass away until all these things take place. Every one of them did happen, in AD 70. Then v. 32 turns the corner: But concerning that day or that hour, no one knows. From there, the opposite of everything before — no sign, no date, nobody knows. Read this way, Jesus was not mistaken by a day: the temple fell in their lifetime as he said, and his own coming remains unmarked as he said.

Not even the Son (v. 32) is the verse most often used against Christ's deity, from Arius onwards. The answer is not a dodge but the heart of the incarnation: the one person, the eternal Son, took a complete human nature without ceasing to be fully God. As God he knows the hour; as man he increased in wisdom (Luke 2:52), which a mind that already knew everything could not do. It is the same structure as sleeping in a boat from exhaustion and then silencing the storm with a word (4:38–39) — the one as a weary man, the other as Lord of creation.

And Mark set the proof one verse earlier. In v. 31 the same speaker says heaven and earth will pass away, but my words will not pass away — a claim no creature could dare make, setting his own sentences above the created order. In v. 32 the same mouth says he does not know the day. The starkest claim to deity and the starkest confession of human limitation, one breath apart, both true. This verse is not a problem for his deity; it is one of the clearest windows in the Gospel onto the two natures in the one Christ.

And the signs will work (v. 22). Jesus does not say the wonders will be faked. Pharaoh's magicians duplicated the plagues (Ex. 7:22); Deuteronomy legislates for a prophet whose sign comes to pass and who then leads you to other gods (Deut. 13:1–3). The supernatural is not self-authenticating. It works is never by itself a reason to follow anybody; the test is always the doctrine underneath (1 Jn. 4:2–3).
13.examples:
Then: in the evening, or at midnight, or when the rooster crows, or in the morning — the four watches of the Roman night, listed as the hours at which the master might come home.

And Mark writes all four into the next two chapters, in order. When it was evening, he came with the twelve (14:17). At midnight, Gethsemane — where he asks them to watch, comes back and finds them sleeping, three times, and says could you not watch one hour? (14:37). At cockcrow, the courtyard, and immediately the rooster crowed a second time (14:72). And as soon as it was morning, the chief priests delivered him to Pilate (15:1).

The parable's own words are the passion narrative's words. Lest he come suddenly and find you asleep — and he came to them in the garden at his hour of greatest need and found them asleep.

Now: do not read that as an indictment only. The men who failed it in the garden are the men he died for, restored on a beach, and sent to the ends of the earth. But do not imagine you would have stayed awake either. They loved him, they meant it, they were exhausted — and they could not manage an hour.

And note how the closing parable defines watchfulness: the servants are given jobs, each with his work. Not scanning the road; working. The man who is ready is not the one who calculated the date but the one found at his post when the door opens. So the question this chapter finally asks is answerable this week: what did he leave me to do, and am I doing it?

14.title: The Cup, the Kiss, and the Fire
14.text: <sup>1</sup>It was now two days before the Passover and the Feast of Unleavened Bread. And the chief priests and the scribes were seeking how to arrest him by stealth and kill him, <sup>2</sup>for they said, “Not during the feast, lest there be an uproar from the people.” <sup>3</sup>And while he was at Bethany in the house of Simon the leper, as he was reclining at table, a woman came with an alabaster flask of ointment of pure nard, very costly, and she broke the flask and poured it over his head. <sup>4</sup>There were some who said to themselves indignantly, “Why was the ointment wasted like that? <sup>5</sup>For this ointment could have been sold for more than three hundred denarii and given to the poor.” And they scolded her. <sup>6</sup>But Jesus said, “Leave her alone. Why do you trouble her? She has done a beautiful thing to me. <sup>7</sup>For you always have the poor with you, and whenever you want, you can do good for them. But you will not always have me. <sup>8</sup>She has done what she could; she has anointed my body beforehand for burial. <sup>9</sup>And truly, I say to you, wherever the gospel is proclaimed in the whole world, what she has done will be told in memory of her.” <sup>10</sup>Then Judas Iscariot, who was one of the twelve, went to the chief priests in order to betray him to them. <sup>11</sup>And when they heard it, they were glad and promised to give him money. And he sought an opportunity to betray him. <sup>12</sup>And on the first day of Unleavened Bread, when they sacrificed the Passover lamb, his disciples said to him, “Where will you have us go and prepare for you to eat the Passover?” <sup>13</sup>And he sent two of his disciples and said to them, “Go into the city, and a man carrying a jar of water will meet you.
