Follow him, <sup>14</sup>and wherever he enters, say to the master of the house, ‘The Teacher says, Where is my guest room, where I may eat the Passover with my disciples?’ <sup>15</sup>And he will show you a large upper room furnished and ready; there prepare for us.” <sup>16</sup>And the disciples set out and went to the city and found it just as he had told them, and they prepared the Passover. <sup>17</sup>And when it was evening, he came with the twelve. <sup>18</sup>And as they were reclining at table and eating, Jesus said, “Truly, I say to you, one of you will betray me, one who is eating with me.” <sup>19</sup>They began to be sorrowful and to say to him one after another, “Is it I?” <sup>20</sup>He said to them, “It is one of the twelve, one who is dipping bread into the dish with me. <sup>21</sup>For the Son of Man goes as it is written of him, but woe to that man by whom the Son of Man is betrayed! It would have been better for that man if he had not been born.” <sup>22</sup>And as they were eating, he took bread, and after blessing it broke it and gave it to them, and said, “Take; this is my body.” <sup>23</sup>And he took a cup, and when he had given thanks he gave it to them, and they all drank of it. <sup>24</sup>And he said to them, “This is my blood of the covenant, which is poured out for many. <sup>25</sup>Truly, I say to you, I will not drink again of the fruit of the vine until that day when I drink it new in the kingdom of God.” <sup>26</sup>And when they had sung a hymn, they went out to the Mount of Olives. <sup>27</sup>And Jesus said to them, “You will all fall away, for it is written, ‘I will strike the shepherd, and the sheep will be scattered.’ <sup>28</sup>But after I am raised up, I will go before you to Galilee.” <sup>29</sup>Peter said to him, “Even though they all fall away, I will not.” <sup>30</sup>And Jesus said to him, “Truly, I tell you, this very night, before the rooster crows twice, you will deny me three times.” <sup>31</sup>But he said emphatically, “If I must die with you, I will not deny you.” And they all said the same. <sup>32</sup>And they went to a place called Gethsemane. And he said to his disciples, “Sit here while I pray.” <sup>33</sup>And he took with him Peter and James and John, and began to be greatly distressed and troubled. <sup>34</sup>And he said to them, “My soul is very sorrowful, even to death. Remain here and watch.” <sup>35</sup>And going a little farther, he fell on the ground and prayed that, if it were possible, the hour might pass from him. <sup>36</sup>And he said, “Abba, Father, all things are possible for you. Remove this cup from me. Yet not what I will, but what you will.” <sup>37</sup>And he came and found them sleeping, and he said to Peter, “Simon, are you asleep? Could you not watch one hour? <sup>38</sup>Watch and pray that you may not enter into temptation. The spirit indeed is willing, but the flesh is weak.” <sup>39</sup>And again he went away and prayed, saying the same words. <sup>40</sup>And again he came and found them sleeping, for their eyes were very heavy, and they did not know what to answer him. <sup>41</sup>And he came the third time and said to them, “Are you still sleeping and taking your rest? It is enough; the hour has come. The Son of Man is betrayed into the hands of sinners. <sup>42</sup>Rise, let us be going; see, my betrayer is at hand.” <sup>43</sup>And immediately, while he was still speaking, Judas came, one of the twelve, and with him a crowd with swords and clubs, from the chief priests and the scribes and the elders. <sup>44</sup>Now the betrayer had given them a sign, saying, “The one I will kiss is the man. Seize him and lead him away under guard.” <sup>45</sup>And when he came, he went up to him at once and said, “Rabbi!” And he kissed him. <sup>46</sup>And they laid hands on him and seized him. <sup>47</sup>But one of those who stood by drew his sword and struck the servant of the high priest and cut off his ear. <sup>48</sup>And Jesus said to them, “Have you come out as against a robber, with swords and clubs to capture me? <sup>49</sup>Day after day I was with you in the temple teaching, and you did not seize me. But let the Scriptures be fulfilled.” <sup>50</sup>And they all left him and fled. <sup>51</sup>And a young man followed him, with nothing but a linen cloth about his body. And they seized him, <sup>52</sup>but he left the linen cloth and ran away naked. <sup>53</sup>And they led Jesus to the high priest. And all the chief priests and the elders and the scribes came together. <sup>54</sup>And Peter had followed him at a distance, right into the courtyard of the high priest. And he was sitting with the guards and warming himself at the fire. <sup>55</sup>Now the chief priests and the whole council were seeking testimony against Jesus to put him to death, but they found none. <sup>56</sup>For many bore false witness against him, but their testimony did not agree. <sup>57</sup>And some stood up and bore false witness against him, saying, <sup>58</sup>“We heard him say, ‘I will destroy this temple that is made with hands, and in three days I will build another, not made with hands.’” <sup>59</sup>Yet even about this their testimony did not agree. <sup>60</sup>And the high priest stood up in the midst and asked Jesus, “Have you no answer to make? What is it that these men testify against you?” <sup>61</sup>But he remained silent and made no answer. Again the high priest asked him, “Are you the Christ, the Son of the Blessed?” <sup>62</sup>And Jesus said, “I am, and you will see the Son of Man seated at the right hand of Power, and coming with the clouds of heaven.” <sup>63</sup>And the high priest tore his garments and said, “What further witnesses do we need? <sup>64</sup>You have heard his blasphemy. What is your decision?” And they all condemned him as deserving death. <sup>65</sup>And some began to spit on him and to cover his face and to strike him, saying to him, “Prophesy!” And the guards received him with blows. <sup>66</sup>And as Peter was below in the courtyard, one of the servant girls of the high priest came, <sup>67</sup>and seeing Peter warming himself, she looked at him and said, “You also were with the Nazarene, Jesus.” <sup>68</sup>But he denied it, saying, “I neither know nor understand what you mean.” And he went out into the gateway and the rooster crowed. <sup>69</sup>And the servant girl saw him and began again to say to the bystanders, “This man is one of them.” <sup>70</sup>But again he denied it. And after a little while the bystanders again said to Peter, “Certainly you are one of them, for you are a Galilean.” <sup>71</sup>But he began to invoke a curse on himself and to swear, “I do not know this man of whom you speak.” <sup>72</sup>And immediately the rooster crowed a second time. And Peter remembered how Jesus had said to him, “Before the rooster crows twice, you will deny me three times.” And he broke down and wept.
14.overview:
The longest chapter in Mark, and the clock runs in hours. Two days before Passover the chief priests decide to take him quietly — not during the feast — and are overruled by their own accomplice, so that the Lamb dies at Passover after all.

Mark wraps that plot around a woman in Bethany who breaks a flask of nard worth a year's wages over his head. The room calls it waste; he calls it beautiful, and says she has anointed him for burial. Then Judas goes out and sells him for less than the perfume cost.

In a borrowed upper room he takes the Passover bread — the meal that had looked backwards to Egypt for fourteen centuries — and turns it round: this is my body, and this is my blood of the covenant, which is poured out for many. Then they sing the Hallel and walk out into the dark.

What follows is the most exposed scene in the Gospels. In an olive grove, appalled and shaking, he asks his Father to take away the cup — the Old Testament's cup of wrath — and adds the words that hold the world together: yet not what I will, but what you will. Three times he comes back to friends who cannot stay awake for an hour.

Then a kiss, an armed crowd, and every one of them running. Upstairs in the high priest's house he answers the direct question at last — I am — and is condemned for it. Downstairs, at a charcoal fire, Peter says, in effect, "I am not", three times, and a bird calls.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–26 — Anointing, Betrayal, and the Last Supper
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The plot and the perfume (vv. 1–11). Two days before Passover the chief priests are looking for a way to take him quietly. Mark then interrupts them with a woman in a house in Bethany breaking a flask of nard over his head — and closes the sandwich with Judas going to the priests for money. The plot frames the anointing, and the anointing interprets the plot: while men calculate the price of his death, a woman prepares his body for burial.

The upper room (vv. 12–21). Two disciples are sent into the city with a sign — a man carrying a water jar — and find everything as he said. And at the table, with the twelve reclining round him, he says that one of them will hand him over, and none of them looks at Judas.

The Supper (vv. 22–26). He takes the bread of the Passover, the meal that had commemorated the exodus for fourteen centuries, and says this is my body. He takes the cup and says this is my blood of the covenant, which is poured out for many.

Then they sing, and go out into the night.
verseByVerse.theology:
He is not attending the Passover. He is the Passover.

For fourteen hundred years Israel had killed a lamb, put its blood where the destroyer would see it, and eaten a meal standing up, ready to leave — and told their children that this was the night God brought them out. Every element of that meal pointed backwards.

Jesus takes it and turns it round. The bread is his body. The cup is my blood of the covenant — which is Moses's phrase at Sinai, where he threw blood over the people and said behold the blood of the covenant that the LORD has made with you (Ex. 24:8), and it is Jeremiah's promise of a new covenant written on hearts, with sins remembered no more (Jer. 31:31–34).

So there is a new exodus, and he is the lamb of it, and the blood goes not on a doorframe but into a cup that is handed round a table and drunk.

And poured out for many is Isaiah 53 — the Servant who poured out his soul to death and bore the sin of many (Isa. 53:12) — and it is his own word from 10:45, where the Son of Man gives his life as a ransom for many. Not a tragedy that overtook him. A ransom, deliberately paid, for a definite number of people whom he knew by name.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: a woman breaks a flask worth a year's wages over his head, and the room objects that it could have been sold for the poor.

The objection is not stupid. Three hundred denarii would have fed a great many families, and the New Testament is fierce about the poor. But Jesus quotes Deuteronomy 15:11 at them — you always have the poor with you — and it is worth knowing that the verse he is quoting goes on: therefore I command you, You shall open wide your hand to your brother, to the needy and to the poor, in your land. He is not excusing anyone from generosity. He is saying that this particular week will not come again.

Now: and then the sentence for everyone who has ever felt they had nothing worth giving: she has done what she could.

Not what she should have. Not what somebody more capable would have. What she could — which was one thing, and she did it, and he called it beautiful and said it would be told wherever the gospel went. It has been, for two thousand years, and Mark does not even record her name.

That is the measure. Not the scale of the service but whether it was the whole of what you had.

verseByVerse.quote: It was now two days before the Passover and the Feast of Unleavened Bread. And the chief priests and the scribes were seeking how to arrest him by stealth and kill him, for they said, "Not during the feast, lest there be an uproar from the people."
verseByVerse.commentary:
It was now two days before the Passover and the Feast of Unleavened Bread. The chief priests and the scribes were looking for a way to arrest Jesus by stealth and kill him, for they said: not during the feast, or there may be an uproar from the people.

Meaning first. Mark 14 is the longest chapter in this Gospel, and it covers less than a day. It opens with a plot to kill Jesus quietly and ends with the leader of his disciples weeping in a courtyard before dawn. Between them come the great scenes of the passion. A woman pours a year’s wages over his head, and he calls it beautiful; Judas sells him for silver. Jesus eats the Passover with the twelve, names the betrayer at the table, and gives them bread and cup as his body and his blood of the covenant, poured out for many. On the way to the Mount of Olives he tells them they will all fall away, and in the same breath tells them where he will meet them after he is raised. In Gethsemane he falls on the ground and asks the Father to remove the cup of wrath, and then says not my will but yours, while his friends sleep. He is betrayed with a kiss and deserted by everyone. Before the council the witnesses cannot agree, until he himself answers the high priest: I am, and you will see the Son of Man at God’s right hand. Downstairs Peter denies him three times. The chapter shows sin at its worst, in friends and in rulers, and a Saviour who walks into it all with open eyes, of his own will, for those who fail him.

The setting. The passion narrative proper begins. Chapters 14–15 cover about thirty-six hours, told in great detail. The early church told this story more than any other, and Mark’s account was probably shaped by years of preaching it.

It was now two days before the Passover and the Feast of Unleavened Bread. Mark starts the clock. From here to the end of the chapter, time is measured in hours. And the setting is not incidental. Passover (Hebrew Pesach) was the feast of deliverance, the night God brought Israel out of Egypt and the angel of death passed over the houses marked with a lamb’s blood (Exodus 12). The lamb was sacrificed on the afternoon of 14 Nisan and eaten that evening, which by Jewish reckoning was the start of 15 Nisan. The Feast of Unleavened Bread was the week that followed (Exodus 12:15–20), and the two were spoken of together. The city was full. Josephus gives figures that are surely inflated, but every account agrees that the population swelled several times over; pilgrims camped on the hillsides, and lambs were being counted into the temple by the thousand. Jesus will die as the true Passover lamb (1 Corinthians 5:7).

And the chief priests and the scribes were seeking how to arrest him by stealth and kill him. They have wanted this since chapter 3, when Pharisees and Herodians walked out of a synagogue together to plan it (3:6), and the plot grew in Jerusalem (11:18; 12:12). What has changed is that it is now an operational question: not whether, but how. By stealth means by cunning, by a trick. They need him away from the crowd, in the dark, with no witnesses.

For they said, Not during the feast, lest there be an uproar from the people. Jerusalem was packed with pilgrims, many from Galilee who supported Jesus. Passover, the feast of liberation, was a time of high nationalist feeling, and the Roman governor brought extra troops to the city. A public arrest could start a riot. So this is a decision of policy, taken by the highest religious authority in Israel on grounds of crowd control. Their considered judgment was: not this week. Wait until the pilgrims have gone home and the city is quiet. And he died on the Friday of that very feast. They did not change their minds because they were persuaded. They changed them because an opportunity arrived they had not counted on: a man from the inside, offering to do it quietly, that night (v. 10). So the timetable of the crucifixion was set not by the Sanhedrin’s plan but against it.

The date was not negotiable. That matters more than it might seem. The lamb had to die at Passover, and every element of the timing had been fixed since Exodus 12, fourteen centuries earlier. So watch what happens in this chapter. The most powerful men in Jerusalem make a plan and are overruled by their own accomplice. Judas thinks he is arranging a transaction. The priests think they are managing a problem of public order. Pilate will think he is settling a provincial dispute. Every one of them is a free agent doing exactly what he wants, and every one of them is running to a schedule set before the world was made: this Jesus, delivered up according to the definite plan and foreknowledge of God, you crucified and killed by the hands of lawless men (Acts 2:23). Both halves of that sentence are true, and Mark holds them together without embarrassment from here to the end.

If God planned it, were the plotters really guilty? Yes, entirely. They did what they wanted to do, for their own reasons, and God did not put one evil desire into their hearts. What God did was rule over their evil, so that it accomplished the very thing they never intended: the salvation of the world. Joseph said it to his brothers: you meant evil against me, but God meant it for good (Genesis 50:20). Scripture never explains how both are true together, but it never lets go of either. That is a comfort, not a puzzle, for anyone who has been wronged: the people who hurt you are answerable, and they are not in charge.

In a sentence. Two days before Passover, the leaders plotted to arrest and kill Jesus quietly, intending to wait until after the feast for fear of the crowds.

On a Tuesday. Human plans are made, but God’s purpose stands (Proverbs 19:21). Think of the plans being made this week that could hurt you or people you love: the meeting about your job, the diagnosis, the decision of a government. Write one of them down and beside it write: not during the feast. The most carefully laid plan in Jerusalem was overruled within forty-eight hours. Even the plots of his enemies serve his timing, and so do the plans of yours.

For worship. The Lamb of God was never a victim of the calendar. Fourteen centuries before, God had written the date into the law of Moses, and on that date, against the wishes of the most powerful men in the land, his Son died. Kings and councils take counsel together against the LORD and his Anointed, and he who sits in the heavens laughs. Every hour of this chapter is in his hand, and every hour of ours. The plot to kill Jesus quietly became the most public act of love the world has ever seen, at exactly the moment God had appointed.
verseByVerse.note: Passover recalled Israel’s rescue from Egypt; Unleavened Bread was the week-long feast that followed it. Jerusalem swelled with pilgrims.

parallels.desc: the council resolves to kill him

verseByVerse.quote: And while he was at Bethany in the house of Simon the leper, as he was reclining at table, a woman came with an alabaster flask of ointment of pure nard, very costly, and she broke the flask and poured it over his head. There were some who said to themselves indignantly, "Why was the ointment wasted like that?
verseByVerse.commentary:
While he was at Bethany in the house of Simon the leper, as he was reclining at table, a woman came with an alabaster flask of ointment of pure nard, very costly. She broke the flask and poured it over his head. There were some who said to themselves indignantly: why was the ointment wasted like that?

The structure. Another of Mark’s sandwiches. The plot of the leaders (vv. 1–2) and the betrayal by Judas (vv. 10–11) are the bread; the woman’s devotion is the filling. Hatred and treachery on either side, and in the middle, extravagant love.

And while he was at Bethany in the house of Simon the leper. Bethany is the village over the ridge from Jerusalem where he has been sleeping all week (11:11). And the house belongs to Simon the leper, a man who is plainly not a leper any longer, since he is hosting a dinner and people are reclining at his table. A leper could do neither; he lived outside the town and shouted unclean at anyone who came near (Leviticus 13:45–46). So presumably somebody healed him, the nickname stuck, and now the man who used to warn strangers away has the Son of God at his table two days before the cross. Mark does not tell us the story. He does not need to. Chapter 1 told us that a leper knelt before Jesus and Jesus touched him (1:40–42). Whether or not this is the same man, it is the same kind of house, and it is where the Lord chose to spend one of his last evenings. John places this dinner six days before Passover, and Mark may have placed it here for its meaning rather than its date (John 12:1–8).

As he was reclining at table. At a formal dinner guests lay on couches around a low table, leaning on the left elbow, with their feet away from the table. That is why a woman could come up behind him.

A woman came. Mark does not name her. John tells us she was Mary, the sister of Martha and Lazarus (John 12:3). Luke records a different anointing earlier, by a sinful woman in Galilee (Luke 7:36–50).

With an alabaster flask of ointment of pure nard, very costly. Every word is doing work. Alabaster was a soft translucent stone carved into small flasks for perfume, often with a long sealed neck and no stopper; the neck had to be snapped off. Nard (spikenard) was an oil from the root of a plant that grows in the Himalayas. It came overland thousands of miles from India, and its price reflected the journey. Mark’s word for pure (pistikēs) may mean genuine, unadulterated: this is not the diluted version. Very costly: verse 5 gives the figure, about a year of a working man’s income in a bottle. It may have been a family treasure, her dowry or her savings. Perfume was a way of storing wealth in portable form, and for a woman with few property rights a sealed flask of nard might be everything she had against old age.

And she broke the flask and poured it over his head. She snaps the neck, and once it is broken it cannot be resealed. There is no using half and keeping half. The breaking is a decision that all of it is going somewhere. And then she pours it over his head, which is not what you do with perfume. A drop on the wrist is the normal use. This is the whole flask, running down his hair and his beard and onto his clothes and the floor, until the house could smell nothing else. It is also, though nobody in that house says so, how kings were made (1 Samuel 10:1; 2 Kings 9:6). Messiah means anointed one. Without perhaps knowing it, she anointed the King. John says she also anointed his feet (John 12:3).

There were some who said to themselves indignantly, Why was the ointment wasted like that? And the room turns on her. Matthew says the disciples said it (Matthew 26:8); John, that Judas led them (John 12:4–5). Wasted: that is their verdict, and it is the only verdict available to a calculating mind. Something valuable has been destroyed and there is nothing to show for it. Love always looks like waste to those who calculate.

Was this the same woman as the sinful woman in Luke? Almost certainly not. Luke’s anointing happens in Galilee, much earlier, in the house of a Pharisee also named Simon, and the woman is known in the town as a sinner who weeps over Jesus’ feet (Luke 7:36–50). This one is in Bethany, in the last week, and John names her as Mary of Bethany. Simon was a common name, and anointing an honoured guest was a known custom. The two stories teach different things: Luke’s, the love of the forgiven; this one, the love that sees what is coming and gives everything before it is too late.

In a sentence. At a dinner in Bethany, a woman broke an alabaster jar of very expensive perfume and poured it all on Jesus’ head, and some were indignant at the waste.

On a Tuesday. Ask what in your life is sealed in an alabaster flask: the thing you have kept back because it is too precious to spend on him. Your time on a Sunday afternoon, a career plan, a sum of money, a child you have never really handed over, a reputation. Then notice the instinct that rises when you think of giving it, and the word it uses. It will almost certainly say waste. That word is the clue that you have found the flask.

For worship. She broke the flask because he was about to be broken. The fragrance that filled Simon’s house was a small picture of what his death would do: he loved us and gave himself up for us, a fragrant offering and sacrifice to God (Ephesians 5:2). She poured out a year’s wages; he poured out his soul to death. Nothing given to him is wasted, because he gave himself without measure, and there is no flask in any house on earth worth as much as the head she anointed.
verseByVerse.note: John names the woman as Mary, sister of Martha and Lazarus. Nard was a costly perfume imported from India. Alabaster was a soft stone used for perfume flasks.

verseByVerse.quote: For this ointment could have been sold for more than three hundred denarii and given to the poor." And they scolded her.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For this ointment could have been sold for more than three hundred denarii and given to the poor. And they scolded her.

For this ointment could have been sold for more than three hundred denarii and given to the poor. Here is the objection stated in full, and it must be taken seriously rather than brushed aside, because it is a good objection. A denarius was a day’s wage for a labourer, so three hundred denarii was about a year’s wages, allowing for no work on Sabbaths and feast days. It would have fed a great many families in a city where the poor were everywhere and there was no safety net but almsgiving. It was customary to give to the poor at Passover. And the New Testament is fierce about this. Religion that is pure and undefiled before God is to visit orphans and widows in their affliction (James 1:27). Jesus himself told a rich man to sell everything and give to the poor four chapters ago (10:21). So this is not a stupid objection, and it is not obviously a wicked one. It is the objection any sensible, socially concerned, morally serious person would make. Which is exactly why the passage is so searching.

And they scolded her. The word (enebrimōnto) is strong: they snorted at her, went at her. Picture it. She has just done the most extravagant thing she will ever do, in public, in a room full of men, on an impulse she probably could not have explained, and the room rounds on her and tells her she has wasted money that should have gone to the hungry. She says nothing. Mark records not one word from her in the whole account.

Who started it. John tells us, and it changes the flavour entirely. It was Judas, who said this not because he cared about the poor, but because he was a thief, and having charge of the moneybag he used to help himself to what was put into it (John 12:6). So the objection about the poor came first from a man stealing from the fund for the poor. And the rest of the room agreed with him, because it was a reasonable thing to say. The mechanism has not aged. A perfectly sound principle can be used as cover, and the people repeating it need not be insincere; most of the men in that room were not. It is very easy to criticise somebody else’s costly devotion in the name of a good cause, to feel morally serious while doing it, and to give nothing yourself.

Two kinds of exchange. Within two days Judas will have his silver, and this woman will have nothing left. Mark has put them side by side on purpose: one person in this chapter turns Jesus into money, and one turns money into worship.

How do I balance generosity to the poor with gifts for worship? Not by choosing one. Jesus does not say the poor do not matter; in the next verse he reminds them of the command to open wide your hand. The same Lord who received the perfume told the rich man to sell everything for the poor. The real contrast in this passage is not between worship and charity but between love and calculation. A heart that has given everything to Christ will be generous to the poor, because he loves them. So give regularly to the needy, give gladly to the work of the gospel, and when someone else gives extravagantly to Christ, do not appoint yourself auditor of their gift.

In a sentence. They complained that the perfume, worth a year’s wages, should have been sold and given to the poor, and they harshly rebuked her.

On a Tuesday. Be slow to criticise others’ devotion to Christ; pious-sounding objections can hide a cold heart. The next time you catch yourself thinking that someone is overdoing it, giving too much, praying too long, going too far for the gospel, ask two questions before you say anything. What have I given myself? And whose voice in the room is this objection really coming from?

For worship. Christ was silent when they scolded the woman only until he spoke for her, and he has never stopped speaking for those who love him. The world will always call devotion to him a waste, and it will always be wrong, because he is worth more than every denarius ever minted. The one whose life was sold for silver is the one for whom no price could ever be too high. The perfume ran down to the floor and was gone; the love it expressed is remembered wherever the gospel goes.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that a denarius was a day’s wage; three hundred denarii was about a year’s wages. John says the complaint came from Judas.

verseByVerse.quote: But Jesus said, "Leave her alone. Why do you trouble her? She has done a beautiful thing to me. For you always have the poor with you, and whenever you want, you can do good for them. But you will not always have me. She has done what she could; she has anointed my body beforehand for burial. And truly, I say to you, wherever the gospel is proclaimed in the whole world, what she has done will be told in memory of her."
verseByVerse.commentary:
But Jesus said: leave her alone. Why do you trouble her? She has done a beautiful thing to me. For you always have the poor with you, and whenever you want, you can do good for them. But you will not always have me. She has done what she could; she has anointed my body beforehand for burial. And truly, I tell you, wherever the gospel is proclaimed in the whole world, what she has done will be told in memory of her.

Leave her alone. Why do you trouble her? He defends her before he explains her, which is worth noticing. The first thing out of his mouth is not theology but protection: get off her. Why do you trouble her is tender. He has seen what the room is doing to a woman who cannot answer back.

She has done a beautiful thing to me. The word is kalos: good, fine, lovely. Not merely permissible; beautiful. And that word is the whole answer to waste. The disciples were applying the only category they had, which is usefulness: what did it achieve, what could have been bought, what was the return. Jesus introduces another category altogether, one a purely practical religion has no room for. There is a place for the beautiful and the useless. Worship is precisely that. Nobody is fed by it and nothing is produced, and God calls it lovely, which is why he commanded gold and blue and scarlet and fine twined linen for a tent in a desert. Love for Jesus that does not count the cost is beautiful to him.

For you always have the poor with you, and whenever you want, you can do good for them. This sentence has been misused for centuries as a shrug, the poor are a permanent feature so do not exert yourself, and it must be rescued, because it is a quotation and the original settles it. He is quoting Deuteronomy 15:11: there will never cease to be poor in the land; therefore I command you, you shall open wide your hand to your brother, to the needy and to the poor. The permanence of poverty is the reason for open-handedness, not an excuse from it. Every Jew in that room knew how the verse ended. And note his own clause, found only in Mark: whenever you want, you can do good for them. It assumes they will, and should.

But you will not always have me. There is the point. This is not a general principle about extravagance against charity. It is a statement about a week that will not come again. He has two days left. The opportunity to do anything at all for the physical body of Jesus of Nazareth is closing, and this woman is the only person in Jerusalem who appears to have noticed.

She has done what she could. Only Mark has this, and it is one of the loveliest sentences in the Gospel. It should be laid up by anyone who has ever felt that what they have to offer is not worth offering. Not what she should have done. Not what a more capable person would have managed. What she could: one thing, done once, with everything she had, and he called it beautiful. That is the measure, and it is a mercy. The question is never the scale of the service. It is whether it was the whole of what you had. Two small coins from a widow outweighed the treasury (12:44); a flask from a woman with nothing else outweighed the criticism of twelve apostles.

She has anointed my body beforehand for burial. And now he tells them what she has actually done, and it is more than she knew. Bodies were anointed with spices and perfumes for burial. Jesus would die as a criminal, there would be no time to anoint his body properly, and the women who came to do it on Sunday morning would find the tomb empty (16:1). This woman is the only person who managed it, and she managed it while he was still alive. Did she understand? Perhaps more than the disciples, who had been told three times and never heard it. Either way, Jesus gives her act its meaning. She came to honour him; he tells her she has buried him.

Wherever the gospel is proclaimed in the whole world, what she has done will be told in memory of her. A remarkable prediction, two days before his death: the gospel will be preached throughout the world (13:10). It has been, for two thousand years on every continent, and her story with it, as you read this. The disciples criticised her; Jesus made her famous. And here is the last touch: Mark does not tell us her name. So the promise is kept in a strange way. The whole world knows what she did, and the Gospel that promises she will be remembered does not say who she was. She is not famous; the deed is. And the one who noticed it and made sure it was written down is the same one who watched a widow put in two coins nobody heard.

Is it right to spend money on beautiful buildings, music and worship? It can be, within limits this passage itself sets. God cares about beauty; he commanded it for the tabernacle and he called this woman’s act beautiful. Worship offered with care, skill and cost honours him. But the gift was love poured on Christ himself, not display. Beauty that serves pride, or that is bought while the church neglects its poor, or that replaces the preaching of the gospel, has lost the point. The test is the one Jesus applies: is this done to me? A plain room where Christ is adored is more beautiful to him than a cathedral where he is ignored.

What if what I can do for Christ is very small? Then you are exactly the person this verse was written for. Perhaps you are ill, elderly, poor, housebound, caring for small children, or simply ordinary. He does not ask what a gifted or wealthy person could do; he asks what you can. A prayer offered faithfully every day, a meal taken to a neighbour, a note to a missionary, a hard conversation had in love: he sees it, and he calls it beautiful. No one will be asked on the last day why they did not do what someone else could. The only question is whether you gave him what was yours.

In a sentence. Jesus defended the woman, calling her act beautiful, an anointing of his body for burial, and promised it would be told wherever the gospel is preached.

On a Tuesday. Do what you can for Christ. It may not seem much, but he calls it beautiful. Name one thing you could do this week that would be costly, unnoticed and done simply because you love him, and do it before Sunday. And if you have a habit of measuring every Christian act by its results, practise one act of worship this week whose only purpose is that he deserves it.

For worship. Here is a Lord who notices. He sees past the scolding room to the trembling woman, past the cost to the love, past the perfume to the heart. He receives what we bring, small and clumsy as it is, and calls it beautiful, and writes it down for ever. And he was himself the great extravagance of heaven: the Father did not spare his own Son, but poured him out for us. The one anointed for burial in Bethany is the one who rose, and the fragrance of what he did has filled the whole world.
verseByVerse.note: Bodies were anointed with spices for burial.

parallels.desc: there will never cease to be poor in the land

verseByVerse.quote: Then Judas Iscariot, who was one of the twelve, went to the chief priests in order to betray him to them. And when they heard it, they were glad and promised to give him money. And he sought an opportunity to betray him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then Judas Iscariot, who was one of the Twelve, went to the chief priests to betray him to them. When they heard it, they were glad and promised to give him money. And he looked for an opportunity to betray him.

Then Judas Iscariot, who was one of the twelve, went to the chief priests in order to betray him to them. The sandwich closes. Plot, anointing, plot, and Mark’s arrangement makes the contrast unavoidable: a woman pours out a year’s wages on him, and a man goes out to sell him. Iscariot may mean man of Kerioth, a town in southern Judea, which would make him the only one of the Twelve not from Galilee; some think it comes from sicarius, dagger-man, a revolutionary. He went to them; they did not come to him.

Who was one of the twelve. Mark says it here, and Jesus will say it at the table (v. 20), and Mark will say it again when the mob arrives (v. 43). Three times in one chapter, as though he cannot stop. It is the thing that will not go away. Not a follower, not a sympathiser. One of the twelve: appointed on the mountain (3:19), sent out two by two with authority over unclean spirits, present at every private explanation, a man who had shared his life for three years.

And when they heard it, they were glad. That is the word, and it is chilling in its ordinariness. The men who had just decided not during the feast are delighted, because the problem they could not solve has just walked through the door and offered to solve itself. An insider could tell them where to find Jesus at night, away from the crowds.

And promised to give him money. Mark does not give the figure; Matthew does: thirty pieces of silver (Matthew 26:15). That is the compensation the Law fixed for a slave gored by an ox (Exodus 21:32), and the wage thrown to the rejected shepherd in Zechariah with the LORD’s own dry comment, the lordly price at which I was priced by them (Zechariah 11:12–13). Set the two halves of this passage against each other and the arithmetic is unbearable. The perfume was three hundred denarii. Thirty pieces of silver was perhaps a hundred and twenty. A woman spent more on his head than the priests paid for his life.

And he sought an opportunity to betray him. Mark’s word is eukairōs: a good moment, a convenient time. So it does not happen at once. Judas goes back to the group and waits, and eats with them, and watches for a gap. He sat through the supper knowing. He heard one of you will betray me and said, is it I?, with the rest.

Why did he do it? The Gospels give several reasons, and it is worth resisting the urge to supply more. Greed: he was a thief (John 12:6) and asked what they would give him (Matthew 26:15). Satan: Satan entered into him (Luke 22:3; John 13:2, 27). Perhaps also disillusionment: Jesus was not the political Messiah he expected, and kept talking about dying, and the waste of a year’s wages may have been the last straw. What Mark gives us is not a motive but a mechanism, and it is more useful. The betrayal of Jesus works by an opportune time: privately, quietly, when nobody is watching and the cost of loyalty has suddenly become visible and a reasonable-looking alternative has appeared. That is how it always works. Almost nobody decides to abandon Christ. A moment simply arrives in which it is very much easier not to be associated with him, and there is a way out that can be explained to yourself, and it is taken. Judas found his gap in a garden after dark. Peter will find his beside a fire within hours. The difference between them is not the failure. It is verse 72.

What it does not mean. Not that Judas was a helpless puppet, forced by God or Satan. He chose freely and was fully responsible (v. 21). Yet his evil act was within God’s plan, foretold in Scripture (Psalm 41:9; John 13:18; Acts 1:16). God’s sovereignty and human responsibility are both fully true (Acts 2:23).

Was Judas ever a true believer? No. John says Jesus knew from the beginning who would betray him, and called him a devil while he was still among the twelve (John 6:64, 70). He was called to be an apostle and given real gifts, but he never belonged to Christ in the heart; Jesus calls him the son of destruction (John 17:12). That is a warning, not a riddle. A person can be near Jesus, active in his work and respected by his people, and still love something else more. Gifts, office and experience are not the same as faith.

Could I turn out to be a Judas? If you are asking with fear, that is already a good sign, because Judas never asked it with fear. The question to ask is not whether you have ever failed, since every disciple in that room failed that night, but whether you are still coming to Christ as your Saviour and treasure. Judas’s heart was set on money and he hid it. If you bring your sins into the light, grieve over them and run to Christ, you are on Peter’s road, not his. Examine yourself, as Scripture says (2 Corinthians 13:5), and then look away from yourself to the one who keeps all who come to him.

In a sentence. Judas, one of the Twelve, went to the chief priests offering to betray Jesus, and they gladly promised him money.

On a Tuesday. Being close to Jesus outwardly is no guarantee of a true heart, so guard against the love of money (1 Timothy 6:10) and every quiet compromise. Ask where your opportune time is likely to come: the meeting where saying nothing would be easier, the deal where no one would know, the friendship where Christ is never mentioned. Decide now, in the light, what you will do then. And if you handle money for others, at church or at work, be scrupulously open about it. Judas began with the moneybag.

For worship. He knew. He chose Judas, washed his feet, gave him bread from his own hand, and warned him to his face, and he went on loving the eleven who would run. The Son of God was sold for the price of a slave so that slaves could be bought back for God. The silver bought a potter’s field for burying strangers; his blood bought a people from every nation. No traitor’s bargain could stop the plan of grace. It only fixed the price, and he paid it.
verseByVerse.note: Matthew says the price was thirty pieces of silver.

verseByVerse.quote: And on the first day of Unleavened Bread, when they sacrificed the Passover lamb, his disciples said to him, "Where will you have us go and prepare for you to eat the Passover?" And he sent two of his disciples and said to them, "Go into the city, and a man carrying a jar of water will meet you. Follow him,
verseByVerse.commentary:
On the first day of Unleavened Bread, when they sacrificed the Passover lamb, his disciples said to him: where do you want us to go and prepare for you to eat the Passover? He sent two of his disciples and said to them: go into the city, and a man carrying a jar of water will meet you. Follow him.

On the first day of Unleavened Bread, when they sacrificed the Passover lamb. The Thursday, 14 Nisan. Strictly the feast of Unleavened Bread began on 15 Nisan, but in popular usage the day the lambs were sacrificed was included. And Mark’s clause is worth pausing over: when they sacrificed the Passover lamb. That afternoon in the temple the slaughter went on for hours. Each household, or group of at least ten, brought a lamb; it was killed in the court, the priests caught the blood in basins and passed it along a line to be poured at the base of the altar, and the carcass was taken home to be roasted whole and eaten that night within the walls of Jerusalem. The noise and the smell of it filled the city. And while that was happening, the Lamb of God was arranging where he would eat.

The date of the Last Supper. Mark, Matthew and Luke present the Last Supper as a Passover meal. John seems to place Jesus’ death on the afternoon when the Passover lambs were being slaughtered (John 18:28; 19:14), which would make the supper a day earlier. Many explanations have been offered: that different groups used different calendars that year, that Jesus held the meal a day early, or that John’s phrases refer to the whole week of the feast and its sacrifices, with Preparation meaning the day before the Sabbath of Passover week (see 15:42). The last is the most likely. However it is resolved, both accounts present Jesus’ death as the fulfilment of Passover.

Where will you have us go and prepare for you to eat the Passover? A practical question and a real problem. The Passover had to be eaten inside the walls, and the city was heaving; every room was spoken for. Preparation involved buying and sacrificing the lamb, and preparing the unleavened bread, wine, bitter herbs and sauce.

Go into the city, and a man carrying a jar of water will meet you. Follow him. The instruction is almost comically thin. No address, no name, no directions: go into a city of hundreds of thousands and look for a man with a jug. And it works, because the sign is not as vague as it sounds. Carrying water in a jar was normally women’s work; men carried water in skins. A man with a water pot on his shoulder would stand out in that street from fifty yards. Either Jesus foreknew it, as with the colt (11:2), or he had arranged it secretly. Mark does not say which.

Why the secrecy? This is the part that repays thinking about. Judas has already been to the priests and is waiting for his opportunity. If the place of the meal had been announced in the morning, the arrest could have happened in the middle of it, and the Last Supper would never have taken place. So Jesus arranges a rendezvous that even his own disciples cannot disclose, because they do not know it. Two men are sent, and they cannot tell anybody where they are going until they get there. He is buying an evening. He has something to say and to give to those men that has to be done before the arrest, and he takes precise practical measures to make sure he gets the time. Nothing in this chapter happens to him by accident. He knows what Judas has done and what the priests want, and he plans around them, which is a very different thing from being caught.

In a sentence. On the day the Passover lambs were sacrificed, Jesus sent two disciples into the city to follow a man carrying a water jar to the place where they would eat the Passover.

On a Tuesday. Jesus prepares the way for what he asks you to do. Follow his instructions one step at a time, even when you cannot see the address. And notice that his sovereignty did not make him careless: he made practical arrangements, kept a plan quiet, and guarded the time that mattered. Trusting God and planning wisely are not rivals. Guard the hours this week that matter most for your soul and your family as carefully as he guarded that evening.

For worship. While the city slaughtered its lambs, the true Lamb walked its streets, choosing where he would give himself to his friends. He was not hunted into the cross; he went to it by appointment, keeping every promise of the old Passover and arranging every detail of the new. The blood poured at the base of the altar that afternoon had never taken away a single sin. The blood he was about to pour out would take away the sin of the world.
verseByVerse.note: The lambs were sacrificed at the temple on the afternoon before the Passover meal. Carrying water was usually women’s work, so a man with a jar would stand out.

verseByVerse.quote: and wherever he enters, say to the master of the house, 'The Teacher says, Where is my guest room, where I may eat the Passover with my disciples?' And he will show you a large upper room furnished and ready; there prepare for us." And the disciples set out and went to the city and found it just as he had told them, and they prepared the Passover.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And wherever he enters, say to the master of the house: the Teacher says, where is my guest room, where I may eat the Passover with my disciples? He will show you a large upper room, furnished and ready; prepare for us there. The disciples set out, went to the city, found it just as he had told them, and prepared the Passover.

And wherever he enters, say to the master of the house, The Teacher says, Where is my guest room? The password again, as with the colt (11:3). The Teacher says, and apparently that is enough. So there is a man in Jerusalem who knows exactly who the Teacher is, has a room ready and asks no questions: another of the anonymous people in this Gospel whose property was requested and who did not say no. Perhaps he was a disciple. Note also the confidence of my guest room. Not a room; he speaks as a man with an arrangement. Guest room (katalyma) is the very word used for the inn in Bethlehem where there was no room (Luke 2:7). At his birth there was no room. At his last meal, a room is ready.

And he will show you a large upper room furnished and ready; there prepare for us. Two details, and both are Mark’s own eye. Large: big enough for thirteen men to recline. Passover was eaten reclining, a deliberate contrast with the first Passover eaten standing with sandals on, because a free man reclines at table and a slave does not. Furnished and ready: spread with couches and cushions, reached by an outside stair. Somebody has prepared it already.

A room that may turn up again. Many think this was the house of Mark’s mother, Mary, where the church later met in Jerusalem (Acts 12:12), and perhaps the upper room where the disciples gathered after the ascension, about a hundred and twenty of them (Acts 1:13–15). This cannot be proved, but it would explain some of Mark’s detailed knowledge. Whether or not it is the same house, the church’s first address in Jerusalem was an upstairs room lent by somebody nobody bothered to name.

And the disciples set out and went to the city and found it just as he had told them. It is the pattern of the colt (11:4–6), and it is deliberate. In the last week, the things Jesus predicts keep turning out exactly right, in small matters and large. He said there would be a colt; there was. He said there would be a man with a jar; there was. He said the room would be ready; it was. And in a few hours he will say one of you will betray me, you will all fall away, and before the rooster crows twice you will deny me three times, and those will turn out exactly right too.

And they prepared the Passover. That meant work: taking a lamb to the temple, waiting in the queue, holding it while its throat was cut, carrying it back, roasting it whole, and setting out the unleavened bread, the bitter herbs, the sauce and the wine. Two disciples spent that afternoon preparing a lamb for the man who was about to become one.

Does Jesus still guide his people in such specific ways? He guides us as surely, but not usually in this way. These detailed instructions belonged to his unique hour, and to the apostolic age when new revelation was being given. Today he guides us through his finished word, which is sufficient for every good work (2 Timothy 3:16–17), through wisdom, counsel and the ordinary providence that arranges the details of our lives without announcing them. You should not expect a man with a water jar, or wait for a sign before obeying what Scripture already says. But you can be sure that the rooms of your life are prepared before you arrive in them.

In a sentence. The disciples found the large upper room exactly as Jesus had said, and prepared the Passover there.

On a Tuesday. If Jesus’ word is reliable in such small details, it can be trusted in everything. Think of one promise of his that you find hardest to believe for yourself, perhaps that he will never leave you, or that all things work together for good to those who love God, and set it beside this verse: they found it just as he had told them. And if you have a room, a car, a table or a spare evening, ask whether the Teacher might be asking for it. The church still runs on borrowed upper rooms.

For worship. The Lord who had nowhere to lay his head had a room ready on the night he was betrayed, because his Father provides for his Son and his Son provides for his friends. There was no room at the inn when he came into the world; there was a furnished room when he gave himself for it. And he has gone ahead of us to prepare another: in my Father’s house are many rooms (John 14:2). We will find it just as he told us.
verseByVerse.note: Larger houses had an upper room reached by an outside stair.

verseByVerse.quote: And when it was evening, he came with the twelve. And as they were reclining at table and eating, Jesus said, "Truly, I say to you, one of you will betray me, one who is eating with me." They began to be sorrowful and to say to him one after another, "Is it I?" He said to them, "It is one of the twelve, one who is dipping bread into the dish with me. For the Son of Man goes as it is written of him, but woe to that man by whom the Son of Man is betrayed! It would have been better for that man if he had not been born."
verseByVerse.commentary:
When it was evening, he came with the Twelve. As they were reclining at table and eating, Jesus said: truly, I tell you, one of you will betray me, one who is eating with me. They began to be sorrowful and to say to him one after another: is it I? He said: it is one of the Twelve, one who is dipping bread into the dish with me. For the Son of Man goes as it is written of him, but woe to that man by whom the Son of Man is betrayed! It would have been better for that man if he had not been born.

And when it was evening, he came with the twelve. The Passover was eaten at night, after sunset (Exodus 12:8). And this is the first of the four watches from the parable two nights ago: in the evening, or at midnight, or when the rooster crows, or in the morning (13:35). Mark’s reader is meant to feel the clock start.

Truly, I say to you, one of you will betray me, one who is eating with me. The meal is under way, and he does not open with an accusation but with the amen-formula, which in this Gospel introduces things that must not be missed. One who is eating with me does not narrow anything, since all twelve are eating with him. It is there for the weight of it. In that culture sharing a meal created a bond of loyalty; to eat a man’s bread and then harm him was the deepest treachery available. And the phrase is a quotation: even my close friend in whom I trusted, who ate my bread, has lifted his heel against me (Psalm 41:9), a psalm Jesus quotes in John’s account of this evening (John 13:18).

They began to be sorrowful and to say to him one after another, Is it I? Here is one of the most instructive moments in the Gospel, and it goes by in a line. Nobody looks at Judas. Eleven men have spent three years with him, walked hundreds of miles with him, slept in the same fields. He held the money bag, which means they trusted him with it. And when the Lord says one of them is a traitor, not one of them turns his head. So Judas was not obviously a Judas. There was no tell. And it tells you something about them too. The Greek expects the answer no, surely not I?, so it is not a confession but a fearful hope. Still, every one of them, hearing that a betrayer was in the room, looked first at himself. That instinct is the healthiest thing in the chapter, and the exact opposite of Peter’s boast ten verses later. Self-suspicion is not morbid; it is sanity. Let anyone who thinks that he stands take heed lest he fall (1 Corinthians 10:12).

It is one of the twelve, one who is dipping bread into the dish with me. At the Passover they dipped unleavened bread and bitter herbs into a common bowl of sauce (charoseth, made of fruit and nuts), and several might share one bowl. He does not name him. Matthew and John record a further exchange that identified him to those close enough to hear; Mark leaves it as a description that fits everyone at the table. So Judas is given every chance, up to the last minute, to stop. The warning is public and the identification is private. Nobody drags him out. He could have got up.

For the Son of Man goes as it is written of him. Goes means to his death. As it is written: in Isaiah 53, in Psalm 22, in Psalm 41, in Zechariah. The cross is not an accident or a defeat. It is not the failure of the plan; it is the plan.

But woe to that man by whom the Son of Man is betrayed! Yet God’s plan does not excuse Judas by an inch. Woe is a cry of lament and of judgment together. Here, in one sentence, are the two truths Mark refuses to separate. The Son of Man goes as it is written; and the man who betrays him is fully answerable. Scripture holds both without apology and never resolves them into a formula.

It would have been better for that man if he had not been born. The most terrible sentence Jesus ever spoke about anybody, and it should not be softened. It means that non-existence would have been preferable to what Judas has coming, a plain statement that there is something worse than never having lived. That implies conscious, everlasting loss, not annihilation, and shows that Judas was not saved in the end (John 17:12). And notice that it is said in his hearing, at the table, while he could still have moved. It is not a verdict pronounced afterwards. It is a last warning delivered to a man’s face, which is what makes it mercy as well as judgment.

Is it fair that Judas was lost if his betrayal was written beforehand? Yes. God foretold what Judas would do; he did not make Judas want it. Judas acted from his own greed and unbelief, after three years of seeing Christ’s goodness and receiving his warnings. Nobody will be condemned for what God planned, but for what they themselves chose and loved. That God can rule over a sinner’s free choice to bring about salvation for others is a mystery beyond us, but it is not injustice. And notice how Jesus spoke of it: not with satisfaction, but with woe.

Should I live in fear that I might betray him? Live in humility, not in terror. The disciples’ question is a good one to ask yourself, because it keeps you from trusting your own strength. But the answer to it is not found by staring inward. It is found at the table, where Christ gives himself to sinners who know they are weak. The eleven all failed that night, and all but one were restored, because their hope was in him and not in themselves. Ask is it I?, and then take the bread.

In a sentence. At the Passover meal, Jesus revealed that one of the Twelve who shared his dish would betray him, as Scripture foretold, yet woe to that man.

On a Tuesday. Is it I? is a good question to ask yourself, so never assume you are beyond the capacity for betrayal. When you hear a sermon on sin this Sunday, notice whether your first thought is of someone else who needed to hear it. Then turn the question round, without despair: where am I most like the man who ate his bread and lifted his heel? Name it to God, and ask him to keep you.

For worship. He ate with the man who would betray him and shared the dish with him. He knew every heart at that table and loved them still. The Lord of the Passover was not taken by surprise; he went as it was written, into the hands of the one he had fed. And the same love that warned Judas holds out bread to every sinner who will take it. There is no treachery he has not seen, and no failure that can surprise him, and he goes to the cross for people who say, is it I?, and mean it.
verseByVerse.note: Dipping bread in a shared dish was a mark of close fellowship.

parallels.desc: my close friend, who ate my bread, has lifted his heel against me

verseByVerse.quote: And as they were eating, he took bread, and after blessing it broke it and gave it to them, and said, "Take; this is my body." And he took a cup, and when he had given thanks he gave it to them, and they all drank of it. And he said to them, "This is my blood of the covenant, which is poured out for many.
verseByVerse.commentary:
As they were eating, he took bread, and after blessing it broke it and gave it to them, and said: take; this is my body. And he took a cup, and when he had given thanks he gave it to them, and they all drank from it. He said to them: this is my blood of the covenant, which is poured out for many.

The Passover meal. The meal followed a set order. The head of the household explained the meaning of each element, retelling the story of the exodus: the lamb (God passed over our houses), the unleavened bread (we left Egypt in haste), the bitter herbs (the bitterness of slavery). Four cups of wine were drunk at fixed points. Every man at that table had heard the script at every Passover of his life: this is the bread of affliction which our fathers ate in the land of Egypt. Jesus now takes the bread and the cup at their appointed moments and says something else, about himself. The old Passover gives way to the new.

And as they were eating, he took bread, and after blessing it broke it and gave it to them. Four verbs, and by now the reader of this Gospel knows them: he took, he blessed, he broke, he gave. He did the same on a hillside with five loaves (6:41) and again with seven (8:6). What he did for the hungry crowds he now does for the twelve, and this time the bread is himself. Blessing means thanking God over it, in the traditional Jewish blessing: blessed are you, Lord our God, King of the universe, who brings forth bread from the earth.

Take; this is my body. Jesus gives the bread a new meaning: it signifies his body, about to be broken in death for them. Not the bread of affliction from Egypt, but his own body given. And take: they must receive it. Salvation must be personally received. Whatever else the Supper is, it is Christ given, and given to be received: not looked at, not admired, not discussed. Taken.

And he took a cup, and when he had given thanks he gave it to them, and they all drank of it. Given thanks (eucharistēsas), from which we get Eucharist. Probably the third cup of the Passover meal, the cup of blessing (1 Corinthians 10:16), drunk after the meal (Luke 22:20; 1 Corinthians 11:25). They all drank of it: all, including Judas it seems (Luke 22:21), which is a sober warning that to take the sign is not the same as to have the thing it signifies.

This is my blood of the covenant. Every phrase is quarried out of the Old Testament. My blood of the covenant is Moses’ sentence at Sinai. Having read the law to the people, he took the blood of the sacrifices and threw it over them and said: behold the blood of the covenant that the LORD has made with you (Exodus 24:8). A covenant was ratified by sacrifice and blood, and every man at that table would have caught the echo. And it is new, as Luke and Paul both record (Luke 22:20; 1 Corinthians 11:25), which takes us to Jeremiah: a new covenant, in which God writes his law on hearts and remembers sins no more (Jeremiah 31:31–34; Hebrews 8–9). At Sinai the blood was thrown over the people from outside. Here it is put into a cup and handed round to be drunk.

Which is poured out for many. Poured out: the blood of sacrifice poured out at the altar (Leviticus 4:7). Not a death that happened to him, but a death poured out, deliberately, for people. For many is Isaiah 53 again, where the Servant poured out his soul to death and bore the sin of many (Isaiah 53:12), and his own word from 10:45, the Son of Man came to give his life as a ransom for many. His blood is shed in the place of many, for the forgiveness of sins (Matthew 26:28). This is the heart of the gospel: the substitutionary, atoning death of Christ.

For many. This is not a limitation grudgingly admitted but a promise gladly made. There is a great multitude no one can number whose sins were actually and effectively dealt with that Friday, not made able to be dealt with but dealt with, and if you are trusting him tonight, you are one of the many he had in mind while he was holding that cup. Many Christians read for many as a Hebrew way of saying all, the multitude set against the one (see Romans 5:15–19), and so as a death for every person. The reading given here is the Reformed one: Christ’s blood was poured out for his people, and actually secured their forgiveness. But both readings agree that his death is sufficient for all, offered to all, and that no one who comes is turned away.

Where Christians differ: the Lord’s Supper. Four main views. Roman Catholic teaching holds transubstantiation: the substance of the bread and wine becomes the body and blood of Christ, while their appearance remains, and the Mass is a sacrifice. Lutherans hold that Christ’s body and blood are truly present in, with and under the bread and wine. Zwingli taught that the Supper is chiefly a memorial, reading the words this is my body as this represents my body. Calvin and the Reformed confessions teach that Christ is truly and spiritually present, and that believers, by faith and through the Holy Spirit, truly feed on Christ, though his body is in heaven. Verdict: Calvin’s view is the best reading. When Jesus said this is my body, his body was sitting at the table, and the disciples would not have thought they were eating his flesh; he speaks as he did in I am the door. But the Supper is more than a reminder. It is a real communion with Christ by the Spirit (1 Corinthians 10:16), in which believers are nourished by him. And it is not a repeated sacrifice; Christ was offered once for all (Hebrews 9:25–28; 10:10–14).

What all Christians agree on. Do not let the argument cost you the thing itself. Nearly every Christian tradition agrees that this meal is commanded, that it is central, that it is not a bare memory exercise, and that Christ is truly given to faith in it. Nobody who takes Scripture seriously thinks it is nothing. The point of Jesus’ sentence is not first metaphysics. It is that he gave it to them and told them to take it.

What does it mean to feed on Christ by faith? It means more than thinking about him, and less than chewing his flesh. When you eat the bread and drink the cup, trusting his promise, the Holy Spirit unites you to the risen Christ in heaven, so that you truly receive him and all his benefits: his forgiveness, his life, his strength for the week. The bread nourishes the body; Christ, received by faith, nourishes the soul (Westminster 29.7; see also the 1689 Confession 30.7). As surely as you hold the bread in your hand, so surely is he given to you. That is why the Supper strengthens faith, and why it is a meal rather than a lecture.

Who should come to the Lord’s Supper? Those who belong to Christ and have publicly confessed him. In the New Testament the Supper is for the church, those who have repented, believed and been baptised (Acts 2:41–42). Each one is to examine himself and so eat (1 Corinthians 11:28), not to prove he is worthy, but to come as a sinner trusting Christ and at peace with his brothers. This commentary holds, with the 1689 Confession, that baptism is for believers and comes before the table; paedobaptist brothers who baptise their children also generally require a credible profession of faith before admitting them to the Supper. Those who do not yet trust Christ should not take it, but should take him, and then come.

What if I feel unworthy to take it? Then you understand what the table is for. It was given on the night of betrayal to men who would all run away within hours. Nobody comes because he is worthy; the Supper is medicine for the sick, not a reward for the healthy. Paul’s warning about eating in an unworthy manner (1 Corinthians 11:27) is about coming carelessly, despising the body of Christ or one’s brothers, not about coming while feeling weak. If you are holding on to a known sin with no intention of leaving it, or refusing to be reconciled to someone, deal with that first. Otherwise, come. The bread is for the hungry.

In a sentence. At the Passover, Jesus gave the bread as his body and the cup as his blood of the covenant, poured out for many, establishing the new covenant through his death.

On a Tuesday. Before the next Lord’s Supper at your church, prepare for it during the week: read one of the Gospel accounts of this night, confess the sins you know, put right anything between you and another believer, and ask the Spirit to feed you. At the table itself, do not only remember; receive. Hold the bread and say in your heart: this is for me. And let the meal shape the week after it, as people who have been fed and have a new covenant written on their hearts.

For worship. Every time you take the Lord’s Supper, you proclaim his death until he comes (1 Corinthians 11:26). On the night he was betrayed, with Judas at the table and Gethsemane an hour away, he did not think of himself. He took bread and gave thanks. He looked at men who would desert him and gave them a covenant sealed in his own blood, with forgiveness written into it. The Lamb of the Passover became the host of the feast and its food. He is no longer on the table and no longer on the cross. He is risen and reigning, and by his Spirit he still comes to meet his people at his table, and gives them himself.
verseByVerse.note: At the Passover meal the head of the household explained the bread and cups; Jesus gives them a new meaning. The ESV notes that some manuscripts insert “new” before “covenant.”

parallels.desc: he bore the sin of many

verseByVerse.quote: Truly, I say to you, I will not drink again of the fruit of the vine until that day when I drink it new in the kingdom of God." And when they had sung a hymn, they went out to the Mount of Olives.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Truly, I tell you, I will not drink again of the fruit of the vine until that day when I drink it new in the kingdom of God. And when they had sung a hymn, they went out to the Mount of Olives.

Truly, I say to you, I will not drink again of the fruit of the vine. The last thing he says at the table, and it is not about his death. It is about a party. The fruit of the vine is the phrase used in the Jewish blessing over wine. I will not drink again: he is telling them this is the last meal. He knows he will not eat with them again on this side of the cross, and there is a real renunciation in the sentence, a man giving up the ordinary comfort of wine and company because tomorrow is what it is. Some think he did not drink the fourth Passover cup, the cup of completion, and would finish it only in the kingdom.

Until that day when I drink it new in the kingdom of God. And there is the turn, one of the great turns in the Gospel. On the last night of his life, hours from Gethsemane, he looks past the cross entirely, past the arrest, the flogging, the nails, the grave, and speaks with complete confidence about a future meal at which he will be present and drinking. He is not hoping. There is no if in the sentence. And that meal is a real appointment. The prophets had promised it: on this mountain the LORD of hosts will make for all peoples a feast of rich food, a feast of well-aged wine, and he will swallow up death forever (Isaiah 25:6–8; see Matthew 8:11). Revelation names it: blessed are those who are invited to the marriage supper of the Lamb (Revelation 19:9). So every time the church takes this cup it is doing two things at once: looking back to a death and forward to a dinner. He said he would be there. He has never yet failed to keep an appointment.

And when they had sung a hymn. The Passover liturgy ended with the second half of the Hallel, Psalms 115 to 118. Those were the words; there was no choosing. So the last thing Jesus of Nazareth sang before Gethsemane included these lines. The snares of death encompassed me; then I called on the name of the LORD (Psalm 116:3–4). Precious in the sight of the LORD is the death of his saints (Psalm 116:15). I shall not die, but I shall live (Psalm 118:17). The stone that the builders rejected has become the cornerstone (Psalm 118:22), the very verse he had thrown at the chief priests two days earlier (12:10). Bind the festal sacrifice with cords, up to the horns of the altar (Psalm 118:27). And the last line of the last psalm, the final words he sang before he walked out into the dark: Oh give thanks to the LORD, for he is good; for his steadfast love endures forever (Psalm 118:29). He sang that. On the way to Gethsemane, in a voice that would be praying in agony within the hour, he sang that God is good and his love does not stop.

They went out to the Mount of Olives. Across the Kidron valley, east of the city, to Gethsemane. Luke says this was his custom (Luke 22:39), so Judas knew where to find him. He did not change his habits to avoid arrest. He went where he always went.

Will there really be eating and drinking in the kingdom? Scripture speaks of it plainly and often, and we should not thin it out into mere symbol. The risen Jesus ate fish in front of his disciples (Luke 24:42–43), and the resurrection body is a real body. The new creation will be a world, not a cloud, and the feast is a picture of what it will be: fellowship, joy, abundance, and the presence of the King at the head of the table. Exactly what we will eat we do not know. That we will sit down with Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, and with Christ himself, we do.

How can I sing when my heart is breaking? By singing what he sang. The psalms were not written by people whose lives were going well. They hold grief and praise together, as he did on the way to Gethsemane, and they give you words when you have none. You need not feel cheerful to sing that God is good and his love endures; you need only believe it, and sometimes singing it is how you come to believe it again. Paul and Silas sang in prison with their backs bleeding (Acts 16:25). Your song may be quiet and full of tears. It is still a song he has sung before you.

In a sentence. Jesus vowed not to drink wine again until he drank it new in the kingdom of God, and after singing the Passover psalms, they went out to the Mount of Olives.

On a Tuesday. Learn one of the Hallel psalms this week, perhaps Psalm 116 or the last verses of Psalm 118, and sing or say it on the way to something you dread. And the next time you take the Supper, let the cup point you forward as well as back: you are not only remembering a death, you are rehearsing for a wedding.

For worship. Jesus sang on the way to the cross. With the cup of wrath before him and the betrayer already gone into the night, he lifted his voice and gave thanks to the LORD, for he is good. He went out singing to be bound with cords to the altar, so that we would one day sit at his table in the kingdom and drink the new wine with him. The one who renounced the cup that night has promised to lift it again, and on that day his steadfast love, which endured through Gethsemane and Golgotha, will be the song of the whole creation.
verseByVerse.note: The hymn was probably from the Hallel psalms (Pss 113–118), sung at Passover.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The warning (vv. 27–31). On the walk out he tells them they will all fall away — and in the same breath tells them where to meet him afterwards. Peter says he will not, and says it twice, and the rest say the same.

The garden (vv. 32–42). Then the most exposed scene in the Gospels. He takes three men further in, tells them his soul is sorrowful to the point of death, falls on the ground and asks his Father to take the cup away — and adds the words that hold the world together. Three times he comes back and finds them asleep.

The arrest (vv. 43–52). Judas arrives with a crowd carrying swords and clubs, and identifies him with a kiss. A sword is drawn, an ear comes off, and Jesus asks whether they think he is a robber. Then everybody runs — including a young man who gets away leaving his only garment in a soldier's hand.

And in three of the four watches of the parable he preached two nights ago (13:35), the disciples are asleep or running, and he is awake.
verseByVerse.theology:
What is the cup? Everything in Gethsemane depends on it, and the answer is not the general dread of dying.

Men far less brave than Jesus have gone to horrible deaths singing — including thousands of his own martyrs, many of them under torture, some of them within living memory of this night. If the cup were merely execution, the Christian would have the awkward position of a Lord less composed at the prospect than his servants.

The cup is an Old Testament image, and it is fixed. In the hand of the LORD there is a cup with foaming wine, well mixed, and he pours out from it, and all the wicked of the earth shall drain it down to the dregs (Ps. 75:8). Wake yourself, wake yourself, stand up, O Jerusalem, you who have drunk from the hand of the LORD the cup of his wrath (Isa. 51:17). Take from my hand this cup of the wine of wrath, and make all the nations to whom I send you drink it (Jer. 25:15).

The cup is the wrath of God against sin. That is what is set in front of him in that garden, and it is why a man who had faced hurricanes and legions without a flicker is on the ground shaking.

And he drank it. For our sake he made him to be sin who knew no sin (2 Cor. 5:21). Which means there is nothing left in that cup for anyone who is in him — the reason a Christian can face death more calmly than Christ did in the garden is precisely that Christ was not calm in the garden.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: You will all fall away (v. 27) — and then, before Peter has said a word, but after I am raised up, I will go before you to Galilee (v. 28).

Read those two verses in the order he said them, because the order is the gospel. He announces the restoration before the failure has happened. Not after they repent. Not on condition of anything. He tells eleven men who are about to abandon him where to meet him afterwards.

And the word he uses is a shepherd's word — I will go before you, the way a shepherd walks ahead of the flock. He has just quoted Zechariah about the shepherd struck and the sheep scattered (Zech. 13:7); now he says he will gather them again himself.

Now: and the angel at the empty tomb repeats it, with one addition that has comforted more failing Christians than almost any other line in Scripture: go, tell his disciples and Peter that he is going before you to Galilee (16:7).

The one who was named in the failure is named in the restoration. If you have failed him badly and are wondering whether there is a road back, notice that the road was mapped and announced before you ever took the wrong turn.
