verseByVerse.quote: And Jesus said to them, "You will all fall away, for it is written, 'I will strike the shepherd, and the sheep will be scattered.' But after I am raised up, I will go before you to Galilee."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus said to them: you will all fall away, for it is written, I will strike the shepherd, and the sheep will be scattered. But after I am raised up, I will go before you to Galilee.

You will all fall away. Not some. Not one. All of them, and he says it walking down the hill with them in the dark. The verb (skandalisthēsesthe) means to be tripped up, to stumble over something. It is the word used of the seed on rocky ground that falls away when the heat comes (4:17), and of the offence Nazareth took at him (6:3). Not just Judas: all of them will desert him.

For it is written, I will strike the shepherd, and the sheep will be scattered. He quotes Zechariah 13:7, and the striking thing about the quotation is who does the striking. In Zechariah God says: awake, O sword, against my shepherd, against the man who stands next to me; strike the shepherd. Jesus gives it in the first person: I will strike the shepherd. So the hand behind tomorrow is not finally Judas’s, or Caiaphas’s, or Pilate’s. Those men will all act freely and answer for it. But behind them and over them is the settled purpose of the Father: it was the will of the LORD to crush him (Isaiah 53:10). The death of Jesus is God’s act as well as the act of wicked men. The Father strikes the Son, in judgment for the sins of his people. This is penal substitution in the words of the prophet. And the shepherd is the man who stands next to God: no ordinary man is struck here.

The scattering foreknown. Note what that means for the disciples’ failure. Their scattering is not an unforeseen embarrassment. It was written centuries before, in the same sentence as the striking of the shepherd, and he tells them so before it happens.

But after I am raised up, I will go before you to Galilee. And now the sentence that changes everything, and the whole force of it is in where it stands. He says this before the failure, not after it. Peter has not yet boasted. Nobody has run. The garden has not happened, the courtyard has not happened, the fire has not been lit. And into that moment, having just told eleven men that every one of them will abandon him within hours, he tells them where he will meet them afterwards. There is no condition attached. He does not say if you repent, or if you prove yourselves. He says: after I am raised, I will go on ahead, and I will see you in Galilee.

Go before you. The word is a shepherd’s word: to lead out in front of the flock, walking ahead so they can follow (10:32; John 10:4). He has just quoted a prophecy about a struck shepherd and scattered sheep, and in the next breath he says he will be out in front of them again. The scattered sheep will be gathered. And Galilee, of all places: not Jerusalem, where it all went wrong, but home, where they were called off their boats. The promise is repeated by an angel in an empty tomb on Sunday morning, with one addition that has done more for failing Christians than almost any line in the Bible: go, tell his disciples and Peter (16:7).

If the Father struck the Son, was God angry with Jesus? The Father never stopped loving his Son; Jesus was never more pleasing to him than when he obeyed to the death (John 10:17). But on the cross the Son stood in the place of sinners and bore the wrath their sins deserved. God was not angry with Jesus for anything Jesus had done. He poured out on him the judgment due to us, and Jesus willingly drank it. That is what Scripture means when it says the LORD laid on him the iniquity of us all (Isaiah 53:6) and made him to be sin who knew no sin (2 Corinthians 5:21). It is not a Father punishing an unwilling victim. It is the Father and the Son together, in one love, saving the guilty.

In a sentence. Jesus predicted that all his disciples would desert him, fulfilling Zechariah’s prophecy of the struck shepherd, but promised to go ahead of them to Galilee after he was raised.

On a Tuesday. Christ knows your failures before you commit them, and he has already planned your restoration. If you have failed him, really failed him, not a slip but the kind that makes you wonder whether there is any road back, take this in the order Mark gives it. The restoration was announced before the betrayal happened. The meeting place was fixed while they were still swearing they would never need it. Go to him today, where he said he would be: in his word, in prayer, among his people.

For worship. The sword of God’s justice woke against the shepherd, the man who stands beside God, and it fell on him and not on the sheep. He was struck so that we would be spared, scattered so that we would be gathered, forsaken so that we would be found. And before any of them failed him, he had already fixed the place of their restoration. That is grace that runs ahead of our sin: the shepherd goes before the flock even into the grave, and comes out of it first, and waits for them in Galilee.

parallels.desc: strike the shepherd, and the sheep will be scattered
he is going before you to Galilee

verseByVerse.quote: Peter said to him, "Even though they all fall away, I will not." And Jesus said to him, "Truly, I tell you, this very night, before the rooster crows twice, you will deny me three times." But he said emphatically, "If I must die with you, I will not deny you." And they all said the same.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Peter said to him: even though they all fall away, I will not. Jesus said to him: truly, I tell you, this very night, before the rooster crows twice, you will deny me three times. But he said emphatically: if I must die with you, I will not deny you. And they all said the same.

Peter said to him, Even though they all fall away, I will not. You can hear him. It is entirely characteristic and it is meant well, and every word of it is wrong. Even though they all: look at what he has done in four words. He has accepted the prophecy for the other ten and exempted himself, and he has done it in front of them. That is not merely presumption about himself; it is a low estimate of his brothers said aloud in their hearing. He contradicts Jesus, and Scripture. The man who thinks he alone will stand has already begun to fall, because he has stopped needing anybody.

Truly, I tell you, this very night, before the rooster crows twice, you will deny me three times. The answer is not a rebuke but a specification, and Mark’s version is the most precise of the four: today, this very night (Jewish days began at sunset), twice, three times. It is the kind of detail only the man it happened to would remember with that exactness, and this Gospel is Peter’s preaching. He has written down the sentence that broke him, with the numbers in it. A cockcrow around 3 a.m. gave its name to the third watch of the night (13:35).

Why does only Mark say twice? Matthew, Luke and John say before the rooster crows; only Mark says twice. The others give the general warning, before the cockcrow at dawn; Mark, from Peter’s own memory, gives the precise form, with a first crowing that Peter ignored and a second that broke him. There is no contradiction; one account is simply more detailed.

But he said emphatically, If I must die with you, I will not deny you. Emphatically (ekperissōs): vehemently, over and over. Peter is not making a considered statement; he is protesting. And he means it. That is the thing to hold on to, because it is what makes this passage useful rather than merely a story about a boastful man. Peter was not lying. He loved him. In a few hours he will draw a sword against an armed crowd (v. 47; John 18:10), which is more than the other ten manage. Whatever else he was, he was not a coward. But courage in a fight is different from courage alone in a courtyard. He simply did not know himself.

And they all said the same. Mark will not let Peter carry it alone. Every one of them said it, and every one of them ran (v. 50).

The danger of untested confidence. Take the practical lesson, because it is aimed straight at anyone who feels reasonably safe. The danger is not that you might one day decide to abandon Christ. Nobody in this room decided anything. The danger is confidence in a strength that has never been tested: the quiet assumption that you would hold, that you would speak up, that you would not do what those people did. And notice what Jesus does not say. He does not say, then you were never mine. He does not withdraw the promise of verse 28. He tells Peter exactly what he will do, then takes him into the garden anyway, dies for him on the Friday, and has him named by an angel on the Sunday. The boast was hollow. The love behind it was not, and Christ knew the difference.

Is it wrong to promise loyalty to Christ? No. Christians rightly make promises: at baptism, in membership, in marriage, in hymns that say I will follow thee. What went wrong with Peter was not the promise but the ground of it. He put his confidence in his own heart, contradicted his Lord, and compared himself favourably with his brothers. Promise, then, but promise leaning on Christ: by your grace, I will. Pray that he will keep you. And when you hear a warning in Scripture, do not argue with it as Peter did; let it send you to your knees.

In a sentence. Peter insisted he would never desert Jesus, but Jesus predicted that he would deny him three times that very night, and still Peter and the others protested their loyalty.

On a Tuesday. Self-confidence is not faithfulness, so don’t trust your own strength; depend on Christ’s (1 Corinthians 10:12). Think of a temptation you are sure you would never fall into, and pray about it today anyway. And watch the little phrase even though they all. If you ever hear yourself saying that other Christians may compromise but you will not, take it as a fire alarm.

For worship. He knew exactly what Peter would do, to the hour and the count, and loved him without a flicker. He did not cast him off for his boast or wait for him to prove himself. He walked on to the garden and the cross for the man who would deny him, and then sent for him by name. Our Lord is not deceived by our promises, and he is not deterred by our failures. He knows us better than we know ourselves, and he keeps those whom the Father has given him, even when they cannot keep themselves.
verseByVerse.note: Only Mark mentions the rooster crowing twice.

verseByVerse.quote: And they went to a place called Gethsemane. And he said to his disciples, "Sit here while I pray." And he took with him Peter and James and John, and began to be greatly distressed and troubled. And he said to them, "My soul is very sorrowful, even to death. Remain here and watch."
verseByVerse.commentary:
They went to a place called Gethsemane. He said to his disciples: sit here while I pray. He took with him Peter, James and John, and began to be greatly distressed and troubled. He said to them: my soul is very sorrowful, even to death. Remain here and watch.

And they went to a place called Gethsemane. The name means oil press. It was an olive grove on the lower slope of the Mount of Olives, across the Kidron valley, where olives were crushed for their oil. John calls it a garden (John 18:1). Olive trees still grow there, some very old. Here, Jesus will be pressed.

Sit here while I pray. Eight are left at the gate. As at the beginning of his ministry (1:35) and at key moments (6:46), Jesus prays.

And he took with him Peter and James and John. The same three who were taken into Jairus’s house to see a dead girl raised (5:37), and up the mountain to see him transfigured (9:2). They have seen him at his most glorious; now they are taken to see him at his lowest. That is not an accident. Nobody is qualified to speak about the glory who has not also seen the garden. James and John had said they could drink his cup (10:39); Peter had said he would die with him (v. 31). Now they will see what that cup is.

And began to be greatly distressed and troubled. Mark reaches for two of the strongest words available, and it is still not enough. Greatly distressed (ekthambeisthai): overwhelmed with horror, shuddering. Troubled (adēmonein): in anguish, the sort of distress that has no bottom to it. And he began: this is not a settled sorrow he has carried all week. It falls on him in that garden. Jesus, who calmly faced storms, demons and enemies, is overwhelmed. Mark does not soften the picture.

My soul is very sorrowful, even to death. He tells them, in words, what is happening to him, and it is worth noticing that he does. The Son of God, in the worst hour of his life, turns to three friends and says how bad it is. There is a kind of piety that regards that as weakness. It is not in this Gospel. He asked for company and told the truth about his state. The phrase itself echoes the Psalms, where the sufferer says why are you cast down, O my soul? (Psalms 42:5, 11; 43:5), and the word Mark uses is the one the Greek Old Testament uses there. He is praying the Psalms, in the dark, using words that were given to him. Even to death means a sorrow of a weight that could kill a man. Luke the physician records what it did to his body: his sweat became like great drops of blood falling to the ground (Luke 22:44).

Why such anguish? Many martyrs have faced death calmly, even joyfully. Was Jesus less brave than them? No. Jesus faced something no martyr has faced: the cup of God’s wrath against sin (v. 36), separation from the Father (15:34), being made sin for us (2 Corinthians 5:21). It was not death itself but what death meant for him: bearing the judgment of God in the place of sinners. The holy Son, who had known only the Father’s love from eternity, was about to bear his wrath. This is the measure of what our sin deserved, and of his love.

How can the Son of God be so distressed? Because he is truly man as well as God. His human soul shrank from the cup of God’s wrath, as any holy man would, and he said so. But his will was never set against the Father’s; he asked, and then submitted: not what I will, but what you will (v. 36). This is not a crack in the Trinity. It is the obedience of the Son, learned with loud cries and tears (Hebrews 5:7–8).

Remain here and watch. The word from the parable, grēgoreite, stay awake, the same verb he used three times two nights ago (13:34, 35, 37). He is not asking them to fix anything. He is asking them to stay awake near him. He wants their company, and their prayer. That is the plainest description of what friendship costs in somebody else’s grief. You cannot fix it. You are not asked to. You are asked not to go to sleep.

Is it sinful for a Christian to be overwhelmed with sorrow? No. Jesus was sinless, and he was overwhelmed. Grief, dread and anguish are not in themselves failures of faith; they are what a true human heart feels in a fallen world. The Psalms are full of them, and so was Gethsemane. What matters is where you take them. Jesus took his to his friends and to his Father. So do not pretend to a calm you do not have, and do not let anyone tell you that a Christian should never be cast down. Tell God the truth about your state, and tell a friend.

How can I keep watch with someone who is suffering? Stay. Most of the time you will not be able to explain the suffering or end it, and you are not asked to. Be present, be quiet more than you speak, pray with them and for them, and keep coming back. Do not hurry them to feel better or quote verses at them as a way of closing the conversation. Jesus asked for exactly this, and his friends could not give it to him. You can give it to his people, and in doing so you give it to him (Matthew 25:40).

In a sentence. In Gethsemane, Jesus took the three closest disciples with him, and was overwhelmed with horror and sorrow so deep it almost killed him.

On a Tuesday. Think of someone carrying a grief this week, and keep watch with them: a visit, a call, an hour sitting with them, a promise to pray kept daily. And take away this, before anything else in the garden: whatever you are carrying, he is not looking at it from a distance. There is a night in the record when the Son of God was appalled and shaking and told his friends the sorrow was killing him, and he is the one you are bringing yours to.

For worship. Jesus was truly human, and felt horror and grief. He knows the darkness you feel, and he faced a darkness far deeper, for you. The olive press of Gethsemane crushed him so that the oil of gladness could be poured on mourners. He entered the sorrow that our sin deserved, all of it, without anaesthetic, and came out the other side still saying Father. We have a high priest who is able to sympathise with our weaknesses (Hebrews 4:15), because on that night he was weaker than any of us, and loved us through it.
verseByVerse.note: Gethsemane (the name means “oil press”) was an olive grove on the Mount of Olives, across the Kidron Valley.

parallels.desc: why are you cast down, O my soul?

verseByVerse.quote: And going a little farther, he fell on the ground and prayed that, if it were possible, the hour might pass from him. And he said, "Abba, Father, all things are possible for you. Remove this cup from me. Yet not what I will, but what you will."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Going a little farther, he fell on the ground and prayed that, if it were possible, the hour might pass from him. He said: Abba, Father, all things are possible for you. Remove this cup from me. Yet not what I will, but what you will.

And going a little farther, he fell on the ground. Luke says about a stone’s throw (Luke 22:41). Not knelt: fell. Matthew says on his face. Jews normally prayed standing (11:25). This is the man who slept through a hurricane, faced down a legion, and turned over the tables in the temple. He is on the ground in the dirt among the olive roots, prostrate in anguish and submission.

And prayed that, if it were possible, the hour might pass from him. Mark gives us the substance first and then the words. The hour is the appointed time of his suffering and death (v. 41; John 12:27). And note the conditional: if it were possible. He is not demanding. He is asking whether there is another way, and the asking is real.

And he said, Abba, Father. Mark keeps the Aramaic, as he did with Talitha cumi and Ephphatha, and this time it is by far the most significant, because this is the actual sound of Jesus praying. Abba is the ordinary family word a child used for his father in the home. It has sometimes been over-translated as Daddy, which is too small, since grown men used it of their fathers all their lives, but it is unmistakably intimate and domestic, not the language of formal worship. Jewish prayer very rarely, if ever, addressed God that way. Jesus did, because he was the Son. And in the deepest agony of his life, that is the word he reaches for.

The name he handed over. It did not stay his alone. Twice the New Testament says that the Spirit puts this very word into the mouths of ordinary Christians: you have received the Spirit of adoption as sons, by whom we cry, Abba! Father! (Romans 8:15; Galatians 4:6). The name he used in Gethsemane is the name he gave away. We pray as sons and daughters because of the Son, and because he was willing on this night to be treated as though he were not.

All things are possible for you. Before the request, the confession. Jesus believes what he taught (10:27). He does not begin by asking whether God is able. He states that God is able, and then asks, which is the right order, and the reverse of how most of us pray in a crisis.

Remove this cup from me. And here is the request, and everything depends on what the cup is. It is not simply death. That has to be said, because the reading that makes Gethsemane a fear of dying leaves the Christian with a Lord less composed at execution than thousands of his own martyrs, many of whom went to far worse deaths singing. The cup is a fixed Old Testament image for the wrath of God (10:38). In the hand of the LORD there is a cup with foaming wine, and all the wicked of the earth shall drain it down to the dregs (Psalm 75:8). Jerusalem had drunk from the hand of the LORD the cup of his wrath (Isaiah 51:17). Take from my hand this cup of the wine of wrath (Jeremiah 25:15). That is what is standing in front of him in the dark: not the nails, but the undiluted anger of God against every sin of everyone he came to save, and he is to drink it to the dregs. It explains everything about this scene that is otherwise inexplicable. He is not afraid of pain. He is looking into the cup. It is a true request, from a true human will, shrinking from the horror of what lay ahead: if there were any other way to save sinners, let it be found.

Yet not what I will, but what you will. Nine words, and they hold the world together. Notice that he does not withdraw the request. He asks, honestly, for the thing he wants, and then submits. Both are prayer. The asking is not unbelief and the submitting is not resignation. Jesus submits his human will to the Father’s. There was no other way, and he accepted it. This is the obedience that undid Adam’s disobedience (Romans 5:19). In a garden a man was told what the Father’s will was and said, in effect, my will, and the world broke. In a garden a man who could have had anything said not what I will, but what you will, and it was mended. And this is the model for all Christian prayer: honest about our desires, and submitted to God’s will (Matthew 6:10).

What it does not mean. Not that there was conflict or sin in Jesus, or that his will was against the Father’s. His human will naturally shrank from suffering, as it should; to desire suffering for its own sake would be unhealthy. But he willingly submitted it. The early church taught from this passage that Christ has two wills, divine and human, in perfect harmony (the Third Council of Constantinople, 681).

Was there really no other way? Gethsemane is the answer. The Son asked the Father, who can do all things, whether the cup could pass, and the answer was no. If sinners could have been saved by teaching, by example, or by God simply overlooking sin, the Father would not have handed his beloved Son that cup. Sin is so serious, and God so just, that nothing but the death of a perfect substitute could pay for it (Hebrews 9:22; Romans 3:25–26). That should silence every suggestion that there are many roads to God. If there had been another road, the Father would have opened it in that garden.

Is it a lack of faith to pray if it is your will? Not when it means what it meant on Jesus’ lips. Some teach that adding if it be your will undermines faith. But the Son of God prayed it, at the moment of greatest need, and he did not lack faith. Where God has plainly promised something, such as forgiveness to those who confess, pray with confidence. Where he has not told you his will, such as whether a sick friend will recover, ask boldly for what you want, and then entrust it to him. That is not a hedge against disappointment. It is the trust of a child who knows the Father is wiser than he is.

In a sentence. Prostrate on the ground, Jesus asked his Father, if possible, to remove the cup of suffering, yet submitted wholly to the Father’s will.

On a Tuesday. When you pray, tell God honestly what you want, and then pray as Jesus did: not what I will, but what you will. Take the hardest thing you are praying about this week and pray it in two halves, aloud if you can: first the plain request, with nothing held back, then the handing over. And when the answer is no, remember that the cup did not pass from him, and he drank it, and that is why there is nothing left in it for you.

For worship. He fell on the ground so that we could stand. He called God Abba in the dark, and then took the cup that made him cry, my God, my God, why have you forsaken me?, so that we could call God Abba for ever. He drained the wrath of God to the last drop, and handed us instead the cup of blessing. The second Adam in the second garden said not my will, and by his obedience many are made righteous. Every child of God who prays Abba is praying a word that cost him Gethsemane.
verseByVerse.note: “Abba” is Aramaic for “father,” the word a child used at home. The “cup” pictures God’s judgment poured out.

verseByVerse.quote: And he came and found them sleeping, and he said to Peter, "Simon, are you asleep? Could you not watch one hour? Watch and pray that you may not enter into temptation. The spirit indeed is willing, but the flesh is weak."
verseByVerse.commentary:
He came and found them sleeping, and said to Peter: Simon, are you asleep? Could you not watch one hour? Watch and pray that you may not enter into temptation. The spirit indeed is willing, but the flesh is weak.

And he came and found them sleeping. He gets up off the ground, walks back through the trees, and they are asleep. And this is the moment Mark’s reader has been prepared for. Two nights ago, on a hillside overlooking this valley, he told them a parable about a master who comes home in the night, lest he come suddenly and find you asleep (13:36). He came. They were asleep. The parable is being acted out on the men it was told to, within forty-eight hours.

And he said to Peter, Simon, are you asleep? He speaks to Peter, and he uses the old name. Simon: not Peter, the rock, but the name he had when he was pulling nets out of the lake, before any of this. It is the only time in Mark that Jesus addresses him as Simon, and the choice is deliberate and gentle, and devastating. The man who two hours ago said even though they all fall away, I will not, cannot stay awake.

Could you not watch one hour? One hour. Not the night; an hour. It is the smallest possible request, made by a man dying of grief thirty yards away, and it was too much. A gentle reproach, more sad than angry. And before it is used against them, be honest about the circumstances. It was late, they had eaten a heavy meal with four cups of wine, they had walked, and Luke kindly records that they were sleeping for sorrow (Luke 22:45). Grief exhausts people. They were not indifferent; they were shattered. That does not remove the failure, but it does explain it, and Jesus explains it too.

Watch and pray that you may not enter into temptation. Two commands, and they belong together: stay awake, and pray. Temptation (peirasmon) is a test, a trial, the testing that could make them fall, and it is coming within the hour. The reason given is preventative. He is not scolding them for missing something; he is telling them that in about twenty minutes they are going to be tested, and this hour is the preparation for it. Their only defence is watchful prayer. This is the Lord’s Prayer in action: lead us not into temptation (Matthew 6:13). They slept through the preparation, and failed the test.

Where the battle is decided. Take that as the plainest practical lesson in the chapter. The battle is lost or won before the moment of temptation arrives. The man who has not prayed does not fall in the moment; he fell in the hours before it, when nothing seemed to be happening and there was no obvious reason to be on his knees. Gethsemane is where the courtyard was decided.

The spirit indeed is willing, but the flesh is weak. And then, having named their failure, he explains it, with a sympathy that is almost unbearable given who is speaking and what is coming. Spirit here means the human spirit, the inner person with its good intentions; flesh means human nature in its frailty, not wickedness but weakness. The spirit indeed is willing: he grants it. Their intentions were real; Peter meant every word of his boast. But the flesh is weak. He is not saying they are hypocrites. He is saying they are men. Good intentions without prayer fail. This is the experience of every believer (Romans 7:18–25; Galatians 5:17). And notice who is diagnosing it: somebody who at that moment has been on the ground with his own flesh failing under a weight none of them can imagine. He knows exactly how weak it is. He is finding out.

Why does prayer help against temptation? Because temptation is a lie that looks true in the moment, and prayer puts you in the presence of the truth before the moment comes. In prayer you confess your weakness, so you stop trusting your own strength. You ask for help, and God has promised to give it (1 Corinthians 10:13). You set your mind on Christ, so that other loves look smaller. And you are reminded that you are not alone. That is why Jesus said watch and pray, not merely try harder. Willpower is the spirit being willing. Prayer is how weak flesh is held up.

In a sentence. Finding them asleep, Jesus asked Peter why he could not watch one hour, and urged them to watch and pray, since the spirit is willing but the flesh weak.

On a Tuesday. Good intentions are not enough; before temptation comes, pray. Think of the hour of the day when you are most likely to fall, late at night, after a bad meeting, alone with a screen, and pray before it arrives, not during it. Name the temptation to God in the morning. And if you have failed again, hear him call you by your old name, gently, and then hear him say the spirit is willing. He has not given up on you.

For worship. He knows our frame; he remembers that we are dust (Psalm 103:14). Our Lord is not surprised by our weakness and does not despise it. He has been more tired, more frightened and more alone than we have ever been, and he stayed awake for us. While his friends slept, he prayed. While they failed the test, he passed it. And the one who said the flesh is weak took our weak flesh to the cross, so that his strength could be made perfect in it.

verseByVerse.quote: And again he went away and prayed, saying the same words. And again he came and found them sleeping, for their eyes were very heavy, and they did not know what to answer him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Again he went away and prayed, saying the same words. And again he came and found them sleeping, for their eyes were very heavy, and they did not know what to answer him.

And again he went away and prayed, saying the same words. He goes back and prays it again. Do not hurry past that, because it says something important about prayer that many Christians have never been told. There is a way of thinking that treats repetition as a failure of faith, as though asking twice showed you had not believed the first time, or as though prayer needed fresh and eloquent phrasing to be genuine. Jesus prayed the same sentence three times in one hour, in the most important prayer meeting in history. Matthew records the second prayer, and it has moved: my Father, if this cannot pass unless I drink it, your will be done (Matthew 26:42). The submission deepens.

Not vain repetition. Jesus warned against heaping up empty phrases as the pagans do, thinking they will be heard for their many words (Matthew 6:7). That is mechanical repetition to wear God down. This is different: the same cry from the same heart, because the need has not changed. Paul did the same about his thorn: three times I pleaded with the Lord about this (2 Corinthians 12:8). And when there are no words left, the Spirit himself intercedes with groanings too deep for words (Romans 8:26). So if all you can do tonight is say the same desperate sentence over and over, you are not praying badly. You are praying in Gethsemane.

And again he came and found them sleeping, for their eyes were very heavy. The same again. And Mark adds a small human detail: their eyes were weighed down, which is exactly the phrase you would use of yourself at two in the morning. Mark is honest: they could hardly help it, physically. But that is the point. The flesh is weak.

And they did not know what to answer him. This is the saddest clause in the paragraph, and it is unmistakably Peter’s own memory. They woke, he was standing over them, and there was nothing to say. No excuse would work. They had been asked for one hour, twice, and failed twice, and the silence in that grove must have been terrible. Mark has recorded exactly this before. At the transfiguration Peter blurted out a suggestion about tents, for he did not know what to say (9:6). The same three men, on the mountain of glory and in the garden of agony, the two moments when they saw most clearly who he was, both times with nothing to say.

Honest reporting. That is one of the reasons this Gospel reads like testimony rather than legend. Nobody inventing a founding story writes down that the leaders slept through the crisis and had no answer when they were caught. Peter told it against himself for the rest of his life. And there is a mercy in that, because the church has never been able to pretend that its first leaders were made of better material than the rest of us.

What if God says no to my prayer? Then you are in good company. The Father said no to his own beloved Son in this garden, and it was not because he loved him less, but because the no was the way to the greatest yes in history: the salvation of the world and the Son’s exaltation. God’s no to a believer is never indifference. It is the refusal of a Father who sees what you cannot, and who has promised that all things work together for good to those who love him (Romans 8:28). Keep praying, as Jesus did, until your will is shaped to his, and trust him with what you do not understand.

In a sentence. Jesus prayed the same prayer again, and returned to find them asleep again, ashamed and without an answer.

On a Tuesday. It is all right to pray the same prayer more than once. Keep praying until your will is shaped to God’s. If there is a prayer you have stopped praying because you were embarrassed to keep asking, pick it up again this week. And if you have been the sleeping friend, the one who promised to pray and did not, do not hide in silence as they did. Go back, tell him, and start again tonight.

For worship. Three times he prayed in the dark, and three times his friends failed him, and he never once failed them. His intercession did not stop in the garden. He always lives to make intercession for those who draw near to God through him (Hebrews 7:25). While we sleep he watches; when we have no words he is our advocate; when we do not know what to answer, he answers for us. The Son who prayed your will be done in Gethsemane now sits at the Father’s right hand, and the will of God for his people is that not one of them will be lost.

verseByVerse.quote: And he came the third time and said to them, "Are you still sleeping and taking your rest? It is enough; the hour has come. The Son of Man is betrayed into the hands of sinners. Rise, let us be going; see, my betrayer is at hand."
verseByVerse.commentary:
He came the third time and said to them: are you still sleeping and taking your rest? It is enough; the hour has come. The Son of Man is betrayed into the hands of sinners. Rise, let us be going; see, my betrayer is at hand.

And he came the third time and said to them, Are you still sleeping and taking your rest? Three times he prayed; three times he came back; three times they were asleep. And within hours Peter will deny him three times. Mark’s numbers are not accidental. The sentence can be read as a question or as a resigned statement, sleep on now and take your rest, and the Greek allows either. Either way the tone has changed. He is no longer asking them for anything.

Settled in prayer. Something has happened in that third prayer. He went into the grove appalled and shaking; he comes out of it settled, and every sentence from here to the cross has the same steadiness in it. The struggle was real and it is over. He asked, he submitted, the answer was no, and he takes the no and gets up.

It is enough; the hour has come. It is enough (apechei) is an obscure word. It may mean it is settled, or enough of this, or even the account is paid, for it was used on receipts. Whatever its exact meaning, the time for prayer is over and the time of action has come. The hour is the word he used on the ground, praying that the hour might pass from him (v. 35). It has not passed. It has arrived. Mark has been building to it since chapter 1. It does not sneak up on him. He announces it.

The Son of Man is betrayed into the hands of sinners. He has said this three times before, in three passion predictions (8:31; 9:31; 10:33). This is the fourth, and the tense has changed. It is no longer will be. It is happening. And sinners: the leaders, who considered themselves righteous and the Gentiles sinners, are themselves the sinners into whose hands he is given.

Rise, let us be going; see, my betrayer is at hand. One of the most extraordinary sentences in the Gospel, and everything depends on the direction he is facing when he says it. Rise, let us be going sounds for half a second like an escape: get up, we are leaving. It is the opposite. Torches are coming up the path from the Kidron valley and he can see them, and he is walking towards them. The disciples are half asleep. Judas is arriving with an armed crowd. And the man who has spent the last hour on the ground begging for another way stands up and says: come, let us go and meet him. Nobody takes him. He goes. No one takes it from me, but I lay it down of my own accord (John 10:18). And notice the pronoun: my betrayer. Not the betrayer. He still owns him; the man is still, in some terrible sense, his.

How did Jesus go from anguish to such calm? Through prayer, and through submission. He did not talk himself into courage or stop feeling the weight. He laid the whole matter before the Father three times, until his human will rested in the Father’s will. The cup was no smaller, but he had accepted it. That is the peace Paul describes: by prayer and supplication with thanksgiving let your requests be made known to God, and the peace of God will guard your hearts (Philippians 4:6–7). It is not the peace of having your way. It is the peace of having given it up to someone you trust.

In a sentence. Finding them asleep a third time, Jesus announced that the hour of his betrayal had come and rose to go and meet the betrayer.

On a Tuesday. Prayer turns anguish into resolve, so pray until you can rise and face what is coming. If there is something you have been dreading, the appointment, the confession, the conversation, the operation, take it to God until you can say rise, let us be going, and then go and meet it. You will not go alone.

For worship. So Gethsemane ends with the sleeping disciples woken by the sound of their Lord walking towards the men who have come to kill him, having settled the matter in prayer while they slept. He was not dragged to Calvary. He rose from his knees and went, with his face set like flint. The good shepherd lays down his life for the sheep, and he does it with open eyes, at the hour appointed, of his own free will. That is how much he wanted us.

verseByVerse.quote: And immediately, while he was still speaking, Judas came, one of the twelve, and with him a crowd with swords and clubs, from the chief priests and the scribes and the elders. Now the betrayer had given them a sign, saying, "The one I will kiss is the man. Seize him and lead him away under guard." And when he came, he went up to him at once and said, "Rabbi!" And he kissed him. And they laid hands on him and seized him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Immediately, while he was still speaking, Judas came, one of the Twelve, and with him a crowd with swords and clubs, from the chief priests, the scribes and the elders. The betrayer had given them a sign: the one I will kiss is the man. Seize him and lead him away under guard. When he came, he went up to him at once and said: Rabbi! And he kissed him. And they laid hands on him and seized him.

And immediately, while he was still speaking, Judas came, one of the twelve. Mark says it again: one of the twelve, the third time in the chapter. He cannot leave it alone, and neither should we. The horror is that it was one of his own.

And with him a crowd with swords and clubs, from the chief priests and the scribes and the elders. An armed party sent by the Sanhedrin: the temple police probably, with servants, and John adds a detachment of Roman soldiers and their commander with lanterns and torches (John 18:3, 12). Swords for the professionals, clubs for the rest. They have come at night, into a garden, in force, to arrest one unarmed teacher and eleven tired men, a teacher who has been standing in the temple courts all week in broad daylight.

Now the betrayer had given them a sign, saying, The one I will kiss is the man. Here is a detail worth pausing on: they needed a sign. The men sent to arrest him could not reliably pick him out, at night, by torchlight, among a dozen Galileans dressed alike. That is a small, believable piece of realism, and it also tells you that Jesus did not look like anything in particular. No halo. Nothing to distinguish the Son of God from the fishermen standing next to him.

Seize him and lead him away under guard. Under guard (asphalōs) means securely, and it is the professional detail. Judas knows what this man has done to crowds and storms, and that he had passed through hostile crowds before (Luke 4:30). He is taking no chances.

Rabbi! And he kissed him. The kiss was the ordinary greeting of a disciple to his teacher: respect, affection, belonging. And Mark’s verb is emphatic (katephilēsen): not simply kissed but kissed him warmly, repeatedly. So the sign chosen to identify him for execution was the sign of love, and it was performed thoroughly. There is nothing in human wickedness worse than this, and the Bible knows it. Joab kissed Amasa as he killed him (2 Samuel 20:9–10). Faithful are the wounds of a friend; profuse are the kisses of an enemy (Proverbs 27:6). And Rabbi, my teacher: that is what he calls him. Not Lord. It is the last word Judas speaks in this Gospel, a title of respect emptied of everything that made it mean anything. Matthew records the answer, and it is almost unbearable: friend, do what you came to do (Matthew 26:50). Luke records another: Judas, would you betray the Son of Man with a kiss? (Luke 22:48). He let him do it. He did not turn his face away or step back. He received the kiss.

And they laid hands on him and seized him. Eight words, and the Gospel turns. From this moment until the resurrection, Jesus of Nazareth is in custody. Everything from here is done to him: he is led, handed over, questioned, struck, flogged, carried out, nailed up. The Son of Man is in the hands of men. The one who could not be bound by a legion of demons, or a storm, or a fever, or death itself, lets a temple guard put its hands on him in the dark and take him away.

How can someone so close to Jesus betray him? Because closeness of position is not the same as love. Judas had the same sermons, the same miracles, the same meals as Peter. What he did not have was a heart that treasured Christ above everything else, and three years of nearness without love hardened him rather than softened him. That is the danger of familiarity with holy things. The cure is not to stay away from Christ, but to keep asking whether you love him, and to be honest when you find something else on the throne.

In a sentence. Judas arrived with an armed crowd from the leaders and identified Jesus by greeting him warmly as Rabbi and kissing him, and they seized him.

On a Tuesday. It is possible to show outward affection for Jesus while betraying him, so let your love for him be real. Look at the outward signs of devotion in your life: the songs you sing, the words you use, the church you attend. Ask whether any of them has become a kiss without a heart. And if someone has betrayed you with friendship, a colleague, a friend, a spouse, remember that your Lord knows exactly what that is like, and bring it to him.

For worship. He let Judas kiss him. The Lord of glory offered his cheek to the traitor and called him friend, and then held out his hands to be bound. He who held the universe together submitted to the grip of a temple guard. He did not need to be identified; he was going to give himself up. He was handed over by a kiss so that we could be welcomed with one, like the son who came home and was embraced by his father before he could finish his confession.
verseByVerse.note: A kiss was the normal greeting of a disciple to his teacher.

verseByVerse.quote: But one of those who stood by drew his sword and struck the servant of the high priest and cut off his ear. And Jesus said to them, "Have you come out as against a robber, with swords and clubs to capture me? Day after day I was with you in the temple teaching, and you did not seize me. But let the Scriptures be fulfilled." And they all left him and fled.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But one of those who stood by drew his sword and struck the servant of the high priest and cut off his ear. Jesus said to them: have you come out as against a robber, with swords and clubs to capture me? Day after day I was with you in the temple teaching, and you did not seize me. But let the Scriptures be fulfilled. And they all left him and fled.

But one of those who stood by drew his sword and struck the servant of the high priest and cut off his ear. Mark does not name him. John, writing much later when everyone involved was dead, says it was Peter, and that the servant’s name was Malchus (John 18:10), the kind of detail you only get from somebody who knew the household. Perhaps Mark, writing while Peter was alive or recently martyred, protected him. And it is worth being fair to Peter. Eleven men are about to run, and one of them draws a weapon against an armed party sent by the Sanhedrin. He was keeping his promise (v. 31), and whatever else he got wrong tonight, he got it wrong bravely.

The wrong kind of loyalty. He also got it entirely wrong. Aiming at a head and taking an ear suggests a wild swing rather than a swordsman’s stroke; the man was a servant, not a soldier. Jesus’ kingdom does not advance by the sword (John 18:36). And Luke the physician records the last healing miracle of Jesus’ ministry before the cross: he touched the ear and healed him (Luke 22:51). The final act of his freedom was to repair the damage his own disciple had done to a man who came to arrest him, a healing done for an enemy.

Does this forbid Christians to use force? Matthew records Jesus’ rebuke, all who take the sword will perish by the sword (Matthew 26:52), and John his reason, my kingdom is not of this world (John 18:36). Jesus forbids the sword to defend his kingdom or to stop the cross. He does not abolish the state’s sword (Romans 13:4), nor the defence of life (Exodus 22:2). Christians may protect themselves and others; they may never advance Christ’s cause by force.

Have you come out as against a robber, with swords and clubs to capture me? He addresses the arresting party, and the question is a rebuke about their method. Robber (lēstēs) is not a pickpocket but a bandit, an armed insurrectionist. It is the word Josephus uses for the Zealot guerrillas, and the word used of Barabbas’s kind (15:7) and of the two men crucified beside him (15:27). So: you have turned out in force, at night, armed, as though I were a terrorist.

Day after day I was with you in the temple teaching, and you did not seize me. He has been standing in their own building, in public, all week. They could have arrested him at any hour of any day. They did not, because of the crowd (12:12; 14:2). So the whole apparatus of swords and torches and a midnight raid is not a security precaution. It is a confession. Men who take a prisoner in the dark are telling you what they think of their own case.

But let the Scriptures be fulfilled. And with that he stops arguing. He breaks off the rebuke and submits. Not, this is a miscarriage of justice, though it is. Not, my Father will vindicate me, though he will. Simply: this is what was written, it is happening, and I am not going to stop it. Perhaps he has in mind Isaiah 53:12, he was numbered with the transgressors, and Zechariah 13:7, the struck shepherd (v. 27). Jesus is not a victim of circumstance. He submits to the Scriptures, which are his Father’s will.

And they all left him and fled. Mark does not soften it by a syllable. All: the eleven who had said an hour ago that they would die with him; the three who could not stay awake; Peter, who had just drawn a sword. Left him: it is the same verb Mark used in chapter 1 when they left their nets and followed him (1:18). They left everything to follow him; now they leave him. You will all fall away (v. 27) is fulfilled within the hour, exactly as he said. The Shepherd is struck, and the sheep are scattered. From here he is alone. There is not a friendly face in the rest of this chapter.

How should I defend Christ when he is attacked? With truth, love and courage, never with the world’s weapons. Peter’s sword is the model of what not to do: anger, force, a wild swing in the dark. The modern versions are online abuse, mockery of opponents, manipulation, and political power used to coerce faith. The apostles learned the right way after Pentecost: they spoke boldly, suffered patiently, and blessed those who cursed them (Acts 4:29; 1 Peter 3:15–16). Christ does not need protecting. He needs witnesses.

In a sentence. When one disciple struck the high priest’s servant with a sword, Jesus rebuked the crowd for arresting him like a bandit, submitted to the Scriptures, and all the disciples deserted him.

On a Tuesday. Don’t defend Christ with the world’s weapons: violence, anger, manipulation. Think of the last argument you had about your faith, and ask whether you came away more like Peter with the sword or Jesus with his hand on the servant’s ear. And when you have deserted him, remember he went on alone for you, and came back for you.

For worship. He healed the man who came to bind him. He refused the sword that could have saved him and the legions of angels he could have called. He let every friend go, so that none of them would be lost: if you seek me, let these men go (John 18:8). The Shepherd stood alone in the torchlight so that the sheep could run, and then he went to gather them again. There is no loneliness like his that night, and because of it, no believer will ever be truly alone.
verseByVerse.note: John names the swordsman as Peter and the servant as Malchus; Luke adds that Jesus healed the ear.

verseByVerse.quote: And a young man followed him, with nothing but a linen cloth about his body. And they seized him, but he left the linen cloth and ran away naked.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A young man followed him, with nothing but a linen cloth about his body. They seized him, but he left the linen cloth and ran away naked.

Only Mark records this. A strange, brief episode, found in no other Gospel, and it has puzzled readers for nineteen centuries, because on the face of it it is pointless. A person nobody has heard of loses his clothes and runs. Nothing depends on it. The narrative would not miss it. Who was he, and why is it here?

A young man followed him. Many have suggested he was Mark himself, which would explain why the story is included at all. It is far too specific and too embarrassing to be invented; nobody puts an anonymous humiliation into a Gospel for the sake of it. It is the classic signature of an eyewitness who wants to be in the record without being named: a small, undignified detail that only he would know and only he would tell, like an artist painting himself into the corner of a picture. And there is a candidate. If the supper was eaten at his mother’s house (Acts 12:12; see v. 15), a young man in that household might well have heard where they had gone, got up in the night with a sheet round him, and followed at a distance. It cannot be proved, but it is an old and attractive suggestion.

With nothing but a linen cloth about his body. Linen was expensive, suggesting a family of some wealth. He had perhaps been asleep and thrown on a sheet.

And they seized him, but he left the linen cloth and ran away naked. Look at what Mark has just told us: they all left him and fled (v. 50). Now the desertion is given a face, one person caught in the torchlight who would rather lose everything he was wearing than be taken with Jesus. That is what the abandonment looked like from the inside. Not a decision; a bolt. Amos spoke of the day of judgment: he who is stout of heart among the mighty shall flee away naked in that day (Amos 2:16). Everyone deserted Jesus. Not one was left with him.

The contrast. The disciples had left everything to follow Jesus (10:28). Now this young man leaves everything to escape him. And watch the linen. In the next chapter Joseph of Arimathea bought a linen shroud, took the body down and wrapped him in it (15:46). A young man abandons his linen cloth and runs away naked, so that his Lord can be wrapped in one. And there is a last bracket, and it is the loveliest thing here. The word for young man, neaniskos, occurs exactly twice in Mark. Here, running away naked in the dark. And on the first morning of the week, when the women find the stone rolled back: they saw a young man sitting on the right side, dressed in a white robe (16:5). Whatever else that means, Mark has bracketed the passion with two young men: one who fled from Christ stripped and ashamed, and one seated in an empty tomb, clothed in white, announcing that he has risen. That is the gospel in two pictures, and if the young man is Mark himself, the man who wrote it put himself in the first one.

Why would Mark tell such an embarrassing story about himself? For the same reason Peter told the story of his denial: because the gospel is not about how faithful we were, but about how faithful Christ is. A Gospel writer who painted himself as a hero would be pointing at himself. One who shows himself running away naked is pointing away from himself, to the one who did not run. It also tells every reader who has fled from Christ in shame that the story does not end there. Mark, who once deserted Paul as well (Acts 15:37–38), later became useful to him for ministry (2 Timothy 4:11), and wrote this Gospel.

In a sentence. A young man who tried to follow Jesus was seized, but slipped out of his linen cloth and fled naked, a picture of the total desertion of Jesus.

On a Tuesday. If you have ever fled from Jesus in shame, you are in good company, possibly that of the Gospel’s own author, and he restores those who run away. Think of a time you ran: from speaking up, from a costly obedience, from a call you knew was his. Do not bury it. Bring it to him, and let it make you humble and grateful rather than hopeless. Then tell someone else what he did with you.

For worship. Everyone left him. The friends fled, the young man fled, and he was led away alone, stripped of every companion, soon to be stripped of his clothes. He bore the shame of nakedness on the cross so that we could be clothed in his righteousness, and the linen that wrapped his body was left lying in the empty tomb when he rose. The one who ran away naked in the dark wrote the story of the Saviour who never ran, and whose robe of white is given to every sinner who comes back.
verseByVerse.note: Only Mark records the young man. Many have guessed he was Mark himself, but the text does not say.

parallels.desc: he who is stout of heart shall flee away naked in that day

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 53–72 — The Trial and the Denial
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The council (vv. 53–65). He is taken to the high priest's house and the whole Sanhedrin assembles in the middle of the night. They look for evidence to justify a verdict they have already reached, and cannot find any that holds — the witnesses contradict each other, even about the temple saying. He says nothing at all. Then the high priest puts the direct question, under oath, and he answers it in full for the first time in this Gospel: I am — and adds Daniel 7 and Psalm 110 to it. The robes are torn, the sentence is passed, and men begin to spit at him.

The courtyard (vv. 66–72). And Mark cuts, in the same building, to the one disciple who followed. A servant girl looks at Peter across a fire; a second challenge comes; then the bystanders place his accent. Three times, escalating — a denial, a denial, and finally oaths and a curse.

Then a bird calls, and he remembers, and the strongest of the twelve goes to pieces.

Mark has interleaved the two scenes deliberately: upstairs, Christ confesses and is condemned for it; downstairs, Peter denies and is safe.
verseByVerse.theology:
The trial was illegal, and the record shows it. By the standards later codified in the Mishnah, capital cases were to be tried in daytime, in the temple's own hall, never begun on the eve of a Sabbath or a festival, and a conviction could not be handed down on the same day as the trial — an acquittal could, but a death sentence required a night to pass first. This proceeding breaks all of it. It is held at night, in the high priest's residence, at Passover, with sentence passed at once.

How much of that code was in force in AD 30 is genuinely debated. But Mark's own account convicts them without any of it, in one sentence: the chief priests and the whole council were seeking testimony against Jesus to put him to death (v. 55). That is not a court. A court seeks the truth and then decides the penalty; this one had the penalty and went looking for grounds.

And I am is the fullest confession in the Gospel. Nine chapters of demons silenced and healed men hushed, and now, under oath, with nothing left to protect, he answers plainly. Egō eimi — the words of the burning bush (Ex. 3:14) — and then two texts fused: seated at the right hand of Power (Ps. 110:1), which he had put to them as a riddle two days earlier (12:36), and coming with the clouds of heaven (Dan. 7:13).

He tells the court that the man in the dock will be their judge, and they understand him perfectly.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: the high priest tears his garments (v. 63) — the formal gesture required of a judge on hearing blasphemy.

And it is worth knowing what the Law said about that particular man's clothes. The high priest was under a standing prohibition: he shall not let the hair of his head hang loose nor tear his clothes (Lev. 21:10). The office was not permitted the ordinary signs of mourning.

So on the night the Sanhedrin condemned Jesus for blasphemy, the high priest of Israel broke the Law of Moses to do it. Every man in that room was more concerned with the letter of the law than anybody alive, and the one they killed for breaking it was the only one in the building keeping it.

Now: and then they spat at him and covered his face and hit him and said Prophesy! — a game, apparently, of making the blindfolded man name who struck him.

They did not know that he had prophesied, that afternoon and the night before, with total accuracy: that one of the twelve would betray him, that all of them would run, and that Peter would deny him three times before the cock crowed twice.

While they were demanding a prophecy, the last of those predictions was coming true below them, in the courtyard, in the hearing of a servant girl.

verseByVerse.quote: And they led Jesus to the high priest. And all the chief priests and the elders and the scribes came together. And Peter had followed him at a distance, right into the courtyard of the high priest. And he was sitting with the guards and warming himself at the fire.
verseByVerse.commentary:
They led Jesus to the high priest, and all the chief priests, the elders and the scribes came together. Peter had followed him at a distance, right into the courtyard of the high priest, and he was sitting with the guards and warming himself at the fire.

And they led Jesus to the high priest. Caiaphas, high priest from AD 18 to 36 (Matthew 26:57). John records a first hearing before Annas, his father-in-law, a former high priest who was still the power behind the office (John 18:13–24). And Caiaphas was the man who had already said it was better that one man should die for the people (John 11:50).

And all the chief priests and the elders and the scribes came together. The Sanhedrin, the council of seventy-one, or at least a quorum of it, assembled in the middle of the night. That takes organisation: messengers sent round the city, men roused from their beds and brought to one house at an hour when nobody meets. So the arrangements were made in advance; they were waiting for Judas’s signal. A night meeting was irregular. By later Jewish law (the Mishnah), capital trials could not be held at night or on the eve of a feast, and a death sentence could not be passed on the same day as the trial. If those rules applied then, this trial broke them. They were in a hurry, determined to finish before the feast and before the crowds could react.

The structure. Another Mark sandwich. Peter in the courtyard (v. 54), Jesus before the council (vv. 55–65), Peter in the courtyard (vv. 66–72). Inside, Jesus confesses who he is, and is condemned. Outside, Peter denies who he is, and saves himself. Mark begins the second thread here, before the trial, so that the two run side by side in the reader’s mind, and invites us to compare.

And Peter had followed him at a distance. Three words, and they are among the saddest descriptions of discipleship in the New Testament. He has not fled, and that is worth saying loudly, because Peter is easy to despise and he does not deserve it. Ten men are somewhere in the dark on the far side of the Kidron. One followed. But at a distance: close enough to see, far enough not to be associated. That is the most dangerous place in the world to stand, near enough to keep your conscience quiet and far enough to keep your safety. Nobody stays there long. It resolves, one way or the other, within hours.

Right into the courtyard of the high priest. Wealthy houses were built around an open courtyard. John says another disciple, known to the high priest, got Peter through the gate (John 18:15–16).

And he was sitting with the guards and warming himself at the fire. Every word is deliberate, and Mark will repeat it in verse 67 so that we cannot miss it. Sitting with the guards: not standing at the edge. He has sat down among the men who arrested his Lord an hour ago, in the courtyard of the man who is trying him. Warming himself at the fire: spring nights in Jerusalem, at 2,500 feet, can be cold, and there was a charcoal fire in the middle of the yard, and Peter is at it with his hands out. Picture the geometry, because Mark has built it. Upstairs, Jesus stands before the Sanhedrin. Downstairs, in the same building, Peter is warm, sitting with the men who seized him. He has not denied anything yet. He has simply taken a place at the enemy’s fire because it was cold and he wanted to see what would happen, and the next thing that happens is that the firelight falls on his face (v. 67).

Is it wrong to keep quiet about Christ among people who have no time for him? Not always. There are times when silence is wise, and you are not obliged to preach at every lunch table. But there is a version of Peter’s fire in every Christian’s life: the place where you can be near Christ and comfortable at the same time, sitting with people who mock him and saying nothing, because it is warm and leaving would cost something. The question is not whether you speak every time, but whether you have settled in. If the company you keep regularly requires you to hide that you belong to Jesus, it is time either to speak or to move away from the fire.

In a sentence. Jesus was taken to the high priest before the gathered council, while Peter followed at a distance into the courtyard and warmed himself among the guards.

On a Tuesday. Following Jesus at a distance is dangerous, so notice where you are warming yourself, and with whom. Nobody has ever been asked a hard question at a safe distance; they get asked at the fire. Think of the place this week where you are most likely to be identified as a Christian, and decide now that if the question comes you will say yes.

For worship. He was led into the house of his enemies alone, and he went in. While his friend warmed his hands below, he stood in the cold of their hatred and did not flinch. He followed his Father’s will not at a distance but all the way, into the court and onto the cross. And even then he did not lose sight of the man at the fire. The Shepherd who stood trial upstairs was praying for the sheep in the courtyard, that his faith would not fail.
verseByVerse.note: John records a first hearing before Annas, the former high priest.

verseByVerse.quote: Now the chief priests and the whole council were seeking testimony against Jesus to put him to death, but they found none. For many bore false witness against him, but their testimony did not agree.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The chief priests and the whole council were looking for testimony against Jesus to put him to death, but they found none. For many bore false witness against him, but their testimony did not agree.

Now the chief priests and the whole council were seeking testimony against Jesus to put him to death. Read the sentence slowly, because Mark has convicted the court in one line, without any appeal to procedural rules. They are not seeking testimony; they are seeking testimony against him, to put him to death. The verdict is fixed and the evidence is being recruited to fit it. That is the precise inversion of what a court is. A court establishes what happened and then determines the consequence. This body has the consequence and is shopping for the happening. They were not looking for truth, but for evidence to justify a decision already made.

The irregularities. It is worth adding what the later Jewish law code says about capital trials, even granting that we cannot be certain how much of it was in force in AD 30. Capital cases were to be heard in daylight, in the temple’s own hall, never begun on the eve of a Sabbath or a feast; and a guilty verdict could not be returned on the day of the trial. An acquittal could be given at once, but a condemnation had to wait overnight, so that the judges slept on it. This trial is held at night, in a private residence, at Passover, and the sentence is passed within the hour. But Mark does not lean on any of that. His indictment is simpler.

But they found none. Something quietly extraordinary, and very easy to read past. The supreme court of Israel, with every motive in the world and the whole night to work in, and the resources to find and prompt willing witnesses, could not assemble a credible case against him. Three years of public ministry. Thousands of hours of teaching, most of it in the open air, much of it in front of hostile professionals taking notes. Enemies who had followed him from town to town since chapter 2 precisely to catch him out. And they could not find two men who could agree on anything he had done wrong. That is not a small piece of evidence for the sinlessness of Jesus. It is the testimony of a hostile prosecution that had every reason to produce something and could not. He was innocent, the spotless lamb (1 Peter 1:19).

For many bore false witness against him, but their testimony did not agree. They had witnesses; the witnesses were lying; and the lies did not match. They broke the ninth commandment to convict the Son of God (Exodus 20:16), and the psalmist had foretold it: false witnesses have risen against me (Psalm 27:12; 35:11). Under the Law, at least two witnesses whose testimony agreed were required for a conviction, especially in a capital case (Deuteronomy 17:6; 19:15). And the penalty for a false witness in a capital case was the death he had sought to inflict (Deuteronomy 19:18–19). Nobody in that room is charged with anything.

Why did God let an innocent man be convicted? Because only an innocent man could save the guilty. If Jesus had been condemned for real sins of his own, his death would have paid for nothing but those sins. The fact that his enemies could find nothing is the very thing that makes his death a substitution: the righteous for the unrighteous, that he might bring us to God (1 Peter 3:18). God did not approve of the injustice; the men who committed it were guilty. But he wove their injustice into the greatest act of justice in history, in which sin was truly punished and sinners truly pardoned.

In a sentence. The council searched for evidence to justify killing Jesus, but even the false witnesses contradicted each other.

On a Tuesday. If you are falsely accused, remember that Jesus was, and commit your cause to God, who judges justly (1 Peter 2:23). Do not pay back slander with slander. Tell the truth plainly, accept help, and leave the outcome with him. And if you are ever on the other side, deciding about someone with a conclusion already in mind, stop, and ask what you would see if you were actually seeking the truth.

For worship. They searched for a fault and found none, because there was none to find. Every word he had spoken was true, every deed holy, every thought pure. The only man who never deserved to die stood silent before false witnesses, so that we, who deserve condemnation, could stand before the true Judge with no charge against us. Who shall bring any charge against God’s elect? It is God who justifies (Romans 8:33). The court that could not convict him was the court where our guilt was transferred to him.
verseByVerse.note: The council is the Sanhedrin. The law required two agreeing witnesses.

parallels.desc: false witnesses have risen against me

verseByVerse.quote: And some stood up and bore false witness against him, saying, "We heard him say, 'I will destroy this temple that is made with hands, and in three days I will build another, not made with hands.'" Yet even about this their testimony did not agree.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Some stood up and bore false witness against him, saying: we heard him say, I will destroy this temple that is made with hands, and in three days I will build another, not made with hands. Yet even about this their testimony did not agree.

And some stood up and bore false witness against him, saying, We heard him say, I will destroy this temple that is made with hands. This is the best they can manage, and it is worth taking apart, because it is a lie built out of something true, which is how the most effective lies are made. He did say something like it. John records it, at the first cleansing of the temple three years earlier: destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up. And John adds the explanation the witnesses have conveniently lost: he was speaking about the temple of his body (John 2:19–21). He had predicted the temple’s destruction (13:2), but not that he would do it.

Count the alterations. The imperative becomes a threat. He said destroy this temple, addressed to them, a challenge. They report I will destroy this temple, a stated intention, which turns a saying about his own death into a plot against the national sanctuary. And the metaphor is flattened into masonry. He was speaking of his body; they present it as a claim about the building, which in a week when the city was full of pilgrims was as inflammatory a charge as could be devised. Jeremiah nearly lost his life for prophesying against this building (Jeremiah 26:8–11), and Stephen will lose his for the same accusation within a few years (Acts 6:13–14). So the technique is: take his real words, change the person of one verb, and remove the interpretation. Nothing is invented. Everything is turned. That is still the commonest way Christ and his people are misrepresented: not fabrication, but selective reporting with the key removed.

And in three days I will build another, not made with hands. Made with hands was a phrase used of idols (Acts 7:48; 17:24). The witnesses may have been twisting Jesus’ teaching that a new temple was coming, not a building but a people built around himself (1 Corinthians 3:16; Ephesians 2:20–22; 1 Peter 2:5).

Yet even about this their testimony did not agree. And it collapses anyway. Even the best lie in the room could not survive two men telling it. Mark’s little word even carries the exasperation of the prosecution. They had one usable charge and could not get it into evidence. The charge failed on a technicality.

Not convicted on this. Hold on to it, because the whole passion turns on it. He is not convicted of anything the witnesses said, because none of it stood up. The charge that finally kills him will come out of his own mouth in three verses’ time, when the high priest asks him a direct question and he tells the truth. They could not find a crime. So they asked him who he was, and he told them, and that was enough.

The irony. The false testimony was, in a deeper sense, true. By putting Jesus to death they would destroy the temple of his body; in three days he would rise; and his resurrection would bring into being the true temple, not made with hands, the church, in whom the whole structure, being joined together, grows into a holy temple in the Lord (Ephesians 2:21). And the temple made with hands would be destroyed forty years later. The charge will be thrown at him again on the cross (15:29). The false witnesses were accidentally right, and nobody in the room noticed.

How should I respond when my words, or my faith, are twisted? Calmly, and with the truth. Clarify what you actually said, once, without bitterness. Do not be surprised: if they twisted the words of Jesus, they will twist yours. Do not twist theirs in return. And when Christianity itself is misrepresented, by a quotation torn from context or a caricature of what Christians believe, be ready to restore the missing context gently, as John restores it for us in his Gospel. The truth usually needs only to be stated fully to defend itself.

In a sentence. Witnesses twisted Jesus’ words about the temple into a threat to destroy it, but even they could not agree.

On a Tuesday. Before you repeat a report about someone this week, especially a Christian leader or a person you dislike, ask whether you have the whole of what was said, or only a sentence with the key removed. And remember that you are part of the temple not made with hands, built on the risen Christ. Live this week as the place where God dwells.

For worship. They mocked his promise to raise a temple in three days, and on the third day he did. The body they destroyed rose incorruptible, and in him God has built a house of living stones from every nation, a temple no Roman army could burn. The lie they told at his trial became the truth of Easter. And every believer is a stone in that house, so that the presence of God that once filled the Holy of Holies now fills a people for whom he died.

verseByVerse.quote: And the high priest stood up in the midst and asked Jesus, "Have you no answer to make? What is it that these men testify against you?" But he remained silent and made no answer. Again the high priest asked him, "Are you the Christ, the Son of the Blessed?" And Jesus said, "I am, and you will see the Son of Man seated at the right hand of Power, and coming with the clouds of heaven."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The high priest stood up in the middle and asked Jesus: have you no answer to make? What is it that these men testify against you? But he remained silent and made no answer. Again the high priest asked him: are you the Christ, the Son of the Blessed? And Jesus said: I am, and you will see the Son of Man seated at the right hand of Power, and coming with the clouds of heaven.

And the high priest stood up in the midst and asked Jesus, Have you no answer to make? The case has collapsed, and Caiaphas stands up, physically moves into the middle of the room, because the trial is failing and he has to rescue it. His first move is to try to get the prisoner talking. What is it that these men testify against you?

But he remained silent and made no answer. Mark says it twice over, in two ways, because the silence is the point. He does not defend himself. He does not point out that the witnesses contradict each other, which would have ended the proceeding. He does not explain what he actually said about the temple, which would have taken thirty seconds and was completely defensible. He says nothing. And it is a quotation: like a lamb that is led to the slaughter, and like a sheep that before its shearers is silent, so he opened not his mouth (Isaiah 53:7). Take the measure of that silence. Every instinct in a wronged man is to explain. He stands before a court that has already decided, arrested by a mob, accused by liars, on the strength of a friend’s kiss, and he will not say a word in his own defence, because saying it would have worked.

Are you the Christ, the Son of the Blessed? Now the direct question, the question the whole Gospel has been asking since 1:1. The Blessed is a reverent Jewish substitute for the divine name; Caiaphas will not say God aloud. So he is asking: are you the Messiah, the Son of God? Matthew adds that he put him under oath (Matthew 26:63).

And Jesus said, I am. Two words, the plainest claim in Mark. Nine chapters of demons silenced, healed men hushed, disciples told to say nothing to anybody. The whole strategy of secrecy, sustained since the first synagogue in Capernaum, held for three years, because the title would have been misunderstood, because a crowd would have crowned him, because the cross had to define it. Now there is nothing left to protect. He is bound, the crowd cannot reach him, and a crown is not on offer. And the moment it can only cost him his life, he says it plainly. The words are egō eimi, I am, the words he spoke on the water in the dark (6:50), and they may echo the name God gave Moses at the bush (Exodus 3:14).

And you will see the Son of Man seated at the right hand of Power, and coming with the clouds of heaven. He does not stop at the answer. He adds a sentence that fuses two texts, chosen with care. Seated at the right hand of Power is Psalm 110:1, the psalm he had put to these very men as an unanswerable riddle two days ago (12:36). Power is another reverent way of saying God. Coming with the clouds of heaven is Daniel 7:13, the one like a son of man given dominion and glory and a kingdom, whom all peoples serve. Put them together and this is what a bound prisoner says to the court about to sentence him: you will see me on the throne, and you will see me coming as judge. You are judging me now, but I will judge you. The prisoner is the judge. The dock and the bench are about to change places, and everyone present understood him perfectly. That is why the next verse happens.

When would they see this? Some take it as the vindication of Christ after his death, in his resurrection, ascension and the judgment on Jerusalem, since in Daniel the Son of Man comes to the Ancient of Days to receive his kingdom. Others take it as the final coming, when every eye will see him, even those who pierced him (Revelation 1:7). The more likely reading holds both together. From his resurrection Jesus is enthroned at God’s right hand, and those who condemned him saw the signs of it; the coming with the clouds will be seen by all at his return, when these judges stand before their Judge.

Why was he silent before, and then answer? Because the two questions were different.
