The first invited him to defend himself against lies, and he would not; his silence was the silence of the Lamb, who had come to be condemned, not to escape condemnation. The second asked who he was, under oath, and to stay silent then would have been to deny the truth. So he spoke. That is a pattern for his people. We need not always defend our own reputations, and often should not. But when we are asked whether we belong to Christ and who he is, we must answer, whatever it costs.

In a sentence. Silent before false charges, Jesus answered the high priest’s question openly: he is the Messiah, the Son of God, who will sit at God’s right hand and come with the clouds of heaven.

On a Tuesday. Learn the difference between the two silences. When someone criticises you unfairly this week, practise saying less than you want to in your own defence, and leave your reputation with God. But when someone asks you, even casually, whether you really believe in Jesus, do not hide behind vagueness. Say I do, and say who he is.

For worship. He confessed the truth at the cost of his life. He is who he said: the Christ, the Son of God, seated at God’s right hand. The silent Lamb is the enthroned King, and the prisoner who stood before Caiaphas will sit as Judge over all the earth. Every knee that bowed in mockery that night will bow in truth on that day. Bow before him now, while his throne is a throne of grace.
verseByVerse.note: “The Blessed” is a reverent way of saying “God.” Jesus’ “I am” is his plainest claim in Mark.

verseByVerse.quote: And the high priest tore his garments and said, "What further witnesses do we need? You have heard his blasphemy. What is your decision?" And they all condemned him as deserving death. And some began to spit on him and to cover his face and to strike him, saying to him, "Prophesy!" And the guards received him with blows.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The high priest tore his garments and said: what further witnesses do we need? You have heard his blasphemy. What is your decision? And they all condemned him as deserving death. Some began to spit on him, to cover his face and to strike him, saying to him: prophesy! And the guards received him with blows.

And the high priest tore his garments. The formal judicial gesture on hearing blasphemy, a sign of grief or horror, performed so the court can see that the words have been recognised for what they are. And there is something here that ought to be better known. The Law placed a standing prohibition on the high priest’s clothes: the priest who is chief among his brothers shall not let the hair of his head hang loose nor tear his clothes (Leviticus 21:10). He was forbidden the ordinary signs of mourning, even for his own father and mother. This probably referred to his official robes and to mourning, and later practice allowed the gesture at blasphemy. But the irony stands. The most scrupulous men alive, in a room full of experts on the letter of the law, and the only person in the building wholly keeping it was the one they were about to kill for breaking it.

What further witnesses do we need? You have heard his blasphemy. Relief: the problem of the witnesses is solved. And this is the one honest sentence anybody speaks all night, though not in the way Caiaphas intends. He is right that no further witnesses are needed; the case is settled out of the prisoner’s own mouth. And he is right about the logic too. Blasphemy under the Law was punishable by stoning (Leviticus 24:16). Strictly it meant using the divine name irreverently, and claiming to be the Messiah was not in itself blasphemy; others had done it. But claiming to sit at God’s right hand and come on the clouds, sharing God’s throne and his role as judge, was claiming to be equal with God. If it was false, it was blasphemy. If it was true, they were condemning God.

Only two options. There were never more than two options in that room, and there are never more than two now. Either the man in the dock is God’s Son, or he said the most blasphemous thing a human being has ever said. Caiaphas is not being unreasonable; he is being consistent, and he has reached the only conclusion available to someone who has already decided the claim is false. Nobody who has read this trial can go on calling Jesus merely a fine moral teacher.

And they all condemned him as deserving death. All: the verdict was unanimous among those who voted. Joseph of Arimathea, a member of the council, had not consented (Luke 23:51); perhaps he was absent.

And some began to spit on him. Spitting in someone’s face was the deepest contempt available in that culture; the Law used it as the mark of public disgrace (Numbers 12:14; Deuteronomy 25:9). And Isaiah said the Servant would receive it: I gave my back to those who strike, and my cheeks to those who pull out the beard; I hid not my face from disgrace and spitting (Isaiah 50:6).

And to cover his face and to strike him, saying to him, Prophesy! A cruel game. They blindfold him, hit him and demand that he name who did it; Luke spells it out (Luke 22:64). Grown men, the religious leadership of Israel, playing a guessing game with a bound prisoner in the middle of the night. And prophesy! is the cruellest word in the chapter, and the most ironic. Because he had prophesied, that very evening, with total accuracy. He said one of the twelve would betray him, and one had. He said they would all fall away, and they had. He said the temple would come down, and it would. And he said one more thing, which at that exact moment was coming true below them, in the courtyard, in the hearing of a servant girl at the fire.

And the guards received him with blows. Slaps across the face, the treatment of a slave.

Who was responsible for the death of Jesus? Scripture answers: the Jewish leaders who condemned him, the Roman governor who sentenced him, the soldiers who crucified him, and the crowd who called for it, Jew and Gentile together (Acts 4:27). Behind them all stood the purpose of God, who delivered him up for us all (Romans 8:32). And in the deepest sense, every sinner, for it was for our sins that he died (Isaiah 53:5). That rules out forever the wicked charge that the Jews as a people are uniquely guilty, which has caused so much suffering. It also rules out every comfortable view of the cross in which someone else did it. The hymn is right to say: it was my sin that held him there.

In a sentence. The high priest declared Jesus’ claim blasphemy, the council condemned him to death, and some spat on him, blindfolded and struck him, mocking him as a prophet.

On a Tuesday. Make a decision about Jesus’ claim, because neutrality is not one of the options this trial allows. If you are a believer, let the picture of his spat-on face cure you of self-pity the next time you are mocked or treated with contempt for his sake. And refuse to join, even with a laugh, in the mockery of Christ that passes for wit in your office, your family or your feed.

For worship. The King of glory was spat on, struck and mocked, in silence, for you. The face that angels cannot look upon was covered with a rag and slapped by servants. He who will judge the world allowed himself to be condemned by it. He did not hide his face from disgrace and spitting, so that God would never hide his face from us. Let it break your heart, and stir your worship: this is how far the Son of God came down to bring us up.
verseByVerse.note: Tearing one’s garments was a sign of horror or grief.

parallels.desc: I hid not my face from disgrace and spitting

verseByVerse.quote: And as Peter was below in the courtyard, one of the servant girls of the high priest came, and seeing Peter warming himself, she looked at him and said, "You also were with the Nazarene, Jesus." But he denied it, saying, "I neither know nor understand what you mean." And he went out into the gateway and the rooster crowed.
verseByVerse.commentary:
As Peter was below in the courtyard, one of the servant girls of the high priest came. Seeing Peter warming himself, she looked at him and said: you also were with the Nazarene, Jesus. But he denied it, saying: I neither know nor understand what you mean. He went out into the gateway, and the rooster crowed.

And as Peter was below in the courtyard. Below: Mark gives us the architecture, and it is the whole point of the arrangement. Upstairs, Christ on trial, confessing who he is and being struck for it. Downstairs, in the same house, in the open yard, Peter at the fire, about to be asked the same question. Two men, one building, one night, and the same question put to both: are you the Christ?, and, you also were with him. One says I am, and it costs him his life. The other says, in effect, I am not, and it costs him everything else.

One of the servant girls of the high priest came. And look at who breaks him. Not a soldier, not a member of the council, not the temple police who had seen him draw a sword three hours ago. A servant girl, the lowest-status person in the household, a girl on the gate, whose opinion could not have hurt him and who had no power over him whatsoever. The man who swore he would die with him, who had drawn a sword against an armed crowd, collapsed before her.

And seeing Peter warming himself, she looked at him. She fixed her eyes on him, stared, peering across a charcoal fire in the dark, with the light on his face, working out where she had seen him before. And it is precisely because he sat down at that fire that she can see him at all. In the shadows at the edge of the yard, nobody asks you anything.

You also were with the Nazarene, Jesus. Note what the accusation actually is. Not you are a disciple, not you believe his teaching. You were with him. Association, that is all, and being with him was the very purpose for which Peter was chosen (3:14). The Nazarene, from that small town, is faintly contemptuous: the man from that village, that provincial nobody.

But he denied it, saying, I neither know nor understand what you mean. The first denial, and it is not a flat lie so much as a fog. It is a legal form of evasion, I don’t know what you are talking about, the answer of a man buying time, and the sort of thing everybody has said. That is worth being honest about, because we imagine Peter’s denial as something dramatic and unlike us. It begins as an evasion at a fire. Not I renounce Christ; just a vague sentence said to somebody unimportant, to make a moment go away.

And he went out into the gateway and the rooster crowed. He moves, out to the entrance passage, nearer the door, further from the light, closer to escape. Some manuscripts omit the rooster’s crowing here, but it matches Jesus’ twice (v. 30) and the second crowing in verse 72. And a bird calls somewhere in the city, and he does not hear it. That is the mercy in this account, and almost nobody notices it. The first crow was a warning, delivered exactly when Jesus said it would be, to a man who had been told what it meant three hours earlier. There was still time. Two denials had not yet happened. He heard a cock crow and it meant nothing to him at all.

Why do the small denials matter so much? Because they are where the large ones begin, and because they are the ones we commit most. Very few of us will be asked under threat of death whether we follow Jesus. Many of us will be asked, lightly, at work or at a party, whether we are religious, or what we did on Sunday, or what we think of something Christ forbids, and the temptation will be to answer with fog. That is the first step of Peter’s road. The remedy is to decide in advance what you will say, simply and kindly, so that when the servant girl asks, you are not deciding in the firelight.

In a sentence. When a servant girl recognised him as one of Jesus’ followers, Peter pretended not to know what she meant and moved away, and a rooster crowed.

On a Tuesday. Denials of Christ usually begin with small evasions in front of unimportant people, so watch your first steps. Write down one sentence you could say if someone asked this week whether you are a Christian: something true, short and unashamed. And listen for the roosters in your life: the conscience that stings, the verse that comes to mind, the friend’s question. They are mercies, sent while there is still time.

For worship. He was confessing upstairs while Peter was denying downstairs, and he was confessing for Peter. The good confession he made before Caiaphas and Pilate covers every failure of his people to confess him. And he sent the rooster: a small mercy in the dark, a warning from the Lord of creation, timed exactly. Even while he was being struck, he was still caring for the friend who was letting him down.

verseByVerse.quote: And the servant girl saw him and began again to say to the bystanders, "This man is one of them." But again he denied it. And after a little while the bystanders again said to Peter, "Certainly you are one of them, for you are a Galilean."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The servant girl saw him and began again to say to the bystanders: this man is one of them. But again he denied it. After a little while the bystanders again said to Peter: certainly you are one of them, for you are a Galilean.

And the servant girl saw him and began again to say to the bystanders, This man is one of them. She has not let it go, and now she is talking to other people about him. She followed him to the gateway and told everyone. The pressure is widening: the first challenge was private, this one is public. And the wording has hardened. Not you were with him but he is one of them: a category, a group, a party.

But again he denied it. Mark does not even record the words this time. Just the fact. The tense means he kept on denying. The second lie is easier, and it needs less said. That is how it works, and it is the most practically useful thing in this passage. The first denial makes the second one cheap. Having said I neither know nor understand, he now has to defend the first statement as well as himself, and the only way to defend it is to say it again with more force. A man who tells one lie has taken out a loan. Every later lie is interest.

Certainly you are one of them, for you are a Galilean. Third challenge, and now it is not one girl but a group, and they have evidence. It is his accent. Galilean Aramaic was noticeably different from the speech of Jerusalem; the rabbis joked about Galileans swallowing their consonants and confusing their gutturals. Matthew makes it explicit: your accent betrays you (Matthew 26:73). So Peter is trapped by the way he says words. He can deny knowing Jesus; he cannot deny the sound of his own mouth. Every sentence he speaks to defend himself proves the case against him.

Peter’s accent was more faithful than Peter was. There is something in that worth carrying home. He was recognisable, not by a badge or a confession, but by what he could not help: where he came from, how he spoke, the marks of three years in that company. Something about him gave him away before he opened his mouth to lie, and kept giving him away every time he did. That is what following Christ does to a person over time, and it is a mercy even when it is inconvenient.

What should give a Christian away? Not a special vocabulary or a religious manner, but the marks of having been with Jesus (Acts 4:13). The way you speak: without cruelty, gossip or filth, and with grace (Colossians 4:6). The way you handle money: honestly and generously. The way you treat people with no power to help you. The way you face loss, with grief but with hope. The way you refuse certain things without making a show of it. None of these makes you a Christian. But if you are one, they will grow, and people will notice before anything is said. Let your light shine before others, so that they may see your good works and give glory to your Father (Matthew 5:16).

In a sentence. The servant girl told the bystanders that Peter was one of them, he denied it again, and the bystanders insisted, pointing to his Galilean accent.

On a Tuesday. You can’t hide where you come from. If you belong to Christ, let your speech betray you, in the best sense. Ask someone who knows you well what, if anything, marks you out as a follower of Jesus, and listen to the answer. And if you have told one small lie this week to avoid being identified with him, go back and correct it now, before the interest grows.

For worship. Christ marks his people. He takes Galilean fishermen and makes them recognisable as his, so that even their enemies can tell that they have been with him. His Spirit writes his likeness into ordinary lives until it cannot be hidden. And when we deny him, he does not deny the marks he has made: we are his, by purchase and by grace, and the accent of heaven that he has given us will one day be the only language we speak.
verseByVerse.note: Galileans spoke with a recognisable regional accent.

verseByVerse.quote: But he began to invoke a curse on himself and to swear, "I do not know this man of whom you speak." And immediately the rooster crowed a second time. And Peter remembered how Jesus had said to him, "Before the rooster crows twice, you will deny me three times." And he broke down and wept.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But he began to invoke a curse on himself and to swear: I do not know this man of whom you speak. Immediately the rooster crowed a second time. Peter remembered how Jesus had said to him, before the rooster crows twice, you will deny me three times. And he broke down and wept.

But he began to invoke a curse on himself and to swear. And now the bottom. This is not swearing in the sense of bad language. Two things are happening, and both are formal and terrible. He invokes a curse: in the standard oath formula of that world, may God do so to me and more also if I am lying. And he swears: he takes an oath, calling God to witness. Some think the Greek could mean he cursed Jesus, since the verb has no object. Either way the third denial is the worst. Peter calls God as his witness, and calls down God’s curse on his own head, to guarantee a lie about God’s Son. And this is the man who three hours ago said if I must die with you, I will not deny you. He has always been in earnest. That is the horror of it.

I do not know this man of whom you speak. Notice that he will not say the name. Not Jesus, not the Nazarene: this man. He puts as much distance into the sentence as the grammar will allow. And the words are the exact opposite of the truth. He knew him better than almost anyone alive. He had watched him raise a dead girl, still a storm, feed five thousand and shine on a mountain. He had said at Caesarea Philippi, you are the Christ. At that very moment, upstairs, this man was confessing that he is the Son of God.

And immediately the rooster crowed a second time. A bird, in a city, before dawn. Exactly as Jesus had said. God did not send an angel or a thunderclap. He used the most ordinary sound in the world, part of every morning of Peter’s life, and timed it to the second.

And Peter remembered how Jesus had said to him, Before the rooster crows twice, you will deny me three times. The remembering is the turn, and it is everything. The word of Jesus came back to him. And Luke adds the detail that finishes a man: the Lord turned and looked at Peter (Luke 22:61). If the prisoner was being moved across the courtyard at that moment, the two men’s eyes met at the instant the bird called.

And he broke down and wept. Mark’s phrase is unusual (epibalōn eklaien) and hard to translate: perhaps he thought about it and wept, or he threw himself down and wept, or he began to weep. The tense means he wept and went on weeping. Whatever the precise sense, the strongest of the twelve went completely to pieces in a courtyard in the dark. Bitter tears of repentance (Matthew 26:75; Luke 22:62).

Peter and Judas. Two men betrayed Jesus that night. Both were of the twelve. Both had been warned to their faces. Both did exactly what he said they would. Judas betrayed him and despaired, and died by his own hand (Matthew 27:3–5). Peter denied him and wept, and was restored (16:7; John 21:15–19). The difference was not in the size of the sin; denying him three times with oaths is not obviously better than selling him for silver. The difference was in what each did with the wreckage. Judas felt remorse, and it drove him away from Christ. Peter felt grief, and it drove him back. Godly grief produces a repentance that leads to salvation without regret, whereas worldly grief produces death (2 Corinthians 7:10). And on the third morning an angel in an empty tomb will say: go, tell his disciples and Peter (16:7). Named, specifically. The one who denied him is the one singled out to be told.

But did Jesus not say he would deny those who deny him? He did: whoever denies me before men, I also will deny before my Father (Matthew 10:33), and Paul writes, if we deny him, he also will deny us (2 Timothy 2:12). Those words describe a final, settled denial, the denial of someone who will not come back. Peter’s was a terrible fall, but not a final one. Jesus had prayed that his faith would not fail (Luke 22:32), and it did not. A believer can fall badly; Christ keeps him from falling away for good. If you have denied him and your heart is breaking over it, that grief is the proof that you are not the person those verses describe.

Why record this? The early church did not hide the failure of its greatest leader. Mark, probably writing from Peter’s own preaching, records it in detail. Peter told this story against himself, again and again, with the numbers in it, as a testimony to the grace that restored him. No Christian is too great to fall, and no fallen Christian is beyond restoration.

I keep failing in the same way. Is there still a way back? Yes, as many times as you come. Peter did not fall only once; years later he drew back from Gentile believers out of fear and had to be rebuked to his face (Galatians 2:11–14). Restoration is not a single event but the pattern of the Christian life: fall, grieve, return, be received. Do not let the size or the repetition of your failure persuade you that Christ is tired of you. He told Peter to forgive seventy times seven; he will not do less himself. Come back today, confess it plainly, and get up.

In a sentence. Peter swore with a curse that he did not know Jesus; the rooster crowed a second time, and, remembering Jesus’ words, Peter broke down and wept.

On a Tuesday. If you have denied Christ, in word or deed, don’t despair like Judas. Weep like Peter, and come back. He is waiting for you in Galilee. Go to him today in prayer and tell him exactly what you did, without excuse. Then go to the place where he meets his people, his word and his church, and let him restore you there. And if someone you know has fallen, be the angel at the tomb for them: go and tell them, by name, that he is waiting.

For worship. The tears in that courtyard are not the end of Peter. They are the beginning of the man who preached at Pentecost, wrote two letters about standing firm, and died on a cross of his own, and who told this story against himself for the rest of his life, so that everyone who has ever warmed their hands at the wrong fire would know there is a way back. The Lord who turned and looked at Peter is the Lord who was at that moment being condemned for Peter. He bore the curse Peter called down on himself, so that Peter would never have to bear it. That is our Saviour: he looks at us at our worst, with eyes that break our hearts and then heal them.

14.theology:
What is the cup? Everything in Gethsemane turns on it, and it is not the general dread of dying. Thousands of his own martyrs have gone to worse deaths singing; if the cup were merely execution, the Christian would have a Lord less composed than his servants.

The cup is a fixed Old Testament image and it means the wrath of God: in the hand of the LORD there is a cup with foaming wine... and all the wicked of the earth shall drain it down to the dregs (Ps. 75:8); you who have drunk from the hand of the LORD the cup of his wrath (Isa. 51:17); take from my hand this cup of the wine of wrath (Jer. 25:15). That is what stands in front of him in the dark, and it is why a man who slept through a hurricane is on the ground shaking. And he drank it — for our sake he made him to be sin who knew no sin (2 Cor. 5:21) — which is precisely why there is nothing left in it for anyone who is in him.

And Gethsemane reverses Eden. In a garden a man was told the Father's will and said, in effect, "not your will but mine", and the world broke. In a garden a man who could have had anything said not what I will, but what you will, and it was mended.

Abba (v. 36) is one of the Aramaic words Mark preserves, and the most significant: the ordinary family word a child used for his father at home. Jewish prayer very rarely, if ever, addressed God that way. And it did not stay his — twice the New Testament says the Spirit puts this very word into the mouths of ordinary Christians (Rom. 8:15; Gal. 4:6). The name he used in Gethsemane is the name he handed over.

And I am (v. 62) is the fullest confession in the Gospel. Nine chapters of silencing demons and hushing healed men — and now, under oath, in chains, when it can only cost him his life, he answers plainly, in the words of the burning bush, and fuses Psalm 110:1 to Daniel 7:13. He tells the court that the man in the dock will be their judge, and they understand him perfectly.
14.examples:
Then: You will all fall away (v. 27) — and then, before Peter has opened his mouth, but after I am raised up, I will go before you to Galilee (v. 28).

Read those in the order he said them, because the order is the gospel. He announces the restoration before the failure happens. No condition attached — not if you repent, not if you come back. He tells eleven men who are about to abandon him where to meet him afterwards, and the word he uses is a shepherd's word: I will go before you, out in front, the way a shepherd leads. And not Jerusalem, where it all went wrong — Galilee, where they were called off their boats.

Now: the angel at the empty tomb repeats it with one addition — go, tell his disciples and Peter (16:7). The one named in the failure is named in the restoration.

And the chapter ends with two men who betrayed him. Both of the twelve, both warned to their faces, both doing exactly what he said they would. One went out and hanged himself; one went out and wept.

The difference is not the size of the sin — denying him three times with oaths is not obviously better than selling him for silver. It is what each did with the wreckage. Remorse drove Judas away from Christ, to a rope. Grief drove Peter back.

So if you have failed him badly, notice where Peter was standing when it started: at a distance (v. 54), and then warming himself at the fire — near enough to keep his conscience quiet, far enough to keep his safety. Nobody stays there long. And notice that the man who told this story against himself, with the numbers in it, for the rest of his life, is the man whose memories became this Gospel.

15.title: Truly This Man Was the Son of God
15.text: <sup>1</sup>And as soon as it was morning, the chief priests held a consultation with the elders and scribes and the whole council. And they bound Jesus and led him away and delivered him over to Pilate. <sup>2</sup>And Pilate asked him, “Are you the King of the Jews?” And he answered him, “You have said so.” <sup>3</sup>And the chief priests accused him of many things. <sup>4</sup>And Pilate again asked him, “Have you no answer to make? See how many charges they bring against you.” <sup>5</sup>But Jesus made no further answer, so that Pilate was amazed. <sup>6</sup>Now at the feast he used to release for them one prisoner for whom they asked. <sup>7</sup>And among the rebels in prison, who had committed murder in the insurrection, there was a man called Barabbas. <sup>8</sup>And the crowd came up and began to ask Pilate to do as he usually did for them. <sup>9</sup>And he answered them, saying, “Do you want me to release for you the King of the Jews?” <sup>10</sup>For he perceived that it was out of envy that the chief priests had delivered him up. <sup>11</sup>But the chief priests stirred up the crowd to have him release for them Barabbas instead. <sup>12</sup>And Pilate again said to them, “Then what shall I do with the man you call the King of the Jews?” <sup>13</sup>And they cried out again, “Crucify him.” <sup>14</sup>And Pilate said to them, “Why? What evil has he done?” But they shouted all the more, “Crucify him.” <sup>15</sup>So Pilate, wishing to satisfy the crowd, released for them Barabbas, and having scourged Jesus, he delivered him to be crucified. <sup>16</sup>And the soldiers led him away inside the palace (that is, the governor’s headquarters), and they called together the whole battalion. <sup>17</sup>And they clothed him in a purple cloak, and twisting together a crown of thorns, they put it on him. <sup>18</sup>And they began to salute him, “Hail, King of the Jews!” <sup>19</sup>And they were striking his head with a reed and spitting on him and kneeling down in homage to him. <sup>20</sup>And when they had mocked him, they stripped him of the purple cloak and put his own clothes on him. And they led him out to crucify him. <sup>21</sup>And they compelled a passerby, Simon of Cyrene, who was coming in from the country, the father of Alexander and Rufus, to carry his cross. <sup>22</sup>And they brought him to the place called Golgotha (which means Place of a Skull). <sup>23</sup>And they offered him wine mixed with myrrh, but he did not take it. <sup>24</sup>And they crucified him and divided his garments among them, casting lots for them, to decide what each should take. <sup>25</sup>And it was the third hour when they crucified him. <sup>26</sup>And the inscription of the charge against him read, “The King of the Jews.” <sup>27</sup>And with him they crucified two robbers, one on his right and one on his left. <sup>29</sup>And those who passed by derided him, wagging their heads and saying, “Aha! You who would destroy the temple and rebuild it in three days, <sup>30</sup>save yourself, and come down from the cross!” <sup>31</sup>So also the chief priests with the scribes mocked him to one another, saying, “He saved others; he cannot save himself. <sup>32</sup>Let the Christ, the King of Israel, come down now from the cross that we may see and believe.” Those who were crucified with him also reviled him. <sup>33</sup>And when the sixth hour had come, there was darkness over the whole land until the ninth hour. <sup>34</sup>And at the ninth hour Jesus cried with a loud voice, “Eloi, Eloi, lema sabachthani?” which means, “My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?” <sup>35</sup>And some of the bystanders hearing it said, “Behold, he is calling Elijah.” <sup>36</sup>And someone ran and filled a sponge with sour wine, put it on a reed and gave it to him to drink, saying, “Wait, let us see whether Elijah will come to take him down.” <sup>37</sup>And Jesus uttered a loud cry and breathed his last. <sup>38</sup>And the curtain of the temple was torn in two, from top to bottom. <sup>39</sup>And when the centurion, who stood facing him, saw that in this way he breathed his last, he said, “Truly this man was the Son of God!” <sup>40</sup>There were also women looking on from a distance, among whom were Mary Magdalene, and Mary the mother of James the younger and of Joses, and Salome. <sup>41</sup>When he was in Galilee, they followed him and ministered to him, and there were also many other women who came up with him to Jerusalem. <sup>42</sup>And when evening had come, since it was the day of Preparation, that is, the day before the Sabbath, <sup>43</sup>Joseph of Arimathea, a respected member of the council, who was also himself looking for the kingdom of God, took courage and went to Pilate and asked for the body of Jesus. <sup>44</sup>Pilate was surprised to hear that he should have already died. And summoning the centurion, he asked him whether he was already dead. <sup>45</sup>And when he learned from the centurion that he was dead, he granted the corpse to Joseph. <sup>46</sup>And Joseph bought a linen shroud, and taking him down, wrapped him in the linen shroud and laid him in a tomb that had been cut out of the rock. And he rolled a stone against the entrance of the tomb. <sup>47</sup>Mary Magdalene and Mary the mother of Joses saw where he was laid.
15.overview:
Fifteen hours from the garden to the grave, and Mark tells it almost without adjectives.

At first light the council reconvenes to make the night's verdict look regular and hands him to Rome, because they could pass a religious sentence and could not carry one out. Pilate asks one question, gets four words, and then nothing at all — and it astonishes him, because he has never seen a prisoner decline to save himself.

He knows the case is malicious; Mark says so plainly (v. 10). He tries the festival amnesty and the crowd, worked by the chief priests, asks for a murderer instead — a man called Barabbas, guilty of exactly the crime Jesus is falsely charged with. Pilate asks the only honest question of the morning and, getting no answer, hands him over anyway, wishing to satisfy the crowd.

Then a cohort of soldiers stages a coronation as a joke and gets every detail right; a pilgrim from Africa is pressed into carrying the beam and his sons end up in the church at Rome; and Mark records the crucifixion itself in four words.

At noon the light goes out. At three he shouts the first line of Psalm 22 into the dark, and then shouts again and dies — and sixty feet of temple curtain tears from the top down, and a Roman officer who has watched him for six hours says the thing no human being in this Gospel has yet said.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–20 — Before Pilate and the Mocking
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The transfer (vv. 1–5). As soon as it is light the council reconvenes to make the night's verdict look regular, and hands him to Rome — because they could pass a religious sentence and could not carry out an execution. Pilate asks one question and gets four words, and then nothing at all, and it astonishes him.

Barabbas (vv. 6–15). Pilate has read the situation correctly — he perceived that it was out of envy — and tries to release him through a festival custom. The chief priests work the crowd, and the crowd asks for a murderer. Pilate asks the only honest question of the morning, what evil has he done?, gets no answer, and hands him over anyway.

The mockery (vv. 16–20). Then the whole battalion is called together for a game: a purple cloak, a crown twisted out of thorns, a reed, mock salutes and real spitting.

Every element of it is accurate. He is the King; he does receive homage; he will wear purple and a crown. A cohort of Roman soldiers staged a coronation as a joke and got every detail right.
verseByVerse.theology:
Barabbas is the atonement acted out on a platform in Jerusalem.

Mark tells us exactly what he was: a rebel, in prison, who had committed murder in the insurrection — guilty of precisely the crime Jesus is falsely charged with, and guilty in fact.

So two men stand before the crowd. One is guilty; the other is the Son of the Father and is innocent. The crowd is offered a choice, chooses the guilty man, and condemns the innocent one — and the innocent one dies in the guilty man's place, on the cross that had been prepared for him.

Nobody in Jerusalem understood what they were watching. But somewhere in that city, by nine o'clock that morning, there was a murderer walking around free, and the only reason he was free is that Jesus of Nazareth was on his cross.

That is the whole gospel, and it happened to one man literally before it happened to anybody else spiritually. Christ also suffered once for sins, the righteous for the unrighteous, that he might bring us to God (1 Pet. 3:18).
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: What evil has he done? (v. 14) — the right question, asked by the one man in Jerusalem with the authority to act on it, who then did the opposite.

Mark is careful to show that Pilate knew. He perceived that it was out of envy (v. 10). He tried the amnesty. He put the question twice. The Roman governor of Judea conducted a better assessment of the evidence than the Sanhedrin had, and reached the correct conclusion, and signed the order anyway.

Now: and the reason Mark gives is five words long — wishing to satisfy the crowd. Not conviction, not deception, not a legal error. He wanted the noise to stop, and his position was already precarious enough that a riot at Passover could have finished him.

That is the commonest failure of people in authority, and it has never needed a Roman governor to perform it. The doctrine not defended because of who would leave. The wrong not named because of whose son it was. The decision made by counting the room rather than weighing the case.

Pilate did not decide that Jesus was guilty. He decided that being right was more expensive than being popular — which is a different sin, and a far more available one.

verseByVerse.quote: And as soon as it was morning, the chief priests held a consultation with the elders and scribes and the whole council. And they bound Jesus and led him away and delivered him over to Pilate. And Pilate asked him, "Are you the King of the Jews?" And he answered him, "You have said so."
verseByVerse.commentary:
As soon as it was morning, the chief priests held a consultation with the elders, the scribes and the whole council. They bound Jesus, led him away and handed him over to Pilate. Pilate asked him: are you the King of the Jews? He answered him: you have said so.

Meaning first. Mark 15 tells the story of a single day, from dawn to dusk on the Friday, and it is the day on which everything turns. At first light the council binds Jesus and hands him to Pilate, turning a charge of blasphemy into a charge of treason. Jesus will not defend himself. Pilate sees that he is innocent and tries to release him, but the crowd, stirred up by the priests, chooses Barabbas, a murderer, and shouts for crucifixion, and Pilate gives them what they want. Soldiers dress Jesus as a mock king and kneel before him in jest. Simon of Cyrene is made to carry the cross. At nine in the morning Jesus is crucified between two rebels, under a placard that tells the truth: The King of the Jews. Everyone mocks him, and his enemies preach the gospel without meaning to: he saved others; he cannot save himself. From noon to three darkness covers the land, and then Jesus cries out in the words of Psalm 22, My God, my God, why have you forsaken me? With a loud cry he dies, the temple curtain is torn from top to bottom, and a Roman centurion says what no human being in this Gospel has yet said: truly this man was the Son of God. Women watch from a distance, and Joseph of Arimathea, a member of the council, boldly asks for the body and lays it in a rock tomb. This is the chapter in which the Son of God bears the wrath of God for sinners, and opens the way to God for all who come through him.

The setting. The night hearing before the council (14:53–65) is over, Peter has wept in the courtyard (14:72), and the sun is coming up over the Mount of Olives. Jesus has had no sleep. Within nine hours he will be dead.

And as soon as it was morning. The fourth watch of the parable (13:35), and the last of the four. Evening at the supper, midnight in the garden, cockcrow in the courtyard, and now morning, and the disciples have slept or run through every one of them. Early, perhaps around 6 a.m.; Roman officials began their working day at dawn.

The chief priests held a consultation with the elders and scribes and the whole council. They meet again at first light, and the reason is almost certainly procedural. A capital verdict reached at night was irregular even by their own standards; a daylight session could be recorded as the proper trial. So this is a formality performed to make an irregularity look regular, and Mark, who has already told us they had the sentence before they had the evidence (14:55), lets the reader draw the conclusion. They also agreed how to present the case to Pilate. Blasphemy would mean nothing to a Roman governor, so they turned it into a political charge: Jesus claims to be a king, a rival to Caesar (Luke 23:2).

And they bound Jesus and led him away and delivered him over to Pilate. Bound: like a criminal, for the transfer through the streets. Isaac was bound on the altar (Genesis 22:9); the true sacrifice is bound now. Delivered over (paradidōmi) is the word Mark has used for Judas’s betrayal (14:10), for what the Son of Man must undergo (9:31; 10:33), and it will be used of Pilate handing him to the soldiers (v. 15). Everyone in this chapter is handing him on to somebody else. Nobody wants to be the last pair of hands.

Why Pilate at all? Because under Roman rule the council could pass a religious sentence but could not carry out a death sentence (John 18:31). Pontius Pilate was the Roman prefect (governor) of Judea from AD 26 to 36. He normally lived at Caesarea on the coast but came to Jerusalem at festivals with extra troops to keep order. Ancient writers describe him as harsh, stubborn and contemptuous of the Jews; Luke mentions Galileans whose blood he mingled with their sacrifices (Luke 13:1). An inscription bearing his name was found at Caesarea in 1961.

And Pilate asked him, Are you the King of the Jews? The political form of the charge, and the first thing out of his mouth, before any evidence is heard, which tells you what he had been told in advance. King of the Jews is a Gentile phrase; Jews said King of Israel (v. 32). The title runs through this chapter (vv. 2, 9, 12, 18, 26, 32). Judea was a difficult province with a history of messianic risings, and Rome tolerated no king without Caesar’s permission. Pilate is not asking a theological question but an operational one: is this man a threat? His you may be emphatic: you, a bound, beaten Galilean, a king?

And he answered him, You have said so. A guarded yes. It is not evasion; it is a refusal to accept the frame. King of the Jews is Pilate’s phrase, loaded with everything Rome feared: insurrection, a rival throne, tax revolt. Jesus will not deny the kingship, because he is the King. He will not affirm it in Pilate’s terms, because in those terms it means something he has never claimed. John gives the fuller exchange: my kingdom is not of this world; if it were, my servants would have been fighting (John 18:36–37). He is not the rebel Pilate fears. And this is his last recorded answer to a question in this Gospel. From here, almost nothing, until a cry at three in the afternoon.

Should Christians seek political power for Christ’s kingdom? Christians may serve in government, vote, campaign for justice and hold office; Joseph and Daniel did, and the state is God’s servant for good (Romans 13:1–4). But Christ’s kingdom does not come by political power, legislation or force. It comes by the word and the Spirit, through the new birth (John 3:3–5), and it is not of this world. When the church confuses the two, it either tries to make people Christian by law or makes the gospel a political badge, and both betray the King who answered Pilate as he did. Seek the good of your city; do not mistake any party or nation for the kingdom of God.

In a sentence. At dawn the council bound Jesus and handed him over to Pilate, who asked if he was the King of the Jews, and Jesus answered, you have said so.

On a Tuesday. Jesus is the King, though not the kind the world expects, so ask yourself in what sense he is your king. Is he a king you consult on Sundays, or the one whose word decides how you spend your money, treat your family and use your evenings? Pick one area of your life where you have been running a small kingdom of your own, and hand it to him today.

For worship. The King of kings stood bound before a provincial governor and did not deny his crown. He who will judge the living and the dead allowed himself to be passed from hand to hand like a parcel nobody wanted. He did not take his throne by the sword; he took it by the cross, and his kingdom has outlasted Pilate, Caesar and Rome. Of the increase of his government and of peace there will be no end, and every hand that handed him over will one day open before him.
verseByVerse.note: Under Roman rule the council could not carry out a death sentence. Pontius Pilate was the Roman governor of Judea from AD 26 to 36.

verseByVerse.quote: And the chief priests accused him of many things. And Pilate again asked him, "Have you no answer to make? See how many charges they bring against you." But Jesus made no further answer, so that Pilate was amazed.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The chief priests accused him of many things. Pilate again asked him: have you no answer to make? See how many charges they bring against you. But Jesus made no further answer, so that Pilate was amazed.

And the chief priests accused him of many things. Mark does not itemise them, and Luke does: misleading the nation, forbidding tribute to Caesar, and saying that he himself is Christ, a king (Luke 23:2). Every one is false or twisted. He had told them explicitly to pay the tax (12:17); the very men accusing him were there when he said it, and marvelled at the answer. Many things: the strategy is volume. If no single charge will hold, pile them up and hope the weight does the work.

And Pilate again asked him, Have you no answer to make? See how many charges they bring against you. Roman law gave the accused the right to defend himself, and a man who did not was normally convicted. And here is something worth noticing about Pilate: he is trying to help. A governor who wanted a conviction would let the accusations stand and move to sentence. Pilate is prompting the prisoner, say something, they are burying you, because he can see the case is thin and he would rather not do this. Matthew adds that his wife sent word about a dream and told him to have nothing to do with this righteous man (Matthew 27:19). Pilate is not a man in the grip of conviction. He is a man looking for an exit.

But Jesus made no further answer. And he will not take the exit he is offered. As before the high priest (14:61). Take the measure of this, because a single sentence would have done it. He could have said: I told them to pay the tax; ask them. He could have said: my kingdom is not of this world, and here are eleven witnesses that I have never armed a man. The case against him was so weak that a competent defence would have collapsed it in two minutes, and everyone in the room knew it. He says nothing. It is a deliberate fulfilment: he opened not his mouth; like a lamb that is led to the slaughter (Isaiah 53:7). His silence is not weakness but dignity, and submission to the Father’s will. He would not defend himself against lies, or try to escape the death he came to die.

So that Pilate was amazed. Consider what it takes to astonish a Roman governor at a criminal hearing. This man had presided over years of provincial justice. He had seen every kind of defendant: the pleaders, the bribers, the weepers, the men who cursed him, the men who invented alibis. Every one of them fought. He had never seen a man decline to save himself. Isaiah had said it: so shall he sprinkle many nations; kings shall shut their mouths because of him (Isaiah 52:15).

Why would an innocent man refuse to defend himself? Because he had not come to be acquitted. If Jesus had talked his way out, he would have walked free and we would have stayed condemned. He was not on trial to clear his name but to bear our sentence. The silence was not resignation and it was not despair. It was the most deliberate act in the room. That is also why it is not a rule for every Christian in every courtroom. Paul defended himself and appealed to Caesar (Acts 25:10–11). Jesus’ silence belonged to his unique work as the Lamb.

In a sentence. Faced with many accusations, Jesus gave no answer, and Pilate was astonished.

On a Tuesday. There are times when silence is the right answer to false accusation, so trust God to vindicate you (1 Peter 2:23). Notice the next time you feel the urge to have the last word in an argument, especially online or in the family, and ask whether it is truth that needs defending or only your pride. Often the most Christlike reply to an unfair charge is a short, true sentence, and then quiet.

For worship. He kept his mouth shut so that ours could be opened. The Word of God, through whom the worlds were spoken into being, stood silent before liars, because his silence was the price of our acquittal. Kings shut their mouths before him; one day every mouth will be stopped before his throne, and every tongue confess that he is Lord. And because he was silent then, he speaks for us now, as our advocate with the Father, and his defence of his people has never once been refused.

parallels.desc: like a sheep that before its shearers is silent

verseByVerse.quote: Now at the feast he used to release for them one prisoner for whom they asked. And among the rebels in prison, who had committed murder in the insurrection, there was a man called Barabbas. And the crowd came up and began to ask Pilate to do as he usually did for them. And he answered them, saying, "Do you want me to release for you the King of the Jews?" For he perceived that it was out of envy that the chief priests had delivered him up.
verseByVerse.commentary:
At the feast Pilate used to release for them one prisoner for whom they asked. Among the rebels in prison, who had committed murder in the insurrection, there was a man called Barabbas. The crowd came up and began to ask Pilate to do as he usually did for them. He answered them: do you want me to release for you the King of the Jews? For he perceived that it was out of envy that the chief priests had handed him over.

Now at the feast he used to release for them one prisoner for whom they asked. A goodwill custom at Passover, the feast of liberation, so a prisoner is set free. It is attested nowhere outside the Gospels, which some have made an objection; but Roman governors did grant such amnesties elsewhere, and a local custom in one province for one feast is exactly the sort of thing that leaves no other trace.

And among the rebels in prison, who had committed murder in the insurrection, there was a man called Barabbas. Mark is precise, and every detail matters. Among the rebels: not a common criminal but a political prisoner, one of a group. Who had committed murder in the insurrection: Mark says the insurrection, as though his readers knew which one, one of the many uprisings against Rome in those years. Barabbas was a revolutionary, perhaps a Zealot, who had killed someone in it. He is guilty of exactly what Jesus is falsely accused of: sedition against Rome. One of these two men actually did what the other is charged with. Exactly the kind of man Pilate should have feared, and exactly the kind of king many wanted.

Son of the father. And the name. Bar-abbas is Aramaic for son of the father. Some manuscripts of Matthew give his first name as Jesus: Jesus Barabbas (Matthew 27:16–17). So the choice put to the crowd is between two men called son of the father. One is a murderer. The other is the Son of the Father, who prayed Abba a few hours before (14:36).

And the crowd came up and began to ask Pilate to do as he usually did for them. Note that the crowd initiates it. They have come up to the governor’s residence for their prisoner, and they have somebody in mind. And note who this crowd is. It is not necessarily the crowd from Sunday. Those Galilean pilgrims are camped on the hillsides; this is early Friday morning, and the people present are those who could be assembled at short notice by men with influence. Verse 11 tells us who assembled them.

Do you want me to release for you the King of the Jews? Pilate makes his move, and it is shrewd. He offers the amnesty in a way that puts his preferred outcome first, thinking he can free Jesus this way. And the title needles the priests: this is your king? It is his title for Jesus throughout; he uses it here, again in verse 12, and will have it nailed to the cross and refuse to change it (John 19:22).

For he perceived that it was out of envy that the chief priests had delivered him up. Mark tells us plainly what Pilate had worked out, and it settles the question of his culpability. Envy: not concern for public order, not theological outrage. They were not loyal to Caesar. They wanted him dead because the crowds hung on his teaching (11:18; 12:37), because his authority made theirs look like what it was, and because he had walked into their temple and turned the tables over. A Roman politician recognised professional jealousy when he saw it. So Pilate knows the charge is malicious, knows the man is innocent, and knows exactly why he is standing there. Everything that happens next happens with that knowledge in the room. Envy, one of the sins Jesus listed as coming from the heart (7:22), sent him to the cross.

How do I recognise envy in myself? Envy is sorrow at another’s good and quiet pleasure at his harm. It rarely calls itself envy. It calls itself concern, or justice, or high standards. Watch for these signs: you find it hard to rejoice when a colleague, sibling or fellow Christian is praised; you look for flaws in people who succeed; you feel a small lift when someone you resent stumbles; you speak of another’s gifts with a qualification attached. The cure is not to pretend, but to confess it to God, thank him specifically for the other person’s gifts, pray for their good, and remember that in Christ you already have more than you could ever envy (1 Corinthians 3:21–23).

In a sentence. Pilate, knowing the chief priests had handed Jesus over out of envy, offered to release him under the Passover amnesty instead of Barabbas, a murderer and rebel.

On a Tuesday. Envy is a deadly sin. When you resent someone else’s gifts or success, remember what envy did to Jesus. This week, name one person whose success bothers you, and do something deliberately for their good: praise them to someone else, pray for them by name, help them with something. Envy cannot survive long in a heart that is actively seeking the other’s blessing.

For worship. The Son of the Father stood beside the son of a father, and the guilty one was set free. Envy handed him over, and love let it. He had no envy of anyone, though he alone deserved all praise; he rejoiced in his Father’s glory and in his people’s good. The Lord of the feast of liberation was not released, so that every prisoner of sin could be. The amnesty of that Passover set one murderer free for a while. The death it led to sets sinners free for ever.
verseByVerse.note: Barabbas means “son of the father.” The “insurrection” was one of many uprisings against Rome.

verseByVerse.quote: But the chief priests stirred up the crowd to have him release for them Barabbas instead. And Pilate again said to them, "Then what shall I do with the man you call the King of the Jews?" And they cried out again, "Crucify him." And Pilate said to them, "Why? What evil has he done?" But they shouted all the more, "Crucify him."
verseByVerse.commentary:
But the chief priests stirred up the crowd to have him release Barabbas for them instead. Pilate again said to them: then what shall I do with the man you call the King of the Jews? They cried out again: crucify him. Pilate said to them: why? What evil has he done? But they shouted all the more: crucify him.

But the chief priests stirred up the crowd to have him release for them Barabbas instead. Stirred up (aneseisan): they agitated the crowd, shook it, the way you shake a jar. This is the single most important sentence for understanding the next hour, because it tells you the crowd is being worked. They did not arrive with a view about Barabbas. Somebody moved among them and gave them one. Matthew says the same: the chief priests and the elders persuaded the crowd (Matthew 27:20).

How crowds are made. It is worth stopping on, because crowds are still made this way, and it is one of the most frightening things in the Bible. Some of the people shouting in that courtyard may well have been on the road five days earlier with their cloaks in the dust. Nobody in Jerusalem had changed his mind about Jesus on the evidence. There was no new fact. What happened was that people with authority and access told them what to think, and they thought it, and within minutes they were shouting for a man’s execution. A crowd is not a mind. It is an amplifier, and whoever gets to it first decides what it amplifies. That is why the Law says you shall not fall in with the many to do evil (Exodus 23:2).

Then what shall I do with the man you call the King of the Jews? Again: Mark keeps the count. This is Pilate’s second attempt, and there will be a third. And notice the question he has just made public. What shall I do with him?, put to a crowd, out loud, as though it were theirs to answer. It is the question of every person who hears of Jesus, and the tragedy of Pilate is that he asked it in the one way that guaranteed the wrong answer. He asked the room instead of deciding himself.

And they cried out again, Crucify him. Two words. No argument, no charge, no reasoning. A demand for a specific method of execution, and a Roman one, not Jewish: the most shameful death the Romans knew, reserved for slaves, rebels and the worst criminals, meant to deter by its horror. Roman citizens could not be crucified. And the Law said a man hanged on a tree was cursed by God (Deuteronomy 21:23; Galatians 3:13). They wanted not only his death, but his disgrace. The crowd that shouted Hosanna (11:9), or a crowd like it, now shouts for this.

Why? What evil has he done? The third attempt, and the only honest question of the morning. The judge declares him innocent. Luke records that Pilate said three times that he found no guilt in him (Luke 23:4, 14, 22). It is a fair question, and it has an answer: nothing. Mark records no reply, because there was none. Nobody in that courtyard could name a crime, and the silence where the answer should be is the verdict of history on the whole proceeding. The judge’s own words testify that Jesus died not for his own sins, but as the righteous for the unrighteous (1 Peter 3:18).

But they shouted all the more, Crucify him. Louder: that is the reply. The mob does not reason. When a case cannot be made, volume does the work, and it worked.

How do I keep from being carried along by the crowd? Notice when you are agreeing with something mainly because everyone around you does, or because it was said loudly and often. Ask the question Pilate asked and the crowd ignored: why? what is the evidence? Be especially careful online, where crowds form in minutes and outrage is rewarded. Slow down before you share, sign or join. Test what you hear by Scripture rather than by its popularity. And be willing to be the one person in the room who says, quietly, I do not think that is true. The crowd that shouted crucify him was sure it was right.

Is there a neutral answer to Pilate’s question? No. Pilate tried to find one, by handing the question to others, and it did not save him. Every person who hears of Jesus does something with him: bows to him, rejects him, or postpones him, and postponing is a decision too. Jesus himself said whoever is not with me is against me (Matthew 12:30). That is not a threat; it is the plain logic of who he is. If he is the King, the only right answer is to receive him.

In a sentence. Stirred up by the chief priests, the crowd chose Barabbas and, when Pilate asked what evil Jesus had done, only shouted louder for his crucifixion.

On a Tuesday. What will you do with Jesus? Every person must answer, and there is no neutral answer. If you have been putting off a decision about him, or about some part of obedience to him, answer today. And think of one opinion you have picked up recently because it was in the air, about a person, a group, a cause, and examine it honestly before you repeat it again.

For worship. They shouted for his death, and he went to it for them. The Lord who could have silenced the crowd with a word let their cry stand, because the curse they demanded for him was the curse he had come to bear for them. He became a curse for us, hanged on a tree, so that the blessing of Abraham might come to the nations. The question why? what evil has he done? has only one true answer: none. And because he had done none, his death could pay for ours.

verseByVerse.quote: So Pilate, wishing to satisfy the crowd, released for them Barabbas, and having scourged Jesus, he delivered him to be crucified.
verseByVerse.commentary:
So Pilate, wishing to satisfy the crowd, released Barabbas for them, and having scourged Jesus, he handed him over to be crucified.

So Pilate, wishing to satisfy the crowd. Mark gives the motive in one phrase, and it is not a legal judgment. He chose politics over justice. He knows the man is innocent; he has all but said so in his own questions. He has tried the amnesty and the direct question. And he folds, because the noise is rising and his position cannot take a riot at Passover. John records the crowd’s threat: if you release this man, you are not Caesar’s friend (John 19:12). Pilate’s record was already poor. He had provoked riots by bringing military standards bearing the emperor’s image into Jerusalem, and by raiding the temple treasury to build an aqueduct; Philo records a rebuke from Tiberius himself. He was one incident away from trouble, and he knew it. In the end he was recalled anyway, a few years later, after a massacre in Samaria. So a man weighed an innocent life against his own career and chose the career, and lost it in any case, which is very often how that trade turns out.

Washing his hands. Matthew records that he washed his hands to declare himself innocent (Matthew 27:24). But a judge who condemns a man he knows is innocent is not innocent. The church has confessed for centuries that Jesus suffered under Pontius Pilate, and his name is fixed in the creed as a permanent witness that this happened in real history, under a real governor, and that the governor was guilty.

Released for them Barabbas. Somewhere in Jerusalem, before nine o’clock that morning, a convicted murderer walked out into the street a free man and did not know why. The guilty man goes free; the innocent man dies in his place. Barabbas is the first person in history who could say, literally: Jesus died instead of me. He did not repent, or ask, or understand. He did not even know it was happening. Somebody else’s name was called instead of his, and the cross that had been meant for him took another man. This is substitution in a picture: Christ also suffered once for sins, the righteous for the unrighteous, that he might bring us to God (1 Peter 3:18).

And having scourged Jesus. Mark gives it in a few words, and they should not be hurried past, because the reticence of the Gospels here is deliberate and total. Not one of the four describes the physical suffering in detail. Roman scourging (flagellatio) was the normal preliminary to crucifixion. The prisoner was stripped, tied to a post, and beaten with a whip of several leather thongs weighted with pieces of bone or metal. There was no fixed number of strokes as under Jewish law; the soldiers went on until the officer stopped them. It tore the flesh, sometimes to the bone, and men died under it. Partly punishment, partly to shorten the ordeal by weakening the man. So when Simon of Cyrene is pressed into carrying the beam in verse 21, this is why. He was pierced for our transgressions; he was crushed for our iniquities; upon him was the chastisement that brought us peace, and with his wounds we are healed (Isaiah 53:5).

He delivered him to be crucified. The final handing over. The Father gave the Son (Romans 8:32), Judas handed him to the priests, the priests to Pilate, and Pilate to the soldiers.

Was Pilate really guilty if he did not want to do it? Yes. Not wanting to do evil is not the same as refusing to do it. Pilate had the authority, the knowledge and the duty to release an innocent man, and he chose his own safety instead. Scripture names him among those who gathered against God’s holy servant Jesus (Acts 4:27). His reluctance makes him more instructive, not less guilty. Most evil in the world is done not by monsters but by people who know better and give way. That is a warning to every Christian who holds any kind of authority, from a boardroom to a classroom to a home.

Did Jesus die for Barabbas? We do not know whether Barabbas ever believed, and Scripture does not say. What his release gives us is a picture, not a guarantee about him. The picture is exact: a guilty man goes free because an innocent man takes his place, and he contributes nothing to it. That is what happens to every sinner who trusts Christ. The picture becomes your story not by being near the cross, as Barabbas was, but by faith, as you stop pleading your own case and rest on the one who took your place.

In a sentence. To satisfy the crowd, Pilate released Barabbas, had Jesus scourged, and handed him over to be crucified.

On a Tuesday. Ask where you are most tempted this week to do what you know is wrong because the pressure is rising: to sign off something dishonest, to go along with a cruel joke, to stay silent while someone innocent is blamed. Decide now, before the noise, what you will do. And when you take bread or pray tonight, say it plainly to God: I am Barabbas, and he took my place.

For worship. You are Barabbas. The guilty one went free because the innocent one took his place, so give thanks. He was scourged so that we could be healed; he was handed over so that we could be handed back to God; he was condemned by a coward so that cowards and murderers and sinners of every kind could walk out of their prisons free. The cross that was meant for us bore him instead, and nothing remains of our sentence but the scars on his hands.
verseByVerse.note: Roman scourging used a whip weighted with bone or metal; it could itself kill.

parallels.desc: with his wounds we are healed

verseByVerse.quote: And the soldiers led him away inside the palace (that is, the governor's headquarters), and they called together the whole battalion. And they clothed him in a purple cloak, and twisting together a crown of thorns, they put it on him. And they began to salute him, "Hail, King of the Jews!" And they were striking his head with a reed and spitting on him and kneeling down in homage to him. And when they had mocked him, they stripped him of the purple cloak and put his own clothes on him. And they led him out to crucify him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The soldiers led him away inside the palace, that is, the governor’s headquarters, and called together the whole battalion. They clothed him in a purple cloak, twisted together a crown of thorns and put it on him. They began to salute him: hail, King of the Jews! They struck his head with a reed, spat on him, and knelt down in homage to him. When they had mocked him, they stripped him of the purple cloak and put his own clothes on him. And they led him out to crucify him.

And the soldiers led him away inside the palace (that is, the governor’s headquarters). The praetorium, the governor’s residence in Jerusalem, either Herod’s palace on the west side of the city or the Antonia fortress next to the temple. Mark uses the Latin word for his Roman readers.

And they called together the whole battalion. A cohort (speira), nominally six hundred men, though probably only those on hand. Whatever the number, Mark’s point is that this was not two bored guards. They called everybody in. And understand who these men were: not Romans from Italy but auxiliaries, recruited from the non-Jewish peoples of the region, mostly from Samaria and Syria, garrisoned in a province they despised, on riot duty at a festival they did not understand. They loathed the Jews and the feeling was returned. And here is a Jew handed to them as a king. This is entertainment.

And they clothed him in a purple cloak. Purple was the colour of royalty, made from an expensive dye and restricted to the powerful. What they had to hand was probably a faded red soldier’s cloak (Matthew 27:28 says scarlet), passed off as a king’s robe.

And twisting together a crown of thorns, they put it on him. Not a circlet resting on the head but a wreath, a parody of the laurel the emperor wore, perhaps woven from the long thorns of a date palm sticking out like the rays of a crown on coins. And thorns are not incidental to the Bible. They arrive in Genesis 3 as part of the curse on the ground: thorns and thistles it shall bring forth for you (Genesis 3:17–18). The first visible mark of a world under judgment is pressed onto the head of the man who came to lift it. The King bears the curse on his head.

And they began to salute him, Hail, King of the Jews! A parody of the imperial greeting, Ave, Caesar, with the name changed. They are performing an accession, and the joke is that a bleeding provincial is given the honours of an emperor.

And they were striking his head with a reed and spitting on him and kneeling down in homage to him. The reed was his mock sceptre; Matthew says they first put it in his right hand (Matthew 27:29), and then they took it and beat him on the head with it, driving the thorns in. Kneeling down in homage is the language of worship, the verb used of the demoniac falling at his feet (5:6) and the wise men before the child (Matthew 2:11). They are bowing the knee to the Son of God as a joke.

Every element is true. See what Mark has quietly done, without a word of comment. Every element of that mockery is true. He is the King of the Jews; Pilate will nail the words over his head within the hour. He will wear a crown and a robe and receive the homage of the nations. At the name of Jesus every knee will bow (Philippians 2:10–11), including, one day, every knee in that room. A cohort of Roman soldiers staged a coronation as a joke and got the costume, the crown, the sceptre, the acclamation and the kneeling exactly right. They were the only people in Jerusalem that morning conducting the correct ceremony. They simply thought it was funny.

And when they had mocked him, they stripped him of the purple cloak and put his own clothes on him. And they led him out to crucify him. The game ends. The robe comes off, because it belongs to somebody and will be wanted back, and in a few verses they will gamble for the clothes he is standing in. They led him out: out of the city, for Jesus also suffered outside the gate (Hebrews 13:12).

Why did God allow his Son to be so humiliated? Because shame is part of what sin deserves, and he came to bear all of it. Adam and Eve’s first experience of sin was shame, and they hid (Genesis 3:7–10). Jesus was stripped, mocked, spat on and paraded so that sinners covered in shame could be clothed and honoured before God. Hebrews says he endured the cross, despising the shame, for the joy that was set before him (Hebrews 12:2). If you carry shame, for what you have done or what was done to you, he has carried it too, and he can lift your head.

In a sentence. The soldiers dressed Jesus as a mock king in a purple cloak and a crown of thorns, saluted him, beat him and spat on him, before leading him out to be crucified.

On a Tuesday. Notice how easily the things of Christ are made a joke around you: in comedy, at work, perhaps at home, and how easily you laugh along. You need not be grim or self-righteous, but you can refuse to bow the knee in mockery. Then do the opposite on purpose: kneel today, literally if you can, and give him the homage they gave in jest, meaning every word.

For worship. They mocked him as king, and he is the King, so bow to him in truth where they bowed in mockery. The thorns of the curse became his crown, and the reed they struck him with became the sceptre of a kingdom that will never end. He let them strip him so that we could be clothed, and let them spit on him so that God would never turn his face from us. Crown him with many crowns, the Lamb upon his throne: he wore the crown of thorns first.
verseByVerse.note: The governor’s headquarters is the praetorium. The ESV notes that a battalion (cohort) was a tenth of a Roman legion. Purple was the colour of royalty.

parallels.desc: I gave my back to those who strike

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The road and the cross (vv. 21–27). A man on his way in from the country is pressed into carrying the beam, and Mark names his sons, probably because his readers knew them. At Golgotha he refuses the drugged wine, the soldiers gamble for his clothes, and Mark records the crucifixion itself in four words: and they crucified him.

The mockery (vv. 29–32). Three groups take their turn — passers-by, the chief priests, and the two men dying beside him. The taunt is always the same, and it is the wilderness temptation for the third time: come down; save yourself.

The darkness (vv. 33–37). At noon the light goes out for three hours. And at three o'clock he cries out in Aramaic the opening line of Psalm 22, and Mark preserves the sound of it. Then a loud cry, and he is dead.

What the death did (vv. 38–41). Sixty feet of temple curtain tears from the top down. A Roman officer says the thing no human being in this Gospel has yet said. And the women who have been there all along are named.
verseByVerse.theology:
The cry of dereliction (v. 34) is the sentence a suffering reader stops at, and two errors must be kept off it.

The first would soften it — as though Jesus were merely reciting a comforting psalm and was not truly forsaken. He was. The abandonment was real; he was bearing sin, and God's holiness turned from the sin-bearer.

The second would break God in two — as though the Trinity were torn apart, the Father ceasing to love the Son, the Son ceasing to be God. That did not happen and could not. The Son remained the beloved Son and remained God through every moment of the darkness; what he lost was not his Father's love or his own deity but the felt light of the Father's face, borne in our place.

Both are true at once: he entered a real forsakenness, and he entered it still holding on — for notice the word he uses. He does not cry God, why have you abandoned me, but my God, my God: twice claiming as his own the very One he could no longer feel. That is faith stripped of every comfort and still gripping in the dark.

And that is the word for the believer who has prayed into silence. The blackest hour a soul can know — real God-forsakenness, the full weight of it — has already been entered by the Son, so that it would never fall on you. I will never leave you nor forsake you (Heb. 13:5) is bought with this cry. If you must pray in the dark, pray as he did — my God — to the God you cannot feel, and know that he prayed it first, and prayed it there, so that you would never have to pray it alone.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: He saved others; he cannot save himself (v. 31) — the chief priests, standing at the foot of the cross, jeering.

And they have stated the gospel with complete accuracy without meaning a word of it.

Every clause is true. He did save others — a leper, a paralytic, a legion, a dead girl, a boy with a spirit. And he could not save himself — not because the power was gone, since he could have called twelve legions of angels (Matt. 26:53), but because saving himself and saving others were the two things that could not both be done.

Now: the mockers thought they had found a contradiction. They had found the mechanism. The one who saves others cannot save himself; that is not a failure of power but the shape of substitution, and it is why there is a gospel at all.

And notice the demand attached: come down now from the cross that we may see and believe (v. 32). They had the order exactly backwards, and it is the standing human demand — show me and I will trust you.

He did not come down, and that is why anyone believes. Had he come down they would have seen a miracle and gone home unforgiven. He stayed up, and by three o'clock a Roman officer who had asked for no sign at all was saying truly this man was the Son of God.

verseByVerse.quote: And they compelled a passerby, Simon of Cyrene, who was coming in from the country, the father of Alexander and Rufus, to carry his cross. And they brought him to the place called Golgotha (which means Place of a Skull).
verseByVerse.commentary:
They compelled a passer-by, Simon of Cyrene, who was coming in from the country, the father of Alexander and Rufus, to carry his cross. And they brought him to the place called Golgotha, which means Place of a Skull.

And they compelled a passerby, Simon of Cyrene. The condemned man normally carried his own crossbeam (patibulum), perhaps 75–100 pounds (35–45 kg), through the streets to the place of execution, where the upright post was already standing. He cannot carry it. That is what this verse tells us without saying it. After a night of interrogation, a scourging and a cohort’s entertainment, he is physically finished, and a Roman execution detail does not stop for compassion. They needed the prisoner alive at Golgotha. Compelled is a Persian loan-word that had passed into Greek as a technical term for military requisition, the right of a soldier to press a civilian into service. It is the word behind if anyone forces you to go one mile, go with him two (Matthew 5:41). So Simon does not volunteer. A soldier taps him and he has no choice.

Who was coming in from the country. Into the city, as Jesus was being led out. Cyrene was a city in North Africa, in modern Libya, with a large Jewish community. Simon was probably a Jewish pilgrim who had travelled a very long way to keep the Passover, or had settled in Jerusalem. People from Cyrene were at Pentecost (Acts 2:10), and some of the first to preach to Gentiles (Acts 11:20). He has planned this trip for months. And a soldier picks him out of the crowd, and the day is not his any more.

The father of Alexander and Rufus. Only Mark has this, and it is one of the most quietly moving details in the Gospel. Why name the sons? Mark does not tell us who Simon’s wife was, or his age, or what became of him. He names two men, and the only likely reason is that his readers knew them. They were Christians. This Gospel was probably written for the church at Rome, and in Paul’s letter to that church there is a line in the closing greetings: greet Rufus, chosen in the Lord; also his mother, who has been a mother to me as well (Romans 16:13). It cannot be proved, and it does not need to be, because the shape of the thing is clear either way. Mark expects his readers to nod at those names, which means the family of the man pressed into carrying the cross ended up in the church.

What that morning did. A pilgrim from Africa is dragged out of a crowd against his will, humiliated in a public street, made to carry a condemned criminal’s cross for a man he had never met, and it is the making of his household. His sons are named in a Gospel. His wife, perhaps, mothered the apostle Paul. Luke says he carried the cross behind Jesus (Luke 23:26), the very picture of a disciple.
