He literally took up the cross and followed (8:34). Nobody has ever been pressed into carrying something for Christ and been the poorer for it, though it very rarely feels like that at the time.

And they brought him to the place called Golgotha (which means Place of a Skull). Golgotha is Aramaic, which Mark translates for his Roman readers; Calvary comes from the Latin for skull, calvaria. Perhaps a rocky outcrop shaped like a skull, or simply what an execution ground was called. It was outside the city wall then but near it, beside a road, because the whole point of crucifixion was that passers-by should see it (v. 29). The Church of the Holy Sepulchre, inside today’s Old City but outside the wall of Jesus’ day, has a strong claim to be the site.

What does it mean to take up my cross today? It means accepting whatever it costs to follow Jesus, rather than choosing the parts that are convenient. For Simon it was a crossbeam he did not ask for. For you it may be the loss of approval at work, a hard obedience in your marriage, a temptation refused every day, a costly forgiveness, or a call to serve somewhere unglamorous. It is not every hardship of life, such as illness or traffic, but the hardships that come because you belong to him. And notice that Simon carried it behind Jesus. You never carry your cross ahead of him or alone; he has carried the heavier one first.

In a sentence. The soldiers forced Simon of Cyrene, whose sons became known Christians, to carry Jesus’ cross to Golgotha.

On a Tuesday. Simon was forced to carry the cross; you are invited. And God can use an unwanted interruption to change a whole family. Think of the interruption you most resent this week, the request, the illness, the person who takes your time, and ask whether it is a crossbeam handed to you on the road. Carry it behind him, and see what he does with it.

For worship. The Maker of the universe stumbled on a Jerusalem street under a beam of wood, too weak to carry it, so that we could be carried. He let a stranger bear his cross for a few hundred yards, and then bore our sins the whole way to death. And he turned the worst morning of Simon’s pilgrimage into the beginning of a family’s salvation. That is our Lord: he takes what is forced on us and makes it a door, and no one who follows him under the weight of the cross ever regrets it in the end.
verseByVerse.note: Cyrene was a city in North Africa with a large Jewish community. Golgotha is Aramaic for “skull.” Rufus may be the man Paul greets in Rome.

verseByVerse.quote: And they offered him wine mixed with myrrh, but he did not take it. And they crucified him and divided his garments among them, casting lots for them, to decide what each should take.
verseByVerse.commentary:
They offered him wine mixed with myrrh, but he did not take it. And they crucified him and divided his garments among them, casting lots for them, to decide what each should take.

And they offered him wine mixed with myrrh, but he did not take it. The drink was a rough anaesthetic. Wine with myrrh dulled the senses, and Jewish tradition records that the women of Jerusalem provided it as an act of mercy to the condemned, on the strength of Proverbs 31:6: give strong drink to the one who is perishing. Even the Romans allowed it. It cost nothing and made the prisoner easier to handle. He did not take it. A decision. He is about to be nailed to a piece of wood and left for six hours, and he is offered the one thing available in the ancient world that would take the edge off it, and he refuses. He had said the night before that he would not drink wine again until he drank it new in the kingdom (14:25). And more than that, the cup he had been given in Gethsemane was to be drunk to the bottom, undiluted, with a clear mind (14:36). Everything that follows, the mockery, the darkness, the cry, he goes through fully conscious, having deliberately declined the mercy that would have blurred it. He would not be half-present at his own crucifixion. He would not dull what he had come to bear.

And they crucified him. Three words in Greek. That is all Mark says. No description of the nails, the raising, the position of the body. Neither he nor Matthew nor Luke nor John describes the physical process at all, and the restraint is universal and deliberate. Part of the reason is that nobody in the first century needed it explained. The victim was stripped, laid on the crossbeam, and nailed through the wrists and feet, or tied; the beam was hoisted onto the upright post; and he hung there, often for days, struggling to push himself up to breathe, until he died of exhaustion and suffocation. Cicero called it the cruellest and most disgusting penalty, and said the very word should be kept far from the ears of Roman citizens. But there is more to it than that. The Gospels are not trying to move you by the horror. They focus not on the physical suffering but on its meaning. A reader overwhelmed by the physical agony can miss the darkness at noon and the cry at three, which are the heart of what he bore.

And divided his garments among them, casting lots for them, to decide what each should take. The clothing of the executed belonged to the soldiers. A man’s clothes were among his few possessions: an outer cloak, an inner tunic, a belt, sandals, a head covering. So he was stripped, and the shame of it was total and public; Jesus was crucified naked. And four soldiers sat down in the dirt a few feet away and gambled, probably with dice. That is one of the most terrible details in the passion, and it is not the cruelty that makes it so. It is the ordinariness. The Son of God is dying above their heads, and the men closest to him are playing for a coat, because it is a working day.

Psalm 22. Mark does not point out that this is a quotation. He does not have to, because anyone who knew the Psalter would already have gone cold: they divide my garments among them, and for my clothing they cast lots (Psalm 22:18). That is the first line of Psalm 22, the psalm of the righteous sufferer, to surface in this chapter. There will be more. Mark is laying them in quietly, one at a time, until the man on the cross says the first line aloud. And there is an older garden behind it. Adam and Eve were clothed by God after the first sin (Genesis 3:21). Christ was stripped to clothe us in his righteousness.

Is it wrong for a Christian to take painkillers or sedation, since Jesus refused? No. His refusal belonged to his unique work. He had a cup to drink that no one else could drink, and he had to drink it with full awareness as our substitute. You are not bearing God’s wrath, and you are not asked to suffer more than you must. Scripture approves of medicine and relief: Paul told Timothy to take a little wine for his stomach (1 Timothy 5:23), and Luke was a physician. Receive pain relief with thanks as a gift of God’s kindness. What we learn from Jesus here is not to refuse medicine but to marvel at what he chose to endure for us.

In a sentence. Jesus refused the drugged wine and was crucified, and the soldiers gambled for his clothes, as Psalm 22 foretold.

On a Tuesday. Notice what you reach for to dull the edge of a hard day: the screen, the drink, the noise, the shopping. Not all of it is wrong, but some of it keeps you from facing God with what is actually happening. Choose one evening this week to sit with the hard thing in prayer, clear-headed, instead of numbing it. And when you dress in the morning, remember the soldiers at the foot of the cross, and thank him for the robe of righteousness you did not earn.

For worship. He was stripped naked so that you could be clothed in his righteousness (Isaiah 61:10). He refused the cup that would have dulled his pain, because he would not dull his love; he drank the cup of wrath with open eyes, every drop, for us. The soldiers gambled for his tunic, and won a piece of cloth. He gave himself, and won a people. Worship him, the Lamb who was fully present at the cross, so that we could be fully present with him for ever.
verseByVerse.note: Wine mixed with myrrh was a drugged drink to dull pain; Jesus refused it. The clothes of the condemned went to the execution squad.

parallels.desc: they divide my garments among them

verseByVerse.quote: And it was the third hour when they crucified him. And the inscription of the charge against him read, "The King of the Jews." And with him they crucified two robbers, one on his right and one on his left.
verseByVerse.commentary:
It was the third hour when they crucified him. The inscription of the charge against him read: The King of the Jews. And with him they crucified two robbers, one on his right and one on his left.

And it was the third hour when they crucified him. About 9 a.m. by Jewish reckoning, counting from sunrise, which is how Mark counts throughout: the sixth hour is noon (v. 33) and the ninth is three in the afternoon (v. 34). So the timetable is: arrested around midnight, condemned by the council before dawn, before Pilate at first light, crucified at nine, dark at noon, dead by three. Roughly fifteen hours from the garden to the grave.

The hour in John. A difficulty worth naming honestly, because a reader with John open will find one. John says it was about the sixth hour when Pilate handed him over (John 19:14), which on Mark’s reckoning would be noon, three hours after Mark has him crucified. Two answers are usually given, and both are reasonable. Some hold that John is using Roman civil reckoning from midnight, which would put the judgment at six in the morning and fit perfectly. Others point out that both writers work in three-hour blocks, third, sixth, ninth, with no clocks, and that John’s about is doing real work; ancient time-telling rounded heavily. What is not in doubt is that Mark’s own account is consistent to the hour, and that all four Gospels agree on the day, the place, the manner and the outcome.

And the inscription of the charge against him read, The King of the Jews. A placard (titulus) stating the crime was carried before the condemned man or hung around his neck, then fixed to the cross, so that everyone passing could see what this had been done for. Meant as mockery and a warning: this is what happens to rebel kings. Which makes it the only crime in history for which the charge, posted publicly by the state, was the plain truth. John adds that it was written in Aramaic, Latin and Greek, the languages of religion, power and culture, and that when the chief priests asked Pilate to change it, he refused: what I have written I have written (John 19:19–22). The one decisive thing Pilate did all day was to leave a true sentence standing. He proclaimed to the world, in three languages, who Jesus is. On the cross he is enthroned as King, ruling by giving his life.

And with him they crucified two robbers, one on his right and one on his left. Robbers (lēstas) is the word Jesus used at his arrest (14:48), probably meaning rebels like Barabbas, perhaps his companions. Jesus hangs where Barabbas would have hung, in his place. One on his right and one on his left: five chapters ago James and John came asking to sit at his right hand and his left in his glory, and he asked whether they could drink his cup, and told them they did not know what they were asking (10:37–40). This was his glory, and those were the places beside him. These are the men who got them.

Textual note. Some manuscripts add verse 28: And the Scripture was fulfilled that says, He was numbered with the transgressors (Isaiah 53:12, quoted in Luke 22:37). It is missing from the earliest and best manuscripts and was probably added from Luke. The ESV puts it in a footnote. It is true, though not original to Mark. That is why the numbers in your Bible run 27, then 29.

Does a missing verse mean the Bible is unreliable? No. It shows how carefully the text has been preserved and studied. We have thousands of manuscripts of the New Testament, far more than for any other ancient book, and by comparing them scholars can see where a scribe added something, as here, where someone evidently wrote the reference in the margin and a later copyist took it into the text. Modern Bibles tell you openly. The words themselves are true Scripture, from Isaiah and Luke, and nothing of doctrine depends on this verse. The God who inspired the Scriptures has kept them, and their message has come to us intact.

What does it mean that he reigns from the cross? It means the cross was not the interruption of his kingship but the way he exercised it. A king fights for his people and defeats their enemies, and on the cross Jesus defeated sin, death and the devil, disarming the rulers and authorities and triumphing over them (Colossians 2:15). He gave his life for his subjects rather than taking theirs. So the placard was truer than Pilate knew. The Lord we worship is a crucified King, and his crown was won at Golgotha before it was shown on Easter morning.

In a sentence. Jesus was crucified at about 9 a.m. under the charge The King of the Jews, between two rebels, in the places James and John had asked for.

On a Tuesday. If someone looked at your life this week and wrote a single line about what you live for, what would it say? Ask God to make the true title over your life his, not yours. And when you wish for a place of honour, at work, in the church, in the family, remember who sat at his right and left in his glory, and ask whether you want the places beside him on his terms.

For worship. The charge against him was the truth. He reigns from the cross, so worship the crucified King. Pilate wrote it in three languages, and it has since been read in thousands. He was numbered with the transgressors so that transgressors could be numbered with his people. He hung between two rebels at the centre of history, and from that throne he reached out to one of them and promised him paradise. The King of the Jews is the King of all the earth, and his throne is the cross before it is the clouds.
verseByVerse.note: The third hour was about 9 a.m. The ESV notes that some manuscripts insert verse 28: “And the Scripture was fulfilled that says, ‘He was numbered with the transgressors.’”

verseByVerse.quote: And those who passed by derided him, wagging their heads and saying, "Aha! You who would destroy the temple and rebuild it in three days, save yourself, and come down from the cross!"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Those who passed by derided him, wagging their heads and saying: aha! You who would destroy the temple and rebuild it in three days, save yourself, and come down from the cross!

And those who passed by derided him, wagging their heads. The first of three groups to mock, and this one is the general public: people on the road going in and out of the city, because Golgotha was beside a road and that was the point of it. Derided him is literally blasphemed him (eblasphēmoun). Jesus was condemned for blasphemy; now the real blasphemers are those who mock the Son of God. Wagging their heads is a gesture of contempt, and another quotation: all who see me mock me; they make mouths at me; they wag their heads (Psalm 22:7). That is the second line of Psalm 22 in this chapter. The same gesture appears over the ruins of Jerusalem: all who pass along the way clap their hands at you; they hiss and wag their heads (Lamentations 2:15).

Aha! You who would destroy the temple and rebuild it in three days. They are throwing the trial’s charge back at him, the false witness from last night (14:58) which even the court could not get two men to agree on. It has evidently got out and become the street version of what he said. And of all the things they might have mocked, they chose the one that was about to come true. At that very moment the temple of his body was being destroyed, and in three days he would raise it.

Save yourself, and come down from the cross! Recognise the voice. In the wilderness at the beginning, Satan offered him the kingdoms of the world without a cross (Matthew 4:8–9; see Mark 1:13). At Caesarea Philippi Peter took him aside and rebuked him, and was told get behind me, Satan (8:32–33). In Gethsemane, the hour pressed on him. And now, from the ground at the foot of the cross itself: come down. The same offer, again and again, in different voices, an enemy, a friend, a crowd, and always the same: be the Christ without the cross. He could have come down. Twelve legions of angels were at his command (Matthew 26:53). But if he saved himself, he could not save us. The tragedy of the people saying it is that they were asking for the one thing that would have damned them. The only way he could save the men jeering at him was to stay where he was and let them go on jeering.

The standing temptation. The pressure to come down is the standing temptation of every Christian: to have the crown without the cross, the benefits of Christ without the death of self, a faith that costs nothing. It is offered constantly, it always sounds reasonable, and it is always the voice from the wilderness. He did not come down. That is the whole reason there is anything to say.

Could Jesus really have come down from the cross? Yes. He was not held there by the nails or the soldiers but by his own will and his love for his Father and his people. He had said no one takes my life from me, but I lay it down of my own accord (John 10:18). If he had been unable to come down, his staying would not have been obedience. That is what makes his endurance so astonishing. Every minute of those six hours was chosen, and every taunt was an invitation he declined, for us.

In a sentence. Passers-by mocked Jesus with the false charge about the temple and taunted him to save himself and come down from the cross.

On a Tuesday. The world still says to Christians: save yourself. Jesus shows the other way: lose your life and save it (8:35). Listen this week for the voice that says come down: you have suffered enough, you deserve this, nobody will know, protect yourself first. Recognise it, and answer it with his example. And when someone mocks your faith, remember that the first Christian ever mocked was Christ, and he prayed for them.

For worship. They told him to save himself, and he saved them instead. The one who could have stepped down from the cross with a word stayed there with a love stronger than nails. He bore their blasphemy, their scorn and their wagging heads, and he bore our sin with it, until the work was done. Because he would not come down from the cross, we will one day go up to the Father’s house. He refused to save himself, and so he is able to save to the uttermost all who come to God through him.

verseByVerse.quote: So also the chief priests with the scribes mocked him to one another, saying, "He saved others; he cannot save himself. Let the Christ, the King of Israel, come down now from the cross that we may see and believe." Those who were crucified with him also reviled him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
So also the chief priests with the scribes mocked him to one another, saying: he saved others; he cannot save himself. Let the Christ, the King of Israel, come down now from the cross, that we may see and believe. Those who were crucified with him also reviled him.

So also the chief priests with the scribes mocked him to one another. The second group, and the worst. These are not passers-by shouting. This is the religious leadership of Israel, at the foot of the cross, talking to one another, sharing the joke among themselves, with the satisfaction of people whose problem has been solved. They speak to one another, not to him: he is beneath their address. They are the most educated men in the country, in their own holy city, at Passover, gloating at an execution.

He saved others; he cannot save himself. With those words they state the gospel more accurately than anyone else in Mark, and do not believe a syllable of it. Take the two halves. He saved others: a concession, made in mockery, by his enemies, at a moment when they have nothing to gain by it, and therefore about as good a piece of hostile testimony as exists. They are not disputing the miracles; they never did (3:22). He cannot save himself: and that is true too, and it is the most important sentence in the chapter. Not because the power was gone. He could not save himself because saving himself and saving others were the two things that could not both be done. That was the whole choice. If he comes down, he is safe and we are lost. If he stays, we are saved and he is not. He chose not to. Love bound him to the cross more firmly than nails. The priests thought they had found a contradiction. They had found the heart of the atonement, and said it aloud in the one place where it was being accomplished.

Let the Christ, the King of Israel, come down now from the cross that we may see and believe. The Jewish form of the title (compare v. 26), mocking his claim before the council (14:61–62). And it is an offer of belief on their terms, with the order reversed: show us and we will trust you. It is the demand for a sign again, from the same kind of men who demanded one and were refused (8:11–12). And it is a lie, and they had already proved it. They had seen a withered hand restored in their own synagogue and gone out to plan a murder (3:5–6). Within days they will hear that the tomb is empty and pay soldiers to say the body was stolen (Matthew 28:11–15). They would not have believed (Luke 16:31). In three days he would do something greater than coming down from the cross: he would come up from the grave. And still they would not believe.

Why he did not come down. He did not come down, and that is why anyone believes at all. Had he come down, the crowd would have seen a wonder and gone home exactly as they came: impressed, and unforgiven. He stayed up, and within three hours a Roman officer who had asked for no sign whatever was saying truly this man was the Son of God.

Those who were crucified with him also reviled him. The third group, and Mark leaves it there. Two men in the same agony, a few feet away, dying the same death, and they join in. There is no solidarity at Golgotha. Mark, focusing on Jesus’ total abandonment, records only the reviling. But Luke tells us what happened to one of them before the afternoon was out. He stopped, rebuked the other, and said: Jesus, remember me when you come into your kingdom, and was told: today you will be with me in paradise (Luke 23:39–43). So one of the men reviling him in this verse died a few hours later with a promise from Christ in his ears. That is worth remembering about anyone you have given up on, including yourself.

Why does God not give unbelievers the sign they ask for? Because the problem is not a lack of evidence but a refusal to submit. These men had seen miracle after miracle and had already decided. A sign on demand would have made them spectators, not believers. God has given the greatest sign of all, the resurrection (Matthew 12:39–40; Romans 1:4), and he gives his Spirit to open blind eyes through the preaching of Christ crucified (1 Corinthians 1:22–24). So when a friend says, I would believe if God showed himself, do not despair of them, and do not try to manufacture wonders. Point them to the cross and the empty tomb, and pray for the Spirit to do what signs cannot.

In a sentence. The religious leaders mocked Jesus, saying he saved others but could not save himself, and challenged him to come down so they might believe; even the criminals beside him reviled him.

On a Tuesday. Think of someone you have written off: a family member hostile to Christ, a colleague who mocks, perhaps your own heart on a bad day. Remember the robber who reviled him at noon and was in paradise by evening, and pray for that person again today, by name. And if you have been waiting for God to prove himself on your terms before you trust him, stop waiting. He has already done more than come down from the cross.

For worship. He did not save himself, so that he could save you. That is the gospel in the mouth of his enemies. The priests meant it as the final insult, and God made it the eternal hymn of his people: he saved others. He saved a reviling thief in his last hours; he saved a centurion at his death; he saved Peter after his denial and Paul after his persecution; and he has saved a multitude no one can number, by refusing to save himself. Worthy is the Lamb who was slain.

verseByVerse.quote: And when the sixth hour had come, there was darkness over the whole land until the ninth hour. And at the ninth hour Jesus cried with a loud voice, "Eloi, Eloi, lema sabachthani?" which means, "My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
When the sixth hour had come, there was darkness over the whole land until the ninth hour. At the ninth hour Jesus cried with a loud voice: Eloi, Eloi, lema sabachthani? which means, My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?

And when the sixth hour had come, there was darkness over the whole land until the ninth hour. Noon until three, the three brightest hours of a Middle Eastern spring day, and the light goes out. It is not an eclipse; Passover falls at full moon, when a solar eclipse is impossible, and no eclipse lasts three hours. Mark offers no explanation and no mechanism. He simply reports that the sun failed over the land for three hours while the Son of God was dying, and leaves it. The ninth hour was about 3 p.m., the time of the evening sacrifice in the temple (Acts 3:1).

Darkness in Scripture. A reader who knows the prophets will hear something. On that day, declares the Lord GOD, I will make the sun go down at noon and darken the earth in broad daylight; I will turn your feasts into mourning; I will make it like the mourning for an only son (Amos 8:9–10). Darkness at noon, at a feast, mourning for an only son: Amos said it eight hundred years earlier. And there was another darkness once in Egypt, on the eve of the first Passover, a darkness to be felt, three days of it, and then the night the firstborn died (Exodus 10:21–23). At the first Passover the darkness came before the firstborn was struck, and it does so again. In the Bible darkness at midday is never atmosphere. It is judgment, and it means the day of the LORD has come. God’s judgment on sin is falling, and it falls on Jesus. For three hours nobody sees anything. The mockery stops; Mark records no voice at all during the darkness. Whatever was happening between the Father and the Son in those hours happened where nobody could watch.

And at the ninth hour Jesus cried with a loud voice, Eloi, Eloi, lema sabachthani? Out of the dark comes the loudest sound of the day. Not the faint whisper of a dying man but a cry. A crucified man’s death is a slow suffocation, and every word costs an agonising push up on the nails. This is shouted. Mark keeps the Aramaic, the language Jesus spoke, as he did with Talitha cumi to a dead girl, Ephphatha to a deaf man, and Abba in the garden (5:41; 7:34; 14:36). All of them are moments of extremity, and all are the actual sound of his voice. These are the only words of Jesus from the cross that Mark records.

My God, my God, why have you forsaken me? The darkest words in Scripture. It is Psalm 22:1, and the psalm that has been surfacing all chapter is now named aloud by the one it was written about. Jesus, who always called God Father, Abba (14:36), now says my God. It is the only place in the Gospels where he addresses his Father as anything other than Father. He is not doubting or losing faith; he still says my God, twice, claiming as his own the very One he can no longer feel. But he experiences what no one else ever has: being forsaken by God. Why? Because he was bearing our sin. For our sake God made him to be sin who knew no sin (2 Corinthians 5:21). He became a curse for us (Galatians 3:13). The holy God turns away from sin, and Jesus, bearing it, experienced the abandonment that sinners deserve. This is the essence of hell: separation from the favour of God. Jesus endured it in the place of his people, so that they would never be forsaken. This is penal substitution at its heart.

Psalm 22. Quoting the first line of a psalm brought the whole psalm to mind. Psalm 22 moves from abandonment (vv. 1–21) through mockery (vv. 7–8), pierced hands and feet (v. 16) and the dividing of garments (v. 18), to victory and praise: all the ends of the earth shall remember and turn to the LORD (vv. 22–31). Its last words are: he has done it. Jesus’ cry is real dereliction; but it is also the cry of one who knows the end of the psalm.

Two errors kept off this verse. The first would soften it, as though he were merely quoting a psalm that ends in triumph and was not truly forsaken. He was. The abandonment was real. The second would break God in two, as though the Trinity were torn. That did not happen and could not.

What it does not mean. Not that the Trinity was broken, or that the Father stopped loving the Son. The Father was never more pleased with the Son than in this act of obedience (John 10:17; Ephesians 5:2). The Son, in his human nature, bore the Father’s wrath against sin and experienced the withdrawal of all sense of his favour. He remained the beloved Son and remained God through every moment of the dark. What he lost was not his Father’s love or his own deity, but the felt light of the Father’s face, borne in our place. The mystery is beyond us. But the fact is clear: he was forsaken so that we would be accepted.

Did Jesus descend into hell? The Apostles’ Creed says he descended into hell, and Christians have understood the phrase in different ways. Scripture does not teach that he went to a place of torment after death; he told the dying thief, today you will be with me in paradise (Luke 23:43), and committed his spirit to the Father (Luke 23:46). Calvin and the Heidelberg Catechism (Q. 44) take the phrase to mean the hellish agony he suffered in soul on the cross, above all in this cry. Others understand it simply as his remaining under the power of death until the third day (Westminster Larger Catechism Q. 50). Either way, the hell he entered was the forsakenness of these hours, and he entered it so that we never will.

What if I feel forsaken by God? Then pray as he did: my God, to the God you cannot feel. The blackest hour a soul can know, real God-forsakenness with its full weight, has already been entered by the Son, so that it would never fall on you. A believer may feel abandoned, as the psalmists often did, but he is never actually forsaken; I will never leave you nor forsake you (Hebrews 13:5) was bought with this cry. Keep praying, even if all you can say is why. Keep going to his people and his word. The darkness is not proof that he has let go; the cross is proof that he never will.

In a sentence. After three hours of supernatural darkness, Jesus cried out in the words of Psalm 22, asking why God had forsaken him, as he bore the judgment of God against sin.

On a Tuesday. Read Psalm 22 through slowly this week, all thirty-one verses, and notice how much of this chapter is in it, and how it ends. Then, when you next sin, do not tell yourself it is small. Look at the darkness at noon and hear the cry, and know what it cost. And when you next feel far from God, do not conclude that he is far from you. He was forsaken in your place.

For worship. Because he was forsaken, you never will be (Hebrews 13:5). Let this cry move you to grateful, wondering worship. The eternal Son, who had known only the Father’s delight from before the foundation of the world, cried my God into the dark, and the dark did not answer, so that every child of God could cry Abba and be heard. He drank the cup to the last drop. He bore the hell we deserved. And Psalm 22 ends where his work ends: he has done it.
verseByVerse.note: The sixth hour was about noon, the ninth about 3 p.m. Jesus cries out in Aramaic the opening words of Psalm 22.

parallels.desc: my God, my God, why have you forsaken me?
I will make the sun go down at noon

verseByVerse.quote: And some of the bystanders hearing it said, "Behold, he is calling Elijah." And someone ran and filled a sponge with sour wine, put it on a reed and gave it to him to drink, saying, "Wait, let us see whether Elijah will come to take him down."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Some of the bystanders who heard it said: look, he is calling Elijah. Someone ran and filled a sponge with sour wine, put it on a reed and gave it to him to drink, saying: wait, let us see whether Elijah will come to take him down.

And some of the bystanders hearing it said, Behold, he is calling Elijah. They mishear, or deliberately misunderstand. Eloi sounds like Eliyahu, Elijah, and a shouted word from a dying man could be taken either way. Popular Jewish belief held that Elijah, who had not died, came to help the righteous in trouble. So the deepest sentence ever spoken on this earth is misheard as a superstition. That is exactly what has happened all through this Gospel. The crowd hears the words and gets the meaning wrong. They thought he was John the Baptist, or Elijah, or one of the prophets (8:28). He is praying Scripture in his agony, and they think he is calling for a folk hero. They mock even his dying cry.

And someone ran and filled a sponge with sour wine, put it on a reed and gave it to him to drink. Sour wine (oxos) is cheap vinegary wine cut with water, the standard drink of soldiers and labourers. There would have been a jar of it at the site, because the detail had to stand there all day. Put on a reed to reach his mouth; crosses were not necessarily very tall. Note what this is not. It is not the drugged wine of verse 23, which he refused. It is a mouthful of liquid for a man dying of thirst, and it may have been an act of kindness: somebody ran. John records that Jesus said I thirst and received it (John 19:28–30). It is also Psalm 69:21: for my thirst they gave me sour wine to drink. Another psalm, another line fulfilled.

Saying, Wait, let us see whether Elijah will come to take him down. And there is the reason given, and it turns the kindness into something else: keep him going a little longer, so we can see whether anything happens. Mockery to the end. The whole crowd has become an audience waiting for an ending.

The irony. Consider what nobody at Golgotha knew. Elijah had already come. Jesus had said so on the way down from the mountain: Elijah has come, and they did to him whatever they pleased (9:13), meaning John the Baptist, who had preached in Elijah’s spirit and lost his head to a girl’s request at a party. So they stand under the cross wondering whether Elijah will come and rescue him. Elijah had come, and been beheaded in a prison for telling a king the truth, and nobody rescued him either. There was never going to be a rescue. That was the entire point, and it is why he is on the cross rather than in the crowd.

Was the man with the sponge being kind or cruel? Perhaps both, as people often are. He ran, which suggests pity; the words that follow sound like curiosity and mockery, and in Mark they may come from him or from those around him. We need not decide. What matters is that even this small act fulfilled Scripture, and that Jesus, who refused the anaesthetic, accepted the drink. He thirsted truly, as a man, so that he could give living water to all who thirst (John 7:37). No kindness done to him, however mixed, went unnoticed.

In a sentence. Mishearing his cry, bystanders said Jesus was calling Elijah, and someone gave him sour wine, mocking to see whether Elijah would come.

On a Tuesday. Jesus was misunderstood and mocked even in his dying words, so if you are misunderstood for your faith, he knows. When someone twists what you believe this week, answer gently, and do not be surprised. And look for one small mercy you can do for someone who is suffering, a drink, a visit, a word, even if your motives are mixed. Christ notices cups of water.

For worship. He who made the rivers and the seas was given sour wine on a sponge. He thirsted so that we could drink from the fountain of life freely. No Elijah came down to take him off the cross, because no one could, and because he would not be taken until the work was finished. The rescue they waited for never came, so that the rescue we needed could. He stayed under the weight of the world’s mockery and his Father’s wrath, alone, until he could say it was done.
verseByVerse.note: Sour wine was the cheap wine soldiers drank.

parallels.desc: for my thirst they gave me sour wine

verseByVerse.quote: And Jesus uttered a loud cry and breathed his last.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And Jesus uttered a loud cry and breathed his last.

And Jesus uttered a loud cry. Two things in that short sentence are extraordinary, and both are the observations of people who were standing there. A loud cry: this is not how crucified men die, and the centurion in the next verse knows it better than we do. Crucifixion kills by exhaustion and asphyxiation. Death comes when a man has no strength left to push himself up for another breath, and the end is a slow suffocation in which speech has long since become impossible. He shouted. Twice in four verses Mark records a loud voice, and the second is at the very moment of death. John tells us what he said: it is finished (John 19:30), tetelestai, a word that could be written on receipts: paid in full. Luke records: Father, into your hands I commit my spirit (Luke 23:46), from Psalm 31:5. That is not a man dying of exhaustion. It is a man finishing something.

And breathed his last. Mark’s verb is exepneusen: he breathed out. He died, a real death, of a real man. The Son of God died. Set it beside a sentence Mark wrote long before: the Son of Man came not to be served but to serve, and to give his life as a ransom for many (10:45). To give: nobody took it. No one takes it from me, but I lay it down of my own accord (John 10:18). His death was not defeat, but completion. He gave up his life at the moment he chose.

Six hours. From the third hour to the ninth. Crucified men often took days to die, and Pilate was surprised he had died so soon (v. 44). He had suffered terribly before the cross, but his early death also shows that he laid down his life when the work was finished. So the death of Jesus is not the moment the Romans finally overcame him. It is the last act of his freedom: a shout, and then a decision, at three o’clock in the afternoon in Passover week, a few hundred yards from the temple where the lambs had been killed. And in that same instant, in that temple, something happened that nobody outside the building could have seen.

What does his finished work mean for me? It means there is nothing left to pay. Everything required to forgive your sins and bring you to God was completed on the cross: the law fully obeyed, the penalty fully borne, the wrath fully satisfied. You cannot add to it by good works, sacraments, suffering or religious effort, and you do not need to. That is why the gospel calls you not to achieve but to receive. When your conscience accuses you, do not answer it with your record; answer it with his receipt.

Where did Jesus go when he died? His body lay in the tomb; his human soul went to the Father, as he said: into your hands I commit my spirit, and today you will be with me in paradise (Luke 23:43, 46). He did not cease to exist, sleep unconsciously or pass through a place of purging. That is also what happens to every believer who dies: absent from the body, at home with the Lord (2 Corinthians 5:8), consciously with Christ, which is far better (Philippians 1:23), waiting for the resurrection of the body. The death of Jesus has turned the death of his people into a homecoming.

In a sentence. With a loud cry, Jesus died.

On a Tuesday. If you have been trying to finish what Christ finished, adding your efforts to make sure God accepts you, stop today. Write down the sins that trouble you most, and across them write: it is finished. Then live this week as a forgiven person, not a person on probation. And if you fear death, for yourself or someone you love, hear his last words: Father, into your hands. They can be yours too.

For worship. It is finished. Nothing is left to pay, so rest in his finished work. He cried with a loud voice because he died as a conqueror, not a victim. He handed his spirit to the Father as a son goes home, and with the same breath he cancelled the record of debt that stood against us, nailing it to the cross. The ransom was paid in full, and no one will ever be asked to pay it again. Hallelujah, what a Saviour.

verseByVerse.quote: And the curtain of the temple was torn in two, from top to bottom.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And the curtain of the temple was torn in two, from top to bottom.

And the curtain of the temple was torn in two, from top to bottom. One sentence, and it may be among the most important in the book. There were two curtains in the temple. The outer one hung at the entrance of the Holy Place. The inner one separated the Holy Place from the Most Holy Place, the inner sanctuary that represented God’s throne room, where the ark of the covenant had once stood. Most interpreters take this to be the inner curtain. Josephus describes the temple veils as embroidered in blue, purple and scarlet, and Jewish tradition says the inner one was enormous, about 60 feet (18 m) high and as thick as a man’s hand.

What the curtain was for. It was a locked door made of cloth. Behind it no one went, ever, except the high priest, once a year, on the Day of Atonement, and never without blood (Leviticus 16:2; Hebrews 9:7). The curtain existed to say one thing, and it said it for fifteen centuries: you cannot come in. It was the standing announcement that sin has separated a holy God from unholy people, and that sinners cannot come into his presence on their own terms.

Was torn in two. Note the moment. Mark puts it in the same breath as the death: the shout, the last breath, the curtain. Not three days later at the resurrection; the instant he died. And the verb (eschisthē) is the one Mark used when the heavens were torn open at Jesus’ baptism (1:10). He uses it exactly twice, at the beginning and at the end. Heaven ripped open at the start, and the veil ripped open at the finish, and between them the whole ministry.

From top to bottom. Heavy woven fabric of that size does not tear. And if men had done it, they would have started at the bottom, because that is where hands reach. This one opened from the top, beyond human reach, and it is Mark’s way of telling you whose hands did it. It was torn by God, not by man. The way into the presence of God was not forced open from our side. It was torn open from his.

Its meaning. Two things together. First, access. Through the death of Jesus, the way into God’s presence is open to all who come through him. We have confidence to enter the holy places by the blood of Jesus, by the new and living way that he opened for us through the curtain, that is, through his flesh (Hebrews 10:19–20). Through his flesh: the veil was his body, and his body was torn so the veil could be. No more priests to go in for us, no more sacrifices; the one sacrifice is complete. Second, judgment. The temple’s system is finished, as Jesus foretold (13:2). The fig tree has withered. God has left the building. The true temple is now Christ, and his people.

Do we still need priests to come to God? No. Every believer has direct access to the Father through Christ, our one great high priest (Hebrews 4:14–16; 1 Timothy 2:5). Pastors and elders are given to teach, shepherd and pray for the church, and we should honour them, but they are not mediators who go into God’s presence on our behalf, and no sacrifice is offered by them. The whole church is a royal priesthood (1 Peter 2:9), offering spiritual sacrifices of praise and service. You do not need anyone’s permission to pray, confess or draw near.

Does the torn curtain mean anyone can come to God any way they like? No, and that would turn its meaning upside down. The curtain was torn at the moment of Christ’s death, because his death is the way through it. The access is real and open to all, but it is through his flesh, by his blood, and in no other way. Jesus said I am the way, and the truth, and the life; no one comes to the Father except through me (John 14:6). The door is wide open, and it has one name on it.

In a sentence. At the moment of Jesus’ death, God tore the temple curtain from top to bottom, opening the way into his presence and signalling the end of the old temple.

On a Tuesday. When you pray tonight, an ordinary person in an ordinary room with an ordinary week’s failures behind you, understand what you are walking through. There is no queue, no annual appointment, no priest to send in on your behalf, and no basin of blood to carry, because the blood has been shed and the door is off its hinges. So pray boldly, about large things and small, and do not hang back as if the curtain were still there.

For worship. You can come into the presence of God today, not by your own merit or through a priest, but through the torn flesh of Jesus. Come boldly (Hebrews 4:16). The most exclusive room in the world was opened to everybody at three o’clock on a Friday afternoon, and the man who opened it did it by dying. The God who once said keep out now says come in, and the hand that tore the veil from top to bottom is the hand of a Father running to meet his children.
verseByVerse.note: The curtain separated the Most Holy Place from the rest of the temple; only the high priest entered, once a year.

parallels.desc: a new and living way through the curtain

verseByVerse.quote: And when the centurion, who stood facing him, saw that in this way he breathed his last, he said, "Truly this man was the Son of God!"
verseByVerse.commentary:
When the centurion, who stood facing him, saw that in this way he breathed his last, he said: truly this man was the Son of God!

And when the centurion, who stood facing him. Here is the sentence the whole Gospel has been travelling towards. A centurion commanded about a hundred soldiers, the backbone of the Roman army, and had risen through the ranks. He was in charge of this execution: a professional soldier, probably twenty years in, a Gentile and a pagan, who had very likely supervised many crucifixions. He had spent the morning watching his own men gamble for the prisoner’s clothes. And he is standing facing him. Mark gives the position: not to one side, not in the crowd, but directly in front of the cross, close enough to see a man’s face, for six hours.

Saw that in this way he breathed his last. What convinced him was not a miracle. It was the way this man died. Mark says it precisely: he saw how he died. The refusal of the drugged wine, the silence under mockery, the absence of cursing, the darkness, the prayer in the dark, and finally a shout from a man who should not have had breath for a whisper. He had watched men die for twenty years and had never seen anything like it.

He said, Truly this man was the Son of God! The climax of Mark’s Gospel. Weigh what Mark has done, because the architecture is exact. He opened his book with these words: the beginning of the gospel of Jesus Christ, the Son of God (1:1). Since then the title has been spoken by the Father at the Jordan and on the mountain (1:11; 9:7), and shrieked by demons who knew perfectly well what he was (3:11; 5:7). And no human being in fifteen chapters has said it. Peter got as far as you are the Christ and then took him aside to argue about the cross. The disciples asked who then is this? and never answered. The first person in this Gospel to look at Jesus of Nazareth and call him the Son of God is a Roman execution officer, not a disciple, not a Jew, but a Gentile soldier, at the cross.

What did he mean? Some translate a son of God, since the Greek has no article, and a Roman might mean only a divine man, a hero. And was, past tense, as of a dead man. The centurion may have understood less than he said. But Mark records the words as the confession his whole book has been building towards (1:1). Whatever the centurion understood, Mark wants us to hear the full confession. And the emperor was called son of god (divi filius) on coins. A Roman soldier gives the title to a crucified Jew instead.

The secret revealed. All through Mark, Jesus silenced those who would announce him. Now, at the cross, the secret is out. He can be proclaimed as Son of God, because the cross shows what that means: not a conqueror who takes life, but one who gives his life as a ransom for many. That is the answer to the question the Gospel keeps asking. You learn who Jesus is by watching him die. Not by the healings; the crowds saw those and stayed baffled. Not by the teaching; the scribes heard it and planned a murder. At the cross, where he looks least like the Son of God, is the one place a human being finally sees it. You cannot understand him as Son of God except as the crucified one.

The wall has been leapt. The confession does not come from Israel. It comes from a foreigner, an occupier, a man with no covenant, no Scriptures and no synagogue, who had almost certainly never heard the name of Jesus before that morning. At the very hour when the chief priests of Israel are standing in the same place jeering, a soldier of the empire that killed him becomes the first man to confess him. The gospel has already leapt the wall. The nations are coming in, and the first of them is standing in front of a cross with blood on his boots.

Did the centurion become a Christian? Scripture does not tell us, and we should not pretend to know. Luke records that he praised God and said, certainly this man was innocent (Luke 23:47). What Mark wants us to see is not his later history but his words, which are the truth about Jesus spoken at the foot of the cross. The question for the reader is not whether the centurion was saved, but whether we will make his confession our own, with all that it means.

In a sentence. Seeing how Jesus died, the Roman centurion in charge of the execution confessed that he was truly the Son of God, the first human being in Mark to say it.

On a Tuesday. Stand where the centurion stood. This week, set aside time to read Mark 15 slowly, from beginning to end, and look at the way Jesus died. Then say his words aloud, as a confession and not a quotation. And remember him when you meet someone who seems far from God, an outsider, a hardened professional, a person of another faith. The first man in Mark to see who Jesus is was the one nobody would have expected.

For worship. Stand where the centurion stood, look at the cross, and make his confession your own: truly this man is the Son of God. The Son of God reveals his glory most clearly where it is most hidden, in weakness, shame and death. Caesar was called son of god on his coins; the true Son of God hung naked on a Roman cross and won the confession of Caesar’s own officer. From that moment the gospel has been running to the ends of the earth, and Gentiles from every nation have looked at the same cross and said the same words.
verseByVerse.note: A centurion commanded about a hundred soldiers.

verseByVerse.quote: There were also women looking on from a distance, among whom were Mary Magdalene, and Mary the mother of James the younger and of Joses, and Salome. When he was in Galilee, they followed him and ministered to him, and there were also many other women who came up with him to Jerusalem.
verseByVerse.commentary:
There were also women looking on from a distance, among them Mary Magdalene, Mary the mother of James the younger and of Joses, and Salome. When he was in Galilee, they followed him and ministered to him, and there were also many other women who came up with him to Jerusalem.

There were also women looking on from a distance. Mark has said little about them for fifteen chapters, and now, when everyone else has gone, he tells you they were there. The men had fled; the women stayed. From a distance is nearly the phrase he used of Peter in the courtyard (14:54). The difference is that Peter’s distance was chosen and theirs was imposed. Women did not stand at the foot of a Roman execution among the soldiers. As near as they were permitted, they were. They watched him die. Nobody made them, there was nothing they could do, and they stayed for six hours. They are witnesses of his death (here), his burial (v. 47) and his empty tomb (16:1–8). The Gospel’s chain of eyewitness rests on them.

Among whom were Mary Magdalene, and Mary the mother of James the younger and of Joses, and Salome. Mark names three, and naming matters: these are witnesses, and named witnesses could be found and questioned by anyone in the early church who wanted to check the story. Mary Magdalene came from Magdala, on the western shore of the Sea of Galilee. Jesus had cast seven demons out of her (Luke 8:2), so she is one of the great trophies of his ministry, and she will be the first person on earth to see him alive (16:9; John 20:11–18). She was not the sinful woman of Luke 7, as later tradition wrongly assumed. Mary the mother of James the younger and of Joses is identified by her sons, presumably because the church knew them; the younger, or the less, distinguishes this James from James son of Zebedee. She was perhaps the wife of Clopas (John 19:25). Salome was probably the mother of James and John (Matthew 27:56), which means the woman who once asked for the best two seats in the kingdom for her sons (Matthew 20:20–21) is standing here watching what those seats actually cost, with two rebels occupying them.

When he was in Galilee, they followed him and ministered to him. Two verbs, and both are large. They followed him: the word for discipleship in this Gospel, used of the fishermen leaving their nets (1:18). Mark applies it to women without comment, in a world where a rabbi did not normally have female disciples. And ministered to him: diēkonoun, served. It is what the angels did for him in the wilderness (1:13), what Peter’s mother-in-law got up and did the moment she was healed (1:31), and the word in the sentence that defines his whole mission: the Son of Man came not to be served but to serve (10:45). Luke adds the practical detail: they provided for him out of their means (Luke 8:3). For three years a group of women funded and fed the ministry of Jesus, and nobody wrote down what it cost them. These women were true disciples.

And there were also many other women who came up with him to Jerusalem. Many: not three, a company. And hold the two halves of this chapter together, because Mark has arranged them. The twelve men who swore they would die with him are not in this chapter. One sold him, one denied him with oaths, and the rest ran in the dark and are hiding somewhere in the city. The women stayed. They watched him die, they watched where he was buried, and they will be at the tomb at dawn on Sunday with spices they had no idea they would not need. The chain of witness runs unbroken from the cross to the empty tomb, and every link in it is a woman, in a culture where a woman’s testimony carried little weight in court, which is precisely why no one inventing a story would have built it this way.

What does this teach about women in the church? That women are full and honoured disciples of Jesus, followers and servants, faithful when men failed, and chosen by God as the first witnesses of the resurrection. The church that forgets this has forgotten its own foundation. Scripture also assigns the office of elder and the authoritative teaching of the church to qualified men (1 Timothy 2:12; 3:1–7), a pattern this commentary holds, with Jesus himself, who chose twelve men as apostles. But that is a difference of calling, not of worth or of devotion, and it is never a licence for men to belittle women. Some of the most faithful service in every church is done by women whose names only Christ records.

In a sentence. Women who had followed and served Jesus since Galilee, including Mary Magdalene, Mary the mother of James and Joses, and Salome, watched his death from a distance when the men had fled.

On a Tuesday. Faithful service that no one notices is noticed by Christ, and he made these women the first witnesses of his resurrection. Thank God for the faithful women in your church, and tell one of them this week, specifically, what her quiet service has meant. And if you are the one who stays when others leave, at a sickbed, in a hard ministry, in a church that is struggling, take heart. Mark wrote your kind into the story at the foot of the cross.

For worship. He who came to serve was served by these women, and he never forgot it. When the men ran, he let the women stay; when the tomb was empty, he showed himself first to a woman out of whom he had cast seven demons. The Lord of glory receives the love of those the world overlooks, and he makes them witnesses of the greatest event in history. Nothing done for him in the shadows is lost; every meal cooked and every coin given in Galilee is remembered in his kingdom.
verseByVerse.note: Salome may be the mother of James and John, named in Matthew as “the mother of the sons of Zebedee.”

parallels.desc: the women who provided for him

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The request (vv. 42–43). Evening is coming and with it the Sabbath, and a body left on a cross overnight would defile the land under the Law. And a member of the very council that condemned him goes to the governor and asks for the corpse.

Mark says he took courage, and he needed it. Joseph of Arimathea is a man of standing who has kept his hopes to himself, and he chooses the moment when Jesus is a convicted criminal and every one of his friends has run — to go public.

The verification (vv. 44–45). Pilate is surprised that he is dead already and sends for the officer in charge to confirm it. So the death of Jesus of Nazareth is certified by a professional executioner and reported to a Roman governor before the body is released.

The tomb (vv. 46–47). A linen shroud, a grave cut in rock, a stone rolled across — and two women sitting where they can see, memorising the address.
verseByVerse.theology:
The burial is not a postscript. It is evidence, and Mark reports it like a man building a case.

Four facts are established in six verses, and every one of them closes off an objection that would be raised later.

He was really dead. Pilate was surprised, because crucifixion normally took two or three days — so he summoned the centurion and asked. A professional soldier who had stood facing him for six hours confirmed it to the governor before the body was signed over. Any theory that Jesus survived the cross has to get past a Roman execution officer's report to his prefect.

He was really buried, in a known place. Not a common grave, which is where crucified bodies usually went, but a rock-cut tomb belonging to a named man of the council — a man the authorities could have produced and questioned.

The tomb was sealed. A stone rolled across the entrance.

And the location was witnessed. Mary Magdalene and Mary the mother of Joses saw where he was laid — Mark's last sentence of the chapter, and it exists to say that the women who go to the tomb on Sunday morning went to the right one.

There is no room in this account for a mistaken address, a swoon, or a grave nobody could find.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Joseph of Arimathea, a respected member of the council... took courage and went to Pilate.

John tells us he had been a disciple of Jesus, but secretly, for fear of the Jews (John 19:38), and Luke that he had not consented to the council's decision (Luke 23:51). So here is a man who had believed quietly for some time and had never said so.

And of all the moments to come out, he chooses this one.

Not the Sunday, when the tomb is empty and there is something to be glad about. Not the triumphal entry, when the crowds were shouting and it would have cost him nothing. He declares himself on the Friday afternoon, when Jesus is a convicted blasphemer executed by Rome, when the movement is finished, when every one of the twelve has vanished — and he does it by walking into the governor's residence and asking, as a member of the Sanhedrin, for the body of the man his own colleagues had just killed.

Now: he had everything to lose and nothing to gain. There was no upside. Association with a crucified criminal ended a career in that city, and he must have known it.

Which is worth putting to any Christian who has been quiet for a long time and is waiting for an easier moment to speak. The easier moment does not come, and it is not supposed to. Joseph's courage arrived on the worst possible day, and it is why he is in the Bible.

verseByVerse.quote: And when evening had come, since it was the day of Preparation, that is, the day before the Sabbath, Joseph of Arimathea, a respected member of the council, who was also himself looking for the kingdom of God, took courage and went to Pilate and asked for the body of Jesus.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When evening had come, since it was the day of Preparation, that is, the day before the Sabbath, Joseph of Arimathea, a respected member of the council, who was also himself looking for the kingdom of God, took courage, went to Pilate and asked for the body of Jesus.

And when evening had come, since it was the day of Preparation, that is, the day before the Sabbath. Late afternoon, before sunset. The Sabbath would begin at sunset, and no burial could be done on it. Mark explains the term for his Roman readers. Friday was the day you got ready: cooking, cleaning, finishing anything that could not be done once the Sabbath began. And there is a legal urgency behind the clock. The Law required that an executed man’s body not remain all night on the tree, but be buried the same day, for a hanged man is cursed by God (Deuteronomy 21:22–23). Paul quotes that verse about this event: Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law by becoming a curse for us (Galatians 3:13). So there are perhaps three hours of daylight left, a body on a cross, and no one to claim it. Roman practice was often to leave corpses hanging as a deterrent, or throw them into a common pit.

How is Friday to Sunday three days? In Jewish reckoning any part of a day counted as a day, so after three days and on the third day mean the same span (compare Esther 4:16 with 5:1). Even Jesus’ three days and three nights (Matthew 12:40) is a way of saying three days, not a count of seventy-two hours. Some have argued for a Wednesday or Thursday crucifixion, but Mark is plain that Jesus died on the day before the Sabbath. And when John calls this Friday the day of Preparation of the Passover (John 19:14), that most likely means the Friday of Passover week, the preparation for that week’s Sabbath, which is exactly how Mark explains the term here (see 14:12).

Joseph of Arimathea. A man walks out of nowhere into the last hours of the Gospel. Arimathea was a town in Judea, probably about 20 miles (30 km) north-west of Jerusalem. He appears in all four Gospels, and only here, at the burial. Matthew says he was rich, a disciple of Jesus (Matthew 27:57); John says secretly, for fear of the Jews (John 19:38).

A respected member of the council. The Sanhedrin, the same body that condemned Jesus at midnight. Luke tells us he was a good and righteous man who had not consented to their decision and action (Luke 23:50–51). He is somebody: he has a position, colleagues, a reputation and a rock-cut tomb, which was an expensive thing to own. And Isaiah had said it: they made his grave with the wicked and with a rich man in his death (Isaiah 53:9).

Who was also himself looking for the kingdom of God. Mark’s phrase is gentle, and it is a believer’s description. He had been waiting, expecting, like Simeon and Anna in the temple (Luke 2:25, 38), like all the quiet people in Israel who had read the prophets and were watching for God to act. And John tells us what had kept him silent: he was a disciple, but secretly, because of exactly who his colleagues were.

Took courage and went to Pilate and asked for the body of Jesus. He had to dare, to steel himself. It was a dangerous request. To ask for the body of a man executed for treason was to identify yourself with him, before both Pilate and the council. The bodies of the executed could be given to family or friends at the governor’s discretion, and Jesus’ family was not there to ask. And consider the timing, because it is the whole point of the man. He does not come out on Sunday, when the tomb is empty and there is something to be glad about. He does not come out on the day of the entry, when the crowds were shouting and it would have cost nothing. He declares himself on the Friday afternoon, when Jesus is a dead criminal, the movement is over, the twelve have vanished, and the only thing to be gained from association is ruin. He walks into the residence of the governor who has just executed the man, identifies himself as a member of the court that asked for it, and requests the corpse. Every person in that building will know where he stands, and so will every colleague on the council by morning. There was no advantage in it. The disciples had fled; Joseph came out of hiding. The cross made a secret disciple brave.

Is a secret believer a real Christian? He may be, for a time, as Joseph and Nicodemus were. Faith can be real and still timid, and Jesus does not break a bruised reed. But faith is not meant to stay hidden. Jesus says whoever is ashamed of me and of my words, of him will the Son of Man be ashamed (8:38), and Paul says that with the mouth one confesses and is saved (Romans 10:10). The normal way to confess him is baptism and joining his church. If you have believed quietly for a long time, Joseph’s story is not permission to stay hidden but a summons to come out, and a promise that the cross will give you courage.

In a sentence. As the Sabbath approached, Joseph of Arimathea, a respected council member looking for God’s kingdom, courageously asked Pilate for Jesus’ body.

On a Tuesday. If you have been a secret disciple, let the cross make you brave. Come out and identify yourself with Jesus. The better moment does not arrive, and it is not meant to. Joseph’s courage came on the worst possible day of the worst possible week. Name the person you have never told that you follow Christ, and tell them this week, simply. If you have never been baptised, speak to your pastor about it.

For worship. The crucified Christ draws his people out of hiding. On the day his cause looked dead, he gave a timid man the boldness of a lion. The one who was numbered with transgressors was laid in a rich man’s grave, exactly as the prophet said, because nothing about his death was left to chance. And the courage Joseph found that afternoon is the courage Christ still gives: the power of a love that was not ashamed of us, so that we need never be ashamed of him.
verseByVerse.note: The day of Preparation was Friday, the day before the Sabbath. Arimathea was a town of Judea. Bodies of the crucified were often left unburied.

parallels.desc: not left on the tree overnight

verseByVerse.quote: Pilate was surprised to hear that he should have already died. And summoning the centurion, he asked him whether he was already dead. And when he learned from the centurion that he was dead, he granted the corpse to Joseph.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Pilate was surprised to hear that he had already died. Summoning the centurion, he asked him whether he was already dead. When he learned from the centurion that he was dead, he granted the corpse to Joseph.

Pilate was surprised to hear that he should have already died. This is one of the most useful verses in the chapter, though it looks like an administrative detail. Pilate’s surprise is professional. Crucifixion was designed to be slow; that was its point, as a deterrent. Victims commonly lasted two or three days. It was so slow that soldiers sometimes broke the legs to hasten it, which is exactly what they had done to the two men beside him (John 19:32). Jesus was on the cross six hours. To a governor who had signed a great many of these orders, that was fast enough to be worth checking.

And summoning the centurion, he asked him whether he was already dead. So Pilate does not take Joseph’s word for it, and he does not guess. He sends for the officer commanding the execution detail, very probably the same man who has just said truly this man was the Son of God, a professional in killing who had watched it all, and puts the question to him directly.

And when he learned from the centurion that he was dead. Official confirmation: the body is not released until a professional soldier has confirmed the death to the governor’s face. Jesus really died. That matters, because from early times some have claimed that he only fainted on the cross and revived in the cool of the tomb (the swoon theory). Mark closes that door with a bolt, and he does it simply by reporting the paperwork. The death was doubted by the governor, examined on his instruction, and certified by an officer who had stood facing him for six hours. John adds that a soldier pierced his side, and blood and water came out (John 19:34). He was dead. Any theory that Jesus survived the cross has to get past a Roman officer’s report to a Roman prefect, and then explain how a man scourged, crucified and sealed in a rock tomb for a day and a half without food, water or care rolled away a stone from the inside and convinced terrified men that he was the risen Lord of life.

He granted the corpse to Joseph. Everywhere else the body is called a body. Here, in the sentence where Pilate signs it over, Mark uses ptōma, a corpse, the blunt word you would use of a carcass. He uses it once more in this Gospel, of John the Baptist’s body collected by his disciples (6:29). He is not being callous. He is being exact, because everything depends on it. What Joseph carried down off that cross was a dead man: not a swoon, not a coma, a corpse, with a Roman officer’s word on it and a governor’s signature. The Son of God was a corpse. Perhaps Pilate, believing him innocent, was glad to grant it.

Why does it matter so much that Jesus really died? Because a Saviour who did not die could not pay the penalty of death, and a resurrection without a death is no resurrection at all. The wages of sin is death (Romans 6:23), and he had to receive those wages in full in our place. And because death is the enemy every one of us will face, we need a Lord who has been there and come back. Christ died for our sins, was buried, and was raised (1 Corinthians 15:3–4): every link matters. If he only fainted, your grave is as final as it looks. Because he truly died and truly rose, it is not.

In a sentence. Surprised that Jesus was already dead, Pilate confirmed it with the centurion before giving the body to Joseph.

On a Tuesday. If you are facing death, your own or that of someone you love, or the fear of it, do not look away from this verse. The Lord you trust was a corpse, certified by Rome. He knows death from the inside, and he has the keys of it (Revelation 1:18). Tell him your fear plainly today. And if someone tells you the resurrection is a pious story, show them the paperwork Mark recorded.

For worship. Jesus truly died. And so his resurrection is real resurrection, a real victory over real death, and the hope of all who die in him. The Author of life lay as a corpse in a borrowed shroud, signed over by a Roman official like a piece of property. He went all the way down into death so that he could break its power from the inside. Death, where is your victory? It was certified on Friday, and overturned on Sunday.
verseByVerse.note: Crucified men often lingered for days; a death within hours surprised Pilate.

parallels.desc: the soldiers find him already dead

verseByVerse.quote: And Joseph bought a linen shroud, and taking him down, wrapped him in the linen shroud and laid him in a tomb that had been cut out of the rock. And he rolled a stone against the entrance of the tomb. Mary Magdalene and Mary the mother of Joses saw where he was laid.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Joseph bought a linen shroud, and taking him down, wrapped him in the linen shroud and laid him in a tomb that had been cut out of the rock. He rolled a stone against the entrance of the tomb. Mary Magdalene and Mary the mother of Joses saw where he was laid.

And Joseph bought a linen shroud. Fine linen, costly, bought quickly with his own money before the shops closed for the Sabbath. There is nothing prepared about any of this. A man who woke up that morning a secret disciple is now buying grave clothes for an executed criminal. And the word is sindōn. It appeared a chapter ago: a young man followed Jesus into the garden with nothing but a linen cloth about his body, and when they seized him he left it and ran away naked (14:51–52). One man abandoned his linen cloth to get away from Christ. Another bought one to wrap him in.

And taking him down, wrapped him in the linen shroud. Somebody had to do it. Somebody had to draw the nails, take the weight of the body, carry it and wrap it, and it was a member of the Sanhedrin, in his good clothes, on the eve of the Sabbath, making himself ceremonially unclean for a week by handling a corpse (Numbers 19:11) in the middle of the feast. John adds that Nicodemus, another member of the council, came too, with about seventy-five pounds of myrrh and aloes (John 19:39). A rich man’s burial for a criminal. Two members of the council that condemned him are the only men in Jerusalem attending to his body. It was done in haste, because of the Sabbath; the women would come to complete the anointing afterwards (16:1).

And laid him in a tomb that had been cut out of the rock. Wealthy families had tombs carved into the limestone hillsides around Jerusalem: a chamber with ledges or niches for bodies. Matthew says it was Joseph’s own new tomb (Matthew 27:60); John, that no one had yet been laid in it, in a garden near the place of crucifixion (John 19:41–42). An unused tomb meant there could be no confusion about which body was there. Joseph gives away his own grave. Executed among criminals, buried in a rich man’s tomb: both halves of Isaiah 53:9 happened on the same afternoon.

And he rolled a stone against the entrance of the tomb. Rock tombs were sealed with a large stone, often a disc, rolled down a groove in front of the entrance: easy to roll in, very hard to roll back out, uphill. It took several men, which is why the women will worry about it on Sunday morning (16:3–4). Matthew adds that the authorities sealed it and set a guard (Matthew 27:62–66). And that is the last thing anybody does for Jesus of Nazareth: a stone across a door, and then everyone goes home because the sun is going down.

Mary Magdalene and Mary the mother of Joses saw where he was laid. The last sentence of the chapter, and it is doing a specific job. They are still there. Everyone else has gone; the men who buried him are hurrying home before the Sabbath. Two women stay in the fading light and watch which tomb it is. They knew the right tomb, and on Sunday morning they would not go to the wrong one. Mark carefully records the same women as witnesses of the death (v. 40), the burial (v. 47) and the empty tomb (16:1). The chain is unbroken and the address confirmed. The Apostles’ Creed preserves the sequence: crucified, dead and buried. So does Paul’s summary of the gospel: Christ died for our sins in accordance with the Scriptures, he was buried, he was raised on the third day (1 Corinthians 15:3–4).

The worst silence in the Bible. And so the chapter ends. The King of the Jews is dead. The body is in a borrowed grave with a stone across it. The disciples are hiding. The women are walking home in the dark with nothing to do until the Sabbath is over. Every person who loved him believed that night that it was finished, and they were right, and they had no idea what the word meant. He had told them three times that he would rise again after three days. Not one of them remembered it. And this is Friday.

Why does the burial matter? It confirms the death, and it makes the resurrection unmistakable: a known body in a known tomb, sealed and watched, and found empty. It also means that Jesus has gone where all his people go. He lay in the grave and sanctified it. The Westminster Shorter Catechism says the bodies of believers, being still united to Christ, rest in their graves till the resurrection (Q. 37). When you stand at the grave of a believer, you stand where the Lord himself lay, and it is not the end of the story any more than this tomb was.

How should I live on the Fridays of life? As people who know that Sunday is coming, even when we cannot feel it. The women did the next faithful thing: they watched, they went home, they kept the Sabbath, they prepared spices. They did not understand, but they did not leave. When God seems silent and his cause looks buried, keep to the ordinary means of faithfulness, worship, prayer, service, and wait. The darkest Friday in history was followed by the brightest morning, and the God who did that has not changed.

In a sentence. Joseph wrapped Jesus’ body in linen, laid it in a rock tomb, and rolled a stone across the entrance, while two of the women watched where he was laid.

On a Tuesday. Visit, in your mind or in person, the grave of a believer you have loved, and say over it the words of the creed: crucified, dead and buried, and on the third day he rose again. Let that change the way you grieve. And if you are in a Friday now, a loss, a failure, a silence from God, do the next faithful thing today, and wait for him.

For worship. Jesus lay in a tomb, so that the grave would hold no terror for those who belong to him. He has made the grave a bed of rest. The Lord of glory was wrapped in linen, laid on a ledge of rock and shut in behind a stone, and the whole creation held its breath. He went down into the place of our deepest fear and made it a waiting room. Low in the grave he lay, Jesus our Saviour, and the stone they rolled across the door was only waiting for an angel.
verseByVerse.note: Rock tombs were sealed with a large stone, often disc-shaped, rolled into a groove.

15.theology:
The cry of dereliction (v. 34) has two errors to be kept off it. The first would soften it, as though he were merely reciting a psalm and not truly forsaken — he was; he was bearing sin, and God's holiness turned from the sin-bearer (2 Cor. 5:21; Gal. 3:13). The second would break God in two, as though the Trinity were torn and the Father ceased to love the Son — that did not happen and could not. He remained the beloved Son and remained God through every moment; what he lost was the felt light of his Father's face, borne in our place.

And notice the word he uses. Not God, why have you abandoned me, but my God, my God — twice claiming as his own the very One he could no longer feel. That is faith stripped of every comfort and still gripping in the dark, and it is the only place in the Gospels where he addresses the Father as anything but Father.

The curtain (v. 38) may be the most important sentence in the book. Sixty feet of woven fabric, a handbreadth thick, whose entire purpose for fifteen centuries was to say you cannot come in — torn at the instant he died, and torn from the top, which is beyond human reach. The way in was not forced from our side; it was opened from his.
