And it is the second thing in Mark torn from above: the heavens being torn open at the baptism (1:10), the same violent word, at the beginning and the end. We have confidence to enter the holy places by the blood of Jesus, by the new and living way that he opened for us through the curtain, that is, through his flesh (Heb. 10:19–20).

And the burial is evidence, not postscript. Pilate was surprised he had died so soon — crucifixion normally took days — so he summoned the centurion and asked. The death was doubted by the governor, examined on his order, and certified by the officer who had stood facing him for six hours, before the body was released. Mark even switches words in v. 45 to ptōma, corpse. Any theory that he survived the cross has to get past a Roman execution officer's report to his prefect.
15.examples:
Then: He saved others; he cannot save himself (v. 31) — the chief priests, jeering at the foot of the cross, stating the gospel with complete accuracy and believing none of it.

Both halves are true. He did save others, and his enemies concede it at the moment they have nothing to gain by conceding anything. And he could not save himself — not for lack of power, since he could have called twelve legions of angels (Matt. 26:53), but because saving himself and saving others were the two things that could not both be done. They thought they had found a contradiction; they had found the mechanism of the atonement.

Now: and the demand attached to it — come down now from the cross that we may see and believe — has the order exactly backwards, and it is the standing human demand. Show me and I will trust you.

He did not come down, and that is why anyone believes at all. Had he come down, the crowd would have seen a miracle and gone home impressed and unforgiven. He stayed up; and within three hours a Roman officer who had asked for no sign whatever was saying truly this man was the Son of God.

And notice what converted that officer. Not a wonder — Mark is precise: he saw that in this way he breathed his last. He saw how he died. That is the answer to the question this Gospel keeps asking. You learn who Jesus is by watching him die. The crowds saw the healings and stayed baffled; the scribes heard the teaching and planned a murder; and at the cross, where he looks least like the Son of God, a pagan finally sees it — and he is the first human being in fifteen chapters to say the words Mark opened his book with (1:1).

16.title: He Has Risen; He Is Not Here
16.text: <sup>1</sup>When the Sabbath was past, Mary Magdalene, Mary the mother of James, and Salome bought spices, so that they might go and anoint him. <sup>2</sup>And very early on the first day of the week, when the sun had risen, they went to the tomb. <sup>3</sup>And they were saying to one another, “Who will roll away the stone for us from the entrance of the tomb?” <sup>4</sup>And looking up, they saw that the stone had been rolled back—it was very large. <sup>5</sup>And entering the tomb, they saw a young man sitting on the right side, dressed in a white robe, and they were alarmed. <sup>6</sup>And he said to them, “Do not be alarmed. You seek Jesus of Nazareth, who was crucified. He has risen; he is not here. See the place where they laid him. <sup>7</sup>But go, tell his disciples and Peter that he is going before you to Galilee. There you will see him, just as he told you.” <sup>8</sup>And they went out and fled from the tomb, for trembling and astonishment had seized them, and they said nothing to anyone, for they were afraid. <sup>9</sup>Now when he rose early on the first day of the week, he appeared first to Mary Magdalene, from whom he had cast out seven demons. <sup>10</sup>She went and told those who had been with him, as they mourned and wept. <sup>11</sup>But when they heard that he was alive and had been seen by her, they would not believe it. <sup>12</sup>After these things he appeared in another form to two of them, as they were walking into the country. <sup>13</sup>And they went back and told the rest, but they did not believe them. <sup>14</sup>Afterward he appeared to the eleven themselves as they were reclining at table, and he rebuked them for their unbelief and hardness of heart, because they had not believed those who saw him after he had risen. <sup>15</sup>And he said to them, “Go into all the world and proclaim the gospel to the whole creation. <sup>16</sup>Whoever believes and is baptized will be saved, but whoever does not believe will be condemned. <sup>17</sup>And these signs will accompany those who believe: in my name they will cast out demons; they will speak in new tongues; <sup>18</sup>they will pick up serpents with their hands; and if they drink any deadly poison, it will not hurt them; they will lay their hands on the sick, and they will recover.” <sup>19</sup>So then the Lord Jesus, after he had spoken to them, was taken up into heaven and sat down at the right hand of God. <sup>20</sup>And they went out and preached everywhere, while the Lord worked with them and confirmed the message by accompanying signs.
16.overview:
Three women buy spices when the shops reopen on Saturday evening, and set out at first light to finish a burial. Not one of them expects a resurrection — he had told them three times and it had gone in nowhere. They are carrying ointment for a corpse, and the only thing on their minds is a stone they cannot move.

They arrive and find it moved, and a young man in white sitting inside, and the most important sentence in the book: He has risen; he is not here. See the place where they laid him. Not a symbol and not an experience — an event with an address, and an invitation to inspect the evidence.

Then a message with two extra words in it: tell his disciples and Peter. And they run away and say nothing to anybody, because they are terrified — which is where the oldest manuscripts of this Gospel stop.

The twelve verses that follow are printed in brackets in the ESV and most modern Bibles, and the question they raise is answered here in full rather than buried in a footnote. They summarise appearances recorded elsewhere, give the commission, and end with the Lord Jesus taken up and seated at the right hand of God — exactly as he had told the high priest he would be, on the night they condemned him for saying it.

And the last sentence of Mark is the reversal of verse 8: the people who said nothing went out and preached everywhere.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The errand (vv. 1–4). The Sabbath ends at sunset on Saturday, the shops open, and three women buy spices. They set out at first light on Sunday to finish a burial, and the only thing worrying them on the road is a practical problem they cannot solve: the stone. They arrive and find it solved.

The announcement (vv. 5–7). Inside the tomb a young man in white is sitting on the right, and what he says is the most important sentence in the book. He has risen; he is not here. See the place where they laid him. And then a message with one name added to it that has comforted failing Christians for two thousand years.

The silence (v. 8). And they run, and say nothing to anybody, because they are terrified.

That is where the oldest manuscripts of this Gospel stop — mid-sentence, almost, on the word afraid. Which raises the question this chapter cannot avoid, and which is dealt with plainly below rather than left in a footnote.
verseByVerse.theology:
Why is 16:9–20 in brackets, and can I trust my Bible?

Open the ESV at this page and you will find, before verse 9, a line in square brackets: Some of the earliest manuscripts do not include 16:9–20. That deserves a straight answer, because a reader who meets it for the first time can feel the ground move.

Here are the facts, plainly. The two oldest complete manuscripts of the New Testament we possess — Codex Sinaiticus and Codex Vaticanus, both fourth century — end Mark at verse 8. Eusebius and Jerome, writing in the fourth and fifth centuries, both say that the accurate copies known to them ended there. Some manuscripts have a different, shorter ending; a few have both. And the Greek of verses 9–20 does not read like Mark: it uses more than a dozen words found nowhere else in the book, and verse 9 introduces Mary Magdalene as though for the first time, though she has just been named in verse 1.

The honest conclusion is that Mark very probably did not write these twelve verses, and that they were added early — early enough to be widely known and read in churches by the second century.

And here is what that does not mean. It does not mean anything has been smuggled into your Bible. Every substantial thing in the passage is taught plainly elsewhere: the appearance to Mary Magdalene (John 20), the two on the Emmaus road (Luke 24), the commission to all nations (Matt. 28), the ascension and session at God's right hand (Luke 24; Acts 1; Eph. 1:20). No doctrine of the Christian faith stands or falls here.

So take the reassurance the right way round. The reason you know about this is that the church kept the evidence and printed it in the margin instead of quietly tidying it away. A faith that could not survive its own manuscripts would hide them. This one puts the workings at the bottom of the page — which is precisely why the rest of the text can be trusted.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: tell his disciples and Peter (v. 7).

Two extra words, and they are there because somebody in heaven knew exactly which man in Jerusalem was certain he had forfeited his place.

Peter had denied him three times with oaths and a curse, in a courtyard, to a servant girl, and had gone out and wept. As far as he knew, he was finished — not merely ashamed, but out.

And the first message from the other side of the grave has his name in it, added on, as though the general term might not reach him. In effect: tell the disciples, and make sure you tell Peter.

Now: and notice that this is not new. Jesus had promised it before the failure happened: you will all fall away... but after I am raised up, I will go before you to Galilee (14:27–28). The angel repeats his promise, and adds the name.

So if you are a Christian who has failed badly enough to wonder whether there is a road back, the answer is in two words at the empty tomb. The road was mapped before you took the wrong turn, and when the message came, the one who had failed worst was named.

verseByVerse.quote: When the Sabbath was past, Mary Magdalene, Mary the mother of James, and Salome bought spices, so that they might go and anoint him. And very early on the first day of the week, when the sun had risen, they went to the tomb.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When the Sabbath was over, Mary Magdalene, Mary the mother of James, and Salome bought spices so that they might go and anoint him. Very early on the first day of the week, when the sun had risen, they went to the tomb.

Meaning first. Mark 16 opens on the morning after the longest Sabbath in history. Three women who watched Jesus die and saw where he was buried go to the tomb at sunrise with spices for a corpse, worrying about who will move the stone. They find it rolled back, and inside a young man in white tells them not to be alarmed: Jesus of Nazareth, who was crucified, has risen; he is not here; see the place where they laid him. They are sent to tell his disciples, and Peter by name, that he is going before them to Galilee, just as he told them. They flee, trembling and astonished, and say nothing to anyone, for they were afraid, and there the earliest manuscripts of Mark end. The verses that follow in most Bibles (vv. 9–20) were very probably added early by another hand; they summarise the appearances, the commission to preach the gospel to the whole creation, and the ascension of the Lord Jesus to the right hand of God. The whole chapter says one thing with overwhelming force. The crucified one is alive, death is defeated, failures are called back by name, and the gospel that Mark called a beginning now runs on to the ends of the earth.

The setting. Jesus died at about three o’clock on Friday afternoon and was buried in haste before sunset (15:42–47). Then the Sabbath closed down and nothing could be done for twenty-four hours. That was the longest day in the history of the world, and Mark says nothing about it at all.

When the Sabbath was past. Saturday evening, after sunset, when the shops could open again. They had watched him buried with the light going (15:47).

Mary Magdalene, Mary the mother of James, and Salome bought spices. The same names as at the cross (15:40) and, for two of them, at the burial (15:47). Mark keeps naming them because they are witnesses, and a named witness could be found and questioned. They are the link of eyewitnesses: they saw him die, saw where he was laid, and now go to the same tomb. And they spend money. Somebody’s savings went on those spices, and it was the last thing they expected to be able to do for him.

So that they might go and anoint him. Fragrant oils to pour over the body, an act of love and honour, and to offset the smell of decay. Understand what this errand is, because it decides how you read everything that follows. They are going to a grave to do the last office for a corpse. The burial on Friday had been done at speed, by two men racing the sunset, with no time for the proper anointing, and they are going to finish it. Which means, and it must be said plainly, not one of them expected a resurrection. Nobody in this chapter is going to see whether it worked. They are carrying two days of grief and a bag of spices to a body they expect to be there and to have begun to decay. He had told them three times that he would rise after three days (8:31; 9:31; 10:34). It had gone in nowhere. So whatever else the first Easter morning was, it was not wish-fulfilment. Nobody was hoping. The resurrection was not invented by people who expected it. The story begins with his friends buying ointment for a dead man.

And very early on the first day of the week, when the sun had risen, they went to the tomb. Mark’s timestamps are precise: very early, and yet with the sun up. John says it was still dark when Mary set out (John 20:1); by the time they arrived it was light. And the first day of the week is a phrase that changed the calendar of the world. All four Gospels use it. Within a generation Christians were meeting on it (Acts 20:7; 1 Corinthians 16:2), and by the end of the century John was calling it the Lord’s Day (Revelation 1:10). The Sabbath, the seventh day, commemorated God’s rest after the first creation; the Lord’s Day celebrates the beginning of the new creation in Christ’s resurrection.

Is Sunday the Christian Sabbath? Christians who agree on almost everything else differ here, and both views deserve a fair hearing. Many Reformed and Baptist Christians, following the Westminster Confession (Westminster 21.7–8) and the 1689 Confession (22.7–8), hold that the Sabbath command still stands and has moved, with the resurrection, to the first day, so that the Lord’s Day is to be kept holy as a day of worship and rest. Others hold that the Sabbath, as a sign of the old covenant, is fulfilled in Christ, our true rest (Colossians 2:16–17; Hebrews 4:9–10), and that Christians gather on the first day not as a law but because it is the day of resurrection. Verdict: the second view fits the New Testament best; the Lord’s Day is a gift, gladly set apart for worship, fellowship and rest, and no one may bind another believer’s conscience over it (Romans 14:5). Both agree that the apostles’ churches met on the Lord’s Day from the beginning, that regular rest is God’s gift, and that gathering with God’s people each week is not optional for a Christian.

Why did no one remember that he had said he would rise? Because grief and unbelief are deafening, and because what he said did not fit what they expected of a Messiah. Each time he predicted his death and resurrection, the disciples either argued, misunderstood or were afraid to ask (8:32; 9:32). They heard the death and could not hear the rising. We are not so different. Many of us know the promises of God and forget them the moment trouble comes. That is why Scripture keeps saying remember, and why the angel will soon say: just as he told you.

In a sentence. After the Sabbath, three women who had watched Jesus’ death and burial brought spices to anoint his body, and went to the tomb early on Sunday morning.

On a Tuesday. Every Lord’s Day is a celebration of the resurrection, so plan your week around it rather than fitting it into the gaps. Prepare on Saturday night as these women prepared their spices: go to bed in good time, pray for the preaching, think of someone to welcome. And when you wake on Sunday, say first: he is risen.

For worship. They came with spices for the dead, and found the Lord of life. Their love was real and their hope was gone, and God met them anyway, at sunrise on the first day of a new creation. The Sabbath had rested over a sealed tomb; the first day broke over an empty one. Every Lord’s Day since has carried the light of that morning, and every gathering of his people is a small Easter, until the morning when the sun rises on a world with no graves in it.
verseByVerse.note: The Sabbath ended at sundown on Saturday; the first day of the week is Sunday.

verseByVerse.quote: And they were saying to one another, "Who will roll away the stone for us from the entrance of the tomb?" And looking up, they saw that the stone had been rolled back—it was very large.
verseByVerse.commentary:
They were saying to one another: who will roll away the stone for us from the entrance of the tomb? And looking up, they saw that the stone had been rolled back. It was very large.

And they were saying to one another, Who will roll away the stone for us from the entrance of the tomb? The tense is continuous: they kept saying it, all the way there. This is the conversation on the road, and it is entirely reasonable. They had watched Joseph roll it across on Friday (15:46). The stone was too heavy for three women, and Matthew says it was sealed and guarded as well (Matthew 27:66). These are women carrying jars, on a path outside the city at dawn, and the one thing standing between them and the errand is a piece of stone they cannot move and have no plan for. Note that they set out anyway. They set out to do what love required, without knowing how. A more calculating person stays at home until the problem is solved.

And looking up, they saw that the stone had been rolled back. Looking up: the tomb was perhaps up a slope, or they had been walking with their heads down in grief. Had been rolled back is passive: rolled back by God. Matthew says an angel rolled it away and sat on it (Matthew 28:2).

It was very large. Mark puts the size at the end of the sentence, almost as an afterthought, exactly as somebody tells a story afterwards: and it had been moved, and it was enormous. A blocking stone for a rock-cut tomb was a disc set in a channel, perhaps weighing a ton or more. Getting it into place was downhill work for several men; getting it out again was not. Mark adds this to show that it could not have been moved by accident, or by the women.

Moved so the world could look in. Here is the first thing the resurrection does in this Gospel. The stone was not moved to let Jesus out. A sealed tomb was no obstacle to a risen Christ, who would come through locked doors that same evening (John 20:19). The stone was moved so that the witnesses could look in. And the pastoral point stands, and it is the plainest comfort in the chapter. They spent the walk on a difficulty that had already been settled. God had gone ahead of them in the dark, while they were still grieving and still certain nothing had changed.

Does God always remove the obstacles I worry about? Not always in the way we hope, and we should not promise ourselves that he will. Sometimes the stone stays, and he gives strength to live beside it. But the empty tomb tells you that the greatest obstacle of all, death itself, has already been rolled away, and that nothing you face is beyond his power or outside his care. Very often, the thing you are rehearsing at four in the morning is dealt with before you reach it. When it is not, he walks with you through it. Either way, it is still right to set out in faithful love without having the solution.

In a sentence. Wondering who would roll away the heavy stone for them, the women looked up and saw it had already been rolled back.

On a Tuesday. What stone are you worried about? Go forward in faithful love; God often removes the obstacle before you reach it. Name the thing you are dreading this week, and instead of rehearsing it again, pray about it once, plainly, and then take the next step you know you should take. You may find the stone already moved.

For worship. The stone was very large, and it was nothing to him. The God who rolled back the stone from the grave of his Son rolls back the weight of sin from the hearts of sinners, and one day will roll back the stones from every grave of his people. He goes ahead of us in the dark, while we are still weeping, and does what we could not do. Our anxious questions on the road are answered before we arrive, because the Lord has risen indeed.

verseByVerse.quote: And entering the tomb, they saw a young man sitting on the right side, dressed in a white robe, and they were alarmed.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Entering the tomb, they saw a young man sitting on the right side, dressed in a white robe, and they were alarmed.

And entering the tomb. They go in. A rock-cut tomb of this kind had a low doorway and an outer chamber, with a shelf cut into the rock where the body was laid. So they stoop through and stand up inside a room built for the dead.

They saw a young man sitting on the right side, dressed in a white robe. An angel, in human form, as angels often appear in Scripture (Genesis 18:2; Daniel 9:21). Mark says a young man, describing what they saw; Matthew says plainly that it was an angel (Matthew 28:2–5), and the white robe and the reaction settle it. Dressed in a white robe: the colour of heaven and glory, like Jesus’ clothes on the mountain (9:3).

Sitting on the right side. A small detail with two things in it. He is sitting, which is the posture of somebody whose work is finished and who is waiting. There is no urgency in that tomb. The crisis is over; an angel has sat down. And the right side is the side of honour and good news, the place the sons of Zebedee asked for (10:37), the place where Jesus himself now sits (v. 19).

The two young men. Here is a bracket, one of the loveliest things in this Gospel. The phrase a young man (neaniskos) occurs exactly twice in Mark. The first time was in the garden on the night of the arrest: a young man followed him with nothing but a linen cloth about his body, and when they seized him he left it and ran away naked (14:51–52), perhaps Mark himself, putting his own worst moment into his own book. The second time is here: a young man, sitting down, dressed in white, inside an empty grave, telling women that Christ is risen. One fled from Christ stripped and ashamed in the dark. One sits in the place of death, clothed in white, with the news. The frightened follower who lost his linen cloth gives way to a heavenly messenger in white. Whether or not Mark intended every echo, the picture is the gospel: that is what happens to people between Friday and Sunday.

And they were alarmed. The word (exethambēthēsan) means utterly astonished, overwhelmed with awe, the same strong word used of Jesus in Gethsemane (14:33). They came expecting a corpse and found a living stranger sitting where it should have been. Every reaction to the supernatural in this Gospel is the same, and it is never serene: the disciples in the boat (4:41), the crowd at the demoniac’s healing (5:15), the three on the mountain (9:6). Nobody in the Bible meets the power of God and finds it comfortable. That is why the first word out of the angel’s mouth is the one it always is.

Why do the Gospels differ about the angels? Matthew has one angel, Luke two men in dazzling clothes (Luke 24:4), John two angels; the women and the times vary too. Each Gospel tells the story selectively, and none says there was only one. If there were two, there was certainly one, and a writer may mention only the one who spoke. The women evidently came in more than one group, at slightly different times. Such differences are what you expect from independent witnesses, not from a story agreed in advance. The core is the same in all four: the women came first, the tomb was empty, and the message was that he had risen.

In a sentence. Entering the tomb, the women were overwhelmed to see an angel in the form of a young man in white sitting on the right.

On a Tuesday. The resurrection is not ordinary news, so let it astonish you again. If Easter has become familiar, read the four accounts side by side this week, slowly, and try to stand in that room at sunrise. And notice that the God who sent an angel to sit in a tomb has turned the place of your greatest fear into a place of good news.

For worship. Heaven sat down in the grave. The angel had nothing to guard and nothing to fight, only news to give, because the work was done. The tomb that was cut for the dead became the first pulpit of the resurrection, and the messenger in white sat where the body had lain. Our God turns graves into places of announcement, and terror into worship, and the one who once fled naked in the dark is clothed in white at the end of the story.

verseByVerse.quote: And he said to them, "Do not be alarmed. You seek Jesus of Nazareth, who was crucified. He has risen; he is not here. See the place where they laid him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
He said to them: do not be alarmed. You seek Jesus of Nazareth, who was crucified. He has risen; he is not here. See the place where they laid him.

Do not be alarmed. The same word as the last verse, negated. The first word of the resurrection message is comfort. He deals with their terror before he gives them the news, which is how heaven habitually opens a conversation: fear not is the first thing said to Zechariah, to Mary, to the shepherds, and to John on Patmos.

You seek Jesus of Nazareth, who was crucified. Three things in that identification, and every one is nailed down. Jesus: the personal name. Of Nazareth: the village, the human address, the ordinary origin that made people take offence (6:3). Who was crucified: the perfect participle (estaurōmenon) means the one who has been crucified, and remains the crucified one. There is no ambiguity about who is meant. The risen one is the crucified one; it is the same man, and he still carries the identity. When he appears to Thomas he will still have the wounds (John 20:27). Christianity has never offered a Jesus who got past the cross. It offers a man who went through it and out the other side, and who is known by it for ever: a Lamb standing, as though it had been slain (Revelation 5:6). The cross is not erased by the resurrection; it is vindicated.

He has risen. The heart of the gospel, and the hinge of history. Literally he has been raised (ēgerthē), a passive: God raised him (Acts 2:24; Romans 10:9). That is how the New Testament almost always puts it. The resurrection is the Father’s public verdict on the Son, the answer to the cry from the dark, the reversal of the council’s sentence. The court of heaven has overturned the court of Caiaphas. The rejected stone has become the cornerstone (12:10). It proves that he is who he claimed to be (Romans 1:4), that his sacrifice for sin has been accepted (Romans 4:25), that death has been defeated (1 Corinthians 15:54–57), and that all who belong to him will be raised as he was (1 Corinthians 15:20–23).

He is not here. The empty tomb: a bodily resurrection. Not merely that his spirit lived on, or that his disciples felt his presence, or that his cause continues. It is a claim about a physical location on a spring morning. The body was not in the room, and the room was one the women had personally watched him carried into (15:47). Something had happened to it.

See the place where they laid him. And now the angel does something no myth does: he offers evidence and invites inspection. Look. Come and look at the shelf. There is nothing on it. The faith of the church does not rest on feelings but on facts, on a real tomb, really empty. John records that the grave clothes were still there, lying in place (John 20:5–7). Paul stakes everything on the same ground: if Christ has not been raised, your faith is futile and you are still in your sins (1 Corinthians 15:17). The tomb was open, the location was known, and the authorities had soldiers. All they had to do was walk in and carry out the body. The place was empty, and it still is.

Evidence for the resurrection. The empty tomb, which the authorities never disputed but explained by claiming the disciples stole the body (Matthew 28:11–15). The appearances to many witnesses, including over five hundred at once, most of them still alive when Paul wrote (1 Corinthians 15:5–8). The transformation of frightened, scattered disciples into bold witnesses ready to die. The conversion of sceptics like James and Paul. And the change of the day of worship from Saturday to Sunday by Jewish believers. None of this is explained except by the resurrection.

What will our resurrection bodies be like? Like his. Paul says Christ will transform our lowly body to be like his glorious body (Philippians 3:21). It will be truly your body, recognisably you, as Jesus was recognisably himself, scars and all; he ate, he could be touched, he was not a ghost (Luke 24:39–43). But it will be changed: raised imperishable, in glory and in power, a body fully suited to life in the Spirit (1 Corinthians 15:42–44). No more sickness, ageing, disability or death. The empty tomb is God’s pledge that he does not throw away what he made. He redeems it.

In a sentence. The angel told the women not to be alarmed: Jesus the crucified one had been raised, was not there, and they could see the empty place where he had lain.

On a Tuesday. He is risen, so live this week as someone whose greatest enemy is already beaten. When you are tempted to despair, about your sin, your health, the state of the world, go back in your mind to the empty shelf. And if someone asks why you believe, do not begin with your feelings. Begin where the angel began: with Jesus of Nazareth, who was crucified, and a tomb that was empty.

For worship. He is risen. Your sins are paid for, death is beaten, and he lives for ever, so worship the risen, crucified Lord. The Father has spoken his verdict over the Son, and it is the opposite of the world’s. The stone the builders rejected is the head of the corner; the man condemned as a blasphemer is declared the Son of God in power. Death could not keep its prey. And because he lives, we shall live also, in bodies like his, in a world made new, before a throne where the Lamb who was slain is worshipped for ever.

verseByVerse.quote: But go, tell his disciples and Peter that he is going before you to Galilee. There you will see him, just as he told you."
verseByVerse.commentary:
But go, tell his disciples and Peter that he is going before you to Galilee. There you will see him, just as he told you.

But go, tell his disciples and Peter. The first commission of the new age is given to three women in a graveyard. In a culture where women’s testimony was not accepted in court, God chose women as the first messengers of the resurrection. No one inventing the story would have done that; it is a mark of truth. And notice his disciples: still his disciples, though they deserted him.

And Peter. Two extra words that have done more for failing Christians than almost any other phrase in Scripture. Only Mark has them. Peter was one of the disciples; the word covered him. There was no need to add anything, unless somebody in heaven knew exactly which man in Jerusalem was certain that it no longer did. Peter had denied him three times, in a courtyard, to a servant girl, with oaths and a curse on his own head, and had gone out and broken down (14:71–72). He had spent Saturday somewhere in that city with nothing to think about but that. As far as he knew he was not merely ashamed; he was out. And the first message sent from the other side of the grave has his name attached to the end of it, as though the general term might not reach him. Tell the disciples, and make sure you tell Peter. Jesus singles out the one who failed most. And Mark probably heard the story from Peter himself, who never forgot those two words. The risen Lord appeared to Peter personally (Luke 24:34; 1 Corinthians 15:5), and restored him publicly (John 21:15–19).

That he is going before you to Galilee. This is not new information; it is a quotation. On the walk to Gethsemane, before anybody had failed, Jesus had said: you will all fall away; but after I am raised up, I will go before you to Galilee (14:27–28). The angel repeats it almost word for word. So the restoration was promised before the betrayal happened, and the meeting place was fixed while they were still swearing they would never need it. Go before is a shepherd’s picture, walking out in front of the flock. The struck shepherd is out in front of them again, and the scattered sheep will be gathered (14:27). And Galilee: not Jerusalem, where it all went wrong, but home, the lake, the boats, the towns where they were called off their nets in chapter 1. He takes them back to the beginning to start again.

But did he not appear in Jerusalem first? Yes. Luke and John record appearances in Jerusalem that Sunday and the week after, and Luke has Jesus tell them to stay in the city (Luke 24:49). The Jerusalem appearances came first; the meeting in Galilee followed (Matthew 28:16; John 21); and they returned to Jerusalem to wait for the Spirit. Luke’s command to stay belongs to the end of the forty days. Mark points to Galilee because it was the promised meeting and the place of their calling, not because nothing happened before it.

There you will see him, just as he told you. The last clause is the angel’s own comment, gentle and slightly pointed: just as he told you. He had told them repeatedly. Every element of this weekend had been announced in advance, the betrayal, the scattering, the denial, the death, the third day, and not one of them had held on to any of it. His word has proved true in everything: the colt (11:2–6), the room (14:13–16), the betrayal, Peter’s denial, his death, and now his resurrection. So the message to the disciples on Easter morning is not a rebuke and not a reward. It is a reminder that he had said so, and that he keeps his word even when nobody believed it.

Have I failed too badly to be called back? If Peter was not beyond it, you are not. His failure was public, repeated, sworn and at the worst possible moment, and the first message of the risen Christ named him. Christ does not restore only those whose failures were small. He restores those who come back. Your feelings may tell you that you have used up his patience; his word says that whoever comes to him he will never cast out (John 6:37). Put your own name after the words and Peter, and go to meet him where he has promised to be: in his word, in prayer, among his people.

In a sentence. The angel sent the women to tell the disciples, and especially Peter, that the risen Jesus was going ahead of them to Galilee, where they would see him, as he had promised.

On a Tuesday. And Peter: put your own name there, especially if you have failed him. The risen Lord is calling you back. And then be the messenger for someone else. Think of a believer who has fallen away or failed badly and is staying away out of shame, and send them a message this week that says, in your own words, he is asking for you.

For worship. The risen Lord did not send for the faithful first. He sent for the deserter, by name. Before Peter could find his way back, Christ had sent a message to find him. That is the heart of our Saviour: a shepherd who goes ahead of his scattered sheep, a friend who names the one who denied him, a Lord who keeps every promise even when his people forget them all. Just as he told you: every word of his stands, and the word for failures is come home.
verseByVerse.note: Peter is named — the one who had denied him.

verseByVerse.quote: And they went out and fled from the tomb, for trembling and astonishment had seized them, and they said nothing to anyone, for they were afraid.
verseByVerse.commentary:
They went out and fled from the tomb, for trembling and astonishment had seized them, and they said nothing to anyone, for they were afraid.

And they went out and fled from the tomb, for trembling and astonishment had seized them. They run. Not from unbelief, but from overwhelming awe. Mark’s two words are strong: trembling (tromos), the physical shaking, and ekstasis, being beside oneself, out of one’s senses, the word behind our ecstasy but with none of the pleasantness. They are undone. It is the fitting response to a direct act of God. In Mark, fear and amazement are the constant reaction to Jesus’ divine power (4:41; 5:15, 33, 42; 9:6).

And they said nothing to anyone. At first, at least, on the way. Matthew and Luke tell us they went and told the disciples (Matthew 28:8; Luke 24:9). Their silence was temporary, a stunned silence on the road, not lasting disobedience. And there is a superb irony in it, Mark’s last word about human beings. All through this Gospel, people commanded to be silent could not keep quiet. The cleansed leper was told to say nothing and went out and talked freely (1:45). The crowd in the Decapolis was charged to tell no one, and the more he charged them, the more they proclaimed it (7:36). And here, where the women are commanded to speak, they say nothing at all.

For they were afraid. In Greek the sentence ends with the small word gar, for: they were afraid, for. An extraordinarily abrupt ending, a little like closing a book on because.

Textual note: the ending of Mark. The two oldest complete manuscripts of the New Testament (Codex Sinaiticus and Codex Vaticanus, both fourth century) end Mark’s Gospel here, at verse 8. Early church writers, Eusebius and Jerome, said that most of the Greek manuscripts they knew ended here. Other manuscripts have a short ending of a sentence or two; most later manuscripts have the longer ending (vv. 9–20), which differs from Mark’s style and vocabulary and appears to be a summary drawn from the other Gospels and Acts. The ESV prints verses 9–20 in brackets.

Where Christians differ: did Mark end here? Some think Mark meant to end at verse 8. Others think the original ending was lost, perhaps from the end of a scroll or the last leaf of a codex, or that Mark could not finish; tradition places him in Rome under Nero, when Peter was executed. Verdict: the evidence is strong that verses 9–20 were not written by Mark, but were added early, probably in the second century. Whether Mark meant to end at verse 8 is less certain. But if he did, it is a powerful ending. The resurrection has been announced; Jesus has been seen to be who he said; and the story leaves the reader with the question: what will you do? The women were silent for fear; will you be? Mark’s Gospel began with the beginning of the gospel (1:1). It ends where the church’s preaching begins.

What an ending at verse 8 does. Consider what it does to the reader. The resurrection has been announced, not described. The appearances are promised, there you will see him, not narrated. And the last human beings in the book fail, for a time, to pass the message on. That leaves the story unfinished on purpose and puts it in the reader’s hands. If it ends here, the whole sixteen chapters are only the beginning, and the rest is written by whoever picks it up. The women were told to go to Galilee, where chapter 1 started. The book loops back to its own first page and points the reader at it.

Nothing is lost. Whatever the ending, nothing whatever is lost. The resurrection is stated as fact in verse 6 by a messenger from God. The appearances are recorded in detail by Matthew, Luke, John and Paul, and Paul’s list of witnesses (1 Corinthians 15:3–8) was written down within about twenty-five years of the event, while most of them were still alive to be asked. Mark’s Gospel ends with three frightened women running away from an empty grave. What it does not end with is any doubt about whether the grave was empty.

Why were they afraid, if the news was good? Because it was too good and too great to take in at once. They had come to anoint a corpse and had met an angel, an empty tomb and a message that turned the universe upside down. This is not the fear of punishment but the holy fear of creatures who have seen God act. Matthew says they ran with fear and great joy (Matthew 28:8): both at once. A faith that has never trembled at the resurrection may not have understood it. But such fear is meant to give way to witness, as theirs did.

In a sentence. Seized with trembling and astonishment, the women fled from the tomb and said nothing to anyone, for they were afraid, which is where the earliest manuscripts end Mark’s Gospel.

On a Tuesday. The women were silent at first. You have heard the news: Christ is risen. Don’t be silent; go and tell. Ask what keeps you quiet: fear of ridicule, fear of not having answers, fear of spoiling a friendship. Then pick up the story where Mark leaves it. Tell one person this week, simply, that you believe Jesus rose from the dead, and why.

For worship. The book that began with the beginning of the gospel ends with an empty tomb and trembling witnesses, and the gospel has not stopped since. God did not wait for brave messengers. He used frightened women, and then deserting men, and then a persecutor, and then us. The power of the resurrection does not depend on the courage of those who carry it. It is the power of God, who raised Jesus from the dead, and who still sends the news of it out of the mouths of the weak to the ends of the earth.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that some of the earliest manuscripts end the Gospel here, and brackets verses 9–20.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
What this passage is. Before verse 9 your Bible prints a line in square brackets: Some of the earliest manuscripts do not include 16:9–20. It is the most significant textual question in the New Testament, and it is dealt with fully at verses 9–11 rather than hidden in a note, because a reader who meets it for the first time deserves a straight answer.

What it contains. A summary of resurrection appearances — to Mary Magdalene, to two men walking into the country, and to the eleven at table — with the disciples disbelieving every one of them until Jesus stands in front of them and rebukes them for it.

Then the commission: go into all the world and proclaim the gospel to the whole creation. Then a promise of accompanying signs, including the two sentences about serpents and poison that a handful of churches have built a lethal practice on.

And then the ending. He is taken up into heaven and sits down at the right hand of God — which is exactly what he told the high priest would happen, on the night they condemned him for saying it (14:62).

And the last verse of Mark is the disciples doing the one thing the women in verse 8 could not.
verseByVerse.theology:
Whoever believes and is baptized will be saved (v. 16) can sound, read at speed, as though baptism were half of what saves you. Read closely it says something more careful.

Believing and being baptized are named together in the first half because in the New Testament they belong together — nobody in Acts comes to faith and then quietly declines to be baptized; the washing is the ordinary, public, commanded seal of the faith professed.

But look at the second half, which is where the sentence settles the matter. The condemnation clause is not whoever is not baptized. It is whoever does not believe. Baptism drops out of it entirely.

That asymmetry is doing deliberate work. What saves is Christ, received by faith; baptism is the sign and seal of that faith, not the ground of it. Which is why a dying thief with no water within reach could be told, today you will be with me in paradise (Luke 23:43).

So take the verse whole and let it cut both ways: do not despise baptism, because your Lord commanded it and it is no empty ceremony — and do not lean your weight on it, because it was never the thing holding you up.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: they will pick up serpents with their hands; and if they drink any deadly poison, it will not hurt them (v. 18).

On the strength of that sentence, a handful of churches — mostly in the Appalachian hills — have taken up handling rattlesnakes and drinking strychnine in their services to prove their faith. People have died doing it.

Now: two things must be said, and they are enough.

First, these are among the words whose place in Mark is most doubtful of all. To build a practice on a passage the earliest manuscripts do not contain is unwise twice over.

Second — and this holds even reading the verse at face value — it describes what may happen to Christ's servants, not what they are to seek out. When a viper fastened on Paul's hand on Malta and he shook it off unharmed (Acts 28:3–6), it was an accident of ministry he neither courted nor expected, not a stunt to test God.

Deliberately reaching for a snake or a poison cup to prove one believes is precisely what Satan urged in the wilderness — throw yourself down — and precisely what Jesus refused, with the words you shall not put the Lord your God to the test (Luke 4:12).

Faith trusts God. It does not dare him.

verseByVerse.quote: Now when he rose early on the first day of the week, he appeared first to Mary Magdalene, from whom he had cast out seven demons. She went and told those who had been with him, as they mourned and wept. But when they heard that he was alive and had been seen by her, they would not believe it.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When he rose early on the first day of the week, he appeared first to Mary Magdalene, from whom he had cast out seven demons. She went and told those who had been with him, as they mourned and wept. But when they heard that he was alive and had been seen by her, they would not believe it.

About verses 9–20. These verses are not found in the earliest manuscripts, and were very probably not written by Mark (see the note on v. 8). They were added early, and have been read in the church for centuries, so they are included in our Bibles, in brackets. They largely summarise appearances recorded in the other Gospels and in Acts. Where they agree with the rest of Scripture, they are true and useful. But no doctrine should rest on these verses alone.

The facts, laid out plainly. Immediately before verse 9 the ESV prints, in square brackets, a note that some of the earliest manuscripts do not include 16:9–20. The two oldest complete manuscripts, Sinaiticus and Vaticanus, end Mark at verse 8, and so do some of the oldest versions in other languages. Eusebius, in the early fourth century, says that the accurate copies known to him ended at verse 8; Jerome says the same a century later. Some manuscripts have a much shorter ending instead, and a few have both, one after the other, which is what copyists do when they know of two and cannot decide. And the Greek does not read like Mark. There are more than a dozen words in these twelve verses that appear nowhere else in the book, and the style is noticeably different. Most tellingly, verse 9 introduces Mary Magdalene as though for the first time, from whom he had cast out seven demons, although she was named a few verses earlier (v. 1). That is not how a writer refers to a character he has been following all morning. It is how a different writer begins.

The other view. Some Christians defend the longer ending as Mark’s own. They point out that it is found in the great majority of manuscripts, that Irenaeus quotes verse 19 around AD 180, and that it seems unlikely Mark meant to end with for they were afraid. Their concern is honourable: they do not want to lose any of God’s word. But the oldest manuscripts and early writers who knew the evidence point the other way. The more likely answer is that this is an early and faithful summary added to Mark, not part of what he wrote. It can be read and taught, but nothing should be built on it that is not taught elsewhere in Scripture.

Should this unsettle my confidence in the Bible? No, and here is why. First, nothing has been smuggled in. Every substantial thing in this passage is taught plainly elsewhere: the appearance to Mary in John 20, the two on the road in Luke 24, the commission in Matthew 28 and Acts 1, the ascension in Luke 24, Acts 1 and Hebrews 1:3. No doctrine of the Christian faith stands or falls here. Second, this is what a reliable text looks like. We possess thousands of manuscripts of the New Testament, vastly more and vastly earlier than for any other ancient document, and so we can see exactly where copyists differed. A faith that could not survive its own manuscripts would hide them. This one prints the workings at the bottom of the page. Third, be clear what is not in doubt: the empty tomb, the announcement of the resurrection and the promise of the appearances are all in verses 1–8, in every manuscript there is.

He appeared first to Mary Magdalene, from whom he had cast out seven demons. As John 20:11–18 records. Whoever wrote it got something exactly right. The first person on earth to see the risen Christ was a woman out of whom he had thrown seven demons (Luke 8:2). Not Peter, not John, not his mother, not a priest: a woman with a past so wrecked that her deliverance needed a number attached to it. Grace chooses the unlikely. That is a detail no one would invent, in a culture where a woman’s testimony was not accepted in court. It is in John, and here, because it happened.

She went and told those who had been with him, as they mourned and wept. Note the state of the disciples on Easter Sunday: mourning and weeping. Not waiting hopefully. Grieving. They thought it was over.

But when they heard that he was alive and had been seen by her, they would not believe it. The first of three refusals in four verses. Luke says the same: these words seemed to them an idle tale, and they did not believe them (Luke 24:11). It is entirely consistent with everything Mark has said about the disciples for sixteen chapters. They did not believe the resurrection when they were told. They had to be convinced, against their will, by the man himself. These are not people predisposed to believe. They are the hardest audience in the story.

Why would God allow words not written by Mark into most Bibles? God has preserved his word not by making copyists infallible, but by giving his church so many copies that errors can be seen and corrected. The longer ending was added very early, it teaches nothing contrary to Scripture, and for centuries readers had no means of telling it apart. Now that the earlier manuscripts are known, translations mark it honestly. That is not a failure of God’s care but an example of it: he has kept the text so fully that we can see even the additions. The canon of Scripture is closed, and its message has reached us intact.

In a sentence. The risen Jesus appeared first to Mary Magdalene, but when she told the grieving disciples, they would not believe her.

On a Tuesday. If you struggle to believe, so did the first disciples, so bring your doubts to the risen Christ himself. Write down the question that troubles you most about the resurrection or the Bible, and then read honestly what Scripture says about it, and ask a pastor or a mature friend. Faith that has looked its questions in the face is stronger, not weaker.

For worship. The risen Lord showed himself first to a woman he had delivered from seven demons. He does not choose the impressive; he chooses the rescued. The disciples refused the news, and he did not refuse them. The same Christ who appeared in a garden to Mary still meets the grieving and the doubting with his living presence, and he still turns tears into testimony. He lives, and those he has set free are the first to know it.
verseByVerse.note: These verses are not found in some of the earliest manuscripts; the ESV prints them in brackets. They largely summarise appearances recorded in the other Gospels.

parallels.desc: Mary Magdalene meets the risen Lord
from whom seven demons had gone out

verseByVerse.quote: After these things he appeared in another form to two of them, as they were walking into the country. And they went back and told the rest, but they did not believe them. Afterward he appeared to the eleven themselves as they were reclining at table, and he rebuked them for their unbelief and hardness of heart, because they had not believed those who saw him after he had risen.
verseByVerse.commentary:
After these things he appeared in another form to two of them as they were walking into the country. They went back and told the rest, but they did not believe them. Afterwards he appeared to the eleven themselves as they were reclining at table, and he rebuked them for their unbelief and hardness of heart, because they had not believed those who saw him after he had risen.

After these things he appeared in another form to two of them, as they were walking into the country. This is Luke 24 in one sentence: the road to Emmaus, seven miles out of Jerusalem, the two disciples who walked and talked with him for hours without recognising him, and knew him at last when he broke the bread (Luke 24:13–35). In another form is this writer’s way of accounting for the failure to recognise him, which Luke explains differently: their eyes were kept from recognising him (Luke 24:16). His risen body was the same, but changed and glorified (1 Corinthians 15:42–44), and he could be recognised only when he chose. Mary made the same mistake in the garden and took him for the gardener (John 20:15).

And they went back and told the rest, but they did not believe them. The second refusal. Two more witnesses, and the eleven still will not have it. Luke suggests that by the time they returned the others had already heard he had appeared to Simon (Luke 24:34), and still there was doubt; this summary emphasises the disciples’ slowness to believe.

Afterward he appeared to the eleven themselves as they were reclining at table. The Twelve minus Judas (Luke 24:36–43; John 20:19–29). The third appearance, and it takes the Lord in person to end the matter. They are at a meal, which is where the risen Christ keeps turning up: at Emmaus, in the upper room where he asks for a piece of fish, on a beach in Galilee cooking breakfast.

And he rebuked them for their unbelief and hardness of heart. Hardness of heart is the phrase used of the men in the synagogue who watched a withered hand restored and went out to plan a murder (3:5), and of the disciples in the boat who had carried the baskets and understood nothing (6:52; 8:17). Unbelief in the face of credible testimony is not a mere intellectual difficulty, but hardness of heart. So the last thing the risen Christ does before commissioning them is to rebuke them, because they had been told plainly, three times, and had refused three separate sets of eyewitnesses. And the risen Christ still rebukes it, lovingly.

Not credulous, and sent anyway. Hold two things together, because the passage puts them side by side. These men were not credulous. The apostles are often accused of having wanted a resurrection so badly that they talked themselves into it. Every account we have says the opposite. They dismissed the women, dismissed the two from the road, and had to be confronted in person, and even then Matthew records that some doubted (Matthew 28:17), and John gives us a whole week of Thomas refusing. And he sends them anyway. In the very next verse this group, men who had run away in a garden, denied him in a courtyard, spent the weekend weeping and refused three reports, is handed the gospel and told to take it to the whole creation. He does not wait for better material. There was none, and there never has been.

Is doubt a sin? Doubt as a struggle is not the same as unbelief as a refusal. Many true believers wrestle with questions and seasons of uncertainty, and Scripture is full of them: Thomas, John the Baptist in prison (Matthew 11:2–3), the father who cried I believe; help my unbelief (9:24). Jesus met those doubts with patience and evidence. What he rebukes here is the hardness that will not believe credible testimony because it does not want to. So bring your doubts to him honestly, as the father did. Do not nurse them as a badge of sophistication, and do not hide them in shame. He has given you the testimony of the eyewitnesses, and he is able to strengthen weak faith.

In a sentence. Jesus appeared to two disciples on the road and then to the eleven, and rebuked them for refusing to believe those who had seen him risen.

On a Tuesday. The testimony of the eyewitnesses has come down to you in Scripture. Believe their word (John 20:29). This week, read 1 Corinthians 15:1–20 slowly, and notice how Paul piles up the witnesses. Then ask whether your own unbelief, in some area of your life, is a question that wants answers or a hardness that does not want to change. Bring either one to him.

For worship. He came to them at table, again and again, and would not let their unbelief have the last word. He walked seven miles with two grieving men, opened the Scriptures to them and broke bread before their eyes. He rebuked his friends because he loved them, and then trusted them with the world. Blessed are those who have not seen and yet have believed, and every one of them believes because the risen Lord first came to the doubters and made them witnesses.

verseByVerse.quote: And he said to them, "Go into all the world and proclaim the gospel to the whole creation. Whoever believes and is baptized will be saved, but whoever does not believe will be condemned.
verseByVerse.commentary:
He said to them: go into all the world and proclaim the gospel to the whole creation. Whoever believes and is baptised will be saved, but whoever does not believe will be condemned.

Go into all the world and proclaim the gospel to the whole creation. The commission, in the form found also in Matthew 28:18–20, Luke 24:47 and Acts 1:8, and every phrase widens it. Go: the movement is outward. The Old Testament pattern was largely that the nations would come to Zion (Isaiah 2:2–3); now the direction reverses and the people of God are sent out. Into all the world: said to eleven men, most of them from one lakeside district of one small province, with no money, no organisation and no standing. Proclaim: the herald’s word (kēryssō), to announce publicly what a king has decreed. A herald does not improve the message; he carries it. To the whole creation: all people everywhere, and more than that, for the rescue is not merely of souls out of a doomed world but the beginning of the repair of everything (Romans 8:21–22; Ephesians 1:10). The gospel that Jesus said must first be preached to all nations (13:10) is now the church’s task.

Whoever believes and is baptized will be saved. A sentence that needs care, because read at speed it can sound as though baptism were half of what saves you. Faith and baptism belong together in the New Testament: those who believed were baptised (Acts 2:41; 8:12; 16:31–33). Nobody in Acts comes to faith and then quietly declines the water. Baptism is the ordinary, public, commanded sign of faith and union with Christ, and a believer who refuses it is refusing his Lord’s plain command.

But whoever does not believe will be condemned. Notice that it does not say whoever is not baptised. The decisive issue is faith. That asymmetry is deliberate and decisive. If baptism were part of what saves, its absence would be part of what condemns, and the sentence carefully does not say so. The thief on the cross was saved without baptism (Luke 23:43). Salvation is by grace through faith (Ephesians 2:8–9). Unbelief condemns (John 3:18, 36).

What it does not mean. Not that baptism itself saves, or that a believer who dies unbaptised is lost. Baptism is commanded, and a believer will want to be baptised in obedience. But it is the sign, not the cause, of salvation. And this verse, from the longer ending, is not a foundation for any doctrine of baptism on its own. Roman Catholic, Lutheran and some other Christians read verses such as Acts 2:38 and 22:16 as teaching that baptism is a means by which God gives forgiveness. But in those verses, as here, baptism is joined to repentance and faith as their outward sign; forgiveness is given to faith (Acts 10:43), and the washing is the picture of it.

Where Christians differ: the order of believing and baptism. Paedobaptists baptise the children of believers before faith; credobaptists baptise on profession of faith. Verdict: this verse, like the New Testament pattern generally, places believing before baptism, which fits the credobaptist position, held charitably toward brothers who differ.

I was baptised as an infant. Should I be baptised now? If you hold, as this commentary does with the 1689 Confession (29.1–4), that baptism is for those who have repented and believed, then yes: your infant baptism was offered in love by your parents, but it was not the baptism of a believer, and you should ask to be baptised now as a public confession of your faith. Many godly paedobaptist Christians, including Calvin and the Westminster divines, would disagree, regarding infant baptism as true baptism that should not be repeated, and they are brothers to be honoured, not opponents to be scorned. Speak to your elders, study the Scriptures, and act on your conscience without contempt for those who differ.

In a sentence. Jesus sent his disciples to proclaim the gospel to all people, promising salvation to those who believe and are baptised, and condemnation to those who do not believe.

On a Tuesday. The commission is yours too. Who in your world needs to hear the gospel? Write down three names, and pray for them by name every day this week, and look for one opportunity to speak. And let the verse cut both ways. Do not despise baptism: if you profess Christ and have never been baptised as a believer, speak to your elders about it this week. And do not lean your weight on it: if your confidence before God rests on something that was done to you with water, you are resting on the sign and not on the thing signified.

For worship. The King who was crucified as a rebel now sends his heralds to the whole creation with a royal decree of pardon. He did not wait for an army; he sent eleven forgiven deserters, and they turned the world upside down. Whoever believes will be saved: no exceptions of race, sin or history, because the blood that was poured out for many is enough for all who come. The Lord of the harvest still sends, and the whole creation still waits for the news that its rescue has begun.

verseByVerse.quote: And these signs will accompany those who believe: in my name they will cast out demons; they will speak in new tongues; they will pick up serpents with their hands; and if they drink any deadly poison, it will not hurt them; they will lay their hands on the sick, and they will recover."
verseByVerse.commentary:
And these signs will accompany those who believe: in my name they will cast out demons; they will speak in new tongues; they will pick up serpents with their hands; and if they drink any deadly poison, it will not hurt them; they will lay their hands on the sick, and they will recover.

And these signs will accompany those who believe. Notice the verb: they will accompany. The signs are not the point; they come behind. Verse 20 says the same, that the Lord confirmed the message by accompanying signs. The message goes first; the signs attend it. The signs listed are found in Acts: casting out demons (Acts 16:18), speaking in tongues (Acts 2:4; 10:46; 19:6), surviving a snake bite (Paul on Malta, Acts 28:3–6), healing by laying on of hands (Acts 28:8). Drinking poison unharmed is not found in the New Testament, though a later legend told it of Barsabbas (Acts 1:23). Signs confirmed the apostles’ message in the founding of the church (Hebrews 2:3–4; 2 Corinthians 12:12).

In my name they will cast out demons; they will speak in new tongues. Both are recorded in Acts, and the name matters: in my name. The authority is borrowed, never possessed, which is the lesson the disciples learned badly at the foot of the mountain in chapter 9. The new tongues were the real languages of Acts 2, understood by those from many nations.

They will pick up serpents with their hands; and if they drink any deadly poison, it will not hurt them. This sentence has done real harm, and it needs a plain word. On the strength of it a handful of churches, mostly in the Appalachian mountains of the United States, have handled venomous snakes in their services and drunk poison to demonstrate their faith. People have been bitten, and some have died, including pastors, some refusing medical treatment on principle. Two things must be said. First, these are among the words whose place in Mark is most doubtful of all, and to build a dangerous practice on a text the oldest copies do not contain is unwise twice over. Second, even taken at face value, the verse describes what may happen to Christ’s servants, not what they are to go looking for. Paul, shipwrecked on Malta, was gathering firewood when a viper fastened on his hand, and he shook it into the fire unharmed (Acts 28:3–6). He did not seek it, was not proving anything, and was engaged in the humble business of collecting sticks to warm shipwrecked strangers. It was an accident of ministry, not a demonstration.

What it does not mean. Not a command to handle snakes or drink poison to prove one’s faith. That would be putting God to the test, which Jesus refused to do (Matthew 4:5–7). Deliberately inviting danger to prove one believes is exactly what Satan urged in the wilderness, quoting a promise of protection to support it (Psalm 91:11–12), and Jesus answered: you shall not put the Lord your God to the test (Luke 4:12). There is a way of treating God’s promises as dares, engineering a crisis to see whether he will come through, refusing the doctor to prove one has faith, and calling it trust. Faith trusts God; it does not dare him. And these verses, not part of Mark’s original text, should not be made the basis of any practice.

Where Christians differ: do the signs continue? Pentecostal and charismatic Christians hold that the miraculous gifts, tongues and healing continue in the church today as normal. Cessationists hold that the sign gifts were given to confirm the apostles and their message while the New Testament was being written, and ceased with the apostolic age. Verdict: the cessationist position fits Scripture best. The signs authenticated the apostles as the foundation of the church (Ephesians 2:20; Hebrews 2:3–4). God still answers prayer, and still heals according to his will (James 5:14–15), but not through the apostolic sign gifts. This is held charitably toward brothers and sisters who differ.

Does God still heal today? Yes, as he wills, in answer to the prayers of his people. James tells the sick to call the elders of the church to pray over them and anoint them in the name of the Lord (James 5:14–15), and that remains the ordinary provision Christ has left in every congregation. God also heals through doctors and medicine, which are his gifts too. What he has not promised is that every sickness will be healed in this life, or that healing can be commanded by a gifted person on demand. Pray boldly for the sick, use every good means, and trust him when the answer is not yet. Every believer’s final healing is certain at the resurrection.

What about Christians I know who say they speak in tongues or prophesy? Treat them as brothers and sisters, not as suspects. Many of them love Christ deeply and are more zealous than we are. You can hold your conviction that the apostolic sign gifts have ceased, and still learn from their prayerfulness and expectancy. Where you differ, test everything by Scripture (1 Thessalonians 5:21), and be clear that no experience adds to the closed canon of God’s word. Speak about it gently, with your Bible open, and do not let it break fellowship over what is not the gospel.

In a sentence. These verses promise that signs, such as those recorded in Acts, would accompany the first believers, confirming their message.

On a Tuesday. The greatest sign of the gospel’s power is a changed life. Pray for the sick, trusting God’s will, and let your life show the power of the risen Christ. Visit someone who is ill this week and pray with them. And if you have been tempted to look for spectacular signs to strengthen your faith, turn instead to the sign God has already given: the empty tomb, and the word that tells of it.

For worship. The Lord who confirmed his word with signs in the days of the apostles still confirms it by the greater wonder of new birth. Every sinner who turns to Christ is a dead man raised. He cast out demons, healed the sick, and protected his servants on the roads of the empire, so that the gospel would be established; and the gospel, once established, has never needed to be proved again. We do not dare God; we trust him, because he raised his Son from the dead, and nothing is too hard for him.

verseByVerse.quote: So then the Lord Jesus, after he had spoken to them, was taken up into heaven and sat down at the right hand of God. And they went out and preached everywhere, while the Lord worked with them and confirmed the message by accompanying signs.
verseByVerse.commentary:
So then the Lord Jesus, after he had spoken to them, was taken up into heaven and sat down at the right hand of God. And they went out and preached everywhere, while the Lord worked with them and confirmed the message by accompanying signs.

So then the Lord Jesus, after he had spoken to them, was taken up into heaven. The full title, the Lord Jesus, common in Acts. The ascension in one sentence, forty days after the resurrection (Luke 24:50–51; Acts 1:9–11), and it is the last thing this book says about Jesus. Was taken up: the Father receives him, as Elijah was taken up (2 Kings 2:11). Luke gives the scene at length: the Mount of Olives, the cloud, the two men in white asking why they are standing there looking up.

And sat down at the right hand of God. Psalm 110:1, the verse Jesus quoted in the temple (12:36) and before the high priest (14:62). Put this beside a night, a few weeks earlier, in the house of the high priest. Bound, mocked, with the case against him in ruins, he had been asked a direct question and answered it: I am, and you will see the Son of Man seated at the right hand of Power. They tore their robes and condemned him for it. And here at the end of the book, in one flat sentence: he sat down at the right hand of God, exactly as he said, within weeks of being executed for saying it. What he claimed at his trial has come true. He is enthroned, reigning, interceding for his people (Romans 8:34; Hebrews 1:3; 7:25), until all his enemies are under his feet.

He sat down because it was done. The sitting is itself the doctrine. Priests in the temple never sat down; there were no chairs in the holy place, because the work of sacrifice was never finished. Hebrews makes the point directly: every priest stands daily at his service, offering repeatedly the same sacrifices, which can never take away sins; but when Christ had offered for all time a single sacrifice for sins, he sat down at the right hand of God (Hebrews 10:11–12).

And they went out and preached everywhere. The book of Acts in a sentence, and the exact reversal of verse 8. There, three women ran from a tomb and said nothing to anyone, for they were afraid. Here, the same terrified company goes out and preaches everywhere. Something happened in between, and it was not a change of temperament. The only thing that turns that group into this one is the risen Christ standing in the room and the Spirit he poured out. Men who would not believe three reports went out and told the world, and most of them died for it, and not one of them ever recanted.

While the Lord worked with them and confirmed the message by accompanying signs. The last clause of the Gospel, and there are two things in it. The Lord worked with them. He has just sat down in heaven, and he is working alongside them on earth in the same sentence. That is not a contradiction; it is the whole shape of the Christian era. The ascended Lord was not absent. He worked with them by his Spirit: behold, I am with you always, to the end of the age (Matthew 28:20). Luke says his first book told what Jesus began to do and teach (Acts 1:1). So the going out was never the disciples carrying on a work he had finished. It was, and is, his work, done through people who had recently proved themselves entirely unreliable. And he confirmed the message by accompanying signs, as Hebrews 2:3–4 describes.

The end of Mark. Whether one reads to verse 8 or 20, Mark’s Gospel ends at a beginning. Look back at its first line: the beginning of the gospel of Jesus Christ, the Son of God (1:1). Mark called sixteen chapters, the baptism, the demons, the storms, the bread, the blind man who saw men like trees, the confession at Caesarea Philippi, the cup in the garden, the cry in the dark, the torn curtain, the empty grave, the beginning. And it has not stopped since. The centurion’s confession was picked up by a church in Rome and carried along the roads of an empire, and to tribes and languages that did not exist when Mark was writing, and it has reached you. The story of Jesus continues in the preaching of his church, and in every person who hears it and believes.

Where is Jesus now, and what is he doing? He is in heaven, bodily, at the right hand of the Father, the same Jesus with the same scars, now glorified. He is reigning over all things for the good of his church (Ephesians 1:20–23). He is praying for his people, and his intercession never fails (Hebrews 7:25). He is building his church by his word and Spirit, working with every faithful preacher and witness. And he is waiting for the day when he will come again, visibly, to judge the living and the dead and make all things new. He is not absent. He is enthroned, and he is busy, and he is with you.

What does this mean for my witness? It means you never speak for Christ alone. When you share the gospel, pray for someone, explain your hope, or serve your neighbour in his name, the Lord works with you. Results are his responsibility; faithfulness is yours. You do not need to be eloquent, brave by nature or theologically trained. The disciples were none of those. You need to go, to tell, and to trust that the King at the Father’s right hand is confirming his own word.

In a sentence. The Lord Jesus ascended and sat at God’s right hand, and the disciples preached everywhere while he worked with them and confirmed their message.

On a Tuesday. Jesus reigns at God’s right hand now, so go out today knowing that the Lord works with those who serve him. Before you leave the house, say it: he is risen, he is reigning, and he is with me. Then look for the place today where you can speak or act for him, and do it, expecting him to be at work there before you arrive.

For worship. The man who was appalled and shaking in a garden, who shouted into three hours of darkness that his God had forsaken him, who lay as a corpse behind a stone, is sitting down at the right hand of God, because the work is finished. The prisoner who stood before Caiaphas is the King before whom Caiaphas will stand. He reigns, he intercedes, he works with his people, and he is coming again. And the last of those he died for will be brought home, from the ends of the earth to the ends of heaven. The beginning of the gospel of Jesus Christ, the Son of God, has no end.

16.theology:
Why is 16:9–20 in brackets, and can I trust my Bible? The facts, plainly. The two oldest complete manuscripts of the New Testament — Sinaiticus and Vaticanus, both fourth century — end Mark at v. 8, as do the oldest Syriac, Armenian and Georgian versions. Eusebius and Jerome both report that the accurate copies known to them ended there. Some manuscripts carry a different, shorter ending; a few carry both. And the Greek does not read like Mark: more than a dozen words appear nowhere else in the book, and v. 9 introduces Mary Magdalene as though for the first time, though she has just been named twice.

The honest conclusion is that Mark very probably did not write these verses, though they were known and read by the middle of the second century.

And here is why that need not unsettle anybody. Nothing has been smuggled in: every substantial thing in the passage is taught plainly elsewhere — Mary Magdalene (John 20), the Emmaus road (Luke 24), the commission (Matt. 28; Acts 1), the ascension and session (Luke 24; Acts 1; Eph. 1:20; Heb. 1:3). No doctrine stands or falls here. And the reason you know about it at all is that the church kept the evidence and printed it in the margin instead of tidying it away. A faith that could not survive its own manuscripts would hide them; this one prints the workings at the bottom of the page — which is precisely why the rest can be trusted. Nothing in the discussion touches vv. 1–8, which are in every manuscript there is.

Does Mark end at v. 8? The last word is gar — for — an extraordinarily abrupt way to end a book, rather like closing on because. Three explanations are offered and we do not know which is right: the last leaf of an early codex was lost; the author was interrupted (tradition places him in Rome under Nero); or he meant to stop there. The third has grown stronger the longer people look at it, because an ending at v. 8 leaves the resurrection announced and not described, the appearances promised and not narrated, and the story unfinished in the reader's hands. Mark called his book the beginning of the gospel (1:1) — and the women are sent to Galilee, where chapter 1 began.
16.examples:
Then: and they said nothing to anyone, for they were afraid (v. 8).

There is a superb irony in that sentence, and it is Mark's last word about human beings. All through this Gospel, people commanded to be silent could not keep quiet — the cleansed leper went out and began to talk freely about it so that Jesus could no longer enter a town openly (1:45); the Decapolis crowd was charged to tell no one, and the more he charged them, the more zealously they proclaimed it (7:36).

And here, where the women are commanded to speak, they say nothing at all.

Now: and the last verse of the chapter is the exact reversal — they went out and preached everywhere. The same frightened company. Something happened in between, and it was not a change of temperament.

These were not credulous people. They dismissed the women, dismissed the two from the road, and had to be confronted in person and rebuked to their faces for unbelief and hardness of heart (v. 14). Every account we have says the apostles were the hardest audience in the story, not the softest.

And he sent them anyway — a company of men who had run from a garden, denied him in a courtyard, spent the weekend weeping and refused three separate eyewitness reports. He did not wait for better material. There was none, and there never has been.
